questions.text:
Consider the following compounds:
Arrange these compounds in the increasing order of reactivity with nitrating mixture.
questions.solution: Step 1: Nitration is an electrophilic substitution, so its rate rises with the electron density of the benzene ring. In c ($\ce{C6H5OCH3}$), the $+R$ effect of $-\ce{OCH3}$ outweighs its $-I$ effect, so the ring is activated and reacts fastest. In a ($\ce{C6H5Cl}$), the $-I$ effect of Cl outweighs its $+R$ effect, so the ring is weakly deactivated. In b ($\ce{C6H5NO2}$), $-\ce{NO2}$ withdraws electrons by both $-I$ and $-R$ effects, so the ring is strongly deactivated and reacts slowest. Increasing order of reactivity towards the nitrating mixture: $\mathrm{b} < \mathrm{a} < \mathrm{c}$. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
The statements that are incorrect about the nickel(II) complex of dimethylglyoxime are:
A. It is red in colour.
B. It has a high solubility in water at $\mathrm{pH}=9$.
C. The Ni ion has two unpaired d-electrons.
D. The $\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{Ni}-\mathrm{N}$ bond angle is almost close to $90^{\circ}$.
E. The complex contains four five-membered metallacycles (metal containing rings).
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Step 1: In bis(dimethylglyoximato)nickel(II), $\ce{Ni^2+}$ ($3d^8$) is bound to the four N atoms of two dimethylglyoximate ions in a square planar $\mathrm{dsp^2}$ arrangement. A is correct: the complex is a rosy red precipitate. B is incorrect: the complex is precipitated from weakly ammoniacal solution (pH about 9) because it is insoluble in water. C is incorrect: in the square planar $\mathrm{dsp^2}$ complex all eight d electrons are paired, so it is diamagnetic. D is correct: adjacent N–Ni–N bond angles in a square planar complex are close to $90^\circ$. E is incorrect: each dimethylglyoximate forms one five-membered chelate ring (Ni–N=C–C=N), so there are only two five-membered metallacycles; the other two rings, closed by O–H···O hydrogen bonds, are six-membered. The incorrect statements are B, C and E. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: Let the domain of the function $f(x)=\log _3 \log _5 \log _7\left(9 x-x^2-13\right)$ be the interval $(\mathrm{m}, \mathrm{n})$. Let the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{\mathrm{a}^2}-\frac{y^2}{\mathrm{~b}^2}=1$ have eccentricity $\frac{\mathrm{n}}{3}$ and the length of the latus rectum $\frac{8 \mathrm{~m}}{3}$. Then $\mathrm{b}^2-\mathrm{a}^2$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \begin{aligned} & \log _5\left(\log _7\left(9 x-x^2-13\right)\right)>0 \ & \Rightarrow \quad 9 x-x^2-13>7 \ & \Rightarrow \quad x \in(4,5)=(m, n) \ & \Rightarrow \quad \text { eccentricity }=\frac{5}{3} \ & L(L R)=\frac{32}{3} \ & \frac{25}{9}=1+\frac{b^2}{a^2} \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,...(1)\end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned} &\frac{2 b^2}{a}=\frac{32}{3} \Rightarrow b^2=\frac{16 a}{3}\ &\text { Substitute in (1) }\ &\begin{aligned} & \frac{16}{9}=\frac{16 a}{3 a^2} \Rightarrow a=3 \ & b^2=16 \ & \therefore b^2-a^2=16-9 \ & =7 \end{aligned} \end{aligned} $$

questions.solution: Step 1: For $L$ to bisect area, line must pass through the centre of rectangle $\left(\frac{3}{2}, 2\right)$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \quad L \equiv(y-2)=\frac{1}{3}\left(x-\frac{3}{2}\right) \ & \Rightarrow \quad 3 y-6=x-\frac{3}{2} \Rightarrow 6 y-12=2 x-3 \ & 6 y-2 x-9=0 \end{aligned} $$ The distance from $L$ of $\left(\frac{1}{2},-5\right)$ is $$ \begin{aligned} & \left|\frac{6(-5)-2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-9}{\sqrt{40}}\right|=\sqrt{40} \ & =2 \sqrt{10} \end{aligned} $$

questions.text:
Let the direction cosines of two lines satisfy the equations: $4 l+m-n=0$ and $2 m n+10 n l+3 l m=0$.
Then the cosine of the acute angle between these lines is:
questions.solution: Step 1: From $4l+m-n=0$, $n=4l+m$. Substituting in $2mn+10nl+3lm=0$: $$2m(4l+m)+10l(4l+m)+3lm=0\Rightarrow 40l^2+21lm+2m^2=0\Rightarrow (8l+m)(5l+2m)=0$$ First line: $m=-8l$, so $n=4l-8l=-4l$; its direction ratios are $(1,-8,-4)$, of magnitude $\sqrt{1+64+16}=9$. Second line: $m=-\dfrac{5l}{2}$, so $n=4l-\dfrac{5l}{2}=\dfrac{3l}{2}$; its direction ratios are $(2,-5,3)$, of magnitude $\sqrt{4+25+9}=\sqrt{38}$. For the acute angle $\theta$ between the lines, $$\cos\theta=\dfrac{|(1)(2)+(-8)(-5)+(-4)(3)|}{9\sqrt{38}}=\dfrac{30}{9\sqrt{38}}=\dfrac{10}{3\sqrt{38}}$$ Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: Let $f(x)=\int \frac{\left(2-x^2\right) \cdot \mathrm{e}^x}{(\sqrt{1+x})(1-x)^{3 / 2}} \mathrm{~d} x$. If $f(0)=0$, then $f\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $f(x)=\int \frac{\left(2-x^2\right) \cdot e^x}{(\sqrt{1+x})(1-x)^{3 / 2}} d x$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $f(x)=\int \frac{\left(2-x^2\right) e^x}{\sqrt{1+x} \sqrt{1-x}(1-x)} d x$ $f(x)=\int \frac{\left(2-x^2\right) \cdot e^x}{\left(\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)(1-x)} d x$ $\begin{aligned} & =\int \frac{\left[1+\left(1-x^2\right)\right] e^x}{\left(\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)(1-x)} d x \ & =\int e^x\left[\frac{1}{\left(\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)(1-x)}+\frac{1+x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\right] d x\end{aligned}$ This integral is of the form $\int e^x\left[g(x)+g^{\prime}(x)\right] d x=e^x \cdot g(x)+C$ Let $g(x)=\frac{1+x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ $g^{\prime}(x)=\frac{(1+x)^{\prime} \cdot \sqrt{1-x^2}-(1+x)\left(\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)^{\prime}}{\left(\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)^2}$ $=\frac{\sqrt{1-x^2}+\frac{\left(x^2+x\right)}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}}{1-x^2}$ $=\frac{1-x^2+x^2+x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}\left(1-x^2\right)}$ $=\frac{(x+1)}{\sqrt{1-x^2}(1-x)(1+x)}$ $$ =\frac{1}{\left(\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)(1-x)} $$ So value of integral $$ f(x)=\frac{e^x \cdot(1+x)}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}+C $$ Apply initial condition $f(0)=0$ to find $C$ $$ 0=\frac{e^0(1+0)}{\sqrt{1-0}}+C \Rightarrow C=-1 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $f(x)=\frac{e^x(1+x)}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}-1$ $$\therefore $$ $f(1 / 2)=\frac{e^{1 / 2}(1+1 / 2)}{\sqrt{1-(1 / 2)^2}}-1$ $=\frac{\sqrt{e} \cdot \frac{3}{2}}{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}}-1=\sqrt{3 e}-1$

questions.text: The vertices B and C of a triangle ABC lie on the line $\frac{x}{1}=\frac{1-y}{-2}=\frac{\mathrm{z}-2}{3}$. The coordinates of A and $B$ are $(1,6,3)$ and $(4,9, \alpha)$ respectively and $C$ is at a distance of 10 units from $B$. The area (in sq. units) of $\triangle A B C$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: The line is $\dfrac{x}{1}=\dfrac{y-1}{2}=\dfrac{z-2}{3}$, with direction $\vec{d}=\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+3\hat{k}$ and $|\vec{d}|=\sqrt{14}$. $B(4,9,\alpha)$ lies on it, so $\dfrac{4}{1}=\dfrac{9-1}{2}=\dfrac{\alpha-2}{3}$, giving $\alpha=14$ and $B(4,9,14)$. $B$ and $C$ lie on the line with $BC=10$, so the area is $\dfrac{1}{2}\times BC\times h$, where $h$ is the distance of $A$ from the line. $\overrightarrow{BA}=(1-4)\hat{i}+(6-9)\hat{j}+(3-14)\hat{k}=-3\hat{i}-3\hat{j}-11\hat{k}$, so BA×d= hati, hatj, hatk\-3, -3, -11\1, 2, 3 =13hati-2hatj-3hatk $$h=\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{BA}\times\vec{d}|}{|\vec{d}|}=\dfrac{\sqrt{169+4+9}}{\sqrt{14}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{182}{14}}=\sqrt{13}$$ $$\text{Area}=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 10\times\sqrt{13}=5\sqrt{13}$$ Hence, the correct option is (B).

Let the mean and variance of 8 numbers $-10,-7,-1, x, y, 9,2,16$ be $\frac{7}{2}$ and $\frac{293}{4}$, respectively.
Then the mean of 4 numbers $x, y, x+y+1,|x-y|$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \begin{aligned} & \text { Mean }=\frac{7}{2} \ & \frac{-10-7-1+x+y+16+2+9}{8}=\frac{7}{2} \ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{x}+\mathrm{y}+9=28 \ & \Rightarrow x+y=19 \ & \text { Variance }=\frac{293}{4} \ & \frac{100+49+1+x^2+y^2+256+4+81}{8}-\frac{49}{4}=\frac{293}{4} \ & \frac{491+x^2+y^2}{8}=\frac{342}{4} \ & x^2+y^2=193 \end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow(x, y)=(7,12) \text { or }(12,7) \ & \text { Mean }=\frac{x+y+x+y+1+|x-y|}{4} \ & =\frac{19+20+5}{4} \ & =11 \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: Number of solutions of $\sqrt{3} \cos 2 \theta+8 \cos \theta+3 \sqrt{3}=0, \theta \in[-3 \pi, 2 \pi]$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Given, trigonometric equation is $$\sqrt{3}\cos 2\theta + 8\cos \theta + 3\sqrt{3} = 0,\ \theta \in [-3\pi, 2\pi]$$ $$\Rightarrow \sqrt{3}\left(2\cos^2 \theta - 1\right) + 8\cos \theta + 3\sqrt{3} = 0$$ $$\Rightarrow 2\sqrt{3}\cos^2 \theta + 8\cos \theta + 2\sqrt{3} = 0$$ $$\Rightarrow (\sqrt{3}\cos \theta + 1)(\cos \theta + \sqrt{3}) = 0$$ $\therefore\ \cos \theta = -\sqrt{3}$ (Not possible because $-1 \leq \cos \theta \leq 1$) $\therefore\ \cos \theta = \dfrac{-1}{\sqrt{3}}$ Hence, $\theta$ will have 5 values in $[-3 \pi, 2 \pi]$.

questions.text:
Let $\alpha$ and $\beta$ respectively be the maximum and the minimum values of the function $f(\theta)=4\left(\sin ^4\left(\frac{7 \pi}{2}-\theta\right)+\sin ^4(11 \pi+\theta)\right)-2\left(\sin ^6\left(\frac{3 \pi}{2}-\theta\right)+\sin ^6(9 \pi-\theta)\right), \theta \in \mathbf{R}$.
Then $\alpha+2 \beta$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \begin{aligned} & f(\theta)=4\left(\sin ^4\left(\frac{7 \pi}{2}-\theta\right)+\sin ^4(11 \pi+\theta)\right) \ & \quad-2\left(\sin ^6\left(\frac{3 \pi}{2}-\theta\right)+\sin ^6(9 \pi-\theta)\right) \ & =4\left(\cos ^4 \theta+\sin ^4 \theta\right)-2\left(\cos ^6 \theta+\sin ^6 \theta\right) \ & =4\left(1-2 \sin ^2 \theta \cos ^2 \theta\right) \ & \quad-2(1)\left(\sin ^4 \theta+\cos ^4 \theta-\sin ^2 \theta \cos ^2 \theta\right) \ & =4-8 \sin ^2 \theta \cos ^2 \theta-2\left(1-3 \sin ^2 \theta \cos ^2 \theta\right) \ & =2-2 \sin ^2 \theta \cos ^2 \theta \ & =2-\frac{(\sin 2 \theta)^2}{2} \ & f(\theta)_{\max }=2=\alpha \quad f(\theta)_{\min }=2-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2}=\beta \ & \alpha+2 \beta=2+3=5 \end{aligned} $$

Step 2: Since $\vec{d}=(\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\times\vec{a}$, the triple-product identity gives $\vec{d}=6\vec{b}+8\vec{a}=(-2,2,-2)$. questions.text: A building construction work can be completed by two masons A and B together in 22.5 days. Mason A alone can complete the construction work in 24 days less than mason B alone. Then mason A alone will complete the construction work in:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \text { Let B's time }=x \text { days } $$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \text { A's time }=(x-24) \text { days } \ & \text { Rate of } \mathrm{A}=\frac{1}{x-24} \ & \text { Rate of } \mathrm{B}=\frac{1}{x} \ & \frac{1}{x-24}+\frac{1}{x}=\frac{1}{22.5} \ & \frac{2 x-24}{x(x-24)}=\frac{1}{22.5} \ & 45 x-540=x^2-24 x \ & x^2-69 x+540=0 \ & (x-60)(x-9)=0 \ & \Rightarrow x=60 \ & \text { A's time }=60-24 \ & =36 \text { days } \end{aligned} $$

II: If $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}x^2+x & x+1 & x-2 \\ 2 x^2+3 x-1 & 3 x & 3 x-3 \\ x^2+2 x+3 & 2 x-1 & 2 x-1\end{array}\right|=\mathrm{p} x+\mathrm{q}$, then $\mathrm{p}^2=196 \mathrm{q}^2$,
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \left|\begin{array}{ccc} 1 \cos \alpha \cos \beta \ \cos \alpha 1 \cos \gamma \ \cos \beta \cos \gamma 1 \end{array}\right|=1\left(\begin{array}{c} \left.1-\cos ^2 \gamma\right)-\cos \alpha(\cos \alpha-\cos \beta \cos \gamma) +\cos \beta(\cos \alpha \cos \gamma-\cos \beta) \end{array}\right. \ =1-\cos ^2 \gamma-\cos ^2 \alpha-\cos ^2 \beta+2 \cos \alpha \cos \beta \cos \gamma \ \left|\begin{array}{ccc} 0 \cos \alpha \cos \beta \ \cos \alpha 0 \cos \gamma \ \cos \beta \cos \gamma 0 \end{array}\right|=-\cos \alpha(-\cos \beta \cos \gamma)+\cos \beta(\cos \alpha \cos \gamma) =2 \cos \alpha \cos \beta \cos \gamma \ \Rightarrow \cos ^2 \alpha+\cos ^2 \beta+\cos ^2 \gamma=1 $$ $$ \because q=\left|\begin{array}{ccc} 0 1 -2 \ -1 0 -3 \ 3 -1 -1 \end{array}\right|=-10-2=-12 \ \text { And }-p+q=\left|\begin{array}{ccc} 0 0 -3 \ -2 -3 -6 \ 2 -3 -3 \end{array}\right|=-36 \ \Rightarrow p=q+36=24 \ \Rightarrow p^2 \neq 196 q^2 \ \text { Option (2) is correct. } $$

questions.text: Let the line $y-x=1$ intersect the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{y^2}{1}=1$ at the points A and B. Then the angle made by the line segment AB at the center of the ellipse is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Given equation of line is $y=x+1$ …(i) and equation of ellipse is $$\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{y^2}{1}=1$$ …(ii) Since, Eq. (i) intersect Eq. (ii), then $$\frac{x^2}{2} + (x+1)^2 = 1 \rightarrow x^2 + 2x^2 + 4x = 0$$ $$\Rightarrow$$ $$x=0,\,-\frac{4}{3}$$ $$\therefore$$ $$y=1,\,-\frac{1}{3}$$ Hence, points $A$ and $B$ are $(0,1)$ and $\left(-\frac{4}{3},-\frac{1}{3}\right)$, respectively. Now, slope of $OB = m_{OB} = \tan\,\theta = \frac{-\frac{1}{3}}{-\frac{4}{3}} = \frac{1}{4}$ $$\Rightarrow$$ $$\theta = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)$$ Hence, $\angle AOB = 90^\circ + \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)$ $$= \frac{\pi}{2} + \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)$$

questions.text:
Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $x^4 \mathrm{~d} y+\left(4 x^3 y+2 \sin x\right) \mathrm{d} x=0, x>0, y\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=0$.
Then $\pi^4 y\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: Since $x^4\,dy+4x^3y\,dx=d\left(x^4y\right)$, the equation is $$d\left(x^4y\right)=-2\sin x\,dx \Rightarrow x^4y=2\cos x+c$$ At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $y=0$: $0=2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}+c$, so $c=0$ and $x^4y=2\cos x$. At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$: $\dfrac{\pi^4}{81}\,y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}=1$, so $$\pi^4\,y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=81$$ Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Let $\mathrm{A}=\{-2,-1,0,1,2,3,4\}$. Let R be a relation on A defined by $x \mathrm{R} y$ if and only if $2 x+y \leqslant 2$. Let $l$ be the number of elements in R. Let m and n be the minimum number of elements required to be added in R to make it reflexive and symmetric relations respectively. Then $l+\mathrm{m}+\mathrm{n}$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Step 1: $A=\{-2,-1,0,1,2,3,4\}$ and $x\,R\,y \iff y\le 2-2x$. Values of $y\in A$ for each $x$: $x=-2$: $y\le6$, 7 values; $x=-1$: $y\le4$, 7 values; $x=0$: $y\le2$, 5 values; $x=1$: $y\le0$, 3 values; $x=2$: $y\le-2$, 1 value; $x=3,4$: none.

Step 2: So $l=7+7+5+3+1=23$. $(x,x)\in R \iff 3x\le2 \iff x\le0$, so $(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(4,4)$ must be added: $m=4$. For symmetry, every $(x,y)\in R$ with $2y+x>2$ needs $(y,x)$ added. These pairs are $(-2,3),(-2,4)$ from $x=-2$; $(-1,2),(-1,3),(-1,4)$ from $x=-1$; $(0,2)$ from $x=0$; none from $x=1,2$. The pairs to add are $(3,-2),(4,-2),(2,-1),(3,-1),(4,-1),(2,0)$: $n=6$. $$l+m+n=23+4+6=33$$ Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: Let $f(x)= \begin{cases}\frac{\mathrm{a} x^2+2 \mathrm{a} x+3}{4 x^2+4 x-3} &, x \neq-\frac{3}{2}, \frac{1}{2} \\ \mathrm{~b} &, x=-\frac{3}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\end{cases}$ be continuous at $x=-\frac{3}{2}$. If $f \circ f(x)=\frac{7}{5}$, then $x$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \begin{aligned} & \lim _{x \rightarrow \frac{-3}{2}} \frac{a x^2+2 a x+3}{4 x^2+4 x-3}=b \ & a x^2+2 a x+3=0 \quad \text { at } x=\frac{-3}{2} \ & \Rightarrow \frac{9 a}{4}-3 a+3=0 \ & \Rightarrow \frac{3 a}{4}=3 \ & \Rightarrow a=4 \ & \lim _{x \rightarrow \frac{-3}{2}} \frac{4 x^2+8 x+3}{4 x^2+4 x-3} \end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned} & =\lim _{x \rightarrow \frac{-3}{2}} \frac{(2 x+1)(2 x+3)}{(2 x-1)(2 x+3)} \ & =\frac{-2}{-4}=\frac{1}{2}=b \ & \therefore f(x)=\frac{2 x+1}{2 x-1} \ & f(f(x))=\frac{7}{5} \ & \therefore \quad \frac{2 f(x)+1}{2 f(x)-1}=\frac{7}{5} \ & \Rightarrow f(x)=3 \ & \frac{2 x+1}{2 x-1}=3 \ & \Rightarrow x=1 \end{aligned} $$

questions.text:
A simple pendulum of string length 30 cm performs 20 oscillations in 10 s. The length of the string required for the pendulum to perform 40 oscillations in the same time duration is
$\_\_\_\_$ cm. [Assume that the mass of the pendulum remains same.]
questions.solution: Step 1: The time period (T) of a simple pendulum is the time taken to complete one full oscillation. For a simple pendulum of the length of the string $(\mathrm{L})$ and the acceleration due to gravity $(\mathrm{g})$ the formula for the time period is, $$ \mathrm{T}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{~L}}{\mathrm{~g}}} $$ So, the time period is directly proportional to the square root of the length $(T \propto \sqrt{L})$. $$ \mathrm{T}^2 \propto \mathrm{~L} \Rightarrow \propto \mathrm{~T}^2 $$ Case - 1 The initial length of the string is $\mathrm{L}_1=30 \mathrm{~cm}$ $\mathrm{N}_1=20$ is the number of oscillations completed in total time $\mathrm{t}_1=10 \mathrm{~s}$ So, the initial time period of oscillation is $$ \mathrm{T}_1=\frac{\text { Total Time }}{\text { Number of Oscillations }}=\frac{10}{20}=0.5 \mathrm{~s} $$ Case - 2 $\mathrm{N}_2=40$ is the number of oscillations completed in the same time $\mathrm{t}_2=\mathrm{t}_1=10 \mathrm{~s}$ So, the final time period of oscillation is, $$ \mathrm{T}_2=\frac{\text { Total Time }}{\text { Number of Oscillations }}=\frac{10}{40}=0.25 \mathrm{~s} $$ We need to find the required length $\left(\mathrm{L}_2\right)$ corresponding to the final length of the string, Using the proportionality $\mathrm{L} \propto \mathrm{T}^2$ $$ \frac{\mathrm{L}_2}{\mathrm{~L}_1}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{T}_2}{\mathrm{~T}_1}\right)^2 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{\mathrm{L}_2}{30}=\left(\frac{0.25}{0.50}\right)^2=\frac{1}{4}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \frac{\mathrm{L}_2}{30}=\frac{1}{4} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~L}_2=\frac{30}{4} \mathrm{~cm}=7.5 \mathrm{~cm} $$ Therefore, the required length of the string is 7.5 cm. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: The de Broglie wavelength of an oxygen molecule at $27^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ is $x \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{~m}$. The value of $x$ is (take Planck's constant $=6.63 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{~J}. \mathrm{s}$, Boltzmann constant $=1.38 \times 10^{-23} \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{K}$, mass of oxygen molecule $=5.31 \times 10^{-26} \mathrm{~kg}$ )
questions.solution: Step 1: Only translational motion gives a molecule linear momentum, so the kinetic energy that fixes $p$ is the translational part $\dfrac{3}{2}k_BT$; the rotational energy of the diatomic $\ce{O2}$ molecule adds no linear momentum. $$p = \sqrt{2m \times \dfrac{3}{2}k_BT} = \sqrt{3mk_BT}$$ With $T = 27 + 273 = 300\ \text{K}$: $$3mk_BT = 3 \times 5.31 \times 10^{-26} \times 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300 = 6.595 \times 10^{-46}$$ $$p = \sqrt{6.595 \times 10^{-46}} = 2.568 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$$ $$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{2.568 \times 10^{-23}} = 2.58 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{m} \approx 26 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{m}$$ So $x \approx 26$. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The strain-stress plot for materials $A, B, C$ and $D$ is shown in the figure. Which material has the largest Young's modulus ?
questions.solution: Step 1: Young's Modulus (Y) is defined as the ratio of Stress $(\sigma)$ to Strain $(\varepsilon)$ within the elastic limit: $$ Y=\frac{\text { Stress }}{\text { Strain }} $$ For the given graph, 1. Y -axis: $\operatorname{Strain}(\varepsilon)$ 2. X -axis: Stress $(\sigma)$ Since Strain is on the Y -axis and Stress is on the X -axis, the slope of the line is given by: $$ \text { Slope }=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{Y}}{\Delta \mathrm{X}}=\frac{\text { Strain }}{\text { Stress }} $$ $$ \text { Slope }=\frac{1}{\mathrm{Y}} $$ It shows that the slope is inversely proportional to Young's Modulus, i.e., higher slope corresponds to smaller Young's Modulus (material is more elastic) whereas lower slope shows larger Young's Modulus (material is less elastic). So, the material with the largest Young's modulus will be the line with the smallest slope. 1. Material A has the highest slope → smallest Y. 2. Material C has the lowest slope → largest Y. Therefore, material C has the largest Young's modulus. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The following diagram shows a Zener diode as a voltage regulator. The Zener diode is rated at $V_z=5 \mathrm{~V}$ and the desired current in load is 5 mA. The unregulated voltage source can supply upto 25 V. Considering the Zener diode can withstand four times of the load current, the value of resistor $R_s$ (shown in circuit) should be $\_\_\_\_$ $\Omega$.
questions.solution: Step 1: The Zener current must not exceed $I_{Z,\max}=4I_L=4\times5\ \text{mA}=20\ \text{mA}$. At the highest input voltage with the load disconnected, the whole current through $R_s$ passes through the diode, so $$R_s=\dfrac{V_{in,\max}-V_Z}{I_{Z,\max}}=\dfrac{25-5}{20\times10^{-3}}=1000\ \Omega$$ With the load connected, the same $20\ \text{mA}$ divides into $I_L=5\ \text{mA}$ and $I_Z=15\ \text{mA}$, so the diode still holds the output at $5\ \text{V}$. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: A 20 m long uniform copper wire held horizontally is allowed to fall under the gravity $\left(g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right)$ through a uniform horizontal magnetic field of 0.5 Gauss perpendicular to the length of the wire. The induced EMF across the wire when it travels a vertical distance of 200 m is $\_\_\_\_$ mV.
questions.solution:
Step 1: When a straight wire falls through a magnetic field, an EMF gets induced across its ends. This is the motional EMF, and it is given by $$\varepsilon = Bvl$$ where $B$ is the magnetic field, $v$ is the speed of the wire, and $l$ is its length. Here the wire is falling freely, so first we need its speed after falling through 200 m. Using the equation of motion with initial velocity zero, $$v^2 = 2gh = 2 \times 10 \times 200 = 4000$$ $$v = \sqrt{4000} = 20\sqrt{10} \ \text{m/s}$$ Now, the magnetic field is given in Gauss, so we convert it to SI units. Since $1$ Gauss $= 10^{-4}$ T, $$B = 0.5 \ \text{Gauss} = 0.5 \times 10^{-4} \ \text{T}$$ The wire is horizontal, the field is horizontal and perpendicular to the wire, and the motion is vertical.

Step 2: So $B$, $v$ and $l$ are all mutually perpendicular, and we can directly use $\varepsilon = Bvl$. $$\varepsilon = 0.5 \times 10^{-4} \times 20\sqrt{10} \times 20$$ $$\varepsilon = 0.5 \times 10^{-4} \times 400\sqrt{10} = 200\sqrt{10} \times 10^{-4} \ \text{V}$$ $$\varepsilon = 0.02\sqrt{10} \ \text{V} = 20\sqrt{10} \ \text{mV}$$ So the induced EMF across the wire is $20\sqrt{10}$ mV, which is Option C.

questions.text:
Match List - I with List - II.

LIST I — Relation
A. $ \oint \vec{E} \cdot \overrightarrow{d l}=-\frac{d}{d t} \oint \vec{B} \cdot \overrightarrow{d a} $
B. $ \oint \vec{B} \cdot \overrightarrow{d l}=\mu_0\left(I+\epsilon_0 \frac{d \phi_E}{d t}\right) $
C. $ \oint \vec{E} \cdot \overrightarrow{d a}=\frac{1}{\epsilon_0} \int_{\mathrm{v}} \rho \mathrm{dv} $
D. $ \oint \vec{B} \cdot \overrightarrow{d l}=\mu_0 I $

LIST II — Law
I. Ampere's circuital law
II. Faraday's laws of electromagnetic induction
III. Ampere - Maxwell law
IV. Gauss's law of electrostatics

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Step 1: For relation A The equation $\oint \vec{E} \cdot d \vec{l}=-\frac{d}{d t}[\oint \vec{B} \cdot d \vec{a}]$ mathematically states that the line integral of the electric field around a closed loop is equal to the negative rate of change of magnetic flux through the loop. This is the integral form of Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction, i.e., $\mathrm{A} \rightarrow$ II For relation B This equation $\oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \cdot \mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{l}}=\mu_0\left(\mathrm{I}+\epsilon_0 \frac{\mathrm{~d} \Phi_{\mathrm{E}}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right)$ relates the magnetic field line integral to both the conduction current (I) and the displacement current $\left(\epsilon_0 \frac{\mathrm{~d} \Phi_{\mathrm{E}}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right)$. This modification to Ampere's Law was introduced by Maxwell to account for changing electric fields. This is the Ampere-Maxwell Law, i.e., $\mathrm{B} \rightarrow$ III For relation C In relation $C, \oint \vec{E} \cdot d \vec{a}=\frac{1}{\epsilon_0} \int_V \rho d V$ the total charge $Q_{\text {enclosed }}$ is represented as $\oint \vec{E} \cdot d \vec{a}$. The equation states that the total electric flux through a closed surface is equal to the enclosed charge divided by $\epsilon_0$. This is Gauss's Law of Electrostatics, i.e., $\mathrm{C} \rightarrow$ IV For relation D This relation $\oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \cdot d \overrightarrow{\mathrm{l}}=\mu_0 \mathrm{I}$ states that the line integral of the magnetic field around a closed loop is equal to $\mu_0$ times the current enclosed by the loop. This is the original form of Ampere's Circuital Law which is valid for steady currents, i.e., $\mathrm{D} \rightarrow \mathrm{I}$ So, the correct match is $\mathrm{A} \rightarrow$ II, $\mathrm{B} \rightarrow$ III, $\mathrm{C} \rightarrow$ IV, $\mathrm{D} \rightarrow$ I. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: Two small balls with masses $m$ and 2 m are attached to both ends of a rigid rod of length $d$ and negligible mass. If angular momentum of this system is $L$ about an axis (A) passing through its centre of mass and perpendicular to the rod then angular velocity of the system about $A$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Let the mass m be at position $\mathrm{x}=0$. The mass 2 m is at position $\mathrm{x}=\mathrm{d}$. The position of the centre of mass $\left(\mathrm{X}_{\mathrm{CM}}\right)$ is given by: $$ \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{CM}}=\frac{\mathrm{m}_1 \mathrm{x}_1+\mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{x}_2}{\mathrm{~m}_1+\mathrm{m}_2} $$ $$ X_{C M}=\frac{m(0)+2 m(d)}{m+2 m}=\frac{2 m d}{3 m}=\frac{2 d}{3} $$ So, the distances of the masses from the centre of mass are: Distance of mass m from $\mathrm{CM}\left(\mathrm{r}_1\right)$: $$ r_1=\frac{2 d}{3} $$ Distance of mass 2 m from CM ( $\mathrm{r}_2$ ): $$ \mathrm{r}_2=\mathrm{d}-\frac{2 \mathrm{~d}}{3}=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{3} $$ The moment of inertia of the system about the axis passing through the CM is the sum of the moments of inertia of the individual masses: $$ \mathrm{I}=\mathrm{m}_1 \mathrm{r}_1^2+\mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{r}_2^2 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $I=m\left(\frac{2 d}{3}\right)^2+2 m\left(\frac{d}{3}\right)^2$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $I=m\left(\frac{4 d^2}{9}\right)+2 m\left(\frac{d^2}{9}\right)$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $I=\frac{4 \mathrm{md}^2}{9}+\frac{2 \mathrm{md}^2}{9}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{I}=\frac{6 \mathrm{md}^2}{9}=\frac{2}{3} \mathrm{md}^2 $$ The angular momentum L is related to the moment of inertia I and angular velocity $\omega$ by the formula: $$ \mathrm{L}=\mathrm{I} \omega $$ $$\Rightarrow \omega=\frac{L}{I}=\frac{L}{\left(\frac{2}{3} \mathrm{md}^2\right)} $$ $$ \Rightarrow \omega=\frac{3}{2} \frac{\mathrm{~L}}{\mathrm{md}^2} $$ Therefore, the angular velocity of the system is $\frac{3}{2} \frac{\mathrm{~L}}{\mathrm{md}^2}$. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: An object is projected with kinetic energy $K$ from a point $A$ at an angle $60^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. The ratio of the difference in kinetic energies at points $B$ and $C$ to that at point $A$ (see figure), in the absence of air friction is:
questions.solution:
Step 1: Let the mass of the object be m and the initial speed be u. The angle of projection is $\theta=60^{\circ}$. At point A The kinetic energy at point $A$ is given as $K$. $$ \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mu}^2=\mathrm{K} $$ At Point B (Maximum Height) At the highest point of a projectile's path, the vertical component of velocity becomes zero $\left(v_y=0\right)$. The object only possesses the horizontal component of velocity ( $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{x}}$ ). The horizontal velocity remains constant throughout the motion (assuming no air resistance): $$ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{u} \cos \theta $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{u} \cos 60^{\circ}=\mathrm{u}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{u}}{2} $$ So, the kinetic energy at B is, $$ \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}\left(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{B}}\right)^2 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}\left(\frac{\mathrm{u}}{2}\right)^2$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}\left(\frac{\mathrm{u}^2}{4}\right)$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mu}^2\right)=\frac{1}{4} \mathrm{~K}_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{\mathrm{K}}{4}$ $$ \Rightarrow \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{\mathrm{K}}{4} $$ At Point C Point C is at the same horizontal level as point
A. By the law of conservation of energy, the speed of the projectile when it hits the ground at the same level is equal to the speed of projection. $$ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{C}}=\mathrm{u} $$ Therefore, the kinetic energy at C is equal to the kinetic energy at
A: $$ \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{C}}=\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{K} $$ The difference in kinetic energies at B and
C: $$ \Delta K_{B C}=\left|K_C-K_B\right|=\left|K-\frac{K}{4}\right|=\frac{3 K}{4} $$ So, the ratio of the difference in kinetic energies at points B and C to that at point A is Ratio $=\frac{\Delta K_{B C}}{K_A}=\frac{(3 / 4) K}{K}=\frac{3}{4}$ Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
In a perfectly inelastic collision, two spheres made of the same material with masses 15 kg and 25 kg, moving in opposite directions with speeds of $10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ and $30 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$, respectively, strike each other and stick together. The rise in temperature (in ${ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ), if all the heat produced during the collision is retained by these spheres, is:
(specific heat of sphere material $31 \mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{kg}.{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $1 \mathrm{cal}=4.2 \mathrm{~J}$ )
questions.solution: Step 1: Before Collision: The masses of the spheres are, $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}}=15 \mathrm{~kg}, \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{B}}=25 \mathrm{~kg}$ The initial velocities of the spheres are, $\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{A}}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}, \mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{B}}=-30 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ Hence, the kinetic energy of system before collision is, $$ \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{i}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{A}}^2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{B}}^2 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{i}}=\frac{1}{2}(15)(10)^2+\frac{1}{2}(25)(30)^2=750+11250=12000 \mathrm{~J} $$ Since the collision is perfectly inelastic, the spheres stick together and move with a common final velocity $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{f}}$. Using conservation of linear momentum, $$ m_A u_A+m_B u_B=\left(m_A+m_B\right) v_f $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $(15)(10)+(25)(-30)=(15+25) v_f$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $150-750=40 v_f$ $$ -600=40 v_f \Rightarrow v_f=-15 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} $$ (The negative sign indicates the combined mass moves in the direction of the 25 kg sphere.) So, the final kinetic energy of the system is $$ \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{f}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{A}}+\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}}\right) \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{f}}^2 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{f}}=\frac{1}{2}(40)(15)^2$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{f}}=4500 \mathrm{~J} $$ The loss in kinetic energy appears as heat (Q). $$ Q=K_i-K_f $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $Q=12000 \mathrm{~J}-4500 \mathrm{~J}$ $$ Q=7500 \mathrm{~J} $$ Using the heat capacity formula $\mathrm{Q}=\operatorname{mc} \Delta \mathrm{T}$. Where, total mass (m) of the spheres is 40 kg, the specific heat (c) of the material of spheres is $31 \mathrm{cal} / \mathrm{kg} \cdot{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. As $1 \mathrm{cal}=4.2 \mathrm{~J}$, so $\mathrm{c}=31 \times 4.2 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{kg} \cdot{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}=130.2 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{kg} \cdot{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ Substituting the values in heat capacity formula, $$ 7500=40 \times 130.2 \times \Delta \mathrm{T} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $7500=5208 \times \Delta \mathrm{T}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \Delta \mathrm{T}=\frac{7500}{5208} \approx 1.44^{\circ} \mathrm{C} $$ Therefore, the rise in temperature is $1.44^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
In hydrogen atom spectrum, ( $R \rightarrow$ Rydberg's constant)
A. the maximum wavelength of the radiation of Lyman series is $\frac{4}{3 R}$
B. the Balmer series lies in the visible region of the spectrum
C. the minimum wavelength of the radiation of Paschen series is $\frac{9}{R}$
D. the minimum wavelength of Lyman series is $\frac{5}{4 R}$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Step 1: For hydrogen, $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$; the longest wavelength of a series comes from $n_2 = n_1 + 1$ and the shortest from $n_2 = \infty$. Statement
A: for Lyman ($n_1 = 1$), the longest wavelength is from $n_2 = 2$: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda_{\max}} = R\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{4}\right) = \dfrac{3R}{4} \Rightarrow \lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{4}{3R}$. Correct. Statement
B: Balmer lines ($n_2 \geq 3 \to n_1 = 2$), such as $656\ \text{nm}$, $486\ \text{nm}$, $434\ \text{nm}$ and $410\ \text{nm}$, lie in the visible region. Correct. Statement
C: for Paschen ($n_1 = 3$), the shortest wavelength is from $n_2 = \infty$: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda_{\min}} = \dfrac{R}{9} \Rightarrow \lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{9}{R}$. Correct. Statement
D: for Lyman, the shortest wavelength is from $n_2 = \infty$: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda_{\min}} = R \Rightarrow \lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{1}{R}$, not $\dfrac{5}{4R}$. Incorrect. Statements A, B and C are correct. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Two point charges $2 q$ and $q$ are placed at vertex $A$ and centre of face $C D E F$ of the cube as shown in figure. The electric flux passing through the cube is:
questions.solution: Step 1: According to Gauss's Law, the total electric flux $\Phi$ through a closed surface is $$ \Phi=\frac{Q_{\text {enclosed }}}{\epsilon_0} $$ For the flux contribution from charge at vertex $\mathrm{A}(2 \mathrm{q})$ As the charge 2 q is placed at a corner (vertex) of the cube. A corner of a cube is a meeting point for 8 identical cubes stacked together Since the charge is shared equally among 8 cubes, the portion of the flux entering the specific cube is $\frac{1}{8}$ of the total flux produced by the charge. $$ \Phi_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{1}{8} \times \frac{2 \mathrm{q}}{\epsilon_0}=\frac{2 \mathrm{q}}{8 \epsilon_0}=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{4 \epsilon_0} $$ For the flux contribution from charge at the centre of face CDEF (q) The charge q is placed at the center of the face CDEF and a face of a cube is shared by exactly 2 identical cubes placed side-by-side. Since the charge is shared equally between 2 cubes, the portion of the flux entering the specific cube is $\frac{1}{2}$ of the total flux produced by the charge. $$ \Phi_{\text {face }}=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{q}{\epsilon_0}=\frac{q}{2 \epsilon_0} $$ The total flux passing through the cube is the sum of the contributions from both charges. $$ \Phi_{\text {total }}=\Phi_{\mathrm{A}}+\Phi_{\text {face }} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\Phi_{\text {total }}=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{4 \epsilon_0}+\frac{\mathrm{q}}{2 \epsilon_0}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \Phi_{\text {total }}=\frac{q+2 q}{4 \epsilon_0}=\frac{3 q}{4 \epsilon_0} $$ Therefore, the total electric flux passing through the cube is $\frac{3 q}{4 \epsilon_0}$. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: The moment of inertia of a square loop made of four uniform solid cylinders, each having radius $R$ and length L(\mathrm{R}
questions.solution: Step 1: Total mass of the square loop is M which is made of 4 identical solid cylinders. So, mass of each cylinder $=m=\frac{M}{4}$ The length of each cylinder is L and radius is R. Axis of rotation passes through the midpoints of two opposite sides. Let's assume the square lies in the xy -plane and the axis bisects the square vertically. For the cylinder B and D The axis passes through the center of these cylinders and is perpendicular to their length. The Moment of Inertia ( $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{B}}, \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{D}}$ ) of a solid cylinder about a transverse axis passing through its center is: $$ \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{D}}=\frac{\mathrm{mL}^2}{12}+\frac{\mathrm{mR}^2}{4} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{B}}+\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{D}}=2\left(\frac{\mathrm{~mL}^2}{12}+\frac{\mathrm{mR}^2}{4}\right)=\left(\frac{\mathrm{mL}^2}{6}+\frac{\mathrm{mR}^2}{2}\right) $$ For the cylinders A and C: The axis is parallel to the length of these cylinders. The axis is at a distance $\mathrm{d}=\frac{\mathrm{L}}{2}$ from the center of each cylinder. The Moment of Inertia ( $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{CM}}$ ) of a solid cylinder about its own longitudinal axis is $\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mR}^2$. Using the Parallel Axis Theorem ( $\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{CM}}+\mathrm{md}^2$ ), the inertia of one such cylinder about the central axis is: $$ \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mR}^2+\mathrm{m}\left(\frac{\mathrm{~L}}{2}\right)^2=\frac{\mathrm{mR}^2}{2}+\frac{\mathrm{mL}^2}{4} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{A}}+\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{C}}=2 \times\left(\frac{\mathrm{mR}^2}{2}+\frac{\mathrm{mL}^2}{4}\right)=\left(\mathrm{mR}^2+\frac{\mathrm{mL}^2}{2}\right) $$ Hence, the total moment of inertia of system about the given axis of rotation is, $$ \mathrm{I}_{\text {total }}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{A}}+\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{B}}+\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{C}}+\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{D}} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{I}_{\text {total }}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{mL}^2}{6}+\frac{\mathrm{mR}^2}{2}\right)+\left(\mathrm{mR}^2+\frac{\mathrm{mL}^2}{2}\right)$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{I}_{\text {total }}=\left(\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}\right) \mathrm{mL}^2+\left(\frac{1}{2}+1\right) \mathrm{mR}^2$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{I}_{\text {total }}=\frac{4}{6} \mathrm{~mL}^2+\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{mR}^2$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{I}_{\text {total }}=\frac{2}{3} \mathrm{~mL}^2+\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{mR}^2$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{I}_{\text {total }}=\frac{2}{3}\left(\frac{\mathrm{M}}{4}\right) \mathrm{L}^2+\frac{3}{2}\left(\frac{\mathrm{M}}{4}\right) \mathrm{R}^2$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{I}_{\text {total }}=\frac{2}{12} \mathrm{ML}^2+\frac{3}{8} \mathrm{MR}^2$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{I}_{\text {total }}=\frac{1}{6} \mathrm{ML}^2+\frac{3}{8} \mathrm{MR}^2 $$ Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
Consider a ferromagnetic material:
Assertion (A): The individual atoms in a ferromagnetic material possess a magnetic dipole moment and interact with one another in such a way that they spontaneously align themselves forming domains.
Reason (R): At high enough temperature, the domain structure of ferromagnetic material disintegrates. Thus, magnetization will disappear at high enough temperature known as Curie temperature.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A)

questions.solution: Step 1: Ferromagnetic materials (like iron, nickel, cobalt) are characterized by the fact that their individual atoms possess a permanent magnetic dipole moment. Due to strong quantum mechanical interactions between neighbouring atoms, these dipoles spontaneously align parallel to each other within small macroscopic regions. These aligned regions are indeed called magnetic domains. Within a domain, the magnetization is saturated, even in the absence of an external field. Hence, the Assertion (A) is True. Temperature represents thermal agitation. As the temperature of a ferromagnetic material increases, the thermal energy tends to randomize the orientation of the magnetic dipoles. At a specific critical temperature called the Curie Temperature ( $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{c}}$ ), the thermal agitation becomes strong enough to overcome the exchange coupling that holds the domains together. The domain structure breaks down (disintegrates), and the material transitions from ferromagnetic to paramagnetic, losing its spontaneous magnetization. So, the Reason (R) is also True. The formation of domains (A) is caused by the minimization of exchange energy and magnetostatic energy. The destruction of domains at high temperature ( R ) is a property of the material's phase transition. Knowing that domains disappear at high heat does not explain the fundamental physical mechanism (exchange interaction) that causes them to align spontaneously at lower temperatures. Both statements are correct facts, but R is not the functional explanation for A, i.e., both $(\mathrm{A})$ and $(\mathrm{R})$ are true but $(\mathrm{R})$ is not the correct explanation of (A). Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: A small bob $A$ of mass $m$ is attached to a massless rigid rod of length 1 m pivoted at point $P$ and kept at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with vertical as shown in figure. At distance of 1 m below point $P$, an identical bob $B$ is kept at rest on a smooth horizontal surface that extends to a circular track of radius $R$ as shown in figure. If bob $B$ just manages to complete the circular path of radius $R$ upto a point $Q$ after being hit elastically by $\operatorname{bob} A$, then radius $R$ is $\_\_\_\_$ m.
questions.solution:
Step 1: Bob A is released from rest at an angle $\theta=60^{\circ}$. It swings down to the lowest point (vertical position) where it hits Bob
B. Length of rod is $\mathrm{l}=1 \mathrm{~m}$. Height lost by $\mathrm{A}(\Delta \mathrm{h})$: $\Delta \mathrm{h}=\mathrm{l}-\mathrm{l} \cos \theta=\mathrm{l}\left(1-\cos 60^{\circ}\right)$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \Delta \mathrm{h}=1(1-0.5)=0.5 \mathrm{~m} $$ Using conservation of energy for Bob
A: $$ \mathrm{mg} \Delta \mathrm{~h}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{~m} \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{A}}^2 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{A}}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~g} \Delta \mathrm{~h}}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{A}}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~g} \times 0.5}=\sqrt{\mathrm{g}} $$ It is given that the collision is elastic. Both bobs are identical (mass m ). Initial velocities: $\operatorname{Bob} A$ has $v_A=\sqrt{g}$, $\operatorname{Bob} B$ is at rest $\left(v_B=0\right)$. In a perfectly elastic collision between two identical masses where one is initially at rest, their velocities are exchanged. So, after collision, bob A comes to rest and bob B acquires the velocity of Bob
A. $$ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{B}}=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{A}}=\sqrt{\mathrm{g}} $$ Bob B moves along the smooth horizontal surface and enters the vertical circular track of radius R. The bob B just manages to complete the circular path up to a point Q. For a particle to just complete a full vertical circle (reach the top), the minimum velocity at the bottom $(\sqrt{5 \mathrm{gR}})$ is required. $$ \mathrm{v}_{\text {bottom }} \geq \sqrt{5 \mathrm{gR}} $$ $\Rightarrow \sqrt{g}=\sqrt{5 g R}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\Rightarrow \mathrm{g}=5 \mathrm{gR}$ $$ \Rightarrow \mathrm{R}=\frac{1}{5} \mathrm{~m} $$ Therefore, the required radius $R$ is $\frac{1}{5} \mathrm{~m}$. Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: A thin prism with angle $5^{\circ}$ of refractive index 1.72 is combined with another prism of refractive index 1.9 to produce dispersion without deviation. The angle of second prism is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution: Step 1: When two thin prisms are combined to produce dispersion without deviation, they are arranged such that their refracting angles are inverted relative to each other. The net deviation produced by the combination is zero. $\delta_{\text {net }}=\delta_1-\delta_2=0$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \delta_1=\delta_2 $$ The deviation $(\delta)$ produced by a thin prism is given by the formula: $$ \delta=(\mu-1) \mathrm{A} $$ where: $\mu$ is the refractive index of the material. A is the angle of the prism. Since the deviations must be equal and opposite: $$ \left(\mu_1-1\right) \mathrm{A}_1=\left(\mu_2-1\right) \mathrm{A}_2 $$ The angle of prism for first prism is $\mathrm{A}_1=5^{\circ}$ and its refractive index is $\mu_1=1.72$ The refractive index of the second prism is $\mu_2=1.9$ $$ (1.72-1) \times 5^{\circ}=(1.9-1) \times \mathrm{A}_2 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ 3.6=0.9 \times \mathrm{A}_2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{~A}_2=\frac{3.6}{0.9}=4^{\circ} $$ Therefore, the angle of the second prism is $4^{\circ}$. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: A wire of uniform resistance $\lambda \Omega / \mathrm{m}$ is bent into a circle of radius $r$ and another piece of wire with length $2 r$ is connected between points $A$ and $B(\mathrm{AOB})$ as shown in figure. The equivalent resistance between points $A$ and $B$ is $\_\_\_\_$ $\Omega$.
questions.solution: Step 1: For the equivalent resistance between points A and B we can identify three distinct paths for the current to flow from node A to node B. These paths are in parallel. The resistance per unit length for the wire is $\lambda \Omega / \mathrm{m}$ The resistance is given by $\mathrm{R}=$ Resistance per unit length × Length $=\lambda \times \mathrm{L}$. Path 1 (Minor Arc AB): The shorter curved wire along the circle's circumference. Since $\angle \mathrm{AOB}=90^{\circ}$ (a quarter circle), the length is $\frac{1}{4}$ of the circumference. $$ \mathrm{L}_1=\frac{1}{4} \times 2 \pi \mathrm{r}=\frac{\pi \mathrm{r}}{2} $$ So, the resistance of path 1 is, $$ \mathrm{R}_1=\lambda\left(\frac{\pi \mathrm{r}}{2}\right) $$ Path 2 (Major Arc AOB): The longer curved wire along the remaining part of the circle. This is $\frac{3}{4}$ of the circumference. $$ \mathrm{L}_2=\frac{3}{4} \times 2 \pi \mathrm{r}=\frac{3 \pi \mathrm{r}}{2} $$ So, the resistance of path 2 is, $$ \mathrm{R}_2=\lambda\left(\frac{3 \pi \mathrm{r}}{2}\right) $$ Path 3 (Wire AOB): The straight wire sections connecting A to the centre O and then O to B. Thus, the two segments AO and OB are in series. It is given that the length of this wire is $2 r$. $$ \mathrm{L}_3=\mathrm{r}+\mathrm{r}=2 \mathrm{r} $$ So, the resistance of path 3 is, $$ \mathrm{R}_{34}=\mathrm{R}_3+\mathrm{R}_4=\lambda(2 \mathrm{r}) $$ Since the three paths are in parallel, the equivalent resistance $\left(R_{e q}\right)$ is, $$ \frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_{34}} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{R_{e q}}=\frac{1}{\lambda \pi r / 2}+\frac{1}{3 \lambda \pi r / 2}+\frac{1}{2 \lambda r}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{R_{e q}}=\frac{2}{\lambda \pi r}+\frac{2}{3 \lambda \pi r}+\frac{1}{2 \lambda r}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\frac{1}{\lambda \mathrm{r}}\left[\frac{2}{\pi}+\frac{2}{3 \pi}+\frac{1}{2}\right]$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\frac{1}{\lambda \mathrm{r}}\left[\frac{12+4+3 \pi}{6 \pi}\right]$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\frac{1}{\lambda \mathrm{r}}\left[\frac{16+3 \pi}{6 \pi}\right]$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\lambda \mathrm{r}\left[\frac{6 \pi}{16+3 \pi}\right]=\frac{6 \lambda \pi \mathrm{r}}{3 \pi+16} $$ Therefore, the equivalent resistance between points A and B is $\frac{6 \lambda \pi \mathrm{r}}{3 \pi+16}$. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: Two blocks with masses 100 g and 200 g are attached to the ends of springs $A$ and $B$ as shown in figure. The energy stored in $A$ is $E$. The energy stored in $B$, when spring constants $k_A, k_B$ of $A$ and $B$, respectively satisfy the relation $4 k_A=3 k_B$, is:
questions.solution: Step 1: When a mass $m$ is suspended from a spring of constant $k$, the spring stretches. If the stretch in spring is $\mathrm{x}, \mathrm{kx}=\mathrm{mg} \Rightarrow \mathrm{x}=\frac{\mathrm{mg}}{\mathrm{k}}$ The potential energy ( $U$ ) stored in the spring is given by: $$ \mathrm{U}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{kx}^2 $$ Substituting $\mathrm{x}=\frac{\mathrm{mg}}{\mathrm{k}}$: $$ \mathrm{U}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{k}\left(\frac{\mathrm{mg}}{\mathrm{k}}\right)^2=\frac{(\mathrm{mg})^2}{2 \mathrm{k}} $$ Mass of block A is $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}}=100 \mathrm{~g}$. The spring constant is $\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}$. So, the stored energy in spring A is $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{E}$. Using the formula: $$ E=\frac{\left(m_A g\right)^2}{2 k_A} $$ Mass of block B is $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}}=200 \mathrm{~g}=2 \times 100 \mathrm{~g}=2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{A}}$ The spring constant of spring B is $\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}$. It is given that $4 \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}=3 \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{4}{3} \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}$. So, the stored energy in spring B is $$ \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{\left(\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{~g}\right)^2}{2 \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}} $$ Substituting $\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}}=2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{4}{3} \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}$: $$ E_B=\frac{\left(2 m_A g\right)^2}{2\left(\frac{4}{3} k_A\right)}$$ $\begin{gathered}\Rightarrow \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{4 \times \frac{3}{8} \times\left(\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{g}\right)^2}{\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}} \ \Rightarrow \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{12}{8} \times \frac{\left(\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{g}\right)^2}{\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}} \ \Rightarrow \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{3}{2} \times \frac{\left(\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{g}\right)^2}{\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}} \ \Rightarrow \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{B}}=3 \times\left(\frac{\left(\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{g}\right)^2}{2 \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}}\right) \ \Rightarrow \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{B}}=3 \mathrm{E}\end{gathered}$

questions.text:
In a screw gauge, the zero of the circular scale lies 3 divisions above the horizontal pitch line when their metallic studs are brought in contact. Using this instrument thickness of a sheet is measured. If pitch scale reading is 1 mm and the circular scale reading is 51 then the correct thickness of the sheet is $\_\_\_\_$ mm.
[Assume least count is 0.01 mm ]
questions.solution: Step 1: The circular scale lies 3 divisions above the horizontal pitch line when the studs are in contact. When the zero mark is above the reference line, the screw has been turned past the zero point. This indicates a negative zero error. The error corresponds to 3 divisions. Hence, the zero error is, $$\mathrm{E}_0=-(3 \times \text { Least Count }) =-(3 \times 0.01 \mathrm{~mm})=-0.03 \mathrm{~mm} $$ The observed reading is the sum of the Pitch Scale Reading (PSR) and the Circular Scale Reading (CSR) multiplied by the Least Count (LC). The given Pitch Scale Reading (PSR) is 1 mm and the Circular Scale Reading (CSR) is 51 So, the observed reading $=\mathrm{PSR}+(\mathrm{CSR} \times \mathrm{LC})$ Observed Reading $=1 \mathrm{~mm}+(51 \times 0.01 \mathrm{~mm})$ Observed Reading $=1 \mathrm{~mm}+0.51 \mathrm{~mm}$ Observed Reading $=1.51 \mathrm{~mm}$ To find the true thickness, we must subtract the zero error from the observed reading. Correct Reading $=$ Observed Reading - Zero Error Correct Reading $=1.51 \mathrm{~mm}-(-0.03 \mathrm{~mm})$ Correct Reading $=1.51 \mathrm{~mm}+0.03 \mathrm{~mm}$ Correct Reading $=1.54 \mathrm{~mm}$ Therefore, the correct thickness of the sheet is 1.54 mm. Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: Consider light travelling from a medium $A$ to medium $B$ separated by a plane interface. If the light undergoes total internal reflection during its travel from medium $A$ to $B$ and the speed of light in media $A$ and $B$ are $2.4 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ and $2.7 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$, respectively, then the value of critical angle is:
questions.solution: Step 1: For total internal reflection to occur, light must travel from a denser medium (lower speed) to a rarer medium (higher speed). The speed of light in medium A (Denser) is $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{A}}=2.4 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ The speed of light in medium $B$ (rarer) is $v_B=2.7 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$ Since $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{A}}<\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{B}}$, medium A is indeed optically denser than medium B, satisfying the condition for TIR. The critical angle is determined by Snell's Law at the boundary where the angle of refraction is $90^{\circ}$: $$ n_A \sin \left(\theta_c\right)=n_B \sin \left(90^{\circ}\right) \Rightarrow \sin \left(\theta_c\right)=\frac{n_B}{n_A} $$ Since the refractive index n is inversely proportional to the speed of light $\left(\mathrm{n}=\frac{\mathrm{c}}{\mathrm{v}}\right)$, $$ \frac{n_B}{n_A}=\frac{c / v_B}{c / v_A}=\frac{v_A}{v_B} $$ So, $$ \sin \left(\theta_c\right)=\frac{v_A}{v_B} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\sin \left(\theta_C\right)=\frac{2.4 \times 10^8}{2.7 \times 10^8}=\frac{8}{9}$ $$ \tan \left(\theta_c\right)=\frac{8}{\sqrt{9^2-8^2}}=\frac{8}{\sqrt{17}} \Rightarrow \theta_c=\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{8}{\sqrt{17}}\right) $$ Therefore, the critical angle is $\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{8}{\sqrt{17}}\right)$. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Four persons measure the length of a rod as $20.00 \mathrm{~cm}, 19.75 \mathrm{~cm}, 17.01 \mathrm{~cm}$ and 18.25 cm. The relative error in the measurement of average length of the rod is:
questions.solution: Step 1: The average (mean) of the measured values is the true value for our error calculation. $$ \bar{x}=\frac{x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4}{4} $$ Substituting the given values: $$ \bar{x}=\frac{20.00+19.75+17.01+18.25}{4}=\frac{75.01}{4} $$ $$ \overline{\mathrm{x}}=18.7525 \approx 18.75 \mathrm{~cm} $$ The absolute error is the magnitude of the difference between each individual measurement and the mean value. $$ \left|\Delta \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}}\right|=\left|\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}}-\overline{\mathrm{x}}\right| $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\left|\Delta \mathrm{x}_1\right|=|20.00-18.75|=1.25$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\left|\Delta \mathrm{x}_2\right|=|19.75-18.75|=1.00$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\left|\Delta x_3\right|=|17.01-18.75|=|-1.74|=1.74$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \left|\Delta \mathrm{x}_4\right|=|18.25-18.75|=|-0.50|=0.50 $$ Then the average of these absolute errors. $$ \Delta \overline{\mathrm{x}}=\frac{\sum\left|\Delta \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}}\right|}{4} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\Delta \bar{x}=\frac{1.25+1.00+1.74+0.50}{4}=\frac{4.49}{4}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \Delta \overline{\mathrm{x}}=1.1225 \approx 1.12 \mathrm{~cm} $$ The relative error is defined as the ratio of the mean absolute error to the mean value. Relative Error $=\frac{\Delta \overline{\mathrm{x}}}{\overline{\mathrm{x}}}$ Relative Error $=\frac{1.1225}{18.7525}$ Relative Error $\approx 0.0598$ Rounding to two decimal places, Relative Error $\approx 0.06$ Therefore, the relative error in the measurement is 0.06. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: At 298 K, the mole percentage of $\mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{~g})$ in air is $80 \%$. Water is in equilibrium with air at a pressure of 10 atm. What is the mole fraction of $\mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{~g})$ in water at 298 K ? $\left(\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{H}}\right.$ for $\mathrm{N}_2$ is $\left.6.5 \times 10^7 \mathrm{~mm} \mathrm{Hg}\right)$
questions.solution: Step 1: The partial pressure of a gas in air is its mole fraction times the total pressure (Dalton's law): $$p_{\ce{N2}} = 0.80 \times 10\ \text{atm} = 8\ \text{atm}$$ Since $K_H$ is given in mm Hg, the pressure is converted with $1\ \text{atm} = 760\ \text{mm Hg}$: $$p_{\ce{N2}} = 8 \times 760 = 6080\ \text{mm Hg}$$ Henry's law, $p = K_H\,x$, gives the mole fraction of $\ce{N2}$ dissolved in water: $$x_{\ce{N2}} = \dfrac{p_{\ce{N2}}}{K_H} = \dfrac{6080}{6.5 \times 10^{7}} = 9.35 \times 10^{-5}$$ Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: The heat of atomisation of methane and ethane are ' x ' $\mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ and ' y ' $\mathrm{kJ} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ respectively. The longest wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) of light capable of breaking the $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C}$ bond can be expressed in SI unit as:
questions.solution: Step 1: For methane: $ \Delta H_\text{atom}(CH_4)=x=\;4D(\text{C–H}) \;\Rightarrow\; D(\text{C–H})=\frac{x}{4} $ For ethane: $ \Delta H_\text{atom}(C_2H_6)=y=6D(\text{C–H})+D(\text{C–C}) $ $ \Rightarrow\; D(\text{C–C})=y-6\left(\frac{x}{4}\right)=y-\frac{6x}{4} =\frac{4y-6x}{4}\quad(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}) $ Energy per molecule needed to break the C–C bond: $ E=\frac{D(\text{C–C})\times 1000}{N_A}\quad(\text{J}) $ Longest wavelength corresponds to minimum photon energy: $ \frac{hc}{\lambda}=E \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{N_Ahc}{1000\,D(\text{C–C})} $ $ \lambda=\frac{N_Ahc}{1000\left(\frac{4y-6x}{4}\right)} =\frac{N_Ahc}{250(4y-6x)} $ Correct option: D.

questions.text: Pair of species among the following having same bond order as well as paramagnetic character will be-
questions.solution:
Step 1: Bond order $= \dfrac{1}{2}(N_b - N_a)$, counting the $1s$ electrons; a species with an unpaired electron is paramagnetic. Up to 14 electrons $\pi_{2p}$ lies below $\sigma_{2p_z}$, beyond 14 electrons $\sigma_{2p_z}$ lies below $\pi_{2p}$. $\ce{N2+}$ (13 electrons): $\sigma_{2p_z}$ holds one electron, $N_b = 9$, $N_a = 4$, bond order 2.5, paramagnetic. $\ce{N2-}$ (15 electrons): one electron in $\pi^*$, $N_b = 10$, $N_a = 5$, bond order 2.5, paramagnetic. $\ce{N2^2-}$ (16 electrons): $(\pi^*_{2p_x})^1(\pi^*_{2p_y})^1$, $N_b = 10$, $N_a = 6$, bond order 2, paramagnetic. $\ce{O2+}$ (15 electrons): $N_b = 10$, $N_a = 5$, bond order 2.5, paramagnetic. $\ce{O2-}$ (17 electrons): $N_b = 10$, $N_a = 7$, bond order 1.5, paramagnetic. The pairs have bond orders (
A) 1.5 and 2.5, (
B) 2.5 and 2, (
C) 1.5 and 2.5, (
D) 2.5 and 2.5; only $\ce{O2+}$ and $\ce{N2-}$ match in bond order while both are paramagnetic. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
Consider the following gaseous equilibrium in a closed container of volume ' $V$ ' at $\mathrm{T}(\mathrm{K})$.
$ \mathrm{P}_2(\mathrm{~g})+\mathrm{Q}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{PQ}(\mathrm{~g}) $
2 moles each of $\mathrm{P}_2(\mathrm{~g}), \mathrm{Q}_2(\mathrm{~g})$ and $\mathrm{PQ}(\mathrm{g})$ are present at equilibrium. Now one mole each of ' $\mathrm{P}_2$ ' and ' $\mathrm{Q}_2$ ' are added to the equilibrium keeping the temperature at $\mathrm{T}(\mathrm{K})$. The number of moles of $\mathrm{P}_2, \mathrm{Q}_2$ and PQ at the new equilibrium, respectively, are
questions.solution: Step 1: For $\ce{P2(g) + Q2(g) 2PQ(g)}$, $\Delta n_g = 0$, so the volume cancels: $$K_c = \dfrac{n_{\mathrm{PQ}}^2}{n_{\mathrm{P_2}}\, n_{\mathrm{Q_2}}}$$ At the first equilibrium, $K_c = \dfrac{2^2}{2 \times 2} = 1$. Just after adding 1 mol each of $\ce{P2}$ and $\ce{Q2}$: $n_{\mathrm{P_2}} = n_{\mathrm{Q_2}} = 3$ mol and $n_{\mathrm{PQ}} = 2$ mol, so $Q_c = \dfrac{2^2}{3 \times 3} = \dfrac{4}{9} < K_c$ and the reaction moves forward by $x$ mol: $$\dfrac{(2 + 2x)^2}{(3 - x)^2} = 1 \Rightarrow 2 + 2x = 3 - x \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{1}{3}$$ At the new equilibrium, $n_{\mathrm{P_2}} = n_{\mathrm{Q_2}} = 3 - \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{8}{3} \approx 2.67$ mol and $n_{\mathrm{PQ}} = 2 + \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{8}{3} \approx 2.67$ mol. Hence, the correct option is (B).
questions.topic: Le-Chatelier's Principle and Factors Affecting Chemical Equilibrium

questions.text: The correct order of $\mathrm{C}, \mathrm{N}, \mathrm{O}$ and F in terms of second ionisation potential is
questions.solution: Step 1: The second ionisation removes an electron from the unipositive ion: $\ce{C+}$ $[\text{He}]\,2s^2 2p^1$, $\ce{N+}$ $[\text{He}]\,2s^2 2p^2$, $\ce{O+}$ $[\text{He}]\,2s^2 2p^3$, $\ce{F+}$ $[\text{He}]\,2s^2 2p^4$. Across the period the nuclear charge increases, so $\mathrm{IE_2}$ increases from C to N to F; fluorine, with the highest nuclear charge, has a larger $\mathrm{IE_2}$ than nitrogen even though $\ce{F^2+}$ formed is half-filled. $\ce{O+}$ has the extra-stable half-filled $2p^3$ configuration, while the electron removed from $\ce{F+}$ ($2p^4$) is a paired electron that suffers extra repulsion, so $\mathrm{IE_2(O)}$ is slightly greater than $\mathrm{IE_2(F)}$. Values ($\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$): C 2353, N 2856, F 3374, O 3388, giving $$\mathrm{C < N < F < O}$$ Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Cross aldol condensation between two different aldehydes will always produce four different products.
Statement II: When semicarbazide reacts with a mixture of benzaldehyde and acetophenone under optimum pH, it forms a condensation product with acetophenone only.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.text: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false but Statement II is true

questions.solution:
Step 1: Statement I: False. A crossed aldol between two different aldehydes gives four products only in the uncontrolled case when both aldehydes have α‑H (2 self‑aldols + 2 crossed). It is not “always”: e.g., benzaldehyde (no α‑H) cannot self‑aldol, so fewer products result; and under controlled conditions you can also avoid mixtures. Statement II: False. Semicarbazide forms semicarbazones with both aldehydes and ketones, and aldehydes (benzaldehyde) generally react faster than ketones (acetophenone) under the usual “optimum pH” conditions.

Step 2: So it will not give a condensation product with acetophenone only. Correct option: B — Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.text: The wavelength of spectral line obtained in the spectrum of $\mathrm{Li}^{2+}$ ion, when the transition takes place between two levels whose sum is 4 and difference is 2, is
questions.solution: Step 1: From $n_1 + n_2 = 4$ and $n_2 - n_1 = 2$: $n_2 = 3$ and $n_1 = 1$. For $\ce{Li^2+}$, $Z = 3$. $$\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H Z^2\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right) = R_H \times 9 \times \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{9}\right) = 8R_H$$ With $R_H = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\ \text{m}^{-1} = 1.097 \times 10^{5}\ \text{cm}^{-1}$: $$\lambda = \dfrac{1}{8 \times 1.097 \times 10^{5}}\ \text{cm} = 1.14 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{cm}$$ Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: Two liquids A and B form an ideal solution at temperature T K. At T K, the vapour pressures of pure A and B are 55 and $15 \mathrm{kN} \mathrm{m}^{-2}$ respectively. What is the mole fraction of A in solution of A and B in equilibrium with a vapour in which the mole fraction of A is 0.8?
questions.solution: Step 1: For an ideal solution, Raoult’s law applies: $ p_A=x_A P_A^*,\qquad p_B=x_B P_B^* $ Total pressure: $ P=p_A+p_B=55x_A+15(1-x_A)=55x_A+15-15x_A=40x_A+15 $ Vapour-phase mole fraction (Dalton’s law): $ y_A=\frac{p_A}{P}=\frac{55x_A}{40x_A+15}=0.8 $ Solve: $ 55x_A=0.8(40x_A+15)=32x_A+12 $ $ 23x_A=12 \Rightarrow x_A=\frac{12}{23}=0.5217 $ Answer: 0.5217 (Option A)
questions.topic: Relative Lowering of Vapour Pressure and Roult’s Law

questions.text:
From the following, how many compounds contain at least one secondary alcohol?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Step 1: A secondary alcohol carries the $\ce{-OH}$ group on a carbon atom bonded to exactly two other carbon atoms. (I) $\ce{HOOC-N(CH2CH2OH)2}$: both alcoholic $\ce{-OH}$ groups are on $\ce{CH2}$ carbons (primary); the remaining $\ce{-OH}$ belongs to the carboxyl group. (II) Butane-1,2-diol, $\ce{CH3CH2CH(OH)CH2OH}$: C-2 is bonded to the ethyl carbon and the $\ce{CH2OH}$ carbon, so it is a secondary alcohol. (III) The ring carbon bearing $\ce{-OH}$ is bonded to two ring carbons and the side-chain carbon, and the side-chain carbon to the ring carbon and two methyl groups; both alcohols are tertiary. (IV) The side-chain $\ce{CH(OH)}$ (bonded to a ring carbon and $\ce{CH2OH}$) and the ring $\ce{CH(OH)}$ (bonded to two ring carbons) are secondary; the ring carbon carrying $\ce{CH3}$ and $\ce{OH}$ is tertiary. (V) 3-Methylpentane-2,3-diol, $\ce{CH3CH2C(OH)(CH3)CH(OH)CH3}$: C-2 is secondary (C-3 is tertiary). (VI) 2,3-Dimethylbutane-1,2,3-triol, $\ce{HOCH2C(CH3)(OH)C(CH3)2OH}$: C-2 and C-3 are each bonded to three carbon atoms (tertiary) and C-1 is primary, so there is no secondary alcohol. Compounds II, IV and V contain at least one secondary alcohol, which makes three. Hence, the correct option is (A).
questions.topic: Properties, Preparation and Uses of Alcohols

questions.text: The number of possible tripeptides formed involving alanine (ala), glycine (gly) and valine (val), where no amino acid has been used more than once is:
questions.solution:
Step 1: A tripeptide in which ala, gly and val are each used at most once must contain all three, one of each, so the count equals the number of orders of three different residues: $3! = 6$. A peptide chain has a direction: it is written from the residue with the free amino group (N-terminus) to the residue with the free carboxyl group (C-terminus).

Step 2: So Gly-Ala-Val (free amino group on gly) and Val-Ala-Gly (free amino group on val) are different compounds, not one chain read backwards. The six tripeptides are Gly-Ala-Val, Gly-Val-Ala, Ala-Gly-Val, Ala-Val-Gly, Val-Gly-Ala and Val-Ala-Gly. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: One mole of $\mathrm{Cl}_2(\mathrm{~g})$ was passed into 2 L of cold 2 M KOH solution. After the reaction, the concentrations of $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}, \mathrm{ClO}^{-}$and $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$are respectively (assume volume remains constant)

questions.text:
Find out the statements which are not true.
A. Resonating structures with more number of covalent bonds and lesser charge separation are more stable.
B. In electromeric effect, an unsaturated system shows +E effect with nucleophile and -E effect with electrophile.
C. Inductive effect is responsible for high melting point, boiling point and dipole moment of polar compounds.
D. The greater the number of alkyl groups attached to the doubly bonded carbon atoms, higher is the heat of hydrogenation.
E. Stability of carbanion increases with the increase in $\mathrm{s}-$ character of the carbon carrying the negative charge.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Step 1: Statement A is true: resonating structures with more covalent bonds and less separation of opposite charges are more stable. Statement B is false: in the $+E$ effect the $\pi$ electrons move to the atom to which the attacking reagent gets attached, which happens with electrophiles (e.g. $\ce{H+}$ adding to an alkene); in the $-E$ effect they move to the atom to which the reagent does not get attached, which happens with nucleophiles (e.g. $\ce{CN-}$ adding to a carbonyl group). The statement reverses the two. Statement C is true: the permanent bond polarisation caused by the inductive effect gives polar compounds their dipole moment and the stronger intermolecular attractions behind their higher melting and boiling points. Statement D is false: alkyl groups on the doubly bonded carbons stabilise the alkene by hyperconjugation, so more alkyl groups mean a lower heat of hydrogenation. Statement E is true: greater s-character holds the lone pair closer to the nucleus, so carbanion stability increases in the order $sp^3 < sp^2 < sp$. The statements that are not true are B and D. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: The smallest positive integral value of $a$, for which all the roots of $x^4-a x^2+9=0$ are real and distinct, is equal to
questions.solution:
Step 1: Put $x^2=t$; the equation becomes $t^2-at+9=0$. A positive root $t$ gives two distinct real roots $x=\pm\sqrt t$, while a negative $t$ gives no real $x$.

Step 2: So all four roots are real and distinct exactly when $t^2-at+9=0$ has two distinct positive roots. Distinct real roots: $D=a^2-36>0 \Rightarrow a 6$. Both roots positive: their product is $9>0$, and their sum $a$ must be positive, so $a>0$. Therefore $a>6$, and the smallest positive integer is $a=7$, for which $t=\dfrac{7\pm\sqrt{13}}{2}$, both positive and distinct. Hence, the correct option is (A).
