questions.text: In the following $p-V$ diagram the equation of state along the curved path is given by $(V-2)^2=4 a p$ where $a$ is a constant. The total work done in the closed path is
questions.solution: Step 1: The work done in a cyclic process represented on a $\mathrm{p}-\mathrm{V}$ diagram is equal to the area enclosed by the closed loop. The path of the cycle is $\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{A}$ in an anti-clockwise direction. In a $\mathrm{p}-\mathrm{V}$ diagram, an anti-clockwise cycle represents negative work done by the system $(\mathrm{W}The equation of curve is $(V-2)^2=4 a p$ (path $A \rightarrow B \rightarrow C$). At $\mathrm{V}=2, \mathrm{p}=0$ (Point B is on the V -axis). At $\mathrm{V}=1$ and $\mathrm{V}=3, \mathrm{p}=\frac{(1)^2}{4 \mathrm{a}}=\frac{1}{4 \mathrm{a}}$. This is the pressure at points A and C. The total work done W is the area under the curve minus the area under the straight line: $$ \mathrm{W}=\int_1^3 \mathrm{pdV}-\operatorname{Area}(\mathrm{CA}) $$ Since the line CA is at $\mathrm{p}=\frac{1}{4 \mathrm{a}}$, its area is: $$ \operatorname{Area}(\mathrm{CA})=\mathrm{p} \times \Delta \mathrm{V}=\frac{1}{4 \mathrm{a}} \times(3-1)=\frac{2}{4 \mathrm{a}}=\frac{1}{2 \mathrm{a}} $$ Work done along the curve is, $$ \int\limits_1^3 \mathrm{pdV}=\int_1^3\left[\frac{(\mathrm{~V}-2)^2}{4 \mathrm{a}}\right] \mathrm{dV}=\frac{1}{4 \mathrm{a}}\left[\frac{(\mathrm{~V}-2)^3}{3}\right]_1^3 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \int\limits_1^3 \mathrm{pdV}=\frac{1}{4 \mathrm{a}}\left[\frac{(3-2)^3}{3}-\frac{(1-2)^3}{3}\right]=\frac{1}{4 \mathrm{a}}\left[\frac{1}{3}-\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)\right]=\frac{1}{4 \mathrm{a}} \times \frac{2}{3}=\frac{1}{6 \mathrm{a}} $$ So, the net work done in the cycle is $$ W_{\text {net }}=\frac{1}{6 a}-\frac{1}{2 a}=\frac{1-3}{6 a}=-\frac{1}{3 a} $$ Therefore, the total work done in closed path is $-\frac{1}{3 a}. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
The ratio of mass percentage (w/w) of
C: H in a hydrocarbon is 12: 1. It has two carbon atoms. The weight (in g) of CO 2 (g) formed when 3.38 g of this hydrocarbon is completely burnt in oxygen is: (Given: Molar mass in g mol –1
C: 12, H: 1, O: 16)
questions.solution: Step 1: Let the hydrocarbon be $C_2H_x$ since it has two carbon atoms. Given, the mass percentage ratio of $C:H$ is $12:1$. So, in the hydrocarbon, mass of carbon $= 2 \times 12 = 24$ mass of hydrogen $= x \times 1 = x$ Now, $$ 24: x = 12: 1 $$ So, $$ \frac{24}{x} = \frac{12}{1} $$ $$ 24 = 12x $$ $$ x = 2 $$ Hence, the hydrocarbon is $$ C_2H_2 $$ Its molar mass is $$ (2 \times 12) + (2 \times 1) = 24 + 2 = 26 \text{ g mol}^{-1} $$ Number of moles of $C_2H_2$ in $3.38$ g: $$ \text{moles of } C_2H_2 = \frac{3.38}{26} = 0.13 \text{ mol} $$ Complete combustion of acetylene: $$ 2C_2H_2 + 5O_2 \rightarrow 4CO_2 + 2H_2O $$ From the equation, $$ 1 \text{ mol } C_2H_2 \rightarrow 2 \text{ mol } CO_2 $$ Therefore, $$ 0.13 \text{ mol } C_2H_2 \rightarrow 0.26 \text{ mol } CO_2 $$ Molar mass of $CO_2$: $$ 12 + (2 \times 16) = 44 \text{ g mol}^{-1} $$ Mass of $CO_2$ formed: $$ 0.26 \times 44 = 11.44 \text{ g} $$ So, the correct answer is $$ \boxed{11.44 \text{ g}} $$ Option B.

questions.text: The first and second ionization constants of a weak dibasic acid H₂A are $8.1 \times 10^{-8}$ and $1.0 \times 10^{-13}$ respectively. 0.1 mol of H₂A was dissolved in 1 L of 0.1 M HCl solution. The concentration of HA - in the resultant solution is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Given: First ionization constant: $$K_{a1} = 8.1 \times 10^{-8}$$ Second ionization constant: $$K_{a2} = 1.0 \times 10^{-13}$$ $0.1$ mol of $H_2A$ is dissolved in $1\ \text{L}$ of $0.1\ \text{M HCl}$ So, in the final solution: Initial concentration of $H_2A = 0.1\ \text{M}$ Since HCl is a strong acid, $$[H^+] = 0.1\ \text{M}$$ We have to find $[HA^-]$. For the first dissociation of dibasic acid: $$H_2A \rightleftharpoons H^+ + HA^-$$ Using the expression of first ionization constant, $$K_{a1} = \frac{[H^+][HA^-]}{[H_2A]}$$ Substitute the known values: $$8.1 \times 10^{-8} = \frac{(0.1)[HA^-]}{0.1}$$ Since $\dfrac{0.1}{0.1} = 1$, we get: $$[HA^-] = 8.1 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{M}$$ Now, because $K_{a2}$ is extremely small, further dissociation of $HA^-$ is negligible in presence of strong acid. Hence, the concentration of $HA^-$ in the resultant solution is $$\boxed{8.1 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{M}}$$ So, the correct option is: $$\boxed{\text{Option C}}$$

questions.text:
SF$_4$ is isostructural with:
A. BrF$_4^\ominus$
B. CH$_4$
C. IF$_4^{\oplus}$
D. XeF$_4$ E. XeO$_2$F$_2$ Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Step 1: $\ce{SF4}$: S has 6 valence electrons, forming 4 bond pairs and keeping 1 lone pair, so 5 electron pairs ($\mathrm{sp^3d}$) give a see-saw shape. $\ce{BrF4-}$ (A): Br has $7 + 1 = 8$ electrons, giving 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs ($\mathrm{sp^3d^2}$), so it is square planar. $\ce{CH4}$ (B): 4 bond pairs and no lone pair ($\mathrm{sp^3}$), so it is tetrahedral. $\ce{IF4+}$ (C): I has $7 - 1 = 6$ electrons, giving 4 bond pairs and 1 lone pair ($\mathrm{sp^3d}$), so it is see-saw. $\ce{XeF4}$ (D): 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs ($\mathrm{sp^3d^2}$), so it is square planar. $\ce{XeO2F2}$ (E): Xe uses 6 of its 8 electrons in two Xe=O and two Xe–F bonds and keeps 1 lone pair, so 4 σ bond pairs and 1 lone pair ($\mathrm{sp^3d}$) give a see-saw shape. $\ce{SF4}$ is isostructural with $\ce{IF4+}$ (C) and $\ce{XeO2F2}$ (E). Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: Gas 'A' undergoes change from state 'X' to state 'Y'. In this process, the heat absorbed and work done by the gas is 10 J and 18 J respectively. Now gas is brought back to state 'X' by another process during which 6 J of heat is evolved. In the reverse process of 'Y' to 'X',

options.text: 18 J of the work is done by the gas 'A'.
2 J of the work is done by the gas 'A'.
12 J of the work is done on the gas 'A' by the surrounding.
14 J of the work is done on the gas 'A' by the surrounding.

questions.solution: Step 1: In the chemistry (IUPAC) sign convention, $\Delta U = q + w$, where $q > 0$ for heat absorbed by the gas and $w > 0$ for work done on the gas. Process X $\rightarrow$ Y: heat absorbed $q = +10\ \text{J}$; 18 J of work is done by the gas, so $w = -18\ \text{J}$. $$\Delta U_{X\rightarrow Y} = 10 + (-18) = -8\ \text{J}$$ Internal energy is a state function, so for the return from Y to X by any path, $\Delta U_{Y\rightarrow X} = +8\ \text{J}$. Process Y $\rightarrow$ X: 6 J of heat is evolved, so $q = -6\ \text{J}$. $$8 = -6 + w \Rightarrow w = +14\ \text{J}$$ A positive $w$ means 14 J of work is done on gas A by the surroundings. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Solution A is prepared by dissolving 1 g of a protein (molar mass = 50,000 g mol -1 ) in 0.5 L of water at 300 K. Its osmotic pressure is $x$ bar. Solution B is made by dissolving 2 g of the same protein in 1 L of water at 300 K. Osmotic pressure of solution B is $y$ bar. Entire solution of A is mixed with entire solution of B at the same temperature. The osmotic pressure of resultant solution is $z$ bar. $x$, $y$ and $z$ respectively are: (R = 0.083 L bar mol -1 K -1 )
questions.solution: Step 1: For osmotic pressure, we use the NCERT relation: $$ \pi = C R T = \frac{n}{V}RT $$ where $\pi$ = osmotic pressure $n$ = number of moles of solute $V$ = volume of solution $R = 0.083 \, \text{L bar mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ $T = 300 \, \text{K}$ Protein molar mass is: $$ M = 50000 \, \text{g mol}^{-1} $$ Now solve each part. For solution A Mass of protein $= 1 \, \text{g}$ Moles of protein: $$ n_A = \frac{1}{50000} = 2 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{mol} $$ Volume: $$ V_A = 0.5 \, \text{L} $$ So concentration: $$ C_A = \frac{2 \times 10^{-5}}{0.5} = 4 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{mol L}^{-1} $$ Hence osmotic pressure: $$ x = \pi_A = C_A RT $$ $$ x = (4 \times 10^{-5})(0.083)(300) $$ First calculate: $$ 0.083 \times 300 = 24.9 $$ So, $$ x = 4 \times 10^{-5} \times 24.9 = 9.96 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{bar} $$ For solution B Mass of protein $= 2 \, \text{g}$ Moles: $$ n_B = \frac{2}{50000} = 4 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{mol} $$ Volume: $$ V_B = 1 \, \text{L} $$ Concentration: $$ C_B = \frac{4 \times 10^{-5}}{1} = 4 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{mol L}^{-1} $$ Thus, $$ y = \pi_B = C_BRT $$ $$ y = (4 \times 10^{-5})(0.083)(300) $$ $$ y = 9.96 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{bar} $$ After mixing A and B Total moles of protein: $$ n_{\text{total}} = 2 \times 10^{-5} + 4 \times 10^{-5} = 6 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{mol} $$ Total volume: $$ V_{\text{total}} = 0.5 + 1 = 1.5 \, \text{L} $$ Concentration after mixing: $$ C_{\text{mix}} = \frac{6 \times 10^{-5}}{1.5} = 4 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{mol L}^{-1} $$ Again, $$ z = \pi_{\text{mix}} = C_{\text{mix}}RT $$ $$ z = (4 \times 10^{-5})(0.083)(300) = 9.96 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{bar} $$ So, $$ x = 9.96 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{bar}, \quad y = 9.96 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{bar}, \quad z = 9.96 \times 10^{-4} \, \text{bar} $$ Therefore, the correct option is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option A}} $$

questions.text: At 25°C, 20.0 mL of 0.2 M weak monoprotic acid HX is titrated against 0.2 M NaOH. The pH of the solution (a) at the start of the titration (when NaOH has not been added) and (b) when 10 mL of NaOH is added respectively, are: Given: $K_a = 5 \times 10^{-4}$ $\mathrm{p}K_a = 3.3$ $\alpha \ll 1$
questions.solution: Step 1: Given data: Concentration of the weak acid $HX$, $C = 0.2 \text{ M}$ Initial volume of $HX = 20.0 \text{ mL}$ Concentration of $NaOH = 0.2 \text{ M}$ Dissociation constant of acid, $K_a = 5 \times 10^{-4}$ $\mathrm{p}K_a = 3.3$ Case (a): At the start of the titration (when NO $NaOH$ has been added) At this point, only the weak acid $HX$ is present in the solution. Since the degree of dissociation $\alpha \ll 1$, we can calculate the hydrogen ion concentration $[H^+]$ using the formula for a weak monoprotic acid: $$ [H^+] = \sqrt{K_a \times C} $$ Substitute the values of $K_a$ and $C$: $$ [H^+] = \sqrt{5 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.2} $$ $$ [H^+] = \sqrt{1 \times 10^{-4}} $$ $$ [H^+] = 10^{-2} \text{ M} $$ The $\text{pH}$ of the solution is: $$ \text{pH} = -\log[H^+] $$ $$ \text{pH} = -\log(10^{-2}) = 2.0 $$ Case (b): When $10 \text{ mL}$ of $0.2 \text{ M } NaOH$ is added When strong base $NaOH$ is added, it reacts with the weak acid $HX$ to form salt $NaX$ and water: $$ HX + NaOH \longrightarrow NaX + H_2O $$ Let us find the number of millimoles (mmol) of acid and base: $$ \text{Initial millimoles of } HX = \text{Molarity} \times \text{Volume in mL} = 0.2 \text{ M} \times 20.0 \text{ mL} = 4.0 \text{ mmol} $$ $$ \text{Millimoles of } NaOH \text{ added} = 0.2 \text{ M} \times 10.0 \text{ mL} = 2.0 \text{ mmol} $$ Since $NaOH$ is the limiting reagent, $2.0 \text{ mmol}$ of $NaOH$ will completely neutralize $2.0 \text{ mmol}$ of $HX$, forming $2.0 \text{ mmol}$ of the salt $NaX$. Let's analyze the composition of the mixture after the reaction: $$ \text{Remaining millimoles of } HX = 4.0 - 2.0 = 2.0 \text{ mmol} $$ $$ \text{Millimoles of salt } NaX \text{ formed} = 2.0 \text{ mmol} $$ Now, the solution contains a weak acid ($HX$) and its salt with a strong base ($NaX$). This constitutes an acidic buffer solution. We can determine the $\text{pH}$ using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: $$ \text{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log \left( \frac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]} \right) $$ Since the volumes are the same, the ratio of their concentrations is simply the ratio of their millimoles: $$ \text{pH} = 3.3 + \log \left( \frac{2.0}{2.0} \right) $$ $$ \text{pH} = 3.3 + \log(1) $$ Since $\log(1) = 0$: $$ \text{pH} = 3.3 + 0 = 3.3 $$ (Note: We can also directly observe that because exactly half the equivalence volume of the base is added, it is the half-neutralization point, where $\text{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a$.) Conclusion: The $\text{pH}$ values for part (a) and (b) are $2.0$ and $3.3$ respectively. Correct Option: Option B

questions.text: The correct set that contains all kinds (basic, acidic, amphoteric and neutral) of oxides is:
questions.solution: Step 1: To find the correct set, we need one oxide of each type: Basic oxide Acidic oxide Amphoteric oxide Neutral oxide Now let us check the given oxides. Important classifications Basic oxides: Usually metallic oxides like $Na_2O$, $K_2O$ Acidic oxides: Usually non-metallic oxides like $Cl_2O_7$ Amphoteric oxides: Oxides that react with both acids and bases, like $Al_2O_3$, $As_2O_3$ Neutral oxides: Neither acidic nor basic, like $CO$, $NO$, $N_2O$ Option A $Na_2O,\ K_2O,\ Al_2O_3,\ As_2O_3$ $Na_2O$ = basic $K_2O$ = basic $Al_2O_3$ = amphoteric $As_2O_3$ = amphoteric This set does not contain acidic and neutral oxides. So, Option A is incorrect. Option B $Al_2O_3,\ As_2O_3,\ CO,\ NO$ $Al_2O_3$ = amphoteric $As_2O_3$ = amphoteric $CO$ = neutral $NO$ = neutral This set does not contain basic and acidic oxides. So, Option B is incorrect. Option C $K_2O,\ Cl_2O_7,\ As_2O_3,\ NO$ $K_2O$ = basic $Cl_2O_7$ = acidic $As_2O_3$ = amphoteric $NO$ = neutral This set contains all four kinds of oxides. So, Option C is correct. Option D $Na_2O,\ N_2O,\ Al_2O_3,\ CO$ $Na_2O$ = basic $N_2O$ = neutral $Al_2O_3$ = amphoteric $CO$ = neutral This set does not contain any acidic oxide. So, Option D is incorrect. Final Answer $$\boxed{\text{Option C}}$$

questions.text: Given below are two statements: Statement I: The second ionization enthalpy of B, Al and Ga is in the order of B > Al > Ga. Statement II: The correct order in terms of first ionization enthalpy is Si < Ge < Pb < Sn. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true

questions.solution: Step 1: For boron family elements, the order of second ionization enthalpy is: $$ \underset{(2427 \mathrm{KJ} / \mathrm{mol})}{\mathrm{B}}>\underset{(1979 \mathrm{KJ} / \mathrm{mol})}{\mathrm{Ga}}>\underset{(1816 \mathrm{KJ} / \mathrm{mol})}{\mathrm{Al}} $$ So, the given order $ \mathrm{B} > \mathrm{Al} > \mathrm{Ga} $ is incorrect. For carbon family elements, the order of first ionization enthalpy is: $$ \underset{(786 \mathrm{KJ} / \mathrm{mol})}{\mathrm{Si}}>\underset{(761 \mathrm{KJ} / \mathrm{mol})}{\mathrm{Ge}}>\underset{(715 \mathrm{KJ} / \mathrm{mol})}{\mathrm{Pb}}>\underset{(708 \mathrm{KJ} / \mathrm{mol})}{\mathrm{Sn}} $$ So, the given order \mathrm{Si} Hence, both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.text: Given below are two statements: Statement I: Among Zn, Mn, Sc and Cu, the energy required to remove the third valence electron is highest for Zn and lowest for Sc. Statement II: The correct order of the following complexes in terms of CFSE is [\text{Co(H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true

questions.solution:
Step 1: Statement I We need to compare the energy required to remove the third valence electron, that is, the third ionization enthalpy. First write the electronic configurations: $Zn: [Ar]\,3d^{10}4s^2$ $Mn: [Ar]\,3d^5 4s^2$ $Sc: [Ar]\,3d^1 4s^2$ $Cu: [Ar]\,3d^{10}4s^1$ Now, after removal of two electrons: $Zn^{2+}: [Ar]\,3d^{10}$ $Mn^{2+}: [Ar]\,3d^5$ $Sc^{2+}: [Ar]\,3d^1$ $Cu^{2+}: [Ar]\,3d^9$ The third electron is now removed from these ions. Which one will have highest third ionization enthalpy? For $Zn^{2+}$, the configuration is $3d^{10}$, which is a completely filled and very stable configuration. Removing one electron from this is difficult. So, third ionization enthalpy is highest for Zn. Which one will have lowest third ionization enthalpy? For $Sc^{2+}$, configuration is $3d^1$. Removing this one electron gives $Sc^{3+}: [Ar]$, which is a noble gas configuration, hence this removal is comparatively easier. So, third ionization enthalpy is lowest for Sc. Therefore, Statement I is true. Statement II We need the order of complexes in terms of CFSE. Given complexes: $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$ $[\text{Co(en)}_3]^{3+}$ Step 1: Find oxidation state and $d$-configuration In $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$, cobalt is $Co^{2+}$ $Co: [Ar]\,3d^7 4s^2$ $Co^{2+}: 3d^7$ In $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$, cobalt is $Co^{3+}$ $Co^{3+}: 3d^6$ In $[\text{Co(en)}_3]^{3+}$, cobalt is also $Co^{3+}$ so it is also $3d^6$ Step 2: Nature of ligand and spin state $H_2O$ is a weak field ligand $en$ is a stronger field ligand than $H_2O$ So: $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$ is octahedral, weak field, $d^7$ generally high spin $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$ is octahedral, $d^6$ because of higher charge on $Co^{3+}$, splitting is larger; this complex is effectively low spin $[\text{Co(en)}_3]^{3+}$ is octahedral, $d^6$, strong field definitely low spin Step 3: Calculate CFSE 1. $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$: high-spin $d^7$ Configuration: $t_{2g}^5 e_g^2$ $$ CFSE = 5(-0.4\Delta_o) + 2(+0.6\Delta_o) = -2.0\Delta_o + 1.2\Delta_o = -0.8\Delta_o $$ Magnitude of CFSE $= 0.8\Delta_o$ 2. $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$: low-spin $d^6$ Configuration: $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$ $$ CFSE = 6(-0.4\Delta_o) = -2.4\Delta_o $$ Magnitude $= 2.4\Delta_o$ 3. $[\text{Co(en)}_3]^{3+}$: low-spin $d^6$ Also $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$, so $$ CFSE = -2.4\Delta_o $$ But here $en$ is stronger field than $H_2O$, so $\Delta_o$ is larger. Hence CFSE magnitude is greater for $[\text{Co(en)}_3]^{3+}$ than for $[\text{Co(H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$.

Step 2: So the order is: $$ [\text{Co(H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+} Therefore, Statement II is also true. Final Answer $$ \boxed{\text{Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true}}

questions.text:
Which of the following complexes will show coordination isomerism?
A. $[\mathrm{Ag(NH}_3)_2][\mathrm{Ag(CN)}_2]$
B. $[\mathrm{Co(NH}_3)_6][\mathrm{Cr(CN)}_6]$
C. $[\mathrm{Co(NH}_3)_6][\mathrm{Co(CN)}_6]$
D. $[\mathrm{Fe(NH}_3)_6][\mathrm{Co(CN)}_6]$ E. $[\mathrm{Co(NH}_3)_6][\mathrm{Fe(CN)}_6]$ Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Step 1: Coordination Isomerism arises from the interchange of ligands between cationic and anionic entities of different metal ions present in a complex. When the complete interchange of ligands takes place, it must result in a new, chemically distinct isomer. Let us evaluate each of the given choices under this concept:
A. $[\mathrm{Ag(NH}_3)_2][\mathrm{Ag(CN)}_2]$: Both the cationic and anionic entities contain the same metal ion ($ \text{Ag} $). If we fully interchange the ligands, we get $[\mathrm{Ag(CN)}_2]^- [\mathrm{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+$, which is exactly the same compound written in reverse order. Further, a partial interchange leads to neutral molecules $[\mathrm{Ag(NH}_3)(\mathrm{CN})]$, which destroys the cation-anion pair. Hence, it does not show coordination isomerism.
B. $[\mathrm{Co(NH}_3)_6][\mathrm{Cr(CN)}_6]$: This complex contains two different metal ions ($ \text{Co} $ and $ \text{Cr} $). By interchanging the ligands between the cationic and anionic coordination spheres, we get a completely new distinct complex: $[\mathrm{Cr(NH}_3)_6][\mathrm{Co(CN)}_6]$. Hence, it shows coordination isomerism. (This is also the classic example mentioned in NCERT).
C. $[\mathrm{Co(NH}_3)_6][\mathrm{Co(CN)}_6]$: Both entities contain the same metal ion ($ \text{Co} $). A complete interchange of all ligands gives $[\mathrm{Co(CN)}_6]^{3-} [\mathrm{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$, which is exactly the same coordination compound. According to the strict NCERT definition requiring different metal ions for complete interchange, it does not exhibit coordination isomerism.
D. $[\mathrm{Fe(NH}_3)_6][\mathrm{Co(CN)}_6]$: This complex has two different metal ions ($ \text{Fe} $ and $ \text{Co} $). Exchanging the primary coordination spheres yields a distinct coordination isomer: $[\mathrm{Co(NH}_3)_6][\mathrm{Fe(CN)}_6]$. Hence, it shows coordination isomerism. E. $[\mathrm{Co(NH}_3)_6][\mathrm{Fe(CN)}_6]$: This complex is exactly the coordination isomer of the complex described in option
D. Since it consists of different metal ions ($ \text{Co} $ and $ \text{Fe} $), exchanging its ligands will yield the complex in
D. Thus, it also shows coordination isomerism. Conclusion: Complexes B, D, and E exhibit coordination isomerism because they possess differently named metal ions in their cationic and anionic parts, allowing the exchange of ligands to produce distinctly new isomers. Correct Answer: Option B (B, D and E Only)

questions.text: Complete combustion of $X$ g of an organic compound gave $0.25$ g of $CO_2$ and $0.12$ g of $H_2O$. If the % of carbon is $25\%$ and of hydrogen is $4.89\%$, then $X = \underline{\phantom{xxx}} \times 10^{-3}$ g. (Nearest integer) (Molar mass of C, H and O are 12, 1 and 16 g mol$^{-1}$ respectively.)
questions.solution:
Step 1: For complete combustion, all the carbon in the compound goes into $CO_2$ and all the hydrogen goes into $H_2O$.

Step 2: So first, let us find the masses of carbon and hydrogen present in the given sample. 1. Mass of carbon from $0.25$ g of $CO_2$ In $44$ g of $CO_2$, mass of carbon is $12$ g. So, in $0.25$ g of $CO_2$, mass of carbon is $$ \text{Mass of C}=\frac{12}{44}\times 0.25 $$ $$ =\frac{3}{44}=0.06818\text{ g} $$ 2. Mass of hydrogen from $0.12$ g of $H_2O$ In $18$ g of $H_2O$, mass of hydrogen is $2$ g. So, in $0.12$ g of $H_2O$, mass of hydrogen is $$ \text{Mass of H}=\frac{2}{18}\times 0.12 $$ $$ =\frac{0.24}{18}=0.01333\text{ g} $$ 3. Use given percentage of carbon The compound contains $25\%$ carbon. If total mass of compound is $X$ g, then mass of carbon in it is $$ \frac{25}{100}X=0.25X $$ But this is equal to the carbon obtained from combustion: $$ 0.25X=0.06818 $$ So, $$ X=\frac{0.06818}{0.25}=0.27272\text{ g} $$ $$ X\approx 0.273\text{ g} $$ Now write it in the form $$ X = \underline{\phantom{xxx}} \times 10^{-3}\text{ g} $$ Since $$ 0.273\text{ g}=273\times 10^{-3}\text{ g} $$ So the required integer is $$ \boxed{273} $$ Therefore, the correct option is A.

questions.text: Given below are two statements: Statement I: In, the carbocation is stabilised by +R effect of –OCH 3 group. Statement II: In, the carbanion is stabilised by –R effect of –NO 2 group. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true

questions.solution: Step 1: Carbocation ($C^+$) has a deficiency of electrons, so it becomes more stable when a group donates electron density towards it. Therefore, carbocations are stabilised by electron donating groups (EDGs) due to $+R,+I,+H$ effect whereas, carbanions ($C^-$) are stabilised by electron withdrawing groups (EWGs) due to $-R,-I,-H$ effect. So, in Statement I, the $-OCH_3$ group shows $+R$ effect (lone pair donation), which stabilises the carbocation by resonance. In Statement II, the $-NO_2$ group shows $-R$ effect (it withdraws electron density), which stabilises the carbanion by resonance.

questions.text: The compound (X) on (i) on heating in the presence of anhydrous AlCl 3 and HCl gas gives 2,4-dimethyl pentane (ii) aromatization gives toluene and (iii) cyclisation gives methyl cyclohexane The correct name of compound (X) is:
questions.solution: Step 1: All three changes are reactions of the alkane n-heptane, $\ce{C7H16}$. Heating n-heptane with anhydrous $\ce{AlCl3}$ and $\ce{HCl}$ gas isomerises it to branched alkanes of the same formula, such as 2,4-dimethylpentane, $\ce{(CH3)2CHCH2CH(CH3)2}$. Aromatisation over $\ce{Cr2O3}$ at 773 K and 10–20 atm cyclises and dehydrogenates the chain to toluene: $$\ce{C7H16 -> C6H5CH3 + 4H2}$$ Cyclisation of the seven-carbon chain gives methylcyclohexane: $$\ce{C7H16 -> C6H11CH3 + H2}$$ Hept-2-ene ($\ce{C7H14}$) and the heptatrienes ($\ce{C7H10}$) cannot give the saturated $\ce{C7H16}$ on $\ce{AlCl3}$/$\ce{HCl}$ isomerisation, since no hydrogen is added. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
Correct statements regarding alkyl halides (R–X) among the following are:
A. Alcohol being less polar solvent as compared to water, alcoholic KOH favours elimination reaction with R–X.
B. Order of reactivity towards S N 1 mechanism is C₆H₅ –CH 2 –Cl > C₆H₅ –CHCl–C₆H₅.
C. Non substituted aryl halides exhibit properties similar to alkyl halides.
D. Vinyl chloride is an example of haloalkene and allyl chloride is an example of haloalkyne. E. R–Cl can be prepared by reacting R–OH with SOCl 2 but Ar–Cl cannot be prepared by reacting Ar–OH with SOCl 2. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Step 1: Check each statement carefully. For $R-X$, alcoholic KOH generally gives elimination, while aqueous KOH gives substitution. This happens because alcohol is less polar than water, so the hydroxide ion is less solvated and behaves more like a base, favouring $\beta$-elimination. So, $A$ is correct. Now $B$: In $S_N1$ reaction, reactivity depends on stability of the carbocation formed. For benzyl chloride: $$C_6H_5-CH_2-Cl \rightarrow C_6H_5-CH_2^+$$ This is a benzyl carbocation, stabilized by resonance. For benzhydryl chloride: $$C_6H_5-CHCl-C_6H_5 \rightarrow C_6H_5-CH^+-C_6H_5$$ This carbocation is stabilized by resonance with two phenyl rings, so it is more stable than benzyl carbocation. Hence reactivity order should be $$C_6H_5-CHCl-C_6H_5 > C_6H_5-CH_2-Cl$$ So statement $B$ is false. Now $C$: Aryl halides do not show properties similar to alkyl halides. They are much less reactive in nucleophilic substitution because the $C-X$ bond in aryl halides has partial double bond character due to resonance.

Step 2: So $C$ is false. Now $D$: Vinyl chloride, $CH_2=CHCl$, is a haloalkene. This part is correct. Allyl chloride, $CH_2=CH-CH_2Cl$, is also a haloalkene, not a haloalkyne.

Step 3: So $D$ is false. Now $E$: Alkyl chlorides can be prepared from alcohols using thionyl chloride: $$R-OH + SOCl_2 \rightarrow R-Cl + SO_2 + HCl$$ But phenols do not give aryl chlorides with $SOCl_2$. In phenol, the $C-O$ bond has partial double bond character due to resonance, so replacement of $OH$ by $Cl$ does not happen this way.

Step 4: So $E$ is correct. The correct statements are $A$ and $E$ only. $$\boxed{\text{Option C}}$$

questions.text:
A molecule (X) with following structure under mild acidic condition is hydrolysed to produce (Y) and (Z). Identify the correct statements about (Y) and (Z).
A. Both (Y) and (Z) have same molar mass.
B. (Y) and (Z) can be distinguished from each other by NaHCO$_3$.
C. (Y) and (Z) react with HCN with same rates.
D. (Y) and (Z) undergo addition reaction with 2,4-DNP. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Step 1: X is $\ce{CH3-CH=CH-O-C(CH3)=CH2}$: the oxygen is bonded to two vinylic carbons, so both sides are enol ethers. Mild acid hydrolysis cleaves both C–O bonds and gives two enols, which tautomerise to carbonyl compounds. The products are propanal, $\ce{CH3CH2CHO}$ (Y), and propanone, $\ce{CH3COCH3}$ (Z). Statement A is correct: both are $\ce{C3H6O}$, molar mass $58\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. Statement B is incorrect: neither compound has an acidic COOH group, so neither reacts with $\ce{NaHCO3}$. Statement C is incorrect: the aldehyde adds HCN faster than the ketone, because its carbonyl carbon is less hindered and more electrophilic. Statement D is correct: both have a C=O group and react with 2,4-DNP (addition followed by loss of water) to give 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazones. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Identify compounds A and E in the following reaction sequence.
questions.solution: Step 1: In 1-ethyl-4-nitrobenzene the ethyl group (activating, ortho/para-directing) and the nitro group (deactivating, meta-directing) both direct to the carbon ortho to the ethyl group, so $\ce{Br2/AlBr3}$ gives A = 2-bromo-1-ethyl-4-nitrobenzene. Sn/HCl reduces $\ce{-NO2}$ to $\ce{-NH2}$, giving B = 3-bromo-4-ethylaniline, and $\ce{NaNO2/HCl}$ at 273–278 K converts it to the diazonium chloride C. Ethanol reduces the diazonium group to H, giving D = 1-bromo-2-ethylbenzene. Hot alkaline $\ce{KMnO4}$ oxidises the ethyl side chain, which has benzylic hydrogens, to a carboxylate, and $\ce{H3O+}$ gives E = 2-bromobenzoic acid; the C–Br bond is unaffected. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: Among $Fe^{2+}$, $Fe^{3+}$, $Cr^{2+}$ and $Zn^{2+}$, the ion that shows positive borax bead test and with highest ionisation enthalpy is:
questions.solution: Step 1: For a positive borax bead test, the ion must generally have unpaired electrons in its $d$-orbitals, because transition metal ions give characteristic bead colours due to electronic transitions. Let us check each ion: $Fe^{2+}: [Ar]\,3d^6$ → has unpaired electrons, so it gives borax bead test. $Fe^{3+}: [Ar]\,3d^5$ → has unpaired electrons, so it gives borax bead test. $Cr^{2+}: [Ar]\,3d^4$ → has unpaired electrons, so it gives borax bead test. $Zn^{2+}: [Ar]\,3d^{10}$ → all electrons are paired, so it does not give a positive borax bead test. So, among the given ions, we compare $Fe^{2+}, Fe^{3+}, Cr^{2+}$ for highest ionisation enthalpy. Now, higher positive charge and greater effective nuclear charge generally mean higher ionisation enthalpy. Also, $Fe^{3+}$ has the stable half-filled configuration: $$ Fe^{3+} = [Ar]\,3d^5 $$ This makes removal of another electron more difficult. Therefore, the ion that: shows positive borax bead test, and has highest ionisation enthalpy is $$ \boxed{Fe^{3+}} $$ So, the correct option is D. $Fe^{3+}$.

questions.text: Let $\alpha, \beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2 - 3x + r = 0$, and $\frac{\alpha}{2}, 2\beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2 + 3x + r = 0$. If the roots of the equation $x^2 + 6x = m$ are $2\alpha + \beta + 2r$ and $\alpha - 2\beta - \frac{r}{2}$, then $m$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: For the equation $x^2 - 3x + r = 0$ with roots $\alpha, \beta$, by using the standard results: $$ \begin{aligned} & \alpha+\beta=3 \ & \frac{\alpha}{2}+2 \beta=-3 \end{aligned} $$ The first line comes from “sum of roots” $= -\dfrac{\text{coefficient of }x}{\text{coefficient of }x^2} = -\dfrac{-3}{1}=3$. The second line comes from the equation $x^2 + 3x + r = 0$, whose roots are $\dfrac{\alpha}{2}$ and $2\beta$. So, their sum is: $$\frac{\alpha}{2} + 2\beta = -\frac{3}{1} = -3$$ Now solve the two equations: $$\alpha+\beta=3 \Rightarrow \alpha=3-\beta$$ Substitute into $\dfrac{\alpha}{2}+2\beta=-3$: $$\frac{3-\beta}{2}+2\beta=-3$$ Multiply by $2$: $$3-\beta+4\beta=-6 \Rightarrow 3+3\beta=-6 \Rightarrow 3\beta=-9 \Rightarrow \beta=-3$$ Then $\alpha=3-(-3)=6$. Now use “product of roots” for $x^2 - 3x + r = 0$: $$\alpha\beta=r \Rightarrow r=6\times(-3)=-18$$ Now consider the equation $x^2 + 6x = m$. Rewrite it in standard form: $$x^2 + 6x - m = 0$$ So, product of its roots $= \dfrac{-m}{1}=-m$. The roots are given as $2\alpha + \beta + 2r$ and $\alpha - 2\beta - \dfrac{r}{2}$. Substitute $\alpha=6$, $\beta=-3$, $r=-18$: First root: $$2\alpha + \beta + 2r = 2(6)+(-3)+2(-18)=12-3-36=-27$$ Second root: $$\alpha - 2\beta - \frac{r}{2} = 6-2(-3)-\frac{-18}{2}=6+6+9=21$$ Now product of roots: $$ \begin{aligned} & =(2 \alpha+\beta+2 \mathrm{r})\left(\alpha-2 \beta-\frac{\mathrm{r}}{2}\right) \ & \Rightarrow-\mathrm{m}=(-27)(21) \ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{m}=567 \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: Let the circles $C_1:|z| = r$ and $C_2:|z - 3 - 4i| = 5$, $z \in \mathbb{C}$, be such that $C_2$ lies within $C_1$. If $z_1$ moves on $C_1$, $z_2$ moves on $C_2$ and $\min |z_1 - z_2| = 2$, then $\max |z_1 - z_2|$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Step 1: $$ \begin{aligned} & |z|=r \ & O A=r \end{aligned} $$ Step 1: Circle $C_1:|z|=r$ has centre $O(0,0)$ and radius $r$ (so $OA=r$).

Step 2: Circle $C_2:|z-3-4i|=5$ has centre at the point $(3,4)$ and radius $5$.

Step 3: Distance between the centres is $$OC=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$$ Step 4: Since $C_2$ lies completely inside $C_1$, the minimum distance between a point $z_1$ on $C_1$ and a point $z_2$ on $C_2$ happens when the two points are on the same line through the centres, on the nearest sides. So, minimum $\left|\mathrm{z}_1-\mathrm{z}_2\right|= r-(OC+5)=r-(5+5)=r-10$ Given minimum $\left|\mathrm{z}_1-\mathrm{z}_2\right|=2$, we get $$ \Rightarrow r-10=2 \Rightarrow r=12 $$ Step 5: The maximum distance $\left|z_1-z_2\right|$ happens when $z_1$ and $z_2$ are on opposite sides along the same line through the centres. Then the farthest distance is $$ \left|z_1-z_2\right|= r+(OC+5)=r+10 $$ Substituting $r=12$, $$ \left|z_1-z_2\right|=12+10=22 $$

questions.text: If the system of equations $x + 5y + 6z = 4$ $2x + 3y + 4z = 7$ $x + 6y + az = b$ has infinitely many solutions, then the point $(a, b)$ lies on the line
questions.solution: Step 1: The given system of equations is: $$x + 5y + 6z = 4$$ $$2x + 3y + 4z = 7$$ $$x + 6y + az = b$$ Find the determinant of the coefficient matrix ($\Delta$) The coefficient matrix is formed by the coefficients of $x$, $y$, and $z$. $$ \Delta = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 5 & 6 \ 2 & 3 & 4 \ 1 & 6 & a \end{vmatrix} $$ Let us expand this determinant along the first row: $$ \Delta = 1(3 \cdot a - 6 \cdot 4) - 5(2 \cdot a - 1 \cdot 4) + 6(2 \cdot 6 - 1 \cdot 3) $$ $$ \Delta = 1(3a - 24) - 5(2a - 4) + 6(12 - 3) $$ $$ \Delta = 3a - 24 - 10a + 20 + 6(9) $$ $$ \Delta = -7a - 4 + 54 $$ $$ \Delta = -7a + 50 $$ For the system to have infinitely many solutions, we equate $\Delta$ to $0$: $$ -7a + 50 = 0 \implies 7a = 50 \implies a = \frac{50}{7} $$ Find the determinant $\Delta_z$ To find $\Delta_z$, we replace the $z$-column (third column) with the constant terms from the right-hand side of the equations. $$ \Delta_z = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 5 & 4 \ 2 & 3 & 7 \ 1 & 6 & b \end{vmatrix} $$ We again expand along the first row: $$ \Delta_z = 1(3 \cdot b - 6 \cdot 7) - 5(2 \cdot b - 1 \cdot 7) + 4(2 \cdot 6 - 1 \cdot 3) $$ $$ \Delta_z = 1(3b - 42) - 5(2b - 7) + 4(12 - 3) $$ $$ \Delta_z = 3b - 42 - 10b + 35 + 4(9) $$ $$ \Delta_z = -7b - 7 + 36 $$ $$ \Delta_z = -7b + 29 $$ Equating $\Delta_z$ to zero for infinitely many solutions, we get: $$ -7b + 29 = 0 \implies 7b = 29 \implies b = \frac{29}{7} $$ Check the options for the point $(a, b)$ We have obtained the point coordinates as $(a, b) = \left( \frac{50}{7}, \frac{29}{7} \right)$. Let us evaluate the difference $a - b$ to find out which linear profile equation matches our outcome: $$ a - b = \frac{50}{7} - \frac{29}{7} $$ $$ a - b = \frac{50 - 29}{7} $$ $$ a - b = \frac{21}{7} = 3 $$ Writing this relation in terms of $x$ and $y$ (where $x = a$ and $y = b$), it perfectly satisfies the line equation: $$ x - y = 3 $$ Thus, the point $(a, b)$ lies on the line given in Option B.

questions.text: Let $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$ be an A.P. and $g_1 = a_1, g_2, g_3, \ldots$ be an increasing G.P. If $a_1 = a_2 + g_2 = 1$ and $a_3 + g_3 = 4$, then $a_{10} + g_5$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: Let the common difference of the given A.P. be $d$ and the common ratio of the given G.P. be $r$. From the general formulas for the $n$-th term of an A.P. and a G.P., we know: $$a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)d$$ $$g_n = g_1 r^{n - 1}$$ We are given that $g_1 = a_1$ and $a_1 = 1$. Thus, the first term of both the A.P. and the G.P. is $1$. So, $g_1 = 1$. Next, we are given the first relationship: $$a_2 + g_2 = 1$$ Using our formulas, we can write the second terms as $a_2 = 1 + d$ and $g_2 = 1 \cdot r = r$. Let us substitute these values into the given equation: $$(1 + d) + r = 1$$ Subtracting $1$ from both sides, we establish a relationship between $d$ and $r$: $$d + r = 0 \implies d = -r$$ We are also given a second relationship: $$a_3 + g_3 = 4$$ Again, applying the $n$-th term formulas, we have the third terms as $a_3 = 1 + 2d$ and $g_3 = 1 \cdot r^2 = r^2$. Substituting these in the equation gives: $$(1 + 2d) + r^2 = 4$$ Now, let us substitute $d = -r$ into this equation to form a quadratic equation in terms of $r$: $$1 + 2(-r) + r^2 = 4$$ $$r^2 - 2r + 1 - 4 = 0$$ $$r^2 - 2r - 3 = 0$$ Let us factorize this quadratic equation by splitting the middle term: $$r^2 - 3r + r - 3 = 0$$ $$r(r - 3) + 1(r - 3) = 0$$ $$(r - 3)(r + 1) = 0$$ This gives us two possible values for $r$: $r = 3$ or $r = -1$. The problem clearly states that the G.P. is an increasing sequence. Since the first term $g_1 = 1$ is positive, an increasing sequence requires the common ratio to be strictly greater than $1$. Therefore, we reject $r = -1$ and take the valid value: $$r = 3$$ Since $d = -r$, we find the common difference of the A.P.: $$d = -3$$ Now, we are asked to find the value of $a_{10} + g_5$. Let us find $a_{10}$ and $g_5$ individually. For the 10th term of the A.P.: $$a_{10} = a_1 + (10 - 1)d$$ $$a_{10} = a_1 + 9d$$ $$a_{10} = 1 + 9(-3)$$ $$a_{10} = 1 - 27 = -26$$ For the 5th term of the G.P.: $$g_5 = g_1 r^{5 - 1}$$ $$g_5 = g_1 r^4$$ $$g_5 = 1 \cdot (3)^4$$ $$g_5 = 81$$ Finally, adding these two values together: $$a_{10} + g_5 = -26 + 81 = 55$$ Therefore, the value of $a_{10} + g_5$ is $55$. Correct Answer: Option D: $55$

questions.text: If for $3 \leq r \leq 30$, $\left({^{30}C_{30-r}}\right) + 3\left({^{30}C_{31-r}}\right) + 3\left({^{30}C_{32-r}}\right) + \left({^{30}C_{33-r}}\right) = {^mC_r}$, then m equals:
questions.solution: Step 1: Given $$ {^{30}C_{30-r}} + 3{^{30}C_{31-r}} + 3{^{30}C_{32-r}} + {^{30}C_{33-r}} = {^mC_r} $$ for $3 \le r \le 30$. We have to find $m$. First, use the symmetry property of combinations: $$ {^nC_k} = {^nC_{n-k}} $$ So, $$ {^{30}C_{30-r}} = {^{30}C_r} $$ $$ {^{30}C_{31-r}} = {^{30}C_{r-1}} $$ because $$ 30-(31-r)=r-1 $$ Similarly, $$ {^{30}C_{32-r}} = {^{30}C_{r-2}} $$ and $$ {^{30}C_{33-r}} = {^{30}C_{r-3}} $$ Therefore the left-hand side becomes $$ {^{30}C_r} + 3{^{30}C_{r-1}} + 3{^{30}C_{r-2}} + {^{30}C_{r-3}} $$ Now notice the coefficients: $$ 1,\ 3,\ 3,\ 1 $$ These are the binomial coefficients in the expansion of $$ (1+x)^3 $$ Also, by Vandermonde’s identity, $$ {^{30}C_r} + 3{^{30}C_{r-1}} + 3{^{30}C_{r-2}} + {^{30}C_{r-3}} = {^{33}C_r} $$ Let us see this through binomial expansion: Coefficient of $x^r$ in $(1+x)^{33}$ is $$ {^{33}C_r} $$ But $$ (1+x)^{33} = (1+x)^{30}(1+x)^3 $$ and $$ (1+x)^3 = 1 + 3x + 3x^2 + x^3 $$ So coefficient of $x^r$ in $(1+x)^{30}(1+3x+3x^2+x^3)$ is $$ {^{30}C_r} + 3{^{30}C_{r-1}} + 3{^{30}C_{r-2}} + {^{30}C_{r-3}} $$ Hence, $$ {^{30}C_r} + 3{^{30}C_{r-1}} + 3{^{30}C_{r-2}} + {^{30}C_{r-3}} = {^{33}C_r} $$ Comparing with $$ {^mC_r} $$ we get $$ m = 33 $$ The correct answer is: $$ \boxed{33} $$ So, Option C.

questions.text: Let $p_n$ denote the total number of triangles formed by joining the vertices of an $n$-side regular polygon. If $p_{n+1} - p_n = 66$, then the sum of all distinct prime divisors of $n$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$P_n = {}^nC_3$$ In an $n$-sided polygon, any $3$ vertices form a triangle, so the total number of triangles is $P_n = {}^nC_3$. $$P_{n+1} - P_n = 66$$ This means when we increase the number of sides from $n$ to $n+1$, the number of triangles increases by $66$. $${}^{n+1}C_3 - {}^nC_3 = 66$$ Now we write both combinations using the formula ${}^nC_3 = \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6}$. $$\Rightarrow \frac{(n+1)n(n-1)}{6} - \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6} = 66$$ Take the common factor $\frac{n(n-1)}{6}$ from both terms. $$\Rightarrow \frac{n(n-1)}{6}[n+1-n+2] = 66$$ Inside the bracket, simplify: $n+1-n+2 = 3$. $$\Rightarrow n(n-1) = 132$$ So we need two consecutive integers whose product is $132$. That gives $n=12$ because $12 \cdot 11 = 132$. $$n = 12$$Prime divisors of 12 are 2, 3 The distinct prime divisors of$12$ are $2$ and $3$. Sum $= 2 + 3 = 5$

questions.text: A man throws a fair coin repeatedly. He gets 10 points for each head he throws and 5 points for each tail he throws. If the probability that he gets exactly 30 points is $\frac{m}{n}$, gcd $(m, n) = 1$, then m + n is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}=(6 \text { tail })+(4 \text { tail }+1 \text { head })+(2 \text { tail }+2 \text { head })+(3 \text { head }) \ & \mathrm{P}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^6+\frac{5!}{1!4!}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^5+\frac{4!}{2!2!}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^4+\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3 \ & \mathrm{P}=\frac{1}{64}+\frac{5}{32}+\frac{3}{8}+\frac{1}{8} \ & \mathrm{P}=\frac{1+10+24+8}{64}=\frac{43}{64}=\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{n}} \ & \mathrm{m}+\mathrm{n}=107\end{aligned}$

questions.text: The mean and variance of n observations are 8 and 16, respectively. If the sum of the first (n − 1) observations is 48 and the sum of squares of the first (n − 1) observations is 496, then the value of n is:
questions.solution: Step 1: The sum of all $n$ observations is $8n$, so the last observation is $x_n=8n-48$. Variance 16 gives $\dfrac{\sum x_i^2}{n}-8^2=16$, so $\sum x_i^2=80n$ and $x_n^2=80n-496$. Equating the two expressions for $x_n$: $$(8n-48)^2=80n-496 \Rightarrow 64(n-6)^2=8(10n-62) \Rightarrow 4(n^2-12n+36)=5n-31$$ $$4n^2-53n+175=0 \Rightarrow (n-7)(4n-25)=0$$ The number of observations is a positive integer, so $n=7$ (then $x_7=8$ and $8^2=64=80\times 7-496$). Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Let a circle pass through the origin and its centre be the point of intersection of two mutually perpendicular lines $x + (k-1)y + 3 = 0$ and $2x + k^2y - 4 = 0$. If the line $x - y + 2 = 0$ intersects the circle at the points A and B, then $(AB)^2$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \begin{aligned} & x+(k-1) y+3=0 \ & 2 x+k^2 y-4=0 \ & \left(\frac{1}{1-k}\right)\left(\frac{2}{k^2}\right)=1 \ & 2=k^2-k^3 \ & k^3-k^2+2=0 \ & k=-1 \end{aligned} $$ Solving: $$ \begin{aligned} & 2(x-2 y+3)=0 \ & 2 x+y-4=0 \ & -5 y+10=0 \ & y=2 \end{aligned} $$ $$ x=1 $$ Centre $(1,2)$ $$ r=\sqrt{5} $$ So circle is $(x-1)^2+(y-2)^2=5$ Chord $\mathrm{x}-\mathrm{y}+2=0$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{p}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \ & \ell=\sqrt{5-\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \ & \mathrm{AB}=\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}} \quad \therefore \mathrm{AB}^2=18 \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: Let O be the origin, and P and Q be two points on the rectangular hyperbola $xy = 12$ such that the midpoint of the line segment PQ is $\left( \frac{1}{2}, -\frac{1}{2} \right)$. Then the area of the triangle OPQ equals:
questions.solution: Step 1: Let $$ P(x_1,y_1), \qquad Q(x_2,y_2) $$ be two points on the rectangular hyperbola $$ xy=12 $$ So, both points satisfy $$ x_1y_1=12 \quad \text{and} \quad x_2y_2=12 $$ Also, the midpoint of $PQ$ is given as $$ \left(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}\right) $$ Using the midpoint formula, $$ \frac{x_1+x_2}{2}=\frac{1}{2}, \qquad \frac{y_1+y_2}{2}=-\frac{1}{2} $$ Hence, $$ x_1+x_2=1, \qquad y_1+y_2=-1 $$ Now we need the area of triangle $OPQ$, where $O=(0,0)$. The area of triangle formed by points $O(0,0)$, $P(x_1,y_1)$, $Q(x_2,y_2)$ is $$ \text{Area}=\frac{1}{2}\left|x_1y_2-x_2y_1\right| $$ So our aim is to find $\left|x_1y_2-x_2y_1\right|$. Since $x_1$ and $x_2$ are the $x$-coordinates of points on the hyperbola, and their sum is $1$, let us use $$ y_1=\frac{12}{x_1}, \qquad y_2=\frac{12}{x_2} $$ Now using $$ y_1+y_2=-1 $$ we get $$ \frac{12}{x_1}+\frac{12}{x_2}=-1 $$ $$ 12\left(\frac{x_1+x_2}{x_1x_2}\right)=-1 $$ Since $x_1+x_2=1$, $$ 12\left(\frac{1}{x_1x_2}\right)=-1 $$ So, $$ x_1x_2=-12 $$ Thus $x_1$ and $x_2$ are roots of the quadratic equation $$ t^2-(x_1+x_2)t+x_1x_2=0 $$ $$ t^2-t-12=0 $$ $$ (t-4)(t+3)=0 $$ Hence, $$ x_1=4,\quad x_2=-3 $$ or vice versa. Then corresponding $y$-coordinates are $$ y_1=\frac{12}{4}=3, \qquad y_2=\frac{12}{-3}=-4 $$ So the points are $$ P(4,3), \qquad Q(-3,-4) $$ Now area of triangle $OPQ$ is $$ \text{Area}=\frac{1}{2}\left|4(-4)-(-3)(3)\right| $$ $$ =\frac{1}{2}\left|-16+9\right| $$ $$ =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 7 $$ $$ =\frac{7}{2} $$ Therefore, the required area is $$ \boxed{\frac{7}{2}} $$ So, the correct option is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option C}} $$

questions.text: Let the parabola $y = x^2 + px + q$ passing through the point $(1, -1)$ be such that the distance between its vertex and the $x$-axis is minimum. Then the value of $p^2 + q^2$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: parabola passes through $(1,-1)$ so $$-1 = 1 + p + q$$ $$p + q = -2$$ $$q = -2 - p \,\,\,\ldots (1)$$ Distance from x-axis $$\frac{-D}{4a} = \frac{-(p^2 - 4q)}{4(1)} = \frac{4q - p^2}{4}$$ $$= \frac{4(-2-p)-p^2}{4} \qquad \text{from (1)}$$ $$= \frac{-8-4p-p^2}{4} = \frac{-(p^2+4p+8)}{4} = \frac{-((p+2)^2+4)}{4}$$ Minimum at $p=-2 \rightarrow q=0$ $$p^2 + q^2 = 4 + 0 = 4$$

questions.text: Let $P = \{ \theta \in [0, 4\pi]: \tan^2 \theta \neq 1 \}$ and $S = \{ a \in \mathbb{Z}: 2(\cos^8 \theta - \sin^8 \theta) \sec 2 \theta = a^2, \theta \in P \}$. Then $n(S)$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: $\begin{aligned} & 2\left(\cos ^8 \theta-\sin ^8 \theta\right) \sec 2 \theta=\mathrm{a}^2 \ & 2\left(\cos ^4 \theta+\sin ^4 \theta\right)\left(\cos ^2 \theta+\sin ^2 \theta\right)\left(\cos ^2 \theta-\sin ^2 \theta\right) \sec 2 \theta=\mathrm{a}^2 \ & 2\left(\cos ^4 \theta+\sin ^4 \theta\right)=\mathrm{a}^2 \ & 2\left(1-2 \sin ^2 \theta \cos ^2 \theta\right)=\mathrm{a}^2 \ & 2\left(1-\frac{\sin ^2 2 \theta}{2}\right)=\mathrm{a}^2, \mathrm{a} \in \mathrm{Z} \ & \mathrm{a}^2=2-\sin ^2 2 \theta \in[1,2] \ & \mathrm{a}^2=1 \text { at } \sin ^2 2 \theta=1 \ & 2 \theta=(2 \mathrm{n}+1) \frac{\pi}{2} \ & \theta=(2 \mathrm{n}+1) \frac{\pi}{4} \notin \mathrm{P} \ & \mathrm{n}(\mathrm{S})=0\end{aligned}$

questions.text: Let the vectors $\vec{a} = -\hat{i} + \hat{j} + 3\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b} = \hat{i} + 3\hat{j} + \hat{k}$. For some $\lambda, \mu \in \mathbb{R}$, let $\vec{c} = \lambda \vec{a} + \mu \vec{b}$. If $\vec{c} \cdot (3\hat{i} - 6\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}) = 10$ and $\vec{c} \cdot (\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}) = -2$, then $|\vec{c}|^2$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$\vec{c}=\lambda \vec{a}+\mu \vec{b}$$ $$\vec{c}=(\mu-\lambda)\hat{i}+(\lambda+3\mu)\hat{j}+(3\lambda+\mu)\hat{k}$$ $$\vec{c}\cdot(3\hat{i}-6\hat{j}+2\hat{k})=10$$ $$3(\mu-\lambda)-6(\lambda+3\mu)+2(3\lambda+\mu)=10$$ $$-3\lambda-13\mu=10 \qquad \ldots (1)$$ $$\vec{c}\cdot(\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k})=-2$$ $$5\mu+3\lambda=-2 \qquad \ldots (2)$$Solving (1), (2)$$\lambda=1,\ \mu=-1$$ $$\vec{c}=-2\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$$ $$|\vec{c}|^2=12$$

questions.text: Let the point A be the foot of perpendicular drawn from the point P$(a, b, 0)$ on the line $\frac{x-1}{2} = \frac{y-2}{1} = \frac{z-\alpha}{3}.$ If the midpoint of the line segment PA is $\left(0, \frac{3}{4}, -\frac{1}{4}\right),$ then the value of $a^2 + b^2 + \alpha^2$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: Let the given line be written in parametric form by taking $$\frac{x-1}{2}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-\alpha}{3}=r.$$ Then a general point $A$ on the line is $$A(1+2r,\;2+r,\;\alpha+3r).$$ Given $P(a,b,0)$ and the midpoint of $PA$ is $\left(0,\frac{3}{4},-\frac{1}{4}\right)$. Using midpoint formula coordinate-wise: $$\begin{aligned} & \frac{2 r+1+a}{2}=0 \Rightarrow 2 r+a=-1 \\ & \frac{r+2+b}{2}=\frac{3}{4} \Rightarrow r+b=-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$ Similarly, from the $z$-coordinate of the midpoint: $$\begin{aligned} & \frac{3 r+\alpha}{2}=\frac{-1}{4} \Rightarrow 3 r+\alpha=\frac{-1}{2} \\ \end{aligned}$$ Now, $A$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the line, so $\overrightarrow{PA}$ is perpendicular to the direction vector of the line. The direction ratios of the line are $(2,1,3)$, so we use the dot product condition: $$2(x_A-a)+1(y_A-b)+3(z_A-0)=0.$$ Using the midpoint point $\left(0,\frac{3}{4},-\frac{1}{4}\right)$, we can write $\overrightarrow{PA}=2\left(\left(0,\frac{3}{4},-\frac{1}{4}\right)-P\right)$, so its components are proportional to $\left(-a,\frac{3}{4}-b,-\frac{1}{4}\right)$. Hence the perpendicularity condition becomes: $$\begin{aligned} & 2 \cdot a+1 \cdot(b-3 / 4)+3 \cdot \frac{1}{4}=0 \Rightarrow a+b=0 \\ \end{aligned}$$ From $2r+a=-1$, we get $a=-1-2r$. From $r+b=-\frac{1}{2}$, we get $b=-\frac{1}{2}-r$. Substitute in $a+b=0$: $$\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 2(-1-2 r)+(-r-1 / 2)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow-3 / 2=3 r=1 \Rightarrow r=-1 / 2, a=0, b=0, \alpha=1 \\ & \therefore a^2+b^2+\alpha^2=1\end{aligned}$$

questions.text: Two adjacent sides of a parallelogram PQRS are given by $\overrightarrow{PQ} = \hat{j} + \hat{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{PS} = \hat{i} - \hat{j}$. If the side PS is rotated about the point P by an acute angle $\alpha$ in the plane of the parallelogram so that it becomes perpendicular to the side PQ, then $\sin^2\left(\frac{5\alpha}{2}\right) - \sin^2\left(\frac{\alpha}{2}\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: Let angle between $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ & $\overrightarrow{PS}$ is $\theta$ $$\cos \theta = \frac{\overrightarrow{PQ}. \overrightarrow{PS}}{\left|\overrightarrow{PQ}\right|\left|\overrightarrow{PS}\right|}$$ $$\cos \theta = \frac{0-1+0}{\sqrt{2}\sqrt{2}}$$ $$\cos \theta = -\frac{1}{2}$$ $$\theta = \frac{2\pi}{3}$$ $$\alpha = \frac{2\pi}{3} - \frac{\pi}{2} \ \text{So} \ \alpha = \frac{\pi}{6}$$ $$\sin^2 \frac{5\alpha}{2} - \sin^2 \frac{\alpha}{2} = \sin\left(\frac{5\alpha}{2} + \frac{\alpha}{2}\right) \sin\left(\frac{5\alpha}{2} - \frac{\alpha}{2}\right)$$ $$= \sin \frac{6\alpha}{2} \times \sin \frac{4\alpha}{2}$$ $$= \sin 3\alpha \times \sin 2\alpha$$ $$= \sin \frac{\pi}{2} \times \sin \frac{\pi}{3}$$ $$= 1 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$

questions.text: The value of $\int\limits_{0}^{20\pi} (\sin^4 x + \cos^4 x) dx$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$I=\int\limits_{0}^{20\pi} \left(1-2\sin^2 x\cos^2 x\right)\cdot dx$$ $$=20\pi-\frac{1}{2}\int\limits_{0}^{20\pi} \sin^2 2x\,dx$$ $$= 20\pi-\frac{1}{2}(40)\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/2} \sin^2 2x$$ $$= 20\pi-\frac{20}{2}\left(x-\frac{\sin 2x}{2}\right)_{0}^{\pi/2}$$ $$= 20\pi-10\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=15\pi$$

questions.text: Let $f(x)$ be a polynomial of degree 5, and have extrema at $x = 1$ and $x = -1$. If $\lim\limits_{x \to 0} \left( \frac{f(x)}{x^3} \right) = -5$, then $f(2) - f(-2)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: Given $f(x)$ is a polynomial of degree $5$ Also, $f'(1)=0$; $f'(-1)=0$. Also $\because\ \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\dfrac{f(x)}{x^3}=-5$ (fixed and finite) $\therefore\ f(0)=0$; $f'(0)=0$; $f''(0)=0$ $$\dfrac{f'''(0)}{6}=-5 \rightarrow f'''(0)=-30$$ Hence, let $$f'(x)=(ax+b)(x-0)(x-1)(x+1)$$ $$\rightarrow f'(x)=ax^4+bx^3-ax^2-bx$$ $$f''(x)=4ax^3+3bx^2-2ax-b$$ $$\therefore\ f''(0)=0 \rightarrow b=0$$ $$f'''(x)=12ax^2+6bx-2a$$ $$\therefore\ f'''(0)=-2a=-30$$ $$\rightarrow a=15$$ $$\therefore\ f'(x)=15x.x.(x-1)(x+1)$$ $$\rightarrow f'(x)=15x^4-15x^2$$ $$\rightarrow f(x)=3x^5-5x^3+C$$ $$\therefore\ f(0)=0 \rightarrow C=0$$ $$\therefore\ f(x)=3x^5-5x^3$$ $$\therefore\ f(2)-f(-2)=112$$

questions.text: Let $f(x) = \int \left( \frac{16x + 24}{x^2 + 2x - 15} \right) dx$. If $f(4) = 14 \log_e(3)$ and $f(7) = \log_e(2^\alpha \cdot 3^\beta)$, $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{N}$, then $\alpha + \beta$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $f(x)=\int \frac{8(2 x+2)+8}{x^2+2 x-15} d x$ $$\Rightarrow f(x)=8\ell n\left|x^2+2x-15\right|+\ell n\left|\frac{x-3}{x+5}\right|+C$$ $$\Rightarrow f(4)=14\ell n3+C$$ $$\Rightarrow 14\ell n3=14\ell n3+C$$ $$\therefore C=0$$ Now, $$f(7)=8\ell n48-\ell n3$$ $$=\ell n\left(\frac{(48)^8}{3}\right)$$ $$\Rightarrow f(7)=\ell n(2^{32}\times 3^7)$$ $$\alpha=32,\ \beta=7\ \Rightarrow\ \alpha+\beta=39$$

questions.text: Let $x = x(y)$ be the solution of the differential equation $2y^2 \frac{dx}{dy} - 2xy + x^2 = 0$, $y > 1$, $x(e) = e$. Then $x(e^2)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$2y(ydx-xdy)+x^2dy=0$$ $$\Rightarrow -2yx^2\,d\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+x^2dy=0$$ $$\Rightarrow -2y\,d\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+dy=0$$ $$\Rightarrow -2d\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+\frac{1}{y}dy=0$$ $$\Rightarrow -\frac{2y}{x}+\log_e y=C$$ Given $x(e)=e$ $$\Rightarrow C=-1$$ $$\therefore -\frac{2y}{x}+\log_e y=-1$$ $$\Rightarrow \frac{2y}{x}-\log_e y=1$$ Put $y=e^2$, we get $$\Rightarrow \frac{2e^2}{x}-2=1 \rightarrow \frac{2e^2}{x}=3 \rightarrow x=\frac{2e^2}{3}$$ $$\Rightarrow x(e^2)=\frac{2e^2}{3}$$

questions.text: Dimensions of universal gravitational constant ($G$) in terms of Planck's constant ($h$), distance ($L$), mass ($M$) and time ($T$) are _______.
questions.solution: Step 1: To find the dimensions of the universal gravitational constant G in terms of Planck's constant h, length L, mass M, and time T, we must first determine the base dimensions of both G and h in the standard MLT system. According to Newton's law of universal gravitation, the force F between two masses $\mathrm{m}_1$ and $\mathrm{m}_2$ separated by a distance $r$ is given by: $$ \mathrm{F}=\frac{\mathrm{Gm}_1 \mathrm{~m}_2}{\mathrm{r}^2} $$ $$ \Rightarrow \mathrm{G}=\frac{\mathrm{Fr}^2}{\mathrm{~m}_1 \mathrm{~m}_2} $$ Substituting the dimensions $\left[M L T^{-2}\right]$ for force, $[L]$ for distance $(r)$, and mass( $m$ ) as $[M]$: $$ [\mathrm{G}]=\frac{\left[\mathrm{MLT}^{-2}\right]\left[\mathrm{L}^2\right]}{[\mathrm{M}][\mathrm{M}]}=\left[\mathrm{M}^{-1} \mathrm{~L}^3 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right] $$ Planck's constant relates the energy $E$ of a photon to its frequency $v$ via the equation: $$ \mathrm{E}=\mathrm{h} \nu $$ Since frequency $v$ has dimensions of inverse time [ $\mathrm{T}^{-1}$ ], and energy E (work done) has dimensions $\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]$, we have: $$ [\mathrm{h}]=\frac{[\mathrm{E}]}{[\mathrm{v}]}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{T}^{-1}\right]}=\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-1}\right] $$ Let assume the relationship is of the form $\mathrm{G}=\mathrm{h}^{\mathrm{a}} \mathrm{L}^{\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{M}^{\mathrm{c}} \mathrm{T}^{\mathrm{d}}$. Comparing the dimensions: $$ \left[\mathrm{M}^{-1} \mathrm{~L}^3 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]=\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-1}\right]^{\mathrm{a}}[\mathrm{~L}]^{\mathrm{b}}[\mathrm{M}]^{\mathrm{c}}[\mathrm{~T}]^{\mathrm{d}} $$ $$ \left[\mathrm{M}^{-1} \mathrm{~L}^3 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]=\left[\mathrm{M}^{\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{c}} \mathrm{~L}^{2 \mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b}} \mathrm{~T}^{-\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{d}}\right] $$ By equating the exponents of $\mathrm{M}, \mathrm{L}$, and T from both sides, we get a system of equations: For $\mathrm{M}: \mathrm{a}+\mathrm{c}=-1 \ldots$ (i) For $\mathrm{L}: 2 \mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b}=3 \ldots$ (ii) For $\mathrm{T}:-\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{d}=-2 \ldots$ (iii) Looking at the provided options, we see that h is with a power of $1, \mathrm{a}=1$ Let's $\mathrm{a}=1$: From eq (i): $1+\mathrm{c}=-1 \Rightarrow \mathrm{c}=-2$ From eq (ii): $2(1)+b=3 \Rightarrow b=1$ From eq (iii): $-1+\mathrm{d}=-2 \Rightarrow \mathrm{~d}=-1$ Substituting these values, we get $G \propto h^1 L^1 M^{-2} T^{-1}$. This corresponds to the dimensional formula $\left[\mathrm{hT}^{-1} \mathrm{LM}^{-2}\right]$. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: A 0.5 kg mass is in contact against the inner wall of a cylindrical drum of radius 4 m rotating about its vertical axis. The minimum rotational speed of the drum to enable the mass to remain stuck to the wall (without falling) is 5 rad/s. The coefficient of friction between the drum’s inner wall surface and mass is _________. (Take $g = 10\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$)
questions.solution: Step 1: In the frame of the drum the mass is at rest under four forces: the normal force $N$ from the wall towards the axis, the centrifugal force $m\omega^2 r$ away from the axis, the weight $mg$ downwards and static friction $f_s$ upwards. Radial balance gives $N = m\omega^2 r$; vertical balance gives $f_s = mg$, with $f_s \le \mu N$. At the minimum angular speed, friction is limiting: $$\mu m\omega^2 r = mg \Rightarrow \mu = \dfrac{g}{\omega^2 r} = \dfrac{10}{5^2 \times 4} = 0.1$$ Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: Two blocks of masses 2 kg and 1 kg respectively, are tied to the ends of a string which passes over a light frictionless pulley as shown in the figure below. The masses are held at rest at the same horizontal level and then released. The distance traversed by the centre of mass in 2 s is _______ m. (Take $g = 10 \; m/s^2$)
questions.solution: Step 1: Let $\mathrm{m}_1=2 \mathrm{~kg}$ and $\mathrm{m}_2=1 \mathrm{~kg}$. When released, the heavier mass moves downward and the lighter mass moves upward with the same magnitude of acceleration a. As the string connecting two blocks is massless, so tension throughout will be same, T. For block $\mathrm{m}_1$, using Newton's $2^{\text {nd }}$ law of motion; $$ \mathrm{m}_1 \mathrm{~g}-\mathrm{T}=\mathrm{m}_1 \mathrm{a} \ldots(\mathrm{i}) $$ For block $\mathrm{m}_2$, using Newton's $2^{\text {nd }}$ law of motion; $$ \mathrm{T}-\mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{~g}=\mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{a}...(ii)$$ Adding both the equations, $$ \left(m_1-m_2\right) g=\left(m_1+m_2\right) a $$ $$ a=\left(\frac{m_1-m_2}{m_1+m_2}\right) g $$ Substituting the given values $\left(\mathrm{g}=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right)$: $$ \mathrm{a}=\left(\frac{2-1}{2+1}\right) \times 10=\frac{1}{3} \times 10=\frac{10}{3} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2 $$ The acceleration of the centre of mass for a two-body system is defined as: $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{\mathrm{m}_1 \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_1+\mathrm{m}_2 \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_2}{\mathrm{~m}_1+\mathrm{m}_2} $$ Taking the downward direction as positive: $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_1=\mathrm{a}$ (downward) $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_2=-\mathrm{a}$ (upward) $$ \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{\mathrm{m}_1(\mathrm{a})+\mathrm{m}_2(-\mathrm{a})}{\mathrm{m}_1+\mathrm{m}_2}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{m}_1-\mathrm{m}_2}{\mathrm{~m}_1+\mathrm{m}_2}\right) \mathrm{a} $$ Substituting the value of a: $$ \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{cm}}=\left(\frac{2-1}{2+1}\right) \times \frac{10}{3}=\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{10}{3}=\frac{10}{9} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2 $$ The system starts from rest ( $\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{cm}}=0$ ). The distance traversed in time $\mathrm{t}=2 \mathrm{~s}$ is given by the kinematic equation: $$ \mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{cm}}=\mathrm{u}_{\mathrm{cm}} \mathrm{t}+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{cm}} \mathrm{t}^2 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{cm}}=0+\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{10}{9}\right)(2)^2$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{cm}}=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{10}{9} \times 4=\frac{20}{9} \approx 2.22 \mathrm{~m}$ Therefore, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: A particle having charge $10^{-9}$ C moving in $x$-$y$ plane in fields of $0.4 \hat{j}$ N/C and $4 \times 10^{-3} \hat{k}$ T experiences a force of $(4 \hat{i} + 2 \hat{j}) \times 10^{-10}$ N. The velocity of the particle at that instant is _________ m/s.
questions.solution:
Step 1: The force on the charge is $\vec F = q\left(\vec E + \vec v \times \vec B\right)$ with $q = 10^{-9}\ \text{C}$, $\vec E = 0.4\,\hat j\ \text{N C}^{-1}$, $\vec B = 4 \times 10^{-3}\,\hat k\ \text{T}$ and, for motion in the $x$-$y$ plane, $\vec v = v_x\hat i + v_y\hat j$. Using $\hat i \times \hat k = -\hat j$ and $\hat j \times \hat k = \hat i$: $$\vec v \times \vec B = 4 \times 10^{-3}\,v_y\,\hat i - 4 \times 10^{-3}\,v_x\,\hat j$$ Dividing the force by $q$: $$\dfrac{\vec F}{q} = \dfrac{(4\hat i + 2\hat j) \times 10^{-10}}{10^{-9}} = 0.4\,\hat i + 0.2\,\hat j$$ Equating with $\vec E + \vec v \times \vec B$: $$0.4\,\hat i + 0.2\,\hat j = 4 \times 10^{-3}\,v_y\,\hat i + \left(0.4 - 4 \times 10^{-3}\,v_x\right)\hat j$$ Along $\hat i$: $4 \times 10^{-3}\,v_y = 0.4 \Rightarrow v_y = 100\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Along $\hat j$: $0.4 - 4 \times 10^{-3}\,v_x = 0.2 \Rightarrow v_x = 50\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: So $\vec v = \left(50\,\hat i + 100\,\hat j\right)\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Hence, the correct option is (A).
