questions.text: $\max\limits_{0 \leq x \leq \pi}\left(16 \sin \left(\frac{x}{2}\right) \cos ^3\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$E = 16\sin\frac{x}{2}\cos^3\frac{x}{2}$$ $$E = 4\sin x\,[1 + \cos x]$$ $$\frac{dE}{dx} = 4[\cos x + \cos 2x]$$ $$= 8\cos\frac{3x}{2}\cos\frac{x}{2} = 0$$ $$\Rightarrow \cos\frac{3x}{2} = 0 \quad \text{or} \quad \cos\frac{x}{2} = 0$$ $$\Rightarrow x = \left\{\frac{\pi}{3}, \pi\right\} \text{ are critical points of the function}$$ $$E(0) = 0$$ $$E(\pi) = 0$$ $$E\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = 3\sqrt{3}$$ $\therefore$ maximum value of $E = 3\sqrt{3}$

questions.text:
The shortest distance between the lines
$ \vec{r}=\left(\frac{1}{3} \hat{\mathrm{i}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+\frac{8}{3} \hat{\mathrm{k}}\right)+\lambda(2 \hat{\mathrm{i}}-5 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+6 \hat{\mathrm{k}}) $
and $\vec{r}=\left(-\frac{2}{3} \hat{\mathrm{i}}-\frac{1}{3} \hat{\mathrm{k}}\right)+\mu(\hat{\mathrm{j}}-\hat{\mathrm{k}}), \lambda, \mu \in \mathbb{R}$, is:
questions.solution: Step 1: For two skew lines, $$ \vec r=\vec a_1+\lambda \vec b_1 \quad \text{and} \quad \vec r=\vec a_2+\mu \vec b_2, $$ the shortest distance is $$ d=\frac{|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot (\vec b_1\times \vec b_2)|}{|\vec b_1\times \vec b_2|}. $$ Now compare with the given lines. First line: $$ \vec r=\left(\frac13 \hat i+2\hat j+\frac83 \hat k\right)+\lambda(2\hat i-5\hat j+6\hat k) $$ So, $$ \vec a_1=\left(\frac13,2,\frac83\right), \qquad \vec b_1=(2,-5,6) $$ Second line: $$ \vec r=\left(-\frac23 \hat i-\frac13 \hat k\right)+\mu(\hat j-\hat k) $$ So, $$ \vec a_2=\left(-\frac23,0,-\frac13\right), \qquad \vec b_2=(0,1,-1) $$ Now find $$ \vec a_2-\vec a_1 =\left(-\frac23-\frac13,\;0-2,\;-\frac13-\frac83\right) =(-1,-2,-3) $$ Next, calculate $\vec b_1\times \vec b_2$: $$ \vec b_1\times \vec b_2 = \begin{vmatrix} \hat i & \hat j & \hat k\ 2 & -5 & 6\ 0 & 1 & -1 \end{vmatrix} $$ $$ = \hat i\big[(-5)(-1)-6(1)\big] -\hat j\big[2(-1)-6(0)\big] +\hat k\big[2(1)-(-5)(0)\big] $$ $$ = \hat i(5-6)-\hat j(-2)+\hat k(2) = -\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k $$ So, $$ \vec b_1\times \vec b_2=(-1,2,2) $$ Its magnitude is $$ |\vec b_1\times \vec b_2| =\sqrt{(-1)^2+2^2+2^2} =\sqrt{1+4+4} =3 $$ Now find the scalar triple product: $$ (\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot (\vec b_1\times \vec b_2) =(-1,-2,-3)\cdot(-1,2,2) $$ $$ = (-1)(-1)+(-2)(2)+(-3)(2) =1-4-6 =-9 $$ Therefore, $$ d=\frac{|-9|}{3}=3 $$ Hence, the shortest distance is $$ \boxed{3} $$ So, the correct option is Option B.

questions.text: If $\left(2 \alpha+1, \alpha^2-3 \alpha, \frac{\alpha-1}{2}\right)$ is the image of $(\alpha, 2 \alpha, 1)$ in the line $\frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z}{1}$, then the possible value(s) of $\alpha$ is (are)
questions.solution: Step 1: $\therefore \mathrm{P}$ is mid point of AB and lies on the given line $$ \Rightarrow \mathrm{P}\left(\frac{3 \alpha+1}{2}, \frac{\alpha^2-\alpha}{2}, \frac{\alpha+1}{4}\right) $$ Now put coordinates of P in the line $$ \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \frac{\frac{3 \alpha+1}{2}-2}{3}=\frac{\frac{\alpha^2-\alpha}{2}-1}{2}=\frac{\alpha+1}{4} \ & \Rightarrow \frac{\alpha-1}{2}=\frac{\alpha+1}{4}=\frac{\alpha^2-\alpha-2}{4} \ & \Rightarrow \alpha=3 \end{aligned} $$ Now for $\alpha=3$, clearly AB is perpendicular to $3 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+\mathrm{k}$ for $\alpha=3$ point B is image of point A

questions.text: Let $\hat{u}$ and $\hat{v}$ be unit vectors inclined at an acute angle such that $|\hat{u} \times \hat{v}|=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. If $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}}=\lambda \hat{u}+\hat{v}+(\hat{u} \times \hat{v})$, then $\lambda$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: Since $\hat{u}$ and $\hat{v}$ are unit vectors, $$ |\hat{u}\times \hat{v}|=|\hat{u}||\hat{v}|\sin\theta=\sin\theta $$ Given $$ |\hat{u}\times \hat{v}|=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} $$ So, $$ \sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} $$ The angle is acute, hence $$ \theta=60^\circ \quad \Rightarrow \quad \hat{u}\cdot \hat{v}=\cos 60^\circ=\frac{1}{2} $$ Now, $$ \vec A=\lambda \hat{u}+\hat{v}+(\hat{u}\times \hat{v}) $$ We take dot product with $\hat{u}$: $$ \vec A\cdot \hat{u} = \lambda (\hat{u}\cdot \hat{u})+(\hat{v}\cdot \hat{u})+(\hat{u}\times \hat{v})\cdot \hat{u} $$ Now, $$ \hat{u}\cdot \hat{u}=1,\qquad \hat{v}\cdot \hat{u}=\frac{1}{2},\qquad (\hat{u}\times \hat{v})\cdot \hat{u}=0 $$ Therefore, $$ \vec A\cdot \hat{u}=\lambda+\frac{1}{2} $$ So, $$ \lambda=\vec A\cdot \hat{u}-\frac{1}{2} \qquad \text{(1)} $$ Now take dot product with $\hat{v}$: $$ \vec A\cdot \hat{v} = \lambda (\hat{u}\cdot \hat{v})+(\hat{v}\cdot \hat{v})+(\hat{u}\times \hat{v})\cdot \hat{v} $$ Using $$ \hat{u}\cdot \hat{v}=\frac{1}{2},\qquad \hat{v}\cdot \hat{v}=1,\qquad (\hat{u}\times \hat{v})\cdot \hat{v}=0 $$ we get $$ \vec A\cdot \hat{v}=\frac{\lambda}{2}+1 $$ Hence, $$ \frac{\lambda}{2}=\vec A\cdot \hat{v}-1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \lambda=2(\vec A\cdot \hat{v})-2 \qquad \text{(2)} $$ Now let $$ x=\vec A\cdot \hat{u}, \qquad y=\vec A\cdot \hat{v} $$ Then from above, $$ x=\lambda+\frac{1}{2} \quad \text{and} \quad y=\frac{\lambda}{2}+1 $$ From the first, $$ \lambda=x-\frac{1}{2} $$ Also, $$ x-2y=\left(\lambda+\frac{1}{2}\right)-2\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}+1\right) =\lambda+\frac{1}{2}-\lambda-2=-\frac{3}{2} $$ So we form $\lambda$ as a linear combination of $x$ and $y$. Check Option A: $$ \frac{4}{3}x-\frac{2}{3}y = \frac{4}{3}\left(\lambda+\frac{1}{2}\right)-\frac{2}{3}\left(\frac{\lambda}{2}+1\right) $$ $$ = \frac{4\lambda}{3}+\frac{2}{3}-\frac{\lambda}{3}-\frac{2}{3} = \lambda $$ Hence, $$ \lambda=\frac{4}{3}(\vec A\cdot \hat{u})-\frac{2}{3}(\vec A\cdot \hat{v}) $$ So the correct option is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option A}} $$
questions.topic: Scalar or Dot Product of Two Vectors and Its Applications

questions.text: Let for some $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}, f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a function satisfying $f(x+y)=f(x)+2 y^2+y+\alpha x y$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$. If $f(0)=-1$ and $f(1)=2$, then the value of $\sum\limits_{n=1}^5(\alpha+f(n))$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Given $$ f(x+y)=f(x)+2y^2+y+\alpha xy \quad \text{for all } x,y\in \mathbb{R} $$ with $$ f(0)=-1,\qquad f(1)=2. $$ We have to find $$ \sum_{n=1}^5 (\alpha+f(n)). $$ Step 1: Use the given relation to find $\alpha$ Put $x=0$ in $$ f(x+y)=f(x)+2y^2+y+\alpha xy. $$ Then $$ f(y)=f(0)+2y^2+y+\alpha\cdot 0\cdot y $$ so $$ f(y)=-1+2y^2+y. $$ Thus, for every real $y$, $$ f(y)=2y^2+y-1. $$ Now use $f(1)=2$: $$ f(1)=2(1)^2+1-1=2. $$ This is already satisfied, so now we must use the original equation to determine $\alpha$. Substitute $$ f(x+y)=2(x+y)^2+(x+y)-1 $$ and $$ f(x)=2x^2+x-1 $$ into the given equation: $$ 2(x+y)^2+(x+y)-1 = 2x^2+x-1+2y^2+y+\alpha xy. $$ Expand the left side: $$ 2x^2+4xy+2y^2+x+y-1. $$ Right side is: $$ 2x^2+x-1+2y^2+y+\alpha xy. $$ Comparing both sides, $$ 4xy=\alpha xy. $$ Hence, $$ \alpha=4. $$ Step 2: Find $f(n)$ for $n=1$ to $5$ Since $$ f(n)=2n^2+n-1, $$ we get: $$ f(1)=2(1)^2+1-1=2 $$ $$ f(2)=2(2)^2+2-1=8+2-1=9 $$ $$ f(3)=2(3)^2+3-1=18+3-1=20 $$ $$ f(4)=2(4)^2+4-1=32+4-1=35 $$ $$ f(5)=2(5)^2+5-1=50+5-1=54 $$ Step 3: Compute the required sum We need $$ \sum_{n=1}^5 (\alpha+f(n)). $$ Since $\alpha=4$, $$ \alpha+f(1)=4+2=6 $$ $$ \alpha+f(2)=4+9=13 $$ $$ \alpha+f(3)=4+20=24 $$ $$ \alpha+f(4)=4+35=39 $$ $$ \alpha+f(5)=4+54=58 $$ Therefore, $$ 6+13+24+39+58=140. $$ So the required value is $$ \boxed{140}. $$ Hence, the correct option is B.

questions.text:
Let
$\mathrm{A}=\{(a, b, c): a, b, c$ are non-negative integers and $a+b+2 c=22\}$.
Then $n(\mathrm{~A})$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: We need to count the number of ordered triples $(a,b,c)$ of non-negative integers satisfying $$ a+b+2c=22 $$ Since $a,b,c \ge 0$, let us fix $c$ first. For a fixed value of $c$, the equation becomes $$ a+b=22-2c $$ Now, the number of non-negative integer solutions of $$ a+b=n $$ is $$ n+1 $$ So, for fixed $c$, number of solutions is $$ (22-2c)+1=23-2c $$ Now find all possible values of $c$. Since $2c \le 22$, $$ c=0,1,2,\dots,11 $$ Hence total number of solutions is $$ \sum_{c=0}^{11} (23-2c) $$ This is an arithmetic series: first term $=23$ last term $=23-2(11)=1$ number of terms $=12$ So, $$ n(A)=\frac{12}{2}(23+1) $$ $$ n(A)=6 \cdot 24=144 $$ Therefore, $$ n(A)=144 $$ So the correct option is: $$ \boxed{144} $$ Hence, $\boxed{\text{Option C}}$.

questions.text: The area of the region bounded by the curves $x+3 y^2=0$ and $x+4 y^2=1$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: Given curves are $$ x+3y^2=0 \quad \text{and} \quad x+4y^2=1 $$ First, write them in the form $x=$: $$ x=-3y^2 $$ and $$ x=1-4y^2 $$ To find the bounded area, we first find their points of intersection. Set the two values of $x$ equal: $$ -3y^2=1-4y^2 $$ $$ y^2=1 $$ $$ y=\pm 1 $$ So the curves intersect at $y=-1$ and $y=1$. Now, for a fixed value of $y$, the right curve is $$ x=1-4y^2 $$ and the left curve is $$ x=-3y^2 $$ So the horizontal width of the region is $$ (1-4y^2)-(-3y^2)=1-y^2 $$ Hence, area of the enclosed region is $$ A=\int_{-1}^{1}(1-y^2)\,dy $$ Now evaluate: $$ A=\left[y-\frac{y^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{1} $$ $$ A=\left(1-\frac{1}{3}\right)-\left(-1+\frac{1}{3}\right) $$ $$ A=\frac{2}{3}-\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right) $$ $$ A=\frac{4}{3} $$ Therefore, the required area is $$ \boxed{\frac{4}{3}} $$ So, the correct option is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option C}} $$

questions.text:
Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation:
$ \frac{d y}{d x}+\left(\frac{6 x^2+\left(3 x^2+2 x^3+4\right) e^{-2 x}}{\left(x^3+2\right)\left(2+e^{-2 x}\right)}\right) y=2+e^{-2 x} $
$x \in(-1,2)$, satisfying $y(0)=\frac{3}{2}$. If $y(1)=\alpha\left(2+e^{-2}\right)$, then $\alpha$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Step 1: Given differential equation is $$ \frac{dy}{dx}+\left(\frac{6x^2+\left(3x^2+2x^3+4\right)e^{-2x}}{(x^3+2)(2+e^{-2x})}\right)y=2+e^{-2x} $$ with initial condition $$ y(0)=\frac{3}{2}. $$ We have to find $y(1)=\alpha(2+e^{-2})$.

Step 1: Compare with linear differential equation This is of the form $$ \frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)y=Q(x), $$ where $$ P(x)=\frac{6x^2+\left(3x^2+2x^3+4\right)e^{-2x}}{(x^3+2)(2+e^{-2x})}, \qquad Q(x)=2+e^{-2x}. $$ To solve, we find the integrating factor: $$ \text{I.F.}=e^{\int P(x)\,dx}. $$ Step 2: Simplify $P(x)$ Notice that $$ \frac{d}{dx}(x^3+2)=3x^2, $$ and $$ \frac{d}{dx}(2+e^{-2x})=-2e^{-2x}. $$ Now consider $$ \frac{d}{dx}\left[(x^3+2)(2+e^{-2x})\right]. $$ Using product rule, $$ = (3x^2)(2+e^{-2x})+(x^3+2)(-2e^{-2x}) $$ $$ = 6x^2+3x^2e^{-2x}-2x^3e^{-2x}-4e^{-2x}. $$ This does not match directly.

Step 3: So let us try another observation. Write numerator as $$ 6x^2+\left(3x^2+2x^3+4\right)e^{-2x}. $$ Now check $$ \frac{d}{dx}\left[(x^3+2)(2+e^{-2x})\right] =6x^2+\left(3x^2-2x^3-4\right)e^{-2x}. $$ Hence if we take $$ \frac{d}{dx}\left[(x^3+2)(2+e^{-2x})^{-1}\right] $$ it becomes complicated.

Step 4: So instead, let us look for a useful factorization. Observe that $$ 6x^2+\left(3x^2+2x^3+4\right)e^{-2x} =3x^2(2+e^{-2x})+(x^3+2)\cdot 2e^{-2x}. $$ Therefore $$ P(x)=\frac{3x^2(2+e^{-2x})+(x^3+2)\cdot 2e^{-2x}}{(x^3+2)(2+e^{-2x})} $$ $$ =\frac{3x^2}{x^3+2}+\frac{2e^{-2x}}{2+e^{-2x}}. $$ So, $$ P(x)=\frac{3x^2}{x^3+2}+\frac{2e^{-2x}}{2+e^{-2x}}. $$ Step 3: Find integrating factor Now $$ \int P(x)\,dx=\int \frac{3x^2}{x^3+2}\,dx+\int \frac{2e^{-2x}}{2+e^{-2x}}\,dx. $$ For the first integral: Let $u=x^3+2$, then $du=3x^2dx$. So, $$ \int \frac{3x^2}{x^3+2}\,dx=\ln(x^3+2). $$ For the second integral, note that $$ \frac{d}{dx}(2+e^{-2x})=-2e^{-2x}. $$ Hence $$ \int \frac{2e^{-2x}}{2+e^{-2x}}\,dx =-\ln(2+e^{-2x}). $$ Therefore, $$ \int P(x)\,dx=\ln(x^3+2)-\ln(2+e^{-2x}) =\ln\left(\frac{x^3+2}{2+e^{-2x}}\right). $$ So the integrating factor is $$ \text{I.F.}=e^{\int P(x)\,dx} =\frac{x^3+2}{2+e^{-2x}}. $$ Step 4: Multiply the equation by the integrating factor Multiplying throughout by $$ \frac{x^3+2}{2+e^{-2x}}, $$ we get $$ \frac{x^3+2}{2+e^{-2x}}\frac{dy}{dx} +\frac{x^3+2}{2+e^{-2x}}P(x)y =(x^3+2). $$ So the left side becomes $$ \frac{d}{dx}\left[y\cdot \frac{x^3+2}{2+e^{-2x}}\right]. $$ Hence $$ \frac{d}{dx}\left[y\cdot \frac{x^3+2}{2+e^{-2x}}\right]=x^3+2. $$ Integrating both sides, $$ y\cdot \frac{x^3+2}{2+e^{-2x}} =\int (x^3+2)\,dx =\frac{x^4}{4}+2x+C. $$ Thus, $$ y=\frac{2+e^{-2x}}{x^3+2}\left(\frac{x^4}{4}+2x+C\right). $$ Step 5: Use initial condition Given $$ y(0)=\frac{3}{2}. $$ Substitute $x=0$: $$ \frac{3}{2} =\frac{2+e^{0}}{0^3+2}\left(0+0+C\right) =\frac{3}{2}C. $$ So, $$ C=1. $$ Hence solution is $$ y=\frac{2+e^{-2x}}{x^3+2}\left(\frac{x^4}{4}+2x+1\right). $$ Step 6: Find $y(1)$ Substitute $x=1$: $$ y(1)=\frac{2+e^{-2}}{1^3+2}\left(\frac{1}{4}+2+1\right). $$ $$ y(1)=\frac{2+e^{-2}}{3}\left(\frac{1}{4}+3\right) =\frac{2+e^{-2}}{3}\cdot \frac{13}{4} $$ $$ y(1)=\frac{13}{12}(2+e^{-2}). $$ Given that $$ y(1)=\alpha(2+e^{-2}), $$ so $$ \alpha=\frac{13}{12}. $$ Final Answer $$ \boxed{\frac{13}{12}} $$ So, the correct option is D.

questions.text: The integral $\int\limits_0^1 \cot ^{-1}\left(1+x+x^2\right) d x$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Step 1: Let $$ I=\int_0^1 \cot^{-1}(1+x+x^2)\,dx $$ We will use the standard identity $$ \cot^{-1} t=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right)\quad \text{for } t>0 $$ Since $1+x+x^2>0$ on $[0,1]$, we can write $$ I=\int_0^1 \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{1+x+x^2}\right)\,dx $$ Now use the formula $$ \tan^{-1} a-\tan^{-1} b=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{a-b}{1+ab}\right) $$ We try to express $$ \frac{1}{1+x+x^2} $$ in a suitable form. Observe that $$ \tan^{-1}(x+1)-\tan^{-1}x = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{(x+1)-x}{1+x(x+1)}\right) = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{1+x+x^2}\right) $$ Hence, $$ \cot^{-1}(1+x+x^2)=\tan^{-1}(x+1)-\tan^{-1}x $$ So, $$ I=\int_0^1 \left[\tan^{-1}(x+1)-\tan^{-1}x\right]dx $$ Therefore, $$ I=\int_0^1 \tan^{-1}(x+1)\,dx-\int_0^1 \tan^{-1}x\,dx $$ In the first integral, put $u=x+1$. Then when $x=0$, $u=1$, and when $x=1$, $u=2$.

Step 2: So $$ \int_0^1 \tan^{-1}(x+1)\,dx=\int_1^2 \tan^{-1}u\,du $$ Thus, $$ I=\int_1^2 \tan^{-1}u\,du-\int_0^1 \tan^{-1}x\,dx = \int_1^2 \tan^{-1}x\,dx-\int_0^1 \tan^{-1}x\,dx $$ Now use $$ \int \tan^{-1}x\,dx=x\tan^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}\log(1+x^2) $$ So, $$ \int_1^2 \tan^{-1}x\,dx = \left[x\tan^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}\log(1+x^2)\right]_1^2 $$ and $$ \int_0^1 \tan^{-1}x\,dx = \left[x\tan^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}\log(1+x^2)\right]_0^1 $$ Hence, $$ I= \left[x\tan^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}\log(1+x^2)\right]_1^2 - \left[x\tan^{-1}x-\frac{1}{2}\log(1+x^2)\right]_0^1 $$ This becomes $$ I= \left(2\tan^{-1}2-\frac{1}{2}\log 5\right) - \left(\tan^{-1}1-\frac{1}{2}\log 2\right) -\left(\tan^{-1}1-\frac{1}{2}\log 2\right) $$ since at $x=0$, the value is $0$. Now $\tan^{-1}1=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so $$ I=2\tan^{-1}2-\frac{1}{2}\log 5-2\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{1}{2}\log 2\right) $$ $$ I=2\tan^{-1}2-\frac{1}{2}\log 5-\frac{\pi}{2}+\log 2 $$ Now combine the logarithms: $$ \log 2-\frac{1}{2}\log 5 = \frac{1}{2}\log 4-\frac{1}{2}\log 5 = \frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{4}{5}\right) = -\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{5}{4}\right) $$ Therefore, $$ I=2\tan^{-1}2-\frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)-\frac{\pi}{2} $$ So the correct answer is $$ \boxed{2\tan^{-1}2-\frac{1}{2}\log_e\left(\frac{5}{4}\right)-\frac{\pi}{2}} $$ Hence, the correct option is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option D}} $$

questions.text:
Match the LIST-I with LIST-II

LIST I
A. Planck's constant
B. Stopping potential
C. Work function
D. Threshold frequency

LIST II
I. $\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}$
II. $\mathrm{T}^{-1}$
III. $\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-1}$
IV. $\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-3} \mathrm{~A}^{-1}$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Step 1: For the dimensions of Planck's Constant (h) According to the photon energy equation $\mathrm{E}=\mathrm{h} \nu$, where E is energy and $\nu$ is frequency. Planck's constant is given by $\mathrm{h}=\frac{\mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{v}}$ The dimensions of energy (E) are $[\mathrm{E}]=\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]$. The dimensions of frequency ( $v$ ) are $[v]=\left[\mathrm{T}^{-1}\right]$. Therefore, dimensions of h: $$ [\mathrm{h}]=\frac{\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{T}^{-1}\right]}=\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-1}\right] $$ Thus, A → III For the dimensions of stopping potential ( $\mathrm{V}_0$ ) Stopping potential is defined as the potential difference required to stop the fastest moving electrons. The work done by the potential is equal to the kinetic energy, $\mathrm{W}=\mathrm{qV}_0$, where q is charge. So, stopping potential is $\mathrm{V}_0=\frac{\mathrm{w}}{\mathrm{q}}$. The dimensions of work ( W ) are $[\mathrm{W}]=\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]$. The dimensions of charge ( $\mathrm{q}=\mathrm{I} \times \mathrm{t}$ ) are $[\mathrm{q}]=[\mathrm{AT}]$. Therefore, dimensions of stopping potential is: $$ \left[\mathrm{V}_0\right]=\frac{\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]}{[\mathrm{AT}]}=\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-3} \mathrm{~A}^{-1}\right] $$ Thus, $\mathrm{B} \rightarrow$ IV. For the dimensions of work function ( $\phi$ ) The work function is the minimum energy required to eject an electron from a metal surface. Since it is a form of energy, its dimensions are the same as energy (E). So, the dimensions of work function is $[\phi]=\left[\mathrm{ML}^2 \mathrm{~T}^{-2}\right]$ Thus, $\mathrm{C} \rightarrow \mathrm{I}$. For the dimensions of threshold frequency ( $v_0$ ) Threshold frequency is the minimum frequency of incident radiation required for photoelectric emission. Frequency is defined as the reciprocal of the time period $\left(v=\frac{1}{\mathrm{~T}}\right)$. So, the dimensions of threshold frequency is $\left[v_0\right]=\left[\mathrm{T}^{-1}\right]$ Thus, $\mathrm{D} \rightarrow$ II. Therefore, the correct match is A - III, B - IV, C - I, D - II. Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: Two cars $A$ and $B$ are moving in the same direction along a straight line with speeds $100 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}$ and $80 \mathrm{~km} / \mathrm{h}$, respectively such that car $A$ is moving ahead of car $B$. A person in car $B$ throws a stone with a speed $v$ so that it hits the car $A$ with a speed of $5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. The value of $v$ is $\_\_\_\_$ $\mathrm{km} / \mathrm{h}$.
questions.solution:
Step 1: Given $v_A = 100\ \text{km h}^{-1}$ and $v_B = 80\ \text{km h}^{-1}$ in the same direction, with A ahead of
B. The stone is thrown with speed $v$ relative to car B and hits car A with speed $5\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ relative to car
A. Converting, $5\ \text{m s}^{-1} = 5 \times \dfrac{18}{5} = 18\ \text{km h}^{-1}$. Velocity of the stone relative to the ground: $$v_S = v_B + v = 80 + v$$ Velocity of the stone relative to car
A: $$v_S - v_A = (80 + v) - 100 = v - 20$$ Setting this equal to $18\ \text{km h}^{-1}$: $$v - 20 = 18 \Rightarrow v = 38\ \text{km h}^{-1}$$ Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: At $t=0$, a body of mass 100 g starts moving under the influence of a force $(5 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+10 \hat{\mathrm{j}}) \mathrm{N} \cdot$ After 2 s its position is $(2 x \hat{\mathrm{i}}+5 y \hat{\mathrm{j}}) \mathrm{m}$. The ratio $x: y$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution: Step 1: The mass of the body, $\mathrm{m}=100 \mathrm{~g}=0.1 \mathrm{~kg}$ The constant force acting on the body, $\vec{F}=(5 \hat{\imath}+10 \hat{\jmath}) N$ The time interval of motion, $\mathrm{t}=2 \mathrm{~s}$ As the body started from rest, so the initial velocity at $\mathrm{t}=0, \overrightarrow{\mathrm{u}}=0$ The position at $\mathrm{t}=2 \mathrm{~s}, \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}}=(2 \mathrm{xi}+5 \mathrm{y}) \mathrm{j}) \mathrm{m}$ According to Newton's Second Law of Motion: $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=\mathrm{m} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}}{\mathrm{~m}} $$ Substituting the values: $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=\frac{5 \hat{\imath}+10 \hat{\jmath}}{0.1} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}=(50 \hat{\imath}+100 \hat{\jmath}) \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}^2 $$ From the second equation of motion for constant acceleration: $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{s}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{ut}}+\frac{1}{2} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} t^2 $$ Since $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{u}}=0$: $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{s}}=\frac{1}{2} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}} \mathrm{t}^2 $$ Substituting the acceleration and time: $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{s}}=\frac{1}{2}(50 \hat{\imath}+100 \hat{\jmath})(2)^2 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{s}}=\frac{1}{2}(50 \hat{\imath}+100 \hat{\jmath})(4)$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\vec{s}=2(50 \hat{\imath}+100 \hat{\jmath})$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{s}}=(100 i \hat{\imath}+200 \hat{\jmath}) \mathrm{m}$ On comparing the calculated displacement with the given position $(2 x \hat{i}+5 y \hat{j})$: For the x -component: $2 \mathrm{x}=100 \Rightarrow \mathrm{x}=50$ For the $y$-component: $5 y=200 \Rightarrow y=40$ So, the required ratio is, $$ \frac{x}{y}=\frac{50}{40}=5: 4 $$ Therefore, the ratio $\mathrm{x}: \mathrm{y}$ is $5: 4$. Thus, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: If $x$ and $y$ coordinates of a projectile as a function of time $(t)$ are given as $24 t$ and $43.6 t-4.9 t^2$, respectively, then the angle (in degrees) made by the projectile with horizontal when $t=2 \mathrm{~s}$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution: Step 1: Horizontal position of projectile is given as $\mathrm{x}=24 \mathrm{t}$ Vertical position of projectile is given as $\mathrm{y}=43.6 \mathrm{t}-4.9 \mathrm{t}^2$ Velocity is the rate of change of position with respect to time $\left(\vec{V}=\frac{d \vec{r}}{d t}\right)$. For the velocity component along horizontal, $\left(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{x}}\right)$: $$ v_x=\frac{d x}{d t}=\frac{d}{d t}(24 t)=24 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} $$ The horizontal velocity remains constant throughout the motion. For the velocity component along vertical, $\left(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{y}}\right)$: $$ v_y=\frac{d y}{d t}=\frac{d}{d t}\left(43.6 t-4.9 t^2\right) $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{y}}=43.6-(2 \times 4.9) \mathrm{t}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ v_y=43.6-9.8 t $$ So, the velocities at $\mathrm{t}=2 \mathrm{~s}$ is, $$ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{x}}=24 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{y}}=43.6-9.8(2)=43.6-19.6=24 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} $$ The angle $\theta$ that the velocity vector makes with the horizontal is given by $$ \tan \theta=\frac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{y}}}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{x}}} $$ Substituting the values calculated for $\mathrm{t}=2 \mathrm{~s}$: $$ \tan \theta=\frac{24}{24} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\tan \theta=1$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \theta=45^{\circ} $$ Therefore, the angle made by the projectile with the horizontal at $\mathrm{t}=2 \mathrm{~s}$ is $45^{\circ}$. Thus, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
The height in terms of radius of the earth $(R)$, at which the acceleration due to gravity becomes $\frac{g}{9}$, where $g$ is acceleration due to gravity on earth's surface, is
$\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution: Step 1: According to Newton's Law of universal gravitation, the acceleration due to gravity ( $g$ ) on the surface of Earth is, $$ g=\frac{G M}{R^2} \ldots \text { (i) } $$ Where $G$ is the gravitational constant, $M$ is the mass of the Earth, and $R$ is the radius of the Earth. If the body is placed at a height h above the Earth's surface, its total distance from the centre of the Earth becomes $(\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h})$. The acceleration due to gravity at this height is: $$ \mathrm{g}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{GM}}{(\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h})^2}...... (ii) $$ Dividing equation (ii) by equation (i): $$ \frac{\mathrm{g}^{\prime}}{\mathrm{g}}=\frac{\mathrm{GM} /(\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h})^2}{\mathrm{GM} / \mathrm{R}^2} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{g^{\prime}}{g}=\frac{R^2}{(R+h)^2}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{g}^{\prime}=\mathrm{g}\left(\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h}}\right)^2 $$ It is given that the acceleration due to gravity at height h is $\mathrm{g}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{g}}{9}$: $$ \frac{g}{9}=g\left(\frac{R}{R+h}\right)^2 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{9}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h}}\right)^2$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \frac{1}{3}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{\mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{R}+\mathrm{h}=3 \mathrm{R} \Rightarrow \mathrm{~h}=2 \mathrm{R} $$ Therefore, the height at which the acceleration due to gravity becomes $\frac{g}{9}$ is $2 R$. Thus, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: A metal string $A$ is suspended from a rigid support and its free end is attached to a block of mass $M$. Second block having mass 2 M is suspended at the bottom of the first block using a string $B$. The area of cross sections of strings $A$ and $B$ are same. The ratio of lengths of strings of $A$ to B is 2 and the ratio of their Young's moduli $\left(Y_A / Y_B\right)$ is 0.5. The ratio of elongations in $A$ to $B$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution: Step 1: Young's Modulus (Y) is defined as the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain: $$ \mathrm{Y}=\frac{\text { Stress }}{\text { Strain }}=\frac{\mathrm{F} / \mathrm{A}}{\Delta \mathrm{~L} / \mathrm{L}} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \Delta \mathrm{L}=\frac{\mathrm{FL}}{\mathrm{AY}} \ldots (ii)$$ Where, F is the tension in the string, L is the original length, A is the area of cross-section. Y is the Young's Modulus. For string B This string supports only the bottom block of mass 2 M. $$ \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{B}}=2 \mathrm{Mg} $$ For string A This string supports both mass M and the mass 2 M hanging below it. $$ \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{A}}=\mathrm{Mg}+2 \mathrm{Mg}=3 \mathrm{Mg} $$ The ratio of lengths is $\frac{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=2$ The ratio of Young's moduli is $\frac{\mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{B}}}=0.5$. The areas are same, $A_A=A_B=A$. Using the formula of extension in string (i), $$ \frac{\Delta L_A}{\Delta L_B}=\frac{F_A L_A / A_A Y_A}{F_B L_B / A_B Y_B}=\left(\frac{F_A}{F_B}\right) \times\left(\frac{L_A}{L_B}\right)\left(\frac{Y_B}{Y_A}\right) $$ Substituting the values: $$ \frac{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\Delta \mathrm{~L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\left(\frac{3 \mathrm{Mg}}{2 \mathrm{Mg}}\right) \times(2) \times\left(\frac{1}{0.5}\right) $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=\left(\frac{3}{2}\right) \times 2 \times 2$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \frac{\Delta \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{A}}}{\Delta \mathrm{~L}_{\mathrm{B}}}=3 \times 2=6 $$ Therefore, the ratio of elongations in A to B is 6. Thus, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: A water spray gun is attached to a hose of cross sectional area $30 \mathrm{~cm}^2$. The gun comprises of 10 perforations each of cross sectional area of $15 \mathrm{~mm}^2$. If the water flows in the hose with the speed of $50 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}$, calculate the speed at which the water flows out from each perforation. (Neglect any edge effects)
questions.solution: Step 1: For an incompressible fluid, the volume of fluid entering a pipe per unit time must equal the volume of fluid leaving the pipe per unit time. Volume Flow Rate (In) = Volume Flow Rate (Out) $$ A_1 v_1=A_2 v_2 $$ Where A is the area and v is the velocity of the fluid. The area of hose is $\mathrm{A}_1=30 \mathrm{~cm}^2=30 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^2$. The speed in hose is $\mathrm{v}_1=50 \mathrm{~cm} / \mathrm{s}=0.5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. Number of perforations is $\mathrm{n}=10$. The area of one perforation is $\mathrm{a}=15 \mathrm{~mm}^2=15 \times\left(10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}\right)^2=15 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^2$ So, total area of exit is, $\mathrm{A}_2=\mathrm{n} \times \mathrm{a}=10 \times 15 \times 10^{-6}=150 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~m}^2$ Using the equation of continuity: $$ A_1 v_1=A_2 v_2 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ v_2=\frac{A_1 v_1}{A_2} $$ Substituting the values: $$ v_2=\frac{\left(30 \times 10^{-4}\right) \times 0.5}{150 \times 10^{-6}} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $v_2=\frac{15 \times 10^{-4}}{150 \times 10^{-6}}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{v}_2=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s} $$ Therefore, the speed at which the water flows out from each perforation is $10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$. Thus, the correct option is (B).
questions.topic: Equation of Continuity and Bernoulli's Theorem

questions.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R
Assertion A: If the average kinetic energy of $\mathrm{H}_2$ and $\mathrm{O}_2$ molecules, kept in two different sized containers are same, then their temperatures will be same.
Reason R: The r.m.s speed of $\mathrm{H}_2$ and $\mathrm{O}_2$ molecules are same at same temperature.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.text: Both $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ are true and $\mathbf{R}$ is the correct explanation of $\mathbf{A}$
Both $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ are true but $\mathbf{R}$ is NOT the correct explanation of $\mathbf{A}$
A is true but $\mathbf{R}$ is false
A is false but $\mathbf{R}$ is true

questions.solution: Step 1: According to the kinetic theory of gases, the average translational kinetic energy ( $\mathrm{K}_{\text {avg }}$ ) of a gas molecule is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (T). $$ \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{3}{2} \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{~T} $$ Where $\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}$ is the Boltzmann constant. So, the average kinetic energy depends only on the temperature and not on the mass of the molecule or the size/volume of the container. Since $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{avg}}$ is the same for both $\mathrm{H}_2$ and $\mathrm{O}_2$, their temperatures (T) must be identical. Therefore, Assertion A is true. The root mean square (r. m. s.) speed ( $\mathrm{v}_{\text {rms }}$ ) of a gas molecule is given by the formula: $$ v_{r m s}=\sqrt{\frac{3 R T}{M}} $$ Where R is the universal gas constant, T is the absolute temperature, and M is the molar mass of the gas. At the same temperature (T), $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rms}}$ is inversely proportional to the square root of the molar mass (M). Since the molar mass of $\mathrm{H}_2(2 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol})$ is different from $\mathrm{O}_2(32 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol})$, their r.m.s. speeds will be different even at the same temperature. Therefore, Reason R is false. Hence, Assertion A is true, but Reason R is false. So, the correct option is (C).
questions.topic: Pressure of an Ideal Gas and Kinetic Interpretation of Temperature

questions.text:
The temperature of a metal strip having coefficient of linear expansion $\alpha$ is increased from $T_1$ to $T_2$ resulting in increase of its length by $\Delta L_1$. The temperature is further increased from $T_2$ to $T_3$ such that the increase in its length is $\Delta L_2$.
Given $T_3+T_1=2 T_2$ and $T_2-T_1=\Delta T$, the value of $\Delta L_2$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution: Step 1: When a metal of length $L$ having coefficient of linear expansion $\alpha$ is heated by temperature $\Delta T$, then the change in length is given as $\Delta \mathrm{L}=\mathrm{L} \alpha \Delta \mathrm{T}$ For the first interval of heating $\left(\mathrm{T}_1 \rightarrow \mathrm{~T}_2\right)$: The increase in length $\Delta \mathrm{L}_1$ is given by $\Delta \mathrm{L}_1=\mathrm{L}_1 \alpha\left(\mathrm{~T}_2-\mathrm{T}_1\right)$ It is given that $\mathrm{T}_2-\mathrm{T}_1=\Delta \mathrm{T}$: $$ \Delta \mathrm{L}_1=\mathrm{L}_1 \alpha \Delta \mathrm{~T}.....(i) $$ The new length at temperature $\mathrm{T}_2$ is: $$ \mathrm{L}_2=\mathrm{L}_1+\Delta \mathrm{L}_1=\mathrm{L}_1(1+\alpha \Delta \mathrm{T})........(ii)$$ For the second interval of heating, ( $\mathrm{T}_2 \rightarrow \mathrm{~T}_3$ ) The increase in length $\Delta \mathrm{L}_2$ depends on the length at the start of this stage $\left(\mathrm{L}_2\right)$: $$ \Delta \mathrm{L}_2=\mathrm{L}_2 \alpha\left(\mathrm{~T}_3-\mathrm{T}_2\right) $$ From the given condition $\mathrm{T}_3+\mathrm{T}_1=2 \mathrm{~T}_2$: $$ \mathrm{T}_3-\mathrm{T}_2=\mathrm{T}_2-\mathrm{T}_1 $$ Since $\mathrm{T}_2-\mathrm{T}_1=\Delta \mathrm{T}$, then $\mathrm{T}_3-\mathrm{T}_2=\Delta \mathrm{T}$. Substituting this into the $\Delta \mathrm{L}_2$ formula: $$\Delta \mathrm{L}_2=\mathrm{L}_2 \alpha \Delta \mathrm{~T}.......(iii) $$ Substitute the value of $\mathrm{L}_2$ from equation (ii) into equation (iii): $$ \Delta \mathrm{L}_2=\left[\mathrm{L}_1(1+\alpha \Delta \mathrm{T})\right] \alpha \Delta \mathrm{T} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \Delta \mathrm{L}_2=\left(\mathrm{L}_1 \alpha \Delta \mathrm{~T}\right)(1+\alpha \Delta \mathrm{T}) $$ From equation (i), we know $\mathrm{L}_1 \alpha \Delta \mathrm{~T}=\Delta \mathrm{L}_1$. $$ \Delta \mathrm{L}_2=\Delta \mathrm{L}_1(1+\alpha \Delta \mathrm{T}) $$ Therefore, the value of $\Delta L_2$ is $\Delta L_1[1+\alpha \Delta T]$. Thus, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
A uniform disc of radius $R$ and mass $M$ is free to oscillate about the axis $A$ as shown in the figure. For small oscillations the time period is $\_\_\_\_$.
(g is acceleration due to gravity)
questions.solution: Step 1: The axis through A is the tangent to the disc lying in its plane, so the disc swings out of its plane as a physical pendulum with its centre of mass at distance $d = R$ from the axis. By the perpendicular axis theorem, the moment of inertia of a uniform disc about a diameter is $I_d = \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}MR^2\right) = \dfrac{1}{4}MR^2$. The tangent at A is parallel to a diameter at distance $R$, so by the parallel axis theorem $$I_A = \dfrac{1}{4}MR^2 + MR^2 = \dfrac{5}{4}MR^2$$ For a small angular displacement $\theta$, the restoring torque is $\tau = -MgR\,\theta$, so $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I_A}{MgR}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{\frac{5}{4}MR^2}{MgR}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{5R}{4g}}$$ The value $\dfrac{3}{2}MR^2$ belongs to a tangent axis perpendicular to the plane of the disc, which is not the axis shown. Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: A rigid dipole undergoes a simple harmonic motion about its centre in the presence of an electric field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_1=\mathrm{E}_0 \hat{x}$. If another electric field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_2=2 \mathrm{E}_0(\hat{y}+\hat{z})$ is introduced to the system, what will be the percentage change in the frequency of the oscillation (approximate)?
questions.solution: Step 1: When a dipole with dipole moment $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}$ is placed in an electric field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}$, the restoring torque is $\vec{\tau}=-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}$ The magnitude of restoring torque is $\tau=-\mathrm{pE} \sin \theta$. For small $\theta$, $$ \tau \approx-\text { pEθ } $$ The equation of motion is $\mathrm{I} \frac{\mathrm{d}^2 \theta}{\mathrm{dt}^2}=-\mathrm{pE} \theta$, where I is the moment of inertia. The angular frequency is $\omega=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{pE}}{\mathrm{I}}}$, so the frequency f is: $$ f=\frac{\omega}{2 \pi} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{f}=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{pE}}{\mathrm{I}}}$ $\Rightarrow \mathrm{f} \propto \sqrt{\mathrm{E}}$ Where E is the magnitude of the net electric field. Initial electric field is $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_1=\mathrm{E}_0 \widehat{\mathrm{x}}$. Magnitude of initial electric field is $\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{E}_0$. The additional electric field is $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_2=2 \mathrm{E}_0 \hat{\mathrm{y}}+2 \mathrm{E}_0 \hat{\mathrm{z}}$. So, the net electric field is $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_{\mathrm{net}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_1+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}_2=\mathrm{E}_0 \hat{\mathrm{x}}+2 \mathrm{E}_0 \hat{\mathrm{y}}+2 \mathrm{E}_0 \hat{\mathrm{z}} $$ Magnitude of the net electric field is, $$ \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{net}}=\sqrt{\left(\mathrm{E}_0\right)^2+\left(2 \mathrm{E}_0\right)^2+\left(2 \mathrm{E}_0\right)^2}=\sqrt{\mathrm{E}_0^2+4 \mathrm{E}_0^2+4 \mathrm{E}_0^2} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{net}}=\sqrt{9 \mathrm{E}_0^2}=3 \mathrm{E}_0 $$ Let $f_1$ be the initial frequency and $f_2$ be the final frequency. $$ \frac{\mathrm{f}_2}{\mathrm{f}_1}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{f}}}{\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{i}}}}=\sqrt{\frac{3 \mathrm{E}_0}{\mathrm{E}_0}}=\sqrt{3} \approx 1.732 $$ So, the percentage change is $$ \Delta \%=\left(\frac{\mathrm{f}_2-\mathrm{f}_1}{\mathrm{f}_1}\right) \times 100 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\Delta \%=(\sqrt{3}-1) \times 100$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \Delta \%=(1.732-1) \times 100=0.732 \times 100=73.2 \% $$ Therefore, the approximate percentage change in the frequency of oscillation is $73 \%$. Thus, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
From the circuit given below, the capacitance between terminals $A$ and $B$ shown in the circuit is $\_\_\_\_$ $\mu \mathrm{F}$.
(take $C_1=C_2=C_3=1 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ and $C_4=2 \mu \mathrm{~F}$.)
questions.solution:
Step 1: Let the node between $\mathrm{C}_1$ and $\mathrm{C}_2$ be X, The wire (short circuit) connects terminal A to the node between $\mathrm{C}_2$ and $\mathrm{C}_3$. Thus, this node is at the same potential as
A. So, capacitor $\mathrm{C}_1$ is connected between A and X. The capacitor $\mathrm{C}_2$ is connected between A and X. The capacitor $C_3$ is connected between $A$ and $B$. The capacitor $\mathrm{C}_4$ is connected between X and
B. So, the simplified circuit is, Given values of capacitances are, $\mathrm{C}_1=1 \mu \mathrm{~F}, \mathrm{C}_2=1 \mu \mathrm{~F}, \mathrm{C}_3=1 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ and $\mathrm{C}_4=2 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ Both $\mathrm{C}_1$ and $\mathrm{C}_2$ are connected between point A and point X in parallel. The equivalent capacitance $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{AX}}$ is: $$ C_{A X}=C_1+C_2 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ C_{A X}=1 \mu F+1 \mu F=2 \mu F $$ Now, the combination $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{AX}}$ is in series with $\mathrm{C}_4$ because the charge must flow through $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{AX}}$ to reach $\mathrm{C}_4$. So, the equivalent capacitance ( $\mathrm{C}^{\prime}$ ) is $$ \frac{1}{\mathrm{C}^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{AX}}}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{C}_4} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{\mathrm{C}^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{C}^{\prime}=1 \mu \mathrm{~F} $$ The entire top branch ( $C^{\prime}$ ) is now in parallel with $C_3$, as both are connected across the main terminals $A$ and $B$. The total equivalent capacitance $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{eq}}$ is: $$ C_{\mathrm{eq}}=C^{\prime}+C_3 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{eq}}=1 \mu \mathrm{~F}+1 \mu \mathrm{~F}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{eq}}=2 \mu \mathrm{~F} $$ Therefore, the equivalent capacitance between A and B is $2 \mu \mathrm{~F}$. Thus, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason $\mathbf{R}$
Assertion A: In electrostatics, a conductor does not store any net charge inside.
Reason R: Inside the capacitor (with no dielectric medium), the free charge carriers, if placed between the plates of capacitor, experience force and drift.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.text: Both $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ are true and $\mathbf{R}$ is the correct explanation of $\mathbf{A}$
Both $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ are true but $\mathbf{R}$ is NOT the correct explanation of $\mathbf{A}$
A is true but $\mathbf{R}$ is false
A is false but $\mathbf{R}$ is true

questions.solution: Step 1: In electrostatic equilibrium, the electric field inside a conductor is zero $(\mathrm{E}=0)$. According to Gauss's Law $\left(\oint \mathrm{E} \cdot \mathrm{dA}=\frac{\mathrm{q}_{\text {in }}}{\epsilon_0}\right)$, if the electric field is zero everywhere inside, the net charge enclosed ( $\mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{in}}$ ) by any Gaussian surface inside the conductor must also be zero. Therefore, any excess charge resides entirely on the outer surface. Therefore, assertion A is true. Inside a charged capacitor, there is a uniform electric field between the plates. If free charge carriers (like electrons or ions) are placed in this region, they will experience an electric force ( $\mathrm{F}=\mathrm{qE}$ ). This force causes the charges to accelerate or drift toward the plate of opposite polarity. Therefore, reason R is true. While both statements are scientifically true, reason R describes the behaviour of charges in an external field between two conductors (the plates). It does not explain why the net charge inside a solid conductor is zero (which is due to mutual repulsion and the resulting zero internal field). So, both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A. Thus, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
A solenoid has a core made of material with relative permeability 400. The magnetic field produced in the interior of solenoid is 1.0 T. The magnetic intensity in SI units is $\alpha \times 10^5$. The value of $\alpha$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
(Free space permeability $\mu_0=4 \pi \times 10^{-7}$ SI units.)
questions.solution: Step 1: The relative permeability of the core is $\mu_{\mathrm{r}}=400$. The magnetic field applied is, $\mathrm{B}=1.0 \mathrm{~T}$. The permeability of free space is $\mu_0=4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~T} \cdot \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{A}$. The magnetic induction $B$ in a material is related to the magnetic intensity $H$ by the total permeability of the medium ( $\mu$ ): $$ \mathrm{B}=\mu \mathrm{H} \ldots \text { (i) } $$ The total permeability $\mu$ is the product of the permeability of free space and the relative permeability of the material: $$ \mu=\mu_0 \mu_r $$ Substituting this into the first equation: $$ \mathrm{B}=\mu_0 \mu_{\mathrm{r}} \mathrm{H} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$$$ H=\frac{B}{\mu_0 \mu_r} $$ Substituting the given values, $$ H=\frac{1.0}{\left(4 \pi \times 10^{-7}\right) \times 400} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $H=\frac{1}{1600 \pi \times 10^{-7}}$ $$\Rightarrow $$$$ H=\frac{1}{16 \pi} \times 10^5=a \times 10^5 \Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{1}{16 \pi} $$ Therefore, the value of $\alpha$ is $\frac{1}{16 \pi}$. Thus, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: A magnetic field vector in an electromagnetic wave is represented by $\vec{B}=B_0 \sin \left(2 \pi v t-\frac{2 \pi x}{\lambda}\right) \hat{j}$. Its associated electric field vector is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution: Step 1: The argument of the sine function is $\left(2 \pi v t-\frac{2 \pi x}{\lambda}\right)$. This indicates the wave is propagating along the positive x -axis. Let the unit vector for the direction of propagation be $\hat{\mathrm{n}}=\hat{\mathrm{i}}$. In an electromagnetic wave, the electric field vector $(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}})$, the magnetic field vector $(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}})$, and the direction of propagation ( $\widehat{\mathrm{n}}$ ) are mutually perpendicular. Their relationship is given by: $$ \widehat{\mathrm{E}}=\widehat{\mathrm{B}} \times \widehat{\mathrm{n}} $$ It is given that $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}$ is along $\hat{\mathrm{j}}$: $$ \widehat{\mathrm{E}}=\hat{\jmath} \times \hat{\imath}=-\hat{\mathrm{k}} $$ The magnitude of the electric field and magnetic field in a vacuum are related by the speed of light (c): $$ \mathrm{E}_0=\mathrm{cB}_0 $$ The speed of light is the product of frequency and wavelength: $\mathrm{c}=\nu \lambda$. $$ \mathrm{E}_0=v \lambda \mathrm{~B}_0 $$ The electric field must have the same phase as the magnetic field. So, the electric field component is, $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=\mathrm{E}_0 \sin \left(2 \pi v \mathrm{t}-\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{x}}{\lambda}\right)(-\widehat{\mathrm{k}}) $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}}=-v \lambda \mathrm{~B}_0 \sin \left(2 \pi v \mathrm{t}-\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{x}}{\lambda}\right) \hat{\mathrm{k}} $$ Therefore, the associated electric field vector is $-v \lambda \mathrm{~B}_0 \sin \left(2 \pi v \mathrm{t}-\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{x}}{\lambda}\right) \hat{\mathrm{k}}$. Thus, the correct option is (A).
questions.topic: Displacement Current and Properties of EM Waves

questions.text: A convex lens is made from glass material having refractive index of 1.4 with same radius of curvature on both sides. The ratio of its focal length and radius of curvature is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution: Step 1: For a thin lens with two curved surfaces, the focal length ( $f$ ) is related to the refractive index ( $n$ ) and the radii of curvature $\left(\mathrm{R}_1\right.$ and $\left.\mathrm{R}_2\right)$ by Lens Makers' formula, $$ \frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=(\mathrm{n}-1)\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_1}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}_2}\right) $$ The refractive index of the material, $\mathrm{n}=1.4$. The lens is convex with the same radius of curvature on both sides (R). According to the Cartesian sign convention: The first surface is convex towards the incident light, so $\mathrm{R}_1=+\mathrm{R}$. The second surface is concave towards the incident light, so $R_2=-R$. Substituting the values into the formula: $$ \frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=(1.4-1)\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}}-\frac{1}{-\mathrm{R}}\right) $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=(0.4)\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{R}}\right)$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}}=0.4 \times \frac{2}{\mathrm{R}}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{1}{f}=\frac{0.8}{R}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\mathrm{f}=\frac{\mathrm{R}}{0.8}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \frac{\mathrm{f}}{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{1}{0.8}=1.25 $$ Therefore, the ratio of its focal length and radius of curvature is 1.25. Thus, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: An unpolarized light of certain intensity passes through a combination of two polarizers whose transmission axes are at $30^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$, respectively, with respect to the horizontal axis. A third polarizer with its transmission axis at $60^{\circ}$ with the horizontal axis is placed between the two existing polarizers. The ratio of the output intensities with and without the third polarizer is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution: Step 1: When polarized light of intensity $\mathrm{I}_{\text {in }}$ passes through a polarizer, the intensity of the transmitted light $\left(\mathrm{I}_{\text {out }}\right)$ is given by Malus's Law $$ I_{\text {out }}=I_{\text {in }} \cos ^2 \theta $$ Where $\theta$ is the angle between the polarization direction of the incident light and the transmission axis of the polarizer. The initial intensity of unpolarised light $=\mathrm{I}_0$. After the first polarizer (at $30^{\circ}$ ), the light becomes polarized with intensity $\mathrm{I}_1=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I}_0$. This light then hits the second polarizer (at $90^{\circ}$ ). The angle between them is $\theta=90^{\circ}-30^{\circ}=60^{\circ}$. So, the final intensity without third polarizer is, $$ I_{\text {without }}=I_2=I_1 \cos ^2 60^{\circ}=\left(\frac{1}{2} I_0\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{2} I_0 \times \frac{1}{4}=\frac{I_0}{8} $$ The intensity after the first polarizer (at $30^{\circ}$ ) is $\mathrm{I}_1=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{I}_0$. This light hits the middle polarizer (at $60^{\circ}$ ). The angle is $\theta_{12}=60^{\circ}-30^{\circ}=30^{\circ}$. So, intensity after middle polarizer $\left(\mathrm{I}_3\right)$: $$ I_3=I_1 \cos ^2 30^{\circ}=\left(\frac{1}{2} I_0\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{2} I_0 \times \frac{3}{4}=\frac{3 I_0}{8} $$ This light hits the final polarizer (at $90^{\circ}$ ). The angle is $\theta_{23}=90^{\circ}-60^{\circ}=30^{\circ}$. So, final intensity after the final polarizer is $$ \mathrm{I}_{\text {with }}=\mathrm{I}_3 \cos ^2 30^{\circ}=\left(\frac{3 \mathrm{I}_0}{8}\right)\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2=\frac{3 \mathrm{I}_0}{8} \times \frac{3}{4}=\frac{9 \mathrm{I}_0}{32} $$ So, the ratio of the output intensities with and without the third polarizer is, $$ \frac{\mathrm{I}_{\text {with }}}{\mathrm{I}_{\text {without }}}=\frac{\left(\frac{9 \mathrm{I}_0}{32}\right)}{\left(\frac{\mathrm{I}_0}{8}\right)}=\frac{9}{4} $$ Therefore, the ratio of the output intensities with and without the third polarizer is $9 / 4$. Thus, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
In Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment, only a few alpha particles rebound back because
A. The size of gold nucleus is very small as compared to the size of gold atom.
B. Alpha particle and gold nucleus have equal charge.
C. The impact parameter is minimum for a few alpha particles.
D. A few alpha particles have very high kinetic energy.
E. Only a few alpha particles undergo head-on collision with the nuclei.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Step 1: In the experiment, alpha particles (positively charged helium nuclei) are fired at a thin gold foil. Rutherford observed that most particles passed straight through, but a tiny fraction (about 1 in 8000 ) reflected back at angles greater than $90^{\circ}$. Statement
A: Rutherford concluded that the positive charge and most of the mass of the atom are concentrated in an extremely small region called the nucleus. Since the nucleus is tiny compared to the total volume of the atom, the probability of an alpha particle hitting it or coming close enough to be repelled backward is very low. Hence, statement A is true. Statement
B: Alpha particles have a charge of +2 e, while a gold nucleus has a charge of +79 e. They do not have equal charges. Hence, statement B is false. Statement
C: The impact parameter (b) is the perpendicular distance of the initial velocity vector of the alpha particle from the centre of the nucleus. A rebound or large-angle scattering occurs when the impact parameter is very small (close to zero), meaning the particle is heading almost directly toward the nucleus. Only a few particles have such a small impact parameter. Hence, the statement C is true. Statement
D: The kinetic energy of the incident alpha particles is generally uniform in the beam; high kinetic energy would actually make it easier to penetrate closer to the nucleus rather than causing the few rebounds mentioned. Hence, the statement D is false. Statement E: A head-on collision occurs when the particle moves directly toward the centre of the nucleus $(\mathrm{b}=0)$. Because the nucleus is so small, only a very small number of particles are aligned for such a collision. Hence, the statement E is true. Therefore, statements A, C, and E are the correct reasons for the observed phenomenon. Thus, the correct option is (D).
questions.topic: Alpha-Particle Scattering and Rutherford Model of Atom

questions.text: The de Broglie wavelength associated with an electron accelerated through a potential difference V is $\lambda_{\mathrm{e}}$ and the de Broglie wavelength associated with a proton accelerated through the same potential difference is $\lambda_{\mathrm{p}}$. If their corresponding masses are $m_{\mathrm{e}}$ and $m_{\mathrm{p}}$, respectively, then the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths $\left(\frac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p}\right)$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution: Step 1: According to de Broglie's hypothesis, the wavelength associated with a particle of momentum p is: $$ \lambda=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{p}} $$ Where h is Planck's constant. Kinetic energy is given by $\mathrm{K}=\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}^2$. In terms of linear momentum, the kinetic energy can be written as $$ K=\frac{m^2 v^2}{2 m}=\frac{p^2}{2 m} $$ Thus, momentum $\mathrm{p}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mK}}$. When a particle of charge q is accelerated through a potential difference V, the work done on it becomes its kinetic energy: $$ \mathrm{K}=\mathrm{qV} $$ Substituting this into the momentum equation: $$ \mathrm{p}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mqV}} $$ So, the de-Broglie's wavelength is $\lambda=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mqV}}}$ The charge on electron is $\mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{e}}=\mathrm{e}$, so the wavelength for an electron is $\lambda_{\mathrm{e}}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{eV}}}$ The charge on proton is $\mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{p}}=\mathrm{e}$, so the wavelength for a proton is $\lambda_{\mathrm{p}}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{p}} \mathrm{eV}}}$ Taking the ratio $\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{e}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{p}}}$: $$ \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{e}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{p}}}=\frac{\mathrm{h} / \sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{eV}}}{\mathrm{~h} / \sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{p}} \mathrm{eV}}}=\frac{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{p}} \mathrm{eV}}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{eV}}} $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{e}}}{\lambda_{\mathrm{p}}}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{p}}}{\mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{e}}}} $$ Therefore, the ratio of their de Broglie wavelengths is $\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{p}}}{\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{e}}}}$. Thus, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason $\mathbf{R}$
Assertion A: A diode under reverse-biased condition provides very small current which is nearly independent of voltage until a critical limit at which the current increases drastically.
Reason R: Below the critical voltage limit, only majority charge carriers flow which increases drastically above critical voltage.
choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.text: Both $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ are true and $\mathbf{R}$ is the correct explanation of $\mathbf{A}$
Both $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{R}$ are true but $\mathbf{R}$ is NOT the correct explanation of $\mathbf{A}$
A is true but $\mathbf{R}$ is false
A is false but $\mathbf{R}$ is true

questions.solution: Step 1: In reverse bias the p-side is connected to the negative terminal and the n-side to the positive terminal, so the majority carriers are pulled away from the junction and the depletion layer widens. Only minority carriers (electrons in the p-region, holes in the n-region) drift across the junction. Their number is fixed mainly by temperature, so the reverse current is very small (of the order of $\mu\text{A}$) and nearly independent of the applied voltage. At a critical reverse voltage, the breakdown voltage, the reverse current increases sharply. Hence Assertion A is true. Below the breakdown voltage the current is carried by minority carriers, not majority carriers, so Reason R is false. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: A diode has Zener voltage of 10 V and maximum power dissipation of 0.5 W, then the minimum resistance to be used in series with this diode for safety when it is connected to a 25 V power supply is $\_\_\_\_$ $\Omega$.
questions.solution: Step 1: List given data. Step 2: Select formula. Step 3: Substitute and compute. Step 4: State final numeric answer. Answer: 300.

questions.text:

questions.text: Number of moles and number of molecules in 1.4187 L of $\mathrm{SO}_2$ at STP respectively are
questions.solution: Step 1: At STP, according to Avogadro’s law, $1$ mole of any gas occupies $22.4 \, \text{L}$. So, number of moles of $\mathrm{SO_2}$ is $$ n=\frac{V}{22.4}=\frac{1.4187}{22.4} $$ $$ n=0.0633 \text{ mol} $$ Now, number of molecules $$ = n \times N_A $$ where $N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}$ So, $$ \text{Number of molecules} = 0.0633 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} $$ $$ = 3.812 \times 10^{22} $$ Hence, the correct answer is: $$ \boxed{0.0633 \text{ mol; } 3.812 \times 10^{22} \text{ molecules}} $$ So, Option B is correct.

Which of the following is correct set of 4 quantum numbers of $19^{\text {th }}$ electron in Chromium (Atomic number $=24$ ) in accordance with Aufbau principle?
questions.solution: Step 1: Using the Aufbau principle, we fill electrons in the order: $$ 1s,\ 2s,\ 2p,\ 3s,\ 3p,\ 4s,\ 3d,\dots $$ Now let us count electrons one by one up to the $19^{\text{th}}$ electron. $1s^2 \Rightarrow 2$ electrons $2s^2 \Rightarrow 4$ electrons $2p^6 \Rightarrow 10$ electrons $3s^2 \Rightarrow 12$ electrons $3p^6 \Rightarrow 18$ electrons So, the $19^{\text{th}}$ electron enters the $4s$ orbital. For a $4s$ electron: $n=4$ for $s$-orbital, $l=0$ when $l=0$, only possible value of $m$ is $0$ for the first electron in this orbital, $s=+\dfrac{1}{2}$ Thus, the set of four quantum numbers is: $$ n=4,\ l=0,\ m=0,\ s=+\frac{1}{2} $$ So, the correct option is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option D}} $$ Note: Chromium actually has exceptional configuration $[Ar]\,3d^5 4s^1$, but the question clearly says "in accordance with Aufbau principle", so we must place the $19^{\text{th}}$ electron in $4s$.

questions.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: For an ideal gas, heat capacity at constant volume is always greater than the heat capacity at constant pressure.
Statement II: In a constant volume process, no work is produced and all the heat withdrawn goes into the chaotic motion and is reflected by a temperature increase of the ideal gas.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true

questions.solution:
Step 1: For an ideal gas, we know that $$ C_p - C_v = R $$ where $R > 0$. So, $$ C_p > C_v $$ This means Statement I is false, because it says that heat capacity at constant volume is greater than heat capacity at constant pressure. Now look at Statement II. In a constant volume process, $$ \Delta V = 0 $$ So the work done is $$ W = P \Delta V = 0 $$ From the first law of thermodynamics, $$ Q = \Delta U + W $$ Since $W = 0$, $$ Q = \Delta U $$ For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature. Therefore, the heat supplied or withdrawn at constant volume changes the internal energy, which is associated with the random or chaotic motion of molecules, and this is reflected in a change in temperature.

Step 2: So Statement II is true in the NCERT sense. Hence, the correct answer is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option D}} $$ That is, Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.text:
At $\mathrm{T}(\mathrm{K})$, the equilibrium constant of
$\mathrm{A}_2(g)+\mathrm{B}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{C}(g)$ is $2.7 \times 10^{-5}$.
What is the equilibrium constant for
$\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~A}_2(\mathrm{~g})+\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~B}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \rightleftharpoons \frac{1}{3} \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{g})$ at the same temperature?
questions.solution: Step 1: For the reaction $$ \mathrm{A_2(g) + B_2(g) \rightleftharpoons C(g)} $$ the equilibrium constant is given as $$ K = 2.7 \times 10^{-5} $$ Now the new reaction is $$ \frac{1}{3}\mathrm{A_2(g)} + \frac{1}{3}\mathrm{B_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons \frac{1}{3}\mathrm{C(g)} $$ This reaction is obtained by dividing all the coefficients of the original reaction by $3$. According to the rule for equilibrium constants: if the coefficients of a balanced chemical equation are multiplied by $n$, then the new equilibrium constant becomes $K^n$ if the coefficients are divided by $n$, then the new equilibrium constant becomes $K^{1/n}$ So here, $$ K' = K^{1/3} $$ Therefore, $$ K' = \left(2.7 \times 10^{-5}\right)^{1/3} $$ Now calculate: $$ 2.7 = (0.3)^3 \times 100 $$ But it is easier to check directly: $$ (3 \times 10^{-2})^3 = 27 \times 10^{-6} = 2.7 \times 10^{-5} $$ So, $$ \left(2.7 \times 10^{-5}\right)^{1/3} = 3 \times 10^{-2} $$ Hence, the correct answer is: $$ \boxed{3 \times 10^{-2}} $$ So, Option D is correct.

questions.text: In order to oxidise a mixture of 1 mole each of $\mathrm{FeC}_2 \mathrm{O}_4, \mathrm{Fe}_2\left(\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{O}_4\right)_3, \mathrm{FeSO}_4$ and $\mathrm{Fe}_2\left(\mathrm{SO}_4\right)_3$ in acidic medium, the number of moles of $\mathrm{KMnO}_4$ required is
questions.solution: Step 1: In acidic medium, $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ acts as a strong oxidising agent. So, we need to find which species in the given mixture can be oxidised further. The mixture contains $1$ mole each of: $\mathrm{FeC_2O_4}$ $\mathrm{Fe_2(C_2O_4)_3}$ $\mathrm{FeSO_4}$ $\mathrm{Fe_2(SO_4)_3}$ Now let us examine each compound. 1. $\mathrm{FeC_2O_4}$ This is ferrous oxalate, so it contains: $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$: can be oxidised to $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ $\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}$: can be oxidised to $\mathrm{CO_2}$ Oxidation of $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ $$ \mathrm{Fe^{2+} \rightarrow Fe^{3+} + e^-} $$ So, $1$ mole of $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ gives $1$ mole electron. Oxidation of oxalate $$ \mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-} \rightarrow 2CO_2 + 2e^-} $$ So, $1$ mole of $\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}$ gives $2$ moles electrons. Hence, $1$ mole of $\mathrm{FeC_2O_4}$ gives total electrons: $$ 1 + 2 = 3 $$ 2. $\mathrm{Fe_2(C_2O_4)_3}$ This contains: $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$: already in higher oxidation state, so no oxidation $3$ oxalate ions: each can be oxidised Each oxalate ion gives $2$ electrons, so $3$ oxalates give: $$ 3 \times 2 = 6 $$ Thus, $1$ mole of $\mathrm{Fe_2(C_2O_4)_3}$ gives $6$ electrons. 3. $\mathrm{FeSO_4}$ This contains: $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$: can be oxidised to $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$: sulphur is already at maximum oxidation state $+6$, so no oxidation Thus, $1$ mole of $\mathrm{FeSO_4}$ gives: $$ 1 \text{ electron} $$ 4. $\mathrm{Fe_2(SO_4)_3}$ This contains: $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$: cannot be oxidised further here $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$: cannot be oxidised further So, electrons given: $$ 0 $$ Total electrons released $$ 3 + 6 + 1 + 0 = 10 $$ Electrons accepted by $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ in acidic medium In acidic medium: $$ \mathrm{MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O} $$ So, $1$ mole of $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ accepts $5$ moles of electrons. Therefore, moles of $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ required: $$ \frac{10}{5} = 2 $$ Final answer $$ \boxed{2} $$ So, the correct option is Option B.

questions.text:
Consider the first order reaction $\mathrm{R} \rightarrow \mathrm{P}$.
The fraction of molecules decomposed in the given first order reaction can be expressed as
questions.solution: Step 1: For a first order reaction $$ \mathrm{R} \rightarrow \mathrm{P} $$ the integrated rate law is $$ [R]_t = [R]_0 e^{-k_1 t} $$ where: $[R]_0$ = initial concentration of reactant $[R]_t$ = concentration after time $t$ Now, the fraction of molecules left undecomposed after time $t$ is $$ \frac{[R]_t}{[R]_0} = e^{-k_1 t} $$ So, the fraction of molecules decomposed is $$ 1 - \frac{[R]_t}{[R]_0} = 1 - e^{-k_1 t} $$ Hence, the correct answer is $$ \boxed{1 - e^{-k_1 t}} $$ So, Option D is correct.

questions.text: A monoatomic anion $\left(\mathrm{A}^{-}\right)$ has 45 neutrons and 36 electrons. Atomic mass, group in the periodic table and physical state at room temperature of the element (A) respectively are
questions.solution: Step 1: For a monoatomic anion $A^-$: Number of electrons in $A^-$ $= 36$ Since it is an anion with charge $-1$, the neutral atom $A$ must have one electron less. So, number of electrons in neutral atom $A$: $$ 36 - 1 = 35 $$ Hence, atomic number of $A$ is $35$. This element is bromine. Now, number of neutrons $= 45$ So, mass number: $$ \text{Mass number} = \text{protons} + \text{neutrons} = 35 + 45 = 80 $$ Thus, atomic mass number is: $$ 80 $$ Now let us find the group. Bromine $(Z = 35)$ belongs to group 17 in the periodic table. Also, bromine is a liquid at room temperature. So, the correct answer is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option A: } 80,\ 17,\ \text{liquid}} $$

questions.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The covalency of oxygen is generally two but it can exceed upto four. The oxidation state of oxygen in $\mathrm{SO}_2$ is -2 and in $\mathrm{OF}_2$ it is +2.
Statement II: The anomalous behaviour of oxygen when compared to the other elements of group 16 is due to its small size and high electronegativity.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true

questions.solution: Step 1: Analysis of Statement I: Covalency of Oxygen: The electronic configuration of oxygen is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$. In its outermost shell ($n = 2$), it possesses exactly four orbitals available for bonding: one $2s$ orbital and three $2p$ orbitals. Because oxygen is a Period 2 element, it completely lacks empty $d$-orbitals. Consequently, its maximum covalency is restricted to a maximum of 4. While oxygen generally shows a normal covalency of 2 (as seen in $\mathrm{H_2O}$), it can exceed this completely up to 4 in certain scenarios (co-ordinating to maximum four atoms as seen theoretically, and a covalency of 3 is commonly observed in the hydronium ion, $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$). So, the first part of the statement is correct. Oxidation States: In $\mathrm{SO}_2$, oxygen is more electronegative than sulphur. Here, sulphur has an oxidation state of +4, and each oxygen atom securely takes an oxidation state of -2. In $\mathrm{OF}_2$, fluorine is the most electronegative element in the periodic table. Because fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen, each fluorine atom takes an oxidation state of -1. To maintain neutrality in the $\mathrm{OF}_2$ molecule, the oxidation state of oxygen must be +2. Therefore, the second part of the statement is perfectly correct as well. Conclusion: Statement I is true. Analysis of Statement II: In the $p$-block elements, the first member of every group always differs significantly from the heavier members of the same group. According to the NCERT, the anomalous behavior of oxygen compared to the rest of the group 16 elements (like Sulphur, Selenium, etc.) is prominently due to: Its exceptionally small atomic size. Its high electronegativity. The non-availability of $d$-orbitals in its valence shell. Because of its small size and high electronegativity, it readily forms strong $p \pi - p \pi$ double bonds and extensive hydrogen bonds, uniquely distinguishing it from other group elements. The statement accurately lists the main reasons, so it is correct. Conclusion: Statement II is true. Final Conclusion: Since both the provided statements are factually correct based on standard chemical principles, we determine the correct option. Correct Answer: Option A Both Statement I and Statement II are true

questions.text:
The correct statements among the following are,
A. $\mathrm{Mo}(\mathrm{VI})$ and $\mathrm{W}(\mathrm{VI})$ are less stable than $\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{VI})$.
B. $\mathrm{Ce}^{4+}$ and $\mathrm{Tb}^{4+}$ are oxidant while $\mathrm{Eu}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Yb}^{2+}$ are reductant.
C. Cm and Am have seven unpaired electrons.
D. Actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than lanthanoid contraction.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Step 1: Statement A $\mathrm{Mo(VI)}$ and $\mathrm{W(VI)}$ are less stable than $\mathrm{Cr(VI)}$. This statement is incorrect. In group 6 elements: $\mathrm{Cr}$, $\mathrm{Mo}$ and $\mathrm{W}$ commonly show the $+6$ oxidation state. The higher oxidation states become more stable for heavier members of the group. So, $\mathrm{Cr(VI)}$ is strongly oxidising and less stable comparatively, while $\mathrm{Mo(VI)}$ and especially $\mathrm{W(VI)}$ are more stable. Hence, A is false. Statement B $\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}$ and $\mathrm{Tb^{4+}}$ are oxidant while $\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Yb^{2+}}$ are reductant. This statement is correct. Reason: $\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}$ tends to change to $\mathrm{Ce^{3+}}$, so it acts as an oxidising agent. $\mathrm{Tb^{4+}}$ also tends to reduce to $\mathrm{Tb^{3+}}$, so it is an oxidant. $\mathrm{Eu^{2+}}$ tends to change to $\mathrm{Eu^{3+}}$, so it donates electrons and acts as a reducing agent. $\mathrm{Yb^{2+}}$ similarly tends to go to $\mathrm{Yb^{3+}}$, so it is also a reductant. Hence, B is true. Statement C Cm and Am have seven unpaired electrons. This statement is incorrect. Let us see the electronic configurations: $\mathrm{Am}$: $[Rn]\,5f^7 7s^2$ $\mathrm{Cm}$: $[Rn]\,5f^7 6d^1 7s^2$ Now count unpaired electrons: In $\mathrm{Am}$, $5f^7$ gives 7 unpaired electrons In $\mathrm{Cm}$, $5f^7$ gives 7 unpaired, and $6d^1$ gives 1 more unpaired So $\mathrm{Cm}$ has 8 unpaired electrons, not 7. Hence, C is false. Statement D Actinoid contraction is greater from element to element than lanthanoid contraction. This statement is correct. Reason: In actinoids, the $5f$ electrons shield the nuclear charge even more poorly than the $4f$ electrons do in lanthanoids. Therefore, the decrease in atomic and ionic size across actinoids is greater. Hence, D is true. Final conclusion Correct statements are: $$ \boxed{B \text{ and } D \text{ only}} $$ So the correct option is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option C}} $$

questions.text:
Match the LIST-I with LIST-II

LIST I — Complex ion
A. $\left[\mathrm{Cr}\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)_6\right]^{2+}$
B. $\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)_6\right]^{2+}$
C. $\left[\mathrm{Cu}\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)_6\right]^{2+}$
D. $\left[\mathrm{Mn}\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)_6\right]^{2+}$

LIST II — Calculated spin only magnetic moment (BM)
I. 3.87
II. 5.92
III. 4.90
IV. 1.73

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Step 1: For matching, we use the spin-only magnetic moment formula: $$ \mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} \text{ BM} $$ where $n$ = number of unpaired electrons. Since $\mathrm{H_2O}$ is a weak field ligand, all these octahedral complexes will be high spin. Now find oxidation state, electronic configuration, number of unpaired electrons, and then magnetic moment.
A. $\left[\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{H_2O})_6\right]^{2+}$ Here, chromium is in $+2$ oxidation state. Atomic number of Cr = $24$ Neutral Cr: $$ \mathrm{Cr} = [\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1 $$ So, $$ \mathrm{Cr}^{2+} = 3d^4 $$ For high spin $d^4$, number of unpaired electrons: $$ n=4 $$ Thus, $$ \mu = \sqrt{4(4+2)} = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.90 \text{ BM} $$ So, A $\to$ III
B. $\left[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{H_2O})_6\right]^{2+}$ Cobalt is in $+2$ oxidation state. Atomic number of Co = $27$ $$ \mathrm{Co}^{2+} = 3d^7 $$ For high spin $d^7$, number of unpaired electrons: $$ n=3 $$ Thus, $$ \mu = \sqrt{3(3+2)} = \sqrt{15} \approx 3.87 \text{ BM} $$ So, B $\to$ I
C. $\left[\mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{H_2O})_6\right]^{2+}$ Copper is in $+2$ oxidation state. Atomic number of Cu = $29$ $$ \mathrm{Cu}^{2+} = 3d^9 $$ For $d^9$, number of unpaired electrons: $$ n=1 $$ Thus, $$ \mu = \sqrt{1(1+2)} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73 \text{ BM} $$ So, C $\to$ IV
D. $\left[\mathrm{Mn}(\mathrm{H_2O})_6\right]^{2+}$ Manganese is in $+2$ oxidation state. Atomic number of Mn = $25$ $$ \mathrm{Mn}^{2+} = 3d^5 $$ For high spin $d^5$, number of unpaired electrons: $$ n=5 $$ Thus, $$ \mu = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92 \text{ BM} $$ So, D $\to$ II Final matching $$ \boxed{\text{A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II}} $$ So the correct option is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option D}} $$

questions.text:
Increasing order of electron withdrawing power of following functional groups is:
a. -CN
b. -COOH
c. $-\mathrm{NO}_2$
d. $-\mathrm{I}$
questions.solution: Step 1: To understand this question, we need to look at the Inductive effect, specifically the negative inductive effect ($-I$ effect), which determines the electron-withdrawing power of a functional group. According to the principles of organic chemistry laid out in your NCERT textbook, the electron-withdrawing nature of a group depends on the electronegativity of the atoms present in the group and their arrangement. The standard decreasing order of the $-I$ effect (electron-withdrawing power) for various functional groups is: $$ -\mathrm{NO}_2 > -\mathrm{CN} > -\mathrm{COOH} > -\mathrm{F} > -\mathrm{Cl} > -\mathrm{Br} > -\mathrm{I} > -\mathrm{OH} > -\mathrm{OCH}_3 > -\mathrm{C_6H_5} > -\mathrm{H} $$ Let us analyze the functional groups given in the question: $ -\mathrm{NO}_2 $ (c): This group has a nitrogen atom bonded to two highly electronegative oxygen atoms, and the nitrogen carries a formal positive charge. This makes it a very strong electron-withdrawing group. $ -\mathrm{CN} $ (a): The carbon in the cyanide group is $sp$ hybridized, which makes it more electronegative. Coupled with the electronegative nitrogen atom, it exerts a strong $-I$ effect, but it is slightly weaker than $-\mathrm{NO}_2$. $ -\mathrm{COOH} $ (b): This group contains a carbonyl carbon attached to a hydroxyl oxygen. It shows a moderate $-I$ effect, which is weaker than both $-\mathrm{NO}_2$ and $-\mathrm{CN}$. $ -\mathrm{I} $ (d): Iodine is a halogen. While halogens are electronegative, iodine has the largest atomic size and the lowest electronegativity among the common halogens (fluorine, chlorine, bromine). Hence, it has the weakest $-I$ effect out of the groups listed here. Based on this analysis, the decreasing order of their electron-withdrawing power is: $$ \mathrm{c} \ (-\mathrm{NO}_2) > \mathrm{a} \ (-\mathrm{CN}) > \mathrm{b} \ (-\mathrm{COOH}) > \mathrm{d} \ (-\mathrm{I}) $$ Therefore, rearranging them into the increasing order gives: $$ \mathrm{d} This perfectly matches Option C. Correct Answer: Option C $$ \mathrm{d} < \mathrm{b} < \mathrm{a} < \mathrm{c}

questions.text:
Match the LIST-I with LIST-II

LIST I
A. Finkelstein reaction
B. Swarts reaction
C. Sandmeyer's reaction
D. Fittig reaction

LIST II
I. $\mathrm{SbF}_3$
II. Na, dry ether
III. NaI
IV. $\mathrm{Cu}_2 \mathrm{Cl}_2$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Step 1: Finkelstein reaction: This is a halogen exchange reaction used specifically for the preparation of alkyl iodides. In this reaction, alkyl chlorides or bromides are treated with sodium iodide ($ \mathrm{NaI} $) in dry acetone. Therefore, A matches with III.
B. Swarts reaction: This reaction is the preferred method for the synthesis of alkyl fluorides. It involves heating an alkyl chloride or bromide in the presence of a metallic fluoride. Some of the common fluorinating agents used are $ \mathrm{AgF} $, $ \mathrm{Hg}_2\mathrm{F}_2 $, $ \mathrm{CoF}_2 $, or antimony trifluoride ($ \mathrm{SbF}_3 $). Therefore, B matches with I.
C. Sandmeyer's reaction: This reaction is used to prepare haloarenes (like chlorobenzene or bromobenzene) from benzene diazonium chloride. The diazonium salt is treated with a cuprous halide, such as cuprous chloride ($ \mathrm{Cu}_2 \mathrm{Cl}_2 $ or $ \mathrm{CuCl} $), to replace the diazonium group with a halogen. Therefore, C matches with IV.
D. Fittig reaction: This reaction involves aryl halides. When an aryl halide is treated with sodium ($ \mathrm{Na} $) in the presence of dry ether, two aryl groups join together to form a diaryl compound (like biphenyl). Therefore, D matches with II. Summary of Matches: A (Finkelstein reaction) $\rightarrow$ III ($ \mathrm{NaI} $) B (Swarts reaction) $\rightarrow$ I ($ \mathrm{SbF}_3 $) C (Sandmeyer's reaction) $\rightarrow$ IV ($ \mathrm{Cu}_2 \mathrm{Cl}_2 $) D (Fittig reaction) $\rightarrow$ II ($ \mathrm{Na} $, dry ether) Comparing our findings with the given options, the correct combination is A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II. Option B is the correct answer.

questions.text: Amongst the following, the total number of compounds soluble in aqueous NaOH at room temperature is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Aqueous NaOH dissolves a compound at room temperature only if it has an O–H acidic enough to be removed by $\ce{OH-}$, i.e. a phenol ($\mathrm{p}K_a \approx 10$) or a carboxylic acid ($\mathrm{p}K_a \approx 4\text{–}5$); the sodium phenoxide or carboxylate formed is water-soluble. Soluble: II (1-naphthol), III (4-(dimethylamino)phenol) and IV (p-cresol) are phenols; V (benzoic acid) and VII (1-naphthoic acid) are carboxylic acids. Insoluble: I (benzaldehyde) has no acidic H, VI (N,N-dimethylcyclohexylamine) is a base, VIII (1,4-di-tert-butylbenzene) is a hydrocarbon, and IX (1-naphthylmethanol) is an alcohol ($\mathrm{p}K_a \approx 16$), not deprotonated by aqueous NaOH. In IX the OH is on a $\ce{CH2}$ group attached to the ring, so unlike II it is not a phenol. Number of compounds soluble in aqueous NaOH = 5. Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: Given below are two statements: Statement I: The structure of Maltose is given below: Statement II: The structure of Lactose is given below: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Statement I is false but Statement II is true

questions.solution: Step 1: Maltose and lactose are both disaccharides. In each of these structures, one anomeric carbon is used to form the glycosidic linkage, but the other anomeric carbon remains free as a hemiacetal (–OH at anomeric carbon). If a disaccharide has a free hemiacetal group, it can open up to the open-chain form and can reduce mild oxidising agents (like Tollens’ reagent or Fehling’s solution). Therefore, both maltose and lactose are reducing sugars because both contain a hemiacetal linkage (free anomeric carbon).
