questions.text: A thin convex lens and a thin concave lens are kept in contact and are co-axial. Which of the following statements is correct for this combination of two lenses ?

options.text: Focal length of the lens system will change if the positions of two lenses are interchanged

questions.solution:
Step 1: For two thin lenses in contact, the total power P is the sum of their individual powers:
 \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{P}_1+\mathrm{P}_2
 The power of lens is given as $P=\frac{1}{f}$, where $f$ is the focal length of lens in meters.
 \frac{1}{F}=\frac{1}{f_1}+\frac{1}{f_2}
 For a convex lens, the focal length is positive $\Rightarrow \mathrm{f}_1=+\left|\mathrm{f}_{\text {convex }}\right|$. For a concave lens, the focal length is negative $\Rightarrow f_2=-\left|f_{\text {concave }}\right|$. Substituting these into the formula of equivalent power:
 \frac{1}{F}=\frac{1}{\left|f_{\text {convex }}\right|}-\frac{1}{\left|f_{\text {concave }}\right|}

\Rightarrow

 \frac{1}{F}=\frac{\left|f_{\text {concave }}\right|-\left|f_{\text {convex }}\right|}{\left|f_{\text {convex }}\right| \cdot\left|f_{\text {concave }}\right|}
 The combination behaves as a concave lens if the equivalent focal length F is negative ( $\mathrm{F} \left|\mathrm{f}_{\text {concave }}\right|
 Conversely, it behaves as a convex lens if F is positive, which happens when
 \left|\mathrm{f}_{\text {concave }}\right|>\left|\mathrm{f}_{\text {convex }}\right|.
 For thin lenses in contact, the formula $\frac{1}{\mathrm{~F}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}_1}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{f}_2}$ is independent of the order of the lenses. Therefore, interchanging them does not change the focal length. Therefore, the system behaves as a concave lens if $\left|\mathrm{f}_{\text {convex }}\right|>\left|\mathrm{f}_{\text {concave }}\right|. Thus, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: An object $A B$ is placed 15 cm on the left of a convex lens $P$ of focal length 10 cm. Another convex lens $Q$ is now placed 15 cm right of lens $P$. If the focal length of lens $Q$ is 15 cm, the final image is $\_\_\_\_$.

options.text: virtual, formed at 7.5 cm right of lens $Q$, with a size bigger than that of $A B$
real, formed at 7.5 cm right of lens $Q$, with a size same as that of $A B$
real, formed at 7 cm right of lens $Q$, with a size smaller than that of $A B$

questions.solution: Step 1: For lens P: $u_P = -15\ \text{cm}$, $f_P = +10\ \text{cm}$. $$\frac{1}{v_P} = \frac{1}{f_P} + \frac{1}{u_P} = \frac{1}{10} - \frac{1}{15} = \frac{1}{30} \Rightarrow v_P = +30\ \text{cm}$$ $$m_P = \frac{v_P}{u_P} = \frac{30}{-15} = -2$$ Lens Q is 15 cm to the right of P, so the rays leaving P converge towards a point $30 - 15 = 15\ \text{cm}$ to the right of Q. This is a virtual object for Q: $u_Q = +15\ \text{cm}$, $f_Q = +15\ \text{cm}$. $$\frac{1}{v_Q} = \frac{1}{f_Q} + \frac{1}{u_Q} = \frac{1}{15} + \frac{1}{15} = \frac{2}{15} \Rightarrow v_Q = +7.5\ \text{cm}$$ Since $v_Q > 0$, the rays actually meet 7.5 cm to the right of Q, so the final image is real. $$m_Q = \frac{v_Q}{u_Q} = \frac{7.5}{15} = 0.5, \qquad M = m_P\, m_Q = (-2)(0.5) = -1$$ With $|M| = 1$, the final image is real, inverted, 7.5 cm to the right of Q and of the same size as AB. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: The maximum intensity in a Young's double slit experiment is $I_0$. Distance between the slits $(d)$ is $5 \lambda$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength of light used. The intensity of the fringe, exactly opposite to one of the slits on the screen, placed at $D=10 d$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution: Step 1: A point exactly opposite to one of the slits is at a distance $\mathrm{y}=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{2}$ from the central maximum. The slit separation is given as $\mathrm{d}=5 \lambda$ The distance between slits and screen is $\mathrm{D}=10 \mathrm{~d}=50 \lambda$ And the vertical distance of required pointy from the central point is $y=\frac{d}{2}=2.5 \lambda$ For a point on the screen, path difference is approximately: $$ \Delta \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{y} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{~d}}{\mathrm{D}} $$ Substituting the given values: $$ \Delta \mathrm{x}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{2}\right) \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}}{10 \mathrm{~d}}=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{20} $$ Substituting $\mathrm{d}=5 \lambda$: $$ \Delta \mathrm{x}=\frac{5 \lambda}{20}=\frac{\lambda}{4} $$ The relation between phase difference and path difference is: $$ \phi=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \cdot \Delta x $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \phi=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda} \cdot \frac{\lambda}{4}=\frac{\pi}{2}=90^{\circ} $$ The intensity I at a point with phase difference $\phi$ is given by: $$ I=I_0 \cos ^2\left(\frac{\phi}{2}\right) $$ Where $\mathrm{I}_0$ is the maximum intensity of light at the central maxima. Substituting $\phi=\frac{\pi}{2}$: $$ I=I_0 \cos ^2\left(\frac{\pi / 2}{2}\right)=I_0 \cos ^2\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \mathrm{I}=\mathrm{I}_0\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2=\frac{\mathrm{I}_0}{2} $$ Therefore, the intensity of the fringe, exactly opposite to one of the slits on the screen is $\frac{\mathrm{I}_0}{2}$. Thus, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: An electron is travelling with a velocity $v$ in free space and when it enters a medium, its velocity is reduced by $20 \%$. The de Broglie wavelength of electron in the medium is $\alpha \lambda_0$, where $\lambda_0$ is its de Broglie wavelength in free space. The value of $\alpha$ is $\_\_\_\_$.
questions.solution: Step 1: The de Broglie wavelength ( $\lambda$ ) of a particle with mass $m$ and velocity $v$ is given by: $$ \lambda=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{mv}} $$ Where h is Planck's constant. For a particle of constant mass (like an electron), the wavelength is inversely proportional to its velocity: $$ \lambda \propto \frac{1}{v} $$ Let the initial velocity in free space be $\mathrm{v}_0$. The velocity in the medium ( $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{m}}$ ) is reduced by $20 \%$: $$ \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{m}}=\mathrm{v}_0-20 \% \text { of } \mathrm{v}_0=\mathrm{v}_0-0.20 \mathrm{v}_0=0.80 \mathrm{v}_0 $$ Let $\lambda_0$ be the wavelength in free space and $\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}$ be the wavelength in the medium. $$ \frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}}{\lambda_0}=\frac{\mathrm{v}_0}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{m}}} $$ Substituting the value of $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{m}}$: $\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}}{\lambda_0}=\frac{\mathrm{v}_0}{0.80 \mathrm{v}_0}=\frac{1}{0.80}$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{m}}}{\lambda_0}=\frac{100}{80}=1.25$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $\lambda=1.25 \lambda_0=\alpha \lambda_0$ $$\Rightarrow $$$$ \alpha=1.25 $$ Therefore, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
Assuming the experimental mass of ${ }_6^{12} C$ as $12 u$, the mass defect of ${ }_6^{12} C$ atom is $\_\_\_\_$ $\mathrm{MeV} / \mathrm{c}^2$.
(Mass of proton $=1.00727 \mathrm{u}$. mass of neutron $=1.00866 \mathrm{u}, 1 \mathrm{u}=931.5 \mathrm{MeV} / \mathrm{c}^2$ and c is the speed of the light in vacuum).
questions.solution: Step 1: Mass defect $(\Delta \mathrm{m})$ is the difference between the sum of the masses of the individual nucleons (protons and neutrons) and the actual experimental mass of the nucleus. For the atom $\mathrm{C}_6^{12}$, atomic number is $\mathrm{Z}=6$ (Number of protons) Mass number is $\mathrm{A}=12$ Number of neutrons $\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{A}-\mathrm{Z}=12-6=6$ So, mass of 6 protons $=6 \times 1.00727 u=6.04362 u$ And the mass of 6 neutrons $=6 \times 1.00866 u=6.05196 u$ So, total theoretical mass $=6.04362+6.05196=12.09558 \mathrm{u}$ It is given that the experimental mass of $\mathrm{C}_6^{12}=12 \mathrm{u}$: Hence, the mass defect is $$ \Delta \mathrm{m}=\text { (Total theoretical mass) }- \text { (Experimental mass) } $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \Delta \mathrm{m}=12.09558 \mathrm{u}-12 \mathrm{u}=0.09558 \mathrm{u} $$ The energy equivalent of 1 u is given as $931.5 \mathrm{MeV} / \mathrm{c}^2$. $$ \Delta \mathrm{m}\left(\text { in } \mathrm{MeV} / \mathrm{c}^2\right)=0.09558 \times 931.5 $$ $$\Rightarrow $$$$ \Delta \mathrm{m} \approx 89.03277 \approx 89.03 \mathrm{MeV} / \mathrm{c}^{\wedge} 2 $$ Therefore, the mass defect of the $\mathrm{C}_6^{12}$ atom is approximately $89.03 \mathrm{MeV} / \mathrm{c}^2$. Thus, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: In a semiconductor $p$-n diode, the doping concentrations on $p$-side and $n$-side are $10^{15}$ atoms $/ \mathrm{cm}^3$ and $10^{18}$ atoms $/ \mathrm{cm}^3$, respectively. Which one of the following statements is true?

options.text: Widths of depletion region on either side of the interface are equal
The depletion region width is more on p -side compared to that in n -side
The depletion region width is more on $n$-side compared to that in $p$-side
No depletion region forms because of unequal doping concentrations on p and n -sides

questions.solution: Step 1: When a $\mathrm{p}-\mathrm{n}$ junction is formed, holes from the p -side and electrons from the n -side diffuse across the junction, leaving behind immobile ionized dopant atoms. The total negative charge on the p -side of the depletion region must exactly balance the total positive charge on the n -side: $$ \left|Q_p\right|=\left|Q_n\right| $$ The charge in each region is the product of the electronic charge ( e ), the doping concentration and the volume of region (V). $$ \mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{eNV} $$ The volume of region is the product of width of the depletion region ( w ) and the cross-sectional area (A), $$ \mathrm{V}=\mathrm{Aw} $$ So, the charge in each region is $\mathrm{Q}=\mathrm{eNAw}$ On the p -side: $\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{p}}=\mathrm{e} \cdot \mathrm{A} \cdot \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{a}} \cdot \mathrm{w}_{\mathrm{p}} \ldots$ (i) On the n -side: $\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{n}}=\mathrm{q} \cdot \mathrm{A} \cdot \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{d}} \cdot \mathrm{w}_{\mathrm{n}} \ldots$ (ii) Where $w_p$ and $w_n$ are the widths of the depletion layer in the $p$ and $n$ regions, and $N_a$ and $N_d$ are the acceptor and donor concentrations. Equating the two: $$ e A N_a w_p=e A N_d w_n $$ $$\Rightarrow $$ $$ \frac{\mathrm{w}_{\mathrm{p}}}{\mathrm{w}_{\mathrm{n}}}=\frac{\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{d}}}{\mathrm{~N}_{\mathrm{a}}} $$ The acceptor concentration in p -side is $\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{a}}=10^{15}$ atoms $/ \mathrm{cm}^3$ The donor concentration in n -side is $\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{d}}=10^{18}$ atoms $/ \mathrm{cm}^3$ Since $\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{d}}>\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{a}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{p}}>\mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{n}}$. So, the depletion region penetrates deeper into the side that is more lightly doped. Because the p -side has a much lower concentration ( $10^{15}$ ) than the n -side ( $10^{18}$ ), the depletion region width is more on the p-side. Thus, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
How many grams of residue is obtained by heating 2.76 g of silver carbonate?
(Given: Molar mass of $\mathrm{C}, \mathrm{O}$ and Ag are 12, 16 and $108 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ respectively)
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \mathrm{Ag_2CO_3}(s) \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\mathrm{Ag}(s) + \mathrm{CO_2}(g) + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2}(g) $$ From the chemical equation, we can see that carbon dioxide ($ \mathrm{CO_2} $) and oxygen ($ \mathrm{O_2} $) are gases and will easily escape. The only solid residue left behind is silver ($ \mathrm{Ag} $). Next, let us calculate the molar mass of silver carbonate ($ \mathrm{Ag_2CO_3} $) by adding the molar masses of its constituent elements: $$ \text{Molar mass of } \mathrm{Ag_2CO_3} = (2 \times 108) + 12 + (3 \times 16) $$ $$ \text{Molar mass of } \mathrm{Ag_2CO_3} = 216 + 12 + 48 = 276 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} $$ Now, we can find the number of moles of silver carbonate provided in the question. The given mass is $ 2.76 \mathrm{~g} $. $$ \text{Number of moles} = \frac{\text{Given mass}}{\text{Molar mass}} $$ $$ \text{Moles of } \mathrm{Ag_2CO_3} = \frac{2.76 \mathrm{~g}}{276 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}} = 0.01 \mathrm{~mol} $$ Using the stoichiometry from our balanced chemical equation, we know that heating $ 1 \mathrm{~mol} $ of $ \mathrm{Ag_2CO_3} $ yields $ 2 \mathrm{~mol} $ of solid $ \mathrm{Ag} $ residue. Therefore, if we decompose $ 0.01 \mathrm{~mol} $ of $ \mathrm{Ag_2CO_3} $, the number of moles of silver residue produced will be: $$ \text{Moles of residue } (\mathrm{Ag}) = 2 \times 0.01 \mathrm{~mol} = 0.02 \mathrm{~mol} $$ Finally, we convert these moles of silver back to mass in grams. We know the given molar mass of $ \mathrm{Ag} $ is $ 108 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} $. $$ \text{Mass of } \mathrm{Ag} = \text{Moles of } \mathrm{Ag} \times \text{Molar mass of } \mathrm{Ag} $$ $$ \text{Mass of } \mathrm{Ag} = 0.02 \mathrm{~mol} \times 108 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1} = 2.16 \mathrm{~g} $$ The mass of the solid residue obtained is $ 2.16 \mathrm{~g} $. Correct Option: Option B

A. $n=3, l=2, m=+1$

D. $n=5, l=1, m=+1$
E. $n=2, l=1, m=+1$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Step 1: For multi-electron atoms, the energy of an orbital is decided by the $n + l$ rule. The orbital with smaller value of $n+l$ has lower energy. If two orbitals have the same value of $n+l$, then the orbital with smaller $n$ has lower energy. Also, energy does not depend on $m$. Now let us identify each orbital:
A: $n=3,\; l=2$ This is $3d$ $$n+l=3+2=5$$
B: $n=4,\; l=0$ This is $4s$ $$n+l=4+0=4$$
C: $n=6,\; l=1$ This is $6p$ $$n+l=6+1=7$$
D: $n=5,\; l=1$ This is $5p$ $$n+l=5+1=6$$ E: $n=2,\; l=1$ This is $2p$ $$n+l=2+1=3$$ Now arrange in increasing energy: $$ 2p So, $$ \mathrm{E}Hence, the correct answer is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option D}} $$

questions.text:
Identify the correct statements from the following:
A. Heisenberg uncertainty principle is applicable to electrons.
B. The size of $2 p_x$ orbital is less than the size of $3 p_x$ orbital.
C. The energy of 2 s orbital of H atom is equal to the energy of 2 s orbital of Li.
D. The electronic configuration of Cr is $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3 \mathrm{~d}^5 4 \mathrm{~s}^1$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Step 1: Statement A Heisenberg uncertainty principle is applicable to electrons. This statement is correct. According to Heisenberg uncertainty principle, it is impossible to determine simultaneously the exact position and exact momentum of a microscopic particle like an electron. So, A is true. Statement B The size of $2p_x$ orbital is less than the size of $3p_x$ orbital. This statement is correct. As the principal quantum number $n$ increases, the size of the orbital increases. Here, $2p_x$ has $n = 2$ $3p_x$ has $n = 3$ Therefore, size of $3p_x$ orbital is greater than that of $2p_x$ orbital. So, B is true. Statement C The energy of $2s$ orbital of H atom is equal to the energy of $2s$ orbital of Li. This statement is incorrect. For hydrogen atom, energy depends only on principal quantum number $n$. But for multi-electron atoms like lithium, the energy depends on both $n$ and $l$ due to shielding and penetration effects. So, the energy of $2s$ orbital in H and Li is not equal. Thus, C is false. Statement D The electronic configuration of Cr is $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5\,4s^1$ This statement is correct. Chromium is an exception to the expected configuration. Due to extra stability of half-filled $3d$ subshell, its configuration is: $$ [\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^5\,4s^1 $$ So, D is true. Final Answer Correct statements are A, B and D only. Therefore, the correct option is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option B}} $$

questions.text:
What is the mole fraction of water in $10 \%$ by weight $(\mathrm{w} / \mathrm{w})$ of aqueous urea solution?
[Given: Molar mass of $\mathrm{H}, \mathrm{O}, \mathrm{C}$ and N are $1,16,12$ and $14 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ respectively.]
questions.solution: Step 1: For a $10\%$ by weight $(w/w)$ aqueous urea solution, let us take $100 \, \text{g}$ of solution. Then: Mass of urea $= 10 \, \text{g}$ Mass of water $= 90 \, \text{g}$ Now find the molar masses. Urea has formula $NH_2CONH_2$ or $CO(NH_2)_2$ $$ M(\text{urea}) = 12 + 16 + 2(14) + 4(1) = 60 \, \text{g mol}^{-1} $$ Moles of urea: $$ n_{\text{urea}} = \frac{10}{60} = \frac{1}{6} \approx 0.167 $$ Molar mass of water: $$ M(\text{water}) = 2(1) + 16 = 18 \, \text{g mol}^{-1} $$ Moles of water: $$ n_{\text{water}} = \frac{90}{18} = 5 $$ Now, mole fraction of water is $$ X_{\text{water}} = \frac{n_{\text{water}}}{n_{\text{water}} + n_{\text{urea}}} $$ $$ X_{\text{water}} = \frac{5}{5 + \frac{1}{6}} = \frac{5}{\frac{31}{6}} = \frac{30}{31} $$ $$ X_{\text{water}} \approx 0.967 $$ So, the correct answer is: $$ \boxed{0.967} $$ Option D

questions.text: $\mathrm{M}_3 \mathrm{~A}_2$ is a sparingly soluble salt of molar mass $y \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ and solubility $x \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~L}^{-1}$. The ratio of the molar concentration of the anion $\left(\mathrm{A}^{3-}\right)$ to the solubility product of the salt is
questions.solution: Step 1: Given: Solubility of the salt in $\text{g L}^{-1} = x$ Molar mass of the salt in $\text{g mol}^{-1} = y$ The molar solubility $S$ (in $\text{mol L}^{-1}$) is given by: $$ S = \frac{\text{Solubility in g L}^{-1}}{\text{Molar mass}} = \frac{x}{y} $$ Now, let us write the dissociation equation for the sparingly soluble salt $\mathrm{M}_3 \mathrm{A}_2$ in water. According to the stoichiometry, one mole of the salt produces three moles of the cation and two moles of the anion. $$ \mathrm{M}_3\mathrm{A}_2 \rightleftharpoons 3\mathrm{M}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{A}^{3-} $$ If $S$ is the molar solubility of the salt, the equilibrium concentrations of the ions will be: Molar concentration of the cation, $[\mathrm{M}^{2+}] = 3S$ Molar concentration of the anion, $[\mathrm{A}^{3-}] = 2S$ Next, we write the expression for the solubility product constant, $K_{sp}$, which is the product of the molar concentrations of the constituent ions, each raised to the power of its stoichiometric coefficient: $$ K_{sp} = [\mathrm{M}^{2+}]^3 [\mathrm{A}^{3-}]^2 $$ Substituting the equilibrium concentrations into the $K_{sp}$ expression: $$ K_{sp} = (3S)^3 \cdot (2S)^2 $$ $$ K_{sp} = 27S^3 \cdot 4S^2 = 108S^5 $$ We are asked to find the ratio of the molar concentration of the anion $\left(\mathrm{A}^{3-}\right)$ to the solubility product of the salt ($K_{sp}$). Let us set up this ratio: $$ \text{Ratio} = \frac{[\mathrm{A}^{3-}]}{K_{sp}} $$ Substitute $[\mathrm{A}^{3-}] = 2S$ and $K_{sp} = 108S^5$ into the ratio: $$ \text{Ratio} = \frac{2S}{108S^5} $$ $$ \text{Ratio} = \frac{1}{54S^4} $$ Finally, we substitute the value of molar solubility $S = \frac{x}{y}$ back into our ratio: $$ \text{Ratio} = \frac{1}{54 \left( \frac{x}{y} \right)^4} $$ $$ \text{Ratio} = \frac{1}{54} \cdot \frac{y^4}{x^4} $$ Therefore, the ratio of the molar concentration of the anion to the solubility product is $\frac{1}{54} \cdot \frac{y^4}{x^4}$. Option A is the correct answer.

questions.text:
Arrange the following resultant mixtures in increasing order of their pH values
A. $10 \mathrm{~mL} 0.2 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_2+25 \mathrm{~mL} 0.1 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{HCl}$
B. $10 \mathrm{~mL} 0.01 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4+10 \mathrm{~mL} 0.01 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_2$
C. $10 \mathrm{~mL} 0.1 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4+10 \mathrm{~mL} 0.1 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{KOH}$
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Step 1: Mixture
A: The acid is $\mathrm{HCl}$, which furnishes 1 $\mathrm{H}^+$ ion per molecule. $$ \text{Millimoles of } \mathrm{H}^+ = \text{Molarity} \times \text{Volume in mL} \times 1 = 0.1 \times 25 \times 1 = 2.5 \text{ mmol} $$ The base is $\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_2$, which furnishes 2 $\mathrm{OH}^-$ ions per molecule. $$ \text{Millimoles of } \mathrm{OH}^- = \text{Molarity} \times \text{Volume in mL} \times 2 = 0.2 \times 10 \times 2 = 4.0 \text{ mmol} $$ Since the amount of $\mathrm{OH}^-$ ions is greater than $\mathrm{H}^+$ ions ($4.0 > 2.5$), the remaining solution has an excess of $\mathrm{OH}^-$ ions. Therefore, mixture A is basic, which means its pH will be greater than 7. Mixture
B: The acid is $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4$, which furnishes 2 $\mathrm{H}^+$ ions per molecule. $$ \text{Millimoles of } \mathrm{H}^+ = 0.01 \times 10 \times 2 = 0.2 \text{ mmol} $$ The base is $\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_2$, which furnishes 2 $\mathrm{OH}^-$ ions per molecule. $$ \text{Millimoles of } \mathrm{OH}^- = 0.01 \times 10 \times 2 = 0.2 \text{ mmol} $$ Here, the amount of $\mathrm{H}^+$ ions exactly equals the amount of $\mathrm{OH}^-$ ions ($0.2 = 0.2$). This results in complete neutralization. Thus, mixture B is neutral, meaning its pH will be exactly equal to 7. Mixture
C: The acid is $\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4$, furnishing 2 $\mathrm{H}^+$ ions per molecule. $$ \text{Millimoles of } \mathrm{H}^+ = 0.1 \times 10 \times 2 = 2.0 \text{ mmol} $$ The base is $\mathrm{KOH}$, which furnishes 1 $\mathrm{OH}^-$ ion per molecule. $$ \text{Millimoles of } \mathrm{OH}^- = 0.1 \times 10 \times 1 = 1.0 \text{ mmol} $$ Since the amount of $\mathrm{H}^+$ ions is greater than $\mathrm{OH}^-$ ions ($2.0 > 1.0$), there is an excess of $\mathrm{H}^+$ ions in the solution. Therefore, mixture C is acidic, meaning its pH will be down, specifically less than 7. Final Conclusion: Now, let us bring it all together and arrange them in increasing order of their pH values (from most acidic to most basic): Mixture C is acidic ($\mathrm{pH} Mixture B is neutral ($\mathrm{pH} = 7$) Mixture A is basic ($\mathrm{pH} > 7$) The increasing order of their pH values is $\mathrm{C} Therefore, the correct answer is Option C.

questions.text:
First order gas phase reaction
$ \mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{~B}+\mathrm{C} $
$p_i=$ initial pressure of gas $\mathrm{A}, p_t=$ total pressure of the reaction mixture at time $t$
Expression of rate constant ( $k$ ) is
questions.solution: Step 1: So, total pressure at time $t$ is $$ p_t = (p_i - x) + x + x = p_i + x $$ Hence, $$ x = p_t - p_i $$ Now pressure of $\mathrm{A}$ at time $t$ is $$ p_A = p_i - x $$ Substituting $x = p_t - p_i$: $$ p_A = p_i - (p_t - p_i) = 2p_i - p_t $$ For a first-order reaction, $$ k = \frac{1}{t} \ln \frac{[\mathrm{A}]_0}{[\mathrm{A}]_t} $$ Since pressure is proportional to concentration for gases, $$ k = \frac{1}{t} \ln \frac{p_i}{2p_i - p_t} $$ Therefore, the correct expression is $$ \boxed{k = \frac{1}{t} \ln \frac{p_i}{2p_i - p_t}} $$ So, the correct option is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option A}} $$

questions.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The correct order of electronegativity of fluorine, oxygen and nitrogen is $\mathrm{F}>\mathrm{O}>\mathrm{N}$.
Statement II: The oxidation state of oxygen in $\mathrm{OF}_2$ is +2 and in $\mathrm{Na}_2 \mathrm{O}$ is -2.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true

questions.solution: Step 1: Statement I: Electronegativity generally increases across a period from left to right. For the elements nitrogen, oxygen, and fluorine in the second period, the correct order is $$ \mathrm{F} > \mathrm{O} > \mathrm{N} $$ So, Statement I is true. Statement II: Let us check the oxidation state of oxygen in both compounds. In $\mathrm{OF}_2$ Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so its oxidation state is always $-1$. Let the oxidation state of oxygen be $x$. Then, $$ x + 2(-1) = 0 $$ $$ x - 2 = 0 $$ $$ x = +2 $$ So, in $\mathrm{OF}_2$, oxygen has oxidation state $+2$. In $\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{O}$ Sodium has oxidation state $+1$. Let the oxidation state of oxygen be $x$. Then, $$ 2(+1) + x = 0 $$ $$ 2 + x = 0 $$ $$ x = -2 $$ So, in $\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{O}$, oxygen has oxidation state $-2$. Hence, Statement II is also true. Therefore, the correct answer is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option A}} $$ Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.text:
Correct statements from the following are:
A. Nitrogen in oxidation states from +1 to +4 disproportionates in acid medium.
B. Nitrogen has the ability to form $\mathrm{d} \pi$ - $\mathrm{p} \pi$ multiple bonds with itself and other elements with small size and high electronegativity.
C. N-N single bond is stronger than P-P single bond.
D. Nitrogen has highest density in its group due to small size.
E. The maximum covalency of nitrogen is four since it has only four valence orbitals for bonding.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Step 1: Statement
A: Nitrogen in oxidation states from $+1$ to $+4$ disproportionates in acid medium. This statement is correct. All oxidation states of nitrogen from $+1$ to $+4$ tend to undergo disproportionation reactions in an acidic solution. For example, nitrous acid, in which nitrogen is in the $+3$ oxidation state, disproportionates into nitric acid ($+5$) and nitric oxide ($+2$): $$ 3\mathrm{HNO}_2 \rightarrow \mathrm{HNO}_3 + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + 2\mathrm{NO} $$ Statement
B: Nitrogen has the ability to form $\mathrm{d} \pi$ - $\mathrm{p} \pi$ multiple bonds with itself and other elements with small size and high electronegativity. This statement is incorrect. The valence shell electronic configuration of nitrogen is $2\mathrm{s}^2 2\mathrm{p}^3$. Since nitrogen belongs to the second period, it does not possess any empty d-orbitals in its valence shell. Due to the absence of d-orbitals, nitrogen can readily form $\mathrm{p} \pi$ - $\mathrm{p} \pi$ multiple bonds, but it is physically impossible for it to form $\mathrm{d} \pi$ - $\mathrm{p} \pi$ bonds. Statement
C: N-N single bond is stronger than P-P single bond. This statement is incorrect. The single N-N bond is actually weaker than the single P-P bond. Nitrogen atoms are very small, which results in a short N-N bond length. This brings the non-bonding electron pairs (lone pairs) on the two bonded nitrogen atoms very close to each other, leading to high interelectronic repulsion that weakens the chemical bond. Statement
D: Nitrogen has highest density in its group due to small size. This statement is incorrect. As we move down Group 15 from nitrogen to bismuth, the atomic mass increases at a greater rate than the atomic volume. As a result, density smoothly increases down the group. Nitrogen is a diatomic gas at room temperature and has the lowest density in the group, whereas bismuth is a solid and possesses the highest density. Statement E: The maximum covalency of nitrogen is four since it has only four valence orbitals for bonding. This statement is correct. The valence shell of nitrogen consists of only four orbitals available for bonding: one $\mathrm{s}$ orbital ($2\mathrm{s}$) and three $\mathrm{p}$ orbitals ($2\mathrm{p}_x, 2\mathrm{p}_y, 2\mathrm{p}_z$). Without any d-orbitals available to expand its octet, nitrogen is strictly restricted to a maximum covalency of four. Through our step-by-step analysis, we have found that only statements A and E are correct. Correct Answer: Option D (A and E Only)

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a physical or chemical characteristics of interstitial compounds?

options.text: They have high melting points, higher than those of pure metals.
They are very soft and ionic in nature.

Step 1: Interstitial compounds (for example $\ce{TiC}$, $\ce{Mn4N}$, $\ce{Fe3H}$) form when small atoms such as H, C, N or B occupy the interstitial sites of a metal lattice. They have very high melting points (higher than the pure metals), are very hard (some borides approach diamond in hardness), retain metallic conductivity and are chemically inert; they are usually non-stoichiometric.

Step 2: So (A), (
C) and (
D) are characteristics. They are hard, not soft, and the metallic lattice and bonding are retained, so they are not ionic: (
B) is not a characteristic. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
The correct statements about metal carbonyls are
A. The metal-carbon bonds in metal carbonyls possess both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ character.
B. Due to synergic bonding interactions between metal and CO ligand, the metal-carbon bond becomes weak.
C. The metal-carbon $\sigma$ bond is formed by the donation of lone pair of electrons on the carbonyl carbon into a vacant orbital of metal.
D. The metal-carbon $\pi$ bond is formed by the donation of electrons from filled d-orbital of metal into vacant $\pi^*$ orbital of CO.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Step 1: In metal carbonyls, bonding between the metal and CO ligand is explained by synergic bonding. Statement A The metal-carbon bond in metal carbonyls has both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ character. This is correct. CO donates a lone pair from carbon to the metal, forming a $\sigma$ bond. The metal donates electron density back to CO into its vacant $\pi^*$ orbital, forming a $\pi$ bond. So, the bond has both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ character. Statement B Due to synergic bonding interactions between metal and CO ligand, the metal-carbon bond becomes weak. This is incorrect. Synergic bonding actually strengthens the metal-carbon bond because: CO donates electrons to metal by $\sigma$ donation. Metal donates electrons back to CO by $\pi$ back bonding. These two processes reinforce each other, so the M–C bond becomes stronger, not weaker. Statement C The metal-carbon $\sigma$ bond is formed by donation of lone pair of electrons on the carbonyl carbon into a vacant orbital of metal. This is correct. This is exactly the $\sigma$ donation from CO to the metal. Statement D The metal-carbon $\pi$ bond is formed by donation of electrons from filled $d$-orbital of metal into vacant $\pi^*$ orbital of CO. This is correct. This is called $\pi$ back bonding or back donation.

Step 2: So the correct statements are: $$ A,\ C,\ \text{and}\ D $$ Hence, the correct answer is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option B}} $$

Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Each electron in $\mathrm{e}_{\mathrm{g}}$ orbitals destabilizes the orbitals by $+0.6 \Delta_{\mathrm{o}}$ and each electron in the $t_{2 g}$ orbitals stabilizes the orbitals by $-0.4 \Delta_0$ in an octahedral field on the basis of crystal field theory.
Statement II: All the d - orbitals of the transition metals have the same energy in their free atomic state but when a complex is formed the ligands destroy the degeneracy of these orbitals on the basis of crystal field theory.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

questions.solution: Step 1: In an octahedral field the five degenerate $d$ orbitals split into a lower $t_{2g}$ set (three orbitals) and an upper $e_g$ set (two orbitals), separated by $\Delta_o$, with the barycentre unchanged. If $t_{2g}$ is lowered by $x$ and $e_g$ raised by $y$, then $3x = 2y$ and $x + y = \Delta_o$, giving $x = 0.4\Delta_o$ and $y = 0.6\Delta_o$. Each $e_g$ electron therefore destabilises by $+0.6\Delta_o$ and each $t_{2g}$ electron stabilises by $-0.4\Delta_o$, so Statement I is correct. In the free metal atom or ion all five $d$ orbitals have the same energy; the approaching ligands repel electrons in different $d$ orbitals to different extents and remove this degeneracy, so Statement II is correct. Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: On the basis of inductive effect, the order of stability of alkyl carbanions is $\mathrm{CH}_3{ }^{-}>\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2{ }^{-}>\left(\mathrm{CH}_3\right)_2 \mathrm{CH}^{-}>\left(\mathrm{CH}_3\right)_3 \mathrm{C}^{-}$.
Statement II: Allyl and benzyl carbanions are more stabilised by inductive effect and not by resonance effect.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

questions.solution: Step 1: An alkyl group releases electrons by $+I$ effect, which intensifies the negative charge on the carbanionic carbon and destabilises it; each extra alkyl group adds to this destabilisation. $$\ce{CH3^-} > \ce{CH3CH2^-} > \ce{(CH3)2CH^-} > \ce{(CH3)3C^-}$$ So Statement I is correct. In the allyl carbanion $\ce{CH2=CH-CH2^-}$ the negative charge is delocalised by resonance onto the terminal carbon C-3, and in the benzyl carbanion $\ce{C6H5CH2^-}$ it is delocalised onto the ortho and para ring carbons. Their extra stability comes from resonance, not from inductive effect, so Statement II is incorrect. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
" P " is a hydrocarbon of molecular formula:- $\mathrm{C}_8 \mathrm{H}_{14}$. On ozonolysis, " P " forms "Q". "Q" on treatment with alkali under reflux condition produces "R", which on treatment with $\mathrm{I}_2 / \mathrm{NaOH}$ gives a yellow precipitate. Acidification of the solution gives "S". The structure of "S" is given below:-
The correct structure of P is
questions.solution: Step 1: S is 2-methylcyclopent-1-ene-1-carboxylic acid. The yellow precipitate with $\ce{I2}$/NaOH (iodoform) shows that R is a methyl ketone, so R is 1-acetyl-2-methylcyclopent-1-ene; the haloform reaction turns its $\ce{COCH3}$ group into $\ce{COO^-}$ (S after acidification) and $\ce{CHI3}$. R is formed from Q by alkali under reflux, an intramolecular aldol condensation, so Q is the diketone $\ce{CH3CO(CH2)4COCH3}$ (octane-2,7-dione). The enolate at C-3 attacks the C-7 carbonyl to close a five-membered ring, and dehydration gives the ring C=C conjugated with the acetyl group, with $\ce{CH3}$ (C-8) on the other alkene carbon. Q has both carbonyl carbons in one chain of eight carbons, so it comes from ozonolysis of a ring C=C whose two carbons each carry a $\ce{CH3}$. P is therefore 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene, $\ce{C8H14}$ (one ring and one C=C). $$\ce{C8H14 ->[(i) O3][(ii) Zn/H2O] CH3CO(CH2)4COCH3}$$ Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
For the following Friedel Craft's alkylation reaction, which of the statements are correct?
A. Major product is n-propyl benzene.
B. iso-propyl carbocation intermediate is also generated.
C. Multiple substitution is inevitable.
D. Introducing electron-donating substituent on benzene will not produce any alkyl benzene.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Step 1: With anhydrous $\ce{AlCl3}$, 1-chloropropane gives the primary n-propyl carbocation, which rearranges by a 1,2-hydride shift to the more stable secondary isopropyl carbocation; this attacks benzene: The major product is therefore isopropylbenzene (cumene), not n-propylbenzene: A is false and B is true. The alkyl group introduced activates the ring (+I effect and hyperconjugation), so the alkylbenzene is more reactive than benzene and further alkylation takes place: C is true. An electron-donating substituent raises the electron density of the ring and makes Friedel–Crafts alkylation faster, so alkylbenzenes are still formed: D is false. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
Identify the correct statements.
A. Glucose exists in two anomeric forms.
B. Anomers of glucose differ in configuration at $\mathrm{C}-1$ in cyclic hemiacetal structure.
C. Melting point of $\alpha$ - anomer of glucose is greater than $\beta$ - anomer.
D. Specific rotation of $\alpha$ - anomer is $+19^{\circ}$ while for $\beta$ - anomer is $+112^{\circ}$
E. $\alpha$ and $\beta$ - anomers of glucose are prepared by crystallization of saturated glucose solution at 303 K and 371 K respectively.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Step 1: Statement
A: Glucose exists in two anomeric forms. This statement is correct. Glucose exists in two different crystalline forms, which are named as the $\alpha$-form and the $\beta$-form. These are known as anomers. Statement
B: Anomers of glucose differ in configuration at $\mathrm{C}-1$ in cyclic hemiacetal structure. This statement is correct. The $\alpha$ and $\beta$ forms of glucose are cyclic hemiacetals that differ only in the spatial arrangement of the hydroxyl group (-OH) at the first carbon atom ($\mathrm{C}-1$). This specific carbon is referred to as the anomeric carbon. Statement
C: Melting point of $\alpha$ - anomer of glucose is greater than $\beta$ - anomer. This statement is incorrect. According to experimental data, the melting point of the $\alpha$-form of glucose is $419 \text{ K}$, whereas the melting point of the $\beta$-form is slightly higher, at $423 \text{ K}$. Therefore, the melting point of the $\beta$-anomer is greater than that of the $\alpha$-anomer. Statement
D: Specific rotation of $\alpha$ - anomer is $+19^{\circ}$ while for $\beta$ - anomer is $+112^{\circ}$ This statement is incorrect because the values are interchanged. The specific rotation of the pure $\alpha$-anomer is $+112.2^{\circ}$, and the specific rotation of the pure $\beta$-anomer is $+19.2^{\circ}$. Over time, both undergo mutarotation to reach an equilibrium specific rotation of $+52.5^{\circ}$. Statement E: $\alpha$ and $\beta$ - anomers of glucose are prepared by crystallization of saturated glucose solution at 303 K and 371 K respectively. This statement is correct. The $\alpha$-form is typically obtained by the crystallization from a concentrated aqueous solution of glucose at room temperature, around $303 \text{ K}$. On the other hand, the $\beta$-form is obtained by crystallizing it from a hot and saturated aqueous solution at $371 \text{ K}$. From the analysis above, the mathematically and factually correct statements are A, B, and E. Therefore, the correct choice is Option D.

questions.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Sodium dichromate and potassium dichromate are classified as primary standards in titrimetric analysis.
Statement II: Phenolphthalein is a weak base, therefore it dissociates in acidic medium.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are ture
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true

questions.solution: Step 1: Analysis of Statement I: In titrimetric analysis, a primary standard is a substance of high purity that is stable and not hygroscopic, meaning its exact mass can be weighed directly to prepare a standard solution. According to NCERT, potassium dichromate ($K_2Cr_2O_7$) is stable and non-hygroscopic, making it a good primary standard. However, sodium dichromate ($Na_2Cr_2O_7$) is highly hygroscopic (deliquescent). It readily absorbs moisture from the atmosphere, which changes its mass continuously. Due to this property, it cannot be weighed accurately to prepare a standard solution. Therefore, sodium dichromate is not classified as a primary standard. Because of the incorrect claim about sodium dichromate, Statement I is false. Analysis of Statement II: Phenolphthalein is an indicator widely used in acid-base titrations. Chemically, it is a weak organic acid, not a weak base. We often represent it as $HPh$. Since phenolphthalein is a weak acid, its dissociation is governed by the following equilibrium: $$HPh \rightleftharpoons H^+ + Ph^-$$ In an acidic medium, there is already an excess of hydrogen ions ($H^+$). According to Le Chatelier's principle (specifically the common ion effect), the high concentration of $H^+$ suppresses the dissociation of the weak acid $HPh$, causing it to remain mostly in its undissociated, colourless form. It is in a basic medium that phenolphthalein actually dissociates to form the pink-coloured $Ph^-$ ion. Because phenolphthalein is a weak acid and does not dissociate significantly in an acidic medium, Statement II is false. Conclusion: Since both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect, the correct option is Option B. Correct Answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false

questions.text: Let $a, b \in \mathbb{C}$. Let $\alpha, \beta$ be the roots of the equation $x^2+a x+b=0$. If $\beta-\alpha=\sqrt{11}$ and $\beta^2-\alpha^2=3 i \sqrt{11}$, then $\left(\beta^3-\alpha^3\right)^2$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: Given: $\alpha,\beta$ are roots of $x^2+ax+b=0$ $\beta-\alpha=\sqrt{11}$ $\beta^2-\alpha^2=3i\sqrt{11}$ We have to find $\left(\beta^3-\alpha^3\right)^2$. Now, $$ \beta^2-\alpha^2=(\beta-\alpha)(\beta+\alpha) $$ Substituting the given values, $$ 3i\sqrt{11}=\sqrt{11}(\beta+\alpha) $$ Since $\sqrt{11}\neq 0$, we get $$ \beta+\alpha=3i $$ Now use the identity $$ \beta^3-\alpha^3=(\beta-\alpha)(\beta^2+\alpha\beta+\alpha^2) $$ So first let us find $\beta^2+\alpha\beta+\alpha^2$. We know $$ (\beta+\alpha)^2=\beta^2+\alpha^2+2\alpha\beta $$ Also, $$ \alpha\beta=\frac{(\alpha+\beta)^2-(\beta-\alpha)^2}{4} $$ Substitute the values: $$ \alpha+\beta=3i,\qquad \beta-\alpha=\sqrt{11} $$ Thus, $$ \alpha\beta=\frac{(3i)^2-(\sqrt{11})^2}{4} =\frac{-9-11}{4} =\frac{-20}{4} =-5 $$ Now, $$ \alpha^2+\beta^2=(\alpha+\beta)^2-2\alpha\beta $$ So, $$ \alpha^2+\beta^2=(3i)^2-2(-5)=-9+10=1 $$ Hence, $$ \beta^2+\alpha\beta+\alpha^2=1+(-5)=-4 $$ Therefore, $$ \beta^3-\alpha^3=(\beta-\alpha)(\beta^2+\alpha\beta+\alpha^2) =\sqrt{11}\cdot(-4) =-4\sqrt{11} $$ Now square it: $$ \left(\beta^3-\alpha^3\right)^2=\left(-4\sqrt{11}\right)^2=16\cdot 11=176 $$ So the correct answer is: $$ \boxed{176} $$ Hence, Option B is correct.

questions.text: Let the sum of the first $n$ terms of an A.P. be $3 n^2+5 n$. Then the sum of squares of the first 10 terms of the A.P. is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Given, $$ S_n = 3n^2 + 5n $$ where $S_n$ is the sum of the first $n$ terms of the A.P. To get the $n$th term, we use $$ a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} $$ So, $$ S_{n-1} = 3(n-1)^2 + 5(n-1) $$ $$ = 3(n^2 - 2n + 1) + 5n - 5 $$ $$ = 3n^2 - 6n + 3 + 5n - 5 $$ $$ = 3n^2 - n - 2 $$ Now, $$ a_n = (3n^2 + 5n) - (3n^2 - n - 2) $$ $$ a_n = 6n + 2 $$ So the terms of the A.P. are: $$ 8,\ 14,\ 20,\dots $$ Now we need the sum of squares of the first $10$ terms: $$ \sum_{n=1}^{10} (6n+2)^2 $$ Expand: $$ (6n+2)^2 = 36n^2 + 24n + 4 $$ So, $$ \sum_{n=1}^{10} (6n+2)^2 = 36\sum_{n=1}^{10} n^2 + 24\sum_{n=1}^{10} n + 4\sum_{n=1}^{10} 1 $$ Now use the standard sums: $$ \sum_{n=1}^{10} n^2 = \frac{10 \cdot 11 \cdot 21}{6} = 385 $$ $$ \sum_{n=1}^{10} n = \frac{10 \cdot 11}{2} = 55 $$ $$ \sum_{n=1}^{10} 1 = 10 $$ Substitute: $$ 36(385) + 24(55) + 4(10) $$ $$ = 13860 + 1320 + 40 $$ $$ = 15220 $$ So the correct answer is $$ \boxed{15220} $$ Option C

questions.text:
Let A be a $3 \times 3$ matrix such that
$ \mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\left[\begin{array}{l} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l} 5 \\ 2 \\ 2 \end{array}\right], \mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\left[\begin{array}{l} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l} 3 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right], \mathrm{A}\left[\begin{array}{l} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l} 3 \\ 4 \\ 4 \end{array}\right] \text { and } \mathrm{A}\left[\begin{array}{l} 0 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}{l} 1 \\ 3 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]. $
If $\operatorname{det}(A)=1$, then $\operatorname{det}\left(\operatorname{adj}\left(A^2+A\right)\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Step 1: $A^{T}(0,0,1)^{T}$ is the third row of $A$, and $A^{T}(1,0,1)^{T}$ is the sum of the first and third rows.

Step 2: So the third row is $(3,1,1)$ and the first row is $(5,2,2)-(3,1,1) = (2,1,1)$. Similarly, $A(0,0,1)^{T} = (1,3,1)^{T}$ is the third column, and the first column is $(3,4,4)^{T}-(1,3,1)^{T} = (2,1,3)^{T}$. Only the middle entry $b$ remains unknown: $$A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 1\ 1 & b & 3\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$$ $$\det A = 2(b-3)-1(1-9)+1(1-3b) = 3-b = 1 \Rightarrow b = 2$$ $$A+I = \begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & 1\ 1 & 3 & 3\ 3 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}, \qquad \det(A+I) = 3(6-3)-1(2-9)+1(1-9) = 9+7-8 = 8$$ Since $A^{2}+A = A(A+I)$, $\det(A^{2}+A) = \det A \cdot \det(A+I) = 1\times 8 = 8$. For a $3\times 3$ matrix $M$, $\det(\operatorname{adj} M) = (\det M)^{2}$, so $\det\left(\operatorname{adj}(A^{2}+A)\right) = 8^{2} = 64$. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
Consider the system of linear equations in $x, y, z$:
$ \begin{aligned} & x+2 y+t z=0 \\ & 6 x+y+5 t z=0 \\ & 3 x+t^2 y+f(t) z=0 \end{aligned} $
where $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is a differentiable function. If this system has infinitely many solutions for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f$
questions.solution: Step 1: For a homogeneous system of three linear equations in $x,y,z$ to have infinitely many solutions, the coefficient matrix must be singular for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$. So, we form the coefficient matrix: $$ A= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & t\ 6 & 1 & 5t\ 3 & t^2 & f(t) \end{pmatrix} $$ Since the system has infinitely many solutions for all $t$, we must have $$ \det(A)=0 \quad \text{for all } t \in \mathbb{R}. $$ Now compute the determinant. $$ \det(A)= \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 & t\ 6 & 1 & 5t\ 3 & t^2 & f(t) \end{vmatrix} $$ Expanding along the first row, $$ \det(A)= 1\begin{vmatrix}1&5t\ t^2&f(t)\end{vmatrix} -2\begin{vmatrix}6&5t\ 3&f(t)\end{vmatrix} +t\begin{vmatrix}6&1\ 3&t^2\end{vmatrix} $$ Now evaluate each minor: $$ \begin{vmatrix}1&5t\ t^2&f(t)\end{vmatrix} = f(t)-5t^3 $$ $$ \begin{vmatrix}6&5t\ 3&f(t)\end{vmatrix} = 6f(t)-15t $$ $$ \begin{vmatrix}6&1\ 3&t^2\end{vmatrix} = 6t^2-3 $$ So, $$ \det(A)=\big(f(t)-5t^3\big)-2\big(6f(t)-15t\big)+t(6t^2-3) $$ $$ = f(t)-5t^3-12f(t)+30t+6t^3-3t $$ $$ = -11f(t)+t^3+27t $$ Since this is zero for all $t$, $$ -11f(t)+t^3+27t=0 $$ Hence, $$ f(t)=\frac{t^3+27t}{11} $$ Now differentiate: $$ f'(t)=\frac{3t^2+27}{11} =\frac{3(t^2+9)}{11} $$ Since $t^2+9>0$ for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$, we get $$ f'(t)>0 \quad \text{for all } t\in\mathbb{R}. $$ Therefore, $f$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$. Hence, the correct option is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option B}} $$
questions.topic: Solutions of System of Linear Equations in Two or Three Variables using Determinants and Matrices

questions.text: $\sum_{n=1}^{10}\left(\frac{528}{n(n+1)(n+2)}\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Step 1: $ S=\sum_{n=1}^{10}\frac{528}{n(n+1)(n+2)} $ We will simplify the general term using partial fractions.

Step 1: Use the standard identity $ \frac{1}{n(n+1)(n+2)}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{n(n+1)}-\frac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)}\right) $ So, $ \frac{528}{n(n+1)(n+2)} =528\cdot \frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{n(n+1)}-\frac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)}\right) $ $ =264\left(\frac{1}{n(n+1)}-\frac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)}\right) $ Hence, $ S=264\sum_{n=1}^{10}\left(\frac{1}{n(n+1)}-\frac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)}\right) $ Step 2: Write a few terms $ S=264\Bigg[\left(\frac{1}{1\cdot 2}-\frac{1}{2\cdot 3}\right) +\left(\frac{1}{2\cdot 3}-\frac{1}{3\cdot 4}\right) +\left(\frac{1}{3\cdot 4}-\frac{1}{4\cdot 5}\right) +\cdots +\left(\frac{1}{10\cdot 11}-\frac{1}{11\cdot 12}\right)\Bigg] $ Now the middle terms cancel out telescopically.

Step 3: So we get $ S=264\left(\frac{1}{1\cdot 2}-\frac{1}{11\cdot 12}\right) $ $ S=264\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{132}\right) $ Take LCM: $ \frac{1}{2}=\frac{66}{132} $ So, $ \frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{132}=\frac{66-1}{132}=\frac{65}{132} $ Therefore, $ S=264\cdot \frac{65}{132} $ $ S=2\cdot 65=130 $ $ \boxed{130} $ So, the correct option is Option B.

questions.text: Let $\tan A, \tan B$, where $A, B \in\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, be the roots of the quadratic equation $x^2-2 x-5=0$. Then $20 \sin ^2\left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: Let the roots of the equation $$ x^2-2x-5=0 $$ be $\tan A$ and $\tan B$. So, by using relations between roots and coefficients, $$ \tan A+\tan B=2 $$ and $$ \tan A \tan B=-5. $$ We have to find $$ 20\sin^2\left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right). $$ First, find $\tan(A+B)$ using the formula $$ \tan(A+B)=\frac{\tan A+\tan B}{1-\tan A\tan B}. $$ Substituting the values: $$ \tan(A+B)=\frac{2}{1-(-5)}=\frac{2}{6}=\frac{1}{3}. $$ Now let $$ \theta=A+B. $$ Then $$ \tan\theta=\frac{1}{3}. $$ We need $\sin^2 \frac{\theta}{2}$. Using the identity $$ \sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}=\frac{1-\cos\theta}{2}, $$ we first find $\cos\theta$. Since $$ \tan\theta=\frac{1}{3}, $$ take a right triangle with opposite side $1$, adjacent side $3$. Then hypotenuse is $$ \sqrt{1^2+3^2}=\sqrt{10}. $$ So, $$ \cos\theta=\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}. $$ Hence, $$ \sin^2\frac{\theta}{2} = \frac{1-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}}{2}. $$ Therefore, $$ 20\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2} = 20\cdot \frac{1-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}}{2} = 10\left(1-\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\right) = 10-\frac{30}{\sqrt{10}}. $$ Now simplify: $$ \frac{30}{\sqrt{10}}=3\sqrt{10}. $$ So, $$ 20\sin^2\left(\frac{A+B}{2}\right)=10-3\sqrt{10}. $$ Therefore, the correct answer is $$ \boxed{10-3\sqrt{10}} $$ So, Option C is correct.

questions.text: A letter is known to have arrived by post either from KANPUR or from ANANTPUR. On the envelope just two consecutive letters AN are visible. The probability, that the letter came from ANANTPUR, is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Let $A$ = event that the letter came from ANANTPUR $K$ = event that the letter came from KANPUR $B$ = event that on the envelope, the two visible consecutive letters are AN We have to find: $$ P(A \mid B) $$ Using Bayes’ theorem, $$ P(A \mid B)=\frac{P(A)\,P(B\mid A)}{P(A)\,P(B\mid A)+P(K)\,P(B\mid K)} $$ Since the letter is known to have come either from ANANTPUR or KANPUR, and no other information is given, we take $$ P(A)=P(K)=\frac{1}{2} $$ So, $$ P(A \mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)}{P(B\mid A)+P(B\mid K)} $$ Now we find these probabilities. 1. Probability of seeing AN in ANANTPUR Word: ANANTPUR Its consecutive pairs are: $$ AN,\ NA,\ AN,\ NT,\ TP,\ PU,\ UR $$ There are $7$ consecutive pairs in all, and AN occurs $2$ times. Therefore, $$ P(B\mid A)=\frac{2}{7} $$ 2. Probability of seeing AN in KANPUR Word: KANPUR Its consecutive pairs are: $$ KA,\ AN,\ NP,\ PU,\ UR $$ There are $5$ consecutive pairs in all, and AN occurs $1$ time. Therefore, $$ P(B\mid K)=\frac{1}{5} $$ 3. Apply Bayes’ theorem $$ P(A \mid B)=\frac{\frac{2}{7}}{\frac{2}{7}+\frac{1}{5}} $$ Take LCM: $$ \frac{2}{7}+\frac{1}{5}=\frac{10+7}{35}=\frac{17}{35} $$ So, $$ P(A \mid B)=\frac{\frac{2}{7}}{\frac{17}{35}} =\frac{2}{7}\cdot\frac{35}{17} =\frac{10}{17} $$ Therefore, the required probability is $$ \boxed{\frac{10}{17}} $$ So, the correct option is B.

questions.text:
The mean deviation about the mean for the data
$ \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline x_i & 5 & 7 & 9 & 10 & 12 & 15 \\ \hline f_i & 8 & 6 & 2 & 2 & 2 & 6 \\ \hline \end{array} $
is equal to:
questions.solution:
Step 1: For a discrete frequency distribution, the mean deviation about the mean is $$ \text{M.D. about mean}=\frac{\sum f_i |x_i-\bar{x}|}{\sum f_i} $$ First, find the mean $\bar{x}$.

Step 1: Calculate $\sum f_i$ and $\sum f_i x_i$ |c|c|c|c| x_i , f_i , f_i x_i \ 5 , 8 , 40 \ 7 , 6 , 42 \ 9 , 2 , 18 \ 10 , 2 , 20 \ 12 , 2 , 24 \ 15 , 6 , 90 \ Now, $$ \sum f_i = 8+6+2+2+2+6=26 $$ and $$ \sum f_i x_i = 40+42+18+20+24+90=234 $$ So, the mean is $$ \bar{x}=\frac{\sum f_i x_i}{\sum f_i}=\frac{234}{26}=9 $$ Step 2: Calculate $\sum f_i |x_i-\bar{x}|$ Since $\bar{x}=9$, we find $|x_i-9|$: |c|c|c|c| x_i , f_i , |x_i-9| , f_i|x_i-9| \ 5 , 8 , 4 , 32 \ 7 , 6 , 2 , 12 \ 9 , 2 , 0 , 0 \ 10 , 2 , 1 , 2 \ 12 , 2 , 3 , 6 \ 15 , 6 , 6 , 36 \ Now, $$ \sum f_i |x_i-\bar{x}| = 32+12+0+2+6+36=88 $$ Step 3: Find mean deviation about the mean $$ \text{M.D. about mean}=\frac{88}{26}=\frac{44}{13} $$ So, the correct answer is $$ \boxed{\frac{44}{13}} $$ Hence, Option C is correct.

questions.text: Let a focus of the ellipse $\mathrm{E}: \frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ be $\mathrm{S}(4,0)$ and its eccentricity be $\frac{4}{5}$. If the point $\mathrm{P}(3, \alpha)$ lies on E and O is the origin, then the area of $\triangle \mathrm{POS}$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Step 1: For the ellipse $$ E:\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1 $$ a focus is $S(4,0)$ and eccentricity is $$ e=\frac{4}{5} $$ We need the area of $\triangle POS$, where $P(3,\alpha)$ lies on the ellipse and $O=(0,0)$. Since the focus is on the $x$-axis, the ellipse has major axis along the $x$-axis. For such an ellipse, focus is at $(\pm ae,0)$. Given one focus is $(4,0)$, so $$ ae=4 $$ and $e=\frac{4}{5}$. Therefore, $$ a\cdot \frac{4}{5}=4 $$ $$ a=5 $$ Now, $$ c=ae=4 $$ and for ellipse, $$ b^2=a^2-c^2 $$ So, $$ b^2=25-16=9 $$ Hence the ellipse is $$ \frac{x^2}{25}+\frac{y^2}{9}=1 $$ Since $P(3,\alpha)$ lies on the ellipse, substitute $x=3$: $$ \frac{3^2}{25}+\frac{\alpha^2}{9}=1 $$ $$ \frac{9}{25}+\frac{\alpha^2}{9}=1 $$ $$ \frac{\alpha^2}{9}=1-\frac{9}{25} =\frac{16}{25} $$ $$ \alpha^2=\frac{144}{25} $$ $$ \alpha=\pm \frac{12}{5} $$ Now find the area of triangle with vertices $$ O(0,0),\quad P(3,\alpha),\quad S(4,0) $$ Using base $OS$: $$ OS=4 $$ Since $OS$ lies on the $x$-axis, the height from $P$ to $OS$ is $|\alpha|$.

Step 2: So area is $$ \frac{1}{2}\times 4\times |\alpha| =2|\alpha| $$ $$ =2\times \frac{12}{5} =\frac{24}{5} $$ Therefore, the area of $\triangle POS$ is $$ \boxed{\frac{24}{5}} $$ So, the correct option is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option C}} $$

questions.text: Let P be a moving point on the circle $x^2+y^2-6 x-8 y+21=0$. Then, the maximum distance of P from the vertex of the parabola $x^2+6 x+y+13=0$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: First, find the vertex of the parabola. The parabola is $$ x^2+6x+y+13=0 $$ Rewrite it by completing the square: $$ x^2+6x+y+13=0 $$ $$ x^2+6x+9+y+13-9=0 $$ $$ (x+3)^2+y+4=0 $$ $$ y=-(x+3)^2-4 $$ So, the vertex of the parabola is $$ (-3,-4) $$ Now, find the centre and radius of the circle. Given circle: $$ x^2+y^2-6x-8y+21=0 $$ Complete the squares: $$ x^2-6x+y^2-8y+21=0 $$ $$ (x^2-6x+9)+(y^2-8y+16)+21-9-16=0 $$ $$ (x-3)^2+(y-4)^2-4=0 $$ $$ (x-3)^2+(y-4)^2=4 $$ Hence, centre of the circle is $$ (3,4) $$ and radius is $$ r=2 $$ Now we need the maximum distance of a point $P$ on this circle from the vertex $(-3,-4)$. Let $V=(-3,-4)$ and centre of circle be $C=(3,4)$. First find $VC$: $$ VC=\sqrt{(3+3)^2+(4+4)^2} =\sqrt{6^2+8^2} =\sqrt{36+64} =\sqrt{100} =10 $$ For a point moving on a circle, the maximum distance from an external point is $$ VC+r $$ So, $$ \text{Maximum distance}=10+2=12 $$ Therefore, the correct answer is $$ \boxed{12} $$ So, Option C is correct.

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: In an equilateral triangle $P Q R$, let the vertex $P$ be at $(3,5)$ and the side $Q R$ be along the line $x+y=4$. If the orthocentre of the triangle PQR is $(\alpha, \beta)$, then $9(\alpha+\beta)$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
Step 1: Since $QR$ lies on the line $$ x+y=4, $$ and $P=(3,5)$, first find the altitude from $P$ to the side $QR$. In an equilateral triangle, all altitudes, medians and angle bisectors coincide. Also, the orthocentre lies on the altitude from each vertex and divides the altitude in the ratio $2:1$ from the vertex.

Step 2: So let us proceed step by step. The line $QR$ has equation $$ x+y-4=0. $$ Distance of point $P(3,5)$ from this line is $$ d=\frac{|3+5-4|}{\sqrt{1^2+1^2}} =\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}} =2\sqrt{2}. $$ This is the altitude of the equilateral triangle from vertex $P$. Now, the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to the line $x+y=4$ lies on the altitude. Since in an equilateral triangle the orthocentre lies at $\frac{2}{3}$ of the altitude from the vertex, we can find it along the perpendicular direction. The slope of $x+y=4$ is $-1$, so the perpendicular slope is $1$. Hence the altitude through $P(3,5)$ is $$ y-5=1(x-3) $$ or $$ y=x+2. $$ The orthocentre lies on this line. Now find the foot of perpendicular from $P$ to $x+y=4$ by solving $$ y=x+2 $$ and $$ x+y=4. $$ Substitute $y=x+2$ into $x+y=4$: $$ x+(x+2)=4 $$ $$ 2x=2 $$ $$ x=1,\quad y=3. $$ So the foot is $(1,3)$. Thus the altitude segment is from $P(3,5)$ to $(1,3)$. The orthocentre divides this altitude in the ratio $2:1$ from vertex $P$. Therefore, $$ H=\left(\frac{2\cdot 1+1\cdot 3}{3},\frac{2\cdot 3+1\cdot 5}{3}\right) $$ This is incorrect ratio placement, so let us use the correct section carefully: If $H$ divides the segment from $P$ to foot $D$ in the ratio $2:1$, then $$ H=P+\frac{2}{3}(D-P). $$ Here, $$ D-P=(1-3,\,3-5)=(-2,-2). $$ So $$ H=(3,5)+\frac{2}{3}(-2,-2) =\left(3-\frac{4}{3},\,5-\frac{4}{3}\right) =\left(\frac{5}{3},\,\frac{11}{3}\right). $$ Thus, $$ \alpha=\frac{5}{3},\qquad \beta=\frac{11}{3}. $$ So, $$ \alpha+\beta=\frac{5}{3}+\frac{11}{3}=\frac{16}{3}. $$ Therefore, $$ 9(\alpha+\beta)=9\cdot \frac{16}{3}=48. $$ Hence the correct answer is $$ \boxed{48} $$ So, Option D is correct.

questions.text: The sum of all the integral values of $p$ such that the equation $3 \sin ^2 x+12 \cos x-3=p, x \in \mathbb{R}$, has at least one solution, is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Given $$ 3\sin^2 x + 12\cos x - 3 = p,\qquad x\in \mathbb{R} $$ We need all integral values of $p$ for which this equation has at least one real solution. Now use the identity $$ \sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x $$ So, $$ 3(1-\cos^2 x)+12\cos x-3 = p $$ Simplifying, $$ 3 - 3\cos^2 x + 12\cos x - 3 = p $$ $$ -3\cos^2 x + 12\cos x = p $$ Let $$ t = \cos x $$ Then $$ -1 \le t \le 1 $$ So we have $$ p = -3t^2 + 12t $$ Now we need the range of $$ f(t) = -3t^2 + 12t,\qquad -1 \le t \le 1 $$ This is a downward opening parabola. Find its values at the endpoints: $$ f(-1) = -3(1) + 12(-1) = -3 - 12 = -15 $$ $$ f(1) = -3(1) + 12(1) = -3 + 12 = 9 $$ Also, $$ f'(t) = -6t + 12 $$ For $-1 \le t \le 1$, we have $$ -6t + 12 > 0 $$ so $f(t)$ is increasing on $[-1,1]$. Hence the range of $p$ is $$ -15 \le p \le 9 $$ Therefore all integral values of $p$ are $$ -15,-14,-13,\dots,9 $$ This is an AP with first term $-15$, last term $9$. Number of terms: $$ n = 9-(-15)+1 = 25 $$ Sum: $$ S = \frac{n}{2}(a+l) = \frac{25}{2}(-15+9) = \frac{25}{2}(-6) = -75 $$ Hence, the required sum is $$ \boxed{-75} $$ So, the correct option is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option C}} $$

questions.text: The square of the distance of the point $\mathrm{P}(5,6,7)$ from the line $\frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y-5}{3}=\frac{z-2}{4}$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: Write the given line in vector form. From $$ \frac{x-2}{2}=\frac{y-5}{3}=\frac{z-2}{4}, $$ a point on the line is $$ A(2,5,2) $$ and its direction vector is $$ \vec{b} = 2\hat{i}+3\hat{j}+4\hat{k}. $$ Given point is $$ P(5,6,7). $$ Now, $$ \overrightarrow{AP} = (5-2)\hat{i}+(6-5)\hat{j}+(7-2)\hat{k} = 3\hat{i}+\hat{j}+5\hat{k}. $$ The distance $d$ of point $P$ from the line is given by $$ d = \frac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times \vec{b}|}{|\vec{b}|}. $$ Since we need the square of the distance, $$ d^2=\frac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\times \vec{b}|^2}{|\vec{b}|^2}. $$ Now calculate the cross product: $$ \overrightarrow{AP}\times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k}\ 3 & 1 & 5\ 2 & 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix} $$ $$ = \hat{i}(1\cdot 4-5\cdot 3)-\hat{j}(3\cdot 4-5\cdot 2)+\hat{k}(3\cdot 3-1\cdot 2) $$ $$ = \hat{i}(4-15)-\hat{j}(12-10)+\hat{k}(9-2) $$ $$ = -11\hat{i}-2\hat{j}+7\hat{k}. $$ So, $$ |\overrightarrow{AP}\times \vec{b}|^2 = (-11)^2+(-2)^2+7^2 = 121+4+49=174. $$ Also, $$ |\vec{b}|^2 = 2^2+3^2+4^2=4+9+16=29. $$ Therefore, $$ d^2=\frac{174}{29}=6. $$ So, the square of the distance is $$ \boxed{6} $$ Hence, the correct option is Option C.

questions.text: Let $\vec{a}=\sqrt{7} \hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{b}=\hat{j}+2 \hat{k}$. If $\vec{r}$ is a vector such that $\vec{r} \times \vec{a}+\vec{a} \times \vec{b}=\overrightarrow{0}$ and $\vec{r} \cdot \vec{a}=0$, then $|3 \vec{r}|^2$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $\vec{r}\times\vec{a}+\vec{a}\times\vec{b}=\vec{0}\Rightarrow\vec{r}\times\vec{a}=\vec{b}\times\vec{a}\Rightarrow(\vec{r}-\vec{b})\times\vec{a}=\vec{0}$, so $\vec{r}=\vec{b}+\lambda\vec{a}$ for some scalar $\lambda$. $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=0+1-2=-1$, $|\vec{a}|^2=7+1+1=9$ and $|\vec{b}|^2=0+1+4=5$. $\vec{r}\cdot\vec{a}=0\Rightarrow\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}+\lambda|\vec{a}|^2=0\Rightarrow -1+9\lambda=0\Rightarrow\lambda=\dfrac{1}{9}$. $$|\vec{r}|^2=|\vec{b}|^2+2\lambda(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})+\lambda^2|\vec{a}|^2=5-\frac{2}{9}+\frac{9}{81}=\frac{44}{9}$$ $$|3\vec{r}|^2=9|\vec{r}|^2=44$$ Hence, the correct option is (A).
questions.topic: Vector or Cross Product of Two Vectors and Its Applications

questions.text:
The square of the distance of the point of
intersection of the lines $\vec{r}=(\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k})+\lambda(a \hat{i}-\hat{j}), a \neq 0$ and $\vec{r}=(4 \hat{i}-\hat{k})+\mu(2 \hat{i}+a \hat{k})$ from the origin is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Let the two given lines be: $$\vec{r} = (1 + a\lambda)\hat{i} + (1 - \lambda)\hat{j} - \hat{k}$$ $$\vec{r} = (4 + 2\mu)\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} + (-1 + a\mu)\hat{k}$$ At the point of intersection, the position vectors from both equations must be identical. Comparing the coefficients of $\hat{i}$, $\hat{j}$, and $\hat{k}$ gives three equations: $$1 + a\lambda = 4 + 2\mu \quad \text{--- (1)}$$ $$1 - \lambda = 0 \quad \text{--- (2)}$$ $$-1 = -1 + a\mu \quad \text{--- (3)}$$ From equation (2), we get: $$\lambda = 1$$ From equation (3), we get: $$a\mu = 0$$ Since it is given that $a \neq 0$, we must have: $$\mu = 0$$ Now, substituting $\lambda = 1$ and $\mu = 0$ into equation (1): $$1 + a(1) = 4 + 2(0)$$ $$1 + a = 4$$ $$a = 3$$ To find the coordinates of the point of intersection, substitute $\mu = 0$ into the equation of the second line: $$\vec{r} = 4\hat{i} + 0\hat{j} - \hat{k}$$ So, the point of intersection is $(4, 0, -1)$. The square of the distance of this point from the origin $(0, 0, 0)$ is: $$d^2 = 4^2 + 0^2 + (-1)^2$$ $$d^2 = 16 + 0 + 1 = 17$$ The correct option is Option C.

questions.text: The area of the region $\mathrm{R}=\left\{(x, y): x y \leq 27,1 \leq y \leq x^2\right\}$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $\begin{aligned} & \text { Area }=\int_1^3\left(x^2-1\right) d x+\int_3^{27}\left(\frac{27}{x}-1\right) d x \ & =\left[\frac{x^3}{3}-x\right]_1^3+[27 \ell n x-x]_3^{27} \ & =\frac{26}{3}-2+27 \ln 9-24 \ & =27 \ln 9-\frac{26 \times 2}{3} \ & =54 \ln 3-\frac{52}{3}\end{aligned}$

questions.text:
The product of all possible values of $\alpha$, for which
$\lim \limits_{x \rightarrow 0}\left(\frac{1-\cos (\alpha x) \cos ((\alpha+1) x) \cos ((\alpha+2) x)}{\sin ^2((\alpha+1) x)}\right)=2$, is:
questions.solution: Step 1: For small $\theta$, $\cos\theta=1-\dfrac{\theta^2}{2}+O(\theta^4)$, so $$\cos(\alpha x)\cos((\alpha+1)x)\cos((\alpha+2)x)=1-\frac{\alpha^2+(\alpha+1)^2+(\alpha+2)^2}{2}x^2+O(x^4)$$ Also $\sin^2((\alpha+1)x)=(\alpha+1)^2x^2+O(x^4)$, where $\alpha\neq -1$ (otherwise the denominator is identically zero). Therefore $$\lim\limits_{x\to 0}\frac{1-\cos(\alpha x)\cos((\alpha+1)x)\cos((\alpha+2)x)}{\sin^2((\alpha+1)x)}=\frac{\alpha^2+(\alpha+1)^2+(\alpha+2)^2}{2(\alpha+1)^2}=2$$ $$\alpha^2+(\alpha+2)^2=3(\alpha+1)^2\Rightarrow 2\alpha^2+4\alpha+4=3\alpha^2+6\alpha+3\Rightarrow \alpha^2+2\alpha-1=0$$ Its roots $\alpha=-1\pm\sqrt{2}$ are real and different from $-1$, so the product of all possible values of $\alpha$ is $-1$. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: The value of the integral $\int\limits_0^{\infty} \frac{\log _e(x)}{x^2+4} d x$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Let $$ I=\int_0^{\infty}\frac{\ln x}{x^2+4}\,dx $$ We will use a standard substitution, as done in NCERT-type definite integral problems. Take $$ x=2t $$ Then $$ dx=2\,dt $$ and when $x=0,\ t=0$, and when $x\to\infty,\ t\to\infty$. So, $$ I=\int_0^{\infty}\frac{\ln(2t)}{(2t)^2+4}\cdot 2\,dt $$ Simplify the denominator: $$ (2t)^2+4=4t^2+4=4(1+t^2) $$ Hence, $$ I=\int_0^{\infty}\frac{\ln(2t)}{4(1+t^2)}\cdot 2\,dt =\frac12\int_0^{\infty}\frac{\ln(2t)}{1+t^2}\,dt $$ Now use $$ \ln(2t)=\ln 2+\ln t $$ So, $$ I=\frac12\int_0^{\infty}\frac{\ln 2}{1+t^2}\,dt+\frac12\int_0^{\infty}\frac{\ln t}{1+t^2}\,dt $$ That is, $$ I=\frac{\ln 2}{2}\int_0^{\infty}\frac{dt}{1+t^2}+\frac12\int_0^{\infty}\frac{\ln t}{1+t^2}\,dt $$ Now, $$ \int_0^{\infty}\frac{dt}{1+t^2}=\left[\tan^{-1} t\right]_0^{\infty}=\frac{\pi}{2} $$ Also, let $$ J=\int_0^{\infty}\frac{\ln t}{1+t^2}\,dt $$ Using the substitution $t=\frac1u$, we get $$ dt=-\frac{1}{u^2}\,du $$ Then $$ J=\int_{\infty}^{0}\frac{\ln(1/u)}{1+1/u^2}\left(-\frac{1}{u^2}\right)du $$ This simplifies to $$ J=\int_0^{\infty}\frac{-\ln u}{1+u^2}\,du =-J $$ Therefore, $$ J=0 $$ So, $$ I=\frac{\ln 2}{2}\cdot \frac{\pi}{2} =\frac{\pi\ln 2}{4} $$ Hence, the value of the integral is $$ \boxed{\frac{\pi\ln 2}{4}} $$ So, the correct option is: $$ \boxed{\text{Option B}} $$

questions.text: Let $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ be a differentiable function such that $f\left(\frac{x+y}{3}\right)=\frac{f(x)+f(y)}{3}$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$, and $f^{\prime}(0)=3$. Then the minimum value of the function $g(x)=3+e^x f(x)$, is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Given $$ f\left(\frac{x+y}{3}\right)=\frac{f(x)+f(y)}{3}\quad \text{for all }x,y\in \mathbb{R}, $$ and $$ f'(0)=3. $$ We have to find the minimum value of $$ g(x)=3+e^x f(x). $$ Step 1: Find the form of $f(x)$ We are given a functional equation. We will use it carefully. Let $$ \frac{x+y}{3}=t. $$ Then $$ x+y=3t. $$ The relation becomes $$ f(t)=\frac{f(x)+f(y)}{3}\quad \text{whenever }x+y=3t. $$ We now choose suitable values. Put $x=y=0$ Then $$ f(0)=\frac{f(0)+f(0)}{3}=\frac{2f(0)}{3}. $$ So, $$ 3f(0)=2f(0)\implies f(0)=0. $$ Put $y=0$ Then $$ f\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)=\frac{f(x)+f(0)}{3}=\frac{f(x)}{3}. $$ Thus, $$ f(x)=3f\left(\frac{x}{3}\right). $$ Now differentiate both sides with respect to $x$: $$ f'(x)=3\cdot f'\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)\cdot \frac{1}{3}=f'\left(\frac{x}{3}\right). $$ So, $$ f'(x)=f'\left(\frac{x}{3}\right). $$ Repeating this, $$ f'(x)=f'\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)=f'\left(\frac{x}{3^2}\right)=\cdots=f'\left(\frac{x}{3^n}\right). $$ As $n\to\infty$, $$ \frac{x}{3^n}\to 0. $$ Since $f$ is differentiable, $f'$ is defined at $0$, so we get $$ f'(x)=f'(0)=3. $$ Hence, $$ f'(x)=3\quad \text{for all }x. $$ Therefore, $$ f(x)=3x+c. $$ But $f(0)=0$, so $$ c=0. $$ Thus, $$ f(x)=3x. $$ Step 2: Write $g(x)$ Now $$ g(x)=3+e^x f(x)=3+e^x(3x)=3+3xe^x. $$ So, $$ g(x)=3\bigl(1+xe^x\bigr). $$ Step 3: Minimise $xe^x$ Let $$ h(x)=xe^x. $$ Then $$ h'(x)=e^x+xe^x=e^x(1+x). $$ Since $e^x>0$ for all $x$, we have $$ h'(x)=0 \iff 1+x=0 \iff x=-1. $$ Now, for $x for $x>-1$, $h'(x)>0$, so $h$ is increasing. Hence $h(x)$ has a minimum at $x=-1$. Its minimum value is $$ h(-1)=(-1)e^{-1}=-\frac{1}{e}. $$ Therefore, $$ g_{\min}=3\left(1-\frac{1}{e}\right)=3\left(\frac{e-1}{e}\right). $$ Final Answer \boxed{3\left(\frac{e-1}{e}\right)} $ So the correct option is B.

questions.text: The value of the integral $\int\limits_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}\left(\frac{4-\operatorname{cosec}^2 x}{\cos ^4 x}\right) d x$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Let the given integral be $$I = \int\limits_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \left(\frac{4 - \operatorname{cosec}^2 x}{\cos^4 x}\right) dx$$ We can rewrite $\frac{1}{\cos^4 x}$ as $\sec^4 x$: $$I = \int\limits_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} (4 - \operatorname{cosec}^2 x)\sec^4 x \, dx$$ Using the trigonometric identity $\operatorname{cosec}^2 x = 1 + \cot^2 x$, the term inside the bracket simplifies to: $$4 - \operatorname{cosec}^2 x = 4 - (1 + \cot^2 x) = 3 - \cot^2 x$$ Expressing $\cot x$ in terms of $\tan x$, we get: $$3 - \cot^2 x = 3 - \frac{1}{\tan^2 x} = \frac{3\tan^2 x - 1}{\tan^2 x}$$ We also know that $\sec^4 x = (1 + \tan^2 x)\sec^2 x$. Substituting these into the integral gives: $$I = \int\limits_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \left(\frac{3\tan^2 x - 1}{\tan^2 x}\right)(1 + \tan^2 x)\sec^2 x \, dx$$ Now, let us use the substitution method. Put $t = \tan x$, so that $dt = \sec^2 x \, dx$. Next, we change the limits of integration: When $x = \frac{\pi}{6}$, $t = \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ When $x = \frac{\pi}{3}$, $t = \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \sqrt{3}$ The integral transforms to: $$I = \int\limits_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}^{\sqrt{3}} \left(\frac{3t^2 - 1}{t^2}\right)(1 + t^2) \, dt$$ Simplify the integrand: $$\left(3 - \frac{1}{t^2}\right)(1 + t^2) = 3 + 3t^2 - \frac{1}{t^2} - 1 = 3t^2 + 2 - \frac{1}{t^2}$$ Now, integrate each term with respect to $t$: $$I = \int\limits_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}^{\sqrt{3}} \left(3t^2 + 2 - t^{-2}\right) dt$$ $$I = \left[ t^3 + 2t + \frac{1}{t} \right]_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}^{\sqrt{3}}$$ Substitute the upper limit $t = \sqrt{3}$: $$(\sqrt{3})^3 + 2(\sqrt{3}) + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = 3\sqrt{3} + 2\sqrt{3} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = 5\sqrt{3} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{16}{\sqrt{3}}$$ Substitute the lower limit $t = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$: $$\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^3 + 2\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) + \sqrt{3} = \frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}} + \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} + \sqrt{3} = \frac{1 + 6 + 9}{3\sqrt{3}} = \frac{16}{3\sqrt{3}}$$ Subtracting the lower limit value from the upper limit value: $$I = \frac{16}{\sqrt{3}} - \frac{16}{3\sqrt{3}} = \frac{16}{\sqrt{3}}\left(1 - \frac{1}{3}\right) = \frac{16}{\sqrt{3}} \times \frac{2}{3} = \frac{32}{3\sqrt{3}}$$ Thus, the correct option is Option C.
