The area enclosed by the closed curve $\mathrm{C}$ given by the differential equation $\frac{d y}{d x}+\frac{x+a}{y-2}=0, y(1)=0$ is $4 \pi$.
Let $P$ and $Q$ be the points of intersection of the curve $\mathrm{C}$ and the $y$-axis. If normals at $P$ and $Q$ on the curve $\mathrm{C}$ intersect $x$-axis at points $R$ and $S$ respectively, then the length of the line segment $R S$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{d y}{d x}+\frac{x+a}{y-2}=0 \\ & \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{x+a}{2-y} \\ & (2-y) d y=(x+a) d x \\ & 2 y-\frac{y^2}{2}=\frac{x^2}{2}+\mathrm{ax}+\mathrm{c} \\ & \mathrm{a}+\mathrm{c}=-\frac{1}{2} \text { as } \mathrm{y}(1)=0 \\ & \mathrm{x}^2+\mathrm{y}^2+2 \mathrm{ax}-4 \mathrm{y}-1-2 \mathrm{a}=0 \\ & \pi \mathrm{r}^2=4 \pi \\ & \mathrm{r}^2=4 \\ & 2=\sqrt{a^2+4+1+2 a} \\ & (\mathrm{a}+1)^2=0 \end{aligned} $$ $$ P, Q=(0,2 \pm \sqrt{3}) $$ Equation of normal at $\mathrm{P}, \mathrm{Q}$ are $\mathrm{y}-2=\sqrt{3}(\mathrm{x}-1)$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{y}-2=-\sqrt{3}(\mathrm{x}-1) \\ & \mathrm{R}=\left(1-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, 0\right) \\ & \mathrm{S}=\left(1+\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, 0\right) \\ & \mathrm{RS}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{3}}=4 \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \end{aligned} $$

questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \mathrm{m}=-\frac{1}{2} $$ Here $\mathrm{m_{BH}} \times \mathrm{m_{AC}}=-1$ $$ \begin{array}{ll} & \left(\frac{\beta-3}{\alpha-2}\right)\left(\frac{1}{-2}\right)=-1 \\ & \beta-3=2 \alpha-4 \\ & \beta=2 \alpha-1 \\ & \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{AH}} \times \mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{BC}}=-1 \\ \Rightarrow & \left(\frac{\beta-2}{\alpha-1}\right)(-2)=-1 \\ \Rightarrow & 2 \beta-4=\alpha-1 \\ \Rightarrow & 2(2 \alpha-1)=\alpha+3 \\ \Rightarrow & 3 \alpha=5 \\ & \alpha=\frac{5}{3}, \beta=\frac{7}{3} \Rightarrow \mathrm{H}\left(\frac{5}{3}, \frac{7}{3}\right) \\ & \alpha+4 \beta=\frac{5}{3}+\frac{28}{3}=\frac{33}{3}=11 \\ & \beta+4 \alpha=\frac{7}{3}+\frac{20}{3}=\frac{27}{3}=9 \\ & \mathrm{x}^2-20 \mathrm{x}+99=0 \end{array} $$

questions.text: If $y=y(x)$ is the solution curve of the differential equation $\frac{d y}{d x}+y \tan x=x \sec x, 0 \leq x \leq \frac{\pi}{3}, y(0)=1$, then $y\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: Step 1: $\frac{d y}{d x}+y \tan x=x \sec x$ $\therefore $ I.F $=e^{\int \tan x d x}=\sec x$ $\Rightarrow y \sec x=\int x \sec ^{2} x d x$ $\Rightarrow y \sec x=x \tan x-\ln |\sec x|+c$ Given, $$ y(0)=1 $$ $\Rightarrow 1=c$ $$ \therefore $$ $ y \sec x=x \tan x-\ln |\sec x|+1$ $\Rightarrow y=x \sin x-\cos x \ln |\sec x|+\cos x$ Now, at $x=\pi / 6$, we have $$ \begin{aligned} & y=\frac{\pi}{12}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \log _e \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ & =\frac{\pi}{12}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\left[\log _e \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}-\log _e e\right]\\ &=\frac{\pi}{12}-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \log _e\left(\frac{2}{e \sqrt{3}}\right) \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: A proton moving with one tenth of velocity of light has a certain de Broglie wavelength of $\lambda$. An alpha particle having certain kinetic energy has the same de-Broglie wavelength $\lambda$. The ratio of kinetic energy of proton and that of alpha particle is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Since $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}$, the same de Broglie wavelength means the same momentum $p$ for the proton and the alpha particle (the proton's speed $c/10$ only fixes the common value of $\lambda$). Kinetic energy in terms of momentum is $K = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, so for equal $p$, $K \propto \dfrac{1}{m}$. $$\dfrac{K_p}{K_\alpha} = \dfrac{m_\alpha}{m_p} = \dfrac{4m_p}{m_p} = 4$$ So $K_p: K_\alpha = 4: 1$. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Acceleration due to gravity is different at different places on the surface of earth.
Statement II: Acceleration due to gravity increases as we go down below the earth's surface.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false

questions.solution: Step 1: Statement I is true. The acceleration due to gravity varies slightly over the surface of the Earth, being affected by factors such as latitude (because of the Earth's oblate shape or its equatorial bulge), altitude (it decreases with height above the Earth's surface), and local geological variations in the Earth's density. Statement II is false. The acceleration due to gravity actually decreases as we go down below the Earth's surface. This is because the mass that is "above" or outside the location begins to pull the object away from the Earth's center, and the net gravitational acceleration decreases. Therefore, Option D: Statement I is true but Statement II is false, is the correct answer.
questions.topic: Acceleration due to Gravity and its Variation

questions.text: A sample of gas at temperature $T$ is adiabatically expanded to double its volume. The work done by the gas in the process is $\left(\mathrm{given}, \gamma=\frac{3}{2}\right)$:
questions.solution: Step 1: $\gamma=\frac{3}{2}$ $$ \begin{aligned} & W =\frac{n R \Delta T}{1-\gamma}=\frac{n R T_{f}-n R T_{i}}{1-\gamma} \\ & =\frac{(P V)_{f}-\left(P V_{i}\right)}{1-\gamma} \quad \ldots \text { (1) } \\ & P V^{\gamma}=\text { constant } \\ & P_{i} V_{i}^{\gamma}=P_{f}\left(2 V_{i}\right)^{\gamma} \Rightarrow P_{f}=\frac{P_{i}}{2^{\gamma}}=\frac{P_{i}}{2 \sqrt{2}}......(2) \end{aligned} $$ From (1) and (2) $$ \begin{aligned} & W=\frac{\frac{P_{i}}{2 \sqrt{2}} 2 V_{i}-P_{i} V_{i}}{1-\gamma}=\frac{P_{i} V_{i}}{-1 / 2}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}-1\right) \\ & =-n R T(\sqrt{2}-2) \\ & =n R T(2-\sqrt{2}) \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: A block of mass $5 \mathrm{~kg}$ is placed at rest on a table of rough surface. Now, if a force of $30 \mathrm{~N}$ is applied in the direction parallel to surface of the table, the block slides through a distance of $50 \mathrm{~m}$ in an interval of time $10 \mathrm{~s}$. Coefficient of kinetic friction is (given, $g=10 \mathrm{~ms}^{-2}$):
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \begin{aligned} & S=u t+\frac{1}{2} a t^2 \\ & 50=0+\frac{1}{2} \times a \times 100 \\ & a=1 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2 \\ & F-\mu m g=m a \\ & 30-\mu \times 50=5 \times 1 \\ & 50 \mu=25 \\ & \mu=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: The number of s-electrons present in an ion with 55 protons in its unipositive state is
questions.solution: Step 1: The number of protons in an element determines its atomic number, which is the number of electrons in a neutral atom of the element. The unipositive state of an ion indicates that it has lost one electron. Therefore, the number of electrons in a unipositive ion is one less than the atomic number. The element with 55 protons is cesium (Cs), which is in group 1 of the periodic table. Group 1 elements have one valence electron in the s sublevel of their outermost energy level. In a neutral atom of cesium, there are 55 electrons, with the electron configuration [Xe] 6s1. When cesium loses one electron to form a unipositive ion (Cs+), the resulting ion has 54 electrons. Out of this 54 electrons s subshell has 10 electrons in 1s2, 2s2, 3s2, 4s2, 5s2.

questions.text: What is the number of unpaired electron(s) in the highest occupied molecular orbital of the following species: $\mathrm{{N_2};N_2^ +;{O_2};O_2^ + }$ ?
questions.solution: Step 1: For molecules up to $\ce{N2}$ the $\sigma 2p_z$ orbital lies above $\pi 2p_x$, $\pi 2p_y$; from $\ce{O2}$ onwards it lies below them. $\ce{N2}$ (14 electrons): $\sigma 1s^2\,\sigma^*1s^2\,\sigma 2s^2\,\sigma^*2s^2\,\pi 2p_x^2 = \pi 2p_y^2\,\sigma 2p_z^2$. The HOMO $\sigma 2p_z$ holds a pair, so it has 0 unpaired electrons. $\ce{N2+}$ (13 electrons): the HOMO is $\sigma 2p_z^1$, so 1 unpaired electron. $\ce{O2}$ (16 electrons): $\sigma 1s^2\,\sigma^*1s^2\,\sigma 2s^2\,\sigma^*2s^2\,\sigma 2p_z^2\,\pi 2p_x^2 = \pi 2p_y^2\,\pi^*2p_x^1 = \pi^*2p_y^1$. The HOMO is the degenerate $\pi^*2p$ pair with one electron in each, so 2 unpaired electrons. $\ce{O2+}$ (15 electrons): the HOMO is $\pi^*2p_x^1$, so 1 unpaired electron. The numbers are 0, 1, 2, 1. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R
Assertion A: Benzene is more stable than hypothetical cyclohexatriene
Reason R: The delocalised $\pi$ electron cloud is attracted more strongly by nuclei of carbon atoms.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.solution: Step 1: Benzene is more stable than hypothetical cyclohexatriene due to the delocalization of electrons in the π electron cloud of the aromatic ring. This delocalization of electrons leads to a more stable electronic configuration in benzene, as the electrons are shared more evenly between all six carbon atoms in the ring. This is in agreement with Assertion A. Reason R is also correct, as the delocalized π electron cloud in the aromatic ring is attracted more strongly by the nuclei of the carbon atoms. This is due to the fact that the π electrons in the ring are more spread out and are not localized to a single atom, which makes them more attracted to the positively charged nuclei of the carbon atoms. This explanation supports Assertion A.

questions.text:
A student has studied the decomposition of a gas AB$_3$ at 25$^\circ$C. He obtained the following data.
p (mm Hg)
50
100
200
400
relative t$_{1/2}$ (s)
4
2
1
0.5
The order of the reaction is
questions.solution: Step 1: For a reaction of order $n$, the half-life depends on the initial pressure as $$t_{1/2} \propto p_0^{\,1-n}$$ From the data, each doubling of $p_0$ (50 to 100 mm Hg) halves $t_{1/2}$ (4 s to 2 s): $$\dfrac{4}{2} = \left(\dfrac{50}{100}\right)^{1-n} \Rightarrow 2 = 2^{\,n-1} \Rightarrow n - 1 = 1 \Rightarrow n = 2$$ The other pairs (200 to 400 mm Hg, 1 s to 0.5 s) give the same ratio, so $t_{1/2} \propto \dfrac{1}{p_0}$, which is characteristic of a second order reaction. Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: Let $f(x)$ be a function such that $f(x+y)=f(x).f(y)$ for all $x,y\in \mathbb{N}$. If $f(1)=3$ and $\sum\limits_{k = 1}^n {f(k) = 3279} $, then the value of n is
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{y})=\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x}) \cdot \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{y}) \forall \mathrm{x}, \mathrm{y} \in \mathrm{N}, \mathrm{f}(1)=3 \\ & \mathrm{f}(2)=\mathrm{f}^2(1)=3^2 \\ & \mathrm{f}(3)=\mathrm{f}(1) \mathrm{f}(2)=3^3 \\ & \mathrm{f}(4)=3^4 \\ & \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{k})=3^{\mathrm{k}} \\ & \sum_{\mathrm{k}=1}^{\mathrm{n}} \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{k})=3279 \\ & \mathrm{f}(1)+\mathrm{f}(2)+\mathrm{f}(3)+\ldots \ldots \ldots+\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{k})=3279 \\ & 3+3^2+3^3+\ldots \ldots \ldots 3^{\mathrm{k}}=3279 \\ & \frac{3\left(3^{\mathrm{k}}-1\right)}{3-1}=3279 \\ & \frac{3^{\mathrm{k}}-1}{2}=1093 \\ & 3^{\mathrm{k}}-1=2186 \\ & 3^{\mathrm{k}}=2187 \\ & \text{So, } \mathrm{k}=7 \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: The number of real solutions of the equation $3\left( {{x^2} + {1 \over {{x^2}}}} \right) - 2\left( {x + {1 \over x}} \right) + 5 = 0$, is
questions.solution: Step 1: $3\left(x^{2}+\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right)-2\left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)+5=0$ $3\left[\left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)^{2}-2\right]-2\left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)+5=0$ Put $x+\frac{1}{x}=t \Rightarrow t \in(-\infty,-2] \cup[2, \infty)$ $$ \begin{aligned} & 3 t^{2}-2 t-1=0 \\ & 3 t^{2}-3 t+t-1=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 3 t(t-1)+1(t-1)=0 \Rightarrow t=1,=-\frac{1}{3} \\ & \Rightarrow \quad t=1,-\frac{1}{3} \\ & \because t \in(-\infty,-2] \cup[2, \infty) \end{aligned} $$ No real value of $t \Rightarrow$ no real value of $x$.

questions.text: Let $\overrightarrow \alpha = 4\widehat i + 3\widehat j + 5\widehat k$ and $\overrightarrow \beta = \widehat i + 2\widehat j - 4\widehat k$. Let ${\overrightarrow \beta _1}$ be parallel to $\overrightarrow \alpha $ and ${\overrightarrow \beta _2}$ be perpendicular to $\overrightarrow \alpha $. If $\overrightarrow \beta = {\overrightarrow \beta _1} + {\overrightarrow \beta _2}$, then the value of $5{\overrightarrow \beta _2}\,.\left( {\widehat i + \widehat j + \widehat k} \right)$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Let $\vec{\beta}_1=\lambda \vec{\alpha}$ Now $\vec{\beta}_2=\vec{\beta}-\vec{\beta}_1$ $$ \begin{aligned} & =(\hat{\mathrm{i}}+2 \hat{\mathrm{j}}-4 \hat{\mathrm{k}})-\lambda(4 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+3 \hat{\mathrm{j}}+5 \hat{\mathrm{k}}) \\ & =(1-4 \lambda) \hat{\mathrm{i}}+(2-3 \lambda) \hat{\mathrm{j}}-(5 \lambda+4) \hat{\mathrm{k}} \\ & \vec{\beta}_2 \cdot \vec{\alpha}=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 4(1-4 \lambda)+3(2-3 \lambda)-5(5 \lambda+4)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 4-16 \lambda+6-9 \lambda-25 \lambda-20=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 50 \lambda=-10 \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{-1}{5} \\ & \vec{\beta}_2=\left(1+\frac{4}{5}\right) \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\left(2+\frac{3}{5}\right) \hat{\mathrm{j}}-(-1+4) \hat{\mathrm{k}} \\ & \vec{\beta}_2=\frac{9}{5} \hat{\mathrm{i}}+\frac{13}{5} \hat{\mathrm{j}}-3 \hat{\mathrm{k}} \\ & 5 \vec{\beta}_2=9 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+13 \hat{\mathrm{j}}-15 \hat{\mathrm{k}} \\ & 5 \vec{\beta}_2 \cdot(\hat{\mathrm{i}}+\hat{\mathrm{j}}+\hat{\mathrm{k}})=9+13-15=7 \end{aligned} $$

questions.text:
If the system of equations
$x+2y+3z=3$
$4x+3y-4z=4$
$8x+4y-\lambda z=9+\mu$
has infinitely many solutions, then the ordered pair ($\lambda,\mu$) is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: For infinite many solution, $\Delta=0$ and $\Delta_x=0$ $$ \Delta=\left|{ccc} 1 2 3 \ 4 3 -4 \ 8 4 -\lambda \right|=0; \Rightarrow 1(-3 \lambda+16)-2(-4 \lambda+32)+3(16-24)=0; \Rightarrow 16-3 \lambda+8 \lambda-64-24=0 \Rightarrow 5 \lambda=72; \therefore \lambda=\frac{72}{5}; \Delta_x=\left|{ccc} 3 2 3 \ 4 3 -4 \ 9+\mu 4 -\lambda \right|=0 $$ $$ \Rightarrow \quad 3(-3 \lambda+16)-2(-4 \lambda+36+4 \mu)+3(16-27-3 \mu)=0; \Rightarrow-9 \lambda+48+8 \lambda-72-8 \mu-33-9 \mu=0; \Rightarrow-\lambda-17 \mu=57; \Rightarrow-17 \mu=57+\lambda; \therefore -\mu=\frac{57+\frac{72}{5}}{17}; \Rightarrow \mu=\frac{-357}{85}=\frac{-21}{5} $$ $$ \text { Thus, }(\lambda, \mu) \equiv\left(\frac{72}{5}, \frac{-21}{5}\right) $$

questions.solution: Step 1: $$\mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to a} \left( {[x - 5] - [2x + 2]} \right) = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow \mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to a} \left( {[x] - 5 - [2x] - 2} \right) = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow \mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to a} [x] - [2x] - 7 = 0$$ Case 1: If $$a \in \left[ {n,n + {1 \over 2}} \right)$$ then $$\mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to a} \left( {[x] - [2x] - 7} \right) = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow n - 2n - 7 = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow n = - 7$$ $$\therefore$$ $$a \in \left[ { - 7, - 6.5} \right)$$ Case 2: If $$a \in \left[ {n + {1 \over 2},n + 1} \right)$$ then $$\mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to a} \left( {[x] - [2x] - 7} \right) = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow n - (2n + 1) - 7 = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow - n - 8 = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow n = - 8$$ $$\therefore$$ $$a \in \left[ { - 7.5, - 7} \right)$$ $$R.H.L = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to - {{7.5}^ + }} \left( {\left[ x \right] - \left[ {2x} \right] - 7} \right)$$ $$ = - 8 - \left( { - 15} \right) - 7$$ $$ = - 8 + 15 - 7 = 0$$ $eqalign, L.H.L = mathop lim limits_x to - 7.5^ - ( [ x ] - [ 2x ] - 7 ) cr \, = - 8 - ( - 16 ) - 7 cr \, = - 8 + 16 - 7 = 1 cr$ $$ \therefore $$ R.H.L $$ \ne $$ L.H.L $$ \therefore $$ At x = -7.5, limit does not exist. $$\therefore$$ $$a \in \left( { - 7.5, - 6.5} \right)$$

questions.text: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $(x^2-3y^2)dx+3xy~dy=0,y(1)=1$. Then $6y^2(e)$ is equal to
questions.solution: Step 1: Given, $$\left( {{x^2} - 3{y^2}} \right)dx + 3xydy = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow {x^2}dx - 3{y^2}dx + 3xydy = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow {{{x^2}dx} \over {3xdx}} - {{3{y^2}dx} \over {3xdx}} + {{3xydy} \over {3xdx}} = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow {x \over 3} - {{{y^2}} \over x} + y{{dy} \over {dx}} = 0$$ Let $${y^2} = t$$ $$2y{{dy} \over {dx}} = {{dt} \over {dx}}$$ $$\therefore$$ $${1 \over 2}{{dt} \over {dx}} - {t \over x} + {x \over 3} = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow {{dt} \over {dx}} - {{2t} \over x} = - {{2x} \over 3}$$ This is linear Differential Equation. $$ \text { I.F. }=e^{\int-\frac{2}{x} d x}=e^{-2 \ln |x|}=e^{\ln \frac{1}{x^2}}=\frac{1}{x^2} $$ So, $t \cdot \frac{1}{x^2}=\int \frac{1}{x^2}\left(\frac{-2 x}{3}\right) d x $ $\Rightarrow \frac{y^2}{x^2}=\frac{-2}{3} \ln |x|+C$ When, $x=1, y=1$ $$ 1=\frac{-2}{3} \ln (1)+C \Rightarrow C=1 $$ $$ \therefore \frac{y^2}{x^2}=\frac{-2}{3} \ln |x|+1 $$ At $x=e, \frac{y^2(e)}{e^2}=\frac{-2}{3}+1 $ $\Rightarrow y^2(e)=\frac{e^2}{3} $ $\Rightarrow 6 y^2(e)=2 e^2$

questions.text: If $f(x) = {{{2^{2x}}} \over {{2^{2x}} + 2}},x \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f\left( {{1 \over {2023}}} \right) + f\left( {{2 \over {2023}}} \right)\, + \,...\, + \,f\left( {{{2022} \over {2023}}} \right)$ is equal to
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \begin{aligned} & f(x)=\frac{4^x}{4^x+2} \\ & f(x)+f(1-x)=\frac{4^x}{4^x+2}+\frac{4^{1-x}}{4^{1-x}+2} \\ & =\frac{4^x}{4^x+2}+\frac{4}{4+2\left(4^x\right)} \\ & =\frac{4^x}{4^{\mathrm{x}}+2}+\frac{2}{2+4^{\mathrm{x}}} \\ & =1 \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{f}(\mathrm{x})+\mathrm{f}(1-\mathrm{x})=1 \\ & \text { Now } \mathrm{f}\left(\frac{1}{2023}\right)+\mathrm{f}\left(\frac{2}{2023}\right)+\mathrm{f}\left(\frac{3}{2023}\right)+\ldots \ldots.+ \\ & \ldots \ldots \ldots..+\mathrm{f}\left(1-\frac{3}{2023}\right)+\mathrm{f}\left(1-\frac{2}{2023}\right)+\mathrm{f}\left(1-\frac{1}{2023}\right) \end{aligned} $$ Now sum of terms equidistant from beginning and end is 1 $$ \begin{aligned} & \text { Sum }=1+1+1+\ldots \ldots \ldots+1 \text { (1011 times }) \\ & =1011 \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: The value of ${\left( {{{1 + \sin {{2\pi } \over 9} + i\cos {{2\pi } \over 9}} \over {1 + \sin {{2\pi } \over 9} - i\cos {{2\pi } \over 9}}}} \right)^3}$ is
questions.solution: Step 1: Since $\sin\dfrac{2\pi}{9}=\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{18}$ and $\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{9}=\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{18}$, write $\theta=\dfrac{5\pi}{18}$. The numerator is $$1+\cos\theta+i\sin\theta = 2\cos^2\dfrac{\theta}{2}+2i\sin\dfrac{\theta}{2}\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2} = 2\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2}\,e^{i\theta/2}$$ The denominator $1+\cos\theta-i\sin\theta$ is its conjugate, $2\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2}\,e^{-i\theta/2}$, and $\cos\dfrac{\theta}{2}\ne 0$, so the fraction equals $$\dfrac{e^{i\theta/2}}{e^{-i\theta/2}} = e^{i\theta} = e^{i5\pi/18}$$ Cubing, $$\left(e^{i5\pi/18}\right)^3 = e^{i5\pi/6} = \cos\dfrac{5\pi}{6}+i\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{6} = -\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}+\dfrac{i}{2} = -\dfrac12\left(\sqrt3-i\right)$$ Hence, the correct option is (B).

Step 1: $$ f(x)=x^3-x^2 f^{\prime}(1)+x f^{\prime \prime}(2)-f^{\prime \prime \prime}(3), x \in R $$ Let $\mathrm{f}^{\prime}(1)=\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{f}^{\prime \prime}(2)=\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{f}^{\prime \prime \prime}(3)=\mathrm{c}$ $$ \begin{aligned} & f(x)=x^3-a x^2+b x-c \\ & f^{\prime}(x)=3 x^2-2 a x+b \\ & f^{\prime \prime}(x)=6 x-2 a \\ & f^{\prime \prime \prime}(x)=6 \\ & c=6, a=3, b=6 \\ & f(x)=x^3-3 x^2+6 x-6 \\ & f(1)=-2, f(2)=2, f(3)=12, f(0)=-6 \\ & 2 f(0)-f(1)+f(3)=2=f(2) \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: When a beam of white light is allowed to pass through convex lens parallel to principal axis, the different colours of light converge at different points on the principal axis after refraction. This is called:
questions.solution: Step 1: The phenomenon described in the statement is called chromatic aberration. Chromatic aberration is a type of optical aberration that occurs when a lens is unable to focus different colors of light at the same point after refraction. This causes the different colors of light to converge at different points on the principal axis, resulting in blurred or distorted images. In the case of a convex lens, the refractive index of the lens is different for different colors of light. The blue light, having the shortest wavelength, refracts the most and the red light, having the longest wavelength, refracts the least. This causes the blue light to converge at a point closer to the lens than the red light, resulting in a blurred image. Spherical aberration, on the other hand, is a type of optical aberration that occurs when a spherical lens is unable to focus all the incident light rays at a single point, resulting in a blurred image. Polarization refers to the orientation of the electric field of light waves, and scattering refers to the phenomenon of light being redirected in different directions due to interaction with matter.

questions.solution: Step 1: Assertion A states that steel is used in the construction of buildings and bridges, which is true. Steel is a widely used material for construction due to its high strength, durability, and resistance to corrosion. Reason R states that steel is more elastic and has a higher elastic limit compared to other common construction materials like concrete, and this is why it is preferred in construction. This statement is also true. Steel's high elasticity and high elastic limit make it an ideal material for use in construction as it can withstand greater stress before it becomes permanently deformed. Therefore, both Assertion A and Reason R are true statements. However, to determine the most appropriate answer, we need to see if Reason R explains Assertion A. Reason R does indeed explain why steel is used in the construction of buildings and bridges. Its high elasticity and high elastic limit allow it to withstand greater stress than other common construction materials before becoming permanently deformed, making it a preferred material for construction. So, the correct answer is Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.text: If the distance of the earth from Sun is 1.5 $\times$ 10$^6$ km. Then the distance of an imaginary planet from Sun, if its period of revolution is 2.83 years is:
questions.solution: Step 1: We can use Kepler's third law to solve this problem. Kepler's third law states that the square of the period of revolution of a planet around the Sun is proportional to the cube of its average distance from the Sun. Let $T$ be the period of revolution of the imaginary planet in years, and let $d$ be its average distance from the Sun in kilometers. We can use the following equation to solve for $d$: $$\frac{T_1^2}{T_2^2} = \frac{d_1^3}{d_2^3}$$ where $T_1$ and $d_1$ are the period of revolution and an average distance of the Earth from the Sun, respectively, and $T_2$ is the period of revolution of the imaginary planet. Substituting the given values, we get: $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}=\left(\frac{d_{1}}{d_{2}}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \\ & \Rightarrow\left(\frac{1 \text { year }}{2.83 \text { year }}\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}=\left(\frac{1.5 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~km}}{d_{2}}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{1}{2}=\frac{1.5 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~km}}{d_{2}} \\ & d_{2}=3 \times 10^{6} \mathrm{~km} \end{aligned} $$

Statement I is incorrect but statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect

questions.solution: Step 1: The most appropriate answer is Statement I is correct but statement II is incorrect. Statement I is correct as acceleration due to Earth's gravity decreases as you move away from its surface either upward or downward. This is because the gravity of the Earth follows an inverse square law, which means that the gravitational force decreases as the square of the distance between two objects increases. However, statement II is incorrect because acceleration due to Earth's gravity is not the same at a height and depth from Earth's surface, even if they are equal in magnitude. This is because the Earth is not a perfect sphere and has a non-uniform distribution of mass, which causes variations in the strength of gravity at different locations. Therefore, the acceleration due to Earth's gravity will be different at a certain height and depth, even if they are equal.

questions.text: A body of mass 200g is tied to a spring of spring constant 12.5 N/m, while the other end of spring is fixed at point O. If the body moves about O in a circular path on a smooth horizontal surface with constant angular speed 5 rad/s, then the ratio of extension in the spring to its natural length will be:
questions.solution: Step 1: Let $\ell$ be the natural length and $x$ the extension. The body moves in a circle of radius $\ell + x$, and the spring force supplies the centripetal force: $$kx = m\omega^2(\ell + x)$$ With $m = 0.2\ \text{kg}$ and $\omega = 5\ \text{rad s}^{-1}$, $m\omega^2 = 0.2 \times 25 = 5\ \text{N m}^{-1}$: $$12.5x = 5(\ell + x) \Rightarrow 7.5x = 5\ell \Rightarrow \dfrac{x}{\ell} = \dfrac{5}{7.5} = \dfrac{2}{3}$$ The natural length itself is not needed, since only the ratio $x: \ell = 2: 3$ is fixed by $k$, $m$ and $\omega$. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: The primary and secondary valencies of cobalt respectively in $\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]Cl_2}$ are:
questions.solution: Step 1: In Werner's theory the primary valency of the metal equals its oxidation state and the secondary valency equals its coordination number. The complex ion is $\ce{[Co(NH3)5Cl]^2+}$; with x as the oxidation state of Co, $$x + 5(0) + (-1) = +2 \Rightarrow x = +3$$ So the primary valency is 3: two chlorides are ionisable counter-ions, and the coordinated chloride satisfies one primary and one secondary valency at the same time. Five $\ce{NH3}$ and one $\ce{Cl-}$ are bonded to Co, so the secondary valency (coordination number) is 6. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
Assertion A: Hydrolysis of an alkyl chloride is a slow reaction but in the presence of NaI, the rate of the hydrolysis increases.
Reason R: I$^{-}$ is a good nucleophile as well as a good leaving group.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below

options.text: A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

questions.solution: Step 1: Hydrolysis of an alkyl chloride is slow because $\ce{Cl-}$ is only a moderate leaving group and water is a weak nucleophile. $\ce{I-}$ is large and highly polarisable, so it is a strong nucleophile and rapidly displaces chloride: $\ce{R-Cl + I- -> R-I + Cl-}$. $\ce{I-}$ is also an excellent leaving group (weakest C–X bond, weakest base among halides), so the alkyl iodide is hydrolysed much faster: $\ce{R-I + H2O -> R-OH + H+ + I-}$. The $\ce{I-}$ is regenerated and acts as a catalyst; this dual role, stated in R, is exactly why the rate increases in A. Hence, the correct option is (C).

Step 1: Lactone Y is 3-hydroxy-4,4-dimethyloxolan-2-one: the ring $\ce{C=O}$ carbon is bonded to a $\ce{CH(OH)}$ carbon, then a $\ce{C(CH3)2}$ carbon, then a $\ce{CH2}$ carbon joined to the ring oxygen. It is the cyclic ester of 2,4-dihydroxy-3,3-dimethylbutanoic acid, $\ce{HOCH2C(CH3)2CH(OH)COOH}$. X is 2-methylpropanal, $\ce{(CH3)2CHCHO}$. Its single $\alpha$-hydrogen lets KOH form the enolate, which adds to HCHO (crossed aldol) to give 3-hydroxy-2,2-dimethylpropanal: $$\ce{(CH3)2CHCHO + HCHO ->[KOH] HOCH2C(CH3)2CHO}$$ Cyanide adds to the aldehyde to form the cyanohydrin; $\ce{H3O+}$ hydrolyses $\ce{-CN}$ to $\ce{-COOH}$, and the resulting 4-hydroxy acid closes to the five-membered lactone: $$\ce{HOCH2C(CH3)2CHO ->[KCN] HOCH2C(CH3)2CH(OH)CN ->[H3O+] HOCH2C(CH3)2CH(OH)COOH -> Y + H2O}$$ Compound (
C) is the aldol product itself; having no $\alpha$-hydrogen, it would only undergo a crossed Cannizzaro reaction with HCHO and KOH, and the straight-chain aldehydes (
B) and (
D) cannot supply the gem-dimethyl carbon of Y. Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
Increasing order of stability of the resonance structures is:
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Step 1: All four are resonance structures of $\ce{OHC-CH=CH-CH=CH-NH2}$; each carries one positive and one negative charge, so stability depends on complete octets and on whether each charge sits next to a group that stabilises it. In D every atom has a complete octet: the positive charge is on nitrogen as $\ce{=N^+H2}$ and the negative charge is on the carbon next to $\ce{CHO}$, where it is delocalised onto the carbonyl oxygen. D is the most stable. In B the carbanion is next to the electron-withdrawing $\ce{CHO}$ and the carbocation is next to the lone pair of $\ce{NH2}$, so both charges are stabilised, but the cationic carbon has only a sextet. In A the carbocation is next to the electron-withdrawing $\ce{CHO}$ and the carbanion is next to the lone pair of $\ce{NH2}$, so both charges are destabilised, and one carbon has only a sextet. In C the positive charge is on the electronegative oxygen, which has only one bond and an incomplete octet, and the negative charge is next to $\ce{NH2}$; C is the least stable. Increasing order of stability: $\text{C} < \text{A} < \text{B} < \text{D}$. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.solution: Step 1: $${\left( {1 - \sqrt 3 i} \right)^{200}}$$ $$ = {\left[ {2\left( {{1 \over 2} - {{\sqrt 3 } \over 2}i} \right)} \right]^{200}}$$ $$ = {2^{200}}{\left( {\cos {\pi \over 3} - i\sin {\pi \over 3}} \right)^{200}}$$ $$ = {2^{200}}\left( {\cos {{200\pi } \over 3} - i\sin {{200\pi } \over 3}} \right)$$ $$ = {2^{200}}\left( {\cos \left( {66\pi + {{2\pi } \over 3}} \right) - i\sin \left( {66\pi + {{2\pi } \over 3}} \right)} \right)$$ $$ = {2^{200}}\left( {\cos {{2\pi } \over 3} - i\sin {{2\pi } \over 3}} \right)$$ $$ = {2^{200}}\left( { - {1 \over 2} - {{\sqrt 3 } \over 2}i} \right)$$ $$ = {2^{199}}\left( { - 1 - \sqrt 3 i} \right)$$ $$ = {2^{199}}\left( {p + iq} \right)$$ $$\therefore$$ p = $$-$$1 and q = $$- \sqrt3$$ Now, $$p - q + {q^2} = - 1 + \sqrt 3 + 3 = 2 + \sqrt 3 = \alpha $$ and $$p + q + {q^2} = - 1 - \sqrt 3 + 3 = 2 - \sqrt 3 = \beta $$ $$\therefore$$ $$\alpha + \beta = 4$$ $$\alpha \beta = \left( {2 + \sqrt 3 } \right)\left( {2 - \sqrt 3 } \right) = 4 - 3 = 1$$ $$\therefore$$ Quadratic equation is $${x^2} - (\alpha + \beta )x + \alpha \beta = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow {x^2} - 4x + 1 = 0$$

questions.solution: Step 1: By the classical definition of probability (a finite sample space of equally likely outcomes), $P(A)=\frac{n(A)}{n(\Omega)}$. (S1): $P(A)=0 \Rightarrow n(A)=0 \Rightarrow A=\phi$, so (S1) is true. (S2): $P(A)=1 \Rightarrow n(A)=n(\Omega) \Rightarrow A=\Omega$, so (S2) is true. Hence both (S1) and (S2) are true, which is NTA's answer (option A). Remark: this rests on the classical definition used in JEE. For a continuous sample space it fails: choosing a point on a wire $[0,1]$, the event $A=\left\{\frac{1}{2}\right\}$ has $P(A)=0$ although $A\neq\phi$, and its complement has probability 1 although it is not $\Omega$.

questions.text: The equation ${x^2} - 4x + [x] + 3 = x[x]$, where $[x]$ denotes the greatest integer function, has:
questions.solution: Step 1: $${x^2} - 4x + [x] + 3 = x[x]$$ $$ \Rightarrow {x^2} - 4x + [x] + 3 - x[x] = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow (x - 1)(x - 3) - [x](x - 1) = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow (x - 1)(x - [x] - 3) = 0$$ $$\therefore$$ $$x = 1$$ or $$x - [x] - 3 = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow \{ x\} - 3 = 0$$ [As $$\{ x\} = x - [x]$$] $$ \Rightarrow \{ x\} = 3$$ But we know, $$0 \le \{ x\} $$\therefore$$ $$\{ x\} \ne 3$$ $$\therefore$$ $$x$$ has only one solution in ($$-\infty,\infty$$) which is $$x = 1.

questions.text: If A and B are two non-zero n $\times$ n matrices such that $\mathrm{A^2+B=A^2B}$, then:
questions.solution: Step 1: Given: $A^{2}+B=A^{2} B\quad...(i)$ $\Rightarrow A^{2}+B-I=A^{2} B-I$ $\Rightarrow A^{2} B-A^{2}-B+I=I$ $\Rightarrow A^{2}(B-I)-I(B-I)=I$ $\Rightarrow\left(A^{2}-I\right)(B-I)=I$ $\therefore A^{2}-I$ is the inverse matrix of $B-I$ and vice versa. So, $(B-I)\left(A^{2}-I\right)=I$ $\Rightarrow B A^{2}-B-A^{2}+I=I$ $\therefore A^{2}+B=B A^{2} \quad...(ii)$ So, by (i) and (ii) $A^{2} B=B A^{2}$

questions.text: For three positive integers p, q, r, ${x^{p{q^2}}} = {y^{qr}} = {z^{{p^2}r}}$ and r = pq + 1 such that 3, 3 log$_yx$, 3 log$_zy$, 7 log$_xz$ are in A.P. with common difference $\frac{1}{2}$. Then r-p-q is equal to
questions.solution: Step 1: The terms $3,\ 3\log_y x,\ 3\log_z y,\ 7\log_x z$ are in A.P. with common difference $\dfrac12$, so $$3\log_y x=\dfrac72,\qquad 3\log_z y=4,\qquad 7\log_x z=\dfrac92.$$ Thus $\log_y x=\dfrac76$ and $\log_z y=\dfrac43$, i.e. $x=y^{7/6}$ and $z=y^{3/4}$; these agree with $\log_x z=\dfrac{9}{14}$, since $\dfrac76\times\dfrac43\times\dfrac{9}{14}=1$. Substituting in $x^{pq^2}=y^{qr}=z^{p^2r}$: $$y^{\frac76pq^2}=y^{qr}=y^{\frac34p^2r} \Rightarrow \dfrac76pq^2=qr=\dfrac34p^2r.$$ First equality: $7pq=6r$. With $r=pq+1$, $7pq=6pq+6 \Rightarrow pq=6$ and $r=7$. Second equality: $q=\dfrac34p^2$, so $p\times\dfrac34p^2=6 \Rightarrow p^3=8 \Rightarrow p=2,\ q=3$. $r-p-q=7-2-3=2$. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Let PQR be a triangle. The points A, B and C are on the sides QR, RP and PQ respectively such that ${{QA} \over {AR}} = {{RB} \over {BP}} = {{PC} \over {CQ}} = {1 \over 2}$. Then ${{Area(\Delta PQR)} \over {Area(\Delta ABC)}}$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: Let the position vector of $P, Q, R$ be $\overrightarrow{0}, \overrightarrow{a}, \overrightarrow{b}$ $\Rightarrow$ Position vector of $A=\frac{2 \overrightarrow{a}+\overrightarrow{b}}{3}, $ Position vector of $B=\frac{2 \overrightarrow{b}}{3}$ and Position vector of $C=\frac{\overrightarrow{a}}{3}$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \therefore \overrightarrow{A B}=\frac{2 \vec{b}}{3}-\left(\frac{2 \vec{a}+\vec{b}}{3}\right)=\frac{\vec{b}}{3}-\frac{2 \vec{a}}{3}=\frac{\vec{b}-2 \vec{a}}{3} \\ & \overrightarrow{C A}=\frac{2 \vec{a}+\vec{b}}{3}-\frac{\vec{a}}{3}=\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}}{3} \\ & \text { Area of } \triangle P Q R=\frac{1}{2}|\overrightarrow{P Q} \times \overrightarrow{P R}|=\frac{1}{2}|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| \\ & \text { Area of } \triangle A B C=\frac{1}{2}|\overrightarrow{C A} \times \overrightarrow{A B}| \ & =\frac{1}{2}\left|\left(\frac{\vec{a}+\vec{b}}{3}\right) \times\left(\frac{\vec{b}-2 \vec{a}}{3}\right)\right|=\frac{1}{2}\left|\frac{\vec{a} \times \vec{b}}{3}\right| \\ & \therefore \frac{\text { Area }(\triangle P Q R)}{\text { Area }(\triangle A B C)}=\frac{\frac{1}{2}|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|}{\frac{1}{2}\left|\frac{\vec{a} \times \vec{b}}{3}\right|}=3 \end{aligned} $$

questions.text:
Let f(x) = matrix x^2sin ( 1 over x ),,\,x ne 0 cr 0,,\,x = 0 cr.
Then at $x=0$

options.text: $f$ is continuous but $f'$ is not continuous

questions.solution: Step 1: Given, $f(x) = matrix x^2sin ( 1 over x ),, x ne 0 cr 0,, x = 0 cr.$ $$\therefore$$ $$f'(x) = 2x\sin \left( {{1 \over x}} \right) - \cos \left( {{1 \over x}} \right)$$ Now, $$\mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to 0} f'(x) = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to 0} \left[ {2x\sin \left( {{1 \over x}} \right) - \cos \left( {{1 \over x}} \right)} \right]$$ $$ = 0 - \mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to 0} \cos \left( {{1 \over x}} \right)$$ = Does not exist $$\therefore$$ $$f'(x)$$ is discontinuous function at $$x = 0$$. L.H.D. $$ = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{h \to {0^ + }} {{f(0 - h) - f(0)} \over { - h}}$$ $$ = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{h \to {0^ + }} {{f( - h)} \over { - h}}$$ $$ = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{h \to {0^ + }} {{ - {h^2}\sin \left( {{1 \over h}} \right)} \over { - h}} = 0$$ R.H.D. $$ = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{h \to {0^ + }} {{f(0 + h) - f(0)} \over h}$$ $$ = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{h \to {0^ + }} {{f(h)} \over h}$$ $$ = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{h \to {0^ + }} {{{h^2}\sin \left( {{1 \over h}} \right)} \over h} = 0$$ $$\therefore$$ L.H.D. = R.H.D. $$ \Rightarrow f(x)$$ is differentiable at $$x = 0$$. So, f(x) is continuous.

questions.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: If the Brewster's angle for the light propagating from air to glass is $\mathrm{\theta_B}$, then the Brewster's angle for the light propagating from glass to air is $\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta_B$
Statement II: The Brewster's angle for the light propagating from glass to air is ${\tan ^{ - 1}}({\mu _\mathrm{g}})$ where $\mathrm{\mu_g}$ is the refractive index of glass.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false

questions.solution: Step 1: At the Brewster angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, so the angle of incidence $i_B$ and the angle of refraction $r$ satisfy $i_B + r = 90^\circ$, i.e. $\sin r = \cos i_B$. Air to glass: Snell's law gives $\sin\theta_B = \mu_g \sin r = \mu_g \cos\theta_B$, so $$\tan\theta_B = \mu_g \Rightarrow \theta_B = \tan^{-1}(\mu_g)$$ Glass to air: Snell's law gives $\mu_g \sin\theta_B' = \sin r' = \cos\theta_B'$, so $$\tan\theta_B' = \dfrac{1}{\mu_g} = \dfrac{1}{\tan\theta_B} = \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta_B\right) \Rightarrow \theta_B' = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta_B$$ Hence Statement I is true. Statement II gives $\tan^{-1}(\mu_g)$, which is the Brewster angle for light going from air to glass; for glass to air it is $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\mu_g}\right)$ (for $\mu_g = 1.5$, about $33.7^\circ$ rather than $56.3^\circ$). Hence Statement II is false. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The weight of a body at the surface of earth is 18 N. The weight of the body at an altitude of 3200 km above the earth's surface is (given, radius of earth $\mathrm{R_e=6400~km}$):
questions.solution: Step 1: The weight of an object at a height h from the Earth's surface is given by: $$W' = W \left(\frac{R}{{R + h}}\right)^2$$ where: W' is the weight at height h, W is the weight at the Earth's surface, R is the radius of the Earth, h is the height above the Earth's surface. In this problem, the weight at the Earth's surface W is given as 18 N, the radius of the Earth R is given as 6400 km, and the height h is given as 3200 km. Substituting these values into the equation gives: $$W' = 18 N \left(\frac{6400~km}{{6400~km + 3200~km}}\right)^2 = 18 N \left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^2 = 18 N \cdot \frac{4}{9} = 8 N$$ Therefore, the weight of the body at an altitude of 3200 km above the Earth's surface is 8 N.

questions.text: What is the mass ratio of ethylene glycol ($\mathrm{C_2H_6O_2}$, molar mass = 62 g/mol) required for making 500 g of 0.25 molal aqueous solution and 250 mL of 0.25 molar aqueous solution?
questions.solution: Step 1: Molality is moles of solute per kg of solvent, and $500\ \text{g}$ is the mass of the whole solution. Let the molal solution contain $n$ mol of glycol: mass of glycol $= 62n\ \text{g}$ and mass of water $= (500 - 62n)\ \text{g}$. $$0.25 = \dfrac{n}{(500 - 62n)/1000} \Rightarrow 1000n = 125 - 15.5n \Rightarrow n = 0.1231\ \text{mol}$$ $$w_1 = 62 \times 0.1231 = 7.63\ \text{g}$$ For $250\ \text{mL}$ of $0.25\ \text{M}$ solution, moles $= 0.25 \times 0.250 = 0.0625\ \text{mol}$, so $w_2 = 62 \times 0.0625 = 3.875\ \text{g}$. $$\dfrac{w_1}{w_2} = \dfrac{7.63}{3.875} = 1.97 \approx 2$$ So the mass ratio is $2: 1$. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: Find out the major product from the following reaction.
questions.solution: Step 1: Concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$ protonates the –OH of 2,2,6-trimethylcyclohexan-1-ol, and loss of water gives a secondary carbocation at C-1. C-1 lies between C-2, which carries two $\ce{CH3}$ groups, and C-6, which carries one $\ce{CH3}$ and one H. A 1,2-methyl shift from C-2 gives a tertiary cation at C-2; a 1,2-hydride shift from C-6 gives a tertiary cation at C-6. The C-6 cation can lose a proton only to form trisubstituted alkenes (C-1=C-6 or C-5=C-6, options A and B). The C-2 cation loses the H on C-1 to form 1,2,3-trimethylcyclohex-1-ene, a tetrasubstituted alkene. In hot concentrated acid the protonation, shift and deprotonation steps are reversible, so the alkenes equilibrate and the most substituted, most stable alkene is the major product. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The equations of two sides of a variable triangle are $x=0$ and $y=3$, and its third side is a tangent to the parabola $y^2=6x$. The locus of its circumcentre is:
questions.solution: Step 1: The parabola $y^2 = 6x$ has $4a = 6$, so $a = \dfrac{3}{2}$ and the tangent at the point $\left(\dfrac{3t^2}{2}, 3t\right)$ is $ty = x + \dfrac{3}{2}t^2$. The sides $x = 0$ and $y = 3$ are perpendicular, so the triangle is right-angled at $(0, 3)$ and its circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, which is the side on the tangent. The tangent meets $x = 0$ at $\left(0, \dfrac{3t}{2}\right)$ and $y = 3$ at $\left(3t - \dfrac{3t^2}{2}, 3\right)$. For the circumcentre $(h, k)$: $$2h = 3t - \dfrac{3t^2}{2} \Rightarrow 4h = 6t - 3t^2, \qquad 2k = \dfrac{3t}{2} + 3 \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{4k - 6}{3}$$ Substituting $t$: $$4h = 2(4k - 6) - \dfrac{(4k - 6)^2}{3} \Rightarrow 12h = 24k - 36 - (16k^2 - 48k + 36)$$ $$\Rightarrow 16k^2 - 72k + 12h + 72 = 0 \Rightarrow 4k^2 - 18k + 3h + 18 = 0$$ The locus is $4y^2 - 18y + 3x + 18 = 0$. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: The foot of perpendicular of the point (2, 0, 5) on the line ${{x + 1} \over 2} = {{y - 1} \over 5} = {{z + 1} \over { - 1}}$ is ($\alpha,\beta,\gamma$). Then, which of the following is NOT correct?
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \mathrm{L}: \frac{\mathrm{x}+1}{2}=\frac{y-1}{5}=\frac{z+1}{-1}=\lambda \text { (let) } $$ Let foot of perpendicular is $$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{P}(2 \lambda-1,5 \lambda+1,-\lambda-1) \\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{PA}}=(3-2 \lambda) \hat{\mathrm{i}}-(5 \lambda+1) \hat{\mathrm{j}}+(6+\lambda) \hat{\mathrm{k}} \\ & \text { Direction ratio of line } \Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}}=2 \hat{\mathrm{i}}+5 \hat{\mathrm{j}}-\hat{\mathrm{k}} \\ & \text { Now, } \Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{PA}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{b}}=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 2(3-2 \lambda)-5(5 \lambda+1)-(6+\lambda)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{-1}{6} \\ & \mathrm{P}(2 \lambda-1,5 \lambda+1,-\lambda-1) \equiv \mathrm{P}(\alpha, \beta, \gamma) \\ & \Rightarrow \alpha=2\left(-\frac{1}{6}\right)-1=-\frac{4}{3} \Rightarrow \alpha=-\frac{4}{3} \\ & \Rightarrow \beta=5\left(-\frac{1}{6}\right)+1=\frac{1}{6} \Rightarrow \beta=\frac{1}{6} \\ & \Rightarrow \gamma=-\lambda-1=\frac{1}{6}-1 \Rightarrow \gamma=-\frac{5}{6} \end{aligned} $$

satisfying $f(n) + {1 \over n}f(n + 1) = 1,\forall n \in \{ 1,2,3\} $ is

questions.text: If the function f(x) = matrix (1 + |cos x|)^λ over |cos x|,,, 0 is continuous atx = {\pi \over 2}$, then $9\lambda + 6{\log _e}\mu + {\mu ^6} - {e^{6\lambda }} is equal to
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \rightarrow \frac{\pi^{-}}{2}}(1+|\cos x|)^ \frac{\lambda}{|\cos x|}=e^\lambda $$ And, $$ \begin{aligned} &\mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \rightarrow \frac{\pi^{+}}{2}} e^{\frac{\cot 6 x}{\cot 4 x}}\\ &= \mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to {{{\pi ^ + }} \over 2}} {e^{{{\sin 4x.\cos 6x} \over {\sin 6x.\cos 4x}}}} \\ & =e^{\frac{2}{3}} \end{aligned} $$ Also, $$ f(\pi / 2)=\mu $$ For continuous function, $ \mathrm{e}^{2 / 3}=\mathrm{e}^\lambda=\mu$ $$ \lambda=\frac{2}{3}, \mu=\mathrm{e}^{2 / 3} $$ $$ \therefore $$ $9 \lambda+6 \ln \mu+\mu^{6}-e^{6 \lambda}$ $=6+4+e^{4}-e^{4}=10$

questions.text:
Let A, B, C be 3 $\times$ 3 matrices such that A is symmetric and B and C are skew-symmetric. Consider the statements
(S1) A$^{13}$ B$^{26}$ $-$ B$^{26}$ A$^{13}$ is symmetric
(S2) A$^{26}$ C$^{13}$ $-$ C$^{13}$ A$^{26}$ is symmetric
Then,

options.text: Both S1 and S2 are false
Both S1 and S2 are true

questions.solution: Step 1: $A^{T}=A, B^{T}=-B, C^{T}=-C$ $$ \begin{aligned} P & =A^{13} B^{26}-B^{26} A^{13} \\ P^{T} & =\left(A^{13} B^{26}-B^{26} A^{13}\right)^{T}=\left(A^{13} B^{26}\right)^{T}-\left(B^{26} A^{13}\right)^{T} \\ & =\left(B^{26}\right)^{T}\left(A^{13}\right)^{T}-\left(A^{13}\right)^{T}\left(B^{26}\right)^{T} \\ & =\left(B^{T}\right)^{26}\left(A^{T}\right)^{13}-\left(A^{T}\right)^{13}\left(B^{T}\right)^{26} \\ & =B^{26} A^{13}-A^{13} B^{26}=-\left(A^{13} B^{26}-B^{26} A^{13}\right)=-P \end{aligned} $$ $P$ is skew-symmetric matrix $\Rightarrow S_{1}$ is false $Q=A^{26} C^{13}-C^{13} A^{26}, Q^{T}=\left(A^{26} C^{13}-C^{13} A^{26}\right)^{T}$ $Q^{T}=\left(A^{26} C^{13}\right)^{T}-\left(C^{13} A^{26}\right)^{T}=\left(C^{13}\right)^{T}\left(A^{26}\right)^{T}-\left(A^{26}\right)^{T}\left(C^{13}\right)^{T}$ $=\left(C^{T}\right)^{13}\left(A^{T}\right)^{26}-\left(A^{T}\right)^{26}\left(C^{T}\right)^{13}=-C^{13} A^{26}+A^{26} C^{13}$ $=A^{26} C^{13}-C^{13} A^{26}$ $\Rightarrow Q^{T}=Q \Rightarrow Q$ is symmetric matrix $\Rightarrow S_{2}$ is true.

questions.text: The shortest distance between the lines $x+1=2y=-12z$ and $x=y+2=6z-6$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Writing $x+1=2y=-12z=t$, the line $L_1$ passes through $(-1,0,0)$ with direction $\left(1,\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{12}\right)\parallel(12,6,-1)$. Writing $x=y+2=6z-6=s$, the line $L_2$ passes through $(0,-2,1)$ with direction $\left(1,1,\tfrac{1}{6}\right)\parallel(6,6,1)$. The common perpendicular is along $$(12,6,-1)\times(6,6,1)=(6+6,\,-6-12,\,72-36)=(12,-18,36)=6(2,-3,6)$$ and $|(2,-3,6)|=\sqrt{4+9+36}=7$. The vector joining the two points is $(0,-2,1)-(-1,0,0)=(1,-2,1)$, so $$\text{S.D.}=\frac{|(1,-2,1)\cdot(2,-3,6)|}{7}=\frac{|2+6+6|}{7}=\frac{14}{7}=2$$ Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Let T and C respectively be the transverse and conjugate axes of the hyperbola $16{x^2} - {y^2} + 64x + 4y + 44 = 0$. Then the area of the region above the parabola ${x^2} = y + 4$, below the transverse axis T and on the right of the conjugate axis C is:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$16x^2 + 64x - y^2 + 4y + 44 = 0 \Rightarrow 16(x+2)^2 - (y-2)^2 = 16 \Rightarrow \dfrac{(x+2)^2}{1} - \dfrac{(y-2)^2}{16} = 1$$ The centre is $(-2, 2)$ and the transverse axis is parallel to the $x$-axis, so T: $y = 2$ and C: $x = -2$. The parabola is $y = x^2 - 4$; it meets $y = 2$ where $x^2 = 6$, i.e. $x = \pm\sqrt{6}$. Since $-\sqrt{6} < -2$, the region to the right of $x = -2$ runs from $x = -2$ to $x = \sqrt{6}$, between $y = x^2 - 4$ below and $y = 2$ above. $$A = \int\limits_{-2}^{\sqrt{6}} \left(2 - (x^2 - 4)\right) dx = \left[6x - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-2}^{\sqrt{6}}$$ $$A = \left(6\sqrt{6} - 2\sqrt{6}\right) - \left(-12 + \dfrac{8}{3}\right) = 4\sqrt{6} + \dfrac{28}{3}$$ Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: Let the function $f(x) = 2{x^3} + (2p - 7){x^2} + 3(2p - 9)x - 6$ have a maxima for some value of $x 0$. Then, the set of all values of p is
questions.solution: Step 1: $$f'(x) = 6x^2 + 2(2p-7)x + 3(2p-9)$$ A maximum at some $x 0$ require $f'(x) = 0$ to have two real roots $x_1 0$ require $f'(x) = 0$ to have two real roots $x_1 < 0 < x_2$. Since the leading coefficient of $f'$ is positive, $f'$ changes sign from $+$ to $-$ at $x_1$ (maximum) and from $-$ to $+$ at $x_2$ (minimum). An upward-opening quadratic has its roots on opposite sides of $0$ exactly when its value at $0$ is negative; this also makes the discriminant positive, so the roots are real and distinct. $$f'(0) = 3(2p-9) < 0 \Rightarrow p < \dfrac{9}{2}$$ So $p \in \left(-\infty, \dfrac{9}{2}\right)$. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Let $z$ be a complex number such that $\left| {{{z - 2i} \over {z + i}}} \right| = 2,z \ne - i$. Then $z$ lies on the circle of radius 2 and centre:
questions.solution: Step 1: $\left|\frac{z-2 i}{z+i}\right|=2$ $\Rightarrow (z-2 i)(\bar{z}+2 i)=4(z+i)(\bar{z}-i)$ $\Rightarrow z \bar{z}+2 i z-2 i \bar{z}+4=4(z \bar{z}-z i+\bar{z} i+1)$ $\Rightarrow 3 z \bar{z}-6 i z+6 i \bar{z}=0$ $\Rightarrow z \bar{z}-2 i z+2 i \bar{z}=0$ $\therefore$ Centre $(-2 i)$ or $(0,-2)$ Other Method: $\left|\frac{z-2 i}{z+i}\right|=2, z \neq-i$ Put $z=x+i y$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \left|\frac{x+i y-2 i}{x+i y+i}\right|=2 \\ & \Rightarrow \left|\frac{x+i(y-2)}{x+i(y+1)}\right|^2=4 \\ & \Rightarrow x^2+(y-2)^2=4\left[x^2+(y+1)^2\right] \\ & \Rightarrow x^2+y^2+4-4 y=4\left[x^2+y^2+1+2 y\right] \end{aligned} $$ $\Rightarrow$ $x^2+y^2+4 y=0$ or $x^2+(y+2)^2=2^2$ $$ \therefore $$ Centre is $(0,-2)$.

questions.text: The integral $16\int\limits_1^2 {{{dx} \over {{x^3}{{\left( {{x^2} + 2} \right)}^2}}}} $ is equal to
questions.solution: Step 1: $I=\int \frac{d x}{x^{3}\left(x^{2}+2\right)^{2}}$ $=\frac{1}{4} \int \frac{x}{x^{2}+2} d x+\frac{1}{4} \int \frac{x}{\left(x^{2}+2\right)^{2}}-\frac{1}{4} \int \frac{d x}{x}+\frac{1}{4} \int \frac{d x}{x^{3}}$ $=\frac{1}{8} \ln \left(x^{2}+2\right)-\frac{\ln x}{4}-\frac{1}{8\left(x^{2}+2\right)}-\frac{1}{8 x^{2}}$ Now, $16 \int_{1}^{2} \frac{d x}{x^{3}\left(x^{2}+2\right)^{2}}=2 \ln 6-2 \ln 3-4 \ln 2+\frac{11}{6}$ $=\frac{11}{6}-\ln 4$

questions.text: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function defined by $f(x) = {\log _{\sqrt m }}\{ \sqrt 2 (\sin x - \cos x) + m - 2\} $, for some $m$, such that the range of $f$ is [0, 2]. Then the value of $m$ is _________
questions.solution:
Step 1: Since $\sin x-\cos x=\sqrt{2}\sin\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\in[-\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}]$, the argument of the logarithm satisfies $$\sqrt{2}(\sin x-\cos x)+m-2\in[m-4,\ m]$$ As $f$ is defined for every real $x$, the argument must stay positive, so $m-4>0$, i.e. $m>4$; then the base $\sqrt{m}>1$ and the logarithm is increasing.

Step 2: So the range of $f$ is $\left[\log_{\sqrt{m}}(m-4),\ \log_{\sqrt{m}}m\right]$, and the upper end $\log_{\sqrt{m}}m=2$ for every such $m$. The lower end must be $0$: $\log_{\sqrt{m}}(m-4)=0\Rightarrow m-4=1\Rightarrow m=5$. For $m=4$ the argument reaches $0$, where the logarithm is undefined, so the range cannot be $[0,2]$. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: Let $y=y(t)$ be a solution of the differential equation ${{dy} \over {dt}} + \alpha y = \gamma {e^{ - \beta t}}$ where, $\alpha > 0,\beta > 0$ and $\gamma > 0$. Then $\mathop {\lim }\limits_{t \to \infty } y(t)$
questions.solution: Step 1: $\frac{d y}{d t}+\alpha y=\gamma e^{-\beta t}$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \text { I.F. }=e^{\int \alpha d t}=e^{\alpha t} \\ & \Rightarrow y \cdot e^{\alpha t}=\gamma \int e^{(\alpha-\beta) t} d t=\gamma \frac{e^{(\alpha-\beta) t}}{(\alpha-\beta)}+C \\ & \Rightarrow y=\frac{\gamma}{(\alpha-\beta)} e^{-\beta t}+C e^{-\alpha t} \\ & \lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} y(t)=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty}\left[\frac{\gamma}{(\alpha-\beta)} e^{-\beta t}+C e^{-\alpha t}\right]=0 \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: Let A = [ matrix 1 over √(10), 3 over √(10) cr - 3 over √(10), 1 over √(10) cr ] and B = [ matrix 1, - i cr 0, 1 cr ], where $i = \sqrt { - 1} $. If $\mathrm{M=A^T B A}$, then the inverse of the matrix $\mathrm{AM^{2023}A^T}$ is
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \mathrm{AA}^{\mathrm{T}}=\left[{cc} \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \ \frac{-3}{\sqrt{10}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \right]\left[{cc} \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \frac{-3}{\sqrt{10}} \ \frac{3}{\sqrt{10}} \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}} \right]=\left[{ll} 1 0 \ 0 1 \right] = I; \ \mathrm{B}^2=\left[{cc} 1 -\mathrm{i} \ 0 1 \right]\left[{cc} 1 -\mathrm{i} \ 0 1 \right]=\left[{cc} 1 -2 \mathrm{i} \ 0 1 \right]; \mathrm{B}^3=\left[{cc} 1 -3 \mathrm{i} \ 0 1 \right] $$ Similarly, $$ \mathrm{B}^{2023}=\left[{cc} 1 -2023 \mathrm{i} \ 0 1 \right]; \mathrm{M}=\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathrm{BA}; \mathrm{M}^2=\mathrm{M} \cdot \mathrm{M}=\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathrm{BA} \mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathrm{BA}=\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathrm{B}^2 \mathrm{~A}; \mathrm{M}^3=\mathrm{M}^2 \cdot \mathrm{M}=\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathrm{B}^2 \mathrm{AA}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathrm{BA}=\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathrm{B}^3 \mathrm{~A} $$ Similarly, $$ \mathrm{M}^{2023}= \mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathrm{B}^{2023} \mathrm{~A}; \mathrm{AM}^{2023} \mathrm{~A}^{\mathrm{T}}=\mathrm{AA}^{\mathrm{T}} \mathrm{B}^{2023} \mathrm{AA}^{\mathrm{T}} = \mathrm{I}.\mathrm{B}^{2023}.\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{B}^{2023}; =\left[{cc} 1 -2023 \mathrm{i} \ 0 1 \right] $$ $$ \therefore $$ $$ \text { Inverse of }\left(\mathrm{AM}^{2023} \mathrm{~A}^{\mathrm{T}}\right) \text { is }\left[{cc} 1 2023 i \ 0 1 \right] $$

questions.text: Let $f(x) = 2{x^n} + \lambda,\lambda \in R,n \in N$, and $f(4) = 133,f(5) = 255$. Then the sum of all the positive integer divisors of $(f(3) - f(2))$ is
questions.solution: Step 1: $f(x)=2 x^{n}+\lambda, \lambda \in \mathbb{R}, n \in \mathbb{N}$ $f(4)=2 \cdot 4^{n}+\lambda=133, f(5)=2 \cdot 5^{n}+\lambda=255$ $f(5)-f(4)=2 \cdot\left(5^{n}-4^{n}\right)=122 \Rightarrow n=3$ $\Rightarrow f(3)-f(2)=2 \cdot\left(3^{n}-2^{n}\right)=2 \cdot\left(3^{3}-2^{3}\right)=2 \times 19$ Required sum $=1+2+19+38=60$

questions.text: A particle executes simple harmonic motion between $x=-A$ and $x=+A$. If time taken by particle to go from $x=0$ to $\frac{A}{2}$ is 2 s; then time taken by particle in going from $x=\frac{A}{2}$ to A is

questions.text:
Match List I with List II

LIST I
A. Isothermal Process
B. Adiabatic Process
C. Isochoric Process
D. Isobaric Process

LIST II
I. Work done by the gas decreases internal energy
II. No change in internal energy
III. The heat absorbed goes partly to increase internal energy and partly to do work
IV. No work is done on or by the gas

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \Delta \mathrm{U}=\mathrm{nC}_{\mathrm{v}} \Delta \mathrm{T} $$ For isothermal process $\mathrm{T}$ is constant So $\Delta \mathrm{U}=0$ $\mathrm{A} \longrightarrow \mathrm{II}$ Adiabatic process $$ \begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{Q}=0 \\ & \Delta \mathrm{Q}=\Delta \mathrm{U}+\Delta \mathrm{W} \\ & \Delta \mathrm{U}=-\Delta \mathrm{W} \end{aligned} $$ Work done by gas is positive So $\Delta \mathrm{U}$ is negative $$ \text { B } \longrightarrow \text { I } $$ For Isochoric process $\Delta \mathrm{W}=0$ $$ \mathrm{C} \longrightarrow \mathrm{IV} $$ For Isobaric process $$ \begin{aligned} & \Delta \mathrm{W}=\mathrm{P} \Delta \mathrm{V} \neq 0 \\ & \Delta \mathrm{U}=\mathrm{nC}_{\mathrm{V}} \Delta \mathrm{T} \neq 0 \end{aligned} $$ Heat absorbed goes partly to increase internal energy and partly to do work.

questions.text: Consider a block kept on an inclined plane (incline at 45$^\circ$) as shown in the figure. If the force required to just push it up the incline is 2 times the force required to just prevent it from sliding down, the coefficient of friction between the block and inclined plane($\mu$) is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: To just push the block up, friction acts down the incline with its limiting value $\mu N = \mu mg\cos 45^\circ$: $$F_1 = mg\sin 45^\circ + \mu mg\cos 45^\circ = \dfrac{mg}{\sqrt{2}}(1 + \mu)$$ To just prevent sliding down, friction acts up the incline: $$F_2 = mg\sin 45^\circ - \mu mg\cos 45^\circ = \dfrac{mg}{\sqrt{2}}(1 - \mu)$$ Given $F_1 = 2F_2$: $$1 + \mu = 2(1 - \mu) \Rightarrow 3\mu = 1 \Rightarrow \mu = \dfrac{1}{3} \approx 0.33$$ Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
Every planet revolves around the sun in an elliptical orbit:-
A. The force acting on a planet is inversely proportional to square of distance from sun.
B. Force acting on planet is inversely proportional to product of the masses of the planet and the sun.
C. The Centripetal force acting on the planet is directed away from the sun.
D. The square of time period of revolution of planet around sun is directly proportional to cube of semi-major axis of elliptical orbit.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Step 1: The force acting on a planet is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the sun. This is known as the inverse square law and is described by Newton's law of gravitation.
B. Force acting on a planet is inversely proportional to the product of the masses of the planet and the sun. This is also described by Newton's law of gravitation, but it is not directly related to the planet's elliptical orbit.
C. The centripetal force acting on the planet is directed towards the sun, not away from it.
D. The square of the time period of revolution of a planet around the sun is directly proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of the elliptical orbit. This is known as Kepler's third law. Therefore, only A and D are correct.

questions.text: Two objects are projected with same velocity 'u' however at different angles $\alpha$ and $\beta$ with the horizontal. If $\alpha+\beta=90^\circ$, the ratio of horizontal range of the first object to the 2nd object will be:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \text {Range}=\frac{u^2 \sin 2 \theta}{g} $$ Range for projection angle " $\alpha$ " $$ \mathrm{R}_1=\frac{\mathrm{u}^2 \sin 2 \alpha}{\mathrm{g}} $$ Range for projection angle " $\beta$ " $$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{R}_2=\frac{\mathrm{u}^2 \sin 2 \beta}{\mathrm{g}} \\ & \alpha+\beta=90^{\circ}(\text { Given }) \\ & \Rightarrow \beta=90^{\circ}-\alpha \\ & \mathrm{R}_2=\frac{\mathrm{u}^2 \sin 2\left(90^{\circ}-\alpha\right)}{\mathrm{g}} \\ & \mathrm{R}_2=\frac{\mathrm{u}^2 \sin \left(180^{\circ}-2 \alpha\right)}{\mathrm{g}} \\ & \mathrm{R}_2=\frac{\mathrm{u}^2 \sin 2 \alpha}{\mathrm{g}} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{R}_1}{\mathrm{R}_2}=\frac{\left(\frac{\mathrm{u}^2 \sin 2 \alpha}{\mathrm{g}}\right)}{\left(\frac{\mathrm{u}^2 \sin 2 \alpha}{\mathrm{g}}\right)}=\frac{1}{1} \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: The resistance of a wire is 5 $\Omega$. Its new resistance in ohm if stretched to 5 times of its original length will be:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \mathrm{R}_{\text {initial }}=\frac{\rho \ell}{A}=5 \Omega $$ $\because$ Volume of wire is constant in stretching $$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{f}} \\ & \mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{i}} \ell_{\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{f}} \ell_{\mathrm{f}} \\ & \mathrm{A} \ell=\mathrm{A}^{\prime}(5 \ell) \\ & \mathrm{A}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{A}}{5} \\ & \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{f}}=\frac{\rho \ell_{\mathrm{f}}}{\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{f}}}=\frac{\rho(5 \ell)}{\left(\frac{\mathrm{A}}{5}\right)} \\ & =25\left(\frac{\rho \ell}{\mathrm{A}}\right) \\ & =25 \times 5=125 \Omega \end{aligned} $$

questions.text:
Statement I: When a Si sample is doped with Boron, it becomes P type and when doped by Arsenic it becomes N-type semi conductor such that P-type has excess holes and N-type has excess electrons.
Statement II: When such P-type and N-type semi-conductors, are fused to make a junction, a current will automatically flow which can be detected with an externally connected ammeter.
In the light of above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below

options.text: Statement I is incorrect but statement II is correct
Both Statement I and statement II are correct
Statement I is correct but statement II is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect

questions.solution: Step 1: Boron is trivalent (acceptor), so boron-doped Si is p-type with holes as majority carriers; arsenic is pentavalent (donor), so arsenic-doped Si is n-type with electrons as majority carriers. Statement I is correct. When the two are joined, holes and electrons diffuse across the junction only until the depletion layer and its barrier potential are built up; then the drift current equals the diffusion current and the net current across the junction is zero. With an external ammeter connected, the contact potentials around the closed circuit cancel the barrier potential, so no steady current flows and the ammeter reads zero. Statement II is incorrect. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: The correct order in aqueous medium of basic strength in case of methyl substituted amines is:
questions.solution: Step 1: In the gas phase only the $+I$ effect of the methyl groups operates, giving $\ce{Me3N > Me2NH > MeNH2 > NH3}$ (option (B)), but this order does not hold in water. In water the protonated amine is also stabilised by hydrogen bonding with water molecules; the more $\ce{N-H}$ bonds the cation has, the better it is solvated. $\ce{Me3NH+}$ has only one $\ce{N-H}$ bond and its three methyl groups hinder solvation, so trimethylamine falls below methylamine despite the larger $+I$ effect. The combined $+I$, solvation and steric effects give the aqueous order (pKb in brackets): $$\ce{Me2NH}\,(3.27) > \ce{MeNH2}\,(3.38) > \ce{Me3N}\,(4.22) > \ce{NH3}\,(4.75)$$ Hence, the correct option is (C).

D. $\mathrm{Ba^{2+},Ca^{2+}}$

I. $\mathrm{H_2S}$ gas in presence of dilute HCl
II. $\mathrm{(NH_4)_2CO_3}$ in presence of $\mathrm{NH_4OH}$
III. $\mathrm{NH_4OH}$ in presence of $\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$
IV. H₂S in presence of NH 4 OH

Correct match is -

options.text: A $\to$ i, B $\to$ iii, C $\to$ iv, D $\to$ ii
A $\to$ i, B $\to$ iii, C $\to$ ii, D $\to$ iv
A $\to$ iii, B $\to$ i, C $\to$ iv, D $\to$ ii
A $\to$ iv, B $\to$ ii, C $\to$ iii, D $\to$ i

questions.solution:
Step 1: In qualitative analysis, cations are separated into analytical groups (not periodic-table groups) by group reagents. $\ce{Pb^2+}$, $\ce{Cu^2+}$ (group II): their sulphides have very low $K_{sp}$, so they precipitate with $\ce{H2S}$ even in dilute HCl, where $[\ce{S^2-}]$ is kept low: i. $\ce{Al^3+}$, $\ce{Fe^3+}$ (group III): precipitated as hydroxides by $\ce{NH4OH}$ in the presence of $\ce{NH4Cl}$, which suppresses $[\ce{OH-}]$ so that only these low-$K_{sp}$ hydroxides form: iii. $\ce{Co^2+}$, $\ce{Ni^2+}$ (group IV): their sulphides have higher $K_{sp}$ and precipitate with $\ce{H2S}$ only in ammoniacal medium, where $[\ce{S^2-}]$ is high: iv. $\ce{Ba^2+}$, $\ce{Ca^2+}$ (group V): precipitated as carbonates by $\ce{(NH4)2CO3}$ in the presence of $\ce{NH4OH}$: ii.

Step 2: So A $\to$ i, B $\to$ iii, C $\to$ iv, D $\to$ ii. Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: The vector $\overrightarrow a = - \widehat i + 2\widehat j + \widehat k$ is rotated through a right angle, passing through the y-axis in its way and the resulting vector is $\overrightarrow b $. Then the projection of $3\overrightarrow a + \sqrt 2 \overrightarrow b $ on $\overrightarrow c = 5\widehat i + 4\widehat j + 3\widehat k$ is:
questions.solution:
Step 1: Rotating $\vec a$ through a right angle so that it passes through the y-axis keeps $\vec b$ in the plane of $\vec a$ and $\hat j$, with $\vec b \perp \vec a$ and $|\vec b| = |\vec a| = \sqrt 6$.

Step 2: So $\vec b = \lambda\vec a + \mu\hat j$. $$\vec b \cdot \vec a = 0 \Rightarrow 6\lambda + 2\mu = 0 \Rightarrow \mu = -3\lambda$$ $$\vec b = \lambda(-\hat i + 2\hat j + \hat k) - 3\lambda\hat j = \lambda(-\hat i - \hat j + \hat k)$$ $|\vec b| = \sqrt 3\,|\lambda| = \sqrt 6 \Rightarrow |\lambda| = \sqrt 2$. $\vec a$ makes an angle $\alpha$ with the y-axis where $\cos\alpha = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt 6}$, so $\alpha 0$, so $\lambda = -\sqrt 2$: $$\vec b = \sqrt 2\,\hat i + \sqrt 2\,\hat j - \sqrt 2\,\hat k$$ $$3\vec a + \sqrt 2\,\vec b = (-3\hat i + 6\hat j + 3\hat k) + (2\hat i + 2\hat j - 2\hat k) = -\hat i + 8\hat j + \hat k$$ The projection on $\vec c$ is $$\frac{(-\hat i + 8\hat j + \hat k)\cdot(5\hat i + 4\hat j + 3\hat k)}{|\vec c|} = \frac{-5 + 32 + 3}{\sqrt{50}} = \frac{30}{5\sqrt 2} = 3\sqrt 2$$ Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The minimum value of the function $f(x) = \int\limits_0^2 {{e^{|x - t|}}dt} $ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: For $0\le x\le 2$, split the integral at $t=x$: $$f(x)=\int\limits_0^x e^{x-t}\,dt+\int\limits_x^2 e^{t-x}\,dt=(e^x-1)+(e^{2-x}-1)=e^x+e^{2-x}-2$$ By AM–GM, $e^x+e^{2-x}\ge 2\sqrt{e^x\cdot e^{2-x}}=2e$, with equality at $x=1$, so the least value on $[0,2]$ is $2e-2=2(e-1)$. For $x>2$, $f(x)=\displaystyle\int\limits_0^2 e^{x-t}\,dt=e^{x-2}(e^2-1)>e^2-1$. For $x e^2-1$. Since $e^2-1=(e-1)(e+1)>2(e-1)$, the minimum value of $f$ is $2(e-1)$. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.solution: Step 1: Let $N$ be the number of students. Raising one mark from 8 to 12 increases the total by 4, so the mean increases by $\dfrac{4}{N}$: $$10+\dfrac{4}{N}=10.2 \Rightarrow N=20$$ The original variance gives $\dfrac{\sum x_i^2}{20}-10^2=4$, so $\sum x_i^2=20\times 104=2080$. After the change, $\sum x_i^2=2080-8^2+12^2=2080-64+144=2160$. $$\sigma_{\text{new}}^2=\dfrac{2160}{20}-(10.2)^2=108-104.04=3.96$$ Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.solution: Step 1: $x+y=66$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{x+y}{2} \geq \sqrt{x y} \\ \Rightarrow & 33 \geq \sqrt{x y} \\ \Rightarrow & x y \leq 1089 \\ \therefore & M=1089 \\ S: & x(66-x) \geq \frac{5}{9} \cdot 1089 \\ & 66 x-x^{2} \geq 605 \\ \Rightarrow & x^{2}-66 x+605 \leq 0 \end{aligned} $$ $\Rightarrow(x-55)(x-11) \leq 0; 11 \leq x \leq 55$ Therefore $S=\{11,12,13 \ldots 55\} $ $\Rightarrow n(S)=45$ Elements of $S$ which are multiple of 3 are $$ \begin{aligned} & 12+(n-1) 3=54 \Rightarrow 3(n-1)=42 \Rightarrow n=15 \\ & n(A)=15 \end{aligned} $$ $\Rightarrow P(A)=\frac{15}{45}=\frac{1}{3}$

questions.text: The points of intersection of the line $ax + by = 0,(a \ne b)$ and the circle ${x^2} + {y^2} - 2x = 0$ are $A(\alpha,0)$ and $B(1,\beta )$. The image of the circle with AB as a diameter in the line $x + y + 2 = 0$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: The line $ax+by=0$ passes through the origin, and the circle $x^2+y^2-2x=0$ has centre $(1,0)$ and radius 1. $B(1,\beta)$ lies on the circle: $1+\beta^2-2=0\Rightarrow\beta=\pm1$. It lies on the line: $a+b\beta=0\Rightarrow a=-b\beta$. For $\beta=-1$ this gives $a=b$, which is excluded, so $\beta=1$, $a=-b$ and the line is $y=x$. $A(\alpha,0)$ lies on $y=x$, so $\alpha=0$. Hence $A(0,0)$ and $B(1,1)$. The circle on $AB$ as diameter has centre $\left(\dfrac12,\dfrac12\right)$ and radius $\dfrac{AB}{2}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$. The image of the centre in $x+y+2=0$ is given by $$\frac{x-\frac12}{1}=\frac{y-\frac12}{1}=\frac{-2\left(\frac12+\frac12+2\right)}{1^2+1^2}=-3\Rightarrow\left(-\frac52,-\frac52\right).$$ The image circle has the same radius: $$\left(x+\frac52\right)^2+\left(y+\frac52\right)^2=\frac12\Rightarrow x^2+y^2+5x+5y+\frac{25}{2}-\frac12=0$$ $$\Rightarrow x^2+y^2+5x+5y+12=0$$ Hence, the correct option is (A).

$ax + 2ay - 3az = 1$
$(2a + 1)x + (2a + 3)y + (a + 1)z = 2$
$(3a + 5)x + (a + 5)y + (a + 2)z = 3$
has unique solution and infinitely many solutions. Then

options.text: $\mathrm{n({S_1}) = 2}$ and S$_2$ is an infinite set
S$_1$ is an infinite set and n(S$_2$) = 2

questions.solution: Step 1: The coefficient determinant is D= a, 2a, -3a\2a+1, 2a+3, a+1\3a+5, a+5, a+2 =a 1, 2, -3\2a+1, 2a+3, a+1\3a+5, a+5, a+2. Applying $C_2\to C_2-2C_1$ and $C_3\to C_3+3C_1$: D=a 1, 0, 0\2a+1, 1-2a, 7a+4\3a+5, -5a-5, 10a+17 =a[(1-2a)(10a+17)+(7a+4)(5a+5)]. Here $(1-2a)(10a+17)=-20a^2-24a+17$ and $(7a+4)(5a+5)=35a^2+55a+20$, so $D=a\left(15a^2+31a+37\right)$. The quadratic $15a^2+31a+37$ has discriminant $31^2-4(15)(37)=961-2220<0$, so it is never zero, and $D\neq0$ for every $a\neq0$. The system therefore has a unique solution for every $a\in\mathbb{R}-\{0\}$, so $S_1=\mathbb{R}-\{0\}$ and $S_2=\Phi$. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: Let $y = y(x)$ be the solution curve of the differential equation ${{dy} \over {dx}} = {y \over x}\left( {1 + x{y^2}(1 + {{\log }_e}x)} \right),x > 0,y(1) = 3$. Then ${{{y^2}(x)} \over 9}$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{d y}{d x}-\frac{y}{x}=y^3\left(1+\log _e x\right) \\ & \frac{1}{y^3} \frac{d y}{d x}-\frac{1}{x y^2}=1+\log _e x \\ & \text { Let }-\frac{1}{y^2}=t \Rightarrow \frac{2}{y^3} \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{d t}{d x} \\ & \therefore \frac{d t}{d x}+\frac{2 t}{x}=2\left(1+\log _e x\right) \\ & \text { I.F. }=e^{\int \frac{2}{x} d x}=x^2 \\ & \frac{-x^2}{y^2}=\frac{2}{3}\left(\left(1+\log _e x\right) x^3-\frac{x^3}{3}\right)+C \\ & y(1)=3 \\ & \frac{y^2}{9}=\frac{x^2}{5-2 x^3\left(2+\log _e x^3\right)} \end{aligned} $$

questions.text:
Let $f:(0,1)\to\mathbb{R}$ be a function defined $f(x) = {1 \over {1 - {e^{ - x}}}}$, and $g(x) = \left( {f( - x) - f(x)} \right)$. Consider two statements
(I) g is an increasing function in (0, 1)
(II) g is one-one in (0, 1)
Then,
questions.solution: Step 1: $g(x)=f(-x)-f(x)$ $$ \begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{1-e^{x}}-\frac{1}{1-e^{-x}} \\ & =\frac{1}{1-e^{x}}-\frac{e^{x}}{e^{x}-1} \\ & =\frac{1+e^{x}}{1-e^{x}} \\ g^{\prime}(x) & =\frac{\left(1-e^{x}\right) e^{x}-\left(1+e^{x}\right)\left(-e^{x}\right)}{\left(1-e^{x}\right)^{2}} \\ & =\frac{e^{x}-2 e^{x}+e^{x}+2 e^{x}}{\left(1-e^{x}\right)^{2}}>0 \end{aligned} $$ So both statements are correct

questions.text: A parallel plate capacitor has plate area 40 cm$^2$ and plates separation 2 mm. The space between the plates is filled with a dielectric medium of a thickness 1 mm and dielectric constant 5. The capacitance of the system is:
questions.solution: Step 1: This can be seen as two capacitors in series combination so $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{1}{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{C}_1}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{C}_2} \\ & =\frac{1}{\frac{\mathrm{K} \in_0 \mathrm{~A}}{\mathrm{t}}}+\frac{1}{\frac{\in_0 \mathrm{~A}}{\mathrm{~d}-\mathrm{t}}} \end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned} & =\frac{\mathrm{t}}{\mathrm{K} \in_0 \mathrm{~A}}+\frac{\mathrm{d}-\mathrm{t}}{\epsilon_0 \mathrm{~A}} \\ & =\frac{1 \times 10^{-3}}{5 \in_0 \times 40 \times 10^{-4}}+\frac{1 \times 10^{-3}}{\in_0 40 \times 10^{-4}} \\ & \frac{1}{\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{eq}}}=\frac{1}{20 \in_0}+\frac{1}{4 \in_0} \\ & \mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{20 \times 4 \in_0}{24}=\frac{10 \in_0}{3} \mathrm{~F} \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: In Young's double slits experiment, the position of 5$\mathrm{^{th}}$ bright fringe from the central maximum is 5 cm. The distance between slits and screen is 1 m and wavelength of used monochromatic light is 600 nm. The separation between the slits is:
questions.solution: Step 1: In Young's double-slit experiment, the distance between the slits and the screen, $L = 1 \text{ m}$, the wavelength of the light, $\lambda = 600 \text{ nm} = 600 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}$, and the position of the 5th bright fringe from the central maximum, $y = 5 \text{ cm} = 0.05 \text{ m}$. The distance between the central maximum and the $n$th bright fringe is given by the formula: $$y_n = \frac{n\lambda L}{d}$$ where $d$ is the distance between the two slits. We can rearrange this formula to solve for $d$: $$d = \frac{n\lambda L}{y_n}$$ Substituting the values given in the question, we get: $$d = \frac{5 \times 600 \times 10^{-9} \times 1 \times 100}{5}$$ $$d = 6 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m}$$ $$d = 60 \ \mu\text{m}$$ Therefore, the separation between the slits is $60 \ \mu\text{m}$.

questions.text: T is the time period of simple pendulum on the earth's surface. Its time period becomes $x$ T when taken to a height R (equal to earth's radius) above the earth's surface. Then, the value of $x$ will be:
questions.solution: Step 1: At surface of earth time period $$ \mathrm{T}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\ell}{\mathrm{g}}} $$ At height $\mathrm{h}=\mathrm{R}$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{g}^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{g}}{\left(1+\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\mathrm{R}}\right)^2}=\frac{\mathrm{g}}{4} \\ & \therefore \,\mathrm{xT}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\ell}{(\mathrm{g} / 4)}} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{xT}=2 \times 2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\ell}{\mathrm{g}}} \\ & \Rightarrow \mathrm{xT}=2 \mathrm{~T} \Rightarrow \mathrm{x}=2 \end{aligned} $$

Assume that the earth is a solid sphere of uniform density and a tunnel is dug along its diameter throughout the earth. It is found that when a particle is released in this tunnel, it executes a simple harmonic motion. The mass of the particle is 100 g. The time period of the motion of the particle will be (approximately)
(Take g = 10 m s$^{-2}$, radius of earth = 6400 km)
questions.solution: Step 1: Gravitational acceleration at a distance of $r$ from centre of earth is given by $$ g^{\prime}=\frac{g}{R} r $$ Where $R$ is the radius of earth So, $\frac{d^{2} r}{d t^{2}}=-\frac{g}{R} r$ $\Rightarrow \quad T=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{R}{g}}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{6400000}{10}}$ $=2 \pi \times 800 \mathrm{sec}$ $=5024 ~ \mathrm{sec}$ = 1 hour 24 minutes (approx.)

questions.text: Electron beam used in an electron microscope, when accelerated by a voltage of 20 kV, has a de-Broglie wavelength of $\lambda_0$. IF the voltage is increased to 40 kV, then the de-Broglie wavelength associated with the electron beam would be:
questions.solution: Step 1: When electron is accelerated through potential difference $V$, then $$ \begin{aligned} & \text { K.E. }=\mathrm{eV} \\ & \Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{~m}(\mathrm{KE})}}=\frac{\mathrm{h}}{\sqrt{2 \mathrm{meV}}} \\ & \therefore \lambda \alpha \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mathrm{V}}} \\ & \therefore \frac{\lambda}{\lambda_0}=\sqrt{\frac{20}{40}} \\ & \therefore \lambda=\frac{\lambda_0}{\sqrt{2}} \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: An electromagnetic wave is transporting energy in the negative $z$ direction. At a certain point and certain time the direction of electric field of the wave is along positive $y$ direction. What will be the direction of the magnetic field of the wave at that point and instant?
questions.solution: Step 1: As, poynting vector $$ \overrightarrow{\mathrm{S}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{H}} $$ Given energy transport $=$ negative $\mathrm{z}$ direction Electric field $=$ positive $\mathrm{y}$ direction $(-\hat{\mathrm{k}})=(+\hat{\mathrm{j}}) \times[\hat{\mathrm{i}}]$ Hence according to vector cross product magnetic field should be positive $\mathrm{x}$ direction.

questions.text: An object of mass 8 kg is hanging from one end of a uniform rod CD of mass 2 kg and length 1 m pivoted at its end C on a vertical wall as shown in figure. It is supported by a cable AB such that the system is in equilibrium. The tension in the cable is (Take g = 10 m/s$^2$)
questions.solution: Step 1: The rod's weight $2 \times 10 = 20\ \text{N}$ acts at its midpoint, 0.5 m from the pivot C; the block's weight $8 \times 10 = 80\ \text{N}$ acts at end D, $60 + 40 = 100\ \text{cm} = 1.0\ \text{m}$ from C. The cable meets the rod at B, 0.6 m from the wall, at $30^\circ$. Its horizontal component acts along the rod through the pivot and has no moment; its vertical component $T\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{T}{2}$ has a moment arm of 0.6 m. Torque balance about C: $$\dfrac{T}{2}\times 0.6 = 20 \times 0.5 + 80 \times 1.0 = 90\ \text{N m}$$ $$T = \dfrac{90}{0.3} = 300\ \text{N}$$ Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: In an LC oscillator, if values of inductance and capacitance become twice and eight times, respectively, then the resonant frequency of oscillator becomes $x$ times its initial resonant frequency $\omega_0$. The value of $x$ is:

questions.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The decrease in first ionization enthalpy from B to Al is much larger than that from Al to Ga.
Statement II: The d orbitals in Ga are completely filled.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below

options.text: Statement I is correct but statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect but statement II is correct
Both the statements I and II are correct
Both the statements I and II are incorrect

questions.solution: Step 1: Statement I is correct as the decrease in first ionization enthalpy from B to Al is indeed much larger than from Al to Ga. This is due to the shielding effect of the electron in the outermost shell and the increased effective nuclear charge as one moves from B to Al and from Al to Ga. Statement II is also correct, as the d orbitals in Ga are indeed completely filled. This results in the shielding effect being maximum for Ga and thus, the decrease in first ionization enthalpy from Al to Ga is smaller compared to that from B to Al.

questions.text: The one giving maximum number of isomeric alkenes on dehydrohalogenation reaction is (excluding rearrangement)
questions.solution:
Step 1: Dehydrohalogenation removes Br together with a hydrogen from a β-carbon, so the number of alkenes depends on which β-carbons carry H and on whether the alkenes show geometrical isomerism. (
A) $\ce{CH3-CHBr-C(CH3)2-CH2CH3}$: the β-carbon C-3 is quaternary, so only C-1 can lose H, giving 3,3-dimethylpent-1-ene only (1 alkene). (
B) $\ce{CH3-CHBr-CH3}$: both β-carbons are equivalent, giving propene only (1 alkene). (
C) $\ce{BrCH2-CH(CH3)-CH2CH3}$: the only β-carbon is C-2, giving $\ce{CH2=C(CH3)CH2CH3}$ (2-methylbut-1-ene), which has no geometrical isomers (1 alkene). (
D) $\ce{CH3-CHBr-CH2CH2CH3}$: loss of H from C-1 gives pent-1-ene, and loss of H from C-3 gives pent-2-ene, which exists as cis and trans forms (3 alkenes). Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Find out the major product for the following reaction.
questions.solution: Step 1: Protonation of the OH group and loss of water give a secondary carbocation on the side-chain carbon $\ce{CH(CH3)+}$, which is attached to the quaternary ring carbon carrying a methyl group. A C–C bond of the cyclopentane ring migrates to this cationic carbon (ring expansion). The strained five-membered ring becomes a six-membered ring, and the positive charge moves to the former quaternary carbon, which is now a tertiary carbocation bearing a methyl group; the adjacent ring carbon bears the other methyl group. Loss of a proton from the adjacent $\ce{CH(CH3)}$ carbon gives the most substituted, tetrasubstituted alkene (Saytzeff rule), 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene. Loss of a proton from a ring $\ce{CH2}$ would give only a trisubstituted alkene, and a methyl shift instead of ring expansion would keep the strained five-membered ring. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: The number of 3 digit numbers, that are divisible by either 3 or 4 but not divisible by 48, is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Three-digit multiples of 3: $\left\lfloor \dfrac{999}{3}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor \dfrac{99}{3}\right\rfloor=333-33=300$. Three-digit multiples of 4: $\left\lfloor \dfrac{999}{4}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor \dfrac{99}{4}\right\rfloor=249-24=225$. Numbers divisible by both 3 and 4 are the multiples of 12: $\left\lfloor \dfrac{999}{12}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor \dfrac{99}{12}\right\rfloor=83-8=75$. By inclusion-exclusion, the three-digit numbers divisible by 3 or 4 number $300+225-75=450$. Every multiple of 48 is a multiple of 3, so all of them are among these 450 numbers. Three-digit multiples of 48 run from $48\times 3=144$ to $48\times 20=960$, which is $20-2=18$ numbers. Required count $=450-18=432$. Hence, the correct option is (D).

Then $\cos 2x=2c-1$ and $\sin^2 x=1-c$, so $$\lambda=(2c-1)^2-2(1-c)^2-2c$$ $$=4c^2-4c+1-2+4c-2c^2-2c=2c^2-2c-1=2\left(c-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^2-\dfrac{3}{2}$$ On $[0,1]$ the least value is at $c=\dfrac{1}{2}$, giving $\lambda=-\dfrac{3}{2}$, and the greatest is at $c=0$ or $c=1$, giving $\lambda=2\cdot\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{3}{2}=-1$. questions.text:
Let $f$ and $g$ be the twice differentiable functions on $\mathbb{R}$ such that
$f''(x)=g''(x)+6x$
$f'(1)=4g'(1)-3=9$
$f(2)=3g(2)=12$.
Then which of the following is NOT true?
questions.solution:
Step 1: Given $f'(1)=9$, $g'(1)=3$, $f(2)=12$ and $g(2)=4$. Let $h(x)=f(x)-g(x)$, so $h''(x)=6x$. Integrating: $h'(x)=3x^{2}+C$, and $h'(1)=9-3=6$ gives $C=3$, so $h'(x)=3x^{2}+3$. Integrating again: $h(x)=x^{3}+3x+C'$, and $h(2)=12-4=8$ gives $8+6+C'=8$, so $C'=-6$ and $h(x)=x^{3}+3x-6$. (
A) $g(-2)-f(-2)=-h(-2)=-(-8-6-6)=20$: true. (
B) $h(1)=-2 0$, so $h(x_0)=0$, that is $f(x_0)=g(x_0)$, for some $x_0\in\left(1,\dfrac{3}{2}\right)$: true. (
C) $|f'(x)-g'(x)|=3x^{2}+3 0$, so $h$ increases from $h(-1)=-10$ to $h(2)=8$, taking every value in $(-10,8)$ on $(-1,2)$. For example, $x=-0.8$ lies in $(-1,2)$ and $h(-0.8)=-0.512-2.4-6=-8.912$, so $|f(x)-g(x)|>8$ there: false. Hence, the correct option is (D).
