questions.text: A square loop of area 25 cm$^2$ has a resistance of 10 $\Omega$. The loop is placed in uniform magnetic field of magnitude 40.0 T. The plane of loop is perpendicular to the magnetic field. The work done in pulling the loop out of the magnetic field slowly and uniformly in 1.0 sec, will be
questions.solution: Step 1: Given $B = 40.0\ \text{T}$, $A = 25\ \text{cm}^2 = 25 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2$, $R = 10\ \Omega$ and $t = 1.0\ \text{s}$. Pulling the loop out uniformly reduces the flux from $BA$ to zero at a steady rate, so the induced emf is $$\varepsilon = \dfrac{\Delta \phi}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{40 \times 25 \times 10^{-4}}{1.0} = 0.1\ \text{V}$$ The pull is slow and uniform, so there is no change in kinetic energy and the work done equals the heat produced in the loop: $$W = \dfrac{\varepsilon^2}{R}\,t = \dfrac{(0.1)^2}{10} \times 1.0 = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{J}$$ Hence, the correct option is (A).

E. The final system will have water only.

questions.solution: Step 1: Heat required to raise the temperature of ice to 0$$^\circ$$C is $$ = {{600} \over {1000}}(2222.3)(12)$$ $$ = 16000.5$$ J $$ \approx 16$$ kJ Heat required to melt ice completely $$ = \left( {{{600} \over {1000}}} \right)(336)$$ kJ $$ = 201.6$$ kJ Energy left $$ = (184 - 16) = 168$$ kJ $$\therefore$$ Partial ice will melt $$\therefore$$ $$168 = ({m_{ice\,melted}})336$$ $$0.5$$ kg $$ = ({m_{ice\,melted}})$$ $$\therefore$$ $${m_{ice}}:{m_{water}} = 1:5$$

questions.text:
Identify the correct statements from the following:
A. Work done by a man in lifting a bucket out of a well by means of a rope tied to the bucket is negative.
B. Work done by gravitational force in lifting a bucket out of a well by a rope tied to the bucket is negative.
C. Work done by friction on a body sliding down an inclined plane is positive.
D. Work done by an applied force on a body moving on a rough horizontal plane with uniform velocity is zero.
E. Work done by the air resistance on an oscillating pendulum is negative.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.solution:
Step 1: Work done by a force is $W = Fs\cos\theta$: positive when the force has a component along the displacement, negative when it opposes the displacement.
A: The man pulls the rope upward and the bucket moves upward, so the work done by the man is positive; A is incorrect.
B: Gravity acts downward while the bucket moves upward, so the work done by gravity is negative; B is correct.
C: Friction acts up the incline while the body slides down, so the work done by friction is negative; C is incorrect.
D: At uniform velocity the applied force balances friction and acts along the motion, so it does positive work $Fs$; only the net work is zero, because friction does $-Fs$. D is incorrect. E: Air resistance always opposes the velocity of the bob, so its work is negative; E is correct. The correct statements are B and E only. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The time taken by an object to slide down 45$^\circ$ rough inclined plane is n times as it takes to slide down a perfectly smooth 45$^\circ$ incline plane. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the object and the incline plane is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Smooth case: $$a = g\sin 45^\circ = {g \over {\sqrt 2 }}$$ $${t_1} = \sqrt {{{2L} \over a}} = \sqrt {{{2L} \over {g/\sqrt 2 }}} = \sqrt {{{2\sqrt 2 L} \over g}} $$..... (1) Rough case: $$a = g\sin 45^\circ - \mu g\cos 45^\circ $$ $$ = {g \over {\sqrt 2 }}(1 - \mu )$$ $${t_2} = \sqrt {{{2L} \over a}} = \sqrt {{{2\sqrt 2 L} \over {g(1 - \mu )}}} $$..... (2) From (1) to (2) and $${t_1} = {{{t_2}} \over n}$$ we have $$\sqrt {{{2\sqrt 2 L} \over g}} = {1 \over n}\sqrt {{{2\sqrt 2 L} \over {g(1 - \mu )}}} \Rightarrow \mu = 1 - {1 \over {{n^2}}}$$

questions.text: An object moves at a constant speed along a circular path in a horizontal plane with center at the origin. When the object is at $x=+2~\mathrm{m}$, its velocity is $\mathrm{ - 4\widehat j}$ m/s. The object's velocity (v) and acceleration (a) at $x=-2~\mathrm{m}$ will be
questions.solution: Step 1: Velocity is tangential, so a velocity purely along $-\hat j$ at $x=+2\ \text{m}$ places the object at $(2,\,0)$: the radius is $R=2\ \text{m}$, the speed is $4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and the motion is clockwise. At $x=-2\ \text{m}$, i.e. at $(-2,\,0)$, clockwise motion is along $+\hat j$, so $\vec v=4\hat j\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. At constant speed the acceleration is purely centripetal, pointing from $(-2,\,0)$ towards the origin, i.e. along $+\hat i$: $$a=\dfrac{v^2}{R}=\dfrac{16}{2}=8\ \text{m s}^{-2}\Rightarrow\vec a=8\hat i\ \text{m s}^{-2}$$ Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: A fully loaded boeing aircraft has a mass of $5.4\times10^5$ kg. Its total wing area is 500 m$^2$. It is in level flight with a speed of 1080 km/h. If the density of air $\rho$ is 1.2 kg m$^{-3}$, the fractional increase in the speed of the air on the upper surface of the wing relative to the lower surface in percentage will be. ($\mathrm{g=10~m/s^2}$)
questions.solution: Step 1: Speed of the aircraft: $v = 1080\ \text{km h}^{-1} = 300\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. In level flight the pressure difference between the lower and upper surfaces of the wings supports the weight: $$\Delta P = \dfrac{mg}{A} = \dfrac{5.4\times10^5\times10}{500} = 1.08\times10^4\ \text{Pa}$$ By Bernoulli's principle, with $v_u$ and $v_l$ the air speeds over the upper and lower surfaces and $v_{av} = \dfrac{v_u + v_l}{2} \approx 300\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $$\Delta P = \dfrac{1}{2}\rho\left(v_u^2 - v_l^2\right) = \rho\,v_{av}\left(v_u - v_l\right)$$ $$\dfrac{v_u - v_l}{v_{av}} = \dfrac{\Delta P}{\rho\,v_{av}^2} = \dfrac{1.08\times10^4}{1.2\times(300)^2} = 0.1$$ The fractional increase in speed is $0.1$, that is $10\%$. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
At 300 K, the rms speed of oxygen molecules is $\sqrt {{{\alpha + 5} \over \alpha }} $ times to that of its average speed in the gas. Then, the value of $\alpha$ will be
(used $\pi = {{22} \over 7}$)
questions.solution: Step 1: For a gas of molar mass $M$ at temperature $T$: $$v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{3RT}{M}},\qquad v_{\text{avg}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{8RT}{\pi M}}$$ The ratio is independent of $T$ and $M$: $$\dfrac{v_{\text{rms}}^2}{v_{\text{avg}}^2}=\dfrac{3\pi}{8}=\dfrac{3\times 22}{8\times 7}=\dfrac{33}{28}$$ Given $\dfrac{v_{\text{rms}}}{v_{\text{avg}}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{\alpha+5}{\alpha}}$: $$\dfrac{\alpha+5}{\alpha}=\dfrac{33}{28}\Rightarrow 28\alpha+140=33\alpha\Rightarrow 5\alpha=140\Rightarrow \alpha=28$$ Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: Number of cyclic tripeptides formed with 2 amino acids A and B is:
questions.solution: Step 1: In a cyclic tripeptide the three residues form a ring joined head to tail, so sequences that differ only by a rotation of the ring are the same molecule; for example $\text{A-A-B}$, $\text{A-B-A}$ and $\text{B-A-A}$ give one ring. For three residues, each composition can be arranged in a ring in only one way, and reading the ring in the opposite direction gives one of its own rotations. In the cis isomer the two Cl are adjacent and the two en rings are arranged like a propeller; it has neither a mirror plane nor a centre of symmetry, so it is non-superimposable on its mirror image and is chiral. trans-$\ce{[PtCl2(en)2]^2+}$ has a mirror plane containing Pt and both en rings, and trans-$\ce{[Co(NH3)4Cl2]^+}$ has several mirror planes, so both are achiral; cis-$\ce{[PtCl2(NH3)2]}$ is square planar Pt(II), and its molecular plane is a mirror plane. questions.text: The standard electrode potential $\mathrm{(M^{3+}/M^{2+})}$ for V, Cr, Mn & Co are $-$0.26 V, $-$0.41 V, + 1.57 V and + 1.97 V, respectively. The metal ions which can liberate $\mathrm{H_2}$ from a dilute acid are:
questions.solution: Step 1: An ion $\ce{M^2+}$ liberates $\ce{H2}$ from dilute acid if it reduces $\ce{H+}$, i.e. if $\ce{2M^2+ + 2H+ -> 2M^3+ + H2}$ is spontaneous: $$E^\circ_\text{cell} = E^\circ_{\ce{H+/H2}} - E^\circ_{\ce{M^3+/M^2+}} = 0 - E^\circ_{\ce{M^3+/M^2+}}$$ This is positive only when $E^\circ_{\ce{M^3+/M^2+}}$ is negative. For V, $E^\circ_\text{cell} = +0.26\ \text{V}$ and for Cr, $+0.41\ \text{V}$, so $\ce{V^2+}$ and $\ce{Cr^2+}$ reduce $\ce{H+}$ to $\ce{H2}$. For Mn ($-1.57\ \text{V}$) and Co ($-1.97\ \text{V}$), $E^\circ_\text{cell}$ is negative: $\ce{Mn^2+}$ and $\ce{Co^2+}$ are stable, and $\ce{Mn^3+}$ and $\ce{Co^3+}$ are strong oxidising agents instead. Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: Let $\lambda \ne 0$ be a real number. Let $\alpha,\beta$ be the roots of the equation $14{x^2} - 31x + 3\lambda = 0$ and $\alpha,\gamma$ be the roots of the equation $35{x^2} - 53x + 4\lambda = 0$. Then ${{3\alpha } \over \beta }$ and ${{4\alpha } \over \gamma }$ are the roots of the equation
questions.solution: Step 1: $14 x^{2}-31 x+3 \lambda=0$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \alpha+\beta=\frac{31}{14} \ldots.(1) \text { and } \alpha \beta=\frac{3 \lambda}{14}\quad...(2) \\ & 35 x^{2}-53 x+4 \lambda=0 \\ & \alpha+\gamma=\frac{53}{35} \ldots(3) \text { and } \alpha \gamma=\frac{4 \lambda}{35} \quad\ldots(4) \\ & \frac{(2)}{(4)} \Rightarrow \frac{\beta}{\gamma}=\frac{3 \times 35}{4 \times 14}=\frac{15}{8} \Rightarrow \beta=\frac{15}{8} \gamma \end{aligned} $$ (1) $-(3) \Rightarrow \beta-\gamma=\frac{31}{14}-\frac{53}{35}=\frac{155-106}{70}=\frac{7}{10}$ $\frac{15}{8} \gamma-\gamma=\frac{7}{10} \Rightarrow \gamma=\frac{4}{5}$ $\Rightarrow \beta=\frac{15}{8} \times \frac{4}{5}=\frac{3}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \alpha=\frac{31}{14}-\beta=\frac{31}{14}-\frac{3}{2}=\frac{5}{7}$ $\Rightarrow \lambda=\frac{14}{3} \alpha \beta=\frac{14}{3} \times \frac{5}{7} \times \frac{3}{2}=5$ so, sum of roots $\frac{3 \alpha}{\beta}+\frac{4 \alpha}{\gamma}=\left(\frac{3 \alpha \gamma+4 \alpha \beta}{\beta \gamma}\right)$ $$ \begin{aligned} & =\frac{\left(3 \times \frac{4 \lambda}{35}+4 \times \frac{3 \lambda}{14}\right)}{\beta \gamma}=\frac{12 \lambda(14+35)}{14 \times 35 \beta \gamma} \\ & =\frac{49 \times 12 \times 5}{490 \times \frac{3}{2} \times \frac{4}{5}}=5 \end{aligned} $$ Product of roots $$ =\frac{3 \alpha}{\beta} \times \frac{4 \alpha}{\gamma}=\frac{12 \alpha^{2}}{\beta \gamma}=\frac{12 \times \frac{25}{49}}{\frac{3}{2} \times \frac{4}{5}}=\frac{250}{49} $$ So, required equation is $x^{2}-5 x+\frac{250}{49}=0$ $\Rightarrow 49 \mathrm{x}^{2}-245 \mathrm{x}+250=0$

questions.text: Three rotten apples are mixed accidently with seven good apples and four apples are drawn one by one without replacement. Let the random variable X denote the number of rotten apples. If $\mu$ and $\sigma^2$ represent mean and variance of X, respectively, then $10(\mu^2+\sigma^2)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: Drawing 4 apples one by one without replacement gives the same distribution of the number of rotten apples as drawing 4 together from 10 (3 rotten, 7 good), so $$P(X = k) = \frac{\binom{3}{k}\binom{7}{4-k}}{\binom{10}{4}},\qquad \binom{10}{4} = 210$$ $P(X=0) = \dfrac{35}{210}$, $P(X=1) = \dfrac{3\times35}{210} = \dfrac{105}{210}$, $P(X=2) = \dfrac{3\times21}{210} = \dfrac{63}{210}$, $P(X=3) = \dfrac{1\times7}{210} = \dfrac{7}{210}$. $$\mu = \sum kP(X=k) = \frac{0 + 105 + 126 + 21}{210} = \frac{252}{210} = \frac65$$ $$E(X^2) = \sum k^2P(X=k) = \frac{0 + 105 + 252 + 63}{210} = \frac{420}{210} = 2$$ Since $\sigma^2 = E(X^2) - \mu^2$, $\mu^2 + \sigma^2 = E(X^2) = 2$, and $10(\mu^2 + \sigma^2) = 20$. Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: Let $f(\theta ) = 3\left( {{{\sin }^4}\left( {{{3\pi } \over 2} - \theta } \right) + {{\sin }^4}(3\pi + \theta )} \right) - 2(1 - {\sin ^2}2\theta )$ and $S = \left\{ {\theta \in [0,\pi ]:f'(\theta ) = - {{\sqrt 3 } \over 2}} \right\}$. If $4\beta = \sum\limits_{\theta \in S} \theta $, then $f(\beta )$ is equal to
questions.solution: Step 1: $f(\theta)=3\left(\sin ^{4}\left(\frac{3 \pi}{2}-\theta\right)+\sin ^{4}(3 \pi+\theta)\right)-2\left(1-\sin ^{2} 2 \theta\right)$ $S=\left\{\theta \in[0, \pi]: f^{\prime}(\theta)=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right\}$ $\Rightarrow \mathrm{f}(\theta)=3\left(\cos ^{4} \theta+\sin ^{4} \theta\right)-2 \cos ^{2} 2 \theta$ $\Rightarrow \mathrm{f}(\theta)=3\left(1-\frac{1}{2} \sin ^{2} 2 \theta\right)-2 \cos ^{2} 2 \theta$ $\Rightarrow \mathrm{f}(\theta)=3-\frac{3}{2} \sin ^{2} 2 \theta-2 \cos ^{2} 2 \theta$ $=\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2} \cos ^{2} 2 \theta=\frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1+\cos 4 \theta}{2}\right)$ $f(\theta)=\frac{5}{4}-\frac{\cos 4 \theta}{4}$ $f^{\prime}(\theta)=\sin 4 \theta$ $\Rightarrow f^{\prime}(\theta)=\sin 4 \theta=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ $\Rightarrow 4 \theta=\mathrm{n} \pi+(-1)^{\mathrm{n}} \frac{\pi}{3}$ $\Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\mathrm{n} \pi}{4}+(-1)^{\mathrm{n}} \frac{\pi}{12}$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{12},\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac{\pi}{12}\right),\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{\pi}{12}\right),\left(\frac{3 \pi}{4}-\frac{\pi}{12}\right) \\ & \Rightarrow 4 \beta=\frac{\pi}{4}+\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{3 \pi}{4}=\frac{3 \pi}{2} \\ & \Rightarrow \beta=\frac{3 \pi}{8} \Rightarrow f(\beta)=\frac{5}{4}-\frac{\cos \frac{3 \pi}{2}}{4}=\frac{5}{4} \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: Let $f(x) = x + {a \over {{\pi ^2} - 4}}\sin x + {b \over {{\pi ^2} - 4}}\cos x,x \in R$ be a function which satisfies $f(x) = x + \int\limits_0^{\pi /2} {\sin (x + y)f(y)dy} $. then $(a+b)$ is equal to
questions.solution: Step 1: $f(x)=x+\int\limits_{0}^{\pi / 2}(\sin x \cos y+\cos x \sin y) f(y) d y$ $f(x)=x+\int\limits_{0}^{\pi / 2}((\cos y f(y) d y) \sin x+(\sin y f(y) d y) \cos x)\quad....(1)$ On comparing with $f(x)=x+\frac{a}{\pi^{2}-4} \sin x+\frac{b}{\pi^{2}-4} \cos x, x \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\Rightarrow \frac{a}{\pi^{2}-4}=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \cos y f(y) d y \quad....(2)$ $\Rightarrow \frac{b}{\pi^{2}-4}=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2} \sin y f(y) d y \quad....(3)$ Add (2) and (3) $\frac{a+b}{\pi^{2}-4}=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2}(\sin y+\cos y) f(y) d y \quad....(4)$ $\frac{a+b}{\pi^{2}-4}=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2}(\sin y+\cos y) f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-y\right) d y\quad....(5)$ Add (4) and (5) $\frac{2(a+b)}{\pi^{2}-4}=\int_{0}^{\pi / 2}(\sin y+\cos y)\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{(a+b)}{\pi^{2}-4}(\sin y+\cos y)\right) d y$ $=\pi+\frac{a+b}{\pi^{2}-4}\left(\frac{\pi}{2}+1\right)$ $(a+b)=-2 \pi(\pi+2)$

For two non-zero complex numbers $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$, if $\operatorname{Re}\left(z_{1} z_{2}\right)=0$ and $\operatorname{Re}\left(z_{1}+z_{2}\right)=0$, then which of the following are possible?

questions.solution: Step 1: Let, $${z_1} = {x_1} + i{y_1}$$ and $${z_2} = {x_2} + i{y_2}$$ $$\therefore$$ $${z_1}{z_2} = {x_1}{x_2} - {y_1}{y_2} + i({x_1}{y_2} + {x_2}{y_1})$$ Given, $${\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits} ({z_1} + {z_2}) = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow {x_1} + {x_2} = 0$$...... (1) also given, $${\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits} ({z_1}{z_2}) = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow {x_1}{x_2} - {y_1}{y_2} = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow {x_1}{x_2} = {y_1}{y_2}$$ $$ \Rightarrow {y_1}{y_2} = - x_1^2$$ [$$\because$$ $${x_2} = - {x_1}$$] So, multiplication of imaginary part's of z1 and z2 is negative. (1) Given $$y(1) = e$$ $$\therefore$$ $$x = 1$$ and $$y = e$$ Putting value of x and y in equation (1), we get $$\ln |1| - {1 \over 1} = \ln |e| + C$$ $$ \Rightarrow 0 - 1 = 1 + C$$ $$ \Rightarrow C = - 2$$ $$\therefore$$ Equation (1) becomes, $$\ln |x| - {1 \over x} = \ln |y| - 2$$ $$ \Rightarrow \ln |y| = \ln |x| - {1 \over x} + 2$$ $$ \Rightarrow y = {e^{\ln |x|}}\,.\,{e^{2 - {1 \over x}}}$$ $$ \Rightarrow y = x\,.\,{e^{2 - {1 \over x}}}$$ Now, $$\mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to {0^ + }} y$$ $$ = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to {0^ + }} \left( {x\,.\,{e^{2 - {1 \over x}}}} \right)$$ $$ = 0\,.\,{e^{ - \infty }}$$ $$ = 0$$

questions.text: Let $f:R \to R$ be a function such that $f(x) = {{{x^2} + 2x + 1} \over {{x^2} + 1}}$. Then

options.text: $f(x)$ is one-one in $[1,\infty )$ but not in $( - \infty,\infty )$

questions.solution:
Step 1: $$f(x) = {{{x^2} + 2x + 1} \over {({x^2} + 1)}}$$ $$ \Rightarrow f'(x) = {{({x^2} + 1)(2x + 2) - ({x^2} + 2x + 1)(2x)} \over {{{({x^2} + 1)}^2}}}$$ $$ \Rightarrow f'(x) = {{2 - 2{x^2}} \over {{{({x^2} + 1)}^2}}}$$ $$ = {{2\left( {1 + x} \right)\left( {1 - x} \right)} \over {{{\left( {{x^2} + 1} \right)}^2}}}$$ $$ \therefore $$ $$f'(x) = 0$$ at x = 1 and x = -1. So, x = 1 and x = -1 are point of maxima/minima. Option
A: $$f(x)$$ is many-one in $$( - \infty, - 1)$$. As x = -1 is a point of maxima/minima.

Step 2: So it is a boundary point in the range $$( - \infty, - 1)$$. So, $$f(x)$$ is one-one in $$( - \infty, - 1)$$. $$ \therefore $$ Option A is incorrect. Option
B: $$f(x)$$ is one-one in $$( - \infty,\infty )$$. As, x = 1 and x = -1 are point of maxima/minima which is present inside the range $$( - \infty,\infty )$$. So, $$f(x)$$ is many-one function in $$( - \infty,\infty )$$. $$ \therefore $$ Option B is incorrect. Option
C: $$f(x)$$ is one-one in $$[1,\infty )$$ but not in $$( - \infty,\infty )$$. As x = 1 is a point of maxima/minima.

Step 3: So it is a boundary point in the range $$[1,\infty )$$. So, $$f(x)$$ is one-one in $$[1,\infty )$$. As, x = 1 and x = -1 are point of maxima/minima which is present inside the range $$( - \infty,\infty )$$. So, $$f(x)$$ is many-one function in $$( - \infty,\infty )$$. $$ \therefore $$ Option C is correct. Option
D: $$f(x)$$ is many-one in $$(1,\infty )$$. As x = 1 is a point of maxima/minima.

Step 4: So it is a boundary point in the range $$[1,\infty )$$. So, $$f(x)$$ is one-one in $$[1,\infty )$$. $$ \therefore $$ Option D is incorrect. Note: Methods to Check One-One Function: (i) If a function is one-one, any line parallel to $x$-axis cuts the graph of the function maximum at one point. questions.text: Let $[x]$ denote the greatest integer $\le x$. Consider the function $f(x) = \max \left\{ {{x^2},1 + [x]} \right\}$. Then the value of the integral $\int\limits_0^2 {f(x)dx} $ is
questions.solution: Step 1: Combining both the graph we get, Both graph cuts each other at $$y=2$$ and $$y=1$$ $$\therefore x^2=2$$ $$\Rightarrow x=\sqrt2$$ Two graphs cuts each other at $$x=1$$ and $$x=\sqrt2$$ In 0 to 1, $$f(x) = \max ({x^2},1 + [x]) = 1$$ In 1 to $$\sqrt2$$, $$f(x) = \max ({x^2},1 + [x]) = 2$$ In $$\sqrt2$$ to 2, $$f(x) = \max ({x^2},1 + [x]) = {x^2}$$ $$\therefore$$ $$\int\limits_0^2 {f(x)dx} $$ $$ = \int\limits_0^1 {1\,dx + \int\limits_1^{\sqrt 2 } {2\,dx + \int\limits_{\sqrt 2 }^2 {{x^2}\,dx} } } $$ $$ = \left[ x \right]_0^1 + 2\left[ x \right]_1^{\sqrt 2 } + \left[ {{{{x^3}} \over 3}} \right]_{\sqrt 2 }^2$$ $$ = 1 + 2(\sqrt 2 - 1) + {8 \over 3} - {{2\sqrt 2 } \over 3}$$ $$ = {8 \over 3} - 1 + 2\sqrt 2 - {{2\sqrt 2 } \over 3}$$ $$ = {5 \over 3} + {{6\sqrt 2 - 2\sqrt 2 } \over 3}$$ $$ = {5 \over 3} + {{4\sqrt 2 } \over 3}$$ $$ = {{5 + 4\sqrt 2 } \over 3}$$

questions.text: Find the mutual inductance in the arrangement, when a small circular loop of wire of radius '$R$' is placed inside a large square loop of wire of side $L$ $(L \gg R)$. The loops are coplanar and their centres coincide:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \begin{aligned} & B \text { at centre }=\frac{\mu_{0} i}{4 \pi\left(\frac{L}{2}\right)}\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}\right) \times 4 \\ &= \frac{\sqrt{2} \mu_{0} i}{2 \pi L} \times 4 \\ &=\left(\frac{2 \sqrt{2} \mu_{0} i}{\pi L}\right) \end{aligned} $$ Mutual inductance $=\frac{B \cdot A}{i}$ $$ =\frac{2 \sqrt{2} \mu_{0} i}{\pi L} \times \frac{\pi R^{2}}{i} $$ $$ =\left(\frac{2 \sqrt{2} \mu_{0} R^{2}}{L}\right) $$

questions.text: In a cuboid of dimension $2 \mathrm{~L} \times 2 \mathrm{~L} \times \mathrm{L}$, a charge $q$ is placed at the center of the surface '$\mathrm{S}$' having area of $4 \mathrm{~L}^{2}$. The flux through the opposite surface to '$\mathrm{S}$' is given by
questions.solution: Step 1: Place an identical $2L \times 2L \times L$ cuboid on the other side of face S, sharing S. The two together form a cube of side $2L$, and since $q$ is at the centre of S, it is at the centre of this cube. By Gauss's law the total flux out of the cube is $\dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0}$, and by symmetry each of its six faces carries an equal share, $\dfrac{q}{6\varepsilon_0}$. The face opposite to S in the original cuboid is a $2L \times 2L$ square at distance $L$ from $q$, i.e. one complete face of this cube, so the flux through it is $\dfrac{q}{6\varepsilon_0}$. Each of the four side faces of the original cuboid is half a cube face and carries $\dfrac{q}{12\varepsilon_0}$, so the five faces together carry $\dfrac{q}{6\varepsilon_0} + 4 \times \dfrac{q}{12\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{q}{2\varepsilon_0}$, the flux into the half-space on that side of S. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.solution:
Step 1: The correct answer is
C. It is not correct that a light-emitting diode (LED) emits light only when it is reverse biased. In fact, an LED emits light only when it is forward biased, which is stated correctly in option

questions.solution:
Step 1: $\ce{[Ni(CO)4]}$: Ni(0) is $3d^84s^2$; the strong-field CO pairs these electrons into $3d^{10}$, and the 4s and three 4p orbitals accept the four CO ligands, giving $sp^3$ (tetrahedral): A–I. $\ce{[Cu(NH3)4]^2+}$: in the valence bond description of this square planar complex of $\ce{Cu^2+}$ ($3d^9$), one 3d orbital is made vacant and the hybridisation is $dsp^2$: B–II. $\ce{[Fe(H2O)6]^2+}$: $\ce{H2O}$ is a weak-field ligand, so $\ce{Fe^2+}$ ($3d^6$) keeps 4 unpaired electrons and uses the outer 4d orbitals, giving $sp^3d^2$: D–III. $\ce{[Fe(NH3)6]^2+}$: for the dipositive $\ce{Fe^2+}$ ion the splitting produced by $\ce{NH3}$ is smaller than the pairing energy, so the complex is high spin with 4 unpaired electrons (observed moment about 5 BM) and is also an outer-orbital $sp^3d^2$ complex: C–III, not C–IV. The correct matching is A–I, B–II, C–III, D–III. Options (
B) and (
D) have A–II and B–I, option (
A) has D–IV and option (
C) has C–IV, so no option matches all four complexes; the intended option (

questions.text: The $\mathrm{Cl}-\mathrm{Co}-\mathrm{Cl}$ bond angle values in a fac- $\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{3} \mathrm{Cl}_{3}\right]$ complex is/are:
questions.solution: Step 1: In an octahedral complex any two ligands are either cis to each other (bond angle $90^\circ$) or trans ($180^\circ$). In the fac isomer the three $\ce{Cl-}$ ligands occupy the three corners of one triangular face of the octahedron, so each Cl is trans to an $\ce{NH3}$ and every pair of Cl atoms is mutually cis. All three Cl–Co–Cl angles are therefore $90^\circ$. A $180^\circ$ Cl–Co–Cl angle occurs only in the mer isomer, and $120^\circ$ does not occur in an octahedron. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: $\mathrm{KMnO}_4$ oxidises $\mathrm{I}^{-}$ in acidic and neutral/faintly alkaline solutions, respectively, to:
questions.solution: Step 1: Potassium permanganate ($\mathrm{KMnO}_4$) is a strong oxidizing agent that can oxidize iodide ions ($\mathrm{I}^{-}$) to different products depending on the pH of the solution. In acidic solutions, $\mathrm{KMnO}_4$ oxidizes $\mathrm{I}^{-}$ to molecular iodine ($\mathrm{I}_2$) according to the following equation: $$ 2\mathrm{MnO}_4^{-} + 16\mathrm{H}^{+} + 10\mathrm{I}^{-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 8\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + 5\mathrm{I}_2 $$ In neutral or faintly alkaline solutions, the oxidation product is different because the $\mathrm{I}^{-}$ is oxidized to iodate ion ($\mathrm{IO}_3^{-}$). The reaction in a neutral or slightly alkaline solution is as follows: $$ 2\mathrm{MnO}_4^{-} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} + 10\mathrm{I}^{-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO}_2 + 4\mathrm{OH}^{-} + 5\mathrm{IO}_3^{-} $$ So according to the reactions above, in acidic solutions, $\mathrm{I}^{-}$ is oxidized to $\mathrm{I}_2$ while in neutral or faintly alkaline solutions, $\mathrm{I}^{-}$ is oxidized to $\mathrm{IO}_3^{-}$. Therefore, the correct answer is: Option C: $\mathrm{I}_2 ~\&~ \mathrm{IO}_3^{-}$

A) and (

questions.solution: Step 1: Mixing gives 2 L containing $0.02$ mol of each complex, so each 1 L part contains $0.01$ mol of $\ce{[Co(NH3)5SO4]Br}$ and $0.01$ mol of $\ce{[Co(NH3)5Br]SO4}$. $

Let $a_{1}=1, a_{2}, a_{3}, a_{4}, \ldots.$. be consecutive natural numbers.
Then $\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{1+a_{1} a_{2}}\right)+\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{1+a_{2} a_{3}}\right)+\ldots..+\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{1+a_{2021} a_{2022}}\right)$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $a_{1}=1, a_{2}, a_{3}, a_{4}, \ldots.$. be consecutive natural numbers. $$ \begin{aligned} & \therefore \quad a_2=2, a_3=3, \ldots., a_{2021}=2021, a_{2022}=2022 \\ & \tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{1}{1+a_1 a_2}\right]=\tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{1}{1+1 \cdot 2}\right]=\tan ^{-1}(1)-\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \\ & \tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{1}{1+a_2 a_3}\right]=\tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{1}{1+2 \cdot 3}\right]=\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)-\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{3}\right) \end{aligned} $$.... $$ \begin{aligned} \tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{1}{1+a_{2021} a_{2022}}\right] & =\tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{1}{1+2021 \cdot 2022}\right] \\ & =\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2021}\right)-\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2022}\right) \end{aligned} $$ $$ \therefore $$ $\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{1+a_{1} a_{2}}\right)+\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{1+a_{2} a_{3}}\right)+\ldots..+\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{1+a_{2021} a_{2022}}\right)$ $$ =\tan ^{-1}(1)-\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{2022}\right)=\frac{\pi}{4}-\cot ^{-1}(2022) $$ $$ =\frac{\pi}{4}-\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\tan ^{-1}(2022)\right)=\tan ^{-1}(2022)-\frac{\pi}{4} $$

questions.text: Let $a, b, c>1, a^3, b^3$ and $c^3$ be in A.P., and $\log _a b, \log _c a$ and $\log _b c$ be in G.P. If the sum of first 20 terms of an A.P., whose first term is $\frac{a+4 b+c}{3}$ and the common difference is $\frac{a-8 b+c}{10}$ is $-444$, then $a b c$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: Since $a^3,b^3,c^3$ are in A.P., $2b^3=a^3+c^3$. Since $\log_a b,\ \log_c a,\ \log_b c$ are in G.P., $$(\log_c a)^2=\log_a b\cdot\log_b c=\log_a c\Rightarrow\left(\dfrac{\ln a}{\ln c}\right)^2=\dfrac{\ln c}{\ln a}\Rightarrow(\ln a)^3=(\ln c)^3$$ So $a=c$, and then $2b^3=2a^3$ gives $b=a$. Thus $a=b=c$. First term $=\dfrac{a+4a+a}{3}=2a$ and common difference $=\dfrac{a-8a+a}{10}=-\dfrac{3a}{5}$. $$S_{20}=\dfrac{20}{2}\left[2(2a)+19\left(-\dfrac{3a}{5}\right)\right]=10\cdot\dfrac{20a-57a}{5}=-74a$$ $-74a=-444\Rightarrow a=6$, so $abc=6^3=216$. Hence, the correct option is (B).

Let $f, g$ and $h$ be the real valued functions defined on $\mathbb{R}$ as

Then the value of $\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow 1} g(h(x-1))$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$f(x) = {\mathop{\rm sgn}} (x)$$ $$h(x) = 2[x] - {\mathop{\rm sgn}} (x)$$ If $$x \to {1^ + }$$ then $$h(x - 1) = 2[x] - 2 - {\mathop{\rm sgn}} (x - 1)$$ $$ = 0 - 1 = - 1$$, if$$x \to {1^ - }$$ then $$h(x - 1) = 2[x] - 2 - {\mathop{\rm sgn}} (x - 1)$$ $$ = - 2 + 1 = - 1$$ $$\therefore$$ $$\mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to {1^ + }} g(h(x - 1)) = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to {1^ + }} {{\sin (h(x - 1) + 1)} \over {h(x - 1) + 1}} = 1$$ $$\mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to {1^ - }} g(h(x - 1)) = \mathop {\lim }\limits_{x \to {1^ - }} {{\sin (h(x - 1) + 1)} \over {h(x - 1) + 1}} = 1$$

questions.text: Let $x=(8 \sqrt{3}+13)^{13}$ and $y=(7 \sqrt{2}+9)^9$. If $[t]$ denotes the greatest integer $\leq t$, then:
questions.solution:
Step 1: Since $8\sqrt3 \approx 13.86$, the number $f = (8\sqrt3-13)^{13}$ satisfies $0 < f < 1$. By the binomial theorem, $$x - f = (8\sqrt3+13)^{13} - (8\sqrt3-13)^{13} = 2\sum\limits_{k\ \text{odd}} \binom{13}{k}(8\sqrt3)^{13-k}\,13^{k}.$$ For odd $k$, $13-k$ is even, so $(8\sqrt3)^{13-k} = 192^{(13-k)/2}$ is an integer; hence $x - f = I_1$ is an even integer. Then $x = I_1 + f$ with $0 < f < 1$, so $[x] = I_1$ is even. questions.text: In the wet tests for identification of various cations by precipitation, which transition element cation doesn't belong to group IV in qualitative inorganic analysis?
questions.solution: Step 1: In qualitative inorganic analysis, cations are divided into different groups based on their precipitation reactions. Group IV cations typically include those that form sulfides or hydroxides that are insoluble in water and dilute acids, but soluble in excess ammonia or sodium hydroxide. Co$^{2+}$ (Cobalt) Ni$^{2+}$ (Nickel) Zn$^{2+}$ (Zinc) These cations are generally placed in Group IV because they form precipitates with specific reagents used in the separation process. Fe$^{3+}$ (Iron), on the other hand, is not typically included in Group IV. It belongs to Group III because it forms insoluble hydroxides that precipitate in the presence of ammonia. Thus, the transition element cation that doesn't belong to Group IV is: Option D Fe$^{3+}$

questions.text: The minimum number of elements that must be added to the relation $ \mathrm{R}=\{(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}),(\mathrm{b}, \mathrm{c})\}$ on the set $\{a, b, c\}$ so that it becomes symmetric and transitive is:
questions.solution: Step 1: For symmetry, $(a, b) \in R$ and $(b, c) \in R$ require $(b, a)$ and $(c, b)$. For transitivity, $(a, b)$ and $(b, c)$ give $(a, c)$, and symmetry then requires $(c, a)$. Transitivity also forces the diagonal pairs: $(a, b), (b, a)$ give $(a, a)$; $(b, a), (a, b)$ give $(b, b)$; $(c, b), (b, c)$ give $(c, c)$. These pairs are required by transitivity, not by reflexivity. The relation is now all $9$ pairs of $\{a, b, c\} \times \{a, b, c\}$, which is symmetric and transitive, and every added pair was forced. Pairs added: $(b, a), (c, b), (a, c), (c, a), (a, a), (b, b), (c, c)$, i.e. $9 - 2 = 7$. Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
Let the system of linear equations
$x+y+kz=2$
$2x+3y-z=1$
$3x+4y+2z=k$
have infinitely many solutions. Then the system
$(k+1)x+(2k-1)y=7$
$(2k+1)x+(k+5)y=10$
has:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$x + y + kz = 2$$............(i) $$2x + 3y - z = 1$$..........(ii) $$3x + 4y + 2z = k$$......(iii) (1) + (2) $$3x + 4y + z(k - 1) = 3$$ Comparing with (3) $$k = 3$$ Now, $$4x + 5y = 7$$ $$ \Rightarrow 3x + 3y = 3$$ $$7x + 8y = 10$$ as $${4 \over 7} \ne {5 \over 8}$$ $$\therefore$$ Unique solution satisfying $$x + y = 1$$

questions.text: If [t] denotes the greatest integer $\le \mathrm{t}$, then the value of ${{3(e - 1)} \over e}\int\limits_1^2 {{x^2}{e^{[x] + [{x^3}]}}dx} $ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: For $1\le x<2$, $[x]=1$, so $$I=\dfrac{3(e-1)}{e}\int\limits_1^2 x^2e^{1+[x^3]}\,dx=3(e-1)\int\limits_1^2 x^2e^{[x^3]}\,dx$$ Put $x^3=t$, so $3x^2\,dx=dt$ and the limits become $1$ to $8$: $$I=(e-1)\int\limits_1^8 e^{[t]}\,dt$$ On each interval $[n,n+1)$, $[t]=n$, so $$\int\limits_1^8 e^{[t]}\,dt=e+e^2+\cdots+e^7=\dfrac{e(e^7-1)}{e-1}$$ Therefore $I=(e-1)\cdot\dfrac{e(e^7-1)}{e-1}=e^8-e$. Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: If the coefficient of $x^{15}$ in the expansion of $\left(\mathrm{a} x^{3}+\frac{1}{\mathrm{~b} x^{1 / 3}}\right)^{15}$ is equal to the coefficient of $x^{-15}$ in the expansion of $\left(a x^{1 / 3}-\frac{1}{b x^{3}}\right)^{15}$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive real numbers, then for each such ordered pair $(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b})$:

If the solution of the equation $\log _{\cos x} \cot x+4 \log _{\sin x} \tan x=1, x \in\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, is $\sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{\alpha+\sqrt{\beta}}{2}\right)$, where $\alpha$, $\beta$ are integers, then $\alpha+\beta$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $${\log _{\cos x}}\cot x + 4{\log _{\sin x}}\tan x = 1$$ $$ \Rightarrow {\log _{\cos x}}\cot x - 4{\log _{\sin x}}\cot x = 1$$ $$ \Rightarrow 1 - {\log _{\cos x}}\sin x + 4 - 4{\log _{\sin x}}\cos x = 1$$ Let $${\log _{\cos x}}\sin x = t$$ $$t + {4 \over t} = 4$$ $$ \Rightarrow t = 2$$ $$\sin x = {\cos ^2}x$$ $$ \Rightarrow \sin x = 1 - {\sin ^2}x$$ $$ \Rightarrow {\sin ^2}x + \sin x - 1 = 0$$ $$ \Rightarrow \sin x = {{ - 1\, \pm \,\sqrt 5 } \over 2}$$ as $$x \in \left( {0,{\pi \over 2}} \right)$$ $$\sin x = {{\sqrt 5 - 1} \over 2}$$ $$x = {\sin ^{ - 1}}\left( {{{ - 1 + \sqrt 5 } \over 2}} \right)$$ $$ \Rightarrow \alpha = - 1,\beta = 5$$ $$\alpha + \beta = 4$$

questions.text: If $\tan 15^\circ + {1 \over {\tan 75^\circ }} + {1 \over {\tan 105^\circ }} + \tan 195^\circ = 2a$, then the value of $\left( {a + {1 \over a}} \right)$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: $$\tan 15^\circ + \tan 15^\circ - \tan 15^\circ + \tan 15^\circ $$ $$ = 2\tan 15^\circ $$ $$ = 2\left( {2 - \sqrt 3 } \right) = 2a \Rightarrow a = 2 - \sqrt 3 $$ $$\therefore$$ $${1 \over a} + a \Rightarrow \left( {2 + \sqrt 3 } \right) + \left( {2 - \sqrt 3 } \right) = 4$$

questions.text: Two isolated metallic solid spheres of radii $\mathrm{R}$ and $2 \mathrm{R}$ are charged such that both have same charge density $\sigma$. The spheres are then connected by a thin conducting wire. If the new charge density of the bigger sphere is $\sigma^{\prime}$. The ratio $\frac{\sigma^{\prime}}{\sigma}$ is:
questions.solution: Step 1: Charge on a metallic sphere resides on its surface, so $\sigma$ is the surface charge density of each sphere. Initial charges: $Q_1 = \sigma(4\pi R^2)$ and $Q_2 = \sigma\,4\pi(2R)^2 = 16\pi R^2\sigma$, so the total charge is $Q = 20\pi R^2\sigma$. After connection both spheres are at the same potential: $$\dfrac{kQ_1'}{R} = \dfrac{kQ_2'}{2R} \Rightarrow Q_2' = 2Q_1'$$ So the bigger sphere gets two-thirds of the total charge: $$Q_2' = \dfrac{2}{3}\times 20\pi R^2\sigma = \dfrac{40}{3}\pi R^2\sigma$$ $$\sigma' = \dfrac{Q_2'}{4\pi(2R)^2} = \dfrac{40\pi R^2\sigma}{3\times 16\pi R^2} = \dfrac{5}{6}\sigma \Rightarrow \dfrac{\sigma'}{\sigma} = \dfrac{5}{6}$$ Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
If the gravitational field in the space is given as $\left(-\frac{K}{r^{2}}\right)$. Taking the reference point to be at $\mathrm{r}=2 \mathrm{~cm}$
with gravitational potential $\mathrm{V}=10 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{kg}$. Find the gravitational potential at $\mathrm{r}=3 \mathrm{~cm}$ in SI unit (Given, that $\mathrm{K}=6 \mathrm{~Jcm} / \mathrm{kg}$)
questions.solution: Step 1: The field and potential are related by $E = -\dfrac{dV}{dr}$, so $dV = -E\,dr = \dfrac{K}{r^2}\,dr$. Integrating from the reference point $r = 2\ \text{cm}$ to $r = 3\ \text{cm}$: $$V_3 - V_2 = \int\limits_2^3 \dfrac{K}{r^2}\,dr = K\left[-\dfrac{1}{r}\right]_2^3 = K\left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{3}\right) = \dfrac{K}{6}$$ With $r$ in cm, $\dfrac{1}{6}$ is in $\text{cm}^{-1}$, and $K = 6\ \text{J cm kg}^{-1}$: $$V_3 - V_2 = \dfrac{6}{6} = 1\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$$ $$V_3 = 10 + 1 = 11\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$$ Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R)
Assertion (A): The first ionization enthalpy of $3 \mathrm{~d}$ series elements is more than that of group 2 metals
Reason (R): In 3d series of elements successive filling of d-orbitals takes place.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but $(\mathbf{R})$ is not the correct explanation of (A)

questions.solution:
Step 1: First ionization enthalpies (kJ mol−1): 3d seriesScTiVCrMnFeCoNiCuZn IE631656650653717762758736745906 Group 2BeMgCaSrBaRa IE899737590549503509 Assertion (A): Every 3d element (631 to 906) has a higher first ionization enthalpy than calcium (590), the group 2 metal of the same period (4th), and than the heavier group 2 metals Sr, Ba and Ra.

Step 2: So (A) is true. Reason (R): Across the 3d series the added electrons go successively into the inner $3d$ orbitals, which shield the outer $4s$ electrons poorly. The effective nuclear charge felt by the $4s$ electrons therefore increases, which is why these elements have higher ionization enthalpies than Ca.

Step 3: So (R) is true and is the correct explanation of (A). Hence option A, which is the official NTA answer. (Be and Mg, from earlier periods, have higher values than some 3d elements; the assertion compares elements of the same period.)

questions.text: A hydrocarbon ' $\mathrm{X}$ ' with formula $\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{8}$ uses two moles of $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ on catalytic hydrogenation of its one mole. On ozonolysis, ' $\mathrm{X}$ ' yields two moles of methane dicarbaldehyde. The hydrocarbon ' $\mathrm{X}$ ' is:
questions.solution: Step 1: $\ce{C6H8}$ has $\dfrac{2(6) + 2 - 8}{2} = 3$ degrees of unsaturation. Uptake of 2 mol $\ce{H2}$ per mole shows two C=C bonds, so the third unsaturation is a ring. Methane dicarbaldehyde is $\ce{OHC-CH2-CHO}$. Two such $\mathrm{C}_3$ units from a six-membered ring require each C=C to be separated from the other by one $\ce{CH2}$ on each side, which is cyclohexa-1,4-diene: Cyclohexa-1,3-diene gives $\ce{OHC-CHO}$ and $\ce{OHC-CH2CH2-CHO}$ instead, and hexa-1,3,5-triene takes up 3 mol $\ce{H2}$. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: Upon heating a borax bead dipped in cupric sulphate in a luminous flame, the colour of the bead becomes green
Statement II: The green colour observed is due to the formation of copper(I) metaborate
In light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Statement I is true but Statement II is false

questions.solution: Step 1: In the borax bead test, a bead dipped in a copper(II) salt and heated in the oxidising (non-luminous) flame forms copper(II) metaborate, which gives the blue-green colour: $$\ce{CuSO4 + B2O3 -> Cu(BO2)2 + SO3}$$ In the reducing (luminous) flame, copper(II) metaborate is reduced either to colourless copper(I) metaborate or to metallic copper, which makes the bead red and opaque: $$\ce{2Cu(BO2)2 + 2NaBO2 + C -> 2CuBO2 + Na2B4O7 + CO}$$ $$\ce{2Cu(BO2)2 + 4NaBO2 + 2C -> 2Cu + 2Na2B4O7 + 2CO}$$ So the bead does not become green in the luminous flame, and Statement I is false. Copper(I) metaborate is colourless; the green colour comes from copper(II) metaborate formed in the oxidising flame, so Statement II is also false. Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: The incorrect statement for the use of indicators in acid-base titration is:

options.text: Phenolphthalein is a suitable indicator for a weak acid vs strong base titration.
Methyl orange may be used for a weak acid vs weak base titration.
Methyl orange is a suitable indicator for a strong acid vs weak base titration.
Phenolphthalein may be used for a strong acid vs strong base titration.

questions.solution:
Step 1: An indicator suits a titration when its colour-change range lies inside the steep pH jump at the equivalence point. Methyl orange changes colour at pH 3.1–4.4 and phenolphthalein at pH 8.3–10. (
A) Weak acid vs strong base: the equivalence point is basic and the jump lies at about pH 7–11, covering the range of phenolphthalein. The statement is correct. (
B) Weak acid vs weak base: the pH changes only gradually near the equivalence point, with no sharp jump, so no indicator, methyl orange included, gives a sharp end point. The statement is incorrect. (
C) Strong acid vs weak base: the equivalence point is acidic and the jump lies at about pH 3–7, covering the range of methyl orange. The statement is correct. (
D) Strong acid vs strong base: the jump spans about pH 3–11 around the equivalence point (pH 7), so both phenolphthalein and methyl orange change colour within it. The statement is correct. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: The equation $\mathrm{e}^{4 x}+8 \mathrm{e}^{3 x}+13 \mathrm{e}^{2 x}-8 \mathrm{e}^{x}+1=0, x \in \mathbb{R}$ has:

options.text: two solutions and both are negative
two solutions and only one of them is negative
four solutions two of which are negative

questions.solution: Step 1: $e^{4 x}+8 e^{3 x}+13 e^{2 x}-8 e^{x}+1=0$ Let $\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{t}$ Now, $\mathrm{t}^{4}+8 \mathrm{t}^{3}+13 \mathrm{t}^{2}-8 \mathrm{t}+1=0$ Dividing equation by $\mathrm{t}^{2}$ $$ \begin{aligned} & t^{2}+8 t+13-\frac{8}{t}+\frac{1}{t^{2}}=0 \\ & t^{2}+\frac{1}{t^{2}}+8\left(t-\frac{1}{t}\right)+13=0 \\ & \left(t-\frac{1}{t}\right)^{2}+2+8\left(t-\frac{1}{t}\right)+13=0 \end{aligned} $$ Let $\mathrm{t}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{t}}=\mathrm{z}$ $$ z^{2}+8 z+15=0 $$ $$ \begin{aligned} & (z+3)(z+5)=0 \end{aligned} $$ $$ z=-3 \text { or } z=-5 $$ So, $\mathrm{t}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{t}}=-3$ or $\mathrm{t}-\frac{1}{\mathrm{t}}=-5$ $t^{2}+3 t-1=0$ or $t^{2}+5 t-1=0$ $\mathrm{t}=\frac{-3 \pm \sqrt{13}}{2}$ or $\mathrm{t}=\frac{-5 \pm \sqrt{29}}{2}$ as $t=e^{x}$ so $t$ must be positive, $$ t=\frac{\sqrt{13}-3}{2} \text { or } \frac{\sqrt{29}-5}{2} $$ So, $x=\ln \left(\frac{\sqrt{13}-3}{2}\right)$ or $x=\ln \left(\frac{\sqrt{29}-5}{2}\right)$ Hence two solutions and both are negative.

questions.text:
Let (a, b) $\subset(0,2 \pi)$ be the largest interval for which $\sin ^{-1}(\sin \theta)-\cos ^{-1}(\sin \theta)>0, \theta \in(0,2 \pi)$,
holds. If $\alpha x^{2}+\beta x+\sin ^{-1}\left(x^{2}-6 x+10\right)+\cos ^{-1}\left(x^{2}-6 x+10\right)=0$ and $\alpha-\beta=b-a$, then $\alpha$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $\sin ^{-1} \sin \theta-\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\sin ^{-1} \sin \theta\right)>0$ $\Rightarrow \sin ^{-1} \sin \theta>\frac{\pi}{4}$ $\Rightarrow \sin \theta>\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ So, $\theta \in\left(\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{3 \pi}{4}\right)$ $\theta \in\left(\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{3 \pi}{4}\right)=(\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b})$ $b-a=\frac{\pi}{2}=\alpha-\beta$ $\Rightarrow \beta=\alpha-\frac{\pi}{2}$ $\Rightarrow \alpha x^{2}+\beta \mathrm{x}+\sin ^{-1}\left[(\mathrm{x}-3)^{2}+1\right]+\cos ^{-1}\left[(\mathrm{x}-3)^{2}+1\right]=0$ $x=3,9 \alpha+3 \beta+\frac{\pi}{2}+0=0$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow 9 \alpha+3\left(\alpha-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)+\frac{\pi}{2}=0 \\ & \Rightarrow 12 \alpha-\pi=0 \\ & \alpha=\frac{\pi}{12} \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: Let $\alpha>0$. If $\int\limits_0^\alpha \frac{x}{\sqrt{x+\alpha}-\sqrt{x}} \mathrm{~d} x=\frac{16+20 \sqrt{2}}{15}$, then $\alpha$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $I=\int\limits_{0}^{\alpha} \frac{x}{\sqrt{x+\alpha}-\sqrt{x}} d x, \alpha>0$ $$ \begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{\alpha} \int\limits_{0}^{\alpha} x(\sqrt{x+\alpha}+\sqrt{x}) d x \end{aligned} $$ $eqalign, = 1 over α intlimits_0^α ( x√(x + α ) + xsqrt x ) dx cr, = 1 over α intlimits_0^α [ ( x + α - α )√(x + α ) + x^3 over 2 ] dx cr$ $$ \begin{aligned} & =\frac{1}{\alpha}\int\limits_0^\alpha \left[(x+\alpha)^{3 / 2}-\alpha(x+\alpha)^{1 / 2}+x^{3 / 2}\right] d x \\ & =\frac{1}{\alpha}\left[\frac{2}{5}(x+\alpha)^{5 / 2}-\alpha \frac{2}{3}(x+\alpha)^{3 / 2}+\frac{2}{5} x^{5 / 2}\right]_0^\alpha \\ & =\frac{1}{\alpha}\left(\frac{2}{5}(2 \alpha)^{5 / 2}-\frac{2 \alpha}{3}(2 \alpha)^{3 / 2}+\frac{2}{5} \alpha^{5 / 2}-\frac{2}{5} \alpha^{5 / 2}+\frac{2}{3} \alpha^{5 / 2}\right) \\ & =\frac{1}{\alpha}\left(\frac{2^{7 / 2} \alpha^{5 / 2}}{5}-\frac{2^{5 / 2} \alpha^{5 / 2}}{3}+\frac{2}{3} \alpha^{5 / 2}\right)=\alpha^{3 / 2}\left(\frac{2^{7 / 2}}{5}-\frac{2^{5 / 2}}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\right) \\ & =\frac{\alpha^{3 / 2}}{15}(24 \sqrt{2}-20 \sqrt{2}+10)=\frac{\alpha^{3 / 2}}{15}(4 \sqrt{2}+10) \end{aligned} $$ Now, $\frac{\alpha^{3 / 2}}{15}(4 \sqrt{2}+10)=\frac{16+20 \sqrt{2}}{15}=\frac{2 \sqrt{2}(4 \sqrt{2}+10)}{15}$ $$ \Rightarrow \alpha^{3 / 2}=2 \sqrt{2}=2^{3 / 2} $$ $$\Rightarrow \alpha=2 $$

questions.solution: Step 1: $$ \begin{array}{cll} \quad \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{B} & \mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B} \ \overline{\mathrm{x}}_{1}=40 & \overline{\mathrm{x}}_{2}=55 & \overline{\mathrm{x}}=50 \ \sigma_{1}=\alpha & \sigma_{2}=30-\alpha & \sigma^{2}=350 \ \mathrm{n}_{1}=100 & \mathrm{n}_{2}=\mathrm{n} & 100+\mathrm{n} \\ \overline{\mathrm{x}}=\frac{100 \times 40+55 \mathrm{n}}{100+\mathrm{n}} & \end{array} $$ $$ \begin{aligned} & 5000+50 \mathrm{n}=4000+55 \mathrm{n} \\ & 1000=5 \mathrm{n} \\ & \mathrm{n}=200 \\ & \sigma_{1}^{2}=\frac{\sum \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}}^{2}}{100}-40^{2} \\ & \sigma_{2}^{2}=\frac{\sum \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{j}}^{2}}{200}-55^{2} \\ & 350=\sigma^{2}=\frac{\sum \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{i}}{ }^{2}+\sum \mathrm{x}_{\mathrm{j}}^{2}}{300}-(\overline{\mathrm{x}})^{2} \\ & 350=\frac{\left(1600+\alpha^{2}\right) \times 100+\left[(30-\alpha)^{2}+3025\right] \times 200}{300}-(50)^{2} \\ & 2850 \times 3=\alpha^{2}+2(30-\alpha)^{2}+1600+6050 \\ & 8550=\alpha^{2}+2(30-\alpha)^{2}+7650 \\ & \alpha^{2}+2(30-\alpha)^{2}=900 \\ & \alpha^{2}-40 \alpha+300=0 \\ & \alpha=10,30 \\ & \sigma_{1}^{2}+\sigma_{2}^{2}=10^{2}+20^{2}=500 \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: Let $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$ be an A.P. If $a_7=3$, the product $a_1 a_4$ is minimum and the sum of its first $n$ terms is zero, then $n !-4 a_{n(n+2)}$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $a_{7}=3 \Rightarrow a+6 d=3 \Rightarrow a=3-6 d$ $$ \begin{aligned} & a_{1} \cdot a_{4}=a(a+3 d) \\ & \Rightarrow(3-6 d)(3-6 d+3 d) \\ & \Rightarrow 3(1-2 d) 3(1-d) \\ & \Rightarrow 9\left(2 d^{2}-3 d+1\right) \end{aligned} $$ Let $f(d)=2 d^{2}-3 d+1$ $f^{\prime}(d)=4 d-3 \Rightarrow d=\frac{3}{4}$ $\therefore a=3-6 \cdot \frac{3}{4}=3-\frac{9}{2}=-\frac{3}{2}$ $S_{n}=0$ $\frac{n}{2}(2 a+(n-1) d)=0$ $\Rightarrow 2 \cdot\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)+(n-1)\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)=0$ $\Rightarrow \quad 3=\frac{3}{4}(n-1)$ $\Rightarrow n=5$ Now, $n !-4 \cdot a_{n(n+2)}$ $$ \begin{aligned} & =5 !-4 \cdot a_{35} \\ & =120-4\left(-\frac{3}{2}+34 \cdot \frac{3}{4}\right) \\ & =120-(-6+102) \\ & =120-(96) \\ & =24 \end{aligned} $$

questions.text:
$
\lim\limits_{x \rightarrow \infty} \frac{(\sqrt{3 x+1}+\sqrt{3 x-1})^6+(\sqrt{3 x+1}-\sqrt{3 x-1})^6}{\left(x+\sqrt{x^2-1}\right)^6+\left(x-\sqrt{x^2-1}\right)^6} x^3
$
questions.solution: Step 1: Taking out the dominant powers of $x$: $$(\sqrt{3x+1}+\sqrt{3x-1})^6+(\sqrt{3x+1}-\sqrt{3x-1})^6=x^3\left[\left(\sqrt{3+\tfrac{1}{x}}+\sqrt{3-\tfrac{1}{x}}\right)^6+\left(\sqrt{3+\tfrac{1}{x}}-\sqrt{3-\tfrac{1}{x}}\right)^6\right]$$ $$\left(x+\sqrt{x^2-1}\right)^6+\left(x-\sqrt{x^2-1}\right)^6=x^6\left[\left(1+\sqrt{1-\tfrac{1}{x^2}}\right)^6+\left(1-\sqrt{1-\tfrac{1}{x^2}}\right)^6\right]$$ With the extra factor $x^3$, the powers of $x$ cancel: $\dfrac{x^3\cdot x^3}{x^6}=1$. As $x\to\infty$, the first bracket tends to $(2\sqrt{3})^6+0$ and the second to $2^6+0$, so the limit is $$\frac{(2\sqrt{3})^6}{2^6}=\left(\sqrt{3}\right)^6=27$$ Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation
$\left(3 y^{2}-5 x^{2}\right) y \mathrm{~d} x+2 x\left(x^{2}-y^{2}\right) \mathrm{d} y=0$
such that $y(1)=1$. Then $\left|(y(2))^{3}-12 y(2)\right|$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: The equation gives $$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y(5x^2-3y^2)}{2x(x^2-y^2)},$$ which is homogeneous. Put $y=mx$: $$m+x\dfrac{dm}{dx}=\dfrac{m(5-3m^2)}{2(1-m^2)}\Rightarrow x\dfrac{dm}{dx}=\dfrac{m(3-m^2)}{2(1-m^2)}.$$ Separating the variables and using partial fractions, $$\dfrac{dx}{x}=\dfrac{2(m^2-1)}{m(m^2-3)}\,dm=\left(\dfrac{2}{3m}+\dfrac{4m}{3(m^2-3)}\right)dm.$$ Integrating, $$\ln|x|=\dfrac{2}{3}\ln|m|+\dfrac{2}{3}\ln|m^2-3|+C\Rightarrow |m(m^2-3)|=k\,|x|^{3/2}.$$ At $x=1$, $y=1$: $m=1$ and $|1-3|=k$, so $k=2$. With $m=\dfrac{y}{x}$ and $x>0$: $$\left|\dfrac{y(y^2-3x^2)}{x^3}\right|=2x^{3/2}\Rightarrow\left|y^3-3x^2y\right|=2x^{9/2}.$$ At $x=2$: $$\left|(y(2))^3-12\,y(2)\right|=2\cdot 2^{9/2}=2\cdot 16\sqrt{2}=32\sqrt{2}.$$ Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The set of all values of $a^{2}$ for which the line $x+y=0$ bisects two distinct chords drawn from a point $\mathrm{P}\left(\frac{1+a}{2}, \frac{1-a}{2}\right)$ on the circle $2 x^{2}+2 y^{2}-(1+a) x-(1-a) y=0$, is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: Dividing by $2$, the circle is $x^2+y^2-2hx-2ky=0$ with $h=\dfrac{1+a}{4}$, $k=\dfrac{1-a}{4}$; its centre is $(h,k)$ and $P$ is $(2h,2k)$. Let a chord through $P$ have its midpoint $M(\lambda,-\lambda)$ on $x+y=0$. By $T=S_1$, the chord is $$\lambda x-\lambda y-h(x+\lambda)-k(y-\lambda)=2\lambda^2-2h\lambda+2k\lambda$$ $P(2h,2k)$ lies on it: $$2h\lambda-2k\lambda-h(2h+\lambda)-k(2k-\lambda)=2\lambda^2-2h\lambda+2k\lambda$$ $$\Rightarrow 2\lambda^2-3(h-k)\lambda+2\left(h^2+k^2\right)=0$$ $P$ is not on $x+y=0$ (its coordinates add to $1$), so each real root gives a genuine chord, and two distinct chords need two distinct real roots: $$9(h-k)^2-16\left(h^2+k^2\right)>0$$ Here $h-k=\dfrac{a}{2}$ and $h^2+k^2=\dfrac{(1+a)^2+(1-a)^2}{16}=\dfrac{1+a^2}{8}$, so $$\dfrac{9a^2}{4}-2\left(1+a^2\right)>0 \Rightarrow a^2-8>0 \Rightarrow a^2\in(8,\infty)$$ Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The number of turns of the coil of a moving coil galvanometer is increased in order to increase current sensitivity by $50 \%$. The percentage change in voltage sensitivity of the galvanometer will be:
questions.solution: Step 1: For a moving coil galvanometer, the current sensitivity is $S_I = \dfrac{\theta}{I} = \dfrac{NAB}{k}$ and the voltage sensitivity is $S_V = \dfrac{\theta}{V} = \dfrac{\theta}{IR} = \dfrac{NAB}{kR}$. $S_I \propto N$, so a $50\%$ rise in current sensitivity needs $N' = 1.5N$. The coil is wound from the same wire, so its length, and hence its resistance, grows in proportion to the number of turns: $R' = 1.5R$. $$S_V' = \dfrac{1.5\,NAB}{k\,(1.5R)} = \dfrac{NAB}{kR} = S_V$$ The voltage sensitivity is unchanged, a change of $0\%$. Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: A body weight $\mathrm{W}$, is projected vertically upwards from earth's surface to reach a height above the earth which is equal to nine times the radius of earth. The weight of the body at that height will be:
questions.solution: Step 1: The weight of an object varies with altitude due to the change in gravitational force. The force of gravity decreases with the square of the distance from the center of the Earth. The gravitational force (weight) at a height h from the surface of the Earth is given by: $$W' = W \left(\frac{R}{{R + h}}\right)^2$$ where: W' is the weight at height h, W is the weight at the Earth's surface, R is the radius of the Earth, h is the height above the Earth's surface. In this problem, the height h is given as nine times the radius of the Earth (h = 9R). Substituting h = 9R into the equation gives: $$W' = W \left(\frac{R}{{R + 9R}}\right)^2 = W \left(\frac{1}{10}\right)^2$$ Simplifying this gives: $$W' = \frac{W}{100}$$ Therefore, the weight of the body at that height will be 1/100th of its weight on the surface of the Earth. The correct answer is Option C: $\frac{W}{100}$.

questions.text: Considering a group of positive charges, which of the following statements is correct ?

options.text: Net potential of the system cannot be zero at a point but net electric field can be zero at that point
Net potential of the system at a point can be zero but net electric field can't be zero at that point.
Both the net potential and the net electric field cannot be zero at a point.
Both the net potential and the net field can be zero at a point.

questions.solution:
Step 1: The net potential is the scalar sum $V = \sum \dfrac{kq_i}{r_i}$. Every $q_i$ is positive and every $r_i$ is positive and finite, so every term is positive and $V > 0$ at every point; the net potential cannot be zero. The net field is the vector sum of the individual fields, which can cancel. At the midpoint of two equal positive charges $q$ a distance $d$ apart, the two fields are equal and opposite, so $E = 0$, while $V = \dfrac{4kq}{d} \neq 0$.

Step 2: So the field can be zero at a point but the potential cannot, which rules out (B), (C) and (D); the point at infinity, where $V = 0$ only because it is chosen as the reference, is not a point at a finite distance from the charges. Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: A long conducting wire having a current I flowing through it, is bent into a circular coil of $\mathrm{N}$ turns. Then it is bent into a circular coil of $\mathrm{n}$ turns. The magnetic field is calculated at the centre of coils in both the cases. The ratio of the magnetic field in first case to that of second case is:
questions.solution: Step 1: The same wire of length $L$ forms $N$ turns of radius $r_1$, so $L = N(2\pi r_1)$ and $r_1 = \dfrac{L}{2\pi N}$. The field at the centre of $N$ turns is $$B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2r_1} = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2}\times\frac{2\pi N}{L} = \frac{\pi\mu_0 I N^2}{L}$$ With $n$ turns, $r_2 = \dfrac{L}{2\pi n}$ and in the same way $B_2 = \dfrac{\pi\mu_0 I n^2}{L}$. $$\frac{B_1}{B_2} = \frac{N^2}{n^2}$$ Hence, the correct option is (A).

uniformly by the same amount as another wire B of length $6.0 \mathrm{~m}$ and a cross section of $3.0 \times 10^{-5}$
$\mathrm{m}^{2}$ stretches. The ratio of the Young's modulus of wire A to that of wire $B$ will be:
questions.solution: Step 1: $\Delta \ell=\frac{F \ell}{S Y}$ $F$ is same for both wire and $\Delta \ell$ is also same $$ \begin{aligned} & \frac{\Delta \ell}{F}=\frac{\ell}{S Y} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{\ell_{A}}{S_{A} Y_{A}}=\frac{\ell_{B}}{S_{B} Y_{B}} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{5}{2.5 \times Y_{A}}=\frac{6}{3 \times Y_{B}} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{Y_{A}}{Y_{B}}=1 \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: A stone of mass $1 \mathrm{~kg}$ is tied to end of a massless string of length $1 \mathrm{~m}$. If the breaking tension of the string is $400 \mathrm{~N}$, then maximum linear velocity, the stone can have without breaking the string, while rotating in horizontal plane, is:

questions.text:
Cobalt chloride when dissolved in water forms pink colored complex $\underline{\mathrm{X}}$ which has
octahedral geometry. This solution on treating with conc $\mathrm{HCl}$ forms deep blue complex, $\underline{\mathrm{Y}}$ which has a $\underline{\mathrm{Z}}$ geometry. $\mathrm{X}, \mathrm{Y}$ and $\mathrm{Z}$, respectively, are
questions.solution: Step 1: In water, $\ce{CoCl2}$ gives the pink octahedral aqua complex $\ce{[Co(H2O)6]^2+}$, with cobalt in the +2 state ($3d^7$). Concentrated HCl supplies a large excess of $\ce{Cl^-}$, which replaces the water ligands without changing the oxidation state; four of the large $\ce{Cl^-}$ ions surround $\ce{Co^2+}$ tetrahedrally, giving the deep blue complex. $$\ce{[Co(H2O)6]^2+ + 4Cl^- [CoCl4]^2- + 6H2O}$$ The options with $\ce{[CoCl6]^3-}$, $\ce{[Co(H2O)6]^3+}$ or $\ce{[Co(H2O)4Cl2]^+}$ need Co(III), which is not formed because neither water nor HCl oxidises Co(II). Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: The number of real roots of the equation $\sqrt{x^{2}-4 x+3}+\sqrt{x^{2}-9}=\sqrt{4 x^{2}-14 x+6}$, is:
questions.solution:
Step 1: Factorise: $x^2-4x+3 = (x-1)(x-3)$, $x^2-9 = (x-3)(x+3)$ and $4x^2-14x+6 = (x-3)(4x-2)$. All three radicands are non-negative only for $x \le -3$ or $x \ge 3$. At $x = 3$ every term is 0, so $x = 3$ is a root. For $x > 3$, dividing by $\sqrt{x-3}$: $\sqrt{x-1} + \sqrt{x+3} = \sqrt{4x-2}$. Squaring, $2x + 2 + 2\sqrt{(x-1)(x+3)} = 4x - 2 \Rightarrow \sqrt{x^2+2x-3} = x - 2 \Rightarrow x^2 + 2x - 3 = x^2 - 4x + 4 \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{7}{6}$, which is not greater than 3. For $x \le -3$, dividing by $\sqrt{3-x}$: $\sqrt{1-x} + \sqrt{-x-3} = \sqrt{2-4x}$. Squaring, $-2x - 2 + 2\sqrt{(1-x)(-x-3)} = 2 - 4x \Rightarrow \sqrt{x^2+2x-3} = 2 - x \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{7}{6}$, which is not $\le -3$.

Step 2: So $x = 3$ is the only real root. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: If the sum and product of four positive consecutive terms of a G.P., are 126 and 1296, respectively, then the sum of common ratios of all such GPs is
questions.solution: Step 1: Let the terms be $a,\ ar,\ ar^2,\ ar^3$ with $a,r>0$. Product: $a^4r^6=1296 \Rightarrow a^2r^3=36 \Rightarrow a=\dfrac{6}{r^{3/2}}$. Sum: $a\left(1+r+r^2+r^3\right)=126 \Rightarrow \dfrac{1+r+r^2+r^3}{r^{3/2}}=21 \Rightarrow \left(r^{3/2}+r^{-3/2}\right)+\left(r^{1/2}+r^{-1/2}\right)=21$. Let $t=\sqrt r+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt r}$, so $t\ge2$ and $r^{3/2}+r^{-3/2}=t^3-3t$. Then $$t^3-3t+t=21 \Rightarrow t^3-2t-21=0 \Rightarrow (t-3)\left(t^2+3t+7\right)=0.$$ The factor $t^2+3t+7$ has discriminant $9-28<0$, so the only real root is $t=3$. $\sqrt r+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt r}=3 \Rightarrow r+1=3\sqrt r \Rightarrow r^2+2r+1=9r \Rightarrow r^2-7r+1=0.$ Both roots $r=\dfrac{7\pm3\sqrt5}{2}$ are positive, so each gives a valid G.P., and the sum of the common ratios is $7$. Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
For the system of linear equations
$x+y+z=6$
$\alpha x+\beta y+7 z=3$
$x+2 y+3 z=14$
which of the following is NOT true ?

options.text: If $\alpha=\beta=7$, then the system has no solution
For every point $(\alpha, \beta) \neq(7,7)$ on the line $x-2 y+7=0$, the system has infinitely many solutions
There is a unique point $(\alpha, \beta)$ on the line $x+2 y+18=0$ for which the system has infinitely many solutions
If $\alpha=\beta$ and $\alpha \neq 7$, then the system has a unique solution

questions.solution:
Step 1: The coefficient determinant is Δ= 1, 1, 1\α, β, 7\1, 2, 3 =(3β-14)-(3α-7)+(2α-β)=2β-α-7, so $\Delta=0$ exactly when $(\alpha,\beta)$ lies on the line $x-2y+7=0$. The first and third equations give $y+2z=8$, so their common solutions are $x=t-2,\ y=8-2t,\ z=t$. Substituting in the second equation gives $$(\alpha-2\beta+7)\,t+(8\beta-2\alpha)=3.$$ For $\alpha=\beta=7$ the second equation becomes $x+y+z=\dfrac{3}{7}$, which contradicts $x+y+z=6$, so there is no solution and (
A) is true. For $\alpha=\beta\neq7$, $\Delta=\alpha-7\neq0$, so the solution is unique and (
D) is true. On the line $\alpha-2\beta+7=0$ the $t$ term vanishes, so there are infinitely many solutions only if $8\beta-2\alpha=3$. With $\alpha=2\beta-7$ this gives $4\beta+14=3$, so $\beta=-\dfrac{11}{4}$ and $\alpha=-\dfrac{25}{2}$; every other point of that line gives no solution, so (
B) is false. The point $\left(-\dfrac{25}{2},-\dfrac{11}{4}\right)$ satisfies $-\dfrac{25}{2}-\dfrac{11}{2}+18=0$, so it lies on $x+2y+18=0$ and is the only point giving infinitely many solutions; (
C) is true. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: Let $\mathrm{R}$ be a relation on $\mathrm{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ defined by $(a, b) ~\mathrm{R}~(c, d)$ if and only if $a d(b-c)=b c(a-d)$. Then $\mathrm{R}$ is

options.text: symmetric and transitive but not reflexive
reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
transitive but neither reflexive nor symmetric
symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive

questions.solution:
Step 1: For $a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{N}$, dividing $ad(b-c) = bc(a-d)$ by $abcd$: $$\frac1c - \frac1b = \frac1d - \frac1a \iff \frac1a + \frac1c = \frac1b + \frac1d$$ Symmetric: the condition is unchanged when $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$ are interchanged, so $(a,b)\,R\,(c,d) \Rightarrow (c,d)\,R\,(a,b)$. Reflexive: $(a,b)\,R\,(a,b) \iff \dfrac2a = \dfrac2b \iff a = b$, so for example $(1,2)$ is not related to itself; $R$ is not reflexive. Transitive: $(2,3)\,R\,(3,2)$ since $\dfrac12 + \dfrac13 = \dfrac13 + \dfrac12$, and $(3,2)\,R\,(5,30)$ since $\dfrac13 + \dfrac15 = \dfrac{8}{15} = \dfrac12 + \dfrac{1}{30}$. But $\dfrac12 + \dfrac15 = \dfrac{21}{30} \ne \dfrac{11}{30} = \dfrac13 + \dfrac{1}{30}$, so $(2,3)$ is not related to $(5,30)$; $R$ is not transitive.

Step 2: So $R$ is symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive. Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.solution:
Step 1: On each interval $[n, n+1)$, $[x] = n$, and $\dfrac{n}{1+x^2}$ decreases for $x > 0$, so each piece takes values from its value at the left end (included) down to its limit at the right end (excluded). $x \in [2,3)$: $f(x) = \dfrac{2}{1+x^2} \in \left(\dfrac15, \dfrac25\right]$ $x \in [3,4)$: $f(x) = \dfrac{3}{1+x^2} \in \left(\dfrac{3}{17}, \dfrac{3}{10}\right]$ $x \in [4,5)$: $f(x) = \dfrac{4}{1+x^2} \in \left(\dfrac{2}{13}, \dfrac{4}{17}\right]$ $x \in [5,6)$: $f(x) = \dfrac{5}{1+x^2} \in \left(\dfrac{5}{37}, \dfrac{5}{26}\right]$ Consecutive pieces overlap: $\dfrac15 < \dfrac{3}{10}$, $\dfrac{3}{17} < \dfrac{4}{17}$ and $\dfrac{2}{13} < \dfrac{5}{26}$.

Step 2: So the union has no gaps and runs from $\dfrac{5}{37}$ (not attained) to $\dfrac25$ (attained at $x = 2$); the four points removed in options (
A) and (
D) all lie inside the first or third piece and are attained. $$\text{Range} = \left(\frac{5}{37}, \frac25\right]$$ Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: A wire of length $20 \mathrm{~m}$ is to be cut into two pieces. A piece of length $l_{1}$ is bent to make a square of area $A_{1}$ and the other piece of length $l_{2}$ is made into a circle of area $A_{2}$. If $2 A_{1}+3 A_{2}$ is minimum then $\left(\pi l_{1}\right): l_{2}$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $ \ell_{1}+\ell_{2}=20 \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d} \ell_{2}}{\mathrm{~d} \ell_{1}}=-1$ $\mathrm{A}_{1}=\left(\frac{\ell_{1}}{4}\right)^{2}$ and $\mathrm{A}_{2}=\pi\left(\frac{\ell_{2}}{2 \pi}\right)^{2}$ Let $\mathrm{S}=2 \mathrm{~A}_{1}+3 \mathrm{~A}_{2}=\frac{\ell_{1}^{2}}{8}+\frac{3 \ell_{2}^{2}}{4 \pi}$ $\frac{\mathrm{ds}}{\mathrm{d} \ell_1}=0 \Rightarrow \frac{2 \ell_{1}}{8}+\frac{6 \ell_{2}}{4 \pi} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d} \ell_{2}}{\mathrm{~d} \ell_{1}}=0$ $\Rightarrow \frac{\ell_{1}}{4}=\frac{6 \ell_{2}}{4 \pi} $ $\Rightarrow \frac{\pi \ell_{1}}{\ell_{2}}=6$

questions.text: Let $\alpha \in (0,1)$ and $\beta = {\log _e}(1 - \alpha )$. Let ${P_n}(x) = x + {{{x^2}} \over 2} + {{{x^3}} \over 3}\, + \,...\, + \,{{{x^n}} \over n},x \in (0,1)$. Then the integral $\int\limits_0^\alpha {{{{t^{50}}} \over {1 - t}}dt} $ is equal to
questions.solution: Step 1: $\int_{0}^{\alpha} \frac{t^{50}}{1-t} d t$ $$ \begin{aligned} & = \int_{0}^{\alpha} \frac{t^{50}-1+1}{1-t}\\ & =-\int_{0}^{\alpha}\left(\frac{1-t^{50}}{1-t}-\frac{1}{1-t}\right) d t\\ & =-\int_{0}^{\alpha}\left(1+t+\ldots..+t^{49}\right)+\int_{0}^{\alpha} \frac{1}{1-t} d t \end{aligned} $$ $=-\left(\frac{\alpha^{50}}{50}+\frac{\alpha^{49}}{49}+\ldots..+\frac{\alpha^{1}}{1}\right)+\left(\frac{\ln (1-\mathrm{t})}{-1}\right)_{0}^{\alpha}$ $=-\mathrm{P}_{50}(\alpha)-\ln (1-\alpha)$ $=-\mathrm{P}_{50}(\alpha)-\beta$

questions.text:
Let the shortest distance between the lines
$L: \frac{x-5}{-2}=\frac{y-\lambda}{0}=\frac{z+\lambda}{1}, \lambda \geq 0$ and
$L_{1}: x+1=y-1=4-z$ be $2 \sqrt{6}$. If $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ lies on $L$,
then which of the following is NOT possible?
questions.solution: Step 1: $\frac{x-5}{-2}=\frac{y-\lambda}{0}=\frac{z+\lambda}{1}, \lambda \geq 0$ $$ \frac{x+1}{1}=\frac{y-1}{1}=\frac{z-4}{-1}; \vec{a}_{1}=5 \hat{i}+\lambda \hat{j}-\lambda \hat{k}_{,} \vec{a}_{2}=-\hat{i}+\hat{j}+4 \hat{k}; \vec{a}_{1}-\vec{a}_{2}=6 \hat{i}+(\lambda-1) \hat{j}-(\lambda+4) \hat{k}; \vec{b}_{1}=-2 \hat{i}+\hat{k}, \vec{b}_{2}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}-\hat{k}; \vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}=\left|{ccc} \hat{i} \hat{j} \hat{k} \ -2 0 1 \ 1 1 -1 \right| \ =-\hat{i}-\hat{j}-2 \hat{k} $$ $\left(\vec{a}_{1}-\vec{a}_{2}\right) \cdot \vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}=-6+1-\lambda+2 \lambda+8=\lambda+3$ and $\left|\vec{b}_{1} \times \vec{b}_{2}\right|=\sqrt{6}$ $\because \frac{|\lambda+3|}{\sqrt{6}}=2 \sqrt{6}$ $\therefore \lambda=9, \because \lambda \geq 0$ $\therefore \quad L: \frac{x-5}{-2}=\frac{y-9}{0}=\frac{z+9}{1}=k$ $\therefore \quad \alpha=-2 k+5, \beta=9, \gamma=k-9$ Here $k$ is real then $\alpha+2 \gamma=-13 \neq 24$. But all other are in terms of $k$ hence possible.

questions.text:
Let $\vec{a}=2 \hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, and $\vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ be two nonzero vectors such that $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}|=|\vec{a}+\vec{b}-\vec{c}|$ and $\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}=0$. Consider the following two statements:
(
A) $|\vec{a}+\lambda \vec{c}| \geq|\vec{a}|$ for all $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$.
(
B) $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{c}$ are always parallel.
Then,

options.text:
both (
A) and (
B) are correct

neither (
A) nor (
B) is correct

questions.solution: Step 1: $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}|=|\vec{a}+\vec{b}-\vec{c}|$ $$ \Rightarrow $$ $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^{2}=|\vec{a}+\vec{b}-\vec{c}|^{2}$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow |\vec{a}|^{2}+|\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{c}|^{2}+2(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+\vec{c} \vec{a}) \\ & =|\vec{a}|^{2}+|\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{c}|^{2}+2(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}-\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}-\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a}) \\ & \Rightarrow \vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a}=0 \Rightarrow \vec{c} \cdot \vec{a}=0 \\ & |\vec{a}+\lambda \vec{c}|^{2}=|\vec{a}|^{2}+\lambda^{2}|\vec{c}|^{2}+0 \geq|\vec{a}|^{2} \end{aligned} $$ So $\mathrm{A}$ is correct. $B$ is incorrect.

questions.text: Let A = ( matrix 1, 0, 0 cr 0, 4, - 1 cr 0, 12, - 3 cr ). Then the sum of the diagonal elements of the matrix ${(A + I)^{11}}$ is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: $A^{2}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 4 & -1 \ 0 & 12 & -3\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 4 & -1 \ 0 & 12 & -3\end{array}\right]$ $$ =\left[\begin{array}{ccc} 1 & 0 & 0 \ 0 & 4 & -1 \ 0 & 12 & -3 \end{array}\right]=A $$ $$\Rightarrow \mathrm{A}^{3}=\mathrm{A}^{4}=.......=\mathrm{A}$$ Now, $$ \begin{aligned} (A+I)^{11} & ={ }^{11} C_{0} A^{11}+{ }^{11} C_{1} A^{10}+\ldots{ }^{11} C_{11} I \\ & =A\left({ }^{11} C_{0}+{ }^{11} C_{1} \ldots{ }^{11} C_{10}\right)+I \\ & =A\left(2^{11}-1\right)+I \end{aligned} $$ Trace of $$ \begin{aligned} (A+I)^{11} & =2^{11}+4\left(2^{11}-1\right)+1-3\left(2^{11}-1\right)+1 \\ & =2 \times 2^{11}-4+3+2 \\ & =2^{12}+1 \\ & =4097 \end{aligned} $$

questions.text: The value of int_(π)/(3)^(π)/(2) ((2+3 sin x))/(sin x(1+cos x)) d x is equal to:
questions.solution: Step 1: Let I = $int_(π)/(3)^(π)/(2) ((2+3 sin x))/(sin x(1+cos x)) d x$ $$ =\int\limits_{\pi / 3}^{\pi / 2} \frac{2}{\sin x(1+\cos x)} d x+\int\limits_{\pi / 3}^{\pi / 2} \frac{3}{1+\cos x} d x $$ $$ \begin{aligned} =\int\limits_{\pi / 3}^{\pi / 2} \frac{2(1-\cos x)}{\sin x\left(1-\cos ^2 x\right)} & d x +\int\limits_{\pi / 3}^{\pi / 2} \frac{3}{1+\cos x} d x \end{aligned} $$ $$ =\int\limits_{\pi / 3}^{\pi / 2} \frac{2(1-\cos x)}{\sin ^3 x} d x+\int\limits_{\pi / 3}^{\pi / 2} \frac{3}{2 \cos ^2 \frac{x}{2}} d x $$ $$ \begin{array}{r} =\int\limits_{\pi / 3}^{\pi / 2} \frac{2}{\sin ^3 x} d x-\int\limits_{\pi / 3}^{\pi / 2} 2 \cot x \operatorname{cosec}^2 x d x +\int\limits_{\pi / 3}^{\pi / 2} \frac{3}{2} \sec ^2 \frac{x}{2} d x \end{array} $$ $$ =2 I_1-2 I_2+\frac{3}{2} I_3 $$ Now, $$ \begin{aligned} I_1 & =\int\limits_{\pi / 3}^{\pi / 2} \operatorname{cosec}^3 x d x \\ & =\int\limits_{\pi / 3}^{\pi / 2} \sqrt{1+\cot ^2 x} \operatorname{cosec}^2 x d x \end{aligned} $$ Put $\cot x=t \Rightarrow-\operatorname{cosec}^2 x d x=d t$ When, $x=\frac{\pi}{3} \Rightarrow t=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \text { and } x=\frac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow t=0$ $$ \begin{aligned} \therefore & I_1=-\int\limits_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}^0 \sqrt{1+t^2} d t \\ = & \int\limits_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}} \sqrt{1+t^2} d t \\ = & {\left[\frac{t}{2} \sqrt{1+t^2}+\frac{1}{2} \log \left[t+\sqrt{1+t^2}\right]\right]_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}} } \\ = & \frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{2} \log \sqrt{3} \end{aligned} $$ $$ I_2=\int\limits_{\pi / 3}^{\pi / 2} \cot x \operatorname{cosec}^2 x d x $$ Put $\cot x=t \Rightarrow \operatorname{cosec}^2 x d x=-d t$ When, $x=\frac{\pi}{3}$ $\Rightarrow t=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ and $x=\frac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow t=0$ $$ \therefore \begin{aligned} I_2 & =-\int\limits_{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}^0 t d t \\ & =\int\limits_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} t} t d t=\left[\frac{t^2}{2}\right]_0^{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}=\frac{1}{6} \end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned} & I_3=\int\limits_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sec ^2 \frac{x}{2} d x \\ = & 2\left(\tan \frac{\pi}{4}-\tan \frac{\pi}{6}\right)=2\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned} & \therefore \quad I=2 I_1-2 I_2+\frac{3}{2} I_3 \\ & =2\left(\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{2} \log \sqrt{3}\right)-2\left(\frac{1}{6}\right) +\frac{3}{2}\left(2\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\right) \end{aligned} $$ $$ \begin{aligned} & =\frac{2}{3}+\log \sqrt{3}-\frac{1}{3}+3-\sqrt{3} \\ & =\frac{10}{3}-\sqrt{3}+\log _e \sqrt{3} \end{aligned} $$

questions.solution: Step 1: $f(x)=\sin ^{3}\left(\frac{\pi}{3} \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{3 \sqrt{2}}\left(-4 x^{3}+5 x^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\right)\right)$ $$ \begin{aligned} & f^{\prime}(x)=3 \sin ^{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{3} \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{3 \sqrt{2}}\left(-4 x^{3}+5 x^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\right)\right) \\ & \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{3} \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{3 \sqrt{2}}\left(-4 x^{3}+5 x^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\right)\right) \\ & \frac{\pi}{3}\left(-\sin \left(\frac{\pi}{3 \sqrt{2}}\left(-4 x^{3}+5 x^{2}+1\right)^{3 / 2}\right)\right) \\ & \frac{\pi}{3 \sqrt{2}} \frac{3}{2}\left(-4 x^{3}+5 x^{2}+1\right)^{1 / 2}\left(-12 x^{2}+10 x\right) \end{aligned} $$ $f^{\prime}(1)=\frac{3 \pi^{2}}{16}$ $$ \begin{aligned} & f(1)=\sin ^{3}\left(\frac{\pi}{3} \cos \left(\frac{\pi}{3 \sqrt{2}} 2 \sqrt{2}\right)\right) \\ &=\sin ^{3}\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{-1}{8} \\ & \therefore 2 f^{\prime}(1)+3 \pi^{2} f(1)=0 \end{aligned} $$

questions.text:
Spherical insulating ball and a spherical metallic ball of same size and mass are dropped from the same height. Choose the correct statement out of the following
{Assume negligible air friction}

options.text: Metal ball will reach the earth's surface earlier than the insulating ball
Both will reach the earth's surface simultaneously.
Insulating ball will reach the earth's surface earlier than the metal ball
Time taken by them to reach the earth's surface will be independent of the properties of their materials

questions.solution:
Step 1: The correct answer is option
C: the insulating ball will reach the earth's surface earlier than the metal ball. When the two balls are dropped from the same height, they will experience the same gravitational force, which will cause them to accelerate downwards. However, According to Faraday’s law of electromagnetic induction motion of metal is opposed by earth magnetic field. Which will slightly reduce its acceleration. On the other hand, the insulating ball will not experience any electromagnetic induction. Therefore, it will accelerate downwards at a slightly faster rate than the metal ball. As a result, the insulating ball will reach the earth's surface earlier than the metal ball. So, option C is the correct statement.

questions.text: The drift velocity of electrons for a conductor connected in an electrical circuit is $\mathrm{V}_{\mathrm{d}}$. The conductor is now replaced by another conductor with same material and same length but double the area of cross section. The applied voltage remains same. The new drift velocity of electrons will be
questions.solution: Step 1: Same material and length with area $2A$: the new resistance is $R'=\dfrac{\rho l}{2A}=\dfrac{R}{2}$, so at the same applied voltage the current doubles, $I'=\dfrac{V}{R'}=2I$. The free-electron density $n$ is unchanged (same material), so from $I=neAv_d$: $$v_d'=\dfrac{I'}{ne(2A)}=\dfrac{2I}{2neA}=v_d$$ The factor $\dfrac{1}{A}$ in $v_d=\dfrac{I}{neA}$ is cancelled by the doubled current; the field $E=\dfrac{V}{l}$ that drives the drift is the same in both conductors. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
A rod with circular cross-section area $2 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$ and length $40 \mathrm{~cm}$ is wound uniformly with 400 turns of an insulated wire. If a current of $0.4 \mathrm{~A}$ flows in the wire windings, the total magnetic flux produced inside windings is $4 \pi \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~Wb}$. The relative permeability of the rod is
(Given: Permeability of vacuum $\mu_{0}=4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{NA}^{-2}$)
questions.solution: Step 1: The number of turns per unit length is $n = \dfrac{400}{0.40\ \text{m}} = 1000\ \text{m}^{-1}$, and $A = 2\ \text{cm}^2 = 2 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2$. The field inside the rod is $B = \mu_0\mu_r nI$, so the flux through the rod is $$\Phi = BA = \mu_0\mu_r nIA$$ $$\mu_r = \dfrac{\Phi}{\mu_0 nIA} = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-6}}{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 1000 \times 0.4 \times 2 \times 10^{-4}}$$ $$\mu_r = \dfrac{10^{-6}}{8 \times 10^{-9}} = 125$$ Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: At a certain depth "d " below surface of earth, value of acceleration due to gravity becomes four times that of its value at a height $\mathrm{3 R}$ above earth surface. Where $\mathrm{R}$ is Radius of earth (Take $\mathrm{R}=6400 \mathrm{~km}$ ). The depth $\mathrm{d}$ is equal to
questions.solution: Step 1: The acceleration due to gravity $$g$$ at a distance $$d$$ below the surface of the earth is given by: $g_{d}=\frac{G M}{R^{3}}(R-d)$ (depth variation) where $$G$$ is the gravitational constant and $$M$$ is the mass of the Earth. At a height $$3R$$ above the surface of the Earth, the acceleration due to gravity $g_{h}$ is given by: $$ g_{h}=\frac{G M}{(R+3R)^{2}} $$ Given, $ g_{d}=4 g_{h} \\$, so we can write: \begin{aligned} & \frac{G M}{R^{3}}(R-d)=4 \frac{G M}{(R+3 R)^{2}} \\ & \Rightarrow R-d=\frac{R}{4} \\ & \Rightarrow d=\frac{3 R}{4} \\ & \Rightarrow d=4800 \mathrm{~km} \end{aligned} $
questions.topic: Acceleration due to Gravity and its Variation

questions.text: 100 balls each of mass $\mathrm{m}$ moving with speed $v$ simultaneously strike a wall normally and reflected back with same speed, in time $\mathrm{t ~s}$. The total force exerted by the balls on the wall is
questions.solution: Step 1: When the balls strike the wall, the change in momentum of each ball is given by: $$\Delta p = mv - (-mv) = 2mv$$ Since there are 100 balls, the total change in momentum of all the balls is $$\Delta P = 2m(100v) = 200mv.$$ The time taken for all the balls to strike the wall is $\mathrm{t}$ seconds. Therefore, the average force exerted on the wall is given by: $$F = \frac{\Delta P}{\mathrm{t}} = \frac{2m(100v)}{\mathrm{t}} = \frac{200mv}{\mathrm{t}}$$ Therefore, the total force exerted by the balls on the wall is $$\boxed{F = \frac{200mv}{\mathrm{t}}}$$

questions.text: If the radius of the first orbit of hydrogen atom is $\alpha_{0}$, then de Broglie's wavelength of electron in $3^{\text {rd }}$ orbit is:
questions.solution: Step 1: In Bohr's model, the angular momentum of an electron in an orbit is quantized, which can be represented as: $$mvr = n \cdot \frac{h}{2\pi}$$ Where: (m) is the mass of the electron, (v) is the velocity of the electron, (r) is the radius of the nth orbit, and (n) is the principal quantum number ((n = 1) for the first orbit, (n = 2) for the second orbit, and so on). The de Broglie wavelength ($\lambda$) is given by: $$\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}$$ For the nth orbit, the radius (r) is $n^2$ times the radius of the first orbit ($r_0$, or $\alpha_0$ in your notation): $$r = n^2 \cdot \alpha_0$$ The circumference of the nth orbit is $2\pi r$, which can be written as: $$2\pi r = n \cdot \lambda$$ Substituting the expression for (r): $$2\pi \cdot n^2 \cdot \alpha_0 = n \cdot \lambda$$ Solving for $\lambda$ gives: $$\lambda = 2\pi \cdot n \cdot \alpha_0$$ For the 3rd orbit ((n = 3)), this simplifies to: $$\lambda = 6\pi \cdot \alpha_0$$

questions.text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as "Assertion A" and the other is labelled as "Reason R"
Assertion A: In the complex $\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CO})_{4}$ and $\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CO})_{5}$, the metals have zero oxidation state.
Reason R: Low oxidation states are found when a complex has ligands capable of $\pi$-donor character in addition to the $\sigma$-bonding.
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below

options.text: A is not correct but R is correct
A is correct but R is not correct
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A

questions.solution: Step 1: CO is a neutral ligand and both $\ce{Ni(CO)4}$ and $\ce{Fe(CO)5}$ are neutral, so the oxidation state of Ni and of Fe is $0$; Assertion A is correct. A metal in a low oxidation state is stabilised by ligands that are $\pi$-acceptors in addition to being $\sigma$-donors: CO donates its lone pair to the metal through a $\sigma$ bond and accepts electron density from filled metal d orbitals into its vacant $\pi^*$ orbitals (synergic bonding), which drains the excess electron density from the metal. Reason R calls this $\pi$-donor character; a $\pi$-donor ligand would push still more electron density onto the metal and cannot stabilise a zero oxidation state, so R is not correct. Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: The IUPAC name of $\mathrm{K}_{3}\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}\right)_{3}\right]$ is:-
questions.solution: Step 1: To determine the IUPAC name of the compound K₃[Co(C₂O₄)₃], let's follow the nomenclature rules for coordination compounds: Identify the Cation and Anion: The compound consists of potassium ions (K⁺) and a complex anion [Co(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻. Name the Cation First: The cation is named first. So, we start with "Potassium." Determine the Ligand Name: The ligand C₂O₄²⁻ is called "oxalato." Count the Number of Ligands: There are three oxalato ligands. Since "oxalato" does not contain any numerical prefixes (like di-, tri-), we use the prefixes "di-", "tri-", etc., for simple ligands. So, we use "trioxalato." Name the Central Metal Atom: Since the complex ion is an anion, the metal name ends with the suffix "-ate." Therefore, "cobalt" becomes "cobaltate." Specify the Oxidation State: The oxidation state of cobalt in this complex can be calculated: Let the oxidation state of Co be x. Each oxalato ligand has a charge of -2. The overall charge of the complex ion is -3. So, x + 3(-2) = -3 ⇒ x -6 = -3 ⇒ x = +3. Therefore, we indicate the oxidation state as (III). Combining all these, the IUPAC name is Potassium trioxalatocobaltate(III). Answer: Option C Potassium trioxalatocobaltate(III)

questions.text: The volume of $0.02 ~\mathrm{M}$ aqueous $\mathrm{HBr}$ required to neutralize $10.0 \mathrm{~mL}$ of $0.01 ~\mathrm{M}$ aqueous $\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$ is (Assume complete neutralization)
questions.solution: Step 1: The reaction between $\mathrm{HBr}$ and $\mathrm{Ba(OH)_2}$ is a neutralization reaction where one $\mathrm{Ba(OH)_2}$ reacts with two $\mathrm{HBr}$ to form $\mathrm{BaBr_2}$ and $2\mathrm{H_2O}$: $\mathrm{Ba(OH)_2} + 2\mathrm{HBr} \rightarrow \mathrm{BaBr_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}$ We can use the stoichiometry of the reaction to find the volume of $\mathrm{HBr}$ required. The number of moles of $\mathrm{Ba(OH)_2}$ is given by its molarity times the volume in liters: $n(\mathrm{Ba(OH)_2}) = 0.01 \, \mathrm{M} \times \frac{10.0 \, \mathrm{mL}}{1000 \, \mathrm{mL/L}} = 0.0001 \, \mathrm{moles}$ From the balanced equation, we can see that the reaction requires $2$ moles of $\mathrm{HBr}$ for each mole of $\mathrm{Ba(OH)_2}$: $n(\mathrm{HBr}) = 2 \times n(\mathrm{Ba(OH)_2}) = 2 \times 0.0001 \, \mathrm{moles} = 0.0002 \, \mathrm{moles}$ Then, we find the volume of the $\mathrm{HBr}$ solution by dividing the number of moles by the molarity: $V(\mathrm{HBr}) = \frac{n(\mathrm{HBr})}{0.02 \, \mathrm{M}} = \frac{0.0002 \, \mathrm{moles}}{0.02 \, \mathrm{mol/L}} = 0.01 \, \mathrm{L} = 10 \, \mathrm{mL}$ Therefore, the volume of the $0.02 \, \mathrm{M}$ $\mathrm{HBr}$ solution required to neutralize the $\mathrm{Ba(OH)_2}$ solution is $10.0 \, \mathrm{mL}$.
