Combustion reaction :

then volume of xCO 2 $$\Rightarrow$$ V x = 4 V

x = 4

$$V\left( {x + {y \over 4}} \right)$$ = 6V

$$\left( {x + {y \over 4}} \right) = 6$$ ..... (i)

Put value of x = 4 in Eq. (i) we get,

$$4 + {y \over 4} = 6 \Rightarrow y = 8$$

questions.text:
Production of iron in blast furnace follows the following equation

Fe₃O₄ (s) + 4CO(g) $$\to$$ 3Fe(l) + 4CO 2 (g)

when 4.640 kg of Fe₃O₄ and 2.520 kg of CO are allowed to react then the amount of iron (in g) produced is :

[Given : Molar Atomic mass (g mol $$-$$1 ) : Fe = 56, Molar Atomic mass (g mol $$-$$1 ) : O
= 16, Molar Atomic mass (g mol $$-$$1 ) : C = 12]
questions.solution:
Given,

Mass of $$F{e_3}{O_4}$$ = 4.640 kg = 4640 gm

Molar mass of $$F{e_3}{O_4}$$ = 56 $$\times$$ 3 + 16 $$\times$$ 4 = 232 g

$$\therefore$$ Moles of $$F{e_3}{O_4} = {{4640} \over {232}} = 20$$

Also, given

Mass of CO = 2.520 kg = 2520 gm

Molar mass of CO = 12 + 16 = 28 gm

$$\therefore$$ Moles of $$CO = {{2520} \over {28}} = 90$$

Here Fe₃O₄ is limiting reagent as to find limiting reagent, divide the given moles of reactants with their respective stoichiometric coefficient and reactant for which this ratio is minimum will be limiting reagent

For $$F{e_3}{O_4},{{moles} \over {stoichiometric\,coefficient}} = {{20} \over 1}$$

For $$CO,{{moles} \over {stoichiometric\,coefficient}} = {{90} \over 4} = 22.5$$

$$\therefore$$ Fe₃O₄ is limiting reagent.

Now produced Fe = 20 $$\times$$ 3 = 60 mol

$$\therefore$$ Weight of Fe = 60 $$\times$$ 56 = 3360 g

questions.text:
Compound A contains 8.7% Hydrogen, 74% Carbon and 17.3% Nitrogen. The molecular formula of the compound is,

Given : Atomic masses of C, H and N are 12, 1 and 14 amu respectively.

The molar mass of the compound A is 162 g mol $$-$$1 .

Mole ratio of H, C and N

$$ = {{8.7} \over 1}:{{74} \over {12}}:{{17.\,3} \over {14}}$$

$$ = 8\,.7:6.167:1.23$$

$$ = {{8.7} \over {1.23}}:{{6.167} \over {1.23}}:{{1.23} \over {1.23}}$$

$$ = 7:5:1$$

$$\therefore$$ Emperical formula = $${{C_5}{H_7}N}$$

$$\therefore$$ Molecular formula $$ = {\left( {{C_5}{H_7}N} \right)_n}$$

Given molecular mass = 162

Molecular mass of $${\left( {{C_5}{H_7}N} \right)_n}$$

$$ = (5 \times 12 + 7 \times 1 + 14) \times n$$

$$ = (81) \times n$$

$$\therefore$$ $$81 \times n = 162$$

$$ \Rightarrow n = 2$$

$$\therefore$$ Molecular formula = C 10 H 14 N 2

questions.text: The complete combustion of 0.492 g of an organic compound containing 'C', 'H' and 'O' gives 0.793 g of CO 2 and 0.442 g of H₂O. The percentage of oxygen composition in the organic compound is ______________. (nearest integer)

= 0.492 $$-$$ (0.216 + 0.05)

= 0.226 gm

% by mass of oxygen in compound

= $${{0.226} \over {0.492}}$$ $$\times$$ 100 = 46%

questions.text:
CNG is an important transportation fuel. When 100 g CNG is mixed with 208 g oxygen in vehicles, it leads to the formation of CO 2 and H₂O and produces large quantity of heat during this combustion, then the amount of carbon dioxide, produced in grams is ____________. [nearest integer]

[Assume CNG to be methane]
questions.solution:
Initially,

Mass of CNG(CH 4 ) = 100 gm

$$\therefore$$ Moles of CH 4 = $${{100} \over {16}}$$ = 6.25 moles

Mass of O 2 = 208 gm

$$\therefore$$ Moles of O 2 = $${{208} \over {32}}$$ = 6.5 moles

From reaction you can see,

1 mole of CH 4 react with 2 mole of O 2

$$\therefore$$ 6.25 mole of CH 4 react with 6.25 $$\times$$ 2 = 12.5 moles of O 2

But here only 6.5 moles of O 2 present

So, O 2 will act as limiting reagent.

$$\therefore$$ Produced CO 2 will depends on moles of O 2 .

From 2 moles of O 2 1 mole of CO 2

$$\therefore$$ From 6.5 moles of O 2 $${{6.5} \over {2}}$$ moles of CO 2 produced.

$$\therefore$$ Weight of CO 2 = $${{6.5} \over {2}}$$ $$\times$$ 44 = 143 gm

questions.text: On complete combustion 0.30 g of an organic compound gave 0.20 g of carbon dioxide and 0.10 g of water. The percentage of carbon in the given organic compound is _____________. (Nearest integer)
questions.solution:
$${C_x}{H_y} + \left( {x + {y \over 4}} \right){O_2} \to x\,C{O_2} + {y \over 2}{H_2}O$$

Given organic compound C x H y = 0.3 gm

Produced carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) = 0.2 gm

Produced water (H₂O) = 0.1 gm

Moles of CO 2 = $${{0.2} \over {44}}$$

$$\therefore$$ Moles of C atom = $${{0.2} \over {44}}$$

$$\therefore$$ Mass of C atom = $${{0.2} \over {44}}$$ $$\times$$ 12 = 0.0545

Moles of H₂O = $${{0.1} \over {18}}$$

$$\therefore$$ Moles of H atoms = $${{0.1} \over {18}}$$ $$\times$$ 2

$$\therefore$$ Mass of H atoms = $${{0.1} \times2\over {18}}$$ $$\times$$ 1 = 0.0111

$$\therefore$$ % of C atom = $${{0.0545} \over {0.3}}$$ $$\times$$ 100 = 18%

questions.text: The number of N atoms in 681 g of C₇H₅ N₃O₆ is x $$\times$$ 10 21 . The value of x is (N A = 6.02 $$\times$$ 10 23 mol $$-$$1 ) (Nearest Integer)
questions.solution:
First, determine the molar mass of the compound C$_7$H$_5$N$_3$O$_6$:

Carbon (C): 12 g/mol, and there are 7 C atoms: $7 \times 12 = 84 \text{ g/mol}$

Hydrogen (H): 1 g/mol, and there are 5 H atoms: $5 \times 1 = 5 \text{ g/mol}$

Nitrogen (N): 14 g/mol, and there are 3 N atoms: $3 \times 14 = 42 \text{ g/mol}$

Oxygen (O): 16 g/mol, and there are 6 O atoms: $6 \times 16 = 96 \text{ g/mol}$

Calculate the total molar mass:

$ \text{Molar mass of C}_7\text{H}_5\text{N}_3\text{O}_6 = 84 + 5 + 42 + 96 = 227 \text{ g/mol} $

Calculate the number of moles of C$_7$H$_5$N$_3$O$_6$ in 681 grams:

$ \text{Moles of C}_7\text{H}_5\text{N}_3\text{O}_6 = \frac{681 \text{ g}}{227 \text{ g/mol}} = 3 \text{ moles} $

Each molecule of C$_7$H$_5$N$_3$O$_6$ contains 3 nitrogen atoms. Thus, in 3 moles, the total moles of nitrogen atoms is:

$ \text{Moles of N atoms} = 3 \times 3 = 9 \text{ moles} $

Using Avogadro's number, calculate the number of nitrogen atoms:

$ \text{Number of N atoms} = 9 \text{ moles} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} \text{ atoms/mole} $

$ = 54.18 \times 10^{23} = 5.418 \times 10^{24} \text{ N atoms} $

Convert this number to the form $ x \times 10^{21} $:

$ 5.418 \times 10^{24} = 5418 \times 10^{21} $

Thus, the value of $ x $ is:

$ x = 5418 $

questions.text: If we consider that 1/6, in place of 1/12, mass of carbon atom is taken to be the relative atomic mass unit, the mass of one mole of the substance will

options.text: be a function of the molecular mass of the substance

questions.solution:
Taking $\dfrac{1}{6}$ instead of $\dfrac{1}{12}$ of the mass of a carbon-12 atom as the unit only changes the unit in which relative atomic and molecular masses are expressed: every such number is halved.

A mole is a fixed number of particles (Avogadro's number), and the actual mass of that many particles does not depend on the unit chosen.

So the mass of one mole of the substance remains unchanged.

questions.text:
In the reaction

2Al(s) + 6HCl(aq) $$\to$$ 2Al 3+ (aq) + 6Cl - (aq) + 3H 2 (g)

options.text: 11.2 L H 2 (g) at STP is produced for every mole HCl(aq) consumed
6 L HCl(aq) is consumed for every 3L H 2 (g) produced
33.6 L H 2 (g) is produced regardless of temperature and pressure for every mole that reacts
67.2 H 2 (g) at STP is produced for every mole Al that reacts

questions.solution:
Option
A: 6 moles of HCl(aq) produces = 3 moles of H 2 (g)

$$\therefore$$ 1 mole of HCl(aq) produces = $${3 \over 6}$$ moles of H 2 (g) = $${1 \over 2}$$ moles of H 2 (g)

From avogadro hypothesis we know at STP 1 mole of any as occupies 22.4 L.

$$\therefore$$ $${1 \over 2}$$ moles of H 2 (g) occupies = $${1 \over 2} \times 22.4$$ = 11.2 L

$$\therefore$$ Option (
A) is correct.

Option
B: According to avogadro Hypothesis, volume is directly proportional to the no of moles of gases.

Only for gases, no of mole and volume relationship is possible i.e, for two gases if no of moles are same then their volume is also same. But here HCL is in aqueous form and H 2 is in gaseous form so we can't find volume of HCL(aq) using no of moles of HCL(aq).

$$\therefore$$ Option (
B) is wrong.

Option
C: 2 moles of Al(s) produces = 3 moles of H 2 (g)

$$\therefore$$ 1 mole of Al(s) produces = $${3 \over 2}$$ moles of H 2 (g)

From avogadro hypothesis we know at STP 1 mole of any as occupies 22.4 L.

$$\therefore$$ $${3 \over 2}$$ moles of H 2 (g) occupies = $${3 \over 2} \times 22.4$$ = 33.6 L

6 moles of HCl(aq) produces = 3 moles of H 2 (g)

$$\therefore$$ 1 mole of HCl(aq) produces = $${3 \over 6}$$ moles of H 2 (g) = $${1 \over 2}$$ moles of H 2 (g)

$$\therefore$$ $${1 \over 2}$$ moles of H 2 (g) occupies = $${1 \over 2} \times 22.4$$ = 11.2 L

So from every mole of HCl(aq) that reacts only 11.2 L H 2 (g) produces.

Form every mole of Al(s) produces 33.6 L H 2 (g) but from every mole of HCl(aq) that reacts only 11.2 L H 2 (g) produces not 33.6 L.

$$\therefore$$ Option (
C) is wrong.

Option
D: 2 moles of Al(s) produces = 3 moles of H 2 (g)

$$\therefore$$ 1 mole of Al(s) produces = $${3 \over 2}$$ moles of H 2 (g)

From avogadro hypothesis we know at STP 1 mole of any as occupies 22.4 L.

$$\therefore$$ $${3 \over 2}$$ moles of H 2 (g) occupies = $${3 \over 2} \times 22.4$$ = 33.6 L

$$\therefore$$ Option (
D) is wrong.

questions.text: A transition metal $$M$$ forms a volatile chloride which has a vapour density of 94.8. If it contains 74.75% of chlorine the formula of the metal chloride will be
questions.solution:
Molar mass of the chloride $= 2 \times \text{VD} = 2 \times 94.8 = 189.6\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

Mass of chlorine in one mole $= \dfrac{74.75}{100} \times 189.6 = 141.7\ \text{g}$.

Number of Cl atoms per formula unit $= \dfrac{141.7}{35.5} \approx 4$.

Check: mass of metal $= 189.6 - 141.7 = 47.9\ \text{g}$, which is titanium, so the chloride is $\mathrm{TiCl_4}$.

Hence the formula is $\mathrm{MCl_4}$.

questions.solution:
$\mathrm{O_3}$: $\dfrac{16.0}{48} = \dfrac{1}{3}\ \mathrm{mol}$ of molecules, so $3\times\dfrac{1}{3} = 1\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{O}$ atoms.

$\mathrm{CO}$: $\dfrac{28.0}{28} = 1\ \mathrm{mol}$ of molecules, so $1\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{O}$ atoms.

$\mathrm{O_2}$: $\dfrac{16.0}{32} = \dfrac{1}{2}\ \mathrm{mol}$ of molecules, so $2\times\dfrac{1}{2} = 1\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{O}$ atoms.

questions.text: A gaseous compound of nitrogen and hydrogen contains 12.5% (by mass) of hydrogen. The density of the compound relative to hydrogen is 16. The molecular formula of the compound is :
questions.solution:
Mass percentages: $\mathrm{H} = 12.5$, $\mathrm{N} = 87.5$.

Mole ratio $\mathrm{N : H} = \dfrac{87.5}{14} : \dfrac{12.5}{1} = 6.25 : 12.5 = 1 : 2$, so the empirical formula is $\mathrm{NH_2}$ (formula mass $16$).

Vapour density $= 16$, so molar mass $= 2 \times 16 = 32\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.

$n = \dfrac{32}{16} = 2$, so the molecular formula is $\mathrm{(NH_2)_2 = N_2H_4}$.

Check: in $\mathrm{N_2H_4}$, $\%\,\mathrm{H} = \dfrac{4}{32}\times100 = 12.5$.

So the molecular formula is $\mathrm{N_2H_4}$ (hydrazine).

questions.text:
A sample of a hydrate of barium chloride weighing 61 g was heated until all the
water of hydration is removed. The dried sample weighed 52 g. The formula of the
hydrated salt is : (atomic mass, Ba = 137 amu, Cl = 35.5 amu)
questions.solution:
Water lost $= 61 - 52 = 9\ \mathrm{g}$, i.e. $n_{\mathrm{H_2O}} = \dfrac{9}{18} = 0.5\ \mathrm{mol}$.

For $\mathrm{BaCl_2}$, $M = 137 + 2(35.5) = 208\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$, so $n_{\mathrm{BaCl_2}} = \dfrac{52}{208} = 0.25\ \mathrm{mol}$.

Mole ratio $\mathrm{H_2O} : \mathrm{BaCl_2} = 0.5 : 0.25 = 2 : 1$.

Check: $0.25 \times (208 + 36) = 0.25 \times 244 = 61\ \mathrm{g}$, the mass of the sample taken.

So the formula of the hydrated salt is $\mathrm{BaCl_2 \cdot 2H_2O}$.

questions.text:
The average molar mass of chlorine is
35.5 g mol –1 . The ratio of 35 Cl to 37 Cl in naturally
occuring chlorine is close to :
questions.solution:
Let the mole ratio of $^{35}\text{Cl}$ to $^{37}\text{Cl}$ be $x : y$. The average molar mass is the mole-weighted mean:

$$35.5 = \dfrac{35x + 37y}{x + y}$$

$$35.5x + 35.5y = 35x + 37y \Rightarrow 0.5x = 1.5y$$

$$\dfrac{x}{y} = \dfrac{1.5}{0.5} = 3$$

So $^{35}\text{Cl} : {}^{37}\text{Cl} = 3 : 1$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: A 1.84 mg sample of polyhydric alcoholic compound 'X' of molar mass 92.0 g/mol gave 1.344 mL of $$\mathrm{H}_{2}$$ gas at STP. The number of alcoholic hydrogens present in compound 'X' is ________.
questions.solution:
STP conditions define the volume of 1 mole of any gas as $22.4$ liters or $22400$ mL. The volume of hydrogen gas evolved here is $1.344$ mL, so we can calculate the number of moles of hydrogen gas ($H_2$) using the formula:

$n = \frac{V}{V_m}$

where:

$n$ is the number of moles,

$V$ is the volume of the gas, and

$V_m$ is the molar volume of the gas.

Substituting in the given values:

$n = \frac{1.344 \text{ mL}}{22400 \text{ mL/mol}} = 6.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol}$

Each molecule of $H_2$ contains $2$ atoms of hydrogen. Therefore, the number of moles of hydrogen atoms is twice the number of moles of hydrogen gas:

$n_H = 2 \times n = 2 \times 6.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol} = 1.2 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}$

This number of moles of hydrogen represents the number of moles of alcoholic hydrogen atoms in the $1.84$ mg sample of the compound 'X'.

We can determine the number of moles of compound 'X' in the sample by dividing the mass of the sample by the molar mass of the compound:

$n_X = \frac{m}{M}$

where:

$n_X$ is the number of moles of 'X',

$m$ is the mass of 'X', and

$M$ is the molar mass of 'X'.

Substituting in the given values:

$n_X = \frac{1.84 \text{ mg}}{92 \text{ g/mol}} = \frac{1.84 \times 10^{-3} \text{ g}}{92 \text{ g/mol}} = 2.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol}$

The number of alcoholic hydrogens per molecule of 'X' is then given by the ratio of the number of moles of hydrogen to the number of moles of 'X':

$\frac{n_H}{n_X} = \frac{1.2 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol}}{2.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol}} = 6$

So, compound 'X' contains $6$ alcoholic hydrogens.

questions.text:
Hemoglobin contains $$0.34 \%$$ of iron by mass. The number of Fe atoms in $$3.3 \mathrm{~g}$$ of hemoglobin is

(Given: Atomic mass of Fe is $$56 \,\mathrm{u}, \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{A}}=6.022 \times 10^{23} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$$.)

Iron is $0.34\%$ of the mass of hemoglobin, so the mass of iron in $3.3\ \text{g}$ of hemoglobin is

$$m_{\ce{Fe}} = \dfrac{0.34}{100} \times 3.3 = 1.122 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{g}$$

Moles of iron:

$$n_{\ce{Fe}} = \dfrac{1.122 \times 10^{-2}}{56} = 2.004 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{mol}$$

Number of Fe atoms:

$$N = n_{\ce{Fe}} \times N_A = 2.004 \times 10^{-4} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.21 \times 10^{20}$$

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: Two elements A and B which form 0.15 moles of A₂B and AB 3 type compounds. If both A₂B and AB 3 weigh equally, then the atomic weight of A is _____________ times of atomic weight of B.
questions.solution:
Let atomic weight of A = x

and atomic weight of B = y

$$\therefore$$ Molar mass of A₂B = 2x + y

and molar mass of AB 3 = x + 3y

Now, weight of 0.15 moles of A₂B = (2x + y) 0.15

and weight of 0.15 moles of AB 3 = (x + 3y) 0.15

Given, weight of 0.15 moles of A₂B and AB 3 are equal.

$$\therefore$$ (2x + y)0.15 = (x + 3y)0.15

$$\Rightarrow$$ x = 2y

$$ \Rightarrow {x \over y} = 2$$

$$\therefore$$ Atomic weight of A is 2 times of atomic weight of B.

questions.text: 1 L aqueous solution of H 2 SO 4 contains 0.02 m mol H 2 SO 4 . 50% of this solution is diluted with deionized water to give 1 L solution (A). In solution (A), 0.01 m mol of H 2 SO 4 are added. Total m mols of H 2 SO 4 in the final solution is ___________ $$\times$$ 10 3 m mols.
questions.solution:
Half of the original solution contains $\dfrac{0.02}{2} = 0.01\ \text{mmol}$ of $\ce{H2SO4}$; diluting it to $1\ \text{L}$ does not change this amount, so solution (A) contains $0.01\ \text{mmol}$.

After $0.01\ \text{mmol}$ more is added, the final solution contains $0.01 + 0.01 = 0.02\ \text{mmol}$ of $\ce{H2SO4}$.

In the required form, $0.02\ \text{mmol} = 2 \times 10^{-5} \times 10^{3}\ \text{mmol}$, so the blank is $2 \times 10^{-5}$, which is 0 to the nearest integer.

Hence, the answer is 0.

questions.text: Amongst the following statements, that which was not proposed by Dalton was :

options.text:
Chemical reactions involve reorganization of atoms. These are neither created nor destroyed in
a chemical reaction.

When gases combine or are produced in a chemical reaction they do so in a simple ratio by
volume provided all gases are at the same T & P.
All the atoms of a given element have identical properties including identical mass. Atoms of different elements differ in mass.

questions.solution:
Dalton's atomic theory states that matter consists of indivisible atoms; all atoms of a given element have identical properties including identical mass, while atoms of different elements differ in mass; compounds form when atoms of different elements combine in a fixed ratio; and chemical reactions involve only reorganisation of atoms, which are neither created nor destroyed.

Statements (A), (
B) and (
D) are therefore postulates of Dalton's theory.

Statement (C), that gases combine or are produced in a simple ratio by volume at the same temperature and pressure, is Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes, which Dalton did not propose.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: 56.0 L of nitrogen gas is mixed with excess hydrogen gas and it is found that 20 L of ammonia gas is produced. The volume of unused nitrogen gas is found to be _________ L.

$$

Volume of $$\mathrm{N}_{2}$$ left $$=56-10$$

$$
=46 \mathrm{~L}
$$

questions.text: The moles of methane required to produce 81 g of water after complete combustion is _____________ $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$2 mol. [nearest integer]
A protein 'A' contains 0.30% of glycine (molecular weight 75). The minimum molar mass of the protein 'A' is __________ $$\times$$ 10 3 g mol $$-$$1 [nearest integer]
questions.solution:
The molar mass of protein A is least when each molecule contains the smallest possible amount of glycine, that is, exactly one glycine unit (molar mass $75\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$) per molecule.

Glycine then makes up $0.30\%$ of the minimum molar mass $M_{\text{min}}$:

$$\dfrac{0.30}{100} \times M_{\text{min}} = 75$$

$$M_{\text{min}} = \dfrac{75 \times 100}{0.30} = 25000\ \text{g mol}^{-1} = 25 \times 10^{3}\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$$

Hence, the answer is 25.

questions.text: With increase of temperature, which of these changes?
questions.solution:
Molarity =
Number of moles of solute

Volume of solution (in L)

Molality =
Number of moles of solute

Mass of solvent (in kg)

Mole fraction =
Number of moles of component

Total number of moles of all components

Weight fraction of solute =
Weight of a component

Total weight of solution

$$ \times $$ 100

KEY Concept : Those units which are volume related will be affected by the change in temperature.

The definition of molarity is - Number of moles of solute present in one litre of solution. From definition you can see it depends on volume which increases with increasing temperature
and decreases with decreasing temperature.

All the other three options (Molality, Mole fraction, Weight fraction of solute) are mass related units and temperature has no effect on mass.

questions.text: 25 ml of a solution of barium hydroxide on titration with a 0.1 molar solution of hydrochloric acid gave a titre value of 35 ml. The molarity of barium hydroxide solution was

questions.text: To neutralise completely 20 mL of 0.1 M aqueous solution of phosphorous acid (H 3 PO 3 ), the volume of 0.1 M aqueous KOH solution required is

questions.text: Two solutions of a substance (non electrolyte) are mixed in the following manner. 480 ml of 1.5 M first solution + 520 ml of 1.2 M second solution. What is the molarity of the final mixture?
questions.solution:
Short Cut Method : Molarity, Normality, Average Atomic Mass, Average Molar Mass, Average Density, Average Vapour Pressure all of those values will be between the solutions which are going to be mixed.

Here molarity of first solution is 1.2 and molarity of second solution is 1.5.

So the molarity of the mixture will always be more than 1.2 and less than 1.5. Remember the molarity of mixture can't be either 1.2 or 1.5.

So from the option you an see only 1.344 M can be the right answer.

Normal method :

The formula for molarity of mixture of two substance is = $${{{M_1}{V_1} + {M_2}{V_2}} \over {{V_1} + {V_2}}}$$

Here $${M_1} = 1.5$$, $${V_1} = 480$$, $${M_2} = 1.2$$, $${V_2} = 520$$

$$\therefore$$ Molarity of mixture = $${{1.5 \times 480 + 1.2 \times 520} \over {480 + 520}}$$

= $${{720 + 624} \over {1000}}$$

= $${{1344} \over {1000}}$$

= 1.344

questions.text: Density of a 2.05M solution of acetic acid in water is 1.02 g/mL. The molality of the solution is
questions.solution:
2.05M solution of acetic acid in water means in 1 litre solution 2.05 moles of CH 3 COOH present.

Density of solution = 1.02 g/ml (Given)

Assume the volume of solution = 1 litre = 1000 ml

$$\therefore$$ Mass of solution = 1000 $$ \times $$ 1.02 = 1020 gm

Molar mass of CH 3 COOH = 60

So Mass of CH 3 COOH (m solute ) = 2.05 $$ \times $$ 60 = 123

$$\therefore$$ Mass of solvent (m solvent ) = 1020 - 123 = 897 gm = 0.897 kg

Formula of molality (m) = $${{no\,of\,moles\,of\,solute} \over {weight\,of\,solvent\,in\,kg}}$$

$$\therefore$$ m = $${{2.05} \over {0.897}}$$ = 2.28

Using Formula :

Molality (m) = $${{1000 \times M} \over {1000 \times d - M \times {M_{solute}}}}$$

Here M = molarity, M solute = molecular mass of solute, d = density of solution

$$\therefore$$ m = $${{1000 \times 2.05} \over {1000 \times 1.02 - 2.05 \times 60}}$$ = 2.28

questions.text: The density (in g mL -1 ) of a 3.60 M sulphuric acid solution that is 29% H 2 SO 4 (molar mass = 98 g mol -1 ) by mass will be
questions.solution:

M = $${{10 \times \% w/w \times d} \over {{M_{solute}}}}$$

Here M = 3.6, % w/w = 29, d = density, M solute = 98

$$\therefore$$ 3.6 = $${{10 \times 29 \times d} \over {98}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow d = 1.22$$

questions.text:
A 5.2 molal aqueous solution of methyl alcohol, CH 3 OH, is supplied. What is the mole fraction of methyl
alcohol in the solution ?
questions.solution:
The formula between Mole fraction and Molality is
$$m = {{{X_{solute}}} \over {{X_{solvent}}}} \times {{1000} \over {{M_{solvent}}}}$$

$$m$$ = molality, X solute = Mole fraction of solute, X solvent = Mole fraction of solvent, M solvent = Molar mass of solvent

Here solute is methyl alcohol(CH 3 OH) and solvent is water(H₂O). Here water is solvent because question says solution is aqueous.

Assume mole fraction of methyl alcohol = X

So mole fraction of water = 1 - X

and given molality (m) = 5.2

M solvent = 18 (as molar mass of H₂O = 18)

$$\therefore$$ 5.2 = $$ {X \over {1 - X}} \times {{1000} \over {18}}$$

by solving this we get,

X = 0.086

questions.text: An aqueous solution of oxalic acid dihydrate contains its $$6.3\ \mathrm{g}$$ in $$250\ \mathrm{mL}$$. The volume of $$0.1\ \mathrm{N}\ \mathrm{NaOH}$$ required to completely neutralize $$10\ \mathrm{mL}$$ of this solution
questions.solution:
Oxalic acid dihydrate, $\mathrm{(COOH)_2\cdot 2H_2O}$, has molar mass $126\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$ and is dibasic, so its equivalent mass is $63\ \mathrm{g}$.

Equivalents in the solution $= \dfrac{6.3}{63} = 0.1$, so its normality $= \dfrac{0.1}{0.250} = 0.4\ \mathrm{N}$.

At neutralization, $N_1V_1 = N_2V_2$: $0.4 \times 10 = 0.1 \times V$.

So $V = 40\ \mathrm{mL}$ of $\mathrm{NaOH}$ is required.

questions.text: The ppm level of $$\mathrm{F^-}$$ in a $$500\ \mathrm{g}$$ sample of a tooth paste containing $$0.2\ \mathrm{g}\ \mathrm{F^-}$$ is
questions.solution:
ppm by mass $= \dfrac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{mass of sample}} \times 10^6$.

$= \dfrac{0.2}{500} \times 10^6 = 400$.

So the fluoride level is $400\ \mathrm{ppm}$.

questions.text: The concentrated sulphuric acid that is peddled commercially is $$95\%\ \mathrm{H_2SO_4}$$ by weight. If the density of this commercial acid is $$1.834\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$$, the molarity of this solution is
questions.solution:
Take $100\ \mathrm{g}$ of the acid: it contains $95\ \mathrm{g}$ of $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$.

Moles of $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ $= \dfrac{95}{98} = 0.969\ \mathrm{mol}$.

Volume of this solution $= \dfrac{100}{1.834} = 54.5\ \mathrm{cm^3} = 0.0545\ \mathrm{L}$.

Molarity $= \dfrac{0.969}{0.0545} = 17.8\ \mathrm{M}$.

Check with $M = \dfrac{10\times d\times w}{M_\mathrm{solute}} = \dfrac{10\times1.834\times95}{98} = 17.8$.

So the molarity of the acid is $17.8\ \mathrm{M}$.

questions.text:
The density of a solution prepared by dissolving 120 g of urea (mol. Mass = 60 u ) in 1000g of water is
1.15 g/mL. The molarity of this solution is :
questions.solution:
We know molarity (M) = $${{no\,of\,moles\,of\,solute} \over {volume\,of\,solution\,in\,litre}}$$

Moles of solute = $${{120} \over {60}}$$ = 2

Mass of solution = 1000 + 120 = 1120 gm

Density of solution = 1.15 g/mL

$$\therefore$$ volume of solution = $${{1120} \over {1.15}}$$ = 973.9 mL = $${{973.9} \over {1000}}$$ litre = 0.9739 litre

$$\therefore$$ M = $${2 \over {0.9739}}$$ = 2.05

questions.text: The density of 3M solution of sodium chloride is 1.252 g mL$$^{-1}$$. The molality of the solution will be : (molar mass, NaCl = 58.5 g mol$$^{-1}$$)
questions.solution:
Take $1\ \mathrm{L}$ of solution: mass $= 1000 \times 1.252 = 1252\ \mathrm{g}$.

Mass of $\mathrm{NaCl} = 3 \times 58.5 = 175.5\ \mathrm{g}$.

Mass of water $= 1252 - 175.5 = 1076.5\ \mathrm{g} = 1.0765\ \mathrm{kg}$.

Molality $= \dfrac{3}{1.0765} \approx 2.79\ \mathrm{mol\,kg^{-1}}$.

The molality of the solution is $2.79\ \mathrm{m}$.

questions.text: The molarity of a solution obtained by mixing 750 mL of 0.5 (M) HCl with 250 mL of 2(M) HCl will be:
Dissolving 120 g of a compound of (mol. wt. 60) in 1000 g of water gave a solution of density 1.12 g/mL. The molarity of the solution is :

Mass of solution $= 120 + 1000 = 1120\ \mathrm{g}$

Volume of solution $= \dfrac{1120}{1.12} = 1000\ \mathrm{mL} = 1\ \mathrm{L}$

Moles of solute $= \dfrac{120}{60} = 2\ \mathrm{mol}$

Molarity $= \dfrac{2\ \mathrm{mol}}{1\ \mathrm{L}} = 2.00\ \mathrm{M}$

So the molarity of the solution is $2.00\ \mathrm{M}$.

$${{5V} \over {20}} = 79 \Rightarrow V = 316$$ mL

questions.text: The ratio of mass percent of C and H of an organic compound (C X H Y O Z ) is 6 : 1. If one molecule of the above compound (C X H Y O Z ) contains half as much oxygen as required to burn one molecule of compound C X H Y completely to CO 2 and H₂O. The empirical formula of compound C X H Y O Z is
questions.solution:
$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ The ratio of no of atoms of C and H in one molecule of C x H y O z = 1 : 2

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ y = 2x

In one molecule of C x H y O z compound contain z atoms of oxygen.

According to the question, no of atoms of oxygen required to burn C x H y completely should be twice of z atoms of oxygen.

C x H y + (x + $${y \over 4}$$) O 2 $$ \to $$ xCO 2 + $${y \over 2}$$ H₂O

No. of O 2 molecules required = (x + $${y \over 4}$$)

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ No. of O atoms required = 2 (x + $${y \over 4}$$)

According to question,

$$2\left( {x + {y \over 4}} \right) = 2z$$

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,\,2\left( {x + {{2x} \over 4}} \right) = 2z\,\,\,$$ [ Putting y = 2x ]

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,\,\,{{3x} \over 2} = z$$

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ x : y : z

= x : 2x : $${{3x} \over 2}$$

= 2 : 4 : 3

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ Empirical formula = C₂H₄ O 3

We know,

molality(m) = $${{{x_{solute}}} \over {{x_{solvent}}}} \times {{1000} \over {molar\,weight\,of\,solvent}}$$

Here solvent is H₂O

x solvent = 0.8

$$ \therefore $$ x solute = 0.2

$$ \therefore $$ Molality = $${{0.2} \over {0.8}} \times {{1000} \over {18}}$$ = 13.88

     =  11.11

questions.text: 25 ml of the given HCl solution requires 30 mL of 0.1 M sodium carbonate solution. What is the volume of this HCl solution required to titrate 30 mL of 0.2 M aqueous NaOH solutions ?
questions.solution:
Standardisation: $\ce{Na2CO3 + 2HCl -> 2NaCl + H2O + CO2}$, so 1 mol of $\ce{Na2CO3}$ reacts with 2 mol of HCl.

Moles of $\ce{Na2CO3} = 0.1 \times 30 = 3$ mmol, so HCl present in 25 mL $= 2 \times 3 = 6$ mmol.

$$M_{\ce{HCl}} = \dfrac{6\ \text{mmol}}{25\ \text{mL}} = 0.24\ \text{M}$$

With NaOH: $\ce{HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O}$ (1 : 1). Moles of NaOH $= 0.2 \times 30 = 6$ mmol.

$$V_{\ce{HCl}} = \dfrac{6\ \text{mmol}}{0.24\ \text{M}} = 25\ \text{mL}$$

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
A solution of two components containing
n 1 moles of the 1 st component and n 2 moles of
the 2 nd component is prepared. M 1 and M 2 are
the molecular weights of component 1 and 2
respectively. If d is the density of the solution
in g mL –1 , C 2 is the molarity and x 2 is the mole
fraction of the 2 nd component, then C 2 can be
expressed as :
questions.solution:
Mass of the solution $= n_1M_1 + n_2M_2$ g, so its volume $= \dfrac{n_1M_1 + n_2M_2}{d}$ mL.

Molarity of component 2:

$$C_2 = \dfrac{n_2 \times 1000}{V(\text{mL})} = \dfrac{1000\,d\,n_2}{n_1M_1 + n_2M_2}$$

Dividing numerator and denominator by $(n_1 + n_2)$, with $x_2 = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1 + n_2}$ and $\dfrac{n_1}{n_1 + n_2} = 1 - x_2$:

$$C_2 = \dfrac{1000\,d\,x_2}{(1 - x_2)M_1 + x_2M_2} = \dfrac{1000\,d\,x_2}{M_1 + x_2(M_2 - M_1)}$$

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
If 80 g of copper sulphate CuSO 4 . 5H 2 O is dissolved in deionised water to make 5L of solution. The concentration of the copper sulphate solution is x $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$3 mol L $$-$$1 . The value of x is _____________.

questions.solution:
Given, mass of CuSO 4 . 5H 2 O = 80 g

The concentration of copper sulphate solution is x $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$3 mol/L.

= 5 $$\times$$ 18 = 249.54 g/mol

Molarity = $${{0.3205} \over 5}$$ = 64.11 $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$3 mol/L

Hence, answer is 64.

questions.text: If m and e are the mass and charge of the revolving electron in the orbit of radius r for hydrogen atom, the total energy of the revolving electron will be :
questions.solution:
In CGS units the electrostatic attraction supplies the centripetal force: $\dfrac{mv^2}{r} = \dfrac{e^2}{r^2}$, so $mv^2 = \dfrac{e^2}{r}$.

Kinetic energy: $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{e^2}{2r}$.

Potential energy: $U = -\dfrac{e^2}{r}$.

Total energy: $E = K + U = \dfrac{e^2}{2r} - \dfrac{e^2}{r} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{e^2}{r}$.

So the total energy of the revolving electron is $-\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{e^2}{r}$.

First excited state ($n = 2$): $E_2 = -13.6 \times \dfrac{9}{4} = -30.6\ \mathrm{eV}$

So the energy of the electron in the (first) excited state of $\mathrm{Li^{2+}}$ is $-30.6\ \mathrm{eV}$.

questions.text:
According to Bohr's atomic theory :

(
A) Kinetic energy of electron is $$ \propto {{{Z^2}} \over {{n^2}}}$$.

(
B) The product of velocity (v) of electron and principal quantum number (n), $$'vn' \propto {Z^2}$$.

(
C) Frequency of revolution of electron in an orbit is $$ \propto {{{Z^3}} \over {{n^3}}}$$.

(
D) Coulombic force of attraction on the electron is $$ \propto {{{Z^3}} \over {{n^4}}}$$.

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
questions.solution:
In Bohr's model for a hydrogen-like species of atomic number $Z$, $r_n \propto \dfrac{n^2}{Z}$ and $v_n \propto \dfrac{Z}{n}$.

(
A) $\text{KE} = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 \propto \dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}$, so (
A) is correct.

(
B) $v \times n \propto \dfrac{Z}{n} \times n = Z$, not $Z^2$, so (
B) is incorrect.

(
C) Frequency of revolution:

$$f = \dfrac{v}{2\pi r} \propto \dfrac{Z/n}{n^2/Z} = \dfrac{Z^2}{n^3}$$

so (
C) is incorrect.

(
D) The nucleus carries charge $Ze$, so the Coulombic force on the electron is

$$F = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{(Ze)(e)}{r^2} \propto \dfrac{Z}{r^2} \propto Z \times \dfrac{Z^2}{n^4} = \dfrac{Z^3}{n^4}$$

so (
D) is correct.

Only (
A) and (
D) are correct.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

(h = 6.626 $$ \times $$ 10 $$-$$34 Js, N A = 6.022 $$ \times $$ 10 23 mol $$-$$1 )
questions.solution:
Energy needed to ionise one atom: $E=\dfrac{495.5\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}}{6.022\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}}=8.228\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$

The lowest frequency is the one whose photon energy just equals this: $h\nu=E$

$\nu=\dfrac{8.228\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}}{6.626\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}}=1.24\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$

Check: $E=\dfrac{8.228\times10^{-19}}{1.602\times10^{-19}}=5.14\ \mathrm{eV}$, the known ionisation energy of sodium.

So the lowest frequency is $1.24\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

questions.text: If $$\lambda $$ 0 and $$\lambda $$ be the threshold wavelength and wavelength of incident light, the velocity of photoelectron ejected from the metal surface is :
questions.solution:
By Einstein's photoelectric equation, $\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = h\nu - h\nu_0 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_0}$.

So $\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = hc\left(\dfrac{\lambda_0 - \lambda}{\lambda\lambda_0}\right)$.

Hence $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2hc}{m}\left(\dfrac{\lambda_0 - \lambda}{\lambda\lambda_0}\right)}$.

Check: at $\lambda = \lambda_0$ (threshold), $v = 0$, as expected.

So the velocity of the ejected electron is $\sqrt{\dfrac{2hc}{m}\left(\dfrac{\lambda_0 - \lambda}{\lambda\lambda_0}\right)}$.

questions.text: Ejection of the photoelectron from metal in the photoelectric experiment can be stopped by applying 0.5 V when the radiation of 250 nm is used. The work function of the metal is :

If p is the momentum of the fastest electron
ejected from a metal surface after the irradiation
of light having wavelength $$\lambda $$, then for 1.5 p
momentum of the photoelectron, the
wavelength of the light should be:
(Assume kinetic energy of ejected
photoelectron to be very high in comparison
to work function)
questions.solution:
From photoelectric effect,

E = $$\phi $$ + KE

$${{hc} \over \lambda } = \phi + {{{p^2}} \over {2m}}$$ ................ (1)

Now when momentum = 1.5p then let wavelength = $${{\lambda _1}}$$

$$ \therefore $$ $${{hc} \over {{\lambda _1}}} = \phi + {{{{\left( {1.5p} \right)}^2}} \over {2m}}$$ ........... (2)

Given,

kinetic energy(KE) of ejected
photoelectron to be very high in comparison
to work function($$\phi $$).

$$ \therefore $$ We can neglect work function($$\phi $$).

$$ \therefore $$ Equation (1) and (2) becomes,

$${{hc} \over \lambda } = {{{p^2}} \over {2m}}$$ ................ (1)

$${{hc} \over {{\lambda _1}}} = {{{{\left( {1.5p} \right)}^2}} \over {2m}}$$ ........... (2)

Dividing (1) by (2) we get,

$${{{\lambda _1}} \over \lambda } = {{{p^2}} \over {{{\left( {1.5p} \right)}^2}}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $${{{\lambda _1}} \over \lambda } = {4 \over 9}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $${\lambda _1} = {4 \over 9}\lambda $$

questions.text: The de Broglie wavelength ($$\lambda $$) associated with a photoelectron varies with the frequency (v) of the incident radiation as, [v 0 is threshold frequency] :
questions.solution:
By photoelectric effect

KE = h$$\nu $$ - h$$\nu $$ o ....(1)

de broglie wavelength,

$$\lambda $$ = $${h \over {mv}}$$ = $${h \over {\sqrt {2m \times K.E} }}$$ ...(2)

Using equation (1) and (2), we get

$$\lambda $$ = $${h \over {\sqrt {2m \times \left( {h\nu - h{\nu _0}} \right)} }}$$

$$ \therefore $$ $$\lambda \,\propto \,{1 \over {{{\left( {v - {v_0}} \right)}^{{1 \over 2}}}}}$$

questions.text:
When light of wavelength 248 nm falls on a metal of threshold energy 3.0 eV, the de-Broglie wavelength of emitted electrons is _______$$\mathop A\limits^o $$. (Round off to the Nearest Integer).

[ Use : $$\sqrt 3 $$ = 1.73, h = 6.63 $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$34 Js

m e = 9.1 $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$31 kg; c = 3.0 $$\times$$ 10 8 ms $$-$$1 ; 1eV = 1.6 $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$19 J]
questions.solution:
Energy of the incident photon:

$$E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.0 \times 10^{8}}{248 \times 10^{-9}} = 8.0 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\ (= 5.0\ \text{eV})$$

Threshold energy $W_0 = 3.0\ \text{eV} = 3.0 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} = 4.8 \times 10^{-19}$ J, so the kinetic energy of the emitted electrons is

$$K = E - W_0 = 8.0 \times 10^{-19} - 4.8 \times 10^{-19} = 3.2 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$$

Momentum of the electron:

$$p = \sqrt{2m_eK} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 3.2 \times 10^{-19}} = 7.63 \times 10^{-25}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$$

de Broglie wavelength:

$$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{7.63 \times 10^{-25}} = 8.7 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m} = 8.7\ \text{Å} \approx 9\ \text{Å}$$

Hence, the answer is 9.

questions.text:

(
A) Li

(
B) Na

(
C) Rb

(
D) Cs
questions.solution:
A photoelectric-cell electrode must emit electrons readily when light falls on it, which needs a very low ionisation enthalpy.

Caesium has the lowest ionisation enthalpy among the alkali metals ($376\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) and is used, along with potassium, as the electrode in photoelectric cells; Li, Na and Rb are not used.

Among Li, Na, Rb and Cs, only Cs qualifies, so the number of such metals is 1.

Hence, the answer is 1.

= 180600 J mol $$-$$1 = 180.6 kJ mol $$-$$1 $$ \simeq $$ 181 kJ mol $$-$$1

questions.text:
If the wavelength for an electron emitted from $$\mathrm{H}$$-atom is $$3.3 \times 10^{-10} \mathrm{~m}$$, then energy absorbed by the electron in its ground state compared to minimum energy required for its escape from the atom, is _________ times. (Nearest integer)

$$\left[\right.$$ Given $$: \mathrm{h}=6.626 \times 10^{-34} \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~s}$$ ]

Mass of electron $$=9.1 \times 10^{-31} \mathrm{~kg}$$
questions.solution:
Momentum of the emitted electron from the de Broglie relation:

$$p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}}{3.3 \times 10^{-10}} = 2.01 \times 10^{-24}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$$

Its kinetic energy:

$$KE = \dfrac{p^2}{2m} = \dfrac{(2.01 \times 10^{-24})^2}{2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31}} = 2.22 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{J}$$

The minimum energy for escape from the ground state is the ionization energy of H, $13.6\ \text{eV} = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{J}$.

Energy absorbed $= 2.18 \times 10^{-18} + 2.22 \times 10^{-18} = 4.40 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{J}$.

$$\dfrac{4.40 \times 10^{-18}}{2.18 \times 10^{-18}} = 2.02 \approx 2$$

Hence, the answer is 2.

questions.text: If the kinetic energy of an electron is increased four times, the wavelength of the de-Broglie wave associated with it would become
questions.solution:
$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}$ and $p = \sqrt{2mK}$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$.

Thus $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{K}}$ for a given particle.

With $K' = 4K$: $\dfrac{\lambda'}{\lambda} = \sqrt{\dfrac{K}{4K}} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.

The wavelength becomes half of its original value.

questions.text: If the radius of first orbit of H atom is $$a_0$$, the de Broglie wavelength of an electron in the third orbit is
questions.solution:
In Bohr's model $r_n = n^2 a_0$, so $r_3 = 9a_0$.

A stationary orbit holds a whole number of de Broglie waves: $2\pi r_n = n\lambda$.

So $\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi r_3}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi \times 9a_0}{3}$.

Hence the de Broglie wavelength in the third orbit is $6\pi a_0$.

questions.text: The de Broglie wavelength of a car of mass 1000 kg and velocity 36 km/hr is :

$\lambda = 6.626\times10^{-38}\ \mathrm{m}$.

questions.text: The de-Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass 6.63 g moving with a velocity of 100 ms $$-$$1 is :
questions.solution:
de Broglie wavelength: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv}$.

Here $m = 6.63\ \mathrm{g} = 6.63 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $v = 100\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

$\lambda = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{6.63 \times 10^{-3} \times 100} = 10^{-33}\ \mathrm{m}$.

So the de Broglie wavelength is $10^{-33}\ \mathrm{m}$.

questions.text: At temperature T, the average kinetic energy of any particle is $${3 \over 2}$$ KT. The de Broglie wavelength follows the order :

options.text: Thermal proton > Visible photon > Thermal electron
Thermal electron > Thermal proton > Visible photon
Visible photon > Thermal electron > Thermal neutron
Visible photon > Thermal neutron > Thermal electron

questions.solution:
For a particle with $KE = \dfrac{3}{2}kT$: $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3mkT}}$, so at a given $T$, $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}}$.

Thermal electron at $300$ K: $\lambda = \dfrac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{\sqrt{3(9.1\times10^{-31})(4.14\times10^{-21})}} \approx 6.2\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m} = 6.2\ \mathrm{nm}$.

A neutron (or proton) is about $1840$ times heavier, so $\lambda \approx \dfrac{6.2}{\sqrt{1840}} \approx 0.15\ \mathrm{nm}$.

A visible photon has $\lambda \approx 400$ to $700\ \mathrm{nm}$, much larger than both.

So the order is visible photon $\gt$ thermal electron $\gt$ thermal neutron.

questions.text:
A stream of electrons from a heated filament was passed between two charged plates kept at a potential
difference V esu. If e and m are charge and mass of an electron, respectively, then the value of h / $$\lambda $$ (where
$$\lambda $$ is wavelength associated with electron wave) is given by :
questions.solution:
We know, Kinetic Energy (K E ) = $${1 \over 2}m{v^2}$$

$$\therefore$$ mv 2 = 2K E

$$ \Rightarrow $$ m 2 v 2 = 2mK E

$$ \Rightarrow $$ mv = $$\sqrt {2m{K_E}} $$

For an electron of charge 'e' which passes through 'V' volt, kinetic energy of electron will be

K E = eV

$$\therefore$$ mv = $$\sqrt {2meV} $$

We know de-Broglie wavelength for an electron$$\left( \lambda \right)$$ = $${h \over p} = {h \over {mv}}$$

$$\therefore$$ $${h \over \lambda }$$ = mv = $$\sqrt {2meV} $$

questions.text:
The wavelength of electrons accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 40 kV is x $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$12 m. The value of x is ___________. (Nearest integer)

Given : Mass of electron = 9.1 $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$31 kg

Charge on an electron = 1.6 $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$19 C

Wavelength of electron is given by

Here q = charge on electron, V = potential difference

$$\lambda = {{6.63 \times {{10}^{ - 34}}} \over {\sqrt {2 \times 9.1 \times {{10}^{ - 31}} \times 1.6 \times {{10}^{ - 19}} \times 40 \times {{10}^3}} }}$$

$$ = {{6.63 \times {{10}^{ - 34}}} \over {\sqrt {1164.8 \times {{10}^{ - 47}}} }} = 6.144 \times {10^{ - 12}} \approx 6 \times {10^{ - 12}}$$

questions.text:
A proton and a Li 3+ nucleus are accelerated by the same potential. If $$\lambda _{Li}$$ and $$\lambda _p$$ denote the
de Broglie wavelengths of Li 3+ and proton respectively, then the value of
$${{{\lambda _{Li}}} \over {{\lambda _p}}}$$ is x $$ \times $$ 10 -1 .

The value of x is ______. (Rounded off to the nearest integer)

[Mass of Li 3+ = 8.3 mass of proton]
questions.solution:
A particle of charge $q$ accelerated through a potential $V$ gains $\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = qV$, so

$$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$$

For the same $V$, $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{mq}}$. The proton has charge $e$; the $\ce{Li^3+}$ nucleus has charge $3e$ and mass $m_{\text{Li}} = 8.3\,m_p$.

$$\dfrac{\lambda_{\text{Li}}}{\lambda_p} = \sqrt{\dfrac{m_p \times e}{8.3\,m_p \times 3e}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{24.9}} = 0.2004 \approx 2 \times 10^{-1}$$

Hence, the answer is 2.

questions.text: When the kinetic energy of an electron is increased nine times, the wavelength of the de-Broglie wave associated with it would become :
questions.solution:
$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}$ and $p = \sqrt{2mK}$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$, i.e. $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{K}}$.

With $K' = 9K$: $\dfrac{\lambda'}{\lambda} = \sqrt{\dfrac{K}{9K}} = \dfrac{1}{3}$.

The de Broglie wavelength becomes one-third of its original value.

questions.text: Uncertainty in position of a minute particle of mass 25 g in space is 10 -5 m. What is the uncertainty in its velocity (in ms -1 ) (h = 6.6 $$\times$$ 10 -34 Js)
questions.solution:
According to Heisenberg's Uncertainty Principle
$$\Delta x . \Delta p \ge { h \over {4\pi}}$$
Where $$\Delta x $$ is uncertainty in position and $$\Delta p $$ is uncertainty in momentum and as in momentum m (mass of object) is always same so we can say
$$\Delta x . m. \Delta v \ge { h \over {4\pi}}$$
Mass of the particle (m) = 25 g = 0.025 kg

Position of the particle ($$\Delta x$$) = 10 -5 m

$$\Delta x . \Delta p $$ = $${ h \over {4\pi}}$$

$$\Delta x . m . \Delta v $$ = $${ h \over {4\pi}}$$

$$\Delta v$$ = $${h \over {4 \times \Delta x \times m \times \pi }}$$

$$\Delta v$$ = $${{6.6 \times {{10}^{ - 34}}} \over {4 \times {{10}^{ - 5}} \times 0.025 \times 3.14}}$$

$$\Delta v$$ = 2.1 $$\times$$ 10 -28

questions.text: Uncertainty in the position of an electron (mass = 9.1 $$\times$$ 10 -31 kg) moving with a velocity 300 ms -1 , accurate up to 0.001% will be (h = 6.63 $$\times$$ 10 -34 Js)

$$ \therefore $$ 0.001 = $${{\Delta V} \over {300}} \times 100$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$\Delta $$V = 3 $$ \times $$ 10 -3

According to Heisenberg uncertainty principle,

$$\Delta x.m\Delta V \ge {h \over {4\pi }}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$\Delta x = {h \over {4\pi m\Delta V}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$\Delta x = {{6.63 \times {{10}^{ - 34}}} \over {4 \times 3.14 \times 9.1 \times {{10}^{ - 31}} \times 3 \times {{10}^{ - 3}}}}$$

             = 1.92 $$ \times $$ 10 -2 m

questions.text:
In an atom, an electron is moving with a speed of 600 m/s with an accuracy of 0.005%. Certainity

questions.text:
An accelerated electron has a speed of 5 $$\times$$ 10 6 ms $$-$$1 with an uncertainty of 0.02%. The uncertainty in finding its location while in motion is x $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$9 m. The value of x is ____________. (Nearest integer)

If the uncertainty in velocity and position of a minute particle in space are, 2.4 $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$26 (m s $$-$$1 ) and 10 $$-$$7 (m) respectively. The mass of the particle in g is ____________. (Nearest integer)

We know from Heisenberg uncertainty principle

questions.text: The limiting line in Balmer series will have a frequency of (Rydberg constant, $$R_\infty = 3.29\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{cycles/s}$$)
questions.solution:
For the Balmer series, $\nu = R_\infty\left(\dfrac{1}{2^2} - \dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)$ with $n = 3, 4, \ldots$

The limiting line (series limit) corresponds to $n \to \infty$.

$\nu = \dfrac{R_\infty}{4} = \dfrac{3.29\times10^{15}}{4}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} = 8.22\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$

Check: the Balmer limit lies near $365\ \mathrm{nm}$, and $\dfrac{3.0\times10^{8}}{365\times10^{-9}} \approx 8.2\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

So the limiting line has frequency $8.22\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

questions.text: The wave number of the first emission line in the Balmer series of H-Spectrum is : (R = Rydberg constant)
questions.solution:
Balmer lines end on $n_1 = 2$; the first line starts from $n_2 = 3$.

$\bar{\nu} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{2^2} - \dfrac{1}{3^2}\right) = R\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{9}\right)$.

$\bar{\nu} = \dfrac{9 - 4}{36}R = \dfrac{5}{36}R$.

The wave number of the first Balmer line is $\dfrac{5}{36}R$.

questions.text:
Energy of an electron is given by $$E = - 2.178 \times {10^{ - 18}}J\left( {{{{Z^2}} \over {{n^2}}}} \right)$$. Wavelength of light required to excite an

then $$\lambda = {{6.62 \times {{10}^{ - 34}} \times 3 \times {{10}^8}} \over {1.6335 \times {{10}^{ - 18}}}}$$

questions.text:
Excited hydrogen atom emits light in the ultraviolet region at 2.47 $$ \times $$ 10 15 Hz. With this frequency, the energy of a single photon is :

questions.text:
Based on the equation :

$$\Delta $$E = $$-$$ 2.0$$ \times $$10 $$-$$18 J $$\left( {{1 \over {n_2^2}} - {1 \over {n_1^2}}} \right)$$

the wavelength of the light that must be absorbed to excite hydrogen electron from level n = 1 to level n = 2 will be :

(h = 6.625 $$ \times $$ 10 $$-$$34 Js,    C = 3 $$ \times $$ 10 8 ms $$-$$1 )

For $n_1 = 1$ to $n_2 = 2$: $\Delta E = -2.0\times10^{-18}\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - 1\right) = 1.5\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J}$.

$\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E} = \dfrac{6.625\times10^{-34} \times 3\times10^{8}}{1.5\times10^{-18}}\ \mathrm{m}$.

$\lambda = \dfrac{19.875\times10^{-26}}{1.5\times10^{-18}} = 1.325\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$.

Check: $\lambda \approx 132.5\ \mathrm{nm}$, in the ultraviolet, as expected for the first Lyman transition.

So the wavelength is $1.325\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$.

questions.text:
The ratio of the shortest wavelength of two spectral series of hydrogen spectrum is found to be about 9. The

questions.text:
For any given series of spectral lines of atomic

questions.text:
For the Balmer series in the spectrum of H atom,

$$\overline \nu = {R_H}\left\{ {{1 \over {n_1^2}} - {1 \over {n_2^2}}} \right\}$$, the correct statements among (I) to (IV)
are :

(I) As wavelength decreases, the lines in the series converge

(II) The integer n 1 is equal to 2

(III) The line of longest wavelength corresponds to n 2 = 3

(IV) The ionization energy of hydrogen can be calculated from wave number of these lines
questions.solution:
In the Balmer series the electron falls to $n_1 = 2$ from $n_2 = 3, 4, 5, \ldots$, so (II) is correct.

The longest wavelength has the smallest wave number, from the smallest jump $n_2 = 3$: $\bar\nu = R_H\left(\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{9}\right) = \dfrac{5R_H}{36}$, so (III) is correct.

As $n_2$ increases, $\bar\nu$ approaches the limit $\dfrac{R_H}{4}$ and successive lines crowd together, so the lines converge as the wavelength decreases; (I) is correct.

The series limit $\dfrac{R_H}{4}$ corresponds to removing the electron from $n = 2$, not from the ground state $n = 1$ (which needs $R_H$), so the ionization energy of hydrogen does not follow from Balmer wave numbers; (IV) is incorrect.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: When the excited electron of a H atom from n = 5 drops to the ground state, the maximum number of emission lines observed are _____________.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathrm{n}_{2}=5 \\
&\mathrm{n}_{1}=1 \\
&\Rightarrow \frac{(5-1)(5-1+1)}{2}=10
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence maximum number of emission lines observed are $10 .$

questions.solution:
As there is no electric and magnetic field so ignore m to calculate the energy of orbital.

As here atom is multi-electron so ( n + l ) rule is applicable here. This rule says those orbitals which have more value of ( n + l ) will have more energy.

questions.text:
Consider the hypothetical situation where the
azimuthal quantum number,
$$l$$, takes values 0,
1, 2, ....., n + 1, where n is the principal
quantum number. Then, the element with
atomic number :
questions.solution:
With $l = 0, 1, \ldots, n+1$, the shell $n = 1$ has $1s$, $1p$ and $1d$ subshells (capacities 2, 6, 10), and $n = 2$ has $2s$, $2p$, $2d$ and $2f$.

Filling each shell completely before the next, in order of increasing $n$ and then $l$, gives the sequence $1s, 1p, 1d, 2s, 2p, \ldots$

$Z = 13$: $1s^2\,1p^6\,1d^5$; the valence $1d$ subshell is half-filled, so (
A) is true.

$Z = 9$ ($1s^2\,1p^6\,1d^1$) is not an alkali metal, $Z = 8$ ($1s^2\,1p^6$) does not complete the $n = 1$ shell, so it is not a noble gas, and $Z = 6$ ($1s^2\,1p^4$) has a $1p$, not a $2p$, valence subshell.

Filling by the $(n+l)$ rule would place $2s$ before $1d$ and make both (
B) and (
C) true, so only the shell-by-shell order gives a single correct option.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
Given below are the quantum numbers for 4 electrons.
A. $$\mathrm{n}=3,l=2, \mathrm{~m}_{l}=1, \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{s}}=+1 / 2$$
B. $$\mathrm{n}=4,l=1, \mathrm{~m}_{l}=0, \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{s}}=+1 / 2$$
C. $$\mathrm{n}=4,l=2, \mathrm{~m}_{l}=-2, \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{s}}=-1 / 2$$
D. $$\mathrm{n}=3,l=1, \mathrm{~m}_{l}=-1, \mathrm{~m}_{\mathrm{s}}=+1 / 2$$

The correct order of increasing energy is :
questions.solution:
The order of increasing energy of electrons in an atom can generally be determined using the principal quantum number ($n$) and the azimuthal quantum number ($l$). The energy can be compared using the rule: the higher the $(n + l)$ value, the higher the energy. If two electrons have the same $(n + l)$ value, the electron with the higher $n$ value has the higher energy.

Analyze each electron's quantum numbers:
A. $$n=3, \ l=2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad n+l = 3+2 = 5$$
B. $$n=4, \ l=1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad n+l = 4+1 = 5$$
C. $$n=4, \ l=2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad n+l = 4+2 = 6$$
D. $$n=3, \ l=1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad n+l = 3+1 = 4$$

Comparing the values of $(n + l)$ and the principal quantum number $n$:
D: $n+l = 4$, and $n=3$.

A and
B: $n+l = 5$, but A has $n=3$ while B has $n=4$. Therefore, A has a slightly lower energy than
B.
C: $n+l = 6$.

Thus, the correct order of increasing energy is:

$$ D < A < B < C $$

Therefore, Option B is correct.

Number of orbital in any subshell = 2$$l$$ + 1.

$$\therefore$$ For h subshell, number of orbitals = 2 $$\times$$ 5 + 1 = 11

questions.text: Which of the following sets of ions represents a collection of isoelectronic species?
Which one of the following constitutes a group of the isoelectronic species?

The following sets of quantum numbers represent four electrons in an atom. (i) $$n = 4, l = 1$$ (ii) $$n = 4, l = 0$$ (iii) $$n = 3, l = 2$$ (iv) $$n = 3, l = 1$$ The sequence representing increasing order of energy, is
questions.solution:
By the $(n+l)$ rule, a lower $(n+l)$ value means lower energy; for equal $(n+l)$, the orbital with lower $n$ has lower energy.

(i) $4p$: $n+l = 5$; (ii) $4s$: $n+l = 4$; (iii) $3d$: $n+l = 5$; (iv) $3p$: $n+l = 4$.

Of (iv) and (ii), $3p$ has the lower $n$, so $3p \lt 4s$.

Of (iii) and (i), $3d$ has the lower $n$, so $3d \lt 4p$.

Hence the increasing order of energy is (iv) $\lt$ (ii) $\lt$ (iii) $\lt$ (i).

questions.text: If the principal quantum number n = 6, the correct sequence of filling of electrons will be :
questions.solution:
By the $(n + l)$ rule, orbitals fill in increasing order of $(n + l)$; for equal $(n + l)$ the orbital with lower $n$ fills first.

For $n = 6$: $6s$ has $n + l = 6$; $4f$ has $4 + 3 = 7$; $5d$ has $5 + 2 = 7$; $6p$ has $6 + 1 = 7$.

Among the orbitals with $n + l = 7$, the order is $4f$ (lowest $n$), then $5d$, then $6p$.

So the sequence is $6s \to 4f \to 5d \to 6p$, i.e. $ns \to (n-2)f \to (n-1)d \to np$.

questions.text: Identify the process in which change in the oxidation state is five :
The oxidation states of nitrogen in NO, NO 2 , N₂O and NO$$_3^ - $$ are in the order of :
questions.solution:
To determine the oxidation states of nitrogen in each compound, we consider the overall charge of the compound and the known oxidation states of other elements involved, typically oxygen.

NO (Nitric Oxide) :

Oxygen generally has an oxidation state of $-2$.

Let the oxidation state of nitrogen in NO be $x$.

The equation: $x + (-2) = 0$.

Solving for $x$, we find $x = +2$.

NO$_2$ (Nitrogen Dioxide) :

Oxygen has an oxidation state of $-2$.

Let the oxidation state of nitrogen be $x$.

The equation: $x + 2(-2) = 0$.

Solving for $x$, we find $x = +4$.

N$_2$O (Dinitrogen Monoxide or Nitrous Oxide) :

Oxygen has an oxidation state of $-2$.

Let each nitrogen atom have an oxidation state of $x$.

The equation: $2x + (-2) = 0$.

Solving for $x$, we find $x = +1$.

NO$_3^-$ (Nitrate Ion) :

Oxygen has an oxidation state of $-2$.

The overall charge of the ion is $-1$.

Let the oxidation state of nitrogen be $x$.

The equation: $x + 3(-2) = -1$.

Solving for $x$, we find $x = +5$.

Therefore, the oxidation states of nitrogen are:

NO: $+2$

NO$_2$: $+4$

N$_2$O: $+1$

NO$_3^-$: $+5$

The order of oxidation states from highest to lowest is:

NO$_3^-$ ($+5$) > NO$_2$ ($+4$) > NO ($+2$) > N$_2$O ($+1$)

Thus, the correct option is:

Option D

NO$$_3^-$$ > NO$_2$ > NO > N$_2$O

questions.text: In basic medium $$Cr{O_4}^{2 - }$$ oxidises $${S_2}{O_3}^{2 - }$$ to form $$S{O_4}^{2 - }$$ and itself changes into $$Cr{(OH)_4}^ - $$. The volume of 0.154 M $$Cr{O_4}^{2 - }$$ required to react with 40 mL of 0.25 M $${S_2}{O_3}^{2 - }$$ is __________ mL. (Rounded off to the nearest integer)
questions.solution:
Cr goes from $+6$ in $\ce{CrO4^2-}$ to $+3$ in $\ce{Cr(OH)4-}$, gaining 3 electrons per ion.

S goes from $+2$ in $\ce{S2O3^2-}$ to $+6$ in $\ce{SO4^2-}$; with two S atoms per ion, each $\ce{S2O3^2-}$ loses 8 electrons.

Equating electrons gives the balanced equation

$$\ce{8CrO4^2- + 3S2O3^2- + 17H2O -> 8Cr(OH)4- + 6SO4^2- + 2OH-}$$

$n(\ce{S2O3^2-}) = 40 \times 0.25 = 10\ \text{mmol}$, so $n(\ce{CrO4^2-}) = \dfrac{8}{3} \times 10 = 26.67\ \text{mmol}$.

$$V = \dfrac{26.67\ \text{mmol}}{0.154\ \text{mmol mL}^{-1}} = 173.2\ \text{mL}$$

Hence, the answer is 173.

questions.text:

options.text: Both $$\mathrm{A}$$ and $$\mathrm{R}$$ are true and $$\mathrm{R}$$ is the correct explanation of $$\mathrm{A}$$
Both $$\mathrm{A}$$ and $$\mathrm{R}$$ are true but $$\mathrm{R}$$ is NOT the correct explanation of $$\mathrm{A}$$

questions.solution:
Assertion A is true: permanganate titrations are carried out in dilute $\ce{H2SO4}$, not in hydrochloric acid.

Reason R is true: acidified permanganate oxidises chloride ions to chlorine.

$$\ce{2KMnO4 + 16HCl -> 2KCl + 2MnCl2 + 8H2O + 5Cl2}$$

Part of the permanganate is then used up by HCl instead of by the substance being titrated, so the titre comes out too high; this side reaction is the reason HCl is avoided, so R correctly explains A.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.solution:
Oxidation state of $\mathrm{S}$: $+4$ in $\mathrm{H_2SO_3}$ and $+6$ in $\mathrm{HSO_4^-}$, so $\mathrm{H_2SO_3}$ is oxidised (loses $2$ electrons).

The species that is oxidised gives electrons to the other and so is the reducing agent; the species reduced is the oxidising agent.

So $\mathrm{H_2SO_3}$ is the reducing agent because it undergoes oxidation, and $\mathrm{Sn^{4+}}$ is the oxidising agent.

questions.text: In the reaction of oxalate with permanganate in acidic medium, the number of electrons involved in producing one molecule of CO 2 is :
questions.solution:
The balanced reaction of oxalate with permanganate in acidic medium is :

$$5 \, \text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} + 2 \, \text{MnO}_4^- + 16 \, \text{H}^+ \rightarrow 10 \, \text{CO}_2 + 2 \, \text{Mn}^{2+} + 8 \, \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

In this redox reaction, the oxalate ion $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ is oxidized to carbon dioxide $\text{CO}_2$, and the permanganate ion $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is reduced to manganese(II) ion $\text{Mn}^{2+}$.

The oxidation half-reaction, representing the change for the oxalate ion, is :

$$\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} \rightarrow 2 \, \text{CO}_2 + 2 \, e^-$$

From this half-reaction, it's clear that each oxalate ion produces two CO 2 molecules and releases two electrons in the process.

So, the number of electrons involved in producing one molecule of CO 2 is :

$$\frac{2 \, e^-}{2 \, \text{CO}_2} = 1 \, e^-/\text{CO}_2$$

Therefore, the correct answer is Option C: One electron is involved in the production of one molecule of CO 2 .

values of $$X, Y$$ and $$Z$$ respectively are
questions.solution:
Mn changes from $+7$ in $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ to $+2$: a gain of $5$ electrons per Mn.

C changes from $+3$ in $\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}$ to $+4$ in $\mathrm{CO_2}$: a loss of $2$ electrons per oxalate ion.

Equal electron transfer needs $2\,\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ for every $5\,\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}$, so $X = 2$ and $Y = 5$.

Oxygen balance: $8 + 20 = 20 + \dfrac{Z}{2}$, so $Z = 16$; charge check: $-2 - 10 + 16 = +4 = 2 \times (+2)$.

So $X, Y, Z = 2, 5, 16$.

questions.text: 50 mL of 0.5 M oxalic acid is needed to neutralize 25 mL of sodium hydroxide solution. The amount of NaOH in 50 mL of the given sodium hydroxide solution is -
questions.solution:
The reaction between sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and oxalic acid (H₂C₂ O 4 ) is as follows :

$$ \text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} $$

We can see that 1 mole of oxalic acid ($\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$) reacts with 2 moles of sodium hydroxide (NaOH).

Given that 50 mL of 0.5 M oxalic acid is needed to neutralize the sodium hydroxide, we can find the number of moles of oxalic acid that reacted :

$$ \text{Moles of H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4 = \text{Molarity} \times \text{Volume (L)} = 0.5 \, \text{mol/L} \times 0.05 \, \text{L} = 0.025 \, \text{mol} $$

Since 1 mole of $\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$ reacts with 2 moles of $\text{NaOH}$, the number of moles of $\text{NaOH}$ in 25 mL solution would be twice that of $\text{H}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$ :

$$ \text{Moles of NaOH} = 0.025 \, \text{mol} \times 2 = 0.05 \, \text{mol} $$

Now, to find the mass of NaOH, we multiply the number of moles by the molar mass of NaOH (40 g/mol) :

$$ \text{Mass of NaOH} = \text{Number of moles} \times \text{Molar mass} = 0.05 \, \text{mol} \times 40 \, \text{g/mol} = 2 \, \text{g} $$

However, the question asks for the amount of $\text{NaOH}$ in 50 mL of the given solution. Since we've found the amount in 25 mL, we just need to double our result to find the amount in 50 mL :

$$ 2 \, \text{g} \times 2 = 4 \, \text{g} $$

So, the correct answer is Option B : 4 g.

questions.text: What happens when an inert gas is added to an equilibrium keeping volume unchanged ?
questions.solution:
At constant volume, adding an inert gas raises the total pressure but does not change the number of moles or the volume available to any reacting species.

So the concentrations (and partial pressures) of all reactants and products stay the same.

Hence the reaction quotient $Q$ still equals $K$, and the equilibrium is not disturbed.

So the equilibrium remains unchanged.

questions.text:
Consider the following equilibrium

AgCl $$ \downarrow $$ + 2NH 3   $$\rightleftharpoons$$   [Ag(NH 3 ) 2 ] +  + Cl $$-$$

White precipitate of AgCl appears on adding which of the following ?
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{AgCl}$ reprecipitates only if the equilibrium shifts to the left, i.e. if free $\mathrm{NH_3}$ is removed.

$\mathrm{HNO_3}$ neutralises ammonia ($\mathrm{NH_3 + H^+ \to NH_4^+}$), so $[\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2}]^+$ breaks up and $\mathrm{Ag^+ + Cl^- \to AgCl}$ precipitates.

Adding $\mathrm{NH_3}$ shifts the equilibrium to the right and dissolves more $\mathrm{AgCl}$.

$\mathrm{NaCl}$ or $\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$ do not remove $\mathrm{NH_3}$, so the excess ammonia keeps $\mathrm{Ag^+}$ complexed and no precipitate forms.

So the white precipitate appears on adding aqueous $\mathrm{HNO_3}$.

questions.text: The increase of pressure on ice $$\rightleftharpoons$$ water system at constant temperature will lead to :

options.text: a decrease in the entropy of the system
a shift of the equilibrium in the forward direction
an increase in the Gibbs energy of the system

questions.solution:
For $\mathrm{H_2O(s) \rightleftharpoons H_2O(l)}$, ice occupies a larger volume than the same mass of liquid water.

By Le Chatelier's principle, an increase in pressure favours the side with the smaller volume, i.e. water.

So ice melts; melting increases the entropy of the system, so the entropy does not decrease.

So the increase in pressure shifts the equilibrium in the forward direction.

For $\ce{2SO2(g) + O2(g) <=> 2SO3(g)}$, $\Delta n_g = 2 - 3 = -1$, so an increase in pressure shifts the equilibrium forward: (
A) is correct.

An equilibrium constant depends only on temperature, and an inert gas added at constant volume leaves every partial pressure unchanged, so neither the equilibrium nor $K$ is affected: (
B) is correct.

The reaction is exothermic ($\Delta H < 0$), so $K$ decreases as the temperature rises: (
D) is correct.

A large $K$ only means that the equilibrium mixture is rich in $\ce{SO3}$; it says nothing about how fast equilibrium is reached. The reaction is very slow without a catalyst, so $\ce{V2O5}$ is used in the contact process to raise the rate, and a catalyst does not change $K$. Statement (
C) is incorrect.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
A vessel at 1000 K contains CO 2 with a pressure of 0.5 atm. Some of the CO 2 is converted into CO on
the addition of graphite. If the total pressure at equilibrium is 0.8 atm, the value of K is :
questions.solution:
To determine the equilibrium constant $ K $, consider the equilibrium reaction:

$ \text{CO}_2 + \text{C (graphite)} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{CO} $

Initially, the pressure of $\text{CO}_2$ is 0.5 atm, and there is no $\text{CO}$:

Initial Pressure: $\text{CO}_2 = 0.5 \text{ atm}, \quad \text{CO} = 0$

At equilibrium, assume that $ x $ atm of $\text{CO}_2$ is converted into $\text{CO}$:

Final Pressure: $\text{CO}_2 = 0.5 - x \text{ atm}, \quad \text{CO} = 2x \text{ atm}$

The total pressure at equilibrium is given as 0.8 atm:

$ 0.5 - x + 2x = 0.5 + x = 0.8 $

Solving for $ x $:

$ x = 0.8 - 0.5 = 0.3 \text{ atm} $

The equilibrium constant $ K_p $ is calculated as:

$ K_p = \frac{(P_{\text{CO}})^2}{P_{\text{CO}_2}} $

Substitute the equilibrium pressures:

$ K_p = \frac{(2x)^2}{0.5 - x} = \frac{(2 \times 0.3)^2}{0.5 - 0.3} = \frac{0.6^2}{0.2} $

$ K_p = \frac{0.36}{0.2} = 1.8 \text{ atm} $

questions.text: One mole of $$\mathrm{O_{2(g)}}$$ and two moles of $$\mathrm{SO_{2(g)}}$$ were heated in a closed vessel of one-litre capacity at $$1098\ \mathrm{K}$$. At equilibrium 1.6 moles of $$\mathrm{SO_{3(g)}}$$ were found. The equilibrium constant $$K_c$$ of the reaction would be
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{2SO_2(g) + O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2SO_3(g)}$

Forming 1.6 mol of $\mathrm{SO_3}$ uses 1.6 mol of $\mathrm{SO_2}$ and 0.8 mol of $\mathrm{O_2}$.

At equilibrium in 1 L: $[\mathrm{SO_2}] = 0.4$, $[\mathrm{O_2}] = 0.2$, $[\mathrm{SO_3}] = 1.6\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

$K_c = \dfrac{[\mathrm{SO_3}]^2}{[\mathrm{SO_2}]^2[\mathrm{O_2}]} = \dfrac{(1.6)^2}{(0.4)^2 \times 0.2} = \dfrac{2.56}{0.032} = 80$

Hence $K_c = 80$.

questions.text: The value of $$K_p$$ for the equilibrium reaction $$\mathrm{N_2O_4}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NO_2}(g)$$ is 2. The percentage dissociation of $$\mathrm{N_2O_4}(g)$$ at a pressure of $$0.5\ \mathrm{atm}$$ is
questions.solution:
Start with 1 mol $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$; at equilibrium there are $(1-\alpha)$ mol $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ and $2\alpha$ mol $\mathrm{NO_2}$, total $(1+\alpha)$ mol.

$K_p = \dfrac{(p_{\mathrm{NO_2}})^2}{p_{\mathrm{N_2O_4}}} = \dfrac{4\alpha^2 P}{1-\alpha^2}$.

$2 = \dfrac{4\alpha^2(0.5)}{1-\alpha^2} \Rightarrow 2 - 2\alpha^2 = 2\alpha^2 \Rightarrow \alpha^2 = 0.5$.

$\alpha = 0.707$; check: $\dfrac{4(0.5)(0.5)}{1-0.5} = 2$.

The percentage dissociation is about 71.

questions.text: $$8\ \mathrm{mol}$$ of $$\mathrm{AB_3}(g)$$ are introduced into a $$1.0\ \mathrm{dm^3}$$ vessel. If it dissociates as $$\mathrm{2AB_3}(g) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{A_2}(g) + \mathrm{3B_2}(g)$$. At equilibrium, $$2\ \mathrm{mol}$$ of $$\mathrm{A_2}$$ are found to be present. The equilibrium constant of this reaction is
questions.solution:
Initially $[\mathrm{AB_3}] = 8\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$.

Forming $2$ mol of $\mathrm{A_2}$ uses $4$ mol of $\mathrm{AB_3}$ and forms $6$ mol of $\mathrm{B_2}$.

At equilibrium in $1\ \mathrm{dm^3}$: $[\mathrm{AB_3}] = 4$, $[\mathrm{A_2}] = 2$, $[\mathrm{B_2}] = 6$.

$K_c = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A_2}][\mathrm{B_2}]^3}{[\mathrm{AB_3}]^2} = \dfrac{2 \times 6^3}{4^2} = \dfrac{432}{16}$.

So $K_c = 27$.

questions.text:
$$K_1, K_2$$ and $$K_3$$ are the equilibrium constants of the following reactions (I), (II) and (III) respectively:
(I) $$\mathrm{N_2 + 2O_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2}$$
(II) $$\mathrm{2NO_2 \rightleftharpoons N_2 + 2O_2}$$
(III) $$\mathrm{NO_2 \rightleftharpoons \frac{1}{2}N_2 + O_2}$$
The correct relation from the following is
questions.solution:
$K_1 = \dfrac{[\mathrm{NO_2}]^2}{[\mathrm{N_2}][\mathrm{O_2}]^2}$

Reaction (II) is the reverse of (I), so $K_2 = \dfrac{1}{K_1}$.

Reaction (III) is (II) divided by 2, so $K_3 = K_2^{1/2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{K_1}}$, i.e. $K_1 = \dfrac{1}{K_3^2}$.

Check: $K_3^2 = \dfrac{[\mathrm{N_2}][\mathrm{O_2}]^2}{[\mathrm{NO_2}]^2} = K_2$.

So $K_1 = \dfrac{1}{K_2} = \dfrac{1}{(K_3)^2}$.

(1) $$N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)$$, $$K_1$$
(2) $$N_2(g) + O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO(g)$$, $$K_2$$
(3) $$H_2(g) + \frac{1}{2}O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons H_2O(g)$$, $$K_3$$
The equation for the equilibrium constant of the reaction $$2NH_3(g) + \frac{5}{2}O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO(g) + 3H_2O(g)$$, $$(K_4)$$ in terms of $$K_1$$, $$K_2$$ and $$K_3$$ is :
questions.solution:
Target: $\mathrm{2NH_3} + \dfrac{5}{2}\mathrm{O_2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{2NO + 3H_2O}$.

Reverse (1): $\mathrm{2NH_3 \rightleftharpoons N_2 + 3H_2}$, constant $\dfrac{1}{K_1}$.

Add (2): $\mathrm{N_2 + O_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NO}$, constant $K_2$.

Add three times (3): $\mathrm{3H_2} + \dfrac{3}{2}\mathrm{O_2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{3H_2O}$, constant $K_3^3$.

Adding equations multiplies their constants: $K_4 = \dfrac{K_2K_3^3}{K_1}$.

questions.text: In reaction $$A + 2B \rightleftharpoons 2C + D$$, initial concentration of B was 1.5 times of [A], but at equilibrium the concentrations of A and B became equal. The equilibrium constant for the reaction is :
questions.solution:
Let $[\mathrm{A}]_0 = a$, so $[\mathrm{B}]_0 = 1.5a$; let $x$ mol/L of A react.

At equilibrium: $[\mathrm{A}] = a - x$, $[\mathrm{B}] = 1.5a - 2x$, $[\mathrm{C}] = 2x$, $[\mathrm{D}] = x$.

$[\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{B}]$ gives $a - x = 1.5a - 2x$, so $x = 0.5a$.

Then $[\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{B}] = 0.5a$, $[\mathrm{C}] = a$, $[\mathrm{D}] = 0.5a$.

$K = \dfrac{[\mathrm{C}]^2[\mathrm{D}]}{[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]^2} = \dfrac{a^2 (0.5a)}{(0.5a)(0.5a)^2} = 4$.

Answer: $K = 4$.

For the decomposition of the compound represented as

NH 2 COONH 4 (s)   $$\rightleftharpoons$$  2NH 3 (g) + CO 2 (g)

the K p = 2.9 $$ \times $$ 10 $$-$$5 atm 3 .

If the reaction is started with 1 mol of the compound, the total pressure at equilibrium would be :
questions.solution:
Only the gases enter $K_p$. If $p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}=p$, then $p_{\mathrm{NH_3}}=2p$, since they form in the ratio $2:1$.

$K_p=p_{\mathrm{NH_3}}^2\,p_{\mathrm{CO_2}}=(2p)^2(p)=4p^3=2.9\times10^{-5}$

$p^3=7.25\times10^{-6}\Rightarrow p\approx1.94\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{atm}$

Total pressure $=2p+p=3p=3\times1.94\times10^{-2}=5.82\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{atm}$

The amount of solid (1 mol) does not affect this, as long as some solid remains.

So the total pressure at equilibrium is $5.82\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{atm}$.

So the equilibrium constant is $0.25$.

questions.text: A solid XY kept in an evacuated sealed container undergoes decomposition to form a mixture of gases X and Y at temperature T. The equilibrium pressure is 10 bar in this vessel. K p for this reaction is :
questions.solution:
To determine the equilibrium constant, $K_p$, for the decomposition reaction of the solid compound XY into its gaseous components X and Y, we need to consider the following reaction:

$$ \text{XY (s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{X (g)} + \text{Y (g)} $$

For a reaction where a solid decomposes into gases, the equilibrium constant $K_p$ is defined in terms of the partial pressures of the gaseous products. Since XY is a solid, its activity is considered to be 1 and does not appear in the equilibrium expression. Hence the expression for $K_p$ is:

$$ K_p = P_X \cdot P_Y $$

Where $P_X$ and $P_Y$ are the partial pressures of the gases X and Y, respectively.

Given that the total pressure at equilibrium is 10 bar, and assuming that X and Y are present in equal amounts due to the stoichiometry of the decomposition reaction (i.e., 1:1), we can write:

$$ P_X = P_Y = \frac{10}{2} = 5 \, \text{bar} $$

Substituting these partial pressures into the expression for $K_p$ gives:

$$ K_p = P_X \cdot P_Y = 5 \, \text{bar} \cdot 5 \, \text{bar} = 25 \, \text{bar}^2 $$

Therefore, the equilibrium constant $K_p$ for this reaction is 25. Thus, the correct answer is:

Option C - 25

$$\ce{NH4SH(s) <=> NH3(g) + H2S(g)}$$

To determine the correct relationship between the equilibrium constants $K_C$ and $K_p$ for the reaction:

$$\text{Fe}_2\text{N(s)} + \frac{3}{2}\text{H}_2\text{(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Fe(s)} + \text{NH}_3\text{(g)}$$

First, consider the general relationship between $K_C$ and $K_p$:

$$ K_p = K_C(RT)^{\Delta n} $$

where $\Delta n$ is the change in the number of moles of gas between the products and the reactants, $R$ is the ideal gas constant, and $T$ is the temperature in Kelvin.

For the given reaction, calculate $\Delta n$:

Moles of gas in products: NH 3(g) = 1 mole

Moles of gas in reactants: $${3 \over 2}$$ H 2(g) = 1.5 moles

Therefore:

$$ \Delta n = 1 - 1.5 = -0.5 $$

Substitute this value into the equation relating $K_C$ and $K_p$:

$$ K_p = K_C(RT)^{-0.5} $$

Rearrange to express $K_C$:

$$ K_C = K_p(RT)^{0.5} $$

Thus, the correct option is:

Option A: $$K_C = K_p(RT)^{1/2}$$

questions.text:
If the equilibrium constant for
A ⇌ B + C is $$K_{eq}^{(1)}$$ and that of

B + C ⇌ P is $$K_{eq}^{(2)}$$, the equilibrium

constant for A ⇌ P is :
questions.solution:
We have two reactions:

$ A \;\rightleftharpoons\; B + C \quad\text{with } K_{eq}^{(1)}$

$ B + C \;\rightleftharpoons\; P \quad\text{with } K_{eq}^{(2)}$

We want the equilibrium constant for the overall reaction

$ A \;\rightleftharpoons\; P. $

How to combine the equilibrium constants
When two reactions are added to yield a net (overall) reaction, the equilibrium constant of the net reaction is the product of the equilibrium constants of the individual reactions . Formally:

$ \text{(Reaction 1)} + \text{(Reaction 2)} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{(Net Reaction)}, $

and

$ K_{\text{net}} \;=\; K_{\text{(Reaction 1)}} \times K_{\text{(Reaction 2)}}. $

Applying it here
Reaction 1 : $A \to B + C$ has $K_{eq}^{(1)}.$

Reaction 2 : $B + C \to P$ has $K_{eq}^{(2)}.$

When we add them,

$ \underbrace{A}_{\text{Reactant 1}} \;\longrightarrow\; \underbrace{B + C}_{\text{Products of Reaction 1}=\text{Reactants of Reaction 2}} \;\longrightarrow\; \underbrace{P}_{\text{Product of Reaction 2}}. $

So the net reaction is $A \to P$, and its equilibrium constant is

$ K_{eq}^{\text{(net)}} \;=\; K_{eq}^{(1)} \times K_{eq}^{(2)}. $

Thus, the correct answer is:

$ \boxed{K_{eq}^{(1)} \, K_{eq}^{(2)}}. $

Hence, the answer (Option D) is correct.

questions.text:
The reaction rate for the reaction

[PtCl 4 ] 2$$-$$ + H₂O $$\rightleftharpoons$$ [Pt(H₂O)Cl 3 ] $$-$$ + Cl $$-$$

was measured as a function of concentrations of different species. It was observed that $${{ - d\left[ {{{\left[ {PtC{l_4}} \right]}^{2 - }}} \right]} \over {dt}} = 4.8 \times {10^{ - 5}}\left[ {{{\left[ {PtC{l_4}} \right]}^{2 - }}} \right] - 2.4 \times {10^{ - 3}}\left[ {{{\left[ {Pt({H_2}O)C{l_3}} \right]}^ - }} \right]\left[ {C{l^ - }} \right]$$.

where square brackets are used to denote molar concentrations. The equilibrium constant K c = ____________ . (Nearest integer)
questions.solution:
The rate equation provided in your question describes the rates of the forward and reverse reactions for this chemical system. The equilibrium constant, $K_c$, is the ratio of the forward rate constant ($k_f$) to the reverse rate constant ($k_r$). At equilibrium, the rate of the forward reaction is equal to the rate of the reverse reaction, so the rate equation simplifies to:

$$k_f[\text{{PtCl}}_4]^{2-} = k_r[\text{{Pt(H}}_2\text{{O)Cl}}_3]^-[\text{{Cl}}^-]$$

Given the rate equation:

$$-\frac{d[\text{{PtCl}}_4]^{2-}}{dt} = 4.8 \times 10^{-5} [\text{{PtCl}}_4]^{2-} - 2.4 \times 10^{-3} [\text{{Pt(H}}_2\text{{O)Cl}}_3]^-[\text{{Cl}}^-]$$

At equilibrium, $-\frac{d[\text{{PtCl}}_4]^{2-}}{dt} = 0$, so:

$$0 = 4.8 \times 10^{-5} [\text{{PtCl}}_4]^{2-} - 2.4 \times 10^{-3} [\text{{Pt(H}}_2\text{{O)Cl}}_3]^-[\text{{Cl}}^-]$$

Rearranging terms, we find:

$$4.8 \times 10^{-5} [\text{{PtCl}}_4]^{2-} = 2.4 \times 10^{-3} [\text{{Pt(H}}_2\text{{O)Cl}}_3]^-[\text{{Cl}}^-]$$

Now, the equilibrium constant $K_c$ is defined as the ratio of the concentrations of the products to the reactants, each raised to the power of their stoichiometric coefficients. For the reaction in question, we have:

$$K_c = \frac{[\text{{Pt(H}}_2\text{{O)Cl}}_3]^-[\text{{Cl}}^-]}{[\text{{PtCl}}_4]^{2-}}$$

Dividing both sides of our rate equation by $[\text{{PtCl}}_4]^{2-}$, we find that:

$$K_c = \frac{4.8 \times 10^{-5}}{2.4 \times 10^{-3}} = \frac{1}{50}$$ = 0.02

So, the equilibrium constant $K_c$ for this reaction is approximately 0, when rounded to the nearest integer.

questions.text:
The equilibrium constant for the reaction

A(s) $$\rightleftharpoons$$ M(s) + $${1 \over 2}$$O 2 (g)

is K p = 4. At equilibrium, the partial pressure of O 2 is _________ atm. (Round off to the nearest integer)
questions.solution:
In the given equilibrium, the solid substances do not contribute to the equilibrium constant expression since their activities are considered to be 1.

For the reaction:

$ \text{A(s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{M(s)} + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2(\text{g}) $

The equilibrium constant, $ K_p $, is given by:

$ K_p = P_{\text{O}_2}^{n} $

where $ P_{\text{O}_2} $ is the partial pressure of $ \text{O}_2 $ and $ n $ represents the stoichiometric coefficient of $ \text{O}_2 $ in the balanced chemical reaction, which is $ \frac{1}{2} $. Therefore, the expression for $ K_p $ becomes:

$ K_p = \left( P_{\text{O}_2} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} $

Given that $ K_p = 4 $, substituting into the equation gives:

$ 4 = \left( P_{\text{O}_2} \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} $

To find $ P_{\text{O}_2} $, square both sides of the equation:

$ 4^2 = P_{\text{O}_2} $

$ 16 = P_{\text{O}_2} $

Thus, the partial pressure of $ \text{O}_2 $ at equilibrium is $\boxed{16}$ atm.

questions.text:
Value of K P for the equilibrium reaction

N₂O₄(g) $$\rightleftharpoons$$ 2NO 2(g) at 288 K is 47.9. The K C for this reaction at same temperature is ____________. (Nearest integer)

(R = 0.083 L bar K $$-$$1 mol $$-$$1 )
questions.solution:
For the equilibrium reaction

$ \text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(g) $

the relationship between $ K_P $ and $ K_C $ is given by the equation:

$ K_P = K_C (RT)^{\Delta n} $

where $ \Delta n $ is the change in the number of moles of gas, $ R $ is the ideal gas constant, and $ T $ is the temperature in Kelvin.

For the given reaction:

$ \Delta n = 2 - 1 = 1 $

Given:

$ K_P = 47.9 $

$ R = 0.083 \, \text{L bar K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1} $

$ T = 288 \, \text{K} $

Substitute these values into the equation:

$ 47.9 = K_C (0.083 \times 288)^{1} $

$ K_C = \frac{47.9}{0.083 \times 288} $

Calculate:

$ 0.083 \times 288 = 23.904 $

$ K_C = \frac{47.9}{23.904} $

$ K_C \approx 2.0033 $

Rounding to the nearest integer, the value of $ K_C $ is

$ \boxed{2} $

p SO 2 = 45 kPa

On putting given values, we get

$$ \Rightarrow {K_p} = {{{{(43)}^2}} \over {{{(45)}^2} \times 0.53}}$$

$$ = {{1849} \over {2025 \times 0.53}} = {{1849} \over {1073.25}}$$

$$ = 1.7228$$

$$ = {{1.7228 \times {{10}^2}} \over {{{10}^2}}} = 172.28 \times {10^{ - 2}} = 172$$

Hence, the equilibrium constant, K p = 172.

Here 4 moles of inert gas argon also present.

n T = 5 + x + 4

= 9 + x

Volume (v) = 100 L

Temperature = 610 K

$${P_T}V = {n_T}RT$$

$$ \Rightarrow x = 3$$

$${K_P} = {{{P_{PC{l_3}}} \times {P_{C{l_2}}}} \over {{P_{PC{l_5}}}}}$$

$$ = {{\left[ {{3 \over {9 + 3}} \times 6} \right] \times \left[ {{3 \over {9 + 3}} \times 6} \right]} \over {\left[ {{{5 - 3} \over {9 + 3}} \times 6} \right]}}$$

$$ = {{27} \over {12}}$$

$$ = {9 \over 4}$$

= 2.25 atm

Inert gas always contribute to total mole and pressure calculation.
