PCl 5 dissociates as

PCl 5 (g) $$\rightleftharpoons$$ PCl 3 (g) + Cl 2 (g)

5 moles of PCl 5 are placed in a 200 litre vessel which contains 2 moles of N 2 and is maintained at 600 K. The equilibrium pressure is 2.46 atm. The equilibrium constant K p for the dissociation of PCl 5 is __________ $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$3 . (nearest integer)

(Given : R = 0.082 L atm K $$-$$1 mol $$-$$1 ; Assume ideal gas behaviour)
questions.solution:
Here 2 moles of N 2 also present that is why 2 moles always have to add in total mole calculation.

At equilibrium,

Pressure (P) = 2.46 atm

Volume (V) = 200 L

Temperature (T) = 600 K

$$\therefore$$ Applying ideal gas equation,

PV = nRT

$$\Rightarrow$$ 2.46 $$\times$$ 200 = (7 + x) $$\times$$ 0.082 $$\times$$ 600

$$\Rightarrow$$ x = 3

Now,

$${K_P} = {{{P_{PC{l_3}}} \times {P_{C{l_2}}}} \over {{P_{PC{l_5}}}}}$$

$$ = {{\left[ {{3 \over {7 + 3}} \times 2.46} \right]\left[ {{3 \over {7 + 3}} \times 2.46} \right]} \over {\left[ {{{5 - 3} \over {7 + 3}} \times 2.46} \right]}}$$

$$ = {{{3 \over {10}} \times {3 \over {10}} \times {{(2.46)}^2}} \over {{2 \over {10}} \times 2.46}}$$

$$ = {9 \over {20}} \times 2.46$$

$$ = 1107 \times {10^{ - 3}}$$ atm

questions.text:
For a reaction at equilibrium

A(g) $$\rightleftharpoons$$ B(g) + $${1 \over 2}$$ C(g)

the relation between dissociation constant (K), degree of dissociation ($$\alpha$$) and equilibrium pressure (p) is given by :
questions.solution:
Now,

$${K_P}$$ or $$K = {{{P_B} \times {{\left( {{P_C}} \right)}^{{1 \over 2}}}} \over {{P_A}}}$$

$$ = {{\left( {{\alpha \over {1 + {\alpha \over 2}}}} \right)P \times {{\left[ {\left( {{{{\alpha \over 2}} \over {1 + {\alpha \over 2}}}} \right)P} \right]}^{{1 \over 2}}}} \over {\left( {{{1 - \alpha } \over {1 + {\alpha \over 2}}}} \right)P}}$$

$$ = {{\left( {{{2\alpha } \over {2 + \alpha }}} \right)P \times {{\left[ {\left( {{\alpha \over {2 + \alpha }}} \right)P} \right]}^{{1 \over 2}}}} \over {\left( {{{2(1 - \alpha )} \over {2 + \alpha }}} \right)P}}$$

$$= {\alpha \over {1 - \alpha }} \times {\left( {{{\alpha P} \over {2 + \alpha }}} \right)^{{1 \over 2}}}$$

$$ = {{{\alpha ^{{3 \over 2}}}\,.\,{P^{{1 \over 2}}}} \over {(1 - \alpha ){{(2 + \alpha )}^{{1 \over 2}}}}}$$

2O 3 (g) $$\rightleftharpoons$$ 3O 2 (g)

At 300 K, ozone is fifty percent dissociated. The standard free energy change at this temperature and 1 atm pressure is ($$-$$) ____________ J mol $$-$$1 . (Nearest integer)

[Given : ln 1.35 = 0.3 and R = 8.3 J K $$-$$1 mol $$-$$1 ]
questions.solution:
$\underset{1-x}{2 \mathrm{O}_3(\mathrm{~g})} \rightleftharpoons \underset{\frac{3 \mathrm{x}}{2}}{3 \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{~g})}$

Given, $x=0.5$

$\therefore \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{p}}=\frac{[3(0.5)]^{3} \times 1}{[2]^{3} \times(0.5)^{2} \times 1.25}$

$\therefore \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{p}}=\frac{27}{8} \times \frac{0.5}{1.25}=1.35$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta \mathrm{G}^{\circ} &=-2.303 \mathrm{RT} \log \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{p}} \\\\
&=-2.303 \times 8.3 \times 300 \log 1.35 \\\\
&=-8.3 \times 300 \ln (1.35) \\\\
&=-747 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

questions.text: Assuming that the degree of hydrolysis is small, the pH of 0.1 M solution of sodium acetate (K a = 1.0 $$ \times $$ 10 $$-$$5 ) will be :
questions.solution:
Acetate ion hydrolyses, $\mathrm{CH_3COO^- + H_2O \rightleftharpoons CH_3COOH + OH^-}$, so the solution is basic.

For a salt of a weak acid and a strong base, $\mathrm{pH} = 7 + \dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{p}K_a + \dfrac{1}{2}\log C$.

$\mathrm{p}K_a = 5$ and $\log 0.1 = -1$, so $\mathrm{pH} = 7 + 2.5 - 0.5 = 9.0$.

Check: $K_h = \dfrac{K_w}{K_a} = 10^{-9}$, $[\mathrm{OH^-}] = \sqrt{K_hC} = \sqrt{10^{-10}} = 10^{-5}$, so $\mathrm{pOH} = 5$.

So the pH is $9.0$.

questions.text: An aqueous solution contains 0.10 M H₂S and 0.20 M HCl. If the equilibrium constants for the formation of HS – from H₂S is 1.0 $$\times$$ 10 –7 and that of S 2- from HS – ions is 1.2 $$\times$$ 10 –13 then the concentration of S 2- ions in aqueous solution is :
questions.solution:
HCl $$ \to $$ H + + Cl $$-$$

H + concentration is = 0.2 M.

H₂S $$\rightleftharpoons$$ H + + HS $$-$$ ; K 1 = 1.0 $$ \times $$ 10 $$-$$7

HS $$-$$ $$\rightleftharpoons$$ H + + S 2$$-$$ ; K 2 = 1.2 $$ \times $$ 10 $$-$$13

H₂S $$\rightleftharpoons$$ S 2$$-$$ + 2H +

K = K 1 $$ \times $$ K 2 = 1.0 $$ \times $$ 10 $$-$$7 $$ \times $$ 1.2 $$ \times $$ 1.0 $$-$$13 = 1.2 $$ \times $$ 10 $$-$$20

as K 1 and K 2 both are very low for this reaction so dissociation of H₂S and HS $$-$$ will be very low so, the produced H + from this reaction will also be very low.

So, we can say the concentration of H + will be almost same as H + in HCl.

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ [ H + ] = 0.2 M.

From the reaction, H₂S $$\rightleftharpoons\,$$ 2H + + S 2$$-$$

We get [ H + ] 2 [ S 2$$-$$ ] = K $$ \times $$ [ H₂S ]

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,\,$$ [ S 2$$-$$ ] = $$ {{1.2 \times {{10}^{ - 20}} \times 0.1} \over {{{\left( {0.2} \right)}^2}}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,\,$$ [ S 2$$-$$ ] = 3 $$ \times $$ 10 $$-$$20 M

questions.text:
Given below are two statements : One is labelled as Assertion A and the other labelled as reason R

Assertion A : During the boiling of water having temporary hardness, Mg(HCO 3 ) 2 is converted to MgCO 3 .

Reason R : The solubility product of Mg(OH) 2 is greater than that of MgCO 3 .

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

options.text: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.solution:
Assertion A is false. On boiling, Mg(HCO 3 ) 2 gives Mg(OH) 2 , not MgCO 3 : $$\mathrm{Mg(HCO_3)_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} Mg(OH)_2 \downarrow + 2CO_2}$$ Mg(OH) 2 precipitates because it is less soluble than MgCO 3 .

Reason R: $$K_{sp}\left[\mathrm{Mg(OH)_2}\right] = 1.8 \times 10^{-11}$$ and $$K_{sp}\left[\mathrm{MgCO_3}\right] = 3.5 \times 10^{-8}$$ (NCERT), so the solubility product of Mg(OH) 2 is actually smaller than that of MgCO 3 .

NTA's answer key marks option (D), "A is false but R is true". With the NCERT values above, statement R as printed is also false, so strictly none of the options is correct.

questions.text:
$$20 \mathrm{~mL}$$ of $$0.1\, \mathrm{M} \,\mathrm{NH}_{4} \mathrm{OH}$$ is mixed with $$40 \mathrm{~mL}$$ of $$0.05 \mathrm{~M} \mathrm{~HCl}$$. The $$\mathrm{pH}$$ of the mixture is nearest to :

(Given : $$\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{b}}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{4} \mathrm{OH}\right)=1 \times 10^{-5}, \log 2=0.30, \log 3=0.48, \log 5=0.69, \log 7=0.84, \log 11= 1.04)$$
questions.solution:
$\ce{NH4OH}$: $20 \times 0.1 = 2$ mmol; $\ce{HCl}$: $40 \times 0.05 = 2$ mmol, so the two neutralise each other completely:

$$[\ce{NH4+}] = \dfrac{2\ \text{mmol}}{60\ \text{mL}} = \dfrac{1}{30}\ \text{M}$$

$\ce{NH4Cl}$ is a salt of a weak base and a strong acid, so its solution is acidic by hydrolysis of $\ce{NH4+}$:

$$\mathrm{pH} = 7 - \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\mathrm{p}K_b + \log C\right) = 7 - \dfrac{1}{2}\left(5 + \log\dfrac{1}{30}\right)$$

With $\log 30 = \log 3 + 1 = 1.48$:

$$\mathrm{pH} = 7 - \dfrac{1}{2}(5 - 1.48) = 7 - 1.76 = 5.24 \approx 5.2$$

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
Three reactions involving $$H_2PO_4^−$$ are given below :

(i) H 3 PO 4 + H₂O $$\to$$ H₃O + + $$H_2PO_4^−$$

(ii) $$H_2PO_4^−$$ + H₂O $$\to$$ $$HPO_4^{2−}$$ + H₃O +

(iii) $$H_2PO_4^−$$ + OH - $$\to$$H 3 PO 4 + O 2-

In which of the above does $$H_2PO_4^−$$ act as an acid?
questions.solution:
To determine in which reactions $ H_2PO_4^- $ acts as an acid, we need to understand the Bronsted-Lowry concept of acids and bases. According to this concept, an acid is a substance that donates a proton (H⁺) to another substance, while a base is a substance that accepts a proton.

Let's analyze each reaction :

1. $ H_3PO_4 + H_2O \to H_3O^+ + H_2PO_4^- $

In this reaction, $ H_3PO_4 $ is donating a proton to $ H_2O $, forming $ H_3O^+ $ and $ H_2PO_4^- $.

$ H_2PO_4^- $ is the product of this reaction and is not acting as an acid here.

2. $ H_2PO_4^- + H_2O \to HPO_4^{2−} + H_3O^+ $

In this reaction, $ H_2PO_4^- $ donates a proton to $ H_2O $, resulting in $ HPO_4^{2−} $ and $ H_3O^+ $.

$ H_2PO_4^- $ is acting as an acid in this reaction.

3. $ H_2PO_4^- + OH^- \to H_3PO_4 + O^{2-} $

This reaction is not correctly balanced and does not follow standard chemical reaction rules. The product $ O^{2-} $ is highly unlikely in aqueous solutions due to its reactivity.

A more correct reaction would be $ H_2PO_4^- + OH^- \to HPO_4^{2−} + H_2O $. In this corrected reaction, $ H_2PO_4^- $ is donating a proton to $ OH^- $, which makes it an acid.

Given the information, the correct option is :

Option A : (ii) only

This is because in reaction (ii), $ H_2PO_4^- $ is clearly acting as an acid by donating a proton to water. In reaction (i), $ H_2PO_4^- $ is not acting as an acid but rather is formed as a product. Reaction (iii) as written is chemically incorrect, but even in a corrected form, it would show $ H_2PO_4^- $ acting as an acid.

questions.text:
In aqueous solution the ionization constants for carbonic acid are

K 1 = 4.2 x 10 –7 and K 2 = 4.8 x 10 –11

Select the correct statement for a saturated 0.034 M solution of the carbonic acid.

options.text:
The concentration of
$$CO_3^{2−}$$ is greater than that of $$HCO_3^{−}$$
The concentration of H + and $$HCO_3^−$$ are approximately equal.
The concentration of H + is double that of $$CO_3^{2−}$$.

questions.solution:
$$\mathop {{H_2}C{O_3}\left( {aq} \right)}\limits_{0.034 - x} \, + \,{H_2}O\left( l \right)\,\rightleftharpoons\,\mathop {HCO_3^ - \left( {aq} \right)}\limits_x \, + \,\mathop {{H_3}{O^ + }\left( {aq} \right)}\limits_x $$

$${K_1} = {{\left[ {HCO_3^ - } \right]\left[ {{H_3}{O^ + }} \right]} \over {\left[ {{H_2}C{O_3}} \right]}}$$

$$ = {{x \times x} \over {0.034 - x}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow 4.2 \times {10^{ - 7}} = {{{x^2}} \over {0.034}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow x = 1.195 \times {10^{ - 4}}$$

As $${H_2}C{O_3}$$ is a weak acid so the concentration of

$${H_2}C{O_3}$$ will remain $$0.034\,\,$$ as $$0.034 > > x.$$

$$x = \left[ {{H^ + }} \right] = \left[ {HCO_3^ - } \right]$$

$$ = 1.195 \times {10^{ - 4}}$$

Now, $$\mathop {HCO_3^ - }\limits_{x - y} \left( {aq} \right) + {H_2}O\left( l \right)\,\rightleftharpoons\,\mathop {CO_3^{2 - }\left( {aq} \right)}\limits_y \, + \,\mathop {{H_3}{O^ + }\left( {aq} \right)}\limits_y $$

As $$HCO_3^ - \,$$ is again a weak acid (weaker than $${H_2}C{O_3})$$

with $$x > > y.$$

$${K_2} = {{\left[ {CO_3^{{2^ - }}} \right]\left[ {{H_3}{O^ + }} \right]} \over {\left[ {HCO_3^ - } \right]}}$$

$$ = {{y \times \left( {x + y} \right)} \over {\left( {x - y} \right)}}$$

Note : $$\left[ {{H_3}{O^ + }} \right] = {H^ + }\,\,$$ from first step $$(x)$$

and from second step $$\left( y \right) = \left( {x + y} \right)$$

[As $$\,\,\,x > > y\,\,$$ so $$\,\,\,x + y \simeq x\,\,\,$$ and $$x - y \simeq x$$]

So, $$\,\,\,{K_2} \simeq {{y \times x} \over x} = y$$

$$ \Rightarrow {K_2} = 4.8 \times {10^{ - 11}}$$

$$ = y = \left[ {CO_3^{{2^ - }}} \right]$$

So the concentration of $$\,\,\,\left[ {{H^ + }} \right] = \left[ {HCO_3^ - } \right] = \,\,\,$$ concentrations obtained from the first step. As the dissociation will be very low in second step so there will be no change in these concentrations.

Thus the final concentrations are

$$\left[ {{H^ + }} \right] = \left[ {HCO_3^ - } \right] = 1.195 \times {10^{ - 4}}$$

$$\& \,\,\,\left[ {CO_3^{2 - }} \right] = 4.8 \times {10^{ - 11}}$$

questions.text:
Given (i) $$\mathrm{HCN}(aq) + \mathrm{H_2O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H_3O^+}(aq) + \mathrm{CN^-}(aq)\quad K_a = 6.2 \times 10^{-10}$$
(ii) $$\mathrm{CN^-}(aq) + \mathrm{H_2O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{HCN}(aq) + \mathrm{OH^-}(aq)\quad K_b = 1.6 \times 10^{-5}$$.
These equilibria show the following order of the relative base strength,
questions.solution:
In (i), $K_a$ is very small, so $\mathrm{HCN}$ is a far weaker acid than $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$; hence its conjugate base $\mathrm{CN^-}$ is a stronger base than $\mathrm{H_2O}$.

In (ii), $K_b \ll 1$, so the equilibrium lies to the left: $\mathrm{OH^-}$ takes a proton from $\mathrm{HCN}$ more readily than $\mathrm{CN^-}$ takes one from water.

So $\mathrm{OH^-}$ is a stronger base than $\mathrm{CN^-}$.

Order of base strength: $\mathrm{OH^- \gt CN^- \gt H_2O}$.

questions.text: Which one of the following arrangements represents the correct order of the proton affinity of the given species :
questions.solution:
Proton affinity of an anion is high when its conjugate acid is weak.

Acid strength: $\mathrm{HI \gt HF \gt H_2S \gt NH_3}$.

So the base strength, and proton affinity, is the reverse: $\mathrm{I^- \lt F^- \lt HS^- \lt NH_2^-}$.

The correct order is $\mathrm{I^- \lt F^- \lt HS^- \lt NH_2^-}$.

questions.text:
Values of dissociation constant, $$K_a$$ are given as follows :
Acid             $$K_a$$
HCN             $$6.2 \times 10^{-10}$$
HF               $$7.2 \times 10^{-4}$$
HNO$$_2$$          $$4.0 \times 10^{-4}$$
Correct order of increasing base strength of $$CN^-$$, $$F^-$$ and $$NO_2^-$$ will be :
questions.solution:
The larger $K_a$, the stronger the acid and the weaker its conjugate base.

Acid strength: $\mathrm{HF}\ (7.2 \times 10^{-4}) \gt \mathrm{HNO_2}\ (4.0 \times 10^{-4}) \gt \mathrm{HCN}\ (6.2 \times 10^{-10})$.

Base strength of the conjugate bases is in the reverse order.

Increasing base strength: $\mathrm{F^-} \lt \mathrm{NO_2^-} \lt \mathrm{CN^-}$.

questions.text: The conjugate base of hydrazoic acid is :
questions.solution:
Hydrazoic acid is $\mathrm{HN_3}$.

A conjugate base is what remains after the acid loses one proton: $\mathrm{HN_3 \rightleftharpoons H^+ + N_3^-}$.

So the conjugate base of hydrazoic acid is the azide ion, $\mathrm{N_3^-}$.

questions.text:
The decreasing order of electrical conductivity of the following aqueous solutions is :

0.1 M Formic acid (A),

0.1 M Acetic acid (B),

0.1 M Benzoic acid (C)
questions.solution:
0.1 M Formic acid(HCOOH) (A),

0.1 M Acetic acid(CH 3 COOH) (B),

0.1 M Benzoic acid(C₆H₅ COOH) (C)

Conductivity (K) depends on no of ions present in unit volume of solution. When no of ions increases conductivity also increases.

Also no of ions depends on degree of dissociation($$\alpha $$).

We know, $$\alpha $$ = $$\sqrt {{{{K_a}} \over C}} $$

For all solutions C = 0.1 M

So, $$\alpha $$ depends on only K $$a$$ here.

K $$a$$ of HCOOH = 10 -4

K $$a$$ of CH 3 COOH = 1.8 $$ \times $$ 10 -5

and K $$a$$ of C₆H₅ COOH = 6 $$ \times $$ 10 -5

$$ \therefore $$ $$\alpha $$(HCOOH) > $$\alpha $$(C₆H₅ COOH) > $$\alpha $$(CH 3 COOH)

Therefore conductivity order = A > C > B

questions.text:
$${K_{{a_1}}}$$, $${K_{{a_2}}}$$ and $${K_{{a_3}}}$$ are the respective ionization constants for the following reactions (a), (b) and (c).

(a) $${H_2}{C_2}{O_4} \rightleftharpoons {H^ + } + H{C_2}O_4^ - $$

(b) $$H{C_2}O_4^ - \rightleftharpoons {H^ + } + {C_2}O_4^{2 - }$$

(c) $${H_2}{C_2}O_4^{} \rightleftharpoons 2{H^ + } + {C_2}O_4^{2 - }$$

The relationship between $${K_{{a_1}}}$$, $${K_{{a_2}}}$$ and $${K_{{a_3}}}$$ is given as :
questions.solution:
$$\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4} \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{2-} \quad \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_{3}}$$

$$\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{HC}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{-} \quad \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_{1}}$$

$$\mathrm{HC}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}^{+}+\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{2-} \quad \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_{2}}$$

$$\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_{3}}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]^{2}\left[\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{2-}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}\right]}$$

$$\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_{1}}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{HC}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{-}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}\right]}, \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_{2}}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{H}^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{2-}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{HC}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}^{-}\right]}$$

$$\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_{3}}=\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_{1}} \times \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}_{2}}$$

$$pH$$ of an acidic solution should be less than $$7.$$ The reason is that from $${H_2}O.\left[ {{H^ + }} \right] = {10^{ - 7}}M$$ which cannot be neglected in comparison to $${10^{ - 8}}M.$$ The $$pH$$ can be calculated as.

from acid, $$\,\,\,\left[ {{H^ + }} \right] = {10^{ - 8}}M.$$

from $${H_2}O,\,\,\left[ {{H^ + }} \right] = {10^{ - 7}}M$$

questions.solution:
In aqueous solution $$BA$$ (salt) hydrolyses to give

$$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,$$ $$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,$$ Base acid

questions.text: NaOH is a strong base. What will be pH of $$5.0 \times 10^{-2}$$ M NaOH solution? (log 2 = 0.3)

$\mathrm{NaOH}$ ionises completely: $[\mathrm{OH^-}] = 5.0 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{M}$.

$\log 5 = 1 - \log 2 = 0.7$.

$\mathrm{pOH} = -\log(5 \times 10^{-2}) = 2 - 0.7 = 1.3$.

$\mathrm{pH} = 14 - 1.3 = 12.70$.

In some solutions, the concentration of H₃O + remains constant even when small amounts of strong acid or strong base are added to them. These solutions are known as :
questions.solution:
A buffer contains a weak acid with its salt (e.g. $\mathrm{CH_3COOH/CH_3COONa}$) or a weak base with its salt.

Added $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$ is consumed by the conjugate base: $\mathrm{CH_3COO^- + H_3O^+ \to CH_3COOH + H_2O}$.

Added $\mathrm{OH^-}$ is consumed by the weak acid: $\mathrm{CH_3COOH + OH^- \to CH_3COO^- + H_2O}$.

Hence $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$, and so the pH, stays almost constant; ideal, colloidal and true solutions have no such reserve.

So these are buffer solutions.

questions.solution:
Methyl orange is a pH indicator frequently used in titrations because of its clear and distinct colour change. Under acidic conditions, it is red or pinkish red and under alkaline conditions, it turns yellow.

Let's consider each of the options :

Option
A: When a weak base is titrated against a strong acid, the solution at the end point is slightly acidic. However, the color change from colorless to pink is not associated with methyl orange.

Option
B: When a strong base is titrated against a strong acid, the solution is neutral at the end point. Methyl orange changes color from pinkish-red in acidic conditions to yellow in basic conditions, so this color change doesn't match the description.

Option
C: When a weak base is titrated against a strong acid, the solution is slightly acidic at the end point. Methyl orange would change from yellow in the basic solution to red in the acidic solution at the end point. This corresponds to a "yellow to pinkish-red" color change.

Option
D: When a strong base is titrated against a strong acid, the solution is neutral at the end point. The color change described here is "pink to colorless" which does not correspond with the characteristic changes of methyl orange.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option
C: Weak base, Strong acid, Yellow to pinkish-red.

questions.text: 20 mL of 0.1 M H 2 SO 4 solution is added to 30 mL of 0.2 M NH 4 OH solution. The pH of the resultant mixture is : [pK b of NH 4 OH = 4.7].
questions.solution:
Millimoles taken: $\ce{H2SO4} = 20 \times 0.1 = 2$ and $\ce{NH4OH} = 30 \times 0.2 = 6$.

$$\ce{H2SO4 + 2NH4OH -> (NH4)2SO4 + 2H2O}$$

2 mmol $\ce{H2SO4}$ consumes 4 mmol $\ce{NH4OH}$ and gives 2 mmol $\ce{(NH4)2SO4}$, that is, 4 mmol $\ce{NH4+}$. The $\ce{NH4OH}$ left is $6 - 4 = 2$ mmol.

The solution contains $\ce{NH4OH}$ and its conjugate acid $\ce{NH4+}$, a basic buffer. Both are in the same volume, so the ratio of millimoles can be used:

$$\text{pOH} = \text{p}K_b + \log\frac{[\ce{NH4+}]}{[\ce{NH4OH}]} = 4.7 + \log\frac{4}{2} = 4.7 + 0.3 = 5.0$$

$$\text{pH} = 14 - 5.0 = 9.0$$

Hence, the correct option is (B).

In 100 L solution H 2 SO 4 present = 9.8 gm

$$ \Rightarrow $$ In 10 L solution moles of H 2 SO 4 present = $${{9.8} \over {98}} \times {{10} \over {100}}$$

In one molecule of H 2 SO 4 two H + ion present.

$$ \therefore $$ In 10 L solution moles of H + present = 2$$ \times $$$${{9.8} \over {98}} \times {{10} \over {100}}$$ = 0.02 moles

Also In 100 L solution NaOH present = 4 gm

$$ \therefore $$ In 40 L solution moles of OH - ion present = $${4 \over {40}} \times {{40} \over {100}}$$ = 0.04 moles

As moles of OH - ion is more than H + ion, so solution is basic.

$$ \therefore $$ Final Conc. of OH – = $${{0.04 - 0.02} \over {40 + 10}}$$ = 4 $$ \times $$ 10 -4

$$ \therefore $$ pOH = – log (4 ×10 –4 ) = 3.4

pH = 14 – 3.4 = 10.6

$$ \therefore $$ The contribution of H + from 2 nd dissociation of H 2 SO 3 can be neglected.

$$pH = - \log [{H^ + }]$$

$$ \approx 1$$

questions.solution:
$\mathrm{AgCl(s) \rightleftharpoons Ag^+ + Cl^-}$, $K_\mathrm{sp} = [\mathrm{Ag^+}][\mathrm{Cl^-}]$.

Let the solubility be $s$; then $[\mathrm{Ag^+}] = s$ and $[\mathrm{Cl^-}] = 0.1 + s \approx 0.1$ (common ion from $\mathrm{KCl}$).

$s\times0.1 = 1.0\times10^{-10}$, so $s = 1.0\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$.

Check: $s \ll 0.1$, so the approximation holds; in pure water $s$ would be $10^{-5}$, so the common ion lowers it as expected.

So the solubility is $1.0\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}$.

For the following Assertion and Reason , the
correct option is

Assertion (A): When Cu (II) and sulphide ions
are mixed, they react together
extremely quickly to give a
solid.

Reason (R): The equilibrium constant of

Cu 2+ (aq) + S 2– (aq) ⇌ CuS(s) is
high because the solubility
product is low.

options.text:
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the
explanation for (A).

Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the
explanation for (A).

questions.solution:
The precipitation $\ce{Cu^2+(aq) + S^2-(aq) -> CuS(s)}$ is an ionic reaction that occurs at once on mixing, so the assertion is true.

For this reaction $K = \dfrac{1}{K_{\text{sp}}(\ce{CuS})}$, and $K_{\text{sp}}$ is of the order of $10^{-36}$, so $K$ is very large and the reason is true.

An equilibrium constant measures how far a reaction proceeds, not how fast it proceeds; $\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}$, for example, has a very large $K$ yet is extremely slow at room temperature, so the reason does not explain the speed stated in the assertion.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: The solubility of AgCN in a buffer solution of pH = 3 is x. The value of x is : [Assume : No cyano complex is formed; K sp (AgCN) = 2.2 $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$16 and K a (HCN) = 6.2 $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$10 ]
questions.solution:
In a buffer of pH 3, $[\ce{H+}] = 10^{-3}\ \text{M}$, which is far larger than $K_a(\ce{HCN}) = 6.2 \times 10^{-10}$. Hence $\dfrac{[\ce{CN-}]}{[\ce{HCN}]} = \dfrac{K_a}{[\ce{H+}]} = 6.2 \times 10^{-7}$, so almost all the cyanide released is present as HCN.

The overall equilibrium is $\ce{AgCN(s) + H+ <=> Ag+ + HCN}$, with $K = \dfrac{K_{sp}}{K_a}$.

With solubility $x$: $[\ce{Ag+}] = x$ and $[\ce{HCN}] \approx x$, while $[\ce{H+}]$ is fixed by the buffer.

$$\frac{x \cdot x}{[\ce{H+}]} = \frac{K_{sp}}{K_a} \Rightarrow x^2 = \frac{K_{sp}[\ce{H+}]}{K_a} = \frac{2.2 \times 10^{-16} \times 10^{-3}}{6.2 \times 10^{-10}} = 3.55 \times 10^{-10}$$

$$x = 1.88 \times 10^{-5} \approx 1.9 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{M}$$

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: The solubility product of PbI 2 is 8.0 $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$9 . The solubility of lead iodide in 0.1 molar solution of lead nitrate is x $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$6 mol/L. The value of x is __________. (Rounded off to the nearest integer) [Given $$\sqrt 2 $$ = 1.41]
questions.solution:
$\ce{Pb(NO3)2}$ is a strong electrolyte, so the solution already has $[\ce{Pb^2+}]=0.1$ M.

Let the solubility of $\ce{PbI2}$ in it be $S$ mol L$^{-1}$:

$$\ce{PbI2(s) <=> Pb^2+(aq) + 2I^-(aq)}$$

Then $[\ce{I-}]=2S$ and $[\ce{Pb^2+}]=0.1+S\approx 0.1$ M, since $S\ll 0.1$.

$$K_{sp}=[\ce{Pb^2+}][\ce{I-}]^2=0.1\times(2S)^2=8.0\times10^{-9}$$

$$4S^2=8.0\times10^{-8}\Rightarrow S^2=2\times10^{-8}\Rightarrow S=\sqrt{2}\times10^{-4}=1.41\times10^{-4}=141\times10^{-6}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

Hence, the answer is 141.

questions.text: The solubility of AgCl will be maximum in which of the following?
questions.solution:
The solubility of AgCl will be maximum in deionized water.

Silver chloride (AgCl) is a sparingly soluble salt. Its solubility in water can be represented by the equilibrium:

$$ \text{AgCl (s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}^+ (aq) + \text{Cl}^- (aq) $$

In the presence of a common ion, the solubility of AgCl decreases due to the common ion effect, which is explained by Le Chatelier's Principle. Here's an analysis of each option:

Option
A: 0.01 M KCl

The presence of additional chloride ions ($\text{Cl}^-$) from KCl will shift the equilibrium to the left, reducing the solubility of AgCl.

Option
B: 0.01 M HCl

Similar to KCl, HCl also provides more chloride ions, which will decrease the solubility of AgCl due to the common ion effect.

Option
C: 0.01 M AgNO$_3$

AgNO$_3$ introduces additional silver ions ($\text{Ag}^+$) into the solution, also shifting the equilibrium to the left, hence decreasing the solubility of AgCl.

Option
D: Deionized water

This option does not introduce additional ions that impact the equilibrium, so there are no additional silver or chloride ions to shift the equilibrium. As a result, the solubility of AgCl will be highest in deionized water, as there is no common ion effect.

Therefore, the solubility of AgCl is highest in deionized water.

questions.text: A solution containing 62 g ethylene glycol in 250 g water is cooled to $$-$$ 10 o C. If K f for water is 1.86 K kg mol $$-$$1 , the amount of water (in g) separated as ice is :
questions.solution:
Ethylene glycol ($\ce{C2H6O2}$, molar mass $62\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$): $n = \dfrac{62}{62} = 1\ \text{mol}$. On cooling, only pure water separates as ice; all the glycol stays in the liquid.

At $-10\ ^\circ\text{C}$, the liquid in equilibrium with ice must have $\Delta T_f = 0 - (-10) = 10\ \text{K}$. If $W$ g of water remains liquid:

$$\Delta T_f = K_f\, m \Rightarrow 10 = 1.86 \times \dfrac{1}{W/1000}$$

$$W = \dfrac{1.86 \times 1000}{10} = 186\ \text{g}$$

Water separated as ice $= 250 - 186 = 64\ \text{g}$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
1 kg of 0.75 molal aqueous solution of sucrose can be cooled up to $$-$$4$$^\circ$$C before freezing. The amount of ice (in g) that will be separated out is __________. (Nearest integer)

[Given : K f (H₂O) = 1.86 K kg mol $$-$$1 ]
questions.solution:
The molar mass of sucrose, $\ce{C12H22O11}$, is $342\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. Let the 1000 g of solution contain $w$ g of water and $n$ mol of sucrose.

Molality gives $\dfrac{n}{w/1000}=0.75$, so $n=7.5\times10^{-4}\,w$; the total mass gives $w+342n=1000$.

$$w(1+0.2565)=1000\Rightarrow w=795.9\ \text{g},\qquad n=0.5969\ \text{mol}$$

On cooling, only pure water separates as ice and all the sucrose stays in the remaining liquid. At $-4\ ^\circ\text{C}$, $\Delta T_f=4\ \text{K}$, so the water left in the solution, $w'$, satisfies

$$4=1.86\times\dfrac{0.5969}{w'}\Rightarrow w'=0.2776\ \text{kg}=277.6\ \text{g}$$

Ice separated $=795.9-277.6=518.3\ \text{g}\approx518\ \text{g}$.

Hence, the answer is 518.

questions.text: A 1 molal K₄Fe(CN) 6 solution has a degree of dissociation of 0.4. $\ce{K4[Fe(CN)6] -> 4K+ + [Fe(CN)6]^4-}$ gives 5 ions, so with $\alpha = 0.4$, $i = 1 + (5 - 1)(0.4) = 2.6$.

Effective molality $= 0.6 + 4(0.4) + 0.4 = 2.6\ \text{m}$ (undissociated salt, $\ce{K+}$ and complex anion).

Equal boiling points need equal effective molality, so the solution of the non-electrolyte A is 2.6 m.

An 18.1 weight percent solution has 18.1 g of A in 100 g of solution, that is in $100 - 18.1 = 81.9\ \text{g} = 0.0819\ \text{kg}$ of water.

$$2.6 = \dfrac{18.1/M}{0.0819} \Rightarrow M = \dfrac{18.1}{2.6 \times 0.0819} = 85.0\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$$

Hence, the answer is 85.

questions.text: In a mixture of A and B, components show negative deviation when :

options.text: A - B interaction is weaker than A - A and B - B interaction
A - B interaction is stronger than A - A and B - B interaction

questions.solution:
In the context of solutions and mixtures, a negative deviation from Raoult's law occurs when the interaction between different molecules (A-B interaction) is stronger than the interaction between similar molecules (A-A and B-B interactions). This is because the molecules prefer to interact with each other rather than themselves, leading to a decrease in the overall vapor pressure compared to what would be expected from Raoult's law.

So, the correct option is :

Option D : A - B interaction is stronger than A - A and B - B interaction

Option A suggests that the change in volume ($\Delta V_{mix}$) and change in entropy ($\Delta S_{mix}$) of the mixture are both greater than zero. This doesn't necessarily indicate a negative deviation from Raoult's law. It's possible for these conditions to be true in both positive and negative deviations or even in ideal solutions. Therefore, this option isn't specifically associated with negative deviations.

Option B suggests that there's no change in the volume of the mixture ($\Delta V_{mix} = 0$) and the change in entropy ($\Delta S_{mix}$) is greater than zero. Again, this doesn't specifically indicate a negative deviation from Raoult's law. The volume change upon mixing can be zero, positive, or negative depending on the nature of the interactions among the molecules.

Raoult's law deviations are primarily dictated by the relative strength of the intermolecular forces among the different components in the mixture. Thus, the change in volume and entropy, while they can be related, do not directly determine whether a solution will show a positive or negative deviation.

questions.text: Liquids A and B form an ideal solution. At $$30^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$$, the total vapour pressure of a solution containing $$1\ \mathrm{mol}$$ of A and $$2\ \mathrm{mol}$$ of B is $$250\ \mathrm{mmHg}$$. The total vapour pressure becomes $$300\ \mathrm{mmHg}$$ when 1 more mol of A is added to the first solution. The vapour pressures of pure A and B at the same temperature are
questions.solution:
Raoult's law: $P = x_A p_A^0 + x_B p_B^0$.

First solution: $x_A = \dfrac{1}{3}$, $x_B = \dfrac{2}{3}$, so $\dfrac{p_A^0}{3} + \dfrac{2p_B^0}{3} = 250$, i.e. $p_A^0 + 2p_B^0 = 750$.

After adding 1 mol of
A: $x_A = x_B = \dfrac{1}{2}$, so $p_A^0 + p_B^0 = 600$.

Subtracting: $p_B^0 = 150\ \mathrm{mmHg}$, and then $p_A^0 = 450\ \mathrm{mmHg}$.

Check: $\dfrac{450 + 2 \times 150}{3} = 250$.

Pure
A: $450\ \mathrm{mmHg}$; pure
B: $150\ \mathrm{mmHg}$.

questions.text: Choose the correct statement with respect to the vapour pressure of a liquid among the following :
questions.solution:
As temperature rises, more molecules have enough kinetic energy to escape the liquid, so vapour pressure increases.

Clausius–Clapeyron equation: $\ln p=-\dfrac{\Delta_{\mathrm{vap}}H}{RT}+C$, i.e. $p=A\,e^{-\Delta_{\mathrm{vap}}H/RT}$

So $p$ grows exponentially with $T$: the $p$–$T$ curve bends upward and is not a straight line (only $\ln p$ against $\dfrac{1}{T}$ is linear).

So vapour pressure increases non-linearly with increasing temperature.

questions.text: For an ideal solution of two components A and B, which of the following is true ?

options.text: A $$-$$ B interaction is stronger than A $$-$$ A and B $$-$$ B interactions
A $$-$$ A, B $$-$$ B and A $$-$$ B interactions are identical

questions.solution:
An ideal solution obeys Raoult's law over the whole range of composition.

This is possible only when the A–B attractions are the same as the A–A and B–B attractions.

Then no heat is absorbed or released and there is no volume change: $\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}H=0$, $\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}V=0$.

$\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}H\lt0$ (stronger A–B attraction) or $\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}H\gt0$ (weaker A–B attraction) means a non-ideal solution.

So in an ideal solution the A–A, B–B and A–B interactions are identical.

questions.text: A solution at 20 o C is composed of 1.5 mol of benzene and 3.5 mol of toluene. If the vapour pressure of pure benzene and pure toluene at this temperature are 74.7 torr and 22.3 torr, respectively, then the total vapour pressure of the solution and the benzene mole fraction in equilibrium with it will be, respectively :
questions.solution:
Mole fractions in the liquid: $x_{\mathrm{B}} = \dfrac{1.5}{5.0} = 0.3$, $x_{\mathrm{T}} = 0.7$.

By Raoult's law, $p_{\mathrm{B}} = 0.3 \times 74.7 = 22.41\ \mathrm{torr}$ and $p_{\mathrm{T}} = 0.7 \times 22.3 = 15.61\ \mathrm{torr}$.

Total pressure: $P_{\mathrm{total}} = 22.41 + 15.61 = 38.02 \approx 38.0\ \mathrm{torr}$.

Mole fraction of benzene in the vapour, $y_{\mathrm{B}} = \dfrac{p_{\mathrm{B}}}{P_{\mathrm{total}}} = \dfrac{22.41}{38.02} = 0.589$.

So the total vapour pressure is $38.0\ \mathrm{torr}$ and the benzene mole fraction in the vapour is $0.589$.

The mole fraction of liquid B is 0.5 in the mixture, The vapour pressure of the final solution, the
mole fractions of components A and B in vapour phase, respectively are :
questions.solution:
Given

$$P_A^0$$ = 400 mm of Hg

$$P_B^0$$ = 600 mm of Hg

Mole fraction of B (x
B) in liquid phase = 0.5

Mole fraction of A (x
A) in liquid phase = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5

Pressure of solution :

P s = x A $$P_A^0$$ + x B $$P_B^0$$

= 0.5 $$ \times $$ 400 + 0.5 $$ \times $$ 600

= 500 mm of Hg

From Raoult's law we know,

Partial pressure of A (P
A) = x A $$P_A^0$$ ......(1)

From Dalton's law we know,

Partial pressure of A (P
A) = y A P s ........(2)

here y A = mole fraction of A in vapour phase

From (1) and (2) we can write,

x A $$P_A^0$$ = y A P s

$$ \Rightarrow $$ y A = $${{{x_A}P_A^0} \over {{P_s}}}$$ = $${{0.5 \times 400} \over {500}}$$ = 0.4

Mole fraction of A in vapour phase = 0.4

$$ \therefore $$ mole fraction of B in vapour phase = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6

Relative lowering in vapour pressure (RLVP)

= $${{P - {P_s}} \over P} = {n \over {n + N}}$$

n $$ \to $$ moles of solute

N $$ \to $$ moles of solvent

$$ \therefore $$ (RLVP) A = $${{{{10} \over {100}}} \over {{{10} \over {100}} + {{180} \over {18}}}}$$

(RLVP) B = $${{{{10} \over {200}}} \over {{{10} \over {200}} + {{180} \over {18}}}}$$

and (RLVP) C = $${{{{10} \over {10000}}} \over {{{10} \over {10000}} + {{180} \over {18}}}}$$

$$ \therefore $$ (RLVP) A > (RLVP) B > (RLVP) C

So, A > B > C

questions.text: At 20$$^\circ$$ C, the vapour pressure of benzene is 70 torr and that of methyl benzene is 20 torr. The mole fraction of benzene in the vapour phase at 20$$^\circ$$C above an equimolar mixture of benzene and methyl benzene is _____________ $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$2 . (Nearest integer)
questions.solution:
Vapour pressure of pure benzene, $$p_A^o$$ = 70 Torr

Vapour pressure of pure methyl benzene, $$p_B^o$$ = 20 Torr

This mixture is equimolar, so number of moles of benzene,

n A = number of moles of methyl benzene, n B

Mole fraction of benzene in vapour phase, y A = $${{{p_A}} \over {{p_T}}}$$ .... (i)

where p A is pressure of benzene in mixture.

$${p_A} = \mathop {p_A^o{\chi _A}}\limits_{Mole\,fraction} = p_A^o \times {{{n_A}} \over {{n_A} + {n_B}}} = p_A^o \times {{{n_A}} \over {2{n_A}}} = {{p_A^o} \over 2}$$

p T is total pressure,

$${p_T} = p_A^o{\chi _A} + p_B^o{\chi _B} = {p_A} + {p_B}$$ (pressure of methyl benzene)

$${p_T} = {{p_A^o} \over 2} + {{p_B^o} \over 2} = {{p_A^o + p_B^o} \over 2}$$

Putting in above equation (i),

$${y_A} = {{{{70} \over 2}} \over {{{(70 + 20)} \over 2}}} = {{70} \over {90}}$$

y A = 0.78 = 78 $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$2

questions.text: A solution containing $$0.85\ \mathrm{g}$$ of $$\mathrm{ZnCl_2}$$ in $$125.0\ \mathrm{g}$$ of water freezes at $$-0.23^\circ\mathrm{C}$$. The apparent degree of dissociation of the salt is ($$K_f$$ for water $$= 1.86\ \mathrm{K\,kg\,mol^{-1}}$$, atomic mass: $$\mathrm{Zn} = 65.3$$ and $$\mathrm{Cl} = 35.5$$)
questions.solution:
Molar mass of $\mathrm{ZnCl_2} = 65.3 + 2 \times 35.5 = 136.3\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.

Molality $m = \dfrac{0.85/136.3}{0.125} = 0.0499\ \mathrm{mol\,kg^{-1}}$.

Without dissociation, $\Delta T_f = K_f m = 1.86 \times 0.0499 = 0.0928\ \mathrm{K}$.

van 't Hoff factor $i = \dfrac{0.23}{0.0928} \approx 2.48$.

$\mathrm{ZnCl_2 \rightarrow Zn^{2+} + 2Cl^-}$ gives $3$ ions, so $i = 1 + 2\alpha$ and $\alpha = \dfrac{2.48 - 1}{2} \approx 0.74$.

So the apparent degree of dissociation is about $74\%$, which matches $73.5\%$.

questions.text: A molecule M associates in a given solvent according to the equation $$M \rightleftharpoons (M)_n$$. For a certain concentration of M, the van't Hoff factor was found to be 0.9 and the fraction of associated molecules was 0.2. The value of n is:
questions.solution:
Let $\alpha = 0.2$ be the fraction of M that associates; $n$ molecules form one $(\mathrm{M})_n$.

Particles from 1 mol of M: $1 - \alpha + \dfrac{\alpha}{n}$, so $i = 1 - \alpha + \dfrac{\alpha}{n}$.

$0.9 = 1 - 0.2 + \dfrac{0.2}{n}$.

$\dfrac{0.2}{n} = 0.1$, so $n = 2$.

$\mathrm{Fe(NH_4)_2(SO_4)_2\to Fe^{2+}+2NH_4^{+}+2SO_4^{2-}}$: $1+2+2=5$ ions, so expected $i=5$.

Where

m = molality of solute

K f = freezing point depression constant.

In this question m = 1 and K f is constant.

So, $$\Delta {T_f}\,\, \propto \,\,i$$

Which solutions have more i, those solutions $$\Delta {T_f}\,$$ will be more.

Now,

Freezing point of an aqueous solution $${f_p} = \, - \,\Delta {T_f}$$

Value of i = 3

Value of i = 2

and [ Co(H₂O) 3 Cl 3 ] . 3H 2 O do not show ionization.

So, its freezing point will be maximum.

Molality of diluted milk,

In a solvent 50% of an acid HA dimerizes and the rest dissociates. The van't Hoff factor of the acid is __________ $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$2 .

(Round off to the nearest integer)
questions.solution:
Let the initial amount of HA be $a$ mol; $0.5a$ mol dimerises and the remaining $0.5a$ mol dissociates.

Dimerisation, $\ce{2HA <=> (HA)2}$, turns $0.5a$ mol of HA into $0.25a$ mol of dimer.

Dissociation, $\ce{HA <=> H+ + A-}$, turns the other $0.5a$ mol of HA into $0.5a$ mol of $\ce{H+}$ and $0.5a$ mol of $\ce{A-}$.

Total particles $= 0.25a + 0.5a + 0.5a = 1.25a$.

$$i = \dfrac{1.25a}{a} = 1.25 = 125 \times 10^{-2}$$

Hence, the answer is 125.

questions.text: Which one of the following 0.06 M aqueous solutions has lowest freezing point?
questions.solution:
To determine which solution has the lowest freezing point, you should consider the van 't Hoff factor $i$, which represents the number of particles the solute dissociates into when dissolved. The freezing point depression is given by:

$$ \Delta T_f = i \cdot K_f \cdot m $$

where:

$\Delta T_f$ is the change in freezing point,

$K_f$ is the freezing point depression constant,

$m$ is the molality of the solution,

$i$ is the van 't Hoff factor, which depends on the dissociation of the solute.

For each solute, the van 't Hoff factor $i$ can be determined as follows:

Option
A: $\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$

Dissociates into 2 Al$^{3+}$ ions and 3 SO$_4^{2-}$ ions.

$i = 2 + 3 = 5$

Option
B: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$ (glucose)

Does not dissociate in solution (non-electrolyte).

$i = 1$

Option
C: $\text{KI}$

Dissociates into K$^+$ and I$^-$ ions.

$i = 1 + 1 = 2$

Option
D: $\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4$

Dissociates into 2 K$^+$ ions and 1 SO$_4^{2-}$ ion.

$i = 2 + 1 = 3$

Comparing the van 't Hoff factors, the solution of $\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$ will have the highest factor ($i = 5$), leading to the greatest freezing point depression. Thus, the $\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$ solution will have the lowest freezing point since the extent of freezing point depression is directly proportional to $i$.

Therefore, the solution of $\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$ has the lowest freezing point.

(Assume solubility of $$\mathrm{O}_{2}$$ in water is too small, nearly negligible)

$$\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{H}} \times \mathrm{X}$$

$0.920 \mathrm{bar}=46.82 \times 10^{3}\, \mathrm{bar} \times \frac{\mathrm{mol} \,\mathrm{of} \,\mathrm{O}_{2}}{\mathrm{~mol} \text { of } \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}}$

$$\Rightarrow n_{O_{2}} = 1.09 \times 10^{-3}$$

$$\Rightarrow \mathrm{m}\, \mathrm{mol}\, \mathrm{of}\, \mathrm{O}_{2}=1$$

questions.text:
An ideal gas undergoes isothermal expansion at constant pressure. During
the process :

options.text: enthalpy remains constant but entropy increases.
Both enthalpy and entropy remain constant.

questions.solution:
In an isothermal expansion process, the temperature of the system remains constant throughout the process. Since, for an ideal gas, U depends only on temperature, we have $$\Delta$$U = 0. The enthalpy change of the system in isothermal expansion is also zero as

$$\Delta$$H = $$\Delta$$U + nR$$\Delta$$T = 0 + 0 = 0

The entropy change foe an isothermal process is given by

$$\Delta S = nR\ln \left( {{{{V_f}} \over {{V_i}}}} \right) \ge 0$$

questions.text:
For one mole of an ideal gas, which of these
statements must be true?

(a) U and H each depends only on temperature

(b) Compressibility factor z is not equal to 1

(c) C P, m – C V, m = R

(d) dU = C V dT for any process
questions.solution:
An ideal gas has no intermolecular forces, so $U$ depends only on $T$; for one mole $H = U + PV = U + RT$, which also depends only on $T$. The nature of the gas fixes the value of $C_V$, not the variables on which $U$ depends. Statement (a) is true.

$PV_m = RT$ in every state, so $Z = \dfrac{PV_m}{RT} = 1$. Statement (b) is false.

$C_{P,m} - C_{V,m} = \dfrac{dH}{dT} - \dfrac{dU}{dT} = \dfrac{d(RT)}{dT} = R$. Statement (c) is true.

Since $U$ depends only on $T$, $dU = \left(\dfrac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V dT = C_V\,dT$ for any change of the ideal gas, whatever the process. Statement (d) is true.

The true statements are (a), (c) and (d).

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
The entropy change associated with the conversion of 1 kg of ice at 273 K to water vapours at 383 K is :

(Specific heat of water liquid and water vapour are 4.2 kJ K $$-$$1 kg $$-$$1 and 2.0 kJ K $$-$$1 kg $$-$$1 ; heat of liquid fusion and vapourisation of water are 334 kJ kg $$-$$1 and 2491 kJ kg $$-$$1 , respectively). (log 273 = 2.436, log 373 = 2.572, log 383 = 2.583)
questions.solution:
The change is carried out in four steps, each for 1 kg.

Melting of ice at 273 K: $\Delta S_1 = \dfrac{\Delta_{fus}H}{T} = \dfrac{334}{273} = 1.223\ \text{kJ kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

Heating water from 273 K to 373 K: $\Delta S_2 = c\ln\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 4.2 \times 2.303 \times (2.572 - 2.436) = 1.315\ \text{kJ kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

Vaporisation at 373 K: $\Delta S_3 = \dfrac{\Delta_{vap}H}{T} = \dfrac{2491}{373} = 6.678\ \text{kJ kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

Heating vapour from 373 K to 383 K: $\Delta S_4 = 2.0 \times 2.303 \times (2.583 - 2.572) = 0.051\ \text{kJ kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

$$\Delta S_{\text{total}} = 1.223 + 1.315 + 6.678 + 0.051 = 9.267\ \text{kJ kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$$

This is 9.26 $\text{kJ kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ within the rounding of the given logarithms; the other options are far from it.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: A heat engine absorbs heat Q 1 at temperature T 1 and heat Q 2 at temperature T 2 . Work done by the engine is J (Q 1 + Q 2 ). This data :

options.text: violates 1 st law of thermodynamics if Q 1 is +ve
violates 1 st law of thermodynamics if Q 1 is -ve
does not violate 1 st law of thermodynamics

questions.solution:
For a complete cycle of the engine the change in internal energy is zero, so by the first law of thermodynamics the work done equals the net heat absorbed.

With $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ in heat units and $J$ the mechanical equivalent of heat, $W = J(Q_1 + Q_2)$ is exactly this energy balance, whatever the signs of $Q_1$ and $Q_2$.

Converting all the absorbed heat into work without rejecting any would conflict with the second law, not the first.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The internal energy change when a system goes from state A to B is 40 kJ/mole. If the system goes from A to B by a reversible path and returns to state A by an irreversible path what would be the net change in internal energy?
questions.solution: For a cyclic process the net change in the internal energy is zero because the change in internal energy does not depend on the path.

questions.text: An ideal gas expands in volume from 1$$\times$$10 -3 m 3 to 1 $$\times$$ 10 -2 m 3 at 300 K against a constant pressure of 1$$\times$$10 5 Nm -2 . The work done is :

An ideal gas is allowed to expand both reversibly and irreversibly in an isolated system. If T i is the
initial temperature and T f is the final temperature, which of the following statements is correct?

options.text:
T f > T i
for reversible process but T f = T i
for irreversible process
T f = T i for both reversible and irreversible processes

questions.solution:
The system is thermally isolated, so $q = 0$ and $\Delta U = w$ for both expansions, with $\Delta U = nC_V\,\Delta T$ for an ideal gas.

For the same expansion, the reversible path works against the largest possible opposing pressure (equal to the gas pressure at every stage), so the gas does more work than in the irreversible expansion against a smaller external pressure.

More work done by the gas means a larger fall in internal energy and hence in temperature, so $(T_f)_{\text{rev}} < (T_f)_{\text{irrev}}$, with both below $T_i$.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
The difference between the reaction enthalpy change $$(\Delta_r H)$$ and reaction internal energy change $$(\Delta_r U)$$ for the reaction:
$$\mathrm{2C_6H_6(l) + 15O_2(g) \longrightarrow 12CO_2(g) + 6H_2O(l)}$$
at $$300\ \mathrm{K}$$ is $$(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}})$$
questions.solution:
$\Delta_r H - \Delta_r U = \Delta n_g RT$, where only gaseous species are counted.

Gaseous products: $12$ mol of $\mathrm{CO_2}$; gaseous reactants: $15$ mol of $\mathrm{O_2}$ (benzene and water are liquids).

$\Delta n_g = 12 - 15 = -3$.

$\Delta_r H - \Delta_r U = -3 \times 8.314 \times 300 = -7482.6\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$.

So the difference is about $-7482\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$.

questions.text: Which of the following statements/relationships is not correct in thermodynamic changes?

options.text: $$\Delta U = 0$$ (isothermal reversible expansion of a gas)
$$w = -nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}$$ (isothermal reversible expansion of an ideal gas)
$$w = nRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}$$ (isothermal reversible expansion of an ideal gas)
For a system of constant volume heat involved directly changes to internal energy.

questions.solution:
For an ideal gas $U$ depends only on $T$, so $\Delta U = 0$ in an isothermal expansion: correct.

Reversible isothermal work: $w = -\int p\,dV = -nRT\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}$, negative because the gas does work: correct.

Hence $w = +nRT\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}$ has the wrong sign: not correct.

At constant volume $w = 0$, so $q_V = \Delta U$: correct.

The incorrect relation is $w = nRT\ln\dfrac{V_2}{V_1}$ for isothermal reversible expansion of an ideal gas.

If 100 mole of H₂O₂ decompose at 1 bar and 300 K, the work done (kJ) by one mole of O 2 (g) as it expands against 1 bar pressure is :

2H 2 O 2 (l)    $$\rightleftharpoons$$    2H 2 O(l) + O 2 (g)

(R = 8.3 J K $$-$$1 mol $$-$$1 )
questions.solution:
For reaction : 2H 2 O 2 (l) $$\rightleftharpoons$$ 2H 2 O(l) + O 2 (g)

Given, p = 1 bar, T = 300 K, R = 8.3 J K $$-$$1 mol $$-$$1

From the equation, 2 mol of H₂O₂ give 1 mol of O 2 , so 100 mol of H₂O₂ give n = 50 mol of O 2 (g), the only gas formed (the volumes of the liquids are negligible).

Work done by the O 2 as it expands against the constant pressure:

= 50 $$\times$$ 8.3 $$\times$$ 300

= 124500 J or 124.5 kJ

(This is the work done by all the O 2 formed. For just one mole of O 2 it would be 2.49 kJ, which is not among the options, so the options refer to the total work.)

questions.text:
A gas undergoes change from state A to state B. In this process, the heat absorbed
and work done by the gas is 5 J and 8 J, respectively. Now gas is brought back to
A by another process during which 3 J of heat is evolved. In this reverse process of
B to A :

options.text: 10 J of the work will be done by the gas.
6 J of the work will be done by the gas.
10 J of the work will be done by the surrounding on gas.
6 J of the work will be done by the surrounding on gas.

questions.solution:
From first law of thermodynamics, we have

$$\Delta$$U = q + w

$$\bullet$$ For state A to
B: q = +5 J, w = $$-$$8 J and

$$\Delta$$U AB = 5 + ($$-$$8) = $$-$$3 J

$$\bullet$$ For state B to
A: q = $$-$$3 J

Since the internal energy is a state function, we have $$\Delta$$U BA = $$-$$ $$\Delta$$U AB . Therefore,

$$\Delta$$U BA = q + w

3 = $$-$$3 + w $$\Rightarrow$$ w = 6 J

Positive value of work indicates that 6 J of work is done by the surrounding on gas.

For adiabatic process :

q = 0

questions.text:
Which one of the following equations does not correctly represent the first law of thermodynamics
for the given processes involving an ideal gas? (Assume non-expansion work is zero)
questions.solution:
From 1 st law of thermodynamics we know,

$$\Delta $$U = q + W

Option
A: In adiabatic process exchage of heat = 0

$$ \therefore $$ q = 0

$$ \therefore $$ From 1st law of thermodynaics, $$\Delta $$U = W

So option A is wrong.

Option
B: U is a state function. In cyclic process, initial state and final state both are same. So change in all the state function in cyclic process will be zero.

$$ \therefore $$ $$\Delta $$U = 0

$$ \therefore $$ From 1st law of thermodynaics,

q + W = 0 $$ \Rightarrow $$ q = -W

So option B is correct..

Option
C: In isochoric process volume (V) is constant. So dV = 0.

We know, W = $$ - \int {{P_{ex}}} dV$$

$$ \therefore $$ W = 0

$$ \therefore $$ From 1st law of thermodynaics,

$$\Delta $$U = q

So option C is correct.

Option
D: In isothermal process temerature (T) is constant. So dT = 0.

We know, $$\Delta $$U = nC v dT

$$ \therefore $$ $$\Delta $$U = 0

$$ \therefore $$ From 1st law of thermodynaics,

q + W = 0 $$ \Rightarrow $$ q = -W

So option D is correct.

questions.text: A system does 200 J of work and at the same time absorbs 150 J of heat. The magnitude of the change in internal energy is ____________ J. (Nearest integer)

At 25$$^\circ$$C, 50 g of iron reacts with HCl to form FeCl 2 . The evolved hydrogen gas expands against a constant pressure of 1 bar. The work done by the gas during this expansion is _________ J. (Round off to the Nearest Integer).

[Given : R = 8.314 J mol $$-$$1 K $$-$$1 . Assume, hydrogen is an ideal gas] [Atomic mass of Fe is 55.85 u]
questions.solution:
$$\ce{Fe + 2HCl -> FeCl2 + H2}$$

One mole of Fe gives one mole of $\ce{H2}$:

$$n_{\ce{H2}} = n_{\ce{Fe}} = \dfrac{50}{55.85} = 0.8953\ \text{mol}$$

Only $\ce{H2}$ is a gas (HCl and $\ce{FeCl2}$ are in aqueous solution), so the volume increase is the volume of hydrogen formed at $p_{\text{ext}} = 1$ bar: $\Delta V = \dfrac{n_{\ce{H2}}RT}{p_{\text{ext}}}$.

The work done by the gas against the constant external pressure is

$$w_{\text{by gas}} = p_{\text{ext}}\Delta V = n_{\ce{H2}}RT = 0.8953 \times 8.314 \times 298 = 2218\ \text{J}$$

In the chemistry sign convention, the corresponding work done on the system is $w = -2218$ J.

Hence, the answer is 2218.

questions.text: Five moles of an ideal gas at 293 K is expanded isothermally from an initial pressure of 2.1 MPa to 1.3 MPa against at constant external pressure 4.3 MPa. The heat transferred in this process is _________ kJ mol $$-$$1 . (Rounded off to the nearest integer) [Use R = 8.314 J mol $$-$$1 K $$-$$1 ]
questions.solution:
The gas performs isothermal irreversible work (W).

where, $$\Delta$$U = 0 (change in internal energy)

From, 1st law of thermodynamics,

$$\Rightarrow$$ $$\Delta$$U = $$\Delta$$Q + W

$$\Rightarrow$$ 0 = $$\Delta$$Q + W

$$\Rightarrow$$ $$\Delta$$Q = $$-$$W

Now, $$W = - {p_{ext}}({V_2} - {V_1})$$

$$ = - {p_{ext}}\left( {{{nRT} \over {{p_2}}} - {{nRT} \over {{p_1}}}} \right) = - {p_{ext}} \times nRT\left( {{1 \over {{p_2}}} - {1 \over {{p_1}}}} \right)$$

Given, p ext = 4.3 MPa, p 1 = 2.1 MPa, p 2 = 1.3 MPa, n = 5 mol, T = 293 K and R = 8.314 J mol $$-$$1 K $$-$$1

$$ = - 4.3 \times 5 \times 8.314 \times 293\left( {{1 \over {1.3}} - {1 \over {2.1}}} \right)$$

= $$-$$ 15347.70 J mol $$-$$1

= $$-$$ 15.347 kJ mol $$-$$1 $$ \simeq $$ $$-$$ 15 kJ mol $$-$$1

$$\Rightarrow$$ $$\Delta$$Q = 15 kJ mol $$-$$1

questions.text:
The reaction of cyanamide, NH 2 CN (s) with oxygen was run in a bomb calorimeter and $$\Delta$$U was found to be $$-$$742.24 kJ mol $$-$$1 . The magnitude of $$\Delta$$H 298 for the reaction

is _________ kJ. (Rounded off to the nearest integer) [Assume ideal gases and R = 8.314 J mol $$-$$1 K $$-$$1 ]
questions.solution:
$$N{H_2}CN(s) + {3 \over 2}{O_2}(g)\buildrel {} \over
\longrightarrow {N_2}(g) + C{O_2}(g) + {H_2}O(l)$$

$$\Delta ng = (1 + 1) - {3 \over 2} = {1 \over 2}$$

$$\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta ng\,RT$$

$$ = - 742.24 + {1 \over 2} \times {{8.314 \times 298} \over {1000}}$$

$$ = - 742.24 + 1.24$$

$$ = -741$$ kJ/mol

questions.text: A gas (Molar mass = 280 $$\mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$$) was burnt in excess $$\mathrm{O}_{2}$$ in a constant volume calorimeter and during combustion the temperature of calorimeter increased from $$298.0 \mathrm{~K}$$ to $$298.45$$ $$\mathrm{K}$$. If the heat capacity of calorimeter is $$2.5 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$$ and enthalpy of combustion of gas is $$9 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$$ then amount of gas burnt is _____________ g. The change in internal energy is $$5000 \mathrm{~J}$$ upon heating it from $$300 \mathrm{~K}$$ to $$500 \mathrm{~K}$$. The number of moles of the gas at constant volume is ____________. questions.solution:
$\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{p}}=20.785 \mathrm{~J} \mathrm{~K}^{-1} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\text { and } \Delta \mathrm{U}=\mathrm{nC}_{\mathrm{v}} \Delta \mathrm{T} \\\\
&\therefore \quad \mathrm{nC}_{\mathrm{v}}=\frac{5000}{200}=25
\end{aligned}
$$

and we know that

\begin{aligned}
&C_{p}-C_{v}=R \\\\
&20.785-\frac{25}{n}=8.314 \\\\
&n=\frac{25}{(20.785-8.314)}=2

$$

questions.text: The enthalpy of neutralisation of $$\mathrm{NH_4OH}$$ with $$\mathrm{HCl}$$ is $$-51.46\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}$$ and the enthalpy of neutralisation of $$\mathrm{NaOH}$$ with $$\mathrm{HCl}$$ is $$-55.90\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}$$. The enthalpy of ionisation of $$\mathrm{NH_4OH}$$ is
questions.solution:
For a strong acid with a strong base, $\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$ releases $55.90\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}$.

With the weak base $\mathrm{NH_4OH}$, part of this heat is used first to ionise it: $\Delta H_{\text{neut}} = \Delta H_{\text{ion}} + (-55.90)$.

$-51.46 = \Delta H_{\text{ion}} - 55.90 \Rightarrow \Delta H_{\text{ion}} = +4.44\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}$.

Ionisation absorbs heat, so a positive value is expected.

The enthalpy of ionisation of $\mathrm{NH_4OH}$ is $+4.44\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}$.

questions.text: The standard enthalpy of formation ($$\Delta $$ f H o 298 ) for methane, CH 4 is $$-$$74.9 kJ mol $$-$$1 . In order to calculate the average energy given out in the formation of a C $$-$$ H bond from this it is necessary to know which one of the following ?

options.text: the dissociation energy of the hydrogen molecule, H 2 .
the first four ionisation energies of carbon.
the dissociation energy of H 2 and enthalpy of sublimation of carbon (graphite) :
the first four ionisation energies of carbon and electron affinity of hydrogen.

questions.solution:
Formation: $\mathrm{C(graphite) + 2H_2(g) \to CH_4(g)}$, $\Delta_f H^\circ = -74.9\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

Bond energy refers to gaseous atoms: $\mathrm{C(g) + 4H(g) \to CH_4(g)}$, $\Delta H = -4\varepsilon_{\mathrm{C-H}}$.

Turning the reactants into gaseous atoms needs $\Delta_{\mathrm{sub}}H$ of graphite ($\mathrm{C(s) \to C(g)}$) and $2\Delta_{\mathrm{diss}}H$ of $\mathrm{H_2}$ ($\mathrm{H_2 \to 2H}$).

By Hess's law, $-4\varepsilon_{\mathrm{C-H}} = \Delta_f H^\circ - \Delta_{\mathrm{sub}}H - 2\Delta_{\mathrm{diss}}H$; no ions are involved, so ionisation energies and electron affinity are not needed.

So the dissociation energy of $\mathrm{H_2}$ and the enthalpy of sublimation of graphite must be known.

questions.text: The standard enthalpy of formation of NH 3 is $$-$$ 46.0 kJ/mol. If the enthalpy of formation of H 2 from its atoms is $$-$$ 436 kJ/mol and that of N 2 is $$-$$ 712 kJ/mol, the average bond enthalpy of N $$-$$ H bond in NH 3 is :
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{N_2} + \dfrac{3}{2}\mathrm{H_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{NH_3}$, $\Delta_f H = -46.0\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

From the data, bond dissociation enthalpies are $\mathrm{H-H} = 436$ and $\mathrm{N \equiv N} = 712\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

$\Delta_f H = \left[\dfrac{1}{2}(712) + \dfrac{3}{2}(436)\right] - 3x$, where $x$ is the $\mathrm{N-H}$ bond enthalpy.

$-46 = 356 + 654 - 3x \Rightarrow 3x = 1056$

$x = +352\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$

So the average $\mathrm{N-H}$ bond enthalpy in $\mathrm{NH_3}$ is $+352\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

questions.text: The heat of atomization of methane and ethane are 360 kJ/mol and 620 kJ/mol, respectively. The longest wavelength of light capable of breaking the C - C bond is (Avogadro number = 6.02 $$ \times $$ 10 23 , h = 6.62 $$ \times $$ 10 $$-$$34 J s) :

From methane: $4E_{\mathrm{C-H}} = 360$, so $E_{\mathrm{C-H}} = 90\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

From ethane: $E_{\mathrm{C-C}} + 6E_{\mathrm{C-H}} = 620$, so $E_{\mathrm{C-C}} = 620 - 540 = 80\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

Energy needed per bond $= \dfrac{80 \times 10^{3}}{6.02 \times 10^{23}} = 1.33 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$.

$\lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{hc}{E} = \dfrac{6.62 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{1.33 \times 10^{-19}} = 1.49 \times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$.

So the longest wavelength is $1.49 \times 10^{3}\ \mathrm{nm}$.

questions.text: At 298 K, the enthalpy of fusion of a solid (X) is 2.8 kJ mol $$-$$1 and the enthalpy of vaporisation of the liquid (X) is 98.2 kJ mol $$-$$1 . The enthalpy of sublimation of the substance (X) in kJ mol $$-$$1 is _____________. (in nearest integer)
questions.solution:
The enthalpy of sublimation is the total amount of energy required to convert a solid directly into a gas. This can be calculated by summing the enthalpy of fusion (solid to liquid) and the enthalpy of vaporization (liquid to gas). Mathematically, this relationship is represented as:

$$ \Delta H_{\text{sublimation}} = \Delta H_{\text{fusion}} + \Delta H_{\text{vaporization}} $$

Given:

Enthalpy of fusion, $$\Delta H_{\text{fusion}} = 2.8 \, \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Enthalpy of vaporization, $$\Delta H_{\text{vaporization}} = 98.2 \, \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Substitute these values into the equation:

$$ \Delta H_{\text{sublimation}} = 2.8 \, \text{kJ mol}^{-1} + 98.2 \, \text{kJ mol}^{-1} = 101.0 \, \text{kJ mol}^{-1} $$

Therefore, the enthalpy of sublimation of the substance (X) is approximately 101 kJ mol $$-1$$ .

Bonds broken in $\ce{C2H6}$, one $\ce{C-C}$ and six $\ce{C-H}$:

Bonds formed, one $\ce{C=C}$ and four $\ce{C-H}$ in $\ce{C2H4}$ and one $\ce{H-H}$ in $\ce{H2}$:

questions.text: If an endothermic reaction is non-spontaneous at freezing point of water and becomes feasible at its boiling point, then :
questions.solution:
TIPS/Formulae :

$$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$$

Since $$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$$ for an endothermic reaction,

$$\Delta H = + ve$$ and at low temperature $$\Delta S = + ve$$

Hence $$\Delta G = \left( + \right)\Delta H - T\left( + \right)\Delta S$$

and if $$T\Delta S < \Delta H$$ (at low temp)

$$\Delta G = + ve$$ (non spontaneous)

But at high temperature, reaction becomes

spontaneous i.e. $$\Delta G = - ve.$$

because at higher temperature $$T\Delta S > \Delta H.$$

questions.solution: For spontaneous reaction, $$dS > 0$$ and $$dG$$ should be negative i.e. $$ < 0.$$

questions.text:
In conversion of lime-stone to lime,

CaCO 3 (s) $$\to$$ CaO(s) + CO 2 (g) the vales of ∆H° and ∆S° are +179.1 kJ mol−1
and 160.2 J/K respectively at 298 K and 1 bar.
Assuming that ∆H° do not change with temperature, temperature above which conversion of
limestone to lime will be spontaneous is :
questions.solution:
$$\Delta {G^ \circ } = \Delta {H^ \circ } - T\Delta {S^ \circ }$$

For a spontaneous reaction $$\Delta {G^ \circ } < 0$$

or $$\,\,\,\Delta {H^ \circ } - T\Delta {S^ \circ } < 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow T > {{\Delta {H^ \circ }} \over {\Delta {S^ \circ }}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow T > {{179.3 \times {{10}^3}} \over {160.2}} > 1117.9K \approx 1118K$$

questions.text:
Standard entropy of X 2 , Y 2 and XY 3 are 60, 40 and 50 JK −1
mol −1 , respectively. For the reaction,

$${1 \over 2} X_2$$ + $${3 \over 2} Y_2 \to$$ XY 3 , $$\Delta H$$ = -30 kJ, to be at equilibrium, the temperature will be :
questions.solution:
For a reaction to be at equilibrium $$\Delta G = 0.$$

Since $$\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$$

so at equilibrium $$\Delta H - T\Delta S = 0$$

or $$\,\,\,\,\Delta H = T\Delta S$$

For the reaction

$${1 \over 2}{X_2} + {3 \over 2}{Y_2} \to X{Y_3};\,\,\,$$

$$\Delta H = - 30kJ\,\,\left( {given} \right)$$

Calculating $$\Delta S$$ for the above reaction, we get

$$\Delta S = 50 - \left[ {{1 \over 2} \times 60 + {3 \over 2} \times 40} \right]J{K^{ - 1}}$$

$$ = 50 - \left( {30 + 60} \right)J{K^{ - 1}}$$

$$ = - 40\,J{K^{ - 1}}$$

At equilibrium, $$\,\,\,T\Delta S = \Delta H$$

[ as $$\,\,\,\Delta G = 0$$ ]

$$\therefore$$ $$\,\,\,\,\,$$ $$T \times \left( { - 40} \right) = - 30 \times 1000$$

[ as $$1kJ=1000J$$ ]

or $$\,\,\,\,\,$$ $$T = {{ - 30 \times 1000} \over { - 40}}$$

or $$\,\,\,\,\,$$ = $$750$$ $$K$$

questions.text:
For a particular reversible reaction at temperature T, ∆H and ∆S were found to be both +ve. If T e is
the temperature at equilibrium, the reaction would be spontaneous when :
questions.solution:
At equilibrium $$\Delta G = 0$$

Hence, $$\Delta G = \Delta H - {T_e}\Delta S = 0$$

$$\therefore$$ $$\,\,\,\,\,\,\Delta H = {T_e}\Delta S\,\,\,$$

or $$\,\,\,\,{T_e} = {{\Delta H} \over {\Delta S}}\,\,$$

For a spontaneous reaction

$$\Delta G$$ must be negative

which is possible only if $$\Delta H < T\Delta S$$

or $$\,\,\,T > {{\Delta H} \over {\Delta S}};{T_e} < T$$

questions.text:
The entropy change involved in the isothermal reversible expansion of 2 moles of an ideal gas from a
volume of 10 dm 3 to a volume of 100 dm 3 at 27 o C is :
questions.solution:
Entropy change for an isothermal reversible process is given by

$$\Delta S = nR{\mkern 1mu} ln{{{V_2}} \over {{V_1}}}$$

$$ = 2 \times 8.314 \times 2.303log\,{{100} \over {10}}$$

$$ = 38.3\,J\,mo{l^{ - 1}}\,\,{K^{ - 1}}$$

questions.text: One mole of an ideal gas is expanded isothermally and reversibly to half of its initial pressure. $$\Delta S$$ for the process in $$\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$$ is [$$\ln 2 = 0.693$$ and $$R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$$]
questions.solution:
For an isothermal reversible change of an ideal gas, $\Delta S = nR\ln\dfrac{P_1}{P_2}$.

Here $n = 1$ and $\dfrac{P_1}{P_2} = 2$.

$\Delta S = 8.314 \times 0.693 = 5.76\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$

Check: $\Delta S = \dfrac{q_{rev}}{T} = \dfrac{RT\ln 2}{T} = R\ln 2$, the same value.

Hence $\Delta S = 5.76\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$.

questions.text: The entropy of a sample of a certain substance increases by $$0.836\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$$ on adding reversibly $$0.3344\ \mathrm{J}$$ of heat at constant temperature. The temperature of the sample is:
questions.solution:
For reversible heat transfer at constant temperature, $\Delta S = \dfrac{q_\mathrm{rev}}{T}$.

So $T = \dfrac{q_\mathrm{rev}}{\Delta S} = \dfrac{0.3344}{0.836}\ \mathrm{K} = 0.4\ \mathrm{K}$.

Check: $0.836\times0.4 = 0.3344$, which is the heat supplied.

So the temperature of the sample is $0.4\ \mathrm{K}$.

questions.text:
The entropy (S 0 ) of the following substances are :

CH 4   (g) 186.2 J K $$-$$1  mol $$-$$1

O 2      (g) 205.0 J K $$-$$1  mol $$-$$1

CO 2   (g) 213.6 J K $$-$$1  mol $$-$$1

H₂O  ($$l$$) 69.9 J K $$-$$1  mol $$-$$1

The entropy change ($$\Delta $$S o ) for the reaction

CH 4 (g) + 2O 2 (g)  $$ \to $$ CO 2 (g) + 2H 2 O($$l$$)  is :
questions.solution:
$\Delta S^\circ = \sum S^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum S^\circ(\text{reactants})$.

Products: $213.6 + 2(69.9) = 353.4\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$.

Reactants: $186.2 + 2(205.0) = 596.2\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$.

$\Delta S^\circ = 353.4 - 596.2 = -242.8\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$.

So the entropy change for the reaction is $-242.8\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$.

questions.text:
The molar heat capacity (C p ) of CD 2 O is 10 cals at 1000 K. The change in entropy associated with cooling of 32 g of CD 2 O vapour from 1000 K to 100 K at constant pressure will be :

(D = deuterium, at. mass = 2 u)
questions.solution:
Molar mass of $\mathrm{CD_2O}$ $= 12 + 2(2) + 16 = 32\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$, so $n = 1\ \mathrm{mol}$.

At constant pressure (taking $C_p$ as constant), $\Delta S = nC_p\ln\dfrac{T_2}{T_1} = 2.303\,nC_p\log\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$.

$\Delta S = 2.303 \times 1 \times 10 \times \log\dfrac{100}{1000} = 2.303 \times 10 \times (-1)$.

$\Delta S = -23.03\ \mathrm{cal\,K^{-1}}$; it is negative because the vapour is cooled.

So the entropy change is $-23.03\ \mathrm{cal\,deg^{-1}}$.

questions.text:
A reaction at 1 bar is non-spontaneous at low temperature but becomes spontaneous
at high temperature. Identify the correct statement about the reaction among the
following :
questions.solution:
We know that $$\Delta$$G = $$\Delta$$H $$-$$ T$$\Delta$$S

At low temperature : $$\Delta$$G is positive (non-spontaneous process), so $$\Delta$$H is positive and $$\Delta$$S is positive (T$$\Delta$$S < $$\Delta$$H as T is low).

At high temperature : $$\Delta$$G is negative (spontaneous process), so $$\Delta$$H is positive and $$\Delta$$S is positive (T$$\Delta$$S > $$\Delta$$H as T is high).

questions.text: At 320 K, a gas A 2 is 20% dissociated to A(g). The standard free energy change at 320 K and 1 atm in J mol -1 is approximately : (R = 8.314 JK -1 mol -1 ; ln2 = 0.693; ln 3 = 1.098)
questions.solution:
$$\ce{A2(g) <=> 2A(g)}$$

Starting from $1\ \text{mol}$ of $\ce{A2}$ with $20\%$ dissociation, at equilibrium $n_{\ce{A2}} = 0.8\ \text{mol}$ and $n_{\ce{A}} = 0.4\ \text{mol}$, total $1.2\ \text{mol}$.

At a total pressure of $1\ \text{atm}$:

$$p_{\ce{A}} = \frac{0.4}{1.2} = \frac{1}{3}\ \text{atm},\qquad p_{\ce{A2}} = \frac{0.8}{1.2} = \frac{2}{3}\ \text{atm}$$

$$K_p = \frac{p_{\ce{A}}^2}{p_{\ce{A2}}} = \frac{1/9}{2/3} = \frac{1}{6}$$

$$\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K_p = RT\ln 6 = 8.314\times320\times(0.693 + 1.098) = 2660.5\times1.791 \approx 4765\ \text{J mol}^{-1}$$

The nearest option is $4763\ \text{J mol}^{-1}$.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

For the equilibrium,

2H 2 O $$\rightleftharpoons$$ H₃O + + OH $$-$$ , the value of $$\Delta $$G o at 298 K is approximately :
questions.solution:
For $\ce{2H2O <=> H3O+ + OH-}$, the activity of pure water is 1, so at 298 K

$$K = [\ce{H3O+}][\ce{OH-}] = K_w = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}$$

$$\Delta G^\circ = -2.303RT\log K = -2.303 \times 8.314 \times 298 \times \log\left(10^{-14}\right)$$

$$\Delta G^\circ = 5705.8 \times 14\ \text{J mol}^{-1} \approx 7.99 \times 10^{4}\ \text{J mol}^{-1} \approx 80\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

The large positive value matches the very small extent of self-ionisation of water.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
For the chemical reaction X $$\rightleftharpoons$$ Y, the standard reaction Gibbs energy depends on temperature T (in K) as
$$\Delta $$ r G o (in kJ mol –1 ) = 120 $$ - {3 \over 8}$$ T.

The major component of the reaction mixture at T is :
questions.solution:
For $\ce{X <=> Y}$, $K = \dfrac{[\ce{Y}]}{[\ce{X}]}$ and $\Delta_r G^\circ = -RT\ln K$.

If $\Delta_r G^\circ > 0$, then $K < 1$ and X is the major component; if $\Delta_r G^\circ < 0$, then $K > 1$ and Y is the major component.

$\Delta_r G^\circ = 0$ when $120 - \dfrac{3}{8}T = 0$, that is, at $T = 320\ \text{K}$.

Below 320 K, $\Delta_r G^\circ > 0$, so X is major at 280 K, 300 K and 315 K; above 320 K, $\Delta_r G^\circ < 0$, so Y is major at 350 K. Only the pairing "X at 315 K" matches.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: For the reaction, 2NO 2 (g) $$\rightleftharpoons$$ N₂O₄ (g), when $$\Delta$$S = $$-$$176.0 JK $$-$$1 and $$\Delta$$H = $$-$$57.8 kJ mol $$-$$1 , the magnitude of $$\Delta$$G at 298 K for the reaction is ___________ kJ mol $$-$$1 . (Nearest integer)
questions.solution:
Given, $$\Delta$$H = $$-$$ 57.8 kJ mol $$-$$1

$$\Delta$$S = $$-$$ 176 JK $$-$$1 mol $$-$$1

T = 298 K

Using Gibb's free energy relation

$$\Delta$$G = $$\Delta$$H $$-$$ T$$\Delta$$S

where, $$\Delta$$G = change in Gibb's free energy

$$\Delta$$H = change in enthalpy

T = temperature

$$\Delta$$S = change in entropy

$$\Delta$$G = $$-$$57.8 kJ/mol $$-$$ [298 K $$\times$$ ($$-$$ 176 Jk $$-$$1 mol $$-$$1 )]

= $$-$$57.8 kJ/mol $$-$$ $$\left( {298 \times {{ - 176} \over {1000}}kJ} \right)$$ [$$\therefore$$ 1 kJ = 1000 J]

= $$-$$ 5.352 kJ/mol

| $$\Delta$$G | = 5.352

Hence, answer is 5.

questions.text: The incorrect expression among the following is :
questions.solution:
(
A) At constant temperature and pressure, $\Delta S_{\text{total}} = -\dfrac{\Delta G_{\text{system}}}{T}$, so $\dfrac{\Delta G_{\text{system}}}{\Delta S_{\text{total}}} = -T$: correct.

(
B) $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ = -RT\ln K$, so $\ln K = -\dfrac{\Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ}{RT}$. The expression in (
B) sets $K$ itself (not $\ln K$) equal to $\dfrac{\Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ}{RT}$ and also drops the minus sign: incorrect.

(
C) $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ gives $K = e^{-\Delta G^\circ/RT}$: correct.

(
D) For a reversible isothermal expansion or compression of an ideal gas, $w_{\text{rev}} = -nRT\ln\dfrac{V_f}{V_i}$: correct.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
During which of the following processes, does entropy decrease?

(
A) Freezing of water to ice at 0$$^\circ$$C

(
B) Freezing of water to ice at $$-$$10$$^\circ$$C

(
C) N 2 (g) + 3H 2 (g) $$ \to $$ 2NH 3 (g)

(
D) Adsorption of CO(g) on lead surface.

(E) Dissolution of NaCl in water

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.solution:
A, B $$ \to $$ Freezing of water will decrease entropy as particles will move closer and forces of
attraction will increase. This leads to decrease in randomness. So entropy decrease.

C $$ \to $$ No. of molecules decreasing

D $$ \to $$ Adsorption will lead to decrease in randomness of gaseous particles.

E $$ \to $$ NaCl(s) $$ \to $$ Na + (aq) + Cl – (aq) $$\Delta $$S > 0

So, (A, B, C, D) decreases entropy.

questions.text:
For a chemical reaction A + B ⇌ C + D

($${\Delta _r}{H^\Theta }$$ = 80 kJ mol $$-$$1 ) the entropy change $${\Delta _r}{S^\Theta }$$ depends on the temperature T (in K) as $${\Delta _r}{S^\Theta }$$ = 2T (J K $$-$$1 mol $$-$$1 ).

Minimum temperature at which it will become spontaneous is ___________ K. (Integer)
questions.solution:
We know, $$\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ $$

For a reaction to be spontaneous

$$\Delta G^\circ < 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$\Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ < 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$T > {{\Delta H^\circ } \over {\Delta S^\circ }}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$T > {{80000} \over {2T}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ 2T 2 > 80000

$$ \Rightarrow $$ T 2 > 40000

$$ \Rightarrow $$ T > 200

The minimum temperature to make it spontaneous is 200 K.

questions.text:
Assuming ideal behaviour, the magnitude of log K for the following reaction at 25$$^\circ$$C is x $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$1 . The value of x is ______________. (Integer answer)

$$3HC \equiv C{H_{(g)}} \rightleftharpoons {C_6}{H_{6(l)}}$$

[Given : $${\Delta _f}{G^o}(HC \equiv CH) = - 2.04 \times {10^5}$$ J mol $$-$$1 ; $${\Delta _f}{G^o}({C_6}{H_6}) = - 1.24 \times {10^5}$$ J mol $$-$$1 ; R = 8.314 J K -1 mol $$-$$1 ]
questions.solution:
Reaction,

$$\mathop {3HC \equiv CH(g)}\limits_{Acetylene} \to \mathop {{C_6}{H_6}(l)}\limits_{Benzene} $$

Given, $$\Delta G_f^o (CH \equiv CH) = - 2.04 \times {10^5}$$ J mol $$-$$1

$$\Delta G_f^o({C_6}{H_6}) = - 1.24 \times {10^5}$$ J mol $$-$$1

Gibb's free energy, $$\Delta G_f^o = - nRT\ln K$$

$$\Delta G_f^o = \sum {{{(\Delta G_F^o)}_P} - \sum {{{(\Delta G_F^o)}_R}} } $$

$$ - nRT\ln K = - n'RT\ln {K_p} - ( - n''RT\ln {K_f})$$

$$ \Rightarrow - RT\ln K = 1 \times ( - 1.24 \times {10^5}) - ( - 3 \times 2.04 \times {10^5}) $$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$- 2.303 \times R \times T\log K = 4.88 \times {10^5}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$\log K = - {{4.88 \times {{10}^5}} \over {2.303 \times 8.314 \times 298}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$n\ln K = n'\ln {K_p} - ( - n''ln{K_f})$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ |log K| = 85.52

$$\Rightarrow$$ |log K| = 855 $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$1

x = 855

questions.text:
Given below are two statements: One is labelled as Assertion $$\mathbf{A}$$ and the other is labelled as Reason $$\mathbf{R}$$

Assertion A : The reduction of a metal oxide is easier if the metal formed is in liquid state than solid state.

Reason $$\mathbf{R}$$ : The value of $$\Delta G ^\Theta$$ becomes more on negative side as entropy is higher in liquid state than solid state.

options.text: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct

questions.text:
A variable, opposite external potential (E ext ) is applied to the cell

$$Zn\left| {Z{n^{2 + }}\left( {1\,M} \right)} \right|\left| {C{u^{2 + }}\,\left( {1\,M} \right)} \right|\,Cu,$$ of potential 1.1 V. When E ext < 1.1 V and E ext > 1.1 V, respectively electrons flow from :

options.text: anode to cathode and cathode to anode
cathode to anode and anode to cathode
cathode to anode in both cases
anode to cathode in both cases

questions.solution:
In the cell $\mathrm{Zn | Zn^{2+} || Cu^{2+} | Cu}$, $E_{\mathrm{cell}} = 1.1\ \mathrm{V}$; $\mathrm{Zn}$ is the anode and $\mathrm{Cu}$ the cathode.

When $E_{\mathrm{ext}} \lt 1.1\ \mathrm{V}$, the cell still works as a galvanic cell: $\mathrm{Zn}$ is oxidised and electrons flow from $\mathrm{Zn}$ to $\mathrm{Cu}$, i.e. from anode to cathode.

When $E_{\mathrm{ext}} \gt 1.1\ \mathrm{V}$, the cell reaction is reversed (electrolytic cell): $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ is reduced and $\mathrm{Cu}$ is oxidised.

Now electrons flow from $\mathrm{Cu}$ to $\mathrm{Zn}$, i.e. from the cathode to the anode of the original cell.

So the electrons flow from anode to cathode and from cathode to anode, respectively.

questions.text: The solubility product of a sparingly soluble salt A₂X₃ is 1.1 $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$23 . If specific conductance of the solution is 3 $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$5 S m $$-$$1 , the limiting molar conductivity of the solution is $$x \,\times$$ 10 $$-$$3 S m 2 mol $$-$$1 . The value of x is ___________.
questions.solution:
For $\ce{A2X3 <=> 2A^3+ + 3X^2-}$ with solubility $s$ (in $\text{mol L}^{-1}$):

$$K_{sp} = (2s)^2(3s)^3 = 108\,s^5 = 1.1 \times 10^{-23}$$

$$s^5 \approx 1.0 \times 10^{-25} \Rightarrow s \approx 1.0 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{mol L}^{-1} = 1.0 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol m}^{-3}$$

A saturated solution of a sparingly soluble salt is so dilute that its molar conductivity equals the limiting molar conductivity:

$$\Lambda_m^\circ = \dfrac{\kappa}{c} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{S m}^{-1}}{1.0 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol m}^{-3}} = 3 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{S m}^2\,\text{mol}^{-1}$$

Hence, the answer is 3.

questions.text: The molar conductivities at infinite dilution of barium chloride, sulphuric acid and hydrochloric acid are 280, 860 and 426 S cm 2 mol $$-$$1 respectively. The molar conductivity at infinite dilution of barium sulphate is _________ S cm 2 mol $$-$$1 . (Round off to the Nearest Integer ).
questions.solution:
From Kohlrausch's law

$$\Lambda _m^\infty (BaS{O_4}) = \lambda _m^\infty (B{a^{2 + }}) + \lambda _m^\infty (SO_4^{2 - })$$

$$\Lambda _m^\infty (BaS{O_4}) = \Lambda _m^\infty (BaC{l_2}) + \Lambda _m^\infty ({H_2}S{O_4}) - 2\Lambda _m^\infty (HCl)$$

$$ = 280 + 860 - 2(426)$$

$$ = 288$$ S cm 2 mol $$-$$1

Oxidation half cell : -

$${H_2}\left( g \right)\buildrel \, \over
\longrightarrow 2{H^ + }\left( {1M} \right) + 2{e^ - }\,\,\,...{P_1}$$

Reduction half cell

$$2{H^ + }\left( {1M} \right) + 2{e^ - }\buildrel \, \over
\longrightarrow {H_2}\left( g \right)\,\,\,...{P_2}$$

The net cell reaction

$$\mathop {{H_2}}\limits_{{P_1}} \left( g \right)\buildrel \, \over
\longrightarrow \mathop {{H_2}}\limits_{{P_2}} \left( g \right)$$

$$E_{cell}^ \circ = 0.00\,V$$ $$\,\,\,\,\,$$ $$n=2$$

$$ = 0 - {{RT} \over {nF}}{\log _e}{{{P_2}} \over {{P_1}}}$$

or $$\,\,\,\,{E_{cell}} = {{RT} \over {2F}}{\log _e}{{{P_1}} \over {{P_2}}}$$

questions.text: Given $$E_{C{r^{3 + }}/Cr}^o$$ = -0.72 V; $$E_{Fe^{2+}/Fe}^o$$ = -0.42 V. The potential for the cell Cr | Cr 3+ (0.1M) || Fe 2+ (0.01 M) | Fe is

From the given representation of the cell, $${E_{cell}}$$ can be found as follows.

$${E_{cell}} = E_{F{e^{2 + }}/Fe}^ \circ - E_{C{r^{3 + }}/Cr}^ \circ - {{0.059} \over 6}\log {{{{\left[ {C{r^{3 + }}} \right]}^2}} \over {{{\left[ {F{e^{2 + }}} \right]}^3}}}$$ $$\left[ {} \right.$$ Nernst - Equ. $$\left. {} \right]$$

$$ = - 0.42 - \left( { - 0.72} \right) - {{0.059} \over 6}\log {{{{\left( {0.1} \right)}^2}} \over {{{\left( {0.01} \right)}^3}}}$$

$$ = - 0.42 + 0.72 - {{0.059} \over 6}\log {{0.1 \times 0.1} \over {0.01 \times 0.01 \times 0.01}}$$

$$ = 0.3 - {{0.059} \over 6}\log {{{{10}^{ - 2}}} \over {{{10}^{ - 6}}}}$$

$$ = 0.3 - {{0.059} \over 6} \times 4$$

$$ = 0.30 - 0.0393 = 0.26\,V$$

Hence option (a) is correct answer.

questions.text:
Given : $$E_{F{e^{3 + }}/Fe}^o$$ = -0.036V; $$E_{F{e^{2 + }}/Fe}^o$$ = -0.439 V

The value of standard electrode potential for the change,

Fe 3+ (aq) + e - $$\to$$ Fe 2+ (aq) will be
questions.solution:
Given

$$F{e^{3 + }} + 3{e^ - } \to Fe,\,\,{E^ \circ }_{F{e^{3 + }}/Fe}$$

$$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = - 0.036V\,\,\,...\left( i \right)$$

$$F{e^{2 + }} + 2{e^ - } \to Fe,\,\,{E^ \circ }_{F{e^{2 + }}/Fe}$$

$$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = - 0.439V\,\,\,...\left( {ii} \right)$$

we have to calculate

$$F{e^{3 + }} + {e^ - } \to F{e^{2 + }},\,\,\Delta G = ?$$

To obtain this equation subtract equ $$(ii)$$ from $$(i)$$ we get

$$F{e^{3 + }} + {e^ - } \to F{e^{2 + }}\,\,\,...\left( {iii} \right)$$

As we know that $$\Delta G = - nFE$$

Thus for reaction $$(iii)$$

$$\Delta G = \Delta {G_1} - \Delta {G_2};\,$$

$$\, - nF{E^ \circ } = - nF{E_1} - \left( { - nF{E_2}} \right)$$

$$\, - nF{E^ \circ } = nF{E_2} - nF{E_1}$$

$$ - 1F{E^ \circ } = 2 \times \left( { - 0.439} \right)F - 3 \times \left( { - 0.036} \right)F$$

$$ - 1F{E^ \circ } = - 0.770\,F$$

$$\therefore$$ $$\,\,\,\,{E^ \circ } = 0.770V$$

$$E^\circ_{Cr_2O_7^{2-}/Cr^{3+}} = 1.33$$ V, $$E^\circ_{MnO_4^-/Mn^{2+}} = 1.51$$ V
The correct order of reducing power of the species (Cr, Cr$$^{3+}$$, Mn$$^{2+}$$ and Cl$$^-$$) will be:
questions.solution:
A species is a stronger reducing agent the lower the $E^\circ$ of the couple in which it is the reduced form.

Cr: $E^\circ(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}/Cr}) = -0.74\ \mathrm{V}$, the strongest reductant.

$\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$: $E^\circ(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}/Cr^{3+}}) = 1.33\ \mathrm{V}$.

$\mathrm{Cl^-}$: $1.36\ \mathrm{V}$; $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$: $1.51\ \mathrm{V}$, the weakest reductant.

Order of reducing power: $\mathrm{Mn^{2+} \lt Cl^- \lt Cr^{3+} \lt Cr}$.
