questions.text:
Electrode potentials (E°) are given below :
$$Cu^+/Cu = +0.52$$ V,
$$Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+} = +0.77$$ V,
$$\frac{1}{2}I_2(s)/I^- = +0.54$$ V,
$$Ag^+/Ag = +0.88$$ V.
Based on the above potentials, strongest oxidizing agent will be :
questions.solution:
The species with the highest standard reduction potential is most easily reduced, so it is the strongest oxidising agent.

Order of the given values: $\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}\ (0.88) \gt \mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}}\ (0.77) \gt \mathrm{I_2/I^-}\ (0.54) \gt \mathrm{Cu^+/Cu}\ (0.52)$.

questions.text:
Given

$$E_{C{r^{2 + }}/Cr}^o$$ = -0.74 V; $$E_{MnO_4^ - /M{n^{2 + }}}^o$$ = 1.51 V

$$E_{C{r_2}O_7^{2 - }/C{r^{3 + }}}^o$$ = 1.33 V; $$E_{Cl/C{l^ - }}^o$$ = 1.36 V

Based on the data given above, strongest oxidising agent will be :
questions.solution:
In electrochemistry, the strongest oxidizing agent will be the one with the highest standard electrode potential (E°), because a higher E° value means a greater tendency to gain electrons, i.e., get reduced. An oxidizing agent gains electrons and in doing so, oxidizes another species.

From the provided data, the species with the highest standard electrode potential (E°) is MnO₄⁻, with an E° of 1.51 V. This means that MnO₄⁻ has the greatest tendency to gain electrons and thus is the strongest oxidizing agent.

Therefore, the correct answer is :

Option C : $$MnO_4^ - $$ .

questions.text:
Given

Fe 3+ (aq) + e $$-$$  $$ \to $$  Fe 2+ (aq);   E o = + 0.77 V

Al 3+ (aq) + 3e $$-$$  $$ \to $$  Al(s); E o = $$-$$ 1.66 V

Br 2 (aq) + 2e $$-$$  $$ \to $$  2Br $$-$$ ;  E o = + 1.09 V

Considering the electrode potentials, which of the following represents the correct order of reducing power ?
questions.solution:
A species is a stronger reducing agent when its couple has a lower (more negative) standard reduction potential.

$E^\circ$ values: $\mathrm{Al^{3+}/Al} = -1.66\ \mathrm{V}$, $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}} = +0.77\ \mathrm{V}$, $\mathrm{Br_2/Br^-} = +1.09\ \mathrm{V}$.

So $\mathrm{Al}$ is the strongest reductant and $\mathrm{Br^-}$ the weakest.

So the order of reducing power is $\mathrm{Br^-} \lt \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} \lt \mathrm{Al}$.

questions.text: The standard electrode potentials $$\left( {E_{{M^ + }/M}^o} \right)$$ of four metals A, B, C and D are $$-$$ 1.2 V,  0.6 V,  0.85 V and $$-$$ 0.76 V, respectively. The sequence of deposition of metals on applying potential is :
questions.solution:
As the applied potential is increased, the metal ion with the highest (most positive) reduction potential is reduced and deposited first.

$E^\circ$: $\mathrm{C}\ (0.85\ \mathrm{V}) \gt \mathrm{B}\ (0.6\ \mathrm{V}) \gt \mathrm{D}\ (-0.76\ \mathrm{V}) \gt \mathrm{A}\ (-1.2\ \mathrm{V})$

The ions are therefore discharged in decreasing order of $E^\circ$.

So the sequence of deposition is C, B, D, A.

questions.text:
To find the standard potential of M 3+ /M electrode, the following cell is constituted : Pt/M/M 3+ (0.001 mol L −1 )/Ag + (0.01 mol L −1 )/Ag

The emf of the cell is found to be 0.421 volt at 298 K. The standard potential of half reaction M 3+ + 3e − $$ \to $$ M at 298 K will be :

(Given $$E_{A{g^ + }\,/\,Ag}^o $$ at 298 K = 0.80 Volt)
questions.solution:
According to Nernst equation, for the cell reaction

M(s) + 3Ag + (aq) $$\to$$ M 3+ (aq) + 3Ag(s)

$${E_{cell}} = E_{cell}^o - {{0.059} \over n}\log {{[{M^{3 + }}]} \over {{{[A{g^ + }]}^3}}}$$

Substituting the values, we get

$$0.421 = E_{cell}^o - {{0.059} \over 3}\log {{0.001} \over {{{(0.01)}^3}}}$$

$$E_{cell}^o = 0.48V$$

We know that $$E_{cell}^o = E_{A{g^ + }/Ag}^o - E_{{M^{3 + }}/M}^o$$

$$0.48 = 0.8 - E_{{M^{3 + }}/M}^o$$

$$E_{{M^{3 + }}/M}^o = 0.32V$$

questions.text:
What is the standard reduction potential (E o ) for Fe 3+ $$ \to $$ Fe ?

Given that :

Fe 2+ + 2e $$-$$ $$ \to $$ Fe; $$E_{F{e^{2 + }}/Fe}^o$$ = $$-$$0.47 V

Fe 3+ + e $$-$$ $$ \to $$ Fe 2+ ; $$E_{F{e^{3 + }}/F{e^{2 + }}}^o$$ = +0.77 V
questions.solution:
For the given reaction :

Fe 3+ + e $$-$$ $$ \to $$ Fe 2+ ; $$E_{F{e^{3 + }}/F{e^{2 + }}}^o$$ = +0.77 V

$$\Delta $$G o = -nFE o

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$\Delta G_1^o = - \left( 1 \right)F\left( {0.77} \right)$$ = -0.77F

For the following reaction :

Fe 2+ + 2e $$-$$ $$ \to $$ Fe; $$E_{F{e^{2 + }}/Fe}^o$$ = $$-$$0.47 V

$$\Delta G_2^o = - \left( 2 \right)F\left( {-0.47} \right)$$ = 0.47$$ \times $$2F

Overall reaction :

Fe 3+ + 3e $$-$$ $$ \to $$ Fe;

$$\Delta G_3^o = - 3FE_3^o$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$\Delta G_1^o$$ + $$\Delta G_2^o$$ = $$ 3FE_3^o$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ -0.77F + 0.47$$ \times $$2F = $$ 3FE_3^o$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$E_3^o = - {{0.17} \over 3}$$ = -0.057 V

$${E^\Theta }_{A{u^{3 + }}/Au} = 1.4\,V$$

The strongest oxidizing agent is :
questions.solution:
Which electrode have higher value of standard reduction potential (SRP), that electrode will be strongest oxidizing agent.

Tendency to gain electron is called standard reduction potential. When tendency to gain electron is more then that electrode will have more oxidizing power.

Here given SRP's are :

$${E^\Theta }_{{O_2}/{H_2}O} = 1.23\,V$$ ;

$${E^\Theta }_{{S_2}O_8^{2 - }/SO_4^{2 - }} = 2.05\,V$$

$${E^\Theta }_{B{r_2}/B{r^ - }} = 1.09\,V$$

$${E^\Theta }_{A{u^{3 + }}/Au} = 1.4\,V$$

You can see $${E^\Theta }_{{S_2}O_8^{2 - }/SO_4^{2 - }} = 2.05$$,

have highest SRP so $${S_2}O_8^{2 - }$$ is the strongest oxidizing agent.

questions.text:
In the cell

Pt(s)|H 2 (g, 1 bar)$$\left| {HCl\left( {aq} \right)} \right|$$AgCl(s)|Ag(s)|Pt(s)

the cell potential is 0.92 V when a 10 –6 molal HCl solution is used. The standard electrode potential of (AgCl/Ag/Cl – ) electrode is :

$$\left\{ {} \right.$$Given,  $${{2.303RT} \over F} = 0.06V$$  at  $$\left. {298} \right\}$$
questions.solution:
The electrode reactions are:

Anode: $\ce{H2(g) -> 2H+(aq) + 2e-}$

Cathode: $\ce{2AgCl(s) + 2e- -> 2Ag(s) + 2Cl-(aq)}$

Overall ($n = 2$): $\ce{H2(g) + 2AgCl(s) -> 2Ag(s) + 2H+(aq) + 2Cl-(aq)}$

Since $E^\circ_{\ce{H+/H2}} = 0$, $E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\ce{Cl-/AgCl/Ag}}$.

In $10^{-6}$ molal HCl, $[\ce{H+}] = [\ce{Cl-}] = 10^{-6}$ and $p_{\ce{H2}} = 1$ bar. By the Nernst equation,

$$E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0.06}{2}\log\dfrac{[\ce{H+}]^2[\ce{Cl-}]^2}{p_{\ce{H2}}}$$

$$0.92 = E^\circ - 0.03\log\left(10^{-24}\right) = E^\circ - 0.03 \times (-24) = E^\circ + 0.72$$

$$E^\circ_{\ce{Cl-/AgCl/Ag}} = 0.92 - 0.72 = 0.20\ \text{V}$$

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
Consider the cell at 25$$^\circ$$C

Zn | Zn 2+ (aq), (1M) || Fe 3+ (aq), Fe 2+ (aq) | Pt(s)

The fraction of total iron present as Fe 3+ ion at the cell potential of 1.500 V is x $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$2 . The value of x is ______________. (Nearest integer)

(Given : $$E_{F{e^{3 + }}/F{e^{2 + }}}^0 = 0.77V$$, $$E_{Z{n^{2 + }}/Zn}^0 = - 0.76V$$)
questions.solution:
In the cell, Zn is the anode and the $\ce{Fe^3+/Fe^2+}$ couple on Pt is the cathode:

$$\ce{Zn + 2Fe^3+ -> Zn^2+ + 2Fe^2+}, \qquad n = 2$$

$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}} = 0.77 - (-0.76) = 1.53\ \text{V}$$

With $\dfrac{2.303RT}{F} = 0.06\ \text{V}$ at 25 °C and $[\ce{Zn^2+}] = 1\ \text{M}$, the Nernst equation gives

$$1.50 = 1.53 - \dfrac{0.06}{2}\log\dfrac{[\ce{Zn^2+}][\ce{Fe^2+}]^2}{[\ce{Fe^3+}]^2} = 1.53 - 0.06\log\dfrac{[\ce{Fe^2+}]}{[\ce{Fe^3+}]}$$

$$\log\dfrac{[\ce{Fe^2+}]}{[\ce{Fe^3+}]} = \dfrac{0.03}{0.06} = 0.5 \Rightarrow \dfrac{[\ce{Fe^2+}]}{[\ce{Fe^3+}]} = \sqrt{10} = 3.16$$

The fraction of the total iron present as $\ce{Fe^3+}$ is

$$\dfrac{[\ce{Fe^3+}]}{[\ce{Fe^2+}] + [\ce{Fe^3+}]} = \dfrac{1}{1 + 3.16} = 0.24 = 24 \times 10^{-2}$$

Hence, the answer is 24.

Both reductions share the same copper half-cell, so their thermodynamic tendencies are equal when the two nitrate electrode potentials are equal. Take $[\ce{H+}] = [\ce{NO3-}] = c$ from $\ce{HNO3}$ and $p_{\ce{NO}} = p_{\ce{NO2}} = 1\ \text{bar}$.

For $\ce{NO3- + 4H+ + 3e- -> NO + 2H2O}$:

$$E_1 = 0.96 - \dfrac{0.059}{3}\log\dfrac{1}{c \cdot c^4} = 0.96 + \dfrac{5 \times 0.059}{3}\log c$$

For $\ce{NO3- + 2H+ + e- -> NO2 + H2O}$:

$$E_2 = 0.79 - 0.059\log\dfrac{1}{c \cdot c^2} = 0.79 + 3 \times 0.059\log c$$

Setting $E_1 = E_2$:

$$0.17 = 0.059\left(3 - \dfrac{5}{3}\right)\log c = 0.0787\log c \Rightarrow \log c = 2.16$$

So $[\ce{HNO3}] = 10^{2.16}\ \text{M}$, $x = 2.16$ and $2x = 4.32 \approx 4$.

Hence, the answer is 4.

questions.text:
The correct order of reduction potentials of the following pairs is
A. Cl 2 /Cl $$-$$
B. I 2 /I $$-$$
C. Ag + /Ag
D. Na + /Na

E. Li + /Li

Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
questions.solution:
Standard reduction potentials of the couples:

$$E^\circ_{\ce{Cl2/Cl^-}} = +1.36\ \text{V},\quad E^\circ_{\ce{Ag^+/Ag}} = +0.80\ \text{V},\quad E^\circ_{\ce{I2/I^-}} = +0.54\ \text{V}$$

$$E^\circ_{\ce{Na^+/Na}} = -2.71\ \text{V},\quad E^\circ_{\ce{Li^+/Li}} = -3.05\ \text{V}$$

In decreasing order, $+1.36 > +0.80 > +0.54 > -2.71 > -3.05$, i.e. A > C > B > D > E. $\ce{Ag^+/Ag}$ lies above $\ce{I2/I^-}$, and Li lies below Na because of the very large hydration enthalpy of the small $\ce{Li^+}$ ion.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: The standard potentials of $$\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}$$, $$\mathrm{Hg_2^{2+}/2Hg}$$, $$\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}$$ and $$\mathrm{Mg^{2+}/Mg}$$ electrodes are 0.80, 0.79, 0.34 and $$-2.37\ \mathrm{V}$$, respectively. questions.solution:
As the voltage is raised, the ion with the highest (most positive) reduction potential is reduced first at the cathode.

Order of $E^\circ$: $\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}\ (0.80) \gt \mathrm{Hg_2^{2+}/Hg}\ (0.79) \gt \mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}\ (0.34)$.

The sequence is Ag, Hg, Cu only.

(Take : F = 96000 C, At. mass of chromium = 52)
______.
questions.solution:
Charge passed: $Q = It = 2 \times 8 \times 60 = 960\ \text{C}$, i.e. $\dfrac{960}{96000} = 0.01$ mol of electrons.

In $\ce{Cr2O7^2- + 14H+ + 6e^- -> 2Cr^3+ + 7H2O}$, 6 mol of electrons give 2 mol of $\ce{Cr^3+}$, i.e. 3 mol of electrons per mol of $\ce{Cr^3+}$ (Cr goes from +6 to +3).

Theoretical mass of $\ce{Cr^3+}$:

$$m = \dfrac{0.01}{3} \times 52 = 0.1733\ \text{g}$$

$$\text{Efficiency} = \dfrac{0.104}{0.1733} \times 100 = 60\%$$

Hence, the answer is 60.

Conductance (G) is reciprocal of resistance (R)

A battery is constructed of $$\mathrm{Cr}$$ and $$\mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7}$$. The unbalanced chemical equation when such a battery discharges is following:
$$\mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7 + Cr + H^+ \rightarrow Cr^{3+} + H_2O + Na^+}$$
If one Faraday of electricity is passed through the battery during the charging, the number of moles of $$\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$$ removed from the solution is
questions.solution:
Balanced discharge reaction: $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 2Cr + 14H^+ \rightarrow 4Cr^{3+} + 7H_2O}$.

The two $\mathrm{Cr}$ atoms go from $0$ to $+3$ and give $6e^-$; the two $\mathrm{Cr}$ of the dichromate go from $+6$ to $+3$ and take $6e^-$.

So $6\ \mathrm{F}$ of charge accompany the formation of $4\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$.

Charging runs this reaction backwards, so $1\ \mathrm{F}$ removes $\dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$.

Check electrode by electrode: $\mathrm{Cr^{3+} + 3e^- \rightarrow Cr}$ uses $\dfrac{1}{3}\ \mathrm{mol}$ per faraday, and $\mathrm{2Cr^{3+} + 7H_2O \rightarrow Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 14H^+ + 6e^-}$ uses another $\dfrac{1}{3}\ \mathrm{mol}$.

So $\dfrac{2}{3}\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$ is removed from the solution.

questions.text: How many electrons would be required to deposit 6.35 g of copper at the cathode during the electrolysis of an aqueous solution of copper sulphate ? (Atomic mass of copper = 63.5 u, N A = Avogadro's constant) :

Electrons needed $= 2 \times 0.1 = 0.2\ \mathrm{mol} = 0.2N_A$.

So the number of electrons required is $\dfrac{N_A}{5}$.

questions.text: A current of 10.0 A flows for 2.00 h through an electrolytic cell containing a molten salt of metal X. This results in the deposition of 0.250 mol of metal X at the cathode. The oxidation state of X in the molten salt is : (F = 96,500 C)

Electrons taken up per metal ion $= \dfrac{0.746}{0.250} \approx 3$, i.e. $\mathrm{X^{3+}} + 3e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{X}$

So the oxidation state of X in the molten salt is $+3$.

questions.text:
Given
$$\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu}} = 0.34\ \mathrm{V},\ \mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}/Cu^{+}}} = 0.15\ \mathrm{V}$$
Standard electrode potential for the half cell $$\mathrm{Cu^+/Cu}$$ is
questions.solution:
Electrode potentials are not additive, but the $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$ values are.

$\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}$: $\Delta G_1^\circ = -2F(0.34) = -0.68F$

$\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + e^- \rightarrow Cu^+}$: $\Delta G_2^\circ = -1F(0.15) = -0.15F$

$\mathrm{Cu^+ + e^- \rightarrow Cu}$: $\Delta G_3^\circ = \Delta G_1^\circ - \Delta G_2^\circ = -0.53F$

$E_3^\circ = \dfrac{-\Delta G_3^\circ}{1 \times F} = 0.53\ \text{V}$

Hence the standard electrode potential of $\mathrm{Cu^+/Cu}$ is $0.53\ \text{V}$.

questions.text: At 298 K, the standard reduction potentials are 1.51 V for MnO$$_4^ - $$ $$\left| {M{n^{2 + }}} \right.,$$ 1.36 V for Cl 2 $$\left| {C{l^ - }} \right.$$, 1.07 V for Br 2 $$\left| {B{r^ - }} \right.$$, and 0.54 V for I 2 $$\left| {{{\rm I}^ - }} \right.$$. At pH = 3, permanganate is expected to oxidize : $$\left( {{{2.303RT} \over F} = 0.059\,V} \right)$$
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \to Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O}$, $E^\circ = 1.51\ \mathrm{V}$.

With $[\mathrm{MnO_4^-}] = [\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}] = 1$: $E = 1.51 - \dfrac{0.059}{5}\log\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{H^+}]^8} = 1.51 - \dfrac{0.059\times8}{5}\,\mathrm{pH}$ (here $0.059$ V is the value of $\dfrac{2.303RT}{F}$).

At pH $= 3$: $E = 1.51 - 0.0944\times3 = 1.51 - 0.283 \approx 1.23\ \mathrm{V}$.

Permanganate can oxidise a halide ion only if this $E$ is greater than the $E^\circ$ of that halogen/halide couple.

$1.23 \gt 1.07$ and $1.23 \gt 0.54$, but $1.23 \lt 1.36$.

So at pH 3 permanganate oxidises $\mathrm{Br^-}$ and $\mathrm{I^-}$ but not $\mathrm{Cl^-}$.

questions.text: For the given cell $\mathrm{Zn(s)\,|\,Zn^{2+}(C_1\ M)\,||\,Zn^{2+}(C_2\ M)\,|\,Zn(s)}$ the change in Gibbs energy ($\Delta G$) will be zero when $\dfrac{C_1}{C_2}$ is equal to ________.
questions.solution:
This is a concentration cell: $E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0$; cell reaction $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}(C_2) \rightarrow Zn^{2+}(C_1)}$, $n = 2$.

$E_{\text{cell}} = 0 - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{C_1}{C_2}$.

$\Delta G = -nFE_{\text{cell}} = 0$ requires $E_{\text{cell}} = 0$, i.e. $\log\dfrac{C_1}{C_2} = 0$.

$\dfrac{C_1}{C_2} = 1$.

questions.text:
For a reaction $${1 \over 2}A \to 2B$$ rate of disappearance of ‘A’ is related to the rate of appearance of ‘B’ by the
expression
questions.solution:
The rates of reactions for the reaction

$${1 \over 2}A \to 2B$$

can be written either as

or $$\,\,\,\,\,$$ $${1 \over 2}{d \over {dt}}\left[ B \right]\,\,\,\,$$ with respect to $$'B'$$

questions.text:

questions.text:
For the reaction, 3A + 2B $$ \to $$ C + D,

the differential rate law can be written as :
questions.solution:
Rate of reaction = rate of change of concentration of a species divided by its stoichiometric coefficient.

Reactants are used up, so their terms carry a minus sign; products carry a plus sign.

Rate $=-\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt}=-\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{B}]}{dt}=\dfrac{d[\mathrm{C}]}{dt}=\dfrac{d[\mathrm{D}]}{dt}=k[\mathrm{A}]^n[\mathrm{B}]^m$

So the rate law is $-\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt}=\dfrac{d[\mathrm{C}]}{dt}=k[\mathrm{A}]^n[\mathrm{B}]^m$.

questions.text:
In the reaction of formation of sulphur trioxide by contact process

2SO 2 + O 2   $$\rightleftharpoons$$   2SO 3 the rate of reaction was measured as

$${{d\left[ {{O_2}} \right]} \over {dt}}$$ = $$-$$ 2.5 $$ \times $$ 10 $$-$$4 mol L $$-$$1 s $$-$$1 .

The rate of reaction in terms of   [SO 2 ] in mol L $$-$$1 s $$-$$1
questions.solution:
For $\mathrm{2SO_2 + O_2 \rightleftharpoons 2SO_3}$, rate $= -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{SO_2}]}{dt} = -\dfrac{d[\mathrm{O_2}]}{dt}$.

So $\dfrac{d[\mathrm{SO_2}]}{dt} = 2\,\dfrac{d[\mathrm{O_2}]}{dt}$.

Here $\dfrac{d[\mathrm{O_2}]}{dt} = -2.5\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$.

$\dfrac{d[\mathrm{SO_2}]}{dt} = 2\times(-2.5\times10^{-4}) = -5.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$.

So the rate in terms of $[\mathrm{SO_2}]$ is $-5.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$.

questions.text:
For the reaction, 2N 2 O 5  $$ \to $$ 4NO 2 + O 2 , the rate equation can be

expressed in two ways $$-$$ $${{d\left[ {{N_2}{O_5}} \right]} \over {dt}}$$  =  k [N₂O₅ ]  

and  + $${{d\left[ {N{O_2}} \right]} \over {dt}}$$ = 
k' [N₂O₅ ]   

k and k' are related as :
questions.solution:
Rate $= -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{NO_2}]}{dt}$.

So $\dfrac{d[\mathrm{NO_2}]}{dt} = 2\left(-\dfrac{d[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]}{dt}\right)$.

Substituting the two rate laws, $k'[\mathrm{N_2O_5}] = 2k[\mathrm{N_2O_5}]$.

So $k$ and $k'$ are related as $2k = k'$.

questions.text: For a chemical reaction A $$\to$$ B, it was found that concentration of B is increased by 0.2 mol L $$-$$ in 30 min. The average rate of the reaction is ____________ $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$1 mol L $$-$$1 h $$-$$1 . (in nearest integer)

For the reaction

$$\mathrm{A \rightarrow B}$$

the average rate in terms of formation of $\mathrm{B}$ is

$$ \text{Average rate}=\frac{\Delta[\mathrm{B}]}{\Delta t} $$

Given,

$$ \Delta[\mathrm{B}]=0.2\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}} $$

and

$$ \Delta t=30\ \mathrm{min}=0.5\ \mathrm{h} $$

Thus,

$$ \text{Average rate}=\frac{0.2}{0.5} =0.4\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,h^{-1}} $$

$$ 0.4=4\times10^{-1} $$

Hence, the nearest integer is

$$\boxed{4}$$

$$\left( {{{{r_2}} \over {{r_1}}}} \right) = 27$$

questions.text:
For a given chemical reaction

$$\gamma$$ 1 A + $$\gamma$$ 2 B $$\to$$ $$\gamma$$ 3 C + $$\gamma$$ 4 D

Concentration of C changes from 10 mmol dm $$-$$3 to 20 mmol dm $$-$$3 in 10 seconds. Rate of appearance of D is 1.5 times the rate of disappearance of B which is twice the rate of disappearance A. The rate of appearance of D has been experimentally determined to be 9 mmol dm $$-$$3 s $$-$$1 . Therefore, the rate of reaction is _____________ mmol dm $$-$$3 s $$-$$1 . (Nearest Integer)
questions.solution:
Rate $=\frac{1}{r_{1}}\left(\frac{-d[A]}{d t}\right)=\frac{1}{r_{2}}\left(\frac{-d[B]}{d t}\right)=\frac{1}{r_{3}}\left(\frac{d[C]}{d t}\right)$

$$
=\frac{1}{r_{4}}\left(\frac{d[D]}{d t}\right)
$$

$\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{D}]}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{\mathrm{r}_{4}}{\mathrm{r}_{2}}\left(\frac{-\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{B}]}{\mathrm{dt}}\right)$

$$
\frac{r_{4}}{r_{2}}=\frac{3}{2}
$$

$\frac{-\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{B}]}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{\mathrm{r}_{2}}{\mathrm{r}_{1}}\left(\frac{-\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{A}]}{\mathrm{dt}}\right) \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{r}_{2}}{\mathrm{r}_{1}}=2$

$r_{2}=2 r_{1}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\mathrm{r}_{4}=1.5 \mathrm{r}_{2}=3 \mathrm{r}_{1} \\\\
&\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{C}]}{\mathrm{dt}}=1 \mathrm{~m} \cdot \mathrm{mol} ~\mathrm{dm}^{-3} \mathrm{sec}^{-1} \\\\
&\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{D}]}{\mathrm{dt}}=9 \mathrm{~m} \cdot \mathrm{mol}~ \mathrm{dm}^{-3} \mathrm{sec}^{-1} \\\\
&\frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{D}]}{\mathrm{dt}}=\frac{\mathrm{r}_{4}}{r_{3}} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{C}]}{\mathrm{dt}} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{r}_{4}}{\mathrm{r}_{3}}=9 \\\\
&\mathrm{r}_{4}=9 \mathrm{r}_{3}=3 \mathrm{r}_{1} \\\\
&\Rightarrow \mathrm{r}_{1}=3 \mathrm{r}_{3} \\\\
&\begin{array}{rr}
3 \mathrm{r}_{3} \mathrm{~A}+6 \mathrm{r}_{3} \mathrm{~B} \rightarrow \mathrm{r}_{3} \mathrm{C}+9 \mathrm{r}_{3} \mathrm{D}
\end{array} \\\\
&\begin{aligned}
\therefore \text { rate of reaction } &=\frac{1}{9} \times 9 \mathrm{~m} \cdot \mathrm{mol}~ \mathrm{dm}^{-3} \mathrm{sec}^{-1} \\\\
&=1 \mathrm{~m} \cdot \mathrm{mol}~ \mathrm{dm}^{-3} \mathrm{sec}^{-1}
\end{aligned}
\end{aligned}
$$

questions.text: In respect of the equation k = Ae -E a /RT in chemical kinetics, which one of the following statements is correct?

options.text: E a is energy of activation

questions.solution:
The Arrhenius equation reads

$$k = A\,e^{-\tfrac{E_a}{RT}}$$

Let’s check each term:

A is the pre-exponential (or frequency) factor, not an adsorption factor.

$E_a$ is indeed the activation energy.

R is the universal gas constant ($\approx8.314$ J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹), not Rydberg’s constant.

k is the rate constant, not the equilibrium constant.

Hence, the correct statement is:

Option B: $E_a$ is energy of activation.

questions.text:
Consider an endothermic reaction, X $$\to$$ Y with the activation energies E b and E f
for the backward and forward reactions, respectively. In general :

options.text: There is no definite relation between E b and E f

questions.solution:
Enthalpy of reaction $$\left( {\Delta H} \right) = {E_{{a_{\left( f \right)}}}} - {E_{{a_{\left( b \right)}}}}$$

for an endothermic reaction $$\Delta H = + ve$$

Hence for $$\Delta H$$ to be negative

$$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,$$ $$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,$$ $${E_{{a_{\left( b \right)}}}} < {E_{{a_{\left( f \right)}}}}$$

questions.text:
Rate of a reaction can be expressed by Arrhenius equation as:

$$$k = A\,{e^{ - E/RT}}$$$
In this equation, E represents

options.text: the energy above which all the colliding molecules will react
the energy below which colliding molecules will not react
the total energy of the reacting molecules at a temperature, T
the fraction of molecules with energy greater than the activation energy of the reaction

questions.solution:
$E$ in the Arrhenius equation is the activation energy, the minimum energy that colliding molecules must possess for a collision to lead to reaction.

Collisions with energy below $E$ never react, while collisions with energy above $E$ react only when the molecules are also properly oriented, so not all of them react and (A) fails.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

The energies of activation for forward and reverse reactions for A 2 + B 2 $$\leftrightharpoons$$ 2AB are 180 kJ mol −1
and 200 kJ mol −1 respectively. The presence of catalyst lowers the activation energy of both (forward and reverse) reactions by 100 kJ mol −1 . The enthalpy change of the reaction ( A 2 + B 2 $$\to$$ 2AB) in the presence of catalyst will be (in kJ mol −1 )

questions.text: The activation energy for a reaction which doubles the rate when the temperature is raised from $$298\ \mathrm{K}$$ to $$308\ \mathrm{K}$$ is
questions.solution:
$\ln\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{R}\left(\dfrac{1}{T_1} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right)$ with $\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = 2$.

$\dfrac{1}{298} - \dfrac{1}{308} = \dfrac{10}{298 \times 308} = 1.0895 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{K}^{-1}$

$E_a = \dfrac{8.314 \times 0.693}{1.0895 \times 10^{-4}} = 5.29 \times 10^{4}\ \text{J mol}^{-1}$

Check with common logs: $E_a = \dfrac{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 0.3010}{1.0895 \times 10^{-4}} \approx 52.9\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Hence $E_a = 52.9\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

questions.text: The reaction X $$\rightarrow$$ Y is an exothermic reaction. Activation energy of the reaction for X into Y is 150 kJ mol$$^{-1}$$. Enthalpy of reaction is 135 kJ mol$$^{-1}$$. The activation energy for the reverse reaction, Y $$\rightarrow$$ X will be :
questions.solution:
The reaction is exothermic, so $\Delta H = -135\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

$\Delta H = E_{a,\mathrm{f}} - E_{a,\mathrm{b}}$.

$E_{a,\mathrm{b}} = E_{a,\mathrm{f}} - \Delta H = 150 - (-135) = 285\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

The activation energy for Y to X is $285\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

questions.text:
The rate of a reaction doubles when its temperature changes from 300K to 310K. Activation energy of such
a reaction will be:(R = 8.314 JK –1 mol –1 and log 2 = 0.301)
questions.solution:
Activation energy can be calculated from the equation

$${{\log \,{k_2}} \over {\log \,{k_1}}} = {{{E_a}} \over {2.303R}}\left( {{1 \over {{T_1}}} - {1 \over {{T_2}}}} \right)$$

given $${{{k_2}} \over {{k_1}}} = 2\,\,{T_2} = 310\,K\,\,{T_1} = 300\,K$$

$$ = \log 2 = {{ - {E_a}} \over {2.303 \times 8.314}}\left( {{1 \over {310}} - {1 \over {300}}} \right)$$

$${E_a} = 53598.6J/mol$$

$$ = 53.6kJ/mol.$$

questions.text: The rate coefficient (k) for a particular reaction is 1.3 $$ \times $$ 10 $$-$$4 M $$-$$1 s $$-$$1 at 100 o C, and 1.3 $$ \times $$ 10 $$-$$3 M $$-$$1 s $$-$$1 at 150 o C. What is the energy of activation (E a ) (in kJ) for this reaction ? (R = molar gas constant = 8.314 JK $$-$$1 mol $$-$$1 )
questions.solution:
Arrhenius equation: $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2.303R}\left(\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1T_2}\right)$.

$\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{1.3 \times 10^{-3}}{1.3 \times 10^{-4}} = 10$, so $\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = 1$; $T_1 = 373\ \mathrm{K}$, $T_2 = 423\ \mathrm{K}$.

$E_a = \dfrac{2.303 \times 8.314 \times 373 \times 423}{50}\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$.

$E_a \approx 6.04 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}} \approx 60\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

So the energy of activation is about $60\ \mathrm{kJ}$.

questions.text: For the equilibrium , A(g) $$\rightleftharpoons$$ B(g), $$\Delta $$H is $$-$$ 40 kJ/mol. If the ratio of the activation energies of the forward (E f ) and reverse (E b ) reactions is $${2 \over 3}$$ then :

options.text: E f = 60 kJ/mol; E b = 100 kJ/mol
E f = 30 kJ/mol; E b = 70 kJ/mol
E f = 80 kJ/mol; E b = 120 kJ/mol
E f = 70 kJ/mol; E b = 30 kJ/mol

questions.solution:
For $\mathrm{A(g) \rightleftharpoons B(g)}$: $\Delta H = E_f - E_b = -40\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

Given $\dfrac{E_f}{E_b} = \dfrac{2}{3}$, let $E_f = 2x$ and $E_b = 3x$.

Then $2x - 3x = -40 \Rightarrow x = 40$.

So $E_f = 80\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ and $E_b = 120\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

questions.text:
The rate of a reaction quadruples when the temperature changes from 300 to 310 K. The activation energy of this reaction is :

(Assume activation energy and preexponential factor are independent of
temperature; ln 2 = 0.693; R = 8.314 J mol −1 K −1 )

$$\log 4 = {{{E_a}} \over {2.303 \times 8.314\,J\,{K^{ - 1}}mo{l^{ - 1}}}}\left( {{{310 - 300} \over {300 \times 310}}} \right)$$

$${E_a} = {{0.602 \times 2.303 \times 8.314 \times 300 \times 310} \over {10}}$$

= 107197.12 J/mol $$-$$1 or 107.2 kJ/mol $$-$$1

questions.text: The rate of a reaction A doubles on increasing the temperature from 300 to 310 K. By how much, the temperature of reaction B should be Increased from 300 K so that rate doubles if activation energy of the reaction B is twice to that of reaction A.

k 2 = A.$${e^{{{ - {E_{{a_2}}}} \over {RT}}}}$$ ......(2)

On dividing equation (2) by (1), we get

$${{{k_2}} \over {{k_1}}} = {e^{{{\left( {{E_{{a_1}}} - {E_{{a_2}}}} \right)} \over {RT}}}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$\ln \left( {{{{k_2}} \over {{k_1}}}} \right) = {{\left( {{E_{{a_1}}} - {E_{{a_2}}}} \right)} \over {RT}}$$ = $${{10,000} \over {8.314 \times 300}}$$ = 4

questions.text:
If a reaction follows the Arrhenius equation, the plot ln k vs $${1 \over {\left( {RT} \right)}}$$ gives straight line with a gradient ($$-$$ y) unit.

questions.text:
The reaction

2N 2 O 5 (g) $$ \to $$ 4NO 2 (g) + O 2 (g)

follows first order kinetics. The pressure of a vessel containing only N₂O₅ was found to increase from 50 mm Hg to 87.5 mm Hg in 30 min. The pressure exerted by the gases after 60 min. will be (Assume temperature remains constant) :
questions.solution:
Let the pressure of $\mathrm{N_2O_5}$ fall by $2x$; then $p_{\mathrm{NO_2}} = 4x$, $p_{\mathrm{O_2}} = x$ and $P_{\mathrm{total}} = 50 + 3x$.

At $30\ \mathrm{min}$: $50 + 3x = 87.5 \Rightarrow x = 12.5$, so $p_{\mathrm{N_2O_5}} = 50 - 25 = 25\ \mathrm{mm\,Hg}$.

The pressure of $\mathrm{N_2O_5}$ halves in $30\ \mathrm{min}$, so for this first-order reaction $t_{1/2} = 30\ \mathrm{min}$.

At $60\ \mathrm{min}$ (two half-lives): $p_{\mathrm{N_2O_5}} = 12.5\ \mathrm{mm\,Hg}$, so $2x = 37.5$ and $x = 18.75$.

Total pressure: $P_{\mathrm{total}} = 50 + 3(18.75) = 106.25\ \mathrm{mm\,Hg}$.

So the pressure after $60\ \mathrm{min}$ is $106.25\ \mathrm{mm\,Hg}$.

$$r = k\left[ {{H_2}{O_2}} \right] = 2.78 \times {10^{ - 2}} \times 0.05$$

$$ = 1.386 \times {10^{ - 3}}\,\,mol\,{\min ^{ - 1}}$$

Now

$$ - {{d\left[ {{H_2}{O_2}} \right]} \over {dt}} = {{d\left[ {{H_2}O} \right]} \over {dt}} = {{2d\left[ {{O_2}} \right]} \over {dt}}$$

$$ = {{1.386 \times {{10}^{ - 3}}} \over 2} = 6.93 \times {10^{ - 4}}\,mol\,{\min ^{ - 1}}$$

questions.text: If 50% of a reaction occurs in 100 second and 75% of the reaction occurs in 200 second, the order of this reaction is :
questions.solution:
Assume initial concentration of the reactant = 1 M

After 100 second, concentration becomes of the reactant

After 200 second, concentration of the reactant becomes

So, in first 100 second reactant concentration becomes half of initial and in the second 100 second concentration becomes 0.5 M to 0.25 M, which is also half of 0.5 M.

So, after each 100 second period, concentration of reactant becomes half of initial concentration.

So, 100 second is the half life period and it is independent of concentration of reactant. This is characteristic of first order reaction.

= $${{2.303} \over {0.0693}}$$ log $$\left( {{4 \over 3}} \right)$$

= 4.1 days.

questions.text:
The inactivation rate of a viral preparation is proportional to the amount of virus. In the first minute after preparation, 10% of the virus is inactivated. The rate constant for viral inactivation is ___________ $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$3 min $$-$$1 . (Nearest integer)

[Use : ln 10 = 2.303; log 10 3 = 0.477; property
of logarithm : log x y = y log x]
questions.solution:
Unit of rate constant is min $$-$$1 , so it must be a first order reaction. For first order reaction,

k $$\times$$ t = 2.303 log$${{{A_0}} \over {{A_t}}}$$

k is the rate constant

t is the time

A 0 is the initial conc.

A t is the conc. at time, t

Using formula,

A 0 = 100, A t = 90 in 1 min

So, K $$\times$$ 1 = 2.303 $$\times$$ log$${{100} \over {90}}$$

= 2.303 $$\times$$ (log 10 $$-$$ 2 log 3)

= 2.303 $$\times$$ (1 $$-$$ 2 $$\times$$ 0.477)

= 0.10593

= 105.93 $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$3

$$\approx$$ 106

Hence, the rate constant for viral inactivation is 106.

A and B decompose via first order kinetics with half-lives 54.0 min and 18.0 min respectively. Starting from an equimolar non reactive mixture of A and B, the time taken for the concentration of A to become 16 times that of B is _________ min. (Round off to the Nearest Integer).
questions.solution:
Initially : $$\left[ {{A_0}} \right] = \left[ {{B_0}} \right] = a$$

After time 't' min : $$\left[ A \right] = 16\left[ B \right]$$

$$\left[ A \right] = \left[ {{A_0}} \right]{e^{ - {k_A}t}}$$

$$\left[ B \right] = \left[ {{B_0}} \right]{e^{ - {k_B}t}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow a\,.\,{e^{ - {k_A}t}} = 16a{e^{ - {k_B}t}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {e^{ - \left( {{k_A} - {k_B}} \right)t}} = 16$$

$$ \Rightarrow \left( {{k_B} - {k_A}} \right)t = \ln 16$$

$$ \Rightarrow \ln 2\left( {{1 \over {18}} - {1 \over {54}}} \right)t = 4\ln 2$$

$$ \Rightarrow t = {{54 \times 18 \times 4} \over {36}} = 108$$ min

It is a first order isomerisation reaction. Integrated rate law for 1st order reaction is

$$kt = \ln {{{{[A]}_0}} \over {{{[A]}_t}}}$$ ...(i)

k = rate constant

t = 1547.95 s = 25.79 min (1 min = 60 s or 1s = $${1 \over {60}}$$ min) = 26 minutes

$\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}}=\frac{\ln 2}{100} ; \mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{\ln 2}{50}$

$\mathrm{A}_{\mathrm{t}}=\mathrm{A}_0 \times \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{k}_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{t}}$

$\frac{\ln 2}{100} \times \mathrm{t}=\ln 4=2 \ln 2$

questions.text: In a chemical reaction $$A$$ is converted into $$B$$. The rates of reaction, starting with initial concentrations of $$A$$ as $$2 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{M}$$ and $$1 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{M}$$, are equal to $$2.40 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{M\,s^{-1}}$$ and $$0.60 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{M\,s^{-1}}$$ respectively. The order of reaction with respect to reactant $$A$$ will be
questions.solution:
Rate $= k[A]^n$.

$\dfrac{2.40 \times 10^{-4}}{0.60 \times 10^{-4}} = \left(\dfrac{2 \times 10^{-3}}{1 \times 10^{-3}}\right)^n$.

$4 = 2^n$, so $n = 2$.

So the reaction is of second order with respect to $A$.

questions.text:
At 518 o C the rate of decomposition of a sample of gaseous acetaldehyde initially at a pressure of 363 Torr,
was 1.00 Torr s –1 when 5% had reacted and 0.5 Torr s –1 when 33% had reacted. The order of the reaction is
questions.solution:
For a n th order reaction, the rate of reaction at time t ,

Rate = K [P t ] n

Here P t = pressure at time t, k = constant.

Note :

Here instead of concentration of product, pressure of product is given.

When 5% is reacted at a rate 1 Toss S $$-$$1

Then un-reacted is 95%..

As initial pressure is 363 Torr

then after 5% reaction completed the pressure will be

= 363 $$ \times $$ $${{95} \over {100}}$$ Torr.

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ 1 = K $${\left[ {363 \times {{95} \over {100}}} \right]^n}$$ . . . . . . . .(1)

When 33% is reacted at a rate 0.5 , Torr S $$-$$1 then un-reacted is 67%

So, after 33% reaction completion, the pressure is = $$363 \times {{67} \over {100}}$$ Torr.

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ 0.5 = K $${\left[ {363 \times {{67} \over {100}}} \right]^n}.......$$ (2)

Dividing (1) by (2), we get

$${1 \over {0.5}} = {{{{\left[ {363 \times {{95} \over {100}}} \right]}^n}} \over {{{\left[ {363 \times {{67} \over {100}}} \right]}^n}}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,2 = {\left[ {{{95} \over {67}}} \right]^n}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,$$ 2 = $${\left[ {1.41} \right]^n}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,$$ 2 = $${\left[ {\sqrt 2 } \right]^n}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,\,\,2 = {2^{{n \over 2}}}$$

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ $${n \over 2}$$ = 1

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,\,\,$$ n = 2

This is a 2nd order reaction.

questions.text: For the reaction, 2A + B $$ \to $$ products, when the concentrations of A and B both were doubled, the rate of the reaction increased from 0.3 mol L $$-$$1 s $$-$$1 to 2.4 mol L $$-$$1 s $$-$$1 . When the concentration of A alone is doubled, the rate increased from 0.3 mol L $$-$$1 s $$-$$1 to 0.6 mol L $$-$$1 s $$-$$1 .

options.text: Total order of the reaction is 4
Order of the reaction with respect to B is 2
Order of the reaction with respect to B is 1
Order of the reaction with respect to A is 2

questions.solution:
For the reaction, write the rate law as

$$ r=k[\mathrm A]^m[\mathrm B]^n $$

where $m$ and $n$ are the orders with respect to $\mathrm A$ and $\mathrm B$.

When only $[\mathrm A]$ is doubled:

$$ \frac{0.6}{0.3}=2^m $$

$$ 2=2^m \Rightarrow m=1 $$

When both concentrations are doubled:

$$ \frac{2.4}{0.3}=2^{m+n} $$

$$ 8=2^{m+n} $$

Since $8=2^3$,

$$ m+n=3 $$

Using $m=1$:

$$ 1+n=3 \Rightarrow n=2 $$

Thus, the order with respect to $\mathrm B$ is $2$.

$$ \boxed{\text{Option B}} $$

Experiments I and II: raising $[\mathrm{B}]$ from $0.20$ to $0.25\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ leaves the rate unchanged, so the reaction is zero order in B.

Experiments I and III: doubling $[\mathrm{A}]$ doubles the rate, so the reaction is first order in A and $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]$.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
$\mathrm{X \rightarrow Y + Z}$

X decomposes at 700 K to give Y and Z. The results of two measurements are :

Initial concentration of X / (mol/L) 6.0 12.0 Half life / s 1.0 2.0
The rate constant for the reaction is ________ (in appropriate unit)
questions.solution:
For an $n$th-order reaction $t_{1/2} \propto [\mathrm{X}]_0^{\,1-n}$.

Doubling $[\mathrm{X}]_0$ (6.0 to 12.0) doubles $t_{1/2}$ (1.0 to 2.0 s), so $1 - n = 1$, $n = 0$ (zero order).

Check: $\dfrac{12.0}{2 \times 2.0} = 3.0$.

questions.text:
Consider the following nuclear reactions

$${}_{92}^{238}M \to {}_Y^XN + 2{}_2^4He$$

$${}_Y^XN \to {}_B^AL + 2{\beta ^ + }$$

The number of neutrons in the element L is
questions.solution:
Each $\alpha$-particle emission lowers the mass number by 4 and the atomic number by 2, so two $\alpha$ emissions from ${}^{238}_{92}\text{M}$ give ${}^{230}_{88}\text{N}$ ($X = 230$, $Y = 88$).

Each $\beta^+$ (positron) emission changes a proton into a neutron, keeping the mass number and lowering the atomic number by 1, so two $\beta^+$ emissions from ${}^{230}_{88}\text{N}$ give ${}^{230}_{86}\text{L}$.

Number of neutrons in L $= 230 - 86 = 144$.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: Hydrogen bomb is based on the principle of
questions.solution:
Option C

Nuclear fusion

Explanation :

A hydrogen bomb, also known as a thermonuclear bomb, uses the principle of nuclear fusion. In a fusion reaction, two lighter atomic nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, and a substantial amount of energy is released in the process. In the case of a hydrogen bomb, isotopes of hydrogen (such as deuterium and tritium) fuse together to form helium, releasing a large amount of energy.

It's worth noting that a hydrogen bomb usually involves a two-stage process. The first stage is a fission bomb (like those used in Hiroshima and Nagasaki) that creates the conditions necessary for the fusion reaction in the second stage. Despite this, the majority of the energy in a hydrogen bomb comes from fusion, which is why it is categorized as a fusion weapon.

questions.text:
Consider the reaction :

Cl 2 (aq) + H₂S(aq) → S(s) + 2H + (aq) + 2Cl – (aq)

The rate equation for this reaction is rate = k [Cl 2 ] [H₂S]

Which of these mechanisms is/are consistent with this rate equation?

(
A) Cl 2 + H₂S $$\to$$ H + + Cl – + Cl + + HS – (slow)

Cl + + HS – $$\to$$ H + + Cl – + S (fast)

(
B) H₂S $$ \Leftrightarrow $$ H + + HS – (fast equilibrium)

Cl 2 + HS – $$\to$$ 2Cl – + H + + S (slow)
questions.solution:
Since the slow step is the rate determining step hence-

if we consider option $$(1)$$ we find

Rate $$ = k\left[ {C{l_2}} \right]\left[ {{H_2}S} \right]$$

Now if we consider option $$(2)$$ we find

Rate $$ = k\left[ {C{l_2}} \right]\left[ {H{S^ - }} \right]\,\,\,\,\,...\left( 1 \right)$$

From equation $$(i)$$

$$k = {{\left[ {{H^ + }} \right]\left[ {H{S^ - }} \right]} \over {{H_2}S}}$$ $$\,\,\,\,\,$$ or

$$\left[ {H{S^ - }} \right] = {{k\left[ {{H_2}S} \right]} \over {{H^ + }}}$$

Substituting this value in equation $$(1)$$ we find

Rate $$ = k\left[ {C{l_2}} \right]K{{\left[ {{H_2}S} \right]} \over {{H^ + }}}$$

$$ = k'{{\left[ {C{l_2}} \right]\left[ {{H_2}S} \right]} \over {\left[ {{H^ + }} \right]}}$$

hence only, mechanism $$(1)$$ is consistent with the given rate equation.

questions.text:
Reaction rate between two substance $$A$$ and $$B$$ is expressed as following:
rate $$= k[A]^n[B]^m$$
If the concentration of $$A$$ is doubled and concentration of $$B$$ is made half of initial concentration, the ratio of the new rate to the earlier rate will be:
questions.solution:
Initial rate: $r_1 = k[A]^n[B]^m$.

New rate: $r_2 = k(2[A])^n\left(\dfrac{[B]}{2}\right)^m = 2^n\,2^{-m}\,k[A]^n[B]^m$.

$\dfrac{r_2}{r_1} = 2^{n-m}$

Check with $n = m = 1$: doubling one concentration and halving the other leaves the rate unchanged, and $2^{0} = 1$.

So the ratio of the new rate to the earlier rate is $2^{(n-m)}$.

questions.text:
The reaction of ozone with oxygen atoms in the presence of chlorine atoms can occur
by a two step process shown below :

O 3 (g) + Cl$${^ \bullet }$$ (g) $$ \to $$ O 2 (g) + ClO$${^ \bullet }$$ (g) . . . . . .(i)

k i = 5.2 × 10 9 L mol −1 s −1

ClO$${^ \bullet }$$(g) + O$${^ \bullet }$$(g) $$ \to $$ O 2 (g) + Cl$${^ \bullet }$$ (g) . . . . . . (ii)

k ii = 2.6 × 10 10 L mol −1 s −1

The closest rate constant for the overall reaction O 3 (g) + O$${^ \bullet }$$ (g) $$ \to $$ 2 O 2 (g) is :
questions.solution:
Adding steps (i) and (ii) gives $\ce{O3} + \mathrm{O}^{\bullet} \rightarrow 2\ce{O2}$, with $\mathrm{Cl}^{\bullet}$ regenerated as a catalyst.

For consecutive steps the overall rate is controlled by the slower step; step (i) has the smaller rate constant ($5.2 \times 10^{9}$ against $2.6 \times 10^{10}\ \text{L mol}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$), so it is rate determining.

The overall rate constant is therefore close to $k_{\text{i}} = 5.2 \times 10^{9}\ \text{L mol}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$; the product $k_{\text{i}}k_{\text{ii}}$ has units $\text{L}^2\text{mol}^{-2}\text{s}^{-2}$ and cannot be the rate constant of this reaction.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

options.text: CO 2 < SiO 2 < SnO 2 < PbO 2 : increasing oxidising power
HF < HCl < HBr < HI : increasing acid strength
NH 3 < PH 3 < AsH 3 < SbH 3 : increasing basic strength
B < C < O < N : increasing first ionization enthalpy

questions.solution:
$$(A)\,\,\,$$ Option A is true.

Here in $$Pb{O_2}$$ oxidation number of $$Pb$$ is $$+4,$$ due to inert pair effect the oxidation number $$+4$$ is not stable for $$Pb$$, So, to become stable oxide $$+2$$ $$Pb$$ will oxidize other and reduced to $$P{b^{ + 2.}}$$ So, $$Pb{O_2}$$ has the highest oxidizing power.

$$(B)\,\,\,\,$$ Option B is true.

Bond length from top to bottom in periodic table increases, So the bond length order is $$HI > HBr > HCl > HF$$

The compound which can give $${H^ + }$$ ion easily that compound has higher acidic strength.

As the bond length between $$H$$ and $$I$$ in $$HI$$ is longest then it will be easier to break the bond between $$H$$ and $$I$$. So $$HI$$ will have highest acidic strength.

$$(C)\,\,\,\,$$ Option C is false.

The structure of those $$4$$ molecules are

Due to the lone pair electron all of them are basic in nature. The molecule which can easily donate the lone pair electron will have more basic strength.

Here, Nitrogen (N) is an element of $$2$$nd period so in $$N$$ new electron is added in the second period and as size of $$N$$ is small so electron density is more on the outer shell, so electron become unstable due to repulsion with each other. That is why electron pair is easily removable from $$N{H_3}.$$

On the other hand $$P$$ is a $$3$$rd period, As is a $$4$$th period and $$Sb$$ is a $$5$$th period element. So, their size is bigger. So, electron density on the outer shell is less and their repulsion also decreases. So, outer shell electrons are more stable and $$P{H_3},As{H_3}$$ and $$Sb{H_3}$$ will have less ability to donate the electron.

So the correct order is $$Sb{H_3} < As{H_3} < P{H_3} < N{H_3}$$

(D) Option (D) is true

Electronic configuration of

$$B\left( 5 \right)\,\,\, = \,\,\,1{s^2}2{s^2}2{p^1}$$

$$C\left( 6 \right)\,\,\, = \,\,\,1{s^2}2{s^2}2{p^2}$$

$$N\left( 7 \right)\,\,\, = \,\,\,1{s^2}2{s^2}2{p^3}$$

$$O\left( 8 \right)\,\,\, = \,\,\,1{s^2}2{s^2}2{p^4}$$

In general in periodic table from left to right effective nuclear charge increases and it becomes more difficult to remove electron from an atom. That is why ionization enthalpy increases.

But for those atoms which has half filled or full filled outer most shell, those atoms will be more stable and more energy is needed to remove electron from those atoms. Here $$N\left( {1{s^2}\,2{s^2}\,2{p^3}} \right)$$ has stable half filled $$2p$$ subshell so it is more stable than $$O.$$

So, correct order is $$B < C < O < N$$

$$O$$ atom is highly electronegative so will add first electron easily by releasing energy. So it is exothermic.

After adding first electron $$O$$ becomes $${O^ - }\,\,$$ and size of $${O^ - }\,\,$$ becomes slightly more than $$O$$ atom. Now when a new electron is trying to add into $$\,\,{O^ - }$$ ion, two forces will act on the new electron $$ \to $$

But repulsion between electrons are more compared to the attraction between nucleus and electron as distance between nucleus and electron is more compared to electrons of outer most shell and new electron.

So, to overcome the repulsion energy should be added.

That is why $${O^ - }\left( g \right) + {e^ - }\buildrel \, \over

questions.text: Which one of the following ions has the highest value of ionic radius?
questions.solution:
From a neutral atom where a electron is removed then it become cation and when a electron is added to the atom then it becomes anion.

For a atom $$x$$ when it loose a electron then it becomes cation $$x - {e^ - } \to {x^ + }$$

Let atomic no. of $$x$$ is $$z$$

then no. of proton in $${x^ + } = z$$

and no. of electron in $${x^ + } = z - 1$$

So the ratio $${z \over e}$$ as no. of electrons decreases. And when no of electron decreases then per electron attraction increases from nucleus and radius of cation deceases.

Similarly when atom $$x$$ becomes $${x^ - }$$ by adding a electron $$\left( {x + {e^ - } \to {x^ - }} \right)$$ then no. of proton in $${x^ - } = z$$ and no. of electron in $${x^ - } = z + 1.$$

Now the ratio of $${z \over e}\,\,$$ in $${x^ - }$$ decreases as no. of electron increases. As electron increases in $${x^ - }$$ then attraction from nucleus decreases on per electron and the distance between electron and nucleus increases so the radius also increase in anion.

All $$4$$ ions are from second period and for $${O^{2 - }}\,\,$$ and $${F^ - }$$ both have $$1s,$$ $$2s$$ and $$2p$$ shell and for $$L{i^ + }\,\,$$ and $${B^{3 + }}$$ both have $$1s$$ shell.

So, size of $${O^{2 - }}\,\,\,$$ and $$\,\,\,{F^ - }\,\,\,$$ are more then $$L{i^ + }\,\,\,\,$$

and $$\,\,\,\,{B^{3 + }}$$ and among $${O^{2 - }}\,\,\,$$ and $$\,\,\,\,{F^ - }$$

For $$\,\,\,$$ $${O^{2 - }},\,\,{z \over e} = {8 \over {10}} = 0.8$$

For $$\,\,\,$$ $${F^ - },\,\,\,{z \over e} = {9 \over {10}} = 0.9$$

as for $${O^{2 - }},\,\,{z \over e}\,\,\,$$ is less so per electron attraction from nucleus decreases and radius increases more than $${F^ - }.$$

Iso-electronic ions have same number of electrons. So, for iso-electronic ions, number of electrons = constant.

If Z of an ion increases then Z effective also increases and if Z of an ion decreases then Z effective also decreases. And when Z effective increases then nuclear attraction towards outermost electrons increase and size of ion decreases. questions.text: Which one of the following has largest ionic radius ?
questions.solution:
Cations are smaller than their atoms; the higher the charge, the smaller the ion: $\mathrm{B^{3+}}$ (about $27\ \mathrm{pm}$) and $\mathrm{Li^+}$ (about $76\ \mathrm{pm}$) are small.

Anions are larger than their atoms: $\mathrm{F^-}$ is about $133\ \mathrm{pm}$.

$\mathrm{O_2^{2-}}$ (peroxide) is a diatomic anion, two O atoms bonded together carrying a $-2$ charge, so it is bigger than the single-atom $\mathrm{F^-}$ ion.

So the peroxide ion $\mathrm{O_2^{2-}}$ has the largest ionic radius.

questions.text: Which of the following arrangements represents the increasing order (smallest to largest) of ionic radii of the given species O 2$$-$$ , S 2$$-$$ ,N 3$$-$$ , P 3$$-$$ ?
questions.solution:
For isoelectronic ions, the radius grows as nuclear charge falls: $\mathrm{N^{3-}}$ ($Z = 7$) is larger than $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ ($Z = 8$), and $\mathrm{P^{3-}}$ ($Z = 15$) is larger than $\mathrm{S^{2-}}$ ($Z = 16$).

Down a group radius increases, so the period-3 ions $\mathrm{S^{2-}}$ and $\mathrm{P^{3-}}$ are larger than the period-2 ions $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ and $\mathrm{N^{3-}}$.

Ionic radii: $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ $140\ \mathrm{pm}$, $\mathrm{N^{3-}}$ $171\ \mathrm{pm}$, $\mathrm{S^{2-}}$ $184\ \mathrm{pm}$, $\mathrm{P^{3-}}$ $212\ \mathrm{pm}$.

So the increasing order is $\mathrm{O^{2-} \lt N^{3-} \lt S^{2-} \lt P^{3-}}$.

questions.text:
Given two statements below :

Statement I : In $$\mathrm{Cl}_{2}$$ molecule the covalent radius is double of the atomic radius of chlorine.

Statement II : Radius of anionic species is always greater than their parent atomic radius.

Choose the most appropriate answer from options given below :

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

questions.solution:
For a non-metal, the atomic radius is its covalent radius: half the distance between the nuclei of two atoms joined by a single bond. In $\ce{Cl2}$ the bond distance is 198 pm, so the covalent (atomic) radius of chlorine is 99 pm.

Thus it is the bond length that is double the atomic radius; the covalent radius equals the atomic radius, so Statement I is incorrect.

An anion has more electrons than its parent atom with the same nuclear charge. The extra electron–electron repulsion and the lower effective nuclear charge per electron expand the electron cloud, so an anion is always larger than its parent atom (for example, $\ce{F-}$ is 136 pm while F is 64 pm). Statement II is correct.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Which pair of elements with the given atomic numbers is expected to have similar properties?
questions.solution:
$Z = 40$ is zirconium and $Z = 72$ is hafnium; both are in group 4 ($4d$ and $5d$ series).

Because of the lanthanoid contraction, Hf is almost the same size as Zr (about $160$ and $159\ \mathrm{pm}$), so their properties are nearly identical.

questions.text: Similarity in chemical properties of the atoms of elements in a group of the Periodic table is most closely related to :
questions.solution:
Chemical reactions involve only the outermost (valence) electrons.

Elements of a group have the same valence-shell configuration, e.g. $ns^1$ in group 1 and $ns^2np^5$ in group 17.

Atomic number, atomic mass and the number of shells all change down a group, so they cannot account for the similarity.

So the similarity in chemical properties is related to the number of valence electrons.

questions.text: In the long form of the periodic table, the valence shell electronic configuration of 5s 2 5p 4 corresponds to the element present in :
questions.solution:
The highest principal quantum number in $5s^2\,5p^4$ is $n = 5$, so the element is in period 5.

The last electron enters a $p$ orbital, so it is a $p$-block element: group number $= 10 + (\text{valence electrons}) = 10 + (2 + 4) = 16$.

The element is tellurium ($\mathrm{Te}$, $Z = 52$).

So it lies in group 16 and period 5.

questions.text:
For Periodic Table which of the following statements are TRUE
A. Shielding increases as we go down in the group.
B. Shielding increases sharply across the period.
C. Ionization enthalpy increases down the group.
D. Metallic character increases down the group.

E. Electronegativity decreases down the group.

Choose the correct answer from the following options :

options.text: A, C, D and E only

questions.solution:
Statement A is true: down a group the number of inner electron shells increases, so the shielding of the valence electrons increases.

Statement B is false: across a period electrons enter the same shell and shield one another poorly, so shielding increases only slightly while the effective nuclear charge increases.

Statement C is false: ionisation enthalpy decreases down a group because atomic size and shielding increase.

Statement D is true: down a group atomic size increases, the valence electrons are lost more easily and metallic character increases.

Statement E is true: down a group the larger atom attracts the shared electron pair less strongly, so electronegativity decreases.

The true statements are therefore A, D and E, and options (
B) and (
D) both give exactly this set.

Hence, the correct options are (
B) and (D).

$$\eqalign{
& \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,V\left( {23} \right) = \left[ {Ar} \right]\,\,\,3{d^3}\,\,\,4{S^2} \cr
& \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,Cr\left( {24} \right) = \left[ {Ar} \right]\,\,\,3{d^5}\,\,\,4{S^1} \cr
& \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,Mn\left( {25} \right) = \left[ {Ar} \right]\,\,\,3{d^5}\,\,\,4{S^2} \cr
& \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,Fe\left( {26} \right) = \left[ {Ar} \right]\,\,\,3{d^6}\,\,\,4{S^2} \cr} $$

After first ionization enthalpy the electronic configuration will be,

$$\eqalign{
& \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,V\left( {23} \right) = \left[ {Ar} \right]\,\,\,3{d^3}\,\,\,4{S^1} \cr
& \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,Cr\left( {24} \right) = \left[ {Ar} \right]\,\,\,3{d^5} \cr
& \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,Mn\left( {25} \right) = \left[ {Ar} \right]\,\,\,3{d^5}\,\,\,4{S^1} \cr
& \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,Fe\left( {26} \right) = \left[ {Ar} \right]\,\,\,3{d^6}\,\,\,4{S^1} \cr} $$

Now in 2nd ionization enthalpy one more electron will be removed. And after second ionization enthalpy electronic configuration will be,

$$\eqalign{
& \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,V\left( {23} \right) = \left[ {Ar} \right]\,\,\,3{d^3} \cr
& \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,Cr\left( {24} \right) = \left[ {Ar} \right]\,\,\,3{d^4} \cr
& \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,Mn\left( {25} \right) = \left[ {Ar} \right]\,\,\,3{d^5} \cr
& \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,Fe\left( {26} \right) = \left[ {Ar} \right]\,\,\,3{d^6} \cr} $$

For $$V(23), Mn (25)$$ and $$Fe (26)$$ electron is removed from $$4S$$ orbital but for $$Cr (24)$$ electron is removed from $$3d$$ orbital.

We know distance of $$4S\,\, > \,\,3d$$ from the nucleus. So, the attraction on the electrons of $$45$$ shell is less compared to $$3d$$ shell by the nucleus. So, the removed of electron will be easier for the electrons of $$4S$$ shell than $$3d$$ shell.

So, for $$Cr(24)$$ second ionization is more than other as electron is removed from $$3d$$ shell.

And for $$Cr(24)$$ outer most shell $$''3d''$$ was half filled after $$1st$$ ionization enthalpy, so $$3d$$ shell was stable. So removal of electron will be difficult from stable shell. That is why also $$2nd$$ ionization enthalpy of $$Cr(24)$$ is higher compare to other given atoms.

questions.text: The increasing order of the first ionization enthalpies of the elements B, P, S and F (lowest first) is :
questions.solution:
The correct order of ionisation enthalpies is $$F > P > S > B$$

NOTE : On moving along a period ionization enthalpy increases from left to right and decreases from top to bottom in a group. But this trend breaks up in case of atom having fully or half filled stable orbitals.

In this case $$P$$ has a stable half filled electronic configuration hence its ionisation enthalpy is greater in comparison to $$S.$$ For B(5) electronic configuration is = 1s 2 2s 2 2p 1 and P(15) electronic configuration is = 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 3s 2 3p 3 . As P has half filled valence shell so removing electron will be harder compare to B. Hence by checking all options the correct possible order is

B < S < P < F

questions.text: Which of the following presents the correct order of second ionization enthalpies of C, N, O and F ?
questions.solution:
The second electron is removed from the unipositive ions: $\mathrm{C^+}\ (2s^2 2p^1)$, $\mathrm{N^+}\ (2s^2 2p^2)$, $\mathrm{O^+}\ (2s^2 2p^3)$, $\mathrm{F^+}\ (2s^2 2p^4)$.

$\mathrm{O^+}$ has a stable half-filled $2p^3$ subshell, so its second ionization enthalpy is the highest.

Of the rest, $\mathrm{F^+}$ has the highest nuclear charge, so it comes next, followed by $\mathrm{N^+}$ and then $\mathrm{C^+}$.

Check with measured values in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$: O 3388, F 3374, N 2856, C 2352.

Hence the order is $\mathrm{O \gt F \gt N \gt C}$.

questions.text: Which among the following elements has the highest first ionization enthalpy?
questions.solution:
Across period 2 the first ionization enthalpy generally rises with nuclear charge: $\mathrm{B \lt C \lt N}$.

Nitrogen has the half-filled, extra-stable configuration $2s^2 2p^3$.

Oxygen ($2p^4$) loses one electron of a paired $2p$ orbital; the pairing repulsion makes this easier, so oxygen lies below nitrogen.

Order: $\mathrm{B \lt C \lt O \lt N}$ ($801, 1086, 1314, 1402\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$).

So nitrogen has the highest first ionization enthalpy.

questions.text: Which is the correct order of second ionization potential of C, N, O and F in the following?
questions.solution:
The second IE removes an electron from the unipositive ion: $\mathrm{C^+}$ ($2s^22p^1$), $\mathrm{N^+}$ ($2s^22p^2$), $\mathrm{O^+}$ ($2s^22p^3$), $\mathrm{F^+}$ ($2s^22p^4$).

$\mathrm{O^+}$ has the stable half-filled $2p^3$ configuration, so removing an electron from it is hardest.

$\mathrm{F^+}$ ($2p^4$) loses a paired electron, which is a little easier, so $\mathrm{IE_2}$ of F is just below that of O.

From C to N, $\mathrm{IE_2}$ rises with nuclear charge.

Order of second ionization potential: $\mathrm{O \gt F \gt N \gt C}$.

questions.text:

questions.solution:
(I) Atomic radius increases down a group, so Be is smaller than Mg; true.

(II) The first ionization enthalpy of Be ($899\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) is higher than that of Al ($577\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$); true.

questions.text:
B has a smaller first ionization enthalpy than
Be. Consider the following statements :

(I) It is easier to remove 2p electron than 2s
electron

(II) 2p electron of B is more shielded from the
nucleus by the inner core of electrons than
the 2s electrons of Be.

(III) 2s electron has more penetration power
than 2p electron.

(IV) atomic radius of B is more than Be
(Atomic number B = 5, Be = 4)

The correct statements are :
questions.solution:
In the first ionization, Be ($1s^2 2s^2$) loses a $2s$ electron while B ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^1$) loses a $2p$ electron.

A $2s$ electron penetrates closer to the nucleus than a $2p$ electron, so statement (III) is correct.

Owing to its lower penetration, the $2p$ electron of B is more effectively shielded from the nucleus by the inner core of electrons than the $2s$ electrons of Be, so statement (II) is correct.

The $2p$ electron of B therefore feels a smaller effective nuclear charge and is easier to remove than the $2s$ electron of Be, so statement (I) is correct; this is why $\Delta_i H_1$ of B is smaller than that of Be.

Atomic radius decreases across a period as the nuclear charge increases, so B (88 pm) is smaller than Be (111 pm) and statement (IV) is incorrect.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The correct order of first ionisation enthalpy is :
The first ionization energy of magnesium is smaller as compared to that of elements X and Y, but higher than that of Z. The elements X, Y and Z, respectively, are :
questions.solution:
We are told:

$\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Mg})$ is smaller than $\mathrm{IE}(X)$ and $\mathrm{IE}(Y)$.

$\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Mg})$ is greater than $\mathrm{IE}(Z)$.

Hence we want:

$ \mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Mg}) < \mathrm{IE}(X), \quad \mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Mg}) < \mathrm{IE}(Y), \quad \mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Mg}) > \mathrm{IE}(Z). $

Approximate first ionization energies (in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) of the relevant elements:

$\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Ne}) \approx 2080$

$\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Na}) \approx 496$

$\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Mg}) \approx 738$

$\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Al}) \approx 578$ (not listed but for reference)

$\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Si}) \approx 787$ (not listed but for reference)

$\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{P}) \approx 1012$ (not listed but for reference)

$\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{S}) \approx 1000$ (not listed but for reference)

$\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Cl}) \approx 1251$

$\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Ar}) \approx 1521$

$\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Li}) \approx 520$

We test each option:

(
A) neon, sodium, chlorine

$X=\mathrm{Ne}$: $\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Ne})=2080 > 738$ ✓

$Y=\mathrm{Na}$: $\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Na})=496 < 738$ ✗ (contradicts “$\mathrm{Mg}$ < $Y$”)

$Z=\mathrm{Cl}$: $\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Cl})=1251 > 738$ ✗ (contradicts “$\mathrm{Mg}$ > $Z$”)

So (
A) does not fit the requirement.

(
B) argon, chlorine, sodium

$X=\mathrm{Ar}$: $\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Ar})=1521 > 738$ ✓

$Y=\mathrm{Cl}$: $\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Cl})=1251 > 738$ ✓

$Z=\mathrm{Na}$: $\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Na})=496 < 738$ ✓

Thus $\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Mg}) < \mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Ar}), \,\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Cl})$ and $\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Mg}) > \mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Na})$.

This matches perfectly .

(
C) chlorine, lithium, sodium

$X=\mathrm{Cl}$: $\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Cl})=1251 > 738$ ✓

$Y=\mathrm{Li}$: $\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Li})=520 < 738$ ✗ (contradicts “$\mathrm{Mg}$ < $Y$”)

$Z=\mathrm{Na}$: $\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Na})=496 < 738$, but the mismatch in $Y$ is enough to discard it.

(
D) argon, lithium, sodium

$X=\mathrm{Ar}$: $\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Ar})=1521 > 738$ ✓

$Y=\mathrm{Li}$: $\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Li})=520 < 738$ ✗ (contradicts “$\mathrm{Mg}$ < $Y$”)

$Z=\mathrm{Na}$: $\mathrm{IE}(\mathrm{Na})=496 < 738$ is fine for $Z$, but $Y$ fails.

Hence only (
B) satisfies all conditions:

$ \boxed{\text{(
B) argon, chlorine, and sodium.}} $

questions.text: The first ionization enthalpy of Na, Mg and Si, respectively, are : 496, 737 and $$786 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$$. The first ionization enthalpy ($$\mathrm{kJ} \,\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$$) of $$\mathrm{Al}$$ is :

Al ($[\mathrm{Ne}]\,3s^2 3p^1$) loses a 3p electron, which is higher in energy and shielded by the filled 3s subshell, whereas Mg ($[\mathrm{Ne}]\,3s^2$) loses a more penetrating electron from a fully filled 3s subshell. $$496 < \Delta_i H(\mathrm{Al}) < 737\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Among the options only $577\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ lies in this range; 768 and 856 exceed the value for Mg and 487 is below that for Na.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.solution:
First ionisation enthalpies (in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) decide each statement.

(
A) Down group 1 the atomic size increases: Li (520) > Na (496) > K (419). The statement is correct.

(
B) In group 18, radon (1037) has a lower first ionisation enthalpy than xenon (1170), so Xe is not the lowest in its group. The statement is correct.

(
C) $Z = 37$ is Rb (403) and $Z = 38$ is Sr (549); the single $5s$ electron of Rb is removed more easily than an electron from the filled $5s^2$ of Sr. The statement is correct.

(
D) $Z = 30$ is Zn, whose fully filled $3d^{10}4s^2$ configuration is stable (906), while Ga (579) loses a single $4p$ electron that is well shielded by the inner electrons. The first ionisation enthalpy of Ga is therefore lower than that of Zn, and the statement is incorrect.

questions.text:
Given below are two statements. One is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R.

Assertion A : The first ionization enthalpy for oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen.

Reason R : The four electrons in 2p orbitals of oxygen experience more electron-electron repulsion.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below.

options.text: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is correct but R is not correct.
A is not correct but R is correct.

questions.solution:
In nitrogen ($2p^3$) the three $2p$ electrons occupy separate orbitals, while in oxygen ($2p^4$) two of the four $2p$ electrons must share one orbital.

The four $2p$ electrons of oxygen therefore experience greater electron–electron repulsion, so the fourth $2p$ electron is removed more easily than a $2p$ electron of nitrogen; the first ionisation enthalpy of O (about $1314\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$) is lower than that of N (about $1402\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$).

Both A and R are correct, and the greater repulsion stated in R is the reason for A.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: The electron affinity of chlorine is $$3.7\ \mathrm{eV}$$. 1 gram of chlorine is completely converted to $$\mathrm{Cl^-}$$ ion in a gaseous state. $$(1\ \mathrm{eV} = 23.06\ \mathrm{kcal\,mol^{-1}})$$. Energy released in the process is

questions.text: Electron gain enthalpy with negative sign of fluorine is less than that of chlorine due to :

options.text: Bigger size of 2p orbital of fluorine

questions.solution:
An electron added to fluorine enters the small, compact $2p$ subshell.

Because the fluorine atom is very small, the incoming electron feels strong repulsion from the electrons already present.

In chlorine the extra electron enters the larger $3p$ subshell, where this repulsion is much weaker.

So less energy is released for F than for Cl.

Answer: the smaller size of the fluorine atom.

questions.text: The correct order of electron gain enthalpy is :
questions.solution:
Oxygen is the second most electronegative element in comparison to fluorine. In group - 16 family $(\mathrm{O}, \mathrm{S}, \mathrm{Se}, \mathrm{Te})$, O-atom is smallest in size. So, electron density on O-atom is very high in group -16
During addition of a free electron to gaseous $\mathrm{O}$-atom,

$$
\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g})+\mathrm{e}^{-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{O}^{-}(\mathrm{g})
$$

We have to supply a significant amount of energy (endothermic) to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between the approaching electron and O-atom of very high electron density. So, the net value of electron affinity (EA) or (negative) electron gain enthalpy $\left[\Delta_{\mathrm{eg}} H\right.$ or $\left.\left|\Delta_{\mathrm{eg}} H\right|\right]$ of oxygen decreases to a higher extent in comparison to other elements of group -16 who have larger size and lower electronegativity.

So, the correct order of EA or $\left|\Delta_{\mathrm{eg}} \mathrm{H}\right|$ of group $-16$ elements will be $\mathrm{S}$ $>\mathrm{Se}>\mathrm{Te}>\mathrm{O}$

questions.text:
The decreasing values of bond angles from NH 3 (106 o ) to SbH 3 (91 o
) down group-15 of the periodic table is due to
questions.solution:
In $\ce{NH3}$, $\ce{PH3}$, $\ce{AsH3}$ and $\ce{SbH3}$ the central atom carries three bond pairs and one lone pair.

Down the group the electronegativity of the central atom decreases, so the bonding pairs are drawn less towards it and lie farther from the central atom.

The bond pairs then repel one another less, and the lone pair pushes them closer together, so the bond angle falls from $106^\circ$ in $\ce{NH3}$ to $91^\circ$ in $\ce{SbH3}$.

A decrease in lone pair–bond pair repulsion would widen the angle, not narrow it.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

$\mathrm{NI_3}$: N has 3 bond pairs and 1 lone pair ($sp^3$), so it is trigonal pyramidal.

$\mathrm{I_3^-}$: the central I has 2 bond pairs and 3 lone pairs ($sp^3d$), so it is linear.

$\mathrm{SO_3^{2-}}$: S has 3 σ bonds and 1 lone pair ($sp^3$), so it is trigonal pyramidal.

questions.text: Which of the following has the square planar structure?
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{XeF_4}$: Xe has 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs, so it is $sp^3d^2$ hybridised with an octahedral electron arrangement.

The two lone pairs occupy opposite (trans) positions, leaving the four F atoms in a square plane.

$\mathrm{NH_4^+}$, $\mathrm{BF_4^-}$ and $\mathrm{CCl_4}$ each have 4 bond pairs and no lone pair on the central atom ($sp^3$), so they are tetrahedral.

Hence the square planar species is $\mathrm{XeF_4}$.

questions.text: The formation of molecular complex $$\mathrm{BF_3-NH_3}$$ results in a change in hybridization of boron
questions.solution:
In $\mathrm{BF_3}$ boron has three bond pairs and no lone pair, so it is $sp^2$ hybridized (trigonal planar) with a vacant $2p$ orbital.

$\mathrm{NH_3}$ donates its lone pair into this vacant orbital, forming the coordinate bond $\mathrm{N \rightarrow B}$.

Boron now has four bond pairs, so it becomes $sp^3$ hybridized (tetrahedral).

So the hybridization of boron changes from $sp^2$ to $sp^3$.

questions.text: The geometry of XeOF 4 by VSEPR theory is :
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{Xe}$ has $8$ valence electrons: $4$ form four $\mathrm{Xe-F}$ bonds and $2$ form the $\mathrm{Xe=O}$ double bond, leaving $1$ lone pair.

The steric number of $\mathrm{Xe}$ is $5\ (\text{bond pairs}) + 1\ (\text{lone pair}) = 6$ (the double bond counts once), so the electron arrangement is octahedral, $sp^3d^2$.

The lone pair occupies one octahedral position, so the five atoms ($4\,\mathrm{F} + 1\,\mathrm{O}$) form a square pyramid with $\mathrm{O}$ at the apex.

So by VSEPR theory $\mathrm{XeOF_4}$ is square pyramidal.

questions.text:
If AB 4 molecule is a polar molecule, a possible
geometry of AB 4 is
questions.solution:
An $\ce{AB4}$ molecule is polar only if its four A–B bond dipoles do not cancel.

Tetrahedral: the four equal A–B dipoles point to the corners of a regular tetrahedron and cancel, so the molecule is non-polar (e.g. $\ce{CH4}$, $\ce{CCl4}$).

Rectangular planar and square planar: every A–B dipole has an equal one pointing the opposite way (at $180^\circ$), so they cancel and both shapes are non-polar (e.g. $\ce{XeF4}$ is square planar).

Square pyramidal: A sits at the apex above the square of four B atoms. The components of the four dipoles in the plane of the base cancel, but their components along the axis all point the same way and add up, so the molecule has a net dipole moment and is polar.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: Lattice energy of an ionic compound depends upon

options.text: Charge on the ion and size of the ion

questions.solution:
The lattice energy of an ionic compound is a measure of the strength of the bonds in that ionic compound. Specifically, it is the energy required to separate one mole of an ionic solid into its constituent ions in the gaseous state. The lattice energy depends on several factors, primarily the charge on the ions and the size (or radius) of the ions.

1. Charge on the ions: The lattice energy is directly proportional to the product of the charges of the cation and the anion. Higher charges result in stronger electrostatic attraction between the ions, thereby increasing the lattice energy. This relationship can be derived from Coulomb's law, which states that the force of attraction between two charged particles is directly proportional to the product of their charges.

Mathematically:

$$U \propto \frac{q_1 \cdot q_2}{r}$$

where $U$ is the lattice energy, $q_1$ and $q_2$ are the charges on the ions, and $r$ is the distance between the centers of the ions.

2. Size of the ions: The lattice energy is inversely proportional to the distance between the ions, which depends on the sum of their ionic radii. Smaller ions can come closer together, increasing the electrostatic attractions between them, thereby increasing the lattice energy. Larger ions, being further apart, result in a lower lattice energy.

Considering these two factors, the correct choice is:

Option D: Charge on the ion and size of the ion

questions.text: Amongst LiCl, RbCl, BeCl 2 and MgCl 2 the compounds with the greatest and the least ionic character, respectively are :
questions.solution:
Fajans' rules: a small, highly charged cation polarises the anion most and gives the most covalent character.

$\mathrm{Rb^+}$ is large and singly charged, the least polarising, so $\mathrm{RbCl}$ is the most ionic (more than $\mathrm{LiCl}$, since $\mathrm{Li^+}$ is small).

$\mathrm{Be^{2+}}$ is very small and doubly charged, the most polarising, so $\mathrm{BeCl_2}$ is the most covalent (more than $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$).

Ionic character: $\mathrm{RbCl}\gt\mathrm{LiCl}\gt\mathrm{MgCl_2}\gt\mathrm{BeCl_2}$

So the greatest ionic character is in $\mathrm{RbCl}$ and the least in $\mathrm{BeCl_2}$.

questions.text: The correct set from the following in which both pairs are in correct order of melting point is :
questions.solution:
Correct option is (D), i.e. LiF > LiCl; MgO > NaCl. Melting point is directly proportional to lattice energy. Lattice energy is the energy required to separate a mole of an ionic solid into gaseous ions. It depends upon charge of ions and size of ions.

$$M.P. \propto L.E. \propto {{Charge} \over {Size}}$$

$$\matrix{
{Li \to + 1} & {Li \to + 1} \cr
{F = - 1} & {Cl \to - 1} \cr

} $$

Both LiF and LiCl having same charge, so melting point will depend on size.

Larger the size of anion, lesser the lattice energy and hence, melting point order is LiF > LiCl.

Similarly, $$\matrix{
{MgO} & {NaCl} \cr
{Mg \to 2 + } & {Na \to 1 + } \cr
{O \to 2 - } & {Cl \to 1 - } \cr

} $$

MgO having + 2 charge which is greater than NaCl (+ 1) charge. So, greater the charge on the ions greater will be lattice energy and hence, melting point order is MgO > NaCl.

questions.text: Although $$\mathrm{CN^-}$$ ion and $$\mathrm{N_2}$$ molecule are isoelectronic, yet $$\mathrm{N_2}$$ molecule is chemically inert because of

options.text: presence of more number of electrons in bonding orbitals

questions.solution:
Both species have $14$ electrons and bond order $3$, so their numbers of bonding electrons are the same.

The $\mathrm{N{\equiv}N}$ bond is very strong (about $946\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$), so a low bond energy cannot be the reason.

In $\mathrm{N_2}$ the two atoms are identical, the electron cloud is shared evenly and the bond is non-polar.

$\mathrm{CN^-}$ has a polar bond and a negative charge, so it readily attacks electrophiles and metal ions.

So $\mathrm{N_2}$ is inert because of the absence of bond polarity.

questions.text: Among the following, the species having the smallest bond is
questions.solution:
Bond order from molecular orbital theory $= \dfrac{N_b - N_a}{2}$.

$\mathrm{NO^+}$ has $14$ electrons (like $\mathrm{N_2}$): bond order $3$.

$\mathrm{NO}$ has $15$ electrons: bond order $2.5$.

$\mathrm{NO^-}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$ have $16$ electrons each: bond order $2$.

Bond length decreases as bond order increases, so the highest bond order gives the shortest bond.

So $\mathrm{NO^+}$ has the smallest (shortest) bond.

questions.text: The internuclear distances in O-O bonds for $$O_2^+$$, $$O_2$$, $$O_2^-$$ and $$O_2^{2-}$$ respectively are :
questions.solution:
By MO theory, bond orders: $\mathrm{O_2^+} = 2.5$, $\mathrm{O_2} = 2$, $\mathrm{O_2^-} = 1.5$, $\mathrm{O_2^{2-}} = 1$.

Higher bond order means a shorter bond.

So bond length increases in the order $\mathrm{O_2^+ \lt O_2 \lt O_2^- \lt O_2^{2-}}$.

The distances are $1.12$, $1.21$, $1.30$ and $1.49\ \mathrm{\AA}$ respectively.

questions.text: Bond order normally gives idea of stability of a molecular species. All the molecules viz. $$H_2$$, $$Li_2$$ and $$B_2$$ have the same bond order yet they are not equally stable. Their stability order is :
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{H_2}$, $\mathrm{Li_2}$ and $\mathrm{B_2}$ all have bond order 1.

$\mathrm{H_2}$: small 1s orbitals overlap strongly; bond energy about $436\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

$\mathrm{B_2}$: the bond comes from two half-filled $\pi$ orbitals of compact 2p orbitals; bond energy about $290\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

$\mathrm{Li_2}$: large diffuse 2s orbitals overlap poorly and the inner 1s shells repel; bond energy only about $105\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

Stability order: $\mathrm{H_2} \gt \mathrm{B_2} \gt \mathrm{Li_2}$.

questions.text: In which of the following ionization processes the bond energy has increased and also the magnetic behaviour has changed from paramagnetic to diamagnetic?
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{NO}$ has 15 electrons: bond order $2.5$ with one unpaired electron in $\pi^*2p$, so it is paramagnetic.

Removing that antibonding electron gives $\mathrm{NO^+}$ (14 electrons, like $\mathrm{N_2}$): bond order $3$, all electrons paired, diamagnetic.

$\mathrm{N_2 \to N_2^+}$ and $\mathrm{C_2 \to C_2^+}$ lose a bonding electron, so bond order falls and the ions become paramagnetic.

$\mathrm{O_2 \to O_2^+}$ raises bond order from $2$ to $2.5$, but both species remain paramagnetic.

Answer: $\mathrm{NO \to NO^+}$.

questions.text: The correct order of bond dissociation energy among N 2 , O 2 , O$$_2^ - $$ is shown in which of the following arrangements ?

questions.text:
After understanding the assertion and reason, choose the correct option.

Assertion :     In the bonding molecular
orbital (MO) of H 2 , electron density is increased between the nuclei.

Reason :     The bonding MO is $${\psi _A}\, + \,{\psi _B},$$ which shows destructive interference of the combining electron waves.

options.text:
Assertion and reason are correct and reason is the correct explanation for
the assertion

Assertion and reason are correct, but reason is not the correct explanation
for the assertion.
Assertion is correct, reason is incorrect.
Assertion is incorrect, reason is correct.

questions.solution:
The assertion is correct .

In the bonding molecular orbital of $H_2$, the two atomic orbitals combine in such a way that the electron density increases between the two nuclei . This helps in holding the nuclei together, so it is a bonding MO.

Now look at the reason :

The bonding MO is written as

$$ \psi_A + \psi_B $$

This combination corresponds to constructive interference , not destructive interference. Because of constructive interference, electron density increases in the internuclear region.

So, the reason is incorrect .

Therefore, the correct option is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option C}} $$

Assertion is correct, reason is incorrect.

questions.text:
Among the following, the molecule expected
to be stabilized by anion formation is :

C 2 , O 2 , NO, F 2
questions.solution:
A molecule is stabilised by forming an anion when the added electron enters a bonding molecular orbital, so the bond order rises.

$\ce{C2}$ (12 electrons): $\sigma 1s^2\,\sigma^*1s^2\,\sigma 2s^2\,\sigma^*2s^2\,\pi 2p_x^2 = \pi 2p_y^2$, bond order $= \dfrac{8-4}{2} = 2$. In $\ce{C2-}$ the 13th electron enters the bonding $\sigma 2p_z$ orbital, so bond order $= \dfrac{9-4}{2} = 2.5$: stabilised.

$\ce{NO}$ (15 electrons) has one electron in $\pi^*2p$, bond order $= \dfrac{10-5}{2} = 2.5$. In $\ce{NO-}$ the extra electron also enters $\pi^*2p$, bond order $= \dfrac{10-6}{2} = 2$: destabilised.

$\ce{O2}$ (16 electrons), bond order $= \dfrac{10-6}{2} = 2$; $\ce{O2-}$ has a third $\pi^*2p$ electron, bond order $= \dfrac{10-7}{2} = 1.5$: destabilised.

$\ce{F2}$ (18 electrons), bond order $= \dfrac{10-8}{2} = 1$; in $\ce{F2-}$ the extra electron enters $\sigma^*2p_z$, bond order $= \dfrac{10-9}{2} = 0.5$: destabilised.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: Two pi and half sigma bonds are present in :
questions.solution:
In molecular orbital terms, a pair of electrons in a bonding orbital counts as one bond and a single electron as half a bond; electrons in antibonding orbitals cancel bonding ones of the same type.

$\ce{N2+}$ (13 electrons): $\sigma 1s^2\,\sigma^*1s^2\,\sigma 2s^2\,\sigma^*2s^2\,\pi 2p_x^2 = \pi 2p_y^2\,\sigma 2p_z^1$. The filled $\pi 2p_x$ and $\pi 2p_y$ give two $\pi$ bonds and the single electron in $\sigma 2p_z$ gives half a $\sigma$ bond (bond order 2.5).

$\ce{O2+}$ (15 electrons): $\sigma 1s^2\,\sigma^*1s^2\,\sigma 2s^2\,\sigma^*2s^2\,\sigma 2p_z^2\,\pi 2p_x^2 = \pi 2p_y^2\,\pi^*2p_x^1$. This is one full $\sigma$ bond and two $\pi$ bonds less half a $\pi$ bond, i.e. one $\sigma$ and one and a half $\pi$ bonds; its bond order is also 2.5, but the half bond is of $\pi$ type.

$\ce{N2}$ has one $\sigma$ and two $\pi$ bonds, and $\ce{O2}$ has one $\sigma$ and one $\pi$ bond.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.solution:
A species is diamagnetic only when all its electrons are paired. Up to 14 electrons the molecular orbitals fill as $\sigma1s,\ \sigma^*1s,\ \sigma2s,\ \sigma^*2s,\ (\pi2p_x=\pi2p_y),\ \sigma2p_z$; further electrons enter the degenerate pair $\pi^*2p_x=\pi^*2p_y$.

$\ce{N2}$ (14 electrons): $\ldots(\pi2p)^4(\sigma2p_z)^2$, all paired, diamagnetic.

$\ce{N2+}$ (13 electrons): $\ldots(\pi2p)^4(\sigma2p_z)^1$, 1 unpaired electron.

$\ce{N2-}$ and $\ce{O2+}$ (15 electrons each): $(\pi^*2p_x)^1$, 1 unpaired electron.

$\ce{N2^2-}$ and $\ce{O2}$ (16 electrons each): $(\pi^*2p_x)^1(\pi^*2p_y)^1$, 2 unpaired electrons.

$\ce{O2-}$ (17 electrons): $(\pi^*2p_x)^2(\pi^*2p_y)^1$, 1 unpaired electron.

$\ce{O2^2-}$ (18 electrons): $(\pi^*2p_x)^2(\pi^*2p_y)^2$, all paired, diamagnetic.

Only $\ce{N2}$ and $\ce{O2^2-}$ are diamagnetic.

Hence, the answer is 2.

questions.text: Dipole moment is shown by
questions.solution:
In 1,2-dichlorobenzene the two C–Cl bond dipoles are at $60^\circ$ to each other, so they add up to a net dipole moment.

In 1,4-dichlorobenzene the two C–Cl bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel.

In each trans alkene the identical groups lie opposite each other across the double bond, so their bond dipoles cancel and the net dipole moment is zero.

Hence only 1,2-dichlorobenzene shows a dipole moment.
