$\mathrm{CH_3Cl}$, $\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}$ and $\mathrm{CHCl_3}$ have both C–H and C–Cl bonds, so the bond dipoles do not cancel and $\mu \gt 0$.

Hence the lowest dipole moment is that of $\mathrm{CCl_4}$.

questions.text: Bond distance in HF is $$9.17 \times 10^{-11}$$ m. Dipole moment of HF is $$6.104 \times 10^{-30}$$ Cm. The percentage ionic character in HF will be : (electron charge = $$1.60 \times 10^{-19}$$ C)
questions.solution:
For a fully ionic bond, $\mu = e\,d = 1.60\times10^{-19}\times9.17\times10^{-11} = 1.467\times10^{-29}\ \mathrm{C\,m}$.

Percentage ionic character $= \dfrac{\mu_{\mathrm{obs}}}{e\,d}\times100 = \dfrac{6.104\times10^{-30}}{1.467\times10^{-29}}\times100$.

$\approx 41.6\%$, i.e. about $41.5\%$ ionic character.

questions.text: Molecule AB has a bond length of 1.617 $$\mathop A\limits^ \bullet $$ and a dipole moment of 0.38 D. The fractional charge on each atom (absolute magnitude) is : (e 0 = 4.802 $$ \times $$ 10 $$-$$10 esu)
questions.solution:
Dipole moment $\mu = q \times d$, so $q = \dfrac{\mu}{d}$.

$\mu = 0.38\ \mathrm{D} = 0.38\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{esu\,cm}$ and $d = 1.617\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}} = 1.617\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}$.

$q = \dfrac{0.38\times10^{-18}}{1.617\times10^{-8}} = 2.35\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{esu}$.

Fractional charge $= \dfrac{q}{e_0} = \dfrac{2.35\times10^{-11}}{4.802\times10^{-10}} \approx 0.049$.

So the fractional charge on each atom is about $0.05$.

smaller size of B - atom as compared to that of C- atom.

questions.solution:
In BF 3 , B is sp 2
hybridised and by Back Bonding method strong p$$\pi $$-p$$\pi $$ bond is created between filled p-orbital of F and vacant p-orbital of
B which leads to shortening of B–F bond length which results in higher bond dissociation energy of

questions.text: The bond dissociation energy of B – F in $$\mathrm{BF_3}$$ is 646 kJ $$\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$$ whereas that of C – F in $$\mathrm{CF_4}$$ is 515 kJ $$\mathrm{mol^{-1}}$$. The correct reason for higher B – F bond dissociation energy as compared to that of C – F is :

options.text: smaller size of B-atom as compared to that of C-atom
stronger $$\sigma$$ bond between B and F in $$\mathrm{BF_3}$$ as compared to that between C and F in $$\mathrm{CF_4}$$
significant $$p\pi - p\pi$$ interaction between B and F in $$\mathrm{BF_3}$$ whereas there is no possibility of such interaction between C and F in $$\mathrm{CF_4}$$.
lower degree of $$p\pi - p\pi$$ interaction between B and F in $$\mathrm{BF_3}$$ than that between C and F in $$\mathrm{CF_4}$$.

questions.solution:
In $\mathrm{BF_3}$, boron is $sp^2$ hybridised and keeps one vacant $2p$ orbital perpendicular to the molecular plane.

Fluorine has filled $2p$ orbitals of similar size and energy, so a lone pair of F is donated into this empty orbital of B ($p\pi$–$p\pi$ back bonding).

This gives each B–F bond partial double-bond character, making it shorter and stronger.

In $\mathrm{CF_4}$, carbon is $sp^3$ hybridised with a complete octet and no vacant orbital, so no such $\pi$ interaction is possible.

Size cannot be the reason, since the B atom is actually larger than the C atom.

Hence the higher B–F bond dissociation energy is due to significant $p\pi$–$p\pi$ interaction in $\mathrm{BF_3}$, which is impossible in $\mathrm{CF_4}$.

questions.text: Which one of the following does not have a pyramidal shape ?
questions.solution:
In $\mathrm{(CH_3)_3N}$ and $\mathrm{P(CH_3)_3}$ the central atom has three bond pairs and one lone pair ($sp^3$), so both are pyramidal.

In $\mathrm{(SiH_3)_3N}$ the lone pair on N is delocalised into vacant 3d orbitals of Si ($p\pi$–$d\pi$ back bonding), so N is $sp^2$ and the molecule is trigonal planar.

In $\mathrm{P(SiH_3)_3}$ the lone pair is in the larger, diffuse 3p orbital of P, so this back bonding is weak and the molecule stays pyramidal.

So $\mathrm{(SiH_3)_3N}$ does not have a pyramidal shape.

Fluorine atoms are small, so six of them fit around Si and $\ce{[SiF6]^2-}$ is well known. Germanium and tin are larger, so $\ce{[GeCl6]^2-}$ and the stannate ion $\ce{[Sn(OH)6]^2-}$ also exist.

questions.text:
Among the following, the number of halide(s) which is/are inert to hydrolysis is _________.

(
A) BF 3

(
B) SiCl 4

(
C) PCl 5

(
D) SF 6
questions.solution:
Hydrolysis of a covalent halide needs a site on the central atom that a water molecule can attack.

$\ce{BF3}$: boron has a vacant 2p orbital, so it is hydrolysed: $\ce{4BF3 + 3H2O -> H3BO3 + 3HBF4}$.

$\ce{SiCl4}$: silicon accepts the lone pair of water into its vacant 3d orbitals: $\ce{SiCl4 + 4H2O -> Si(OH)4 + 4HCl}$.

$\ce{PCl5}$: phosphorus is attacked in the same way: $\ce{PCl5 + 4H2O -> H3PO4 + 5HCl}$.

$\ce{SF6}$: sulphur is coordinatively saturated and sterically shielded by six fluorine atoms, so water cannot reach it and $\ce{SF6}$ is inert to hydrolysis.

Only $\ce{SF6}$ is inert to hydrolysis.

Hence, the answer is 1.

questions.text: The correct order of bond dissociation enthalpy of halogens is :
questions.solution:
Bond dissociation enthalpies of the halogens (in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$): $\ce{Cl2}$ 242.6, $\ce{Br2}$ 192.8, $\ce{F2}$ 158.8 and $\ce{I2}$ 151.1.

From $\ce{Cl2}$ to $\ce{I2}$ the atomic size increases, the bond becomes longer and the orbital overlap poorer, so the bond enthalpy decreases: $\ce{Cl2 > Br2 > I2}$.

$\ce{F2}$ is anomalous: the F–F bond is very short, so the lone pairs on the two small fluorine atoms repel each other strongly and weaken the bond, placing $\ce{F2}$ below $\ce{Br2}$ but still above $\ce{I2}$.

$$\ce{Cl2 > Br2 > F2 > I2}$$

Hence, the correct option is (B).

Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is correct but R is not correct.
A is not correct but R is correct.

questions.solution:
Fluorine forms only one oxoacid, $\ce{HOF}$ (hypofluorous acid, also called fluoric(I) acid). Chlorine, bromine and iodine form series such as $\ce{HOX}$, $\ce{HOXO}$, $\ce{HOXO2}$ and $\ce{HOXO3}$.

Fluorine is the smallest and the most electronegative halogen, so it cannot show positive oxidation states or expand its octet; this is why it forms only one oxoacid. Assertion A and Reason R are both correct, and R is the correct explanation of A.

$\ce{OF2}$ and $\ce{O2F2}$ are oxygen fluorides (oxides), not oxoacids, so they do not affect Assertion A.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
Which of the following paramagnetic ions would exhibit a magnetic moment (spin only) of the order of $$5\ \mathrm{BM}$$?
(At. Nos. $$\mathrm{Mn} = 25, \mathrm{Cr} = 24, \mathrm{V} = 23, \mathrm{Ti} = 22$$)
questions.solution:
Spin-only moment: $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\ \mathrm{BM}$, where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons.

$\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$ is $3d^5$ ($n = 5$): $\mu = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92\ \mathrm{BM}$.

$\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}$ is $3d^4$ ($n = 4$): $\mu = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.90\ \mathrm{BM}$.

$\mathrm{V^{2+}}$ is $3d^3$: $\mu \approx 3.87\ \mathrm{BM}$; $\mathrm{Ti^{2+}}$ is $3d^2$: $\mu \approx 2.83\ \mathrm{BM}$.

The value closest to $5\ \mathrm{BM}$ is $4.90\ \mathrm{BM}$.

Hence the ion is $\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}$.

Answer: $3d^54s^2$.

questions.text: Which one of the following exhibits the largest number of oxidation states ?
questions.solution:
Configurations: Ti $3d^2 4s^2$, V $3d^3 4s^2$, Cr $3d^5 4s^1$, Mn $3d^5 4s^2$.

Both $3d$ and $4s$ electrons can be used in bonding, so the highest oxidation state rises with the number of these electrons up to Mn.

Ti shows $+2$ to $+4$, V $+2$ to $+5$, Cr $+2$ to $+6$, and Mn $+2$ to $+7$.

With seven $(3d + 4s)$ electrons, Mn has the widest range.

So Mn (25) exhibits the largest number of oxidation states.

questions.text: The pair of compounds having metals in their highest oxidation state is :
questions.solution:
The highest oxidation state of Mn is $+7$ and that of Cr is $+6$.

In $\ce{Mn2O7}$: $2x + 7(-2) = 0$, so $x = +7$. In $\ce{CrO2Cl2}$: $x + 2(-2) + 2(-1) = 0$, so $x = +6$. Both metals are in their highest oxidation states.

In the other pairs at least one metal is below its highest state (Fe reaches $+6$, Co and Ni $+4$): Ni $+2$ and Co $+2$ in (B), Fe $+3$ and Cu $+2$ in (C), Fe $+3$ and Co $+3$ in (D).

Hence, the correct option is (A).

$$\mu = \sqrt {n\left( {n + 2} \right)} $$
where n = no. of unpaired electrons i.e. greater the no. of unpaired electron more will be the spin-only magnetic moments.

. Electronic configuration of the given transition
metal ions are

Sc 3+ (Z = 21) = 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 3s 2 3p 6

$$ \therefore $$ n = 0

Ti 2+ (Z = 22) = 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 3s 2 3p 6 3d 2

$$ \therefore $$ n = 2

Ti 3+ (Z = 22) = 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 3s 2 3p 6 3d 1

$$ \therefore $$ n = 1

V 2+ (Z = 23) = 1s 2 2s 2 2p 6 3s 2 3p 6 3d 3

$$ \therefore $$ n = 3

questions.text: The reduction in atomic size with increase in atomic number is a characteristic of elements of
questions.solution:
Across the lanthanides and actinides each added electron enters a 4f or 5f orbital, which shields the outer electrons poorly from the increasing nuclear charge.

The effective nuclear charge therefore rises steadily and the atomic and ionic radii decrease regularly with increasing atomic number; this lanthanide (actinide) contraction is the characteristic property of the f-block elements.

In the d-block the decrease is irregular and the size levels off and rises again near the end of each series, while elements of high atomic mass become larger, not smaller, down a group.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
Which of the following factors may be regarded as the main cause of lanthanide
contraction?

options.text: Poor shielding of one of 4f electron by another in the subshell
Effective shielding of one of 4f electrons by another in the subshell
Poorer shielding of 5d electrons by 4f electrons
Greater shielding of 5d electrons by 4f electrons

questions.solution:
Across the lanthanide series the nuclear charge increases by one at each step, and the added electron enters the 4f subshell.

4f orbitals are diffuse, so one 4f electron shields another 4f electron only poorly from the nucleus.

The effective nuclear charge on the outer electrons therefore rises steadily and pulls the electron cloud inward.

So the main cause of lanthanide contraction is poor shielding of one 4f electron by another in the subshell.

But from group 4 to 12, the size of 3d < 4d but 4d $$ \cong $$ 5d due to lanthanide contraction. That is why Zr and Hf have about the same radius.

questions.text: Lanthanoid contraction is caused due to :

the appreciable shielding on outer electrons by 5d electrons from the nuclear charge

the imperfect shielding on outer electrons by 4f electrons from the nuclear charge

questions.solution:
The main reason of lanthanide contraction is, poor shielding of 4f electrons on the outer most shell electrons. As f orbital is defused nature so shielding of 4f electron is imperfect that is why nucleus can attract outer most shell electron easily and the size of atom decreases.

In lanthanides, there is poorer shielding of $$5d$$ electrons by $$4f$$ electrons resulting in greater attraction of the nucleus over $$5d$$ electrons and reduction of the atomic radii.

questions.text: Which of the following forms stable $$+4$$ oxidation state?
questions.solution:
Ce: $[\mathrm{Xe}]4f^1 5d^1 6s^2$; losing four electrons gives $\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}$ with the noble gas configuration $[\mathrm{Xe}]4f^0$, so the $+4$ state is stable.

La forms only $\mathrm{La^{3+}}$ ($[\mathrm{Xe}]$); Eu shows $+2$ ($4f^7$) and $+3$; Gd is stable as $\mathrm{Gd^{3+}}$ ($4f^7$).

Hence cerium forms a stable $+4$ oxidation state.

questions.text: The number of unpaired electrons in Gadolinium $$[Z = 64]$$ is
questions.solution:
Gd ($Z = 64$): $[\mathrm{Xe}]4f^7 5d^1 6s^2$

The half-filled $4f^7$ subshell has 7 unpaired electrons, $5d^1$ adds one more, and $6s^2$ is paired.

Total unpaired electrons $= 7 + 1 = 8$

Hence gadolinium has 8 unpaired electrons.

questions.text: Magnetic moment of $$\mathrm{Gd^{3+}}$$ ion $$(Z = 64)$$ is
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{Gd}$ ($Z = 64$): $[\mathrm{Xe}]\,4f^7 5d^1 6s^2$.

$\mathrm{Gd^{3+}}$: $[\mathrm{Xe}]\,4f^7$, with $7$ unpaired electrons.

Spin-only moment $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{7 \times 9} = \sqrt{63} \approx 7.94\ \mathrm{BM}$.

For $4f^7$ the orbital contribution is zero ($L = 0$), so this is also the observed value.

So the magnetic moment is about $7.9\ \mathrm{BM}$.

questions.text: Which is not the correct Statement? (At. nos. $$\mathrm{Ce} = 58$$, $$\mathrm{Lu} = 71$$, $$\mathrm{La} = 57$$, $$\mathrm{Yb} = 70$$)
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{La^{3+}}$ is $[\mathrm{Xe}]4f^0$ with no unpaired electron, so it is diamagnetic: correct.

$\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}$ has $58 - 4 = 54$ electrons, $[\mathrm{Xe}]4f^0$: correct.

$\mathrm{Lu^{3+}}$ has $71 - 3 = 68$ electrons, $[\mathrm{Xe}]4f^{14}$: correct.

$\mathrm{Yb^{3+}}$ has $70 - 3 = 67$ electrons, $[\mathrm{Xe}]4f^{13}$; its only $f{-}f$ absorption lies in the near infrared, so the ion is colourless (pink is the colour of $\mathrm{Er^{3+}}$).

So the statement that the $\mathrm{Yb^{3+}}$ ion is pink is not correct.

questions.text: The highest possible oxidation states of uranium and plutonium, respectively are :
questions.solution:
The highest possible oxidation states of uranium and plutonium can be identified by considering the electronic configurations of these elements and noting the number of valence electrons available for bonding.

Uranium (U, atomic number 92) has the electronic configuration:
$ [Rn] 5f^3 6d^1 7s^2 $

Plutonium (Pu, atomic number 94) has the electronic configuration:
$ [Rn] 5f^6 7s^2 $

To find the highest oxidation state, we sum the number of $d$, $f$, and $s$ electrons in the valence shell.

For uranium :

$ 3 (f) + 1 (d) + 2 (s) = 6 $

So the highest oxidation state of uranium is +6.

For plutonium :

$ 6 (f) + 2 (s) = 8 $

So the highest oxidation state of plutonium is +8. However, in practice, plutonium is known to exhibit a highest oxidation state of +7.

Comparing with the given options, the correct answer is :

Option D : 6 and 7.

questions.text: The correct order of atomic radii is :
questions.solution:
N is a period-2 non-metal with a covalent radius of only about 70 pm, far smaller than the radius of any lanthanide, so N is the smallest.

Across the lanthanide series the atomic radius decreases steadily (lanthanide contraction), so Ce (183 pm) is larger than Ho (176 pm).

Eu is an exception to this trend. With the stable half-filled $4f^7$ configuration it gives only its two $6s$ electrons to metallic bonding instead of three, so the metallic bonding is weaker and its atomic (metallic) radius is anomalously large, about 199 pm, which is larger than that of Ce.

So the order of atomic radii is Eu > Ce > Ho > N.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The number of f electrons in the ground state electronic configuration of Np (Z = 93) is ___________. (Nearest integer)
questions.solution:
The ground-state configuration of Np $(Z = 93)$ is

$$[\text{Rn}]\,5f^4\,6d^1\,7s^2, \quad [\text{Rn}] = [\text{Xe}]\,4f^{14}\,5d^{10}\,6s^2\,6p^6$$

The Xe core ($1s$ to $5p$) has no f electrons, so the occupied f subshells are $4f$ with 14 electrons and $5f$ with 4 electrons.

Number of f electrons $= 14 + 4 = 18$

Hence, the answer is 18.

In complex $$C{e^{ + 4}} \to [Xe]4{f^0}5{d^0}6{s^0}$$

questions.text: Which one of the following lanthanoids does not form MO 2 ? [M is lanthanoid metal]
questions.solution:
Lanthanoids mainly show the +3 oxidation state; the +4 state, needed for an oxide $\ce{MO2}$, is shown by Ce, Pr, Nd, Tb and Dy.

Pr ($4f^3\,6s^2$), Nd ($4f^4\,6s^2$) and Dy ($4f^{10}\,6s^2$) are therefore able to form $\ce{MO2}$.

Yb ($4f^{14}\,6s^2$) shows +2 ($\ce{Yb^2+}$, $4f^{14}$) and +3 ($\ce{Yb^3+}$, $4f^{13}$). Reaching +4 would need removal of another electron from the nearly full 4f subshell, which requires very high energy, so Yb does not show +4 and does not form $\ce{YbO2}$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: Which one of the lanthanoids given below is the most stable in divalent form?
questions.solution:
The stability of a divalent state can often be attributed to the stability of the electron configuration of that state. Among the options given, we can evaluate the electron configurations of each element in their divalent state to find out which is the most stable. The electronic configurations of the neutral atoms are :

Ce (Atomic Number 58) : $[Xe] 4f^1 5d^1 6s^2$

Sm (Atomic Number 62) : $[Xe] 4f^6 6s^2$

Eu (Atomic Number 63) : $[Xe] 4f^7 6s^2$

Yb (Atomic Number 70) : $[Xe] 4f^{14} 6s^2$

In their divalent state (+2 oxidation state), the electron configurations would be :

Ce : $[Xe] 4f^1 5d^1$ (removal of the 2 electrons from the 6s orbital)

Sm : $[Xe] 4f^6$ (removal of the 2 electrons from the 6s orbital)

Eu : $[Xe] 4f^7$ (removal of the 2 electrons from the 6s orbital)

Yb : $[Xe] 4f^{14}$ (removal of the 2 electrons from the 6s orbital)

Among these, Eu in its divalent state has a half-filled (4f) shell, which offers extra stability due to symmetrical electron distribution. Therefore, Eu (Atomic Number 63) is the most stable in the divalent form.

So the correct answer is Option C : Eu (Atomic Number 63).

$$\ce{I2 + 2Na2S2O3 -> 2NaI + Na2S4O6}$$

B) and (
C) are therefore correct, while $\ce{CuI2}$ is not formed as a product, so statement (

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: The incorrect statement is :

options.text:
In manganate and permanganate ions, the π-bonding takes place by overlap of p-orbitals
of oxygen and d-orbitals of manganese

Manganate ion is green in colour and
permanganate ion is purple in colour

Manganate and permanganate ions are
paramagnetic

Manganate and permanganate ions are
tetrahedral

questions.solution:
To identify the incorrect statement, let's analyze each option :

Option
A: "In manganate and permanganate ions, the π-bonding takes place by overlap of p-orbitals of oxygen and d-orbitals of manganese."
This statement is true. In both manganate ${MnO}_4^{2-} $ and permanganate ${MnO}_4^- $ ions, the manganese atom is in a high oxidation state (+6 and +7, respectively) and forms bonds with oxygen atoms involving the overlap of p-orbitals of oxygen and d-orbitals of manganese.

Option
B: "Manganate ion is green in colour and permanganate ion is purple in colour."
This statement is true. Manganate ions are indeed green and permanganate ions are purple in aqueous solution.

Option
C: "Manganate and permanganate ions are paramagnetic."
This statement is incorrect. Manganate ion (Mn in +6 state, 3d 1 ) is paramagnetic, but permanganate ion (Mn in +7 state, 3d 0 ) has no unpaired electron and is diamagnetic.

Manganate($$\mathop {Mn}\limits^{ + 6} $$O 4
2– )
,

Mn(25) = [Ar]3d 5 4s 2

Mn +6 (25) = [Ar]3d 1 $$ \to $$ Paramagnetic

Permanganate ($$\mathop {Mn}\limits^{ + 7} $$O 4 - )

Mn(25) = [Ar]3d 5 4s 2

Mn +7 (25) = [Ar]3d 0 $$ \to $$ Diamagnetic
Option
D: "Manganate and permanganate ions are tetrahedral."
This statement is true. Both manganate and permanganate ions have a tetrahedral geometry, with the manganese atom at the center and the four oxygen atoms surrounding it.

Therefore, the incorrect statement is option C.

questions.text: The addition of dilute NaOH to Cr 3+ salt solution will give :
questions.solution:
Hydroxide ions added in small amount to a $\ce{Cr^3+}$ solution give a green gelatinous precipitate. This solid contains no discrete $\ce{Cr(OH)3}$ molecules; it is hydrated chromium(III) oxide, $\ce{Cr2O3}(\ce{H2O})_n$, of variable water content, and $\ce{Cr(OH)3}$ is only an idealised way of writing it.

The precipitate is amphoteric and redissolves only in excess alkali as the soluble chromite ion $[\ce{Cr(OH)4}]^-$ or $[\ce{Cr(OH)6}]^{3-}$, so dilute $\ce{NaOH}$ gives neither a solution of $[\ce{Cr(OH)4}]^-$ nor a precipitate of the soluble anion $[\ce{Cr(OH)6}]^{3-}$.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

The product $\ce{K2MnO4}$ (potassium manganate) is green.

In $\ce{MnO4^2-}$, Mn is in the +6 state, $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^1$, with one unpaired electron, so the product is paramagnetic.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
The correct order of following 3d metal oxides, according to their oxidation numbers is :

(a) CrO 3 , (b) Fe₂O₃ , (c) MnO 2 , (d) V₂O₅ , (e) Cu₂O
questions.solution:
(a) $$\mathop C\limits^{ + 6} r{O_3}$$ : Since there are three oxygen atoms each with an oxidation number of -2, the total oxidation number from the oxygen atoms is -6. To make the compound neutral, Chromium (Cr) must therefore have an oxidation number of +6.

(b) $$\mathop {F{e_2}}\limits^{ + 3} {O_3}$$ : Here, there are three oxygen atoms, contributing a total oxidation number of -6. To balance this, the total oxidation number for the two iron (Fe) atoms must be +6, meaning each Fe atom has an oxidation number of +3.

(c) $$\mathop {Mn}\limits^{ + 4} {O_2}$$ : With two oxygen atoms, the total oxidation number is -4. Thus, the manganese (Mn) atom must have an oxidation number of +4 to balance this.

(d) $$\mathop {{V_2}}\limits^{ + 5} {O_5}$$ : In this case, there are five oxygen atoms for a total oxidation number of -10. To balance this, the total oxidation number for the two vanadium (V) atoms must be +10, meaning each V atom has an oxidation number of +5.

(e) $$\mathop {C{u_2}}\limits^{ + 1} O$$ : Here, there's one oxygen atom with an oxidation number of -2. To balance this, the total oxidation number for the two copper (Cu) atoms must be +2, meaning each Cu atom has an oxidation number of +1.

So, the order of the oxidation numbers from highest to lowest is :

(a) CrO$_3$ > (d) V$_2$O$_5$ > (c) MnO$_2$ > (b) Fe$_2$O$_3$ > (e) Cu$_2$O.

Therefore, the answer is Option C : (a) > (d) > (c) > (b) > (e).

questions.text: Consider the coordination compound, [Co(NH 3 ) 6 ]Cl 3 . In the formation of this complex, the species which acts as the lewis acid is :
questions.solution:
A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair; a Lewis base donates one.

In $[\mathrm{Co(NH_3)_6}]^{3+}$, each $\mathrm{NH_3}$ donates the lone pair on nitrogen to $\mathrm{Co^{3+}}$, which accepts six pairs into its vacant $d^2sp^3$ hybrid orbitals.

So $\mathrm{NH_3}$ is the Lewis base and $\mathrm{Co^{3+}}$ the Lewis acid; $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ is only the counter ion.

So the Lewis acid is $\mathrm{Co^{3+}}$.

questions.text:

questions.solution:
A ligand must donate a lone pair of electrons to the central metal atom or ion.

In $\mathrm{CH_4}$, all four valence electron pairs of carbon are used in $\mathrm{C-H}$ bonds; it has no lone pair (and no vacant orbital for back-bonding).

So $\mathrm{CH_4}$ cannot act as a ligand.

Heteroleptic complexes are those compounds in which central transition metal has more than one type of ligands. So, rest of the options are examples of heteroleptic complexes.

questions.text: The overall stability constant of the complex ion [Cu(NH 3 ) 4 ] 2+ is 2.1 $$\times$$ 10 13 . The overall dissociations constant is y $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$14 . Then y is __________. (Nearest integer)
questions.solution:
The overall stability (formation) constant refers to

$$\ce{Cu^2+ + 4NH3 <=> [Cu(NH3)4]^2+}\qquad \beta_4 = 2.1\times10^{13}$$

The overall dissociation is the reverse reaction, so its constant is the reciprocal of $\beta_4$:

$$K_d = \dfrac{1}{\beta_4} = \dfrac{1}{2.1\times10^{13}} = 4.76\times10^{-14}$$

So $y = 4.76 \approx 5$.

Hence, the answer is 5.

questions.solution:
In the brown ring test, $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ is reduced by $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ to NO, which binds to iron as the nitrosonium ion, $\mathrm{NO^+}$ (an electron passes from NO to Fe).

The complex ion is $\mathrm{[Fe(H_2O)_5(NO)]^{2+}}$ (balanced by $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$), and $\mathrm{H_2O}$ is neutral.

$x + 5(0) + (+1) = +2 \Rightarrow x = +1$.

questions.text:
In the following brown complex, the oxidation state of iron is +_____________.

$${[Fe{({H_2}O)_6}]^{2 + }} + NO \to \mathop {{{[Fe{{({H_2}O)}_5}(NO)]}^{2 + }}}\limits_{\text{Brown complex}} + {H_2}O$$
questions.solution:
To determine the oxidation state of iron in the brown complex ${[Fe({H_2}O)_5(NO)]^{2+}}$, we need to analyze the ligands and their charges, as well as the overall charge of the complex.

Step 1: Understanding the Complex
The complex is:

$ {[Fe({H_2}O)_5(NO)]^{2+}} $

Iron (Fe): The central metal atom whose oxidation state we need to find.

Ligands:

5 Water Molecules ($H_2O$) : Neutral ligands (charge = 0).

1 Nitrosyl Group (NO) : Can have different charges depending on its mode of bonding.

Step 2: Assigning Charges to Ligands
Water ($H_2O$) : Neutral ligand, so it contributes 0 to the overall charge.

Nitrosyl (NO) : Can act as:

NO$^+$ (nitrosonium ion) with a +1 charge.

NO (neutral molecule) with 0 charge.

NO$^-$ (nitroxide ion) with a –1 charge.

Step 3: Setting Up the Oxidation State Equation
Let $ x $ be the oxidation state of Fe.

The sum of the oxidation states of all components equals the overall charge of the complex:

$ x + (5 \times 0) + (\text{Charge of NO}) = +2 $

Simplifying:

$ x + (\text{Charge of NO}) = +2 $

Step 4: Determining the Charge of NO in the Complex
In the brown ring complex , experimental evidence shows that the nitrosyl ligand acts as NO$^+$ . This is because:

The NO ligand forms a linear bond with Fe, characteristic of NO$^+$.

The complex is known to involve a reduction of the oxidation state of Fe to an unusual value.

Thus, Charge of NO = +1 .

Step 5: Calculating the Oxidation State of Fe
Substitute the charge of NO into the equation:

$ x + (+1) = +2 $

Solving for $ x $:

$ x = +2 - (+1) = +1 $

Therefore, the oxidation state of Fe in the brown complex is $ +1 $.

Conclusion
The oxidation state of iron in ${[Fe({H_2}O)_5(NO)]^{2+}}$ is +1 .

questions.text: Ammonia forms the complex ion [Cu(NH 3 ) 4 ] 2+ with copper ions in alkaline solutions but not in acidic solutions. What is the reason for it?

options.text:
In acidic solutions protons coordinate with ammonia molecules forming $$NH^+_4$$ ions and NH 3
molecules are not available

In alkaline solutions insoluble Cu(OH) 2
is precipitated which is soluble in excess of any alkali
Copper hydroxide is an amphoteric substance
In acidic solutions hydration protects copper ions.

questions.solution:
Formation of $\ce{[Cu(NH3)4]^2+}$ requires the lone pair on the nitrogen of $\ce{NH3}$ to be donated to $\ce{Cu^2+}$.

In acidic solution $\ce{NH3}$ accepts a proton:

$$\ce{NH3 + H+ -> NH4+}$$

The nitrogen lone pair is now used in the new $\ce{N-H}$ bond, so $\ce{NH4+}$ cannot act as a ligand and free $\ce{NH3}$ molecules are not available for complex formation.

In alkaline solution $\ce{NH3}$ stays unprotonated and coordinates to $\ce{Cu^2+}$; options (B), (
C) and (
D) do not account for this loss of the donor lone pair in acid.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: The coordination number of central metal atom in a complex is determined by :

options.text: the number of ligands around a metal ion bonded by sigma bonds
the number of only anionic ligands bonded to the metal ion
the number of ligands around a metal ion bonded by sigma and pi- bonds both
the number of ligands around a metal ion bonded by pi-bonds

questions.solution:
The coordination number of the central atom or ion is the number of ligand donor atoms directly bonded to it, and it is determined only by the number of $\sigma$ bonds formed between the ligands and the central atom.

$\pi$ bonds formed between a ligand and the metal, such as the back-bonding in metal carbonyls, are not counted, so a ligand bonded through both $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds contributes only through its $\sigma$ bond.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: [Co 2 (CO) 8 ] displays :

options.text: one Co−Co bond, six terminal CO and two bridging CO
one Co−Co bond, four terminal CO and four bridging CO
no Co−Co bond, six terminal CO and two bridging CO
no Co−Co bond, four terminal CO and four bridging CO

questions.solution:
In its solid-state structure, $\ce{[Co2(CO)8]}$ has the two Co atoms joined by one Co–Co bond and also bridged by two CO groups, the C atom of each bridging CO being bonded to both Co atoms.

Each Co carries three terminal CO groups, so the molecule has $2 \times 3 = 6$ terminal CO and 2 bridging CO, accounting for all 8 CO.

Each Co then has $9 + 3 \times 2 + 2 \times 1 + 1 = 18$ valence electrons (Co, three terminal CO, one electron from each bridging CO, the Co–Co bond), which requires the Co–Co bond.

The unbridged isomer found in solution has 8 terminal CO and no bridging CO, which matches none of the options.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

In $\ce{EDTA^4-}$ the two nitrogen atoms of the ethylenediamine backbone each carry a lone pair, and each of the four $\ce{-CH2COO^-}$ arms binds through one carboxylate oxygen atom.

$$\text{Coordination sites} = 2\ (\text{N}) + 4\ (\text{O}) = 6$$

Hence, the answer is 6.

questions.text:
The oxidation states of iron atoms in
compounds (A), (
B) and (C), respectively, are x,
y and z. The sum of x, y and z is ________.

Na 4 [Fe(CN) 5 (NOS)]

       (
A) Na 4 [FeO 4 ]

       (
B) [Fe 2 (CO) 9 ]

       (C)
questions.solution:
In $\ce{Na4[Fe(CN)5(NOS)]}$ the complex ion forms from nitroprusside and sulfide, $\ce{[Fe(CN)5NO]^2- + S^2- -> [Fe(CN)5(NOS)]^4-}$; iron keeps its +2 state and $\ce{NOS}$ ($\ce{NO+}$ combined with $\ce{S^2-}$) carries a charge of $-1$.

$$4(+1) + x + 5(-1) + (-1) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +2$$

In $\ce{Na4[FeO4]}$: $4(+1) + y + 4(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow y = +4$.

In $\ce{[Fe2(CO)9]}$, CO is a neutral ligand: $2z + 9(0) = 0 \Rightarrow z = 0$.

$$x + y + z = 2 + 4 + 0 = 6$$

Hence, the answer is 6.

questions.text:
Complexes (ML 5 ) of metals Ni and Fe have
ideal square pyramidal and trigonal
bipyramidal geometries, respectively. The sum
of the 90°, 120° and 180° L-M-L angles in the
two complexes is ________.
questions.solution:
Here the required quantity is the total number of L–M–L angles of $90^\circ$, $120^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ in the two complexes.

In ideal square pyramidal $\ce{NiL5}$, four basal ligands sit at the corners of a square around the metal and one apical ligand lies above it.

$90^\circ$: the apical ligand with each of the 4 basal ligands (4) and the 4 pairs of adjacent basal ligands (4), giving 8. $180^\circ$: the 2 pairs of opposite basal ligands, giving 2. Number of angles $= 8 + 2 = 10$.

In ideal trigonal bipyramidal $\ce{FeL5}$, three equatorial ligands lie in a plane around the metal and two axial ligands lie above and below it.

$90^\circ$: each of the 2 axial ligands with each of the 3 equatorial ligands, $2 \times 3 = 6$. $120^\circ$: the 3 pairs of equatorial ligands, giving 3. $180^\circ$: the 1 pair of axial ligands. Number of angles $= 6 + 3 + 1 = 10$.

Total number of $90^\circ$, $120^\circ$ and $180^\circ$ L–M–L angles $= 10 + 10 = 20$.

Hence, the answer is 20.

questions.text: The sum of oxidation states of two silver ions in [Ag(NH 3 ) 2 ] [Ag(CN) 2 ] complex is _____________.
questions.solution:
$\ce{[Ag(NH3)2][Ag(CN)2]}$ is made of the complex cation $\ce{[Ag(NH3)2]+}$ and the complex anion $\ce{[Ag(CN)2]-}$.

In $\ce{[Ag(NH3)2]+}$, $\ce{NH3}$ is a neutral ligand: $x + 2(0) = +1 \Rightarrow x = +1$.

In $\ce{[Ag(CN)2]-}$, each $\ce{CN-}$ carries $-1$: $x + 2(-1) = -1 \Rightarrow x = +1$.

Sum of the oxidation states of the two silver ions $= (+1) + (+1) = 2$.

Hence, the answer is 2.

questions.text:
3 moles of metal complex with formula Co(en) 2 Cl 3 gives 3 moles of silver chloride on treatment with excess of silver nitrate. The secondary valency of Co in the complex is ___________.

(Round off to the nearest integer)
questions.solution:
Three moles of complex give three moles of $\ce{AgCl}$, so each formula unit has one ionisable chloride and the complex is $\ce{[Co(en)2Cl2]Cl}$:

$$\ce{[Co(en)2Cl2]Cl + AgNO3 -> [Co(en)2Cl2]NO3 + AgCl}$$

The secondary valency equals the coordination number: each bidentate en supplies two donor atoms and each coordinated chloride one, so $2 \times 2 + 2 = 6$.

Hence, the answer is 6.

questions.text: The secondary valency and the number of hydrogen bonded water molecule(s) in CuSO 4 . 5H 2 O, respectively, are :
questions.solution:
In $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$, four water molecules are coordinated to the $\ce{Cu^2+}$ ion, so the compound is written as $\ce{[Cu(H2O)4]SO4.H2O}$.

The secondary valency of copper is the number of coordinated water molecules, that is, 4.

The fifth water molecule is not bonded to the metal; it is held in the crystal by hydrogen bonds to the sulphate ion and to the coordinated water molecules, so the number of hydrogen-bonded water molecules is 1.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
Given below are two statements.

$$\bullet$$ Statement I : In CuSO 4 . 5H 2 O, Cu-O bonds are present.

$$\bullet$$ Statement II : In CuSO 4 . 5H 2 O, ligands coordinating with Cu(II) ion are O-and S-based ligands.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below.

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct.
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect.
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct.

questions.solution:
In $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$ four water molecules are coordinated to $\ce{Cu^2+}$ through their oxygen atoms, giving $\ce{[Cu(H2O)4]^2+}$; the fifth water molecule is held by hydrogen bonds between a coordinated water molecule and the sulphate ion.

Cu–O coordinate bonds are therefore present, so Statement I is correct.

In the crystal the remaining two axial positions around Cu are taken by oxygen atoms of sulphate ions. The S atom of sulphate is bonded to four O atoms and carries no lone pair, so it never acts as a donor; every donor atom around $\ce{Cu^2+}$ is oxygen, and Statement II is incorrect.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: In the cobalt-carbonyl complex : [Co 2 (CO) 8 ], number of Co-Co bonds is "X" and terminal CO ligands is "Y". X + Y = ___________.
questions.solution:
In its solid-state structure, $\ce{[Co2(CO)8]}$ has the two Co atoms joined by one Co–Co bond and also bridged by two CO groups.

Each Co carries three terminal CO groups, so the number of terminal CO is $2 \times 3 = 6$; with the 2 bridging CO this accounts for all 8 CO.

$X = 1$ and $Y = 6$, so $X + Y = 1 + 6 = 7$.

Hence, the answer is 7.

questions.text: The IUPAC name of the coordination compound K 3 [Fe(CN) 6 ] is
questions.solution:
In $\ce{K3[Fe(CN)6]}$ each potassium is $+1$ and each cyanide ligand is $-1$, so the oxidation state $x$ of iron follows from

$$3(+1) + x + 6(-1) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +3$$

The complex ion $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^3-}$ is an anion, so the metal takes the Latin-based name with the suffix -ate (ferrate); the cation is named first without a numerical prefix, and the six cyanide ligands are shown by hexa.

The name is potassium hexacyanoferrate(III), written potassium hexacyanidoferrate(III) under the current IUPAC rules. Options (
C) and (
D) use "iron", which is used only for a cationic or neutral complex, and (
A) has the wrong oxidation state.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: The IUPAC name for the complex [Co(NO 2 )(NH 3 ) 5 ]Cl 2 is
questions.solution:
The two $\ce{Cl-}$ ions are counter-ions, so the complex cation is $\ce{[Co(NO2)(NH3)5]^2+}$.

$\ce{NH3}$ is neutral and $\ce{NO2-}$ carries a charge of $-1$:

$$x + (-1) + 5(0) = +2 \Rightarrow x = +3$$

so the metal is cobalt(III).

$\ce{NO2}$ written with N first is bonded through nitrogen and is named nitrito-N; $\ce{NH3}$ is named ammine.

Ligands are named in alphabetical order, ignoring the multiplying prefix: ammine (a) comes before nitrito-N (n), giving pentaamminenitrito-N, followed by the metal and its oxidation state.

The cation is named before the anion: pentaamminenitrito-N-cobalt(III) chloride.

Option (
A) puts nitrito-N before ammine, against alphabetical order, and option (
C) gives cobalt(II) instead of cobalt(III).

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Which among the following will be named as dibromidobis (ethylene diamine) chromium(III) bromide?
questions.solution:
In the name, "dibromido" means two $\ce{Br-}$ ligands and "bis(ethylenediamine)" means two en ligands in the coordination sphere, giving $\ce{[Cr(en)2Br2]}$.

With chromium in the +3 state, the charge on the complex ion is $(+3) + 2(-1) + 2(0) = +1$, so one bromide counter-ion completes the formula: $\ce{[Cr(en)2Br2]Br}$.

$\ce{[Cr(en)Br2]Br}$ contains only one en ligand and would be named dibromido(ethylenediamine)chromium(III) bromide.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
The correct order of magnetic moments (spin only values in B.M.) among is :

(Atomic numbers: Mn = 25; Fe = 26, Co =27)
questions.solution:
The spin-only magnetic moment $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\ \text{BM}$ increases with the number of unpaired electrons $n$.

$\ce{[MnCl4]^2-}$: $\ce{Mn^2+}$ is $3d^5$; with weak-field $\ce{Cl-}$ in a tetrahedral ($sp^3$) complex no pairing occurs, so $n = 5$ and $\mu = \sqrt{35} = 5.92\ \text{BM}$.

$\ce{[CoCl4]^2-}$: $\ce{Co^2+}$ is $3d^7$; the tetrahedral complex is $e^{4}t_2^{3}$, so $n = 3$ and $\mu = \sqrt{15} = 3.87\ \text{BM}$.

$\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^4-}$: $\ce{Fe^2+}$ is $3d^6$; $\ce{CN-}$ is a strong-field ligand, so all six electrons pair up as $t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{0}$ ($d^2sp^3$), giving $n = 0$ and $\mu = 0$. The 4 unpaired electrons of free $\ce{Fe^2+}$ remain only with weak-field ligands.

$$\ce{[MnCl4]^2-} > \ce{[CoCl4]^2-} > \ce{[Fe(CN)6]^4-}$$

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: Which one of the following complexes is an outer orbital complex?
questions.solution:
An inner orbital complex ($d^2sp^3$) needs two vacant $3d$ orbitals; when these are not available the outer $4d$ orbitals are used and the complex is outer orbital ($sp^3d^2$).

$\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^4-}$: $\ce{Fe^2+}$, $3d^6$; strong-field $\ce{CN-}$ pairs the six electrons into three $3d$ orbitals, leaving two vacant, so $d^2sp^3$ (inner).

$\ce{[Co(NH3)6]^3+}$: $\ce{Co^3+}$, $3d^6$; $\ce{NH3}$ pairs the six electrons into three $3d$ orbitals, so $d^2sp^3$ (inner, diamagnetic).

$\ce{[Mn(CN)6]^4-}$: $\ce{Mn^2+}$, $3d^5$; $\ce{CN-}$ packs the five electrons into three $3d$ orbitals (one unpaired), so $d^2sp^3$ (inner).

$\ce{[Ni(NH3)6]^2+}$: $\ce{Ni^2+}$, $3d^8$; eight electrons occupy at least four $3d$ orbitals, so two vacant $3d$ orbitals cannot be obtained whatever the ligand, and the complex is $sp^3d^2$ with two unpaired electrons (outer orbital).

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
Among the properties (a) reducing (b) oxidising (c) complexing, the set of properties shown by CN – ion
towards metal species is :
questions.solution:
$\ce{CN-}$ is a strong-field ligand (a $\sigma$-donor and $\pi$-acceptor) and forms very stable complexes such as $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^4-}$, $\ce{[Ni(CN)4]^2-}$ and $\ce{[Ag(CN)2]-}$, so it is complexing.

Carbon in $\ce{CN-}$ is in the +2 state and is easily oxidised, so $\ce{CN-}$ reduces metal ions; for example, $\ce{Cu^2+}$ is reduced to copper(I):

$$\ce{2Cu^2+ + 4CN- -> 2CuCN + (CN)2}$$

$\ce{CN-}$ is not itself easily reduced, so it does not act as an oxidising agent towards metal species.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
Which one of the following cyano complexes would exhibit the lowest value of
paramagnetic behaviour?

(At. No. Cr = 24, Mn = 25, Fe = 26, Co = 27)
questions.solution:
$\ce{CN-}$ is a strong-field ligand, so all four hexacyanido complexes are low spin and the $t_{2g}$ level fills first.

$\ce{[Cr(CN)6]^3-}$: $\ce{Cr^3+}$, $3d^3$, $t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{0}$, 3 unpaired electrons.

$\ce{[Mn(CN)6]^3-}$: $\ce{Mn^3+}$, $3d^4$, $t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{0}$, 2 unpaired electrons.

$\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^3-}$: $\ce{Fe^3+}$, $3d^5$, $t_{2g}^{5}e_g^{0}$, 1 unpaired electron.

$\ce{[Co(CN)6]^3-}$: $\ce{Co^3+}$, $3d^6$, $t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{0}$, 0 unpaired electrons.

The magnetic moment $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\ \text{BM}$ falls with the number of unpaired electrons $n$, so $\ce{[Co(CN)6]^3-}$ ($n = 0$, $\mu = 0$) shows the lowest paramagnetism; it is in fact diamagnetic.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Which one of the following has a square planar geometry?
questions.solution:
All four are $\ce{MCl4^2-}$ complexes of $\ce{M^2+}$ ions with the weak-field ligand $\ce{Cl-}$.

$\ce{Co^2+}$ ($3d^{7}$), $\ce{Fe^2+}$ ($3d^{6}$) and $\ce{Ni^2+}$ ($3d^{8}$) are 3d ions with small crystal field splitting; with $\ce{Cl-}$ no electron pairing occurs, no $3d$ orbital is vacated, and the metal uses $sp^3$ hybridisation, so these complexes are tetrahedral.

$\ce{Pt^2+}$ is $5d^{8}$. The splitting for a 5d metal is much larger, so even with $\ce{Cl-}$ the eight electrons pair up in four $5d$ orbitals, leaving one $5d$ orbital empty for $dsp^2$ hybridisation: $\ce{[PtCl4]^2-}$ is square planar and diamagnetic.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Nickel (Z = 28) combines with a uninegative monodentate ligand to form a diamagnetic complex [NiL 4 ] 2$$-$$ . The hybridisation involved and the number of unpaired electrons present in the complex are respectively :
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{L}$ is uninegative: $x+4(-1)=-2\Rightarrow x=+2$, and $\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$ is $3d^8$.

A tetrahedral $sp^3$ complex would keep two unpaired $3d$ electrons and be paramagnetic.

Since the complex is diamagnetic, the 8 electrons are paired in four $3d$ orbitals, leaving one $3d$ orbital empty.

That $3d$ orbital with $4s$ and two $4p$ orbitals gives $dsp^2$ hybridisation (square planar).

So the hybridisation is $dsp^2$ and there are zero unpaired electrons.

questions.text: The correct statement about the magnetic properties of  [Fe(CN) 6 ] 3 $$-$$ and [FeF 6 ] 3$$-$$   is :  (Z = 26).

$\mathrm{[FeF_6]^{3-}}$: $\mathrm{F^-}$ is a weak field ligand, high spin $t_{2g}^3 e_g^2$, five unpaired electrons, so paramagnetic.

So both complexes are paramagnetic.

Two inner $3d$ orbitals are left empty and combine with $4s$ and three $4p$ orbitals (inner orbital complex).

So the hybridisation is $d^2sp^3$.

questions.text:
Which one of the following complexes will consume more equivalents of aqueous
solution of Ag(NO 3 )?
questions.solution:
Only chloride outside the coordination sphere is ionisable and precipitated by $\ce{AgNO3}$; chloride bonded to Cr is not.

$\ce{Na3[CrCl6]}$ has all six Cl as ligands, so 0 free $\ce{Cl-}$; $\ce{Na2[CrCl5(H2O)]}$ likewise has 0 free $\ce{Cl-}$.

$\ce{[Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2}$ has 2 free $\ce{Cl-}$, and $\ce{[Cr(H2O)6]Cl3}$ has 3 free $\ce{Cl-}$.

$$\ce{[Cr(H2O)6]Cl3 + 3AgNO3 -> [Cr(H2O)6](NO3)3 + 3AgCl}$$

$\ce{[Cr(H2O)6]Cl3}$ therefore consumes the most $\ce{AgNO3}$, 3 mol per mole of complex.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

The pair having the same magnetic moment is :

$\ce{[Cr(H2O)6]^2+}$: $\ce{Cr^2+}$, $3d^4$, $t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{1}$, 4 unpaired electrons.

$\ce{[Fe(H2O)6]^2+}$: $\ce{Fe^2+}$, $3d^6$, $t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{2}$, 4 unpaired electrons.

Only $\ce{[Cr(H2O)6]^2+}$ and $\ce{[Fe(H2O)6]^2+}$ have the same number of unpaired electrons, so both have $\mu = \sqrt{4(4+2)} = \sqrt{24} = 4.90$ BM.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: In Wilkinson's catalyst, the hybridization of central metal ion and its shape are respectively :
questions.solution:
Wilkinson's catalyst is $\ce{[RhCl(PPh3)3]}$; with $\ce{Cl-}$ as $-1$ and $\ce{PPh3}$ neutral, $x - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow x = +1$.

$\ce{Rh}$ is $[\text{Kr}]4d^{8}5s^{1}$, so $\ce{Rh+}$ is $[\text{Kr}]4d^{8}$.

The crystal field splitting of a $4d$ ion is large and $\ce{PPh3}$ is a strong-field ligand, so the eight $4d$ electrons pair up in four $4d$ orbitals and one $4d$ orbital stays vacant.

The vacant $4d$, the $5s$ and two $5p$ orbitals form four $\mathrm{dsp}^{2}$ hybrid orbitals, which accept the lone pairs of one $\ce{Cl-}$ and three $\ce{PPh3}$. The complex is diamagnetic and square planar, like the other $d^{8}$ complexes of $\ce{Pd^2+}$ and $\ce{Pt^2+}$.

Tetrahedral $\mathrm{sp}^{3}$ bonding would leave two unpaired $4d$ electrons, which the diamagnetic complex does not have.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
The correct statements among I to III are :

(I) Valence bond theory cannot explain the
color exhibited by transition metal
complexes.

(II) Valence bond theory can predict
quantitatively the magnetic properties of
transition metal complexes.

(III) Valence bond theory cannot distinguish
ligands as weak and strong field ones.
questions.solution:
To determine which statements are correct, let's analyze each one individually in the context of Valence Bond Theory (VBT) as it applies to transition metal complexes.

Statement (I):
"Valence bond theory cannot explain the color exhibited by transition metal complexes."

Analysis:

Color in Transition Metal Complexes:

The colors of transition metal complexes arise from electronic transitions between different energy levels of the d-orbitals, specifically d-d transitions .

These transitions occur when an electron absorbs light energy and moves from a lower-energy d-orbital to a higher-energy d-orbital.

Valence Bond Theory Limitations:

VBT focuses on the hybridization of atomic orbitals to form covalent bonds.

It does not account for the splitting of d-orbitals into different energy levels in the presence of ligands (known as crystal field splitting ).

Therefore, VBT cannot explain the origin of color in these complexes because it doesn't address the electronic transitions responsible for color.

Conclusion:

Statement (I) is correct.

Statement (II):
"Valence bond theory can predict quantitatively the magnetic properties of transition metal complexes."

Analysis:

Magnetic Properties:

The magnetic behavior of a complex depends on the number of unpaired electrons in the metal ion.

Quantitative prediction requires calculating the magnetic moment , often using the formula:

$ \mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} \ \text{Bohr Magnetons (BM)} $

where $ n $ is the number of unpaired electrons.

Valence Bond Theory Capabilities:

VBT can provide a qualitative idea about the magnetic properties by indicating whether a complex is paramagnetic (unpaired electrons present) or diamagnetic (no unpaired electrons).

However, VBT does not offer the tools to quantitatively predict the exact magnetic moment.

Accurate quantitative predictions require more advanced theories like Crystal Field Theory (CFT) or Ligand Field Theory (LFT) .

Conclusion:

Statement (II) is incorrect.

Statement (III):
"Valence bond theory cannot distinguish ligands as weak and strong field ones."

Analysis:

Weak and Strong Field Ligands:

Ligands are classified based on their ability to split the d-orbitals of the metal ion, influencing the pairing of electrons.

Strong field ligands cause a large splitting, often leading to low-spin complexes.

Weak field ligands cause small splitting, leading to high-spin complexes.

Valence Bond Theory Limitations:

VBT does not address the energy splitting of d-orbitals.

It assumes that all bonds are formed via overlap of orbitals without considering the effect of ligands on d-orbital energies.

Therefore, VBT cannot distinguish between weak and strong field ligands because it doesn't involve the spectrochemical series or orbital splitting concepts.

Conclusion:

Statement (III) is correct.

Final Answer:
Statements (I) and (III) are correct.

Statement (II) is incorrect.

Answer: Option D

(I) and (III) only

(BM) of the anionic and cationic species of
[Fe(H₂O) 6 ] 2 [Fe(CN) 6 ], respectively, are :
questions.solution:
In $\ce{[Fe(H2O)6]2[Fe(CN)6]}$ the cation is $\ce{[Fe(H2O)6]^2+}$ and the anion is $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^4-}$; iron is $+2$ ($3d^6$) in both.

Anion: $\ce{CN-}$ is a strong-field ligand, so the $d^6$ electrons pair as $t_{2g}^6e_g^0$; $n = 0$ and $\mu = 0$.

Cation: $\ce{H2O}$ is a weak-field ligand, so $d^6$ is high spin, $t_{2g}^4e_g^2$, with $n = 4$:

$$\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{24} = 4.90\ \text{BM}$$

The magnetic moments of the anionic and cationic species are 0 and 4.9 BM respectively.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

options.text: d xy , d xz and d yz
d xz , d yz and d z 2
d xy and d x 2 $$-$$ y 2

questions.solution:
In $\ce{K3[Co(CN)6]}$ the complex ion $\ce{[Co(CN)6]^3-}$ is octahedral, and the six $\ce{CN-}$ ligands approach the metal along the $\pm x$, $\pm y$ and $\pm z$ axes.

The lobes of $d_{x^2-y^2}$ lie along the $x$ and $y$ axes and those of $d_{z^2}$ lie along the $z$ axis, so these two $e_g$ orbitals point directly at the ligands.

The lobes of $d_{xy}$, $d_{yz}$ and $d_{xz}$ (the $t_{2g}$ set) lie between the axes, so they do not face the ligands; this rules out (B), (C) and (D).

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: The difference in the number of unpaired electrons of a metal ion in its high spin and low-spin octahedral complexes is two. The metal ion is :
questions.solution:
The unpaired electrons in the high-spin and low-spin octahedral arrangements of each ion are compared.

$\ce{Mn^2+}$ ($d^5$): high spin $t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{2}$ has 5 and low spin $t_{2g}^{5}e_g^{0}$ has 1, a difference of 4.

$\ce{Fe^2+}$ ($d^6$): high spin $t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{2}$ has 4 and low spin $t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{0}$ has 0, a difference of 4.

$\ce{Co^2+}$ ($d^7$): high spin $t_{2g}^{5}e_g^{2}$ has 3 and low spin $t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{1}$ has 1, a difference of 2.

$\ce{Ni^2+}$ ($d^8$): in any octahedral field the configuration is $t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{2}$ with 2 unpaired electrons, so there is no separate low-spin octahedral state; diamagnetic $\ce{Ni^2+}$ complexes are square planar, not octahedral.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: The highest value of the calculated spin only magnetic moment (in BM) among all the transition metal complexes is :
questions.solution:
The spin-only moment $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM increases with the number of unpaired electrons $n$.

In a complex the valence electrons of the metal are all in the 3d orbitals: the 4s electrons are lost first on ionisation, and the 4s and 4p orbitals receive the ligand electron pairs. The five 3d orbitals hold at most 5 unpaired electrons, in high-spin $d^5$ complexes such as $\ce{[Fe(H2O)6]^3+}$.

The 6 unpaired electrons of the free Cr atom ($3d^54s^1$) do not occur in a complex; even Cr(0) in $\ce{[Cr(CO)6]}$ is $3d^6$.

$$\mu_{\max} = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35} = 5.92\ \text{BM}$$

Hence, the correct option is (A).

The molecule in which hybrid MOs involve only
one d-orbital of the central atom is :
questions.solution:
$\ce{XeF4}$: Xe has 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs, so it is $sp^3d^2$ hybridised (two d orbitals).

$\ce{[Ni(CN)4]^2-}$: $\ce{Ni^2+}$ is $3d^8$; the strong-field $\ce{CN-}$ ligands pair the electrons, leaving one 3d orbital empty, so it is $dsp^2$ hybridised (one d orbital, square planar).

$\ce{[CrF6]^3-}$: $\ce{Cr^3+}$ is $3d^3$, which leaves two inner 3d orbitals empty, so it is $d^2sp^3$ hybridised (two d orbitals).

$\ce{BrF5}$: Br has 5 bond pairs and 1 lone pair, so it is $sp^3d^2$ hybridised (two d orbitals).

Only $\ce{[Ni(CN)4]^2-}$ uses a single d orbital.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
The pair in which both the species have the
same magnetic moment (spin only) is :
questions.solution:
Equal spin-only moments, $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM, need equal numbers of unpaired electrons $n$.

$\ce{[Cr(H2O)6]^2+}$: $\ce{Cr^2+}$, $3d^4$; weak-field $\ce{H2O}$ gives $t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{1}$, $n = 4$.

$\ce{[Fe(H2O)6]^2+}$: $\ce{Fe^2+}$, $3d^6$; weak-field $\ce{H2O}$ gives $t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{2}$, $n = 4$.

$\ce{[Mn(H2O)6]^2+}$: $\ce{Mn^2+}$, $3d^5$, high spin, $n = 5$.

$\ce{[CoCl4]^2-}$ and $\ce{[Co(OH)4]^2-}$: tetrahedral $\ce{Co^2+}$, $3d^7$, $e^{4}t_2^{3}$, $n = 3$.

$\ce{[Fe(NH3)6]^2+}$: $\ce{Fe^2+}$, $3d^6$; $\ce{NH3}$ is not strong enough to pair the electrons of $\ce{Fe^2+}$, so $n = 4$ (a low-spin count would be 0), which differs from the 3 of $\ce{[Co(OH)4]^2-}$ either way.

The pairs give $n$ = 4 and 3 in (A), 3 and 4 in (B), 5 and 4 in (C), and 4 and 4 in (D).

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
For octahedral Mn(II) and tetrahedral Ni(II)
complexes, consider the following statements:

(I) both the complexes can be high spin.

(II) Ni(II) complex can very rarely be low spin.

(III) with strong field ligands, Mn(II) complexes
can be low spin.

(IV) aqueous solution of Mn(II) ions is yellow in
colour.

The correct statements are :
questions.solution:
Octahedral Mn(II) is $d^{5}$. With weak-field ligands ($\Delta_o < P$) the configuration is $t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{2}$ with 5 unpaired electrons (high spin), as in $\ce{[Mn(H2O)6]^2+}$. With strong-field ligands such as $\ce{CN-}$ ($\Delta_o > P$) the electrons pair in $t_{2g}$, giving $t_{2g}^{5}e_g^{0}$ with 1 unpaired electron (low spin), as in $\ce{[Mn(CN)6]^4-}$. So (III) is correct.

Tetrahedral Ni(II) is $d^{8}$, $e^{4}t_2^{4}$ with 2 unpaired electrons (high spin), as in $\ce{[NiCl4]^2-}$. Both complexes can therefore be high spin, so (I) is correct.

The tetrahedral splitting is small ($\Delta_t \approx \dfrac{4}{9}\Delta_o$) and is almost never larger than the pairing energy, so tetrahedral Ni(II) complexes are very rarely low spin; diamagnetic Ni(II) complexes are square planar instead. So (II) is correct.

Aqueous $\ce{Mn^2+}$, present as $\ce{[Mn(H2O)6]^2+}$, is pale pink, not yellow, so (IV) is incorrect.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

(

(

B) $= 2.83$ BM.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: Spin only magnetic moment in BM of [Fe(CO) 4 (C₂O₄ )] + is :
questions.solution:
Oxalate is $\ce{C2O4^2-}$ and CO is neutral, so for $\ce{[Fe(CO)4(C2O4)]+}$: $x + 4(0) + (-2) = +1 \Rightarrow x = +3$.

$\ce{Fe^3+}$ is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5$. The four CO ligands are strong-field $\pi$-acceptors, so the complex is low spin and the five electrons pair up in the $t_{2g}$ set: $t_{2g}^{5}e_g^{0}$, with one unpaired electron.

$$\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{1(1+2)} = \sqrt{3} = 1.73\ \text{BM}$$

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: 1 mol of an octahedral metal complex with formula MCl 3 . 2L on reaction with excess of AgNO 3 gives 1 mol of AgCl. The denticity of Ligand L is ____________. (Integer answer)
questions.solution:
One mole of the complex gives 1 mol of AgCl with excess $\ce{AgNO3}$, so only one $\ce{Cl-}$ is outside the coordination sphere and the other two $\ce{Cl-}$ are bonded to M. The complex is $\ce{[MCl2L2]Cl}$.

An octahedral complex has coordination number 6. The two $\ce{Cl-}$ occupy 2 positions, so the two L ligands fill the remaining 4 positions:

$$2 + 2 \times (\text{denticity of L}) = 6 \Rightarrow \text{denticity of L} = 2$$

L is a bidentate ligand.

Hence, the answer is 2.

questions.text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I : $${[Mn{(CN)_6}]^{3 - }}$$, $${[Fe{(CN)_6}]^{3 - }}$$ and $${[Co{({C_2}{O_4})_3}]^{3 - }}$$ are d 2 sp 3 hybridised.

Statement II : $${[MnC{l_6}]^{3 - }}$$ and $${[Fe{F_6}]^{3 - }}$$ are paramagnetic and have 4 and 5 unpaired electrons, respectively.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :

options.text: Statement I is correct but statement II is false
Both statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is incorrect but statement II is true
Both statement I and statement II are true

questions.solution:
In $\ce{[Mn(CN)6]^3-}$, Mn is +3 with $3d^{4}$. Strong-field $\ce{CN-}$ pairs the electrons as $t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{0}$ (one paired and two single electrons in three 3d orbitals), so two 3d orbitals stay empty and the hybridisation is $d^2sp^3$, with 2 unpaired electrons.

In $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^3-}$, Fe is +3 with $3d^{5}$. Strong-field $\ce{CN-}$ gives $t_{2g}^{5}e_g^{0}$, leaving two 3d orbitals empty: $d^2sp^3$, with 1 unpaired electron.

In $\ce{[Co(C2O4)3]^3-}$, Co is +3 with $3d^{6}$. With $\ce{Co^3+}$, oxalate causes pairing, giving $t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{0}$: $d^2sp^3$ and diamagnetic. Statement I is correct.

In $\ce{[MnCl6]^3-}$, weak-field $\ce{Cl-}$ causes no pairing, so $\ce{Mn^3+}$ ($3d^{4}$) is high spin, $t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{1}$, with 4 unpaired electrons ($sp^3d^2$).

In $\ce{[FeF6]^3-}$, weak-field $\ce{F-}$ causes no pairing, so $\ce{Fe^3+}$ ($3d^{5}$) is high spin, $t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{2}$, with 5 unpaired electrons ($sp^3d^2$). Both are paramagnetic with 4 and 5 unpaired electrons, so Statement II is correct.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.solution:
Spin-only $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM increases with the number of unpaired electrons $n$.

(i) $\ce{[FeF6]^3-}$: $\ce{Fe^3+}$ is $3d^5$ and $\ce{F-}$ is weak-field, so no pairing occurs (outer-orbital $sp^3d^2$) and $n = 5$.

(ii) $\ce{[Co(NH3)6]^3+}$: $\ce{Co^3+}$ is $3d^6$ and $\ce{NH3}$ pairs all six electrons ($t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{0}$, inner-orbital $d^2sp^3$), so $n = 0$.

(iii) $\ce{[NiCl4]^2-}$: $\ce{Ni^2+}$ is $3d^8$ and weak-field $\ce{Cl-}$ gives tetrahedral $sp^3$ with two unpaired electrons, so $n = 2$.

(iv) $\ce{[Cu(NH3)4]^2+}$: $\ce{Cu^2+}$ is $3d^9$ and the complex is square planar ($dsp^2$); nine d electrons always leave one unpaired, so $n = 1$.

The moments are (i) $5.92$, (iii) $2.83$, (iv) $1.73$ and (ii) $0$ BM, so the order is (i) > (iii) > (iv) > (ii).

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.solution:
Oxidation states follow from the charge on each complex ion, with $\ce{CN-}$ and $\ce{Cl-}$ each $-1$.

In $\ce{K3[Cu(CN)4]}$, Cu is $+1$. Cu is $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}4s^{1}$, so $\ce{Cu+}$ is $[\text{Ar}]3d^{10}$ with every electron paired: diamagnetic.

In $\ce{K2[Cu(CN)4]}$, Cu is $+2$, i.e. $3d^{9}$, with one unpaired electron: paramagnetic.

In $\ce{K3[Fe(CN)4]}$, Fe is $+1$ with 25 electrons; an odd number of electrons leaves at least one unpaired: paramagnetic.

In $\ce{K4[FeCl6]}$, Fe is $+2$, i.e. $3d^{6}$; $\ce{Cl-}$ is a weak-field ligand, so the complex is high spin, $t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{2}$, with 4 unpaired electrons: paramagnetic.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I : [Ni(CN) 4 ] 2$$-$$ is square planar and diamagnetic complex, with dsp 2 hybridization for Ni but [Ni(CO) 4 ] is tetrahedral, paramagnetic and with sp 3 -hybridization for Ni.

Statement II : [NiCl 4 ] 2$$-$$ and [Ni(CO) 4 ] both have same d-electron configuration have same geometry and are paramagnetic.

In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is correct but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is correct.

questions.solution:
$\ce{[Ni(CN)4]^2-}$: $\ce{Ni^2+}$ is $3d^8$; strong-field $\ce{CN-}$ pairs the electrons and leaves one 3d orbital empty, giving $dsp^2$ hybridisation, a square planar shape and no unpaired electrons (diamagnetic).

$\ce{[Ni(CO)4]}$: Ni(0) is $3d^8 4s^2$; strong-field CO pairs all ten electrons into 3d ($3d^{10}$), giving $sp^3$ hybridisation, a tetrahedral shape and no unpaired electrons. It is diamagnetic, not paramagnetic, so Statement I is false.

$\ce{[NiCl4]^2-}$: $\ce{Ni^2+}$ is $3d^8$; weak-field $\ce{Cl-}$ causes no pairing, giving $sp^3$ hybridisation, a tetrahedral shape and 2 unpaired electrons (paramagnetic).

$\ce{[NiCl4]^2-}$ ($d^8$, paramagnetic) and $\ce{[Ni(CO)4]}$ ($d^{10}$, diamagnetic) share only the tetrahedral geometry, so Statement II is false.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
Arrange the following coordination compounds in the increasing order of magnetic moments. (Atomic numbers : Mn = 25; Fe = 26)
A. [FeF 6 ] 3$$-$$
B. [Fe(CN) 6 ] 3$$-$$
C. [MnCl 6 ] 3$$-$$ (high spin)
D. [Mn(CN) 6 ] 3$$-$$

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.solution:
Spin-only moment $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM rises with the number of unpaired electrons $n$.
A. $\ce{[FeF6]^3-}$: $\ce{Fe^3+}$, $3d^5$; weak-field $\ce{F-}$ gives high spin $t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{2}$, $n = 5$, $\mu = 5.92$ BM.
B. $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^3-}$: $\ce{Fe^3+}$, $3d^5$; strong-field $\ce{CN-}$ gives low spin $t_{2g}^{5}e_g^{0}$, $n = 1$, $\mu = 1.73$ BM.
C. $\ce{[MnCl6]^3-}$ (high spin): $\ce{Mn^3+}$, $3d^4$, $t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{1}$, $n = 4$, $\mu = 4.90$ BM.
D. $\ce{[Mn(CN)6]^3-}$: $\ce{Mn^3+}$, $3d^4$; strong-field $\ce{CN-}$ puts all four electrons in $t_{2g}$, $t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{0}$, which still leaves 2 unpaired electrons, $\mu = 2.83$ BM.

The increasing order of magnetic moment is $\text{B} < \text{D} < \text{C} < \text{A}$.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

$\ce{BrF5}$: Br has 7 valence electrons; 5 form Br–F bonds and 2 remain as one lone pair, so there are 6 electron pairs and the hybridisation is $sp^3d^2$ (square pyramidal) (IV).

$\ce{PCl5}$: P has 5 bond pairs and no lone pair, so it is $sp^3d$ (trigonal bipyramidal) (I).

$\ce{[Co(NH3)6]^3+}$: $\ce{Co^3+}$ is $3d^6$; strong-field $\ce{NH3}$ pairs these into three 3d orbitals, leaving two inner 3d orbitals for $d^2sp^3$ (II).

questions.text: The most stable ion is :
questions.solution:
The stability of a complex rises with the strength of the metal–ligand bonding. In the spectrochemical series $\ce{Cl-} < \ce{H2O} < \ce{CN-}$, and $\ce{CN-}$ is both a strong $\sigma$ donor and a $\pi$ acceptor.

In $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^3-}$, $\ce{Fe^3+}$ ($3d^5$) is low spin, $t_{2g}^{5}e_g^{0}$, with inner-orbital $d^2sp^3$ hybridisation and CFSE $= -2.0\,\Delta_o$; its formation constant is extremely large.

$\ce{[FeCl6]^3-}$ and $\ce{[Fe(H2O)6]^3+}$ are high-spin outer-orbital ($sp^3d^2$) complexes of weak-field ligands, $t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{2}$ with zero CFSE, so they are far less stable.

The formula in (A) does not correspond to a stable iron ion, since $\ce{Fe^3+}$ with three $\ce{OH-}$ is the neutral $\ce{Fe(OH)3}$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: In which of the following octahedral complexes of Co (at. no. 27), will the magnitude of $$\Delta _o$$ be the highest?
questions.solution: In octahedral complex the magnitude of $${\Delta _o}$$ will be highest in a complex having strongest ligand. Of the given ligands $$C{N^ - }$$ is strongest so $${\Delta _o}$$ will be highest for $${\left( {Co{{\left( {CN} \right)}_6}} \right)^{3 - }}.$$ Thus option $$(a)$$ is correct.

questions.text: The correct order of ligands in the spectrochemical series is
questions.solution:
The spectrochemical series arranges ligands by the crystal field splitting they cause: $\mathrm{I^-} \lt \mathrm{Br^-} \lt \mathrm{SCN^-} \lt \mathrm{Cl^-} \lt \mathrm{F^-} \lt \mathrm{OH^-} \lt \mathrm{H_2O} \lt \mathrm{NCS^-} \lt \mathrm{NH_3} \lt \mathrm{en} \lt \mathrm{CN^-} \lt \mathrm{CO}$.

$\mathrm{CN^-}$ is a strong-field ($\pi$-acceptor) ligand, en is a strong $\sigma$-donor, N-bonded $\mathrm{NCS^-}$ is intermediate and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ is weak-field.

In decreasing order: $\mathrm{CN^-} \gt \mathrm{en} \gt \mathrm{NCS^-} \gt \mathrm{Cl^-}$.

questions.text: The $$d$$-electron configurations of $$\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}$$, $$\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$$, $$\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$$ and $$\mathrm{Co^{2+}}$$ are $$d^4$$, $$d^5$$, $$d^6$$ and $$d^7$$ respectively. Which one of the following will exhibit the lowest paramagnetic behaviour? (Atomic no. $$\mathrm{Cr} = 24$$, $$\mathrm{Mn} = 25$$, $$\mathrm{Fe} = 26$$, $$\mathrm{Co} = 27$$).
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{H_2O}$ is a weak-field ligand, so all four octahedral aqua complexes are high spin.

Unpaired electrons: $d^4$ ($t_{2g}^3e_g^1$) $4$; $d^5$ ($t_{2g}^3e_g^2$) $5$; $d^6$ ($t_{2g}^4e_g^2$) $4$; $d^7$ ($t_{2g}^5e_g^2$) $3$.

Paramagnetism increases with the number of unpaired electrons, $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\ \mathrm{BM}$.

For $\mathrm{Co^{2+}}$, $\mu = \sqrt{15} \approx 3.87\ \mathrm{BM}$, the smallest of the four.

So $[\mathrm{Co(H_2O)_6}]^{2+}$ shows the lowest paramagnetic behaviour.

questions.text: In which of the following octahedral complex species the magnitude of $$\Delta_0$$ will be maximum?
questions.solution:
$\Delta_o$ grows with ligand field strength and with the metal's oxidation state.

Spectrochemical series: $\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-} \lt H_2O \lt NH_3 \lt CN^-}$.

$\mathrm{[Co(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}$ has Co(II) and a weak ligand, so it is lowest.

$\mathrm{[Co(CN)_6]^{3-}}$, with Co(III) and the strongest ligand, has the maximum $\Delta_o$.

questions.text: Among the following species the one which causes the highest CFSE, $$\Delta $$ 0 as a ligand is :
questions.solution:
The crystal field splitting $\Delta_o$ depends on the field strength of the ligand (spectrochemical series).

Order of field strength: $\mathrm{F^- \lt NH_3 \lt CN^- \lt CO}$.

$\mathrm{CO}$ is a $\sigma$-donor and a very strong $\pi$-acceptor (back bonding), which raises $\Delta_o$ the most.

So $\mathrm{CO}$ causes the highest CFSE.

questions.text:
Which one of the following complexes will most likely absorb visible light ?

(At nos. Sc = 21, Ti = 22, V = 23, Zn = 30)
questions.solution:
Visible light is absorbed through d–d transitions, which need a partially filled $d$ subshell.

$\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}$ is $3d^0$, $\mathrm{Ti^{4+}}$ is $3d^0$ and $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ is $3d^{10}$, so no d–d transition is possible and these complexes are colourless.

$\mathrm{V^{3+}}$ is $3d^2$, so d–d transitions occur in the octahedral field.

So $\mathrm{[V(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}$ will absorb visible light.

questions.text: The octahedral complex of a metal ion M 3+ with four monodentate ligands L 1 , L 2 , L 3 and L 4 absorb wavelengths in the region of red, green, yellow and blue, respectively. The increasing order of ligand strength of the four ligands is :
questions.solution:
For a given metal ion, weak field ligands create a complex with smaller $$\Delta $$, which will absorb light of longer $$\lambda $$ and thus lower frequency. Conversely, stronger field ligands create a larger $$\Delta ,$$ absorb light of shorter $$\lambda $$ and thus higher $$\nu$$, i.e. higher energy.

$$\mathop {{\mathop{\rm Re}\nolimits} d}\limits_{\lambda = 650\,nm} \,\,\mathop { < Yellow}\limits_{570\,\,nm} \,\,\mathop { < Green}\limits_{490\,nm} < \mathop {Blue}\limits_{450\,nm} $$

So order of ligand strength is

$${L_1} < {L_3} < {L_2} < {L_4}$$

questions.text: Which of the following complex ions has electrons that are symmetrically filled in both t 2g and e g orbitals ?
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}$: $\mathrm{Co^{3+}}$, $d^6$, weak-field $\mathrm{F^-}$ (high spin): $t_{2g}^4e_g^2$ — $t_{2g}$ unevenly filled.

$\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{2+}}$: $\mathrm{Co^{2+}}$, $d^7$: $t_{2g}^5e_g^2$ — unsymmetrical.

$\mathrm{[Mn(CN)_6]^{4-}}$: $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$, $d^5$ with strong-field $\mathrm{CN^-}$ (low spin): $t_{2g}^5e_g^0$ — unsymmetrical.

$\mathrm{[FeF_6]^{3-}}$: $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$, $d^5$ with weak-field $\mathrm{F^-}$ (high spin): $t_{2g}^3e_g^2$ — every d orbital singly occupied, symmetrical.

So $\mathrm{[FeF_6]^{3-}}$ has electrons symmetrically filled in both $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbitals.

questions.text: Which of the following compounds is not colored yellow?
questions.solution:
$\ce{K3[Co(NO2)6]}$ (potassium cobaltinitrite) is the yellow precipitate used to detect $\ce{K+}$.

$\ce{(NH4)3[As(Mo3O10)4]}$ (ammonium arsenomolybdate) is the yellow precipitate given by arsenate with ammonium molybdate.

$\ce{BaCrO4}$ is a yellow precipitate; its colour comes from charge transfer in the chromate ion.

$\ce{Zn2[Fe(CN)6]}$ (zinc ferrocyanide) is the white precipitate given by $\ce{Zn^2+}$ with potassium ferrocyanide; it contains $\ce{Zn^2+}$ ($3d^{10}$) and low-spin $\ce{Fe^2+}$ ($t_{2g}^{6}$), neither of which has unpaired electrons.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Identify the correct trend given below : (Atomic No.=Ti : 22, Cr : 24 and Mo : 42)
questions.solution:
$$\Delta$$ 0 of complex [Mo(H₂O) 6 ] 2+ is greater than that of [Cr(H₂O) 6 ] 2+ . It is due to the fact that Mo 2+ belongs to second row transition element while Cr 2+ is first row transition element.

Magnitude of crystal field splitting energy ($$\Delta$$ 0 ) depends on the charge on the metal ion. Greater the charge, greater is the crystal field splitting energy. Therefore, [Ti(H₂O) 6 ] 3+ > [Ti(H₂O) 6 ] 2+ .

questions.text: The crystal field stabilization energy (CFSE) of [Fe(H₂O) 6 ]Cl 2 and K 2 [NiCl 4 ] respectively, are :
questions.solution:
In $\ce{[Fe(H2O)6]Cl2}$, iron is $\ce{Fe^2+}$ ($3d^6$) in an octahedral field of weak-field $\ce{H2O}$, so it is high spin, $t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{2}$.

$$\text{CFSE} = 4(-0.4\,\Delta_o) + 2(+0.6\,\Delta_o) = -0.4\,\Delta_o$$

In $\ce{K2[NiCl4]}$, $\ce{[NiCl4]^2-}$ is tetrahedral with $\ce{Ni^2+}$ ($3d^8$). In a tetrahedral field the $e$ set lies lower ($-0.6\,\Delta_t$ per electron) and the $t_2$ set higher ($+0.4\,\Delta_t$ per electron), giving $e^{4}t_{2}^{4}$.

$$\text{CFSE} = 4(-0.6\,\Delta_t) + 4(+0.4\,\Delta_t) = -0.8\,\Delta_t$$

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: The INCORRECT statement is :

options.text: the color of [CoCl(NH 3 ) 5 ] 2+ is violet as it absorbs the yellow light.
the gemstone, ruby, has Cr 3+ ions occupying the octahedral sites of beryl.
the spin-only magnetic moment of [Ni(NH 3 ) 4 (H₂O) 2 ] 2+ is 2.83 BM.
the spin-only magnetic moments of [Fe(H₂O) 6 ] 2+ and [Cr(H₂O) 6 ] 2+ are nearly similar.

questions.solution:
(
A) $\ce{[CoCl(NH3)5]^2+}$ absorbs yellow light (about 535 nm), and the complementary colour violet is observed, so (
A) is correct.

(
B) Ruby is aluminium oxide (corundum, $\ce{Al2O3}$) in which about 0.5–1% of the octahedral $\ce{Al^3+}$ sites are occupied by $\ce{Cr^3+}$ ions; $\ce{Cr^3+}$ in beryl ($\ce{Be3Al2Si6O18}$) gives emerald. So (
B) is incorrect.

(
C) In octahedral $\ce{[Ni(NH3)4(H2O)2]^2+}$, $\ce{Ni^2+}$ is $3d^8$ ($t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{2}$) with 2 unpaired electrons, so $\mu = \sqrt{2(2+2)} = \sqrt{8} = 2.83\ \text{BM}$; (
C) is correct.

(
D) High-spin $\ce{[Fe(H2O)6]^2+}$ ($3d^6$, $t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{2}$) and high-spin $\ce{[Cr(H2O)6]^2+}$ ($3d^4$, $t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{1}$) each have 4 unpaired electrons, so both have $\mu = \sqrt{4(4+2)} = 4.90\ \text{BM}$; (
D) is correct.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
The correct order of the spin-only magnetic moment of metal ions in the following low-spin
complexes, [V(CN) 6 ] 4– ,[Fe(CN) 6 ] 4– , [Ru(NH 3 ) 6 ] 3+ , and [Cr(NH 3 ) 6 ] 2+ , is :
questions.solution:
All four complexes are octahedral and are stated to be low-spin, so the $t_{2g}$ set fills completely before any electron enters $e_g$. Spin-only $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM, where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons.

$\ce{V^2+}$ in $\ce{[V(CN)6]^4-}$: $3d^3 \Rightarrow t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{0}$, $n = 3$, $\mu = \sqrt{15} \approx 3.87$ BM.

$\ce{Cr^2+}$ in $\ce{[Cr(NH3)6]^2+}$: $3d^4$, low-spin $\Rightarrow t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{0}$, $n = 2$, $\mu = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.83$ BM.

$\ce{Ru^3+}$ in $\ce{[Ru(NH3)6]^3+}$: $4d^5$, low-spin $\Rightarrow t_{2g}^{5}e_g^{0}$, $n = 1$, $\mu = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73$ BM.

$\ce{Fe^2+}$ in $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^4-}$: $3d^6$, low-spin $\Rightarrow t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{0}$, $n = 0$, $\mu = 0$.

Option (C) would need high-spin $\ce{Cr^2+}$ ($t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{1}$, $n = 4$), which the stated low-spin condition excludes.

So the order is $\ce{V^2+} > \ce{Cr^2+} > \ce{Ru^3+} > \ce{Fe^2+}$.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
Two complexes [Cr(H₂O) 6 ]Cl 3  (
A) and [Cr(NH 3 ) 6 ]Cl 3  (
B) are violet and yellow coloured, respectively. The incorrect statement regarding them is :

options.text:
$$\Delta $$ 0 values of (
A) and (
B) are calculated from the energies of violet and yellow light, respectively
both are paramagnetic with three unpaired electrons
both absorb energies corresponding to their complementary colors.
$$\Delta $$ 0 value for (A) is less than that of (B).

questions.solution:
Both complexes contain $\ce{Cr^3+}$ ($3d^3$, $t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{0}$), so both are paramagnetic with three unpaired electrons: statement (
B) is correct.

The colour seen is complementary to the colour absorbed, so violet complex (
A) absorbs yellow light and yellow complex (
B) absorbs violet light: statement (
C) is correct.

$\Delta_o$ equals the energy of the light absorbed, $\Delta_o = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{\text{absorbed}}}$, so $\Delta_o$ of (
A) is obtained from yellow light and that of (
B) from violet light, not the other way round: statement (
A) is incorrect.

$\ce{NH3}$ is a stronger field ligand than $\ce{H2O}$, consistent with (
B) absorbing higher-energy violet light, so $\Delta_o$ of (
A) is less than that of (B): statement (
D) is correct.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
For a d 4 metal ion in an octahedral field, the
correct electronic configuration is :
questions.solution:
For a $d^4$ ion in an octahedral field, the first three electrons occupy the $t_{2g}$ orbitals singly. The fourth electron either pairs in $t_{2g}$, costing the pairing energy $P$, or enters $e_g$, costing $\Delta_o$.

When $\Delta_o < P$ (weak field), entering $e_g$ costs less, so the configuration is high spin, $t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{1}$.

When $\Delta_o > P$ (strong field), the electron pairs in $t_{2g}$ to give $t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{0}$; options (
A) and (
B) pair each configuration with the opposite condition, and (
C) fills $e_g$ before $t_{2g}$.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
The values of the crystal field stabilization
energies for a high spin d 6 metal ion in
octahedral and tetrahedral fields, respectively,
are :
questions.solution:
For a high-spin $d^{6}$ ion the splitting is smaller than the pairing energy, so all five orbitals are singly occupied before the sixth electron pairs in the lower set.

Octahedral field: the configuration is $t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{2}$, each $t_{2g}$ electron contributing $-0.4\Delta_o$ and each $e_g$ electron $+0.6\Delta_o$.

$$\text{CFSE} = \left[4(-0.4) + 2(0.6)\right]\Delta_o = (-1.6 + 1.2)\Delta_o = -0.4\Delta_o$$

Tetrahedral field: the order is reversed, the lower $e$ set lying at $-0.6\Delta_t$ and the upper $t_2$ set at $+0.4\Delta_t$, and the configuration is $e^{3}t_{2}^{3}$.

$$\text{CFSE} = \left[3(-0.6) + 3(0.4)\right]\Delta_t = (-1.8 + 1.2)\Delta_t = -0.6\Delta_t$$

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
The Crystal Field Stabilization Energy

(CFSE) of [CoF 3 (H₂O) 3 ] ($$\Delta $$ 0 < P) is :
questions.solution:
$\ce{Co^3+}$ is $3d^6$. Since $\Delta_o < P$, electrons enter $e_g$ before pairing in $t_{2g}$, giving the high-spin configuration $t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{2}$ with 4 unpaired electrons.

$$\text{CFSE} = (-0.4 \times 4 + 0.6 \times 2)\,\Delta_o = (-1.6 + 1.2)\,\Delta_o = -0.4\,\Delta_o$$

The single electron pair of $t_{2g}^{4}e_g^{2}$ is already present in the free $3d^6$ ion, so no extra pairing energy enters; a $P$ term arises only for pairs forced by the field, as in low-spin $t_{2g}^{6}$ ($-2.4\,\Delta_o + 2P$).

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
The one that can exhibit highest paramagnetic
behaviour among the following is :

gly = glycinato; bpy = 2, 2'-bipyridine
questions.solution:
(
A) $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ is $3d^6$; with the strong-field nitrogen donors bpy, en and $\ce{NH3}$ it is low spin, $t_{2g}^6e_g^0$, with no unpaired electron.

(
B) $\ce{Pd^{2+}}$ is $4d^8$ and square planar, with no unpaired electron.

(
C) For cobalt, $x+2(-2)+2(-1)=-1$ gives $x=+5$, so $\ce{Co^{5+}}$ is $3d^4$; with $\Delta_o>P$ it is $t_{2g}^4e_g^0$, with 2 unpaired electrons.

(
D) $\ce{Ti^{3+}}$ is $3d^1$, with 1 unpaired electron.

The cobalt complex has the most unpaired electrons and is the most paramagnetic.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
The electronic spectrum of [Ti(H₂O) 6 ] 3+ shows a single broad peak with a maximum at 20,300 cm -1
.
The crystal field stabilization energy (CFSE) of the complex ion, in kJ mol -1 , is :
(1 kJ mol -1 = 83.7 cm -1 )
questions.solution:
$\ce{Ti^3+}$ is $3d^1$, so in the octahedral field of $\ce{H2O}$ the electron occupies $t_{2g}$ ($t_{2g}^{1}e_g^{0}$).

The single absorption band is the $t_{2g} \rightarrow e_g$ transition of this electron, so its energy equals the splitting: $\Delta_o = 20300\ \text{cm}^{-1}$.

$$\text{CFSE} = -0.4\,\Delta_o = -0.4 \times 20300 = -8120\ \text{cm}^{-1}$$

With $1\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1} = 83.7\ \text{cm}^{-1}$:

$$\text{CFSE} = -\dfrac{8120}{83.7}\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1} = -97\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

The stabilization energy is thus $97\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ in magnitude.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
Consider that a d 6 metal ion (M 2+ ) forms a
complex with aqua ligands, and the spin only
magnetic moment of the complex is 4.90 BM.
The geometry and the crystal field stabilization
energy of the complex is
questions.solution:
A spin-only moment of $4.90\ \text{BM}$ gives $\sqrt{n(n+2)} = 4.90 \Rightarrow n = 4$ unpaired electrons, so the $d^6$ ion is high spin.

In an octahedral field, high-spin $d^6$ is $t_{2g}^4e_g^2$ with CFSE $= 4(-0.4\Delta_o) + 2(0.6\Delta_o) = -0.4\Delta_o$, which matches neither octahedral option; $-2.4\Delta_o + 2P$ is low-spin $t_{2g}^6$ with no unpaired electron.

In a tetrahedral field, $d^6$ is $e^3t_2^3$ with 4 unpaired electrons and CFSE $= 3(-0.6\Delta_t) + 3(0.4\Delta_t) = -0.6\Delta_t$, with no pairing beyond that of the free ion; $-1.6\Delta_t + P$ is the $e^4t_2^2$ arrangement with only 2 unpaired electrons.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
The correct order of the spin-only magnetic
moments of the following complexes is :

(I) [Cr(H₂O) 6 ]Br 2

(II) Na 4 [Fe(CN) 6 ]

(III) Na 3 [Fe(C₂O₄ ) 3 ] ($$\Delta $$ 0 $$>$$ P)

(IV) (Et₄N) 2 [CoCl 4 ]
questions.solution:
Spin-only $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\ \text{BM}$, where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons.

(I) $\ce{[Cr(H2O)6]^2+}$: $\ce{Cr^2+}$ is $3d^4$; $\ce{H2O}$ is a weak-field ligand, so $t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{1}$, $n = 4$, $\mu = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.90\ \text{BM}$.

(II) $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^4-}$: $\ce{Fe^2+}$ is $3d^6$; $\ce{CN-}$ is a strong-field ligand, so $t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{0}$, $n = 0$, $\mu = 0$.

(III) $\ce{[Fe(C2O4)3]^3-}$: $\ce{Fe^3+}$ is $3d^5$; since $\Delta_o > P$, the complex is low spin, $t_{2g}^{5}e_g^{0}$, $n = 1$, $\mu = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73\ \text{BM}$.

(IV) $\ce{[CoCl4]^2-}$: tetrahedral, $\ce{Co^2+}$ is $3d^7$, $e^{4}t_2^{3}$, $n = 3$, $\mu = \sqrt{15} \approx 3.87\ \text{BM}$.

The order is (I) > (IV) > (III) > (II).

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
[Pd(F)(Cl)(Br)(I)] 2– has n number of
geometrical isomers. Then, the spin-only
magnetic moment and crystal field stabilisation
energy [CFSE] of [Fe(CN) 6 ] n–6 , respectively,
are:

[Note : Ignore the pairing energy]
questions.solution:
$\ce{[Pd(F)(Cl)(Br)(I)]^2-}$ is a square planar $\ce{[Mabcd]}$ complex, which has 3 geometrical isomers, so $n = 3$ and the second complex is $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^3-}$.

In $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^3-}$, iron is $\ce{Fe^3+}$ with the configuration $[\ce{Ar}]3d^5$.

$\ce{CN-}$ is a strong-field ligand, and with the pairing energy ignored nothing opposes pairing, so all five electrons enter the $t_{2g}$ set: $t_{2g}^{5}e_g^{0}$, with 1 unpaired electron.

$$\mu = \sqrt{1(1+2)} = \sqrt{3} = 1.73\ \text{BM}$$

Ignoring the pairing energy, the CFSE contains only the $\Delta_0$ terms:

$$\text{CFSE} = (-0.4 \times 5 + 0.6 \times 0)\Delta_0 = -2.0\,\Delta_0$$

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
Among the statements(a)-(d) the incorrect ones are :

(a) Octahedral Co(III) complexes with strong field ligands have very high magnetic moments.

(b) When $$\Delta $$ 0 < P, the d-electron configuration of Co(III) in an octahedral complex is $$t_{2g}^4e_g^2$$

(c) Wavelength of light absorbed by [Co(en) 3 ] 3+ is lower than that of [CoF 6 ] 3-

(d) If the $$\Delta $$ 0 for an octahedral complex of Co(III) is 18,000 cm -1 , the $$\Delta $$ t for its tetrahedral complex with the same ligand will be 16,000 cm -1

(b) If $$\Delta $$ 0 < P configuration of Co 3+ will be $$t_{2g}^4e_g^2$$.

[CoF 6 ] 3– .

So wave length of light absorbed by [Co(en) 3 ] 3+
is lower than that of [CoF 6 ] 3–
