$$ \therefore $$ Statement (a) and (d) are incorrect.

questions.text: The theory that can completely/properly explain the nature of bonding in [Ni(CO) 4 ] is :
questions.solution:
In $\ce{[Ni(CO)4]}$ each CO donates its carbon lone pair into an empty orbital of Ni ($\sigma$ bond), and filled Ni $d$ orbitals donate electron density back into the empty $\pi^*$ orbitals of CO ($\pi$ back-bond).

This synergic bonding strengthens the Ni–C bond and weakens the C–O bond, so the C–O bond is longer and its stretching frequency lower than in free CO.

Valence bond theory gives only the $sp^3$ hybridisation, tetrahedral shape and diamagnetism; it has no description of $\pi$ back-donation. Crystal field theory treats ligands as point charges and cannot explain why neutral CO is a strong-field ligand, and Werner's theory deals only with primary and secondary valencies.

Molecular orbital theory combines the metal orbitals with the CO $\sigma$ and $\pi^*$ orbitals, so it accounts for both the $\sigma$ donation and the $\pi$ back-bonding and explains the bonding completely.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The Crystal Field Stabilization Energy (CFSE) and magnetic moment (spin-only) of an octahedral aqua complex of a metal ion (M z+ ) are $$-$$0.8 $$\Delta$$ 0 and 3.87 BM, respectively. Identify (M z+ ) :

, e g 2

= –0.8 Δ 0

Magnetic moment (spin only) can be calculated as :

$$\mu = \sqrt {n\left( {n + 2} \right)} $$

where, $$\mu $$ = spin only magnetic moment and

n = number of unpaired electrons = 3

= $$\sqrt {3\left( {3 + 2} \right)} = \sqrt {15} $$ = 3.87 BM

questions.text:
Arrange the following Cobalt complexes in the order of increasing Crystal Field Stabilization Energy (CFSE) value.

Complexes : $$\mathop {{{[Co{F_6}]}^{3 - }}}\limits_A ,\mathop {{{[Co{{({H_2}O)}_6}]}^{2 + }}}\limits_B ,\mathop {{{[Co{{(N{H_3})}_6}]}^{3 + }}}\limits_C and \mathop {{{[Co{{({en})}_3}]}^{3 + }}}\limits_D $$

Choose the correct option :
questions.solution:
(i) CFSE $$\propto$$ charge or oxidation no. of central metal ion.

(ii) CFSE $$\propto$$ strength of ligand

en > NH 3 > H₂O > F $$-$$

(iii) The oxidation state of the metal has the larger effect: Co(III) complexes have a much larger crystal field splitting than Co(II) complexes. So the only Co(II) complex, B, comes lowest even though H₂O is a stronger field ligand than F $$-$$ ; the three Co(III) complexes then follow ligand strength (F $$-$$ < NH 3 < en).

$$\therefore$$ order of CFSE

$$\mathop {{{[Co{{(en)}_3}]}^{ + 3}}}\limits^{III} > \mathop {{{[Co{{(N{H_3})}_6}]}^{ + 3}}}\limits^{III} > \mathop {{{[Co{F_6}]}^{ - 3}}}\limits^{III} > \mathop {{{[Co{{({H_2}O)}_6}]}^{ + 2}}}\limits^{II} $$

i.e. increasing order of CFSE : B < A < C < D

questions.text: The total number of unpaired electrons present in [Co(NH 3 ) 6 ]Cl 2 and [Co(NH 3 ) 6 ]Cl 3 is :
questions.solution:
$\ce{[Co(NH3)6]Cl2}$ contains $\ce{Co^2+}$, $[\text{Ar}]3d^7$. For this dipositive ion the splitting produced by $\ce{NH3}$ is smaller than the pairing energy ($\Delta_o < P$), so the complex is high spin, $t_{2g}^{5}e_g^{2}$ (outer-orbital $sp^3d^2$), with 3 unpaired electrons.

$\ce{[Co(NH3)6]Cl3}$ contains $\ce{Co^3+}$, $[\text{Ar}]3d^6$. The higher charge of $\ce{Co^3+}$ raises $\Delta_o$ well above $P$, so the electrons pair as $t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{0}$ (inner-orbital $d^2sp^3$), with 0 unpaired electrons.

Total number of unpaired electrons $= 3 + 0 = 3$.

Hence, the answer is 3.

questions.text: The correct order of intensity of colors of the compounds is :
questions.solution:
In all three complexes nickel is $\ce{Ni^2+}$ ($3d^8$), and the colour comes from absorption of visible light by d–d transitions; the colour is intense when the absorption is strong and lies well inside the visible region.

$\ce{[NiCl4]^2-}$ is tetrahedral with the weak-field ligand $\ce{Cl-}$: the small splitting keeps the absorption inside the visible region, and the absence of a centre of symmetry makes its d–d transitions only partly forbidden, so it absorbs strongly and is intensely coloured.

$\ce{[Ni(H2O)6]^2+}$ is octahedral and centrosymmetric, so its d–d transitions are Laporte-forbidden and weak; it is only pale green.

$\ce{[Ni(CN)4]^2-}$ is square planar (also centrosymmetric) with the strong-field ligand $\ce{CN-}$: the large splitting pushes its absorption towards the violet and ultraviolet, so it is the least coloured (pale yellow).

The order of intensity of colour is therefore $\ce{[NiCl4]^2-} > \ce{[Ni(H2O)6]^2+} > \ce{[Ni(CN)4]^2-}$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: The total number of unpaired electrons present in the complex K 3 [Cr(oxalate) 3 ] is _____________.
questions.solution:
In $\ce{K3[Cr(C2O4)3]}$, with oxalate as $\ce{C2O4^2-}$, the oxidation state $x$ of Cr is given by $3(+1) + x + 3(-2) = 0$, so $x = +3$.

$\ce{Cr^3+}$ ($Z = 24$) is $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{3}$.

In the octahedral complex the three electrons occupy the three $t_{2g}$ orbitals singly, $t_{2g}^{3}e_g^{0}$, whatever the field strength of oxalate; pairing would need a fourth $t_{2g}$ electron, so none occurs.

Number of unpaired electrons = 3.

Hence, the answer is 3.

questions.text: [Ti(H₂O) 6 ] 3+ absorbs light of wavelength 498 nm during a d $$-$$ d transition. The octahedral splitting energy for the above complex is ____________ $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$19 J. (Round off to the Nearest Integer). h = 6.626 $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$34 Js; c = 3 $$\times$$ 10 8 ms $$-$$1
questions.solution:
Octahedral splitting energy = $${{hc} \over \lambda }$$

$$ = {{6.626 \times {{10}^{ - 34}} \times 3 \times {{10}^8}} \over {498 \times {{10}^{ - 9}}}}$$

$$ = 3.99 \times {10^{ - 19}}J$$

$$ \approx 4 \times {10^{ - 19}}$$

questions.text: The calculated magnetic moments (spin only value) for species $${[FeC{l_4}]^{2 - }}$$, $${[Co{({C_2}{O_4})_3}]^{3 - }}$$ and $$MnO_4^{2 - }$$ respectively are :
questions.solution:
In $\ce{[FeCl4]^2-}$, $x + 4(-1) = -2$ gives $\ce{Fe^2+}$, $3d^6$. The complex is tetrahedral and $\ce{Cl-}$ is a weak-field ligand, so $\Delta_t$ is small and no pairing occurs: $e^{3}t_2^{3}$, with $n = 4$.

$$\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{4 \times 6} = \sqrt{24} = 4.90\ \text{BM}$$

In $\ce{[Co(C2O4)3]^3-}$, $x + 3(-2) = -3$ gives $\ce{Co^3+}$, $3d^6$. Oxalate is a weaker ligand than water, but the high charge of $\ce{Co^3+}$ makes $\Delta_o > P$ (as with $\ce{H2O}$ and $\ce{NH3}$), so the complex is low spin: $t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{0}$, with $n = 0$ and $\mu = 0$.

In $\ce{MnO4^2-}$, $x + 4(-2) = -2$ gives $\ce{Mn^6+}$, $3d^1$, with $n = 1$.

$$\mu = \sqrt{1 \times 3} = \sqrt{3} = 1.73\ \text{BM}$$

The values are 4.90, 0 and 1.73 BM.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: In low and high spin octahedral $\mathrm{Co^{3+}}$ complexes the number of electrons in $t_{2g}$ level respectively will be . (given At. no. of Co, 27)
questions.solution:
Co ($Z = 27$): $[\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^7 4s^2$; $\mathrm{Co^{3+}}$: $3d^6$.

Low spin ($\Delta_o \gt P$): all six electrons pair in $t_{2g}$, $t_{2g}^6 e_g^0$, so 6 electrons in $t_{2g}$.

High spin ($\Delta_o \lt P$): $t_{2g}^4 e_g^2$, so 4 electrons in $t_{2g}$.

questions.text: Octahedral complexes of copper(II) undergo structural distortion (Jahn-Teller). Which one of the given copper (II) complexes will show the maximum structural distortion? (en - ethylenediamine; $$\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{~N}-\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{CH}_{2}-\mathrm{NH}_{2}$$)
questions.solution:
$\ce{Cu^2+}$ is $3d^9$. In a regular octahedron its configuration $t_{2g}^{6}e_g^{3}$ is degenerate, because the odd $e_g$ electron can occupy either $d_{z^2}$ or $d_{x^2-y^2}$; the complex therefore distorts, usually by lengthening the two axial bonds, to remove this degeneracy.

The degeneracy, and with it the Jahn–Teller distortion, is greatest when all six ligands are identical, so that the undistorted complex would be a perfect octahedron: this is $\ce{[Cu(H2O)6]^2+}$ in $\ce{[Cu(H2O)6]SO4}$.

In $\ce{[Cu(en)(H2O)4]^2+}$ and in cis- and trans-$\ce{[Cu(en)2Cl2]}$ the mixed ligand sets already lower the symmetry below octahedral and partly split the $e_g$ level, so the additional Jahn–Teller distortion is smaller.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: $$\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}\right]^{3-}$$ should be an inner orbital complex. Ignoring the pairing energy, the value of crystal field stabilization energy for this complex is $$(-)$$ ____________ $$\Delta_{0}$$. (Nearest integer)
questions.solution:
In $\left[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN})^{6}\right]^{3-}$, $\mathrm{Fe}$ is present in (+3) oxidation state $\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{III}) \Rightarrow$ inner orbital complex $\Rightarrow d^{5}$ (with pairing)

Configuration $\Rightarrow t_{2 g}^{5}$

CFSE $=5 \times \frac{-2}{5} \Delta_{0}=-2 \Delta_{0}$

questions.text:
The correct order of energy of absorption for the following metal complexes is :
A: [Ni(en) 3 ] 2+ ,
B: [Ni(NH 3 ) 6 ] 2+ ,
C: [Ni(H₂O) 6 ] 2+
questions.solution:
Stronger is ligand attached to metal ion, greater will be the splitting between $$\mathrm{t}_{2} \mathrm{g}$$ and $e_g$ (hence greater will be $$\Delta \mathrm{U})$$

$$ \therefore$$ Greater will be absorption of energy.

Hence correct order

$$\left[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{en})_{3}\right]^{2+}>\left[\mathrm{Ni}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{6}\right]^{2+}>\left[\mathrm{Ni}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)_{6}\right]^{2+}$$

questions.text:
Consider the following metal complexes :

$$\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{6}\right]^{3+}$$

$$\left[\mathrm{CoCl}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{5}\right]^{2+}$$

$$\left[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}\right]^{3-}$$

$$\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{5}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)\right]^{3+}$$

The spin-only magnetic moment value of the complex that absorbs light with shortest wavelength is _____________ B. M. (Nearest integer)
questions.solution:
In all complexes, Co is present in $+3$ oxidation state and all complexes are low spin or inner orbital complex.

The stronger the ligand, the higher the crystal field splitting.

So, the order of crystal field splitting is

$\left[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{CN})_{6}\right]^{3-}>\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{6}\right]^{3+}>\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{5}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)\right]^{3+}>$ $\left[\mathrm{CoCl}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{5}\right]^{2+}$

Shortest wavelength is shown by complex having maximum crystal field splitting.

Spin only magnetic moment $=\sqrt{0(0+2)}=0$ B.M

questions.text: Spin only magnetic moment of [MnBr 6 ] 4$$-$$ is _________ B.M. (round off to the closest integer)
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} & {\left[\mathrm{MnBr}_6\right]^{4-}} \\\\ & x-6=-4\end{aligned}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
x & =+2 \\\\
\mathrm{Mn} & =[\mathrm{Ar}] 3 d^5 4 s^2 \\\\
\mathrm{Mn}^{2+} & =[\mathrm{Ar}] 3 d^5 4 s^0
\end{aligned}
$$

So, number of unpaired electrons $(n)=5$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu & =\sqrt{n(n+2)} \\\\
\mu & =\sqrt{5(5+2)} \\\\
& =\sqrt{35} \\\\
& =5.91 \text { B.M. } \\\\
& \approx 6 \text { B.M. }
\end{aligned}

questions.text: The spin-only magnetic moment value of an octahedral complex among CoCl 3 .4NH 3 , NiCl 2 .6H 2 O and PtCl 4 .2HCl, which upon reaction with excess of AgNO 3 gives 2 moles of AgCl is ___________ B.M. (Nearest integer)
questions.solution:
From the given information, we are looking for a complex which, upon reaction with excess of AgNO₃, gives 2 moles of AgCl. This implies that the complex has 2 chloride ions involved.

Considering the complexes :

CoCl₃.4NH₃ : This complex has 3 chloride ions, so it's not the one we are looking for.

NiCl₂.6H₂O : This complex has 2 chloride ions, so it's a potential candidate.

PtCl₄.2HCl : This complex has 4 chloride ions, so it's not the one we are looking for.

Therefore, the complex we are interested in is NiCl₂.6H₂O.

$\mathrm{CoCl}_{3} \cdot 4 \mathrm{NH}_{3} \underset{\text { excess }}{\stackrel{\mathrm{AgNO}_{3}}{\longrightarrow}}\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_{3}\right)_{4} \cdot \mathrm{Cl}_{2}\right]+\mathrm{AgCl}$

$$
\left.\left.\mathrm{NiCl}_{2} \cdot 6 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \underset{\text { excess }}{\stackrel{\mathrm{AgNO}_{3}}{\longrightarrow}}\right[ \mathrm{Ni}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)_{6}\right]^{2+}+2 \mathrm{AgCl}
$$

$\mathrm{PtCl}_{4} \cdot 2 \mathrm{HCl} \longrightarrow\left[\mathrm{PtCl}_{6}\right]^{4-}+\mathrm{No} ~\mathrm{AgCl} ~\mathrm{ppt}$
The next step is to find the oxidation state of the nickel ion. The nickel ion must have a charge of +2 to balance the -2 charge from the two chloride ions, thus it is Ni 2+ .

In the case of Ni²⁺, the electron configuration is [Ar]3d 8 . For an octahedral complex, the d-orbitals split into two sets under the influence of ligands: the $e_g$ set which includes d(x²-y²) and d(z²) orbitals, and the $t_{2g}$ set which includes the d(xy), d(xz), and d(yz) orbitals. Electrons will occupy the lower energy $t_{2g}$ orbitals first.

The 3d 8 electron configuration implies there are 8 electrons in the 3d orbitals. The first six electrons pair up in the three $t_{2g}$ orbitals, and the next two electrons will go into the two $e_g$ orbitals, with each one having one unpaired electron.

The spin-only magnetic moment (μ) can be calculated using the formula :

$$
\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} \, \text{B.M.}
$$

where n is the number of unpaired electrons. In this case, n = 2, so

$$
\mu = \sqrt{2 \times (2+2)} = \sqrt{8} \, \text{B.M.}
$$

Rounding to the nearest integer, the spin-only magnetic moment is approximately 3 B.M.

If [Cu(H₂O) 4 ] 2+ absorbs a light of wavelength 600 nm for d-d transition, then the value of octahedral crystal field splitting energy for [Cu(H₂O) 6 ] 2+ will be ____________ $$\times$$ 10 $$-$$21 J. [Nearest Integer]

Transition metal complex with highest value of crystal field splitting ($$\Delta$$ 0 ) will be :
questions.solution:
Crystal field splitting $$\left(\Delta_{0}\right)$$ for octahedral complexes depends on oxidation state of the metal as well as to which transition series the metal belongs. For the same oxidation state, the crystal field splitting $$\left(\Delta_{0}\right)$$ increases as we move from $$3 d \rightarrow 4 d \rightarrow 5 d $$

$$\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}$$ and $$\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$$ belong to $$3 d$$ series, $$\mathrm{Mo}^{3+}$$ belongs to $$4 d$$ series and $$\mathrm{Os}^{3+}$$ belongs to $$5 d$$ series.

Therefore crystal field splitting $$\left(\Delta_{0}\right)$$ is highest for $$\left[\mathrm{Os}\left(\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}\right)_{6}\right]^{3+}$$.

questions.text: The type isomerism present in nitropentammine chromium $$\left( {{\rm I}{\rm I}{\rm I}} \right)$$ chloride is :
questions.solution:
Nitropentamminechromium(III) chloride is $\ce{[Cr(NH3)5(NO2)]Cl2}$.

The ambidentate $\ce{NO2-}$ ligand can bind through N (nitro) or through O (nitrito), giving the linkage isomer $\ce{[Cr(NH3)5(ONO)]Cl2}$.

The counter ion $\ce{Cl-}$ is itself a ligand and can take the place of $\ce{NO2-}$ in the coordination sphere, giving the ionisation isomer $\ce{[Cr(NH3)5Cl]Cl(NO2)}$, which releases $\ce{NO2-}$ instead of a second $\ce{Cl-}$ in solution.

An octahedral $\ce{[MA5B]}$ entity has mirror planes, so no optical isomer exists.

Hence, the correct options are (B) and (C).

questions.text: Which one the following has largest number of isomers? (R = alkyl group, en = ethylenediamine)
questions.solution:
$\ce{[Co(en)2Cl2]+}$ is an octahedral $\mathrm{M(AA)_2b_2}$ complex. The trans isomer has a mirror plane and is optically inactive; the cis isomer is chiral and exists as a pair of enantiomers. Total: 3 stereoisomers.

$\ce{[Ru(NH3)4Cl2]+}$ is an octahedral $\mathrm{Ma_4b_2}$ complex with cis and trans forms, both optically inactive: 2 isomers.

$\ce{[Ir(PR3)2H(CO)]^2+}$ is a square planar $\mathrm{Ma_2bc}$ complex with cis and trans forms: 2 isomers.

$\ce{[Co(NH3)5Cl]^2+}$ is an octahedral $\mathrm{Ma_5b}$ complex with only one arrangement: no isomers.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: Which of the following compounds shows optical isomerism?
questions.solution:
A complex shows optical isomerism when it has no plane or centre of symmetry, so that it and its mirror image are non-superimposable.

$\ce{[Cr(C2O4)3]^3-}$ is an octahedral tris-chelate of the type $\ce{[M(AA)3]}$: the three oxalate rings are arranged like the blades of a propeller and no symmetry plane exists, so the $\Delta$ and $\Lambda$ forms are non-superimposable mirror images.

Square planar $\ce{[Cu(NH3)4]^2+}$, tetrahedral $\ce{[ZnCl4]^2-}$ and octahedral $\ce{[Co(CN)6]^3-}$ each carry only identical ligands and have planes of symmetry, so they are achiral.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: Which of the following has an optical isomer ?
questions.solution:
A complex shows optical isomerism only when it has no plane or centre of symmetry.

(
A) $\ce{[Co(en)(NH3)2]^2+}$ and (
D) $\ce{[Co(NH3)3Cl]+}$ are four-coordinate; in either tetrahedral or square planar geometry each has a plane of symmetry, so neither is chiral.

(
B) $\ce{[Co(H2O)4(en)]^3+}$ is of type $\ce{M(AA)B4}$; the plane containing Co and the en chelate ring is a mirror plane, so it has no enantiomer.

(
C) $\ce{[Co(en)2(NH3)2]^3+}$ is of type $\ce{M(AA)2B2}$. The trans isomer has a mirror plane, but in the cis isomer the two en rings form a propeller-like arrangement with no plane of symmetry, so cis-$\ce{[Co(en)2(NH3)2]^3+}$ exists as a pair of non-superimposable mirror images ($\Delta$ and $\Lambda$).

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
Which one of the following has an optical isomer ?

(en = ethylenediamine)
questions.solution:
For a substance to be optical isomers following conditions should be fulfilled

$$(a)\,\,\,$$ A coordination compound which can rotate the plane of polarized light is said to be optically active.

$$(b)\,\,\,$$ When the coordination compounds have same formula but differ in their abilities to rotate directions of the plane of polarized light are said to exhibit optical isomerism and the molecules are optical isomers. The optical isomers are pair of molecules which are non-super-imposable mirror images of each other.

$$(c)\,\,\,$$ This is due to the absence of elements of symmetry in the complex.

$$(d)\,\,\,$$ Optical isomerism is expected in tetrahedral complexes of the type $$Mabcd.$$

Based on this only option $$(2)$$ shows optical isomerism $${\left[ {Co{{\left( {en} \right)}_3}} \right]^{3 + }}$$

Complexes of $$Z{n^{ + + }}\,\,$$ cannot show optical isomerism as they are tetrahedral complexes with plane of symmetry.

$${\left[ {Co{{\left( {{H_2}O} \right)}_4}\left( {en} \right)} \right]^{3 + }}\,\,$$ have two planes of symmetry hence it is also optically inactive.

Hence the formula of the complex is $$\left[ {Co{{\left( {N{H_3}} \right)}_6}} \right]C{l_3}$$

questions.text: The complex ion $$\mathrm{[Pt(NO_2)(Py)(NH_3)(NH_2OH)]^+}$$ will give
questions.solution:
The charge balance $x - 1 = +1$ gives Pt(II), which with four ligands forms a square planar complex of the type $[\mathrm{Mabcd}]$.

Fix ligand a; any one of the other three (b, c or d) can lie trans to it, and the positions of the remaining two are then fixed.

So there are 3 distinct arrangements: a trans to b, a trans to c, and a trans to d.

Hence the ion gives 3 geometrical isomers.

questions.text: Which of the following complex ions will exhibit optical isomerism? (en = 1,2-diamine ethane).
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^+}$ is an octahedral $\mathrm{[M(AA)_2B_2]}$ complex; its cis form has no plane or centre of symmetry, so it exists as a pair of enantiomers.

$\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^+}$, an $\mathrm{[MA_4B_2]}$ complex, shows only cis–trans isomerism, and both forms have a mirror plane.

$\mathrm{[Zn(en)_2]^{2+}}$ is tetrahedral with symmetric chelates, and four-coordinate $\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_2Cl_2]^+}$ has only monodentate ligands; neither is chiral.

So $\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^+}$ exhibits optical isomerism.

questions.text: Type of isomerism which exists between $$[Pd(C_6H_5)_2(SCN)_2]$$ and $$[Pd(C_6H_5)_2(NCS)_2]$$ is :
questions.solution:
Thiocyanate is an ambidentate ligand: it can bind through S ($\mathrm{SCN^-}$, thiocyanato) or through N ($\mathrm{NCS^-}$, isothiocyanato).

The two complexes have the same formula and differ only in the donor atom of this ligand.

Answer: linkage isomerism.

questions.text: Which of the following complex species is not expected to exhibit optical isomerism?
questions.solution:
$\ce{[Co(NH3)3Cl3]}$ is an octahedral complex of the type $\mathrm{Ma_3b_3}$, which exists only as the fac and mer geometrical isomers.

The fac isomer has three mirror planes, each containing Co, one Cl and the $\ce{NH3}$ trans to it; the mer isomer has a mirror plane containing Co, the three Cl and one $\ce{NH3}$. Both isomers are superimposable on their mirror images, so neither is optically active.

By contrast, cis-$\ce{[Co(en)2Cl2]^+}$, $\ce{[Co(en)3]^3+}$ and the isomer of $\ce{[Co(en)(NH3)2Cl2]^+}$ with both $\ce{NH3}$ cis and both Cl cis have no mirror plane and exist as pairs of enantiomers.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: An octahedral complex with molecular composition M.5NH 3 .Cl.SO 4 has two isomers, A and B. The solution of A gives a white precipitate with AgNO 3 solution and the solution of B gives white precipitate with BaCl 2 solution. The type of isomerism exhibited by the complex is :
questions.solution:
A gives a white precipitate of $\mathrm{AgCl}$ with $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$, so $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ is outside the coordination sphere: A is $\mathrm{[M(NH_3)_5SO_4]Cl}$.

B gives a white precipitate of $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$ with $\mathrm{BaCl_2}$, so $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ is outside: B is $\mathrm{[M(NH_3)_5Cl]SO_4}$.

The two have the same composition but exchange a ligand with the counter-ion, so they give different ions in solution.

So the complex shows ionisation isomerism.

The correct statement on the isomerism associated with the following complex
ions,

(a)    [Ni(H₂O) 5 NH 3 ] 2+ ,

(b)    [Ni(H₂O) 4
(NH 3 ) 2 ] 2+ and

(c)    [Ni(H₂O) 3
(NH 3 ) 3 ] 2+ is :

options.text: (a) and (b) show geometrical and optical isomerism
(b) and (c) show geometrical and optical isomerism

questions.solution:
(a) $\mathrm{[Ni(H_2O)_5(NH_3)]^{2+}}$ is octahedral $\mathrm{[MA_5B]}$: every position of $\mathrm{B}$ is equivalent, so it shows neither geometrical nor optical isomerism.

(b) $\mathrm{[Ni(H_2O)_4(NH_3)_2]^{2+}}$ is $\mathrm{[MA_4B_2]}$: it has cis and trans forms, i.e. geometrical isomerism.

(c) $\mathrm{[Ni(H_2O)_3(NH_3)_3]^{2+}}$ is $\mathrm{[MA_3B_3]}$: it has fac and mer forms, i.e. geometrical isomerism.

With only two kinds of monodentate ligands, every isomer of $\mathrm{[MA_4B_2]}$ and $\mathrm{[MA_3B_3]}$ has a mirror plane, so none is optically active.

So (b) and (c) show only geometrical isomerism.

questions.text:
Which one of the following complexes shows optical isomerism?

(en = ethylenediamine)
questions.solution:
A complex shows optical isomerism only when it has no mirror plane, so that it is non-superimposable on its mirror image.

In cis-$\ce{[Co(en)2Cl2]^+}$ the two en rings and the two mutually cis $\ce{Cl}$ ligands are arranged with no mirror plane, so the complex exists as a pair of enantiomers (d and l).

In trans-$\ce{[Co(en)2Cl2]^+}$ the two en rings lie in one plane between the two axial $\ce{Cl}$ ligands, and that plane is a mirror plane, so it is optically inactive.

$\ce{[Co(NH3)4Cl2]^+}$ (cis and trans) and $\ce{[Co(NH3)3Cl3]}$ (fac and mer) contain only monodentate ligands, and every one of these isomers has a mirror plane; the fac isomer, for example, has three, each containing the metal and one $\ce{Cl-Co-NH3}$ axis, so none of them is optically active.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
Consider the following reaction and statements:

[Co(NH 3 ) 4 Br 2 ] + + Br - $$\to$$ [Co(NH 3 ) 3 Br 3 ] + NH 3

(I) Two isomers are produced if the reactant complex ion is a cis-isomer

(II) Two isomers are produced if the reactant complex ion is a trans-isomer

(III) Only one isomer is produced if the reactant complex ion is a trans-isomer

(IV) Only one isomer is produced if the reactant complex ion is a cis – isomer

The correct statements are
questions.solution:
One $\ce{NH3}$ of $\ce{[Co(NH3)4Br2]+}$ is replaced by $\ce{Br-}$. With the octahedral positions numbered 1 (top), 6 (bottom) and 2, 3, 4, 5 around the equator (2 trans to 4, 3 trans to 5), the product $\ce{[Co(NH3)3Br3]}$ is fac when the three $\ce{Br}$ are mutually cis and mer when two of them are trans.

Cis reactant, $\ce{Br}$ at 1 and 2 and $\ce{NH3}$ at 3, 4, 5, 6: replacing the $\ce{NH3}$ at 3 or 5 puts $\ce{Br}$ at 1, 2, 3 or 1, 2, 5, the fac isomer; replacing the $\ce{NH3}$ at 4 (trans to 2) or 6 (trans to 1) puts $\ce{Br}$ at 1, 2, 4 or 1, 2, 6, the mer isomer. Two isomers form, so (I) is correct and (IV) is incorrect.

Trans reactant, $\ce{Br}$ at 1 and 6 and $\ce{NH3}$ at 2, 3, 4, 5: the four $\ce{NH3}$ are equivalent, and replacing any one keeps the trans pair 1, 6, which always gives the mer isomer. Only one isomer forms, so (III) is correct and (II) is incorrect.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: The total number of possible isomers for square-planar [Pt(Cl)(NO 2 )(NO 3 )(SCN)] 2- is :
questions.solution:
A square-planar $\ce{[Mabcd]}$ complex has three geometrical isomers, fixed by which ligand lies trans to $\ce{Cl-}$: $\ce{NO2-}$, $\ce{NO3-}$ or $\ce{SCN-}$.

$\ce{NO2-}$ is ambidentate (nitro, bonded through N, or nitrito, bonded through O) and $\ce{SCN-}$ is ambidentate (thiocyanato, through S, or isothiocyanato, through N), while $\ce{Cl-}$ and $\ce{NO3-}$ bind in one way only; the donor atoms of ($\ce{NO2-}$, $\ce{SCN-}$) can therefore be (N, S), (N, N), (O, S) or (O, N), which gives $2 \times 2 = 4$ linkage isomers.

Each linkage form can take each of the three geometrical arrangements, and a square-planar complex of achiral ligands has its molecular plane as a mirror plane, so there are no optical isomers.

$$\text{Total isomers} = 3 \times 4 = 12$$

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text:
The species that can have a trans-isomer is :

(en = ethane-1, 2-diamine, ox = oxalate)
questions.solution:
$\ce{[Pt(en)2Cl2]^2+}$ is an octahedral complex of the type $\ce{[M(AA)2B2]}$: each en spans two cis positions, and the two $\ce{Cl-}$ ions can be either adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans), so a trans isomer exists.

In $\ce{[Cr(en)2(ox)]+}$ the three chelate rings fill all six positions, each spanning cis positions, so no trans form is possible; the four-coordinate $\ce{[Pt(en)Cl2]}$ and $\ce{[Zn(en)Cl2]}$ have only one arrangement each, because en must span adjacent positions.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
The total number of isomers for a square planar complex
[M(F)(Cl)(SCN)(NO 2 )] is
questions.solution:
$\ce{[M(F)(Cl)(SCN)(NO2)]}$ is a square planar complex of the type $\ce{[Mabcd]}$, which has 3 geometrical isomers: with F fixed, the ligand trans to it can be Cl, SCN or $\ce{NO2}$.

Two of the ligands are ambidentate: thiocyanate binds through S ($\ce{M-SCN}$) or N ($\ce{M-NCS}$), and nitrite binds through N ($\ce{M-NO2}$) or O ($\ce{M-ONO}$), giving $2 \times 2 = 4$ linkage combinations.

Each linkage combination has 3 geometrical isomers, so the total number of isomers is $4 \times 3 = 12$.

The plane of a square planar complex is a plane of symmetry, so none of these isomers is optically active and no optical isomers are added.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.solution:
In $\ce{[Pt(en)(NO2)2]}$, Pt(II) is square planar. The bidentate en must span two cis positions, so the two nitrite ligands are always cis to each other and there are no geometrical isomers; the molecular plane is a mirror plane, so there are no optical isomers.

$\ce{NO2^-}$ is ambidentate and binds through N (nitro) or through O (nitrito), so the two nitrite ligands can be N,N; N,O; or O,O bonded, giving 3 linkage isomers.

questions.text:
Complex A has a composition of H 12 O₆Cl₃ Cr. If the complex on treatment with conc.H 2 SO 4
loses
13.5% of its original mass, the correct molecular formula of A is :

[Given: atomic mass of Cr = 52 amu and Cl = 35 amu]
questions.solution:
The formula $\ce{H12O6Cl3Cr}$ corresponds to $\ce{CrCl3.6H2O}$, with molar mass

$$M = 6(18) + 3(35) + 52 = 265\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$$

Concentrated $\ce{H2SO4}$ is a dehydrating agent: it removes only water of crystallisation held outside the coordination sphere, not water bonded to Cr and not chloride.

Mass lost per mole $= 0.135 \times 265 = 35.8\ \text{g} \approx 2 \times 18\ \text{g}$, so A contains 2 molecules of lattice water.

The other 4 $\ce{H2O}$ are coordinated to Cr; with coordination number 6, two $\ce{Cl-}$ complete the coordination sphere and the third $\ce{Cl-}$ is the counter ion, giving $\ce{[Cr(H2O)4Cl2]Cl.2H2O}$.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: The complex that can show optical activity is :
questions.solution:
An octahedral complex is optically active only when it has no mirror plane, so that it is non-superimposable on its mirror image.

In $\ce{[Fe(NH3)2(CN)4]^-}$ (type $\ce{MA2B4}$), both the cis and the trans isomers contain a mirror plane through the metal and both $\ce{NH3}$ ligands, so neither is optically active.

In trans-$\ce{[CrCl2(ox)2]^3-}$ the two oxalate rings lie in one plane with the two $\ce{Cl}$ ligands above and below it; that plane is a mirror plane, so the complex is optically inactive.

In cis-$\ce{[CrCl2(ox)2]^3-}$ (type $\ce{[M(AA)2B2]}$) the two chelate rings are arranged like the blades of a propeller and no mirror plane is present, so the complex exists as a pair of non-superimposable d and l forms.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
Complex X of composition Cr(H₂O) 6 Cl n
has a spin only magnetic moment of 3.83
BM. It reacts with AgNO 3 and shows
geometrical isomerism. The IUPAC
nomenclature of X is :
questions.solution:
The spin-only magnetic moment is $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}\ \text{BM}$, where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons. $\mu = 3.83$ BM gives $n = 3$, since $\sqrt{3 \times 5} = 3.87$ BM.

Three unpaired electrons means a $3d^{3}$ ion, i.e. $\ce{Cr^3+}$, so the compound contains three chloride ions: $\ce{CrCl3.6H2O}$.

Its hydrate isomers are $\ce{[Cr(H2O)6]Cl3}$, $\ce{[Cr(H2O)5Cl]Cl2.H2O}$, $\ce{[Cr(H2O)4Cl2]Cl.2H2O}$ and $\ce{[Cr(H2O)3Cl3].3H2O}$. A precipitate with $\ce{AgNO3}$ needs ionisable chloride, which rules out $\ce{[Cr(H2O)3Cl3].3H2O}$.

$\ce{[Cr(H2O)6]^3+}$ (type $\ce{MA6}$) and $\ce{[Cr(H2O)5Cl]^2+}$ (type $\ce{MA5B}$) show no geometrical isomerism, while $\ce{[Cr(H2O)4Cl2]+}$ (type $\ce{MA4B2}$) has cis and trans forms.

So X is $\ce{[Cr(H2O)4Cl2]Cl.2H2O}$. Ligands are named alphabetically (aqua before chlorido) and chromium is $+3$: tetraaquadichloridochromium(III) chloride dihydrate.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

the shape of this complex is tetrahedral this
structure is optically inactive due to the presence
of plane of symmetry.

(b) If the complex MA 2 B 2 is dsp 2 hybridised then
the shape of this complex is square planar.

Both isomers are optically inactive due to the

$$ \therefore $$ Total number of optical isomer is zero in both

questions.text: The number of optical isomers possible for [Cr(C₂O₄ ) 3 ] 3$$-$$ is ____________.
questions.solution:
$\ce{[Cr(C2O4)3]^3-}$ is an octahedral complex of the type $\ce{[M(AA)3]}$, in which each oxalate ion spans two cis positions.

With three identical chelate rings there is only one geometrical arrangement, but it has no plane or centre of symmetry, so its mirror image cannot be superimposed on it.

The complex therefore exists as one pair of enantiomers, the $\Delta$ and $\Lambda$ forms.

Hence, the answer is 2.

questions.text:
The number of geometrical isomers found in the metal
complexes [PtCl 2 (NH 3 ) 2 ], [Ni(CO) 4 ], [Ru(H₂O) 3 Cl 3 ] and [CoCl 2 (NH 3 ) 4 ] + respectively, are :
questions.solution:
$[\ce{PtCl2(NH3)2}]$ is square planar of type $\ce{MA2B2}$: cis and trans forms, so 2 geometrical isomers.

$[\ce{Ni(CO)4}]$ is tetrahedral with four identical ligands; all positions of a tetrahedron are adjacent to one another, so it shows no geometrical isomerism: 0.

$[\ce{Ru(H2O)3Cl3}]$ is octahedral of type $\ce{MA3B3}$: facial and meridional forms, so 2.

$[\ce{CoCl2(NH3)4}]^+$ is octahedral of type $\ce{MA4B2}$: cis and trans forms, so 2.

The numbers are 2, 0, 2, 2.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: The number of geometrical isomers possible in triamminetrinitrocobalt (III) is X and in trioxalatochromate (III) is Y. Then the value of X + Y is _______________.
questions.solution:
Triamminetrinitrocobalt(III) is $\ce{[Co(NH3)3(NO2)3]}$, an octahedral $\mathrm{Ma_3b_3}$ complex. The three $\ce{NO2-}$ groups can lie on one face (fac) or along one meridian (mer), so X = 2. Bonding of the ambidentate $\ce{NO2-}$ through N or O gives linkage isomers, not geometrical isomers.

Trioxalatochromate(III) is $\ce{[Cr(C2O4)3]^3-}$, an $\mathrm{M(AA)_3}$ complex. With three identical symmetrical bidentate ligands only one geometrical arrangement exists; the complex shows only optical isomerism (d and l forms), so Y = 0.

$$X + Y = 2 + 0 = 2$$

Hence, the answer is 2.

questions.text: The equivalents of ethylene diamine required to replace the neutral ligands from the coordination sphere of the trans-complex of CoCl 3 . 4NH 3 is _________. (Round off to the Nearest Integer).
questions.solution:
$\ce{CoCl3.4NH3}$ is $\ce{[Co(NH3)4Cl2]Cl}$; in the trans isomer the two Cl ligands are opposite each other and the four neutral ligands are $\ce{NH3}$.

Ethylenediamine ($\ce{H2N-CH2-CH2-NH2}$, en) is a neutral didentate ligand, so one en replaces two monodentate $\ce{NH3}$.

$$\ce{[Co(NH3)4Cl2]Cl + 2en -> [Co(en)2Cl2]Cl + 4NH3}$$

Replacing all four $\ce{NH3}$ therefore needs 2 equivalents of en.

Hence, the answer is 2.

questions.text: The number of stereoisomers possible for [Co(ox) 2 (Br)(NH 3 )] 2$$-$$ is ___________. [ox = oxalate]
questions.solution:
The coordination compound [Co(ox) 2 (Br)(NH 3 )] 2$$-$$
of general
formula [M(A - A) 2 BC]
can show both geometrical and optical
isomerism (stereoisomerism).

The cis-form produces non-superimposable mirror images, i.e.
enantiomeric pairs (optically active)

The trans-form is optically inactive.

So, total number of stereoisomers possible
= cis( $$ \pm $$ ) + trans = 3

questions.text: Total number of relatively more stable isomer(s) possible for octahedral complex $$\left[\mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{en})_{2}(\mathrm{SCN})_{2}\right]$$ will be _________.
questions.solution:
$\ce{Cu^2+}$ is $d^9$, so the octahedral complex undergoes Jahn-Teller elongation along one axis, giving two long, weak axial bonds.

The two monodentate thiocyanate ligands occupy these trans axial positions while the two en chelates span the equatorial plane, so the trans arrangement is the relatively more stable one and the cis forms are less stable.

Thiocyanate is ambidentate (S- or N-bonded), so the trans isomers are trans-$\ce{[Cu(en)2(SCN)2]}$, trans-$\ce{[Cu(en)2(NCS)2]}$ and trans-$\ce{[Cu(en)2(SCN)(NCS)]}$.

Hence, the answer is 3.

questions.text:
(a) CoCl 3 .4NH 3 ,    (b) CoCl 3 .5NH 3 ,      (c) CoCl 3 .6NH 3    and    (d) CoCl(NO 3 ) 2 .5NH 3 .

Number of complex(es) which will exist in cis-trans form is/are _______________.
questions.solution:
(a) $\ce{CoCl3.4NH3}$ is $\ce{[Co(NH3)4Cl2]Cl}$, an octahedral $\ce{MA4B2}$ complex: the two $\ce{Cl-}$ ligands can be adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans), so it exists in cis-trans forms.

(b) $\ce{CoCl3.5NH3}$ is $\ce{[Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2}$, an $\ce{MA5B}$ complex with only one arrangement.

(c) $\ce{CoCl3.6NH3}$ is $\ce{[Co(NH3)6]Cl3}$, an $\ce{MA6}$ complex with no geometrical isomers.

(d) $\ce{CoCl(NO3)2.5NH3}$ is $\ce{[Co(NH3)5Cl](NO3)2}$ (or its ionisation isomer $\ce{[Co(NH3)5(NO3)]Cl(NO3)}$); either way the complex ion is $\ce{MA5B}$ and has no cis-trans forms.

Only complex (a) exists in cis-trans form.

Hence, the answer is 1.

questions.text: Mn 2 (CO) 10 is an organometallic compound due to the presence of -
questions.solution:
An organometallic compound is one that contains at least one metal–carbon bond.

In $\ce{Mn2(CO)10}$ each carbonyl ligand is bonded to manganese through its carbon atom, so the compound contains Mn–C bonds. The C–O and Mn–Mn bonds do not involve a metal–carbon link, and the compound has no Mn–O bond.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The number of bridging CO ligand(s) and Co-Co bond(s) in Co 2 (CO) 8 , respectively are :
questions.solution:
In the solid state, $\ce{Co2(CO)8}$ has two Co atoms joined by one Co–Co bond and bridged by two CO groups; each Co also carries three terminal CO groups ($2 + 3 + 3 = 8$ CO).

Each Co has 9 valence electrons and gains 6 from its three terminal CO, 1 from each of the two bridging CO and 1 from the Co–Co bond: $9 + 6 + 2 + 1 = 18$.

So $\ce{Co2(CO)8}$ has 2 bridging CO ligands and 1 Co–Co bond.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The potassium ferrocyanide solution gives a Prussian blue colour, when added to :
questions.solution:
Potassium ferrocyanide supplies the hexacyanidoferrate(II) ion, $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^4-}$. With $\ce{Fe^3+}$ ions it forms insoluble iron(III) hexacyanidoferrate(II), Prussian blue, in which $\ce{Fe^3+}$ takes the place of $\ce{K+}$ as the outer cation:

$$\ce{4FeCl3 + 3K4[Fe(CN)6] -> Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3 + 12KCl}$$

With $\ce{Fe^2+}$ (from $\ce{FeCl2}$) only a white precipitate of $\ce{K2Fe[Fe(CN)6]}$ forms, and cobalt salts give no blue colour.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Number of complexes which will exhibit synergic bonding amongst, $$[Cr{(CO)_6}]$$, $$[Mn{(CO)_5}]$$ and $$[M{n_2}{(CO)_{10}}]$$ is ___________.
questions.solution:
Synergic bonding in a metal carbonyl is $\sigma$ donation from the lone pair on the carbon of CO into a vacant metal orbital together with $\pi$ back donation from a filled metal d orbital into the vacant $\pi^*$ orbital of CO; each bond strengthens the other.

$\ce{[Cr(CO)6]}$, $\ce{[Mn(CO)5]}$ and $\ce{[Mn2(CO)10]}$ all contain metal-CO bonds with the metal in the zero oxidation state, so each metal has filled d orbitals for back donation and each complex shows synergic bonding.

Hence, the answer is 3.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is incorrect?

On passing H$$_2$$S into Na$$_2$$ZnO$$_2$$ solution a white ppt of ZnS is formed.

questions.solution:

$\mathrm{H_2S}$ passed into sodium zincate solution gives a white precipitate of $\mathrm{ZnS}$ (true).

questions.text: Sodium Carbonate cannot be used in place of $$(NH_4)_2CO_3$$ for the identification of $$Ca^{2+}$$, $$Ba^{2+}$$ and $$Sr^{2+}$$ ions (in group V) during mixture analysis because :

options.text: Concentration of $$CO_3^{2-}$$ ions is very low.
Sodium ions will react with acid radicals.
$$Na^+$$ ions will interfere with the detection of $$Ca^{2+}$$, $$Ba^{2+}$$, $$Sr^{2+}$$ ions.

questions.solution:
Group V is precipitated with $\mathrm{(NH_4)_2CO_3}$ in the presence of $\mathrm{NH_4Cl}$ and $\mathrm{NH_4OH}$.

The common ion $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ suppresses carbonate ion concentration just enough to exceed $K_{sp}$ of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$, $\mathrm{BaCO_3}$, $\mathrm{SrCO_3}$ but not of $\mathrm{MgCO_3}$.

$\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ is a strong electrolyte giving a high $[\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}}]$, so $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ (group VI) would also precipitate.

Answer: $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ ions would also be precipitated.

questions.text: An aqueous solution of a salt X turns blood red on treatment with SCN $$-$$ and blue on treatment with K 4 [Fe(CN) 6 ]. X also gives a positive chromyl chloride test. The salt X is :
questions.solution:
The blood-red colour with $\mathrm{SCN^-}$ is due to $\mathrm{[Fe(SCN)]^{2+}}$, so $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ is present.

The blue colour (Prussian blue) with $\mathrm{K_4[Fe(CN)_6]}$, $\mathrm{4Fe^{3+} + 3[Fe(CN)_6]^{4-} \to Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3}$, confirms $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$.

A positive chromyl chloride test (orange-red $\mathrm{CrO_2Cl_2}$ vapours on heating with $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}$ and conc. $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$) shows that the anion is $\mathrm{Cl^-}$.

So the salt X is $\mathrm{FeCl_3}$.

questions.text: The cation that will not be precipitated by H₂S in the presence of dil HCl is :
questions.solution:
In dil. $\mathrm{HCl}$, the common ion $\mathrm{H^+}$ suppresses the ionisation of $\mathrm{H_2S}$, so $[\mathrm{S^{2-}}]$ is very low.

Only sulphides with very low $K_{sp}$ (group II cations such as $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{As^{3+}}$) precipitate, as $\mathrm{CuS}$, $\mathrm{PbS}$ and $\mathrm{As_2S_3}$.

$\mathrm{CoS}$ has a much higher $K_{sp}$; $\mathrm{Co^{2+}}$ is a group IV cation, precipitated by $\mathrm{H_2S}$ only in ammoniacal medium.

So $\mathrm{Co^{2+}}$ is not precipitated by $\mathrm{H_2S}$ in dil. $\mathrm{HCl}$.

questions.text: A solution containing a group-IV cation gives a precipitate on passing H₂S. A solution of this precipitate in dil.HCl produces a white precipitate with NaOH solution and bluish-white precipitate with basic potassium ferrocyanide. The cation is :

Cu 2+ and Ni 2+ ions give black precipitate with H₂S in presence of HCl solution.
Ferric ion gives blood red color with potassium thiocyanate.
Cu 2+ ion gives chocolate coloured precipitate with potassium ferrocyanide solution.

Cu 2+ and Ni 2+ ions belong to Group II and Group IV respectively.

Group II sulphides precipitated out even under low concentration of sulphides, while Group IV sulphides require higher concentration of sulphides. To fulfill this reaction condition, dil. HCl is chosen in Group II reagents and NH 4 OH is chosen in Group IV reagents.

questions.text: Acidic ferric chloride solution on treatment with excess of potassium ferrocyanide gives a Prussian blue coloured colloidal species. It is :
questions.solution:
Prussian blue is iron(III) hexacyanidoferrate(II), formed when $\ce{Fe^3+}$ ions meet $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^4-}$ ions.

With excess potassium ferrocyanide, each $\ce{Fe^3+}$ combines with one $\ce{[Fe(CN)6]^4-}$, and the remaining charge is balanced by $\ce{K+}$:

$$\ce{Fe^3+ + K4[Fe(CN)6] -> KFe[Fe(CN)6] + 3K+}$$

$\ce{KFe[Fe(CN)6]}$ is the soluble form of Prussian blue and remains as a colloidal dispersion; the insoluble $\ce{Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3}$ precipitates only when $\ce{Fe^3+}$ is in excess.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text:
To an aqueous solution containing ions such as Al 3+ , Zn 2+ , Ca 2+ , Fe 3+ , Ni 2+ , Ba 2+ and Cu 2+ was added conc. HCl, followed by H₂S.

The total number of cations precipitated during this reaction is/are :
questions.solution:
In conc. HCl the high $[\ce{H+}]$ suppresses the ionisation of $\ce{H2S}$ (common-ion effect), so $[\ce{S^2-}]$ is very low and only sulphides of extremely low $K_{sp}$ (group II) are precipitated.

$\ce{Cu^2+}$ forms black $\ce{CuS}$ ($K_{sp} \approx 10^{-36}$), which precipitates even from strongly acidic solution.

$\ce{Zn^2+}$ and $\ce{Ni^2+}$ need the much higher $[\ce{S^2-}]$ of ammoniacal medium (group IV) to precipitate as $\ce{ZnS}$ and $\ce{NiS}$.

$\ce{Fe^3+}$ is only reduced by $\ce{H2S}$ to $\ce{Fe^2+}$ (with separation of sulphur), and $\ce{FeS}$ does not form in acid; $\ce{Al^3+}$ is precipitated only as $\ce{Al(OH)3}$ in group III; $\ce{Ca^2+}$ and $\ce{Ba^2+}$ give no sulphide precipitate.

So only one cation, $\ce{Cu^2+}$, is precipitated.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: Cu 2+ salt reacts with potassium iodide to give
questions.solution:
Iodide ion is oxidised by $\ce{Cu^2+}$ to iodine, while copper(II) is reduced to copper(I), which precipitates as white copper(I) iodide:

$$\ce{2Cu^2+ + 4I- -> Cu2I2 + I2}$$

With a copper(II) salt such as copper sulphate and potassium iodide:

$$\ce{2CuSO4 + 4KI -> Cu2I2 + 2K2SO4 + I2}$$

Copper(I) iodide is written as $\ce{Cu2I2}$, as in these equations, or by its empirical formula $\ce{CuI}$; both formulas stand for the same compound, the product of the reaction. Hence option (A), $\ce{Cu2I2}$, and option (C), $\ce{CuI}$, are both correct.

$\ce{Cu2I3}$ (with copper in a non-integral oxidation state of $+1.5$) and $\ce{Cu(I3)2}$ are not formed in this reaction.

Hence, the correct options are (A) and (C).

questions.text:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I : The identification of Ni 2+ is carried out by dimethyl glyoxime in the presence of NH 4 OH.

Statement II : The dimethyl glyoxime is a bidentate neutral ligand.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :

options.text: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.solution:
Statement I is true. Dimethyl glyoxime (DMG) is a chelating reagent commonly used for the identification of Ni 2+ ions in aqueous solution. In the presence of ammonium hydroxide (NH 4 OH), Ni 2+ reacts with dimethyl glyoxime to form a deep red-colored complex, which can be used to confirm the presence of Ni 2+ ions.

Statement II is also true. Dimethyl glyoxime is a neutral bidentate ligand, which means it has two donor atoms that can coordinate with a metal ion, and its overall charge is neutral.

questions.text: A pink coloured salt turns blue on heating. The presence of which cation is most likely ?
questions.solution:
Hydrated cobalt(II) salts such as $\mathrm{CoCl_2\cdot6H_2O}$ are pink because of octahedral $\mathrm{[Co(H_2O)_6]^{2+}}$.

On heating they lose water and give blue anhydrous $\mathrm{CoCl_2}$: $\mathrm{CoCl_2\cdot6H_2O \xrightarrow{\Delta} CoCl_2 + 6H_2O}$.

Hydrated $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ salts are blue and turn white on heating, $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ salts are pale green and $\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}$ salts are colourless.

So the cation present is most likely $\mathrm{Co^{2+}}$.

flame.

In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options

questions.text: Which of the following cannot be represented by resonance structures?
questions.solution:
Resonance needs $\pi$ electrons or lone pairs that can delocalise through adjacent $p$ orbitals.

$\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ has three equivalent structures, with the $\mathrm{N{=}O}$ double bond on each oxygen in turn.

$\mathrm{RCOO^-}$ has two equivalent structures that share the negative charge between the two oxygens.

Toluene has the Kekulé structures of its benzene ring.

In $\mathrm{CH_3{-}O{-}CH_3}$ every bond is a $\sigma$ bond, and the lone pairs on oxygen have no adjacent $\pi$ system to delocalise into.

So dimethyl ether cannot be represented by resonance structures.

questions.text: Which one of the following compounds will not be soluble in sodium bicarbonate ?
questions.solution:
A compound dissolves in $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$ (with evolution of $\mathrm{CO_2}$) only if it is a stronger acid than $\mathrm{H_2CO_3}$ ($\mathrm{p}K_a\approx6.4$).

Benzenesulphonic acid ($\mathrm{p}K_a\lt0$), picric acid ($\mathrm{p}K_a\approx0.4$, three $-\mathrm{NO_2}$ groups) and benzoic acid ($\mathrm{p}K_a\approx4.2$) are stronger, so they dissolve.

o-Nitrophenol has only one $-\mathrm{NO_2}$ group and its $\mathrm{OH}$ is held by intramolecular hydrogen bonding; $\mathrm{p}K_a\approx7.2$, weaker than $\mathrm{H_2CO_3}$.

So o-nitrophenol is not soluble in sodium bicarbonate.

questions.text: Which types of isomerism is shown by 2,3-dichlorobutane?
questions.solution:
2,3-Dichlorobutane, $\ce{CH3-CHCl-CHCl-CH3}$, has two chiral carbon atoms bearing identical sets of groups, so it exists as three stereoisomers: the optically active enantiomers (2R,3R) and (2S,3S), and the optically inactive meso form (2R,3S), which has a plane of symmetry.

The existence of the enantiomeric pair means the compound shows optical isomerism; the meso form is only one of its optical isomers, and with no $\ce{C=C}$ bond or ring there is no geometrical isomerism.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: Maleic acid and fumaric acids are
questions.solution:
Both are butenedioic acid, $\mathrm{HOOC-CH=CH-COOH}$, with the same atoms joined in the same order.

In maleic acid the two –COOH groups are on the same side of the C=C bond (cis); in fumaric acid they are on opposite sides (trans).

Rotation about the C=C bond is restricted, so the two forms are separate, stable compounds.

Hence they are geometrical (cis–trans) isomers.

questions.text: How many cyclic structures are possible for $$\mathrm{C_4H_6}$$?
questions.solution:
Degree of unsaturation of $\mathrm{C_4H_6}$ $= \dfrac{2\times4 + 2 - 6}{2} = 2$.

A cyclic structure therefore has one ring and one double bond, or two rings.

One ring and one double bond: cyclobutene, 1-methylcyclopropene, 3-methylcyclopropene and methylenecyclopropane.

Two rings: bicyclo[1.1.0]butane.

So $5$ cyclic structures are possible.

questions.text: How many chiral compounds are possible on monochlorination of 2–methyl butane ?
questions.solution:
Monochlorination of 2-methylbutane, $\ce{(CH3)2CHCH2CH3}$, gives four structural isomers.

In $\ce{ClCH2CH(CH3)CH2CH3}$ (1-chloro-2-methylbutane), C-2 carries H, $\ce{CH3}$, $\ce{CH2Cl}$ and $\ce{C2H5}$, so it is chiral.

In $\ce{(CH3)2CClCH2CH3}$ (2-chloro-2-methylbutane), C-2 carries two $\ce{CH3}$ groups, so it is achiral.

In $\ce{(CH3)2CHCHClCH3}$ (2-chloro-3-methylbutane), C-2 carries H, Cl, $\ce{CH3}$ and $\ce{CH(CH3)2}$, so it is chiral.

In $\ce{(CH3)2CHCH2CH2Cl}$ (1-chloro-3-methylbutane), no carbon carries four different groups, so it is achiral.

Each chiral isomer forms as a pair of enantiomers ($R$ and $S$), giving $2 \times 2 = 4$ chiral compounds.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: Monocarboxylic acids are functional isomers of:
questions.solution:

A monocarboxylic acid $\mathrm{C_nH_{2n}O_2}$ has the same formula as an ester, e.g. $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$ and $\mathrm{HCOOCH_3}$ are both $\mathrm{C_2H_4O_2}$.

Ethers, amines and alcohols have different molecular formulae.

Monocarboxylic acids are functional isomers of esters.

questions.text: Which one of the following acids does not exhibit optical isomerism ?
questions.solution:
Optical isomerism requires a chiral molecule, usually one with an asymmetric carbon.

Lactic acid $\mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)COOH}$ has one chiral carbon, tartaric acid $\mathrm{HOOC{-}CH(OH){-}CH(OH){-}COOH}$ has two, and $\alpha$-amino acids $\mathrm{RCH(NH_2)COOH}$ (except glycine) have one.

Maleic acid, cis-$\mathrm{HOOC{-}CH{=}CH{-}COOH}$, is planar with no chiral carbon, so it shows only geometrical isomerism.

So maleic acid does not exhibit optical isomerism.

questions.text: The number of structural isomers for C₆H 14 is :
questions.solution:
Six-carbon chain: hexane ($1$).

Five-carbon chain with one methyl: 2-methylpentane and 3-methylpentane ($2$).

Four-carbon chain with two methyls: 2,2-dimethylbutane and 2,3-dimethylbutane ($2$).

Total $= 1 + 2 + 2 = 5$.

So $\mathrm{C_6H_{14}}$ has $5$ structural isomers.

questions.text: The optically inactive compound from the following is :
questions.solution:
A compound is optically active if it has a chiral carbon (four different groups) and no plane of symmetry.

2-Chloropropanal, $\mathrm{CH_3CH(Cl)CHO}$: C-2 carries $\mathrm{H, Cl, CH_3, CHO}$, so it is chiral.

2-Chloropentane, $\mathrm{CH_3CH(Cl)CH_2CH_2CH_3}$, and 2-chlorobutane, $\mathrm{CH_3CH(Cl)CH_2CH_3}$: C-2 carries $\mathrm{H, Cl, CH_3}$ and a larger alkyl group, so both are chiral.

2-Chloro-2-methylbutane, $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C(Cl)CH_2CH_3}$: C-2 carries two identical $\mathrm{CH_3}$ groups, so it has no chiral centre.

So 2-chloro-2-methylbutane is the optically inactive compound.

questions.text:
Which of the following compounds will show
the maximum 'enol' content?
questions.solution:
Enol content is high when the $\ce{CH2}$ group lies between two carbonyl groups, so that the enol is stabilised by conjugation and by an intramolecular hydrogen bond.

(
A) Acetone has only one carbonyl group, so its enol content is negligible.

(
B) The enol of acetylacetone, $\ce{CH3C(OH)=CHCOCH3}$, has its C=C conjugated with the second C=O and forms a six-membered intramolecular O–H···O=C hydrogen bond, so the enol form predominates (about 80%).

(
C) and (
D) In the ester and the amide, the lone pair of $\ce{-OC2H5}$ or $\ce{-NH2}$ is already delocalised into its own C=O (cross-conjugation), which makes that C=O a poorer partner for the enol's conjugation and hydrogen bond, so the enol content is much lower (ethyl acetoacetate about 8%, the amide less still).

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: The number of stereoisomers possible for 1, 2-dimethyl cyclopropane is :
questions.solution:
In 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane, C1 and C2 are stereocentres: each carries $\ce{H}$, $\ce{CH3}$ and two different ring paths.

In the cis isomer both methyl groups lie on the same face of the ring; a plane of symmetry passes through C3 and the midpoint of the C1–C2 bond, so it is an achiral meso compound: 1 stereoisomer.

In the trans isomer the methyl groups lie on opposite faces; it has no plane or centre of symmetry (only a $C_2$ axis, which does not make a molecule achiral), so it exists as a pair of enantiomers: 2 stereoisomers.

Total number of stereoisomers $= 1 + 2 = 3$.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The number of acyclic structural isomers (including geometrical isomers) for pentene are ___________
questions.solution:
Acyclic isomers of pentene are the alkenes of formula $\ce{C5H10}$, with a straight or branched five-carbon skeleton.

Straight chain: pent-1-ene, $\ce{CH2=CH-CH2-CH2-CH3}$, has no geometrical isomers; pent-2-ene, $\ce{CH3-CH=CH-CH2-CH3}$, exists as cis and trans forms. This gives 3 isomers.

Branched chain: 2-methylbut-1-ene, $\ce{CH2=C(CH3)-CH2-CH3}$; 3-methylbut-1-ene, $\ce{CH2=CH-CH(CH3)-CH3}$; 2-methylbut-2-ene, $\ce{(CH3)2C=CH-CH3}$. None shows geometrical isomerism, because in each one doubly bonded carbon carries two identical groups. This gives 3 isomers.

The neopentane skeleton has no carbon that can form a C=C with a neighbour, so it adds none.

Total $= 3 + 3 = 6$.

Hence, the answer is 6.

questions.text: The number of isomeric compounds (structural isomers only) possible with the molecular formula $\mathrm{C_5H_{10}O_2}$, which do not react with metallic sodium is ________.
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{C_5H_{10}O_2}$ (one degree of unsaturation): carboxylic acids react with Na (acidic H), esters $\mathrm{RCOOR'}$ have no acidic H and do not.

Formates $\mathrm{HCOOC_4H_9}$: n-butyl, isobutyl, sec-butyl, tert-butyl = 4.

Acetates $\mathrm{CH_3COOC_3H_7}$: n-propyl, isopropyl = 2.

questions.text: Total number of isomers (including stereoisomers) obtained on monochlorination of methylcyclohexane is ___________.
questions.solution:
Methylcyclohexane has five kinds of hydrogen (on the $\ce{CH3}$ group and on ring carbons C1, C2, C3 and C4), so monochlorination gives five structural isomers.

(Chloromethyl)cyclohexane: no stereocentre: 1.

1-Chloro-1-methylcyclohexane: C1 carries two identical ring paths, so there is no stereocentre: 1.

1-Chloro-2-methylcyclohexane: C1 and C2 are both stereocentres and neither isomer has a plane of symmetry, so cis and trans each exist as a pair of enantiomers: 4.

1-Chloro-3-methylcyclohexane: C1 and C3 are both stereocentres (the two ring paths from each are unequal) and neither isomer has a plane of symmetry, so cis and trans each exist as a pair of enantiomers: 4.

1-Chloro-4-methylcyclohexane: a plane through C1, C4, Cl and $\ce{CH3}$ makes both isomers achiral, so only cis and trans exist: 2.

Total number of isomers $= 1 + 1 + 4 + 4 + 2 = 12$.

Hence, the answer is 12.

questions.text: Total number of possible stereoisomers of dimethyl cyclopentane is ____________.
questions.solution:
The positional isomers are 1,1-, 1,2- and 1,3-dimethylcyclopentane.

1,1-Dimethylcyclopentane has no stereocentre and no cis–trans relationship, so it has no stereoisomers.

1,2-Dimethylcyclopentane has two stereocentres: the cis form has a plane of symmetry and is meso, and the trans form is chiral and exists as the enantiomers $(1R,2R)$ and $(1S,2S)$, giving 3 stereoisomers.

1,3-Dimethylcyclopentane likewise gives a meso cis form and the trans enantiomers $(1R,3R)$ and $(1S,3S)$, giving 3 stereoisomers.

Total number of stereoisomers $= 3 + 3 = 6$.

Hence, the answer is 6.

questions.text: The distillation technique most suited for separating glycerol from spent-lye in the soap industry is :
questions.solution:
The best technique for separating glycerol from spent-lye in the soap industry is Distillation under Reduced Pressure, also known as Vacuum Distillation (Option D).

The reason for this is that glycerol has a high boiling point (~$${290^ \circ }$$$$C$$). If we were to use simple or fractional distillation, which involves boiling at standard atmospheric pressure, the high temperature could degrade or decompose the glycerol.

In contrast, vacuum distillation allows the separation to occur at a much lower temperature ( around $${180^ \circ }C$$) by reducing the pressure. This helps to prevent degradation of the glycerol, making it a better method for this particular separation. Steam distillation isn't suitable here, as it's typically used for temperature-sensitive, volatile substances, which isn't the case for glycerol.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is not true about partition chromatography?

options.text: Mobile phase can be a gas
Stationary phase is a finely divided solid adsorbent
Separation depends upon equilibration of solute between a mobile and a stationary phase
Paper chromatography is an example of partition chromatography

questions.solution:
In partition chromatography, which includes paper chromatography, the stationary phase is typically water held by cellulose fibers in the paper. This paper acts as an inert support. When a mixture is applied to the paper, its components partition between this stationary phase and the mobile phase (which can be a liquid or a gas). The varying affinities of the mixture's components for the stationary and mobile phases allow for their separation.

Now, let's address the options :

Option
A: Mobile phase can be a gas - This is true. In partition chromatography, the mobile phase can be either a liquid or a gas.

Option
B: Stationary phase is a finely divided solid adsorbent - This is typically false for partition chromatography. Here, the stationary phase is a liquid (like water in paper chromatography) that's held by an inert solid support (like cellulose paper).

Option
C: Separation depends upon equilibration of solute between a mobile and a stationary phase - This is true. In partition chromatography, the mixture's components equilibrate between the mobile and stationary phases, leading to their separation.

Option
D: Paper chromatography is an example of partition chromatography - This is true. As explained above, in paper chromatography, the stationary phase (water) is held by an inert support (cellulose paper), fitting the definition of partition chromatography.

questions.text: In chromatography, which of the following statements is incorrect for R f ?

options.text: R f value depends on the type of chromatography.

Higher R f
value means higher adsorption.

R f
value is dependent on the mobile phase.

The value of R f

questions.solution:
R f = $${x \over y}$$

$$x$$ = Distance moved by the substance from baseline

$$y$$ = Distance moved by the solvent from baseline

Option
A: Correct. The R f value can depend on the type of chromatography being used because different methods can use different stationary and mobile phases, which can influence how far a substance travels.

Option
B: Incorrect. The R f value is actually inversely related to adsorption. A higher Rf value indicates that the substance is less strongly adsorbed to the stationary phase, and therefore moves further along with the mobile phase.

Option
C: Correct. The nature of the mobile phase can greatly influence the R f value. The more compatible the substance is with the mobile phase, the further it will travel, leading to a higher Rf value.

Option
D: Correct. By definition, the R f value cannot exceed one, as a substance cannot travel further than the solvent.

So, Option B is incorrect for the R f value in chromatography.

questions.text: The principle of column chromatography is :

options.text: Differential adsorption of the substances on the solid phase.
Differential absorption of the substances on the solid phase.

questions.solution:
The principle of column chromatography is based on the differential adsorption of substances on the solid phase. This means that different substances in a mixture will interact with the solid stationary phase to different extents. Some substances will adsorb more strongly to the solid phase and will therefore move more slowly through the column, while others will adsorb less strongly and will therefore move more quickly. This differential adsorption allows for the separation of the substances in the mixture.

So, the correct answer is :

Option C : Differential adsorption of the substances on the solid phase.

questions.text:
A chromatography column, packed with silica gel as stationary phase, was used to separate a
mixture of compounds consisting of (
A) benzanilide (
B) aniline and (
C) acetophenone. When the
column is eluted with a mixture of solvents, hexane : ethyl acetate (20:80), the sequence of
obtained compounds is :
questions.solution:
Silica gel is a polar adsorbent with acidic $\ce{Si-OH}$ groups; a compound is held back in proportion to how strongly it adsorbs by hydrogen bonding and dipolar interaction, and the least strongly adsorbed compound leaves the column first.

Acetophenone, $\ce{C6H5COCH3}$, has no $\ce{N-H}$ bond and only accepts hydrogen bonds through its carbonyl oxygen, so it is held least and elutes first.

Benzanilide, $\ce{C6H5CONHC6H5}$, has a single $\ce{N-H}$ flanked by two phenyl rings, and its nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the carbonyl group, so it is held moderately.

Aniline, $\ce{C6H5NH2}$, has two $\ce{N-H}$ bonds and a basic nitrogen lone pair that binds to the acidic silanol groups, so it is held most and elutes last.

Order of elution: acetophenone, benzanilide, aniline, that is (C), (A), (B).

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: In chromotography technique, the purification of compound is independent of :

options.text: Mobility or flow of solvent system
Physical state of the pure compound
Length of the column or TLC plate

questions.solution:
The purification of a compound using chromatography is dependent on several factors, including the solubility of the compound, the mobility or flow of the solvent system, and the length of the column or TLC plate. However, it is not typically dependent on the physical state of the pure compound. Here's why :

Option
A: The solubility of the compound in the mobile phase and its interaction with the stationary phase are key factors in determining how the compound will migrate in a chromatographic system. Hence, the solubility of the compound does affect its purification.

Option
B: The mobility or flow of the solvent system, often referred to as the mobile phase in chromatography, also plays a significant role in the separation of components in the mixture. The rate at which the mobile phase moves can influence how far and how quickly the components of the mixture will travel.

Option
C: The physical state (solid, liquid, gas) of the pure compound is usually not a factor in the purification process in chromatography. Whether a compound is solid, liquid, or gas does not typically affect its ability to be separated by chromatography, as it is the interactions between the compound and the stationary/mobile phases that are key.

Option
D: The length of the column or TLC plate can impact the degree of separation achieved in chromatography. A longer column or TLC plate can provide more opportunities for the interactions that drive the separation process, often leading to better separation of the components.

So, Option C is correct : The physical state of the pure compound is usually not a factor in its purification by chromatography.

questions.text: The major product obtained in the photobromination of 2-methyl butane is
questions.solution:
Free-radical bromination is highly selective: the bromine atom abstracts the hydrogen that gives the most stable radical.

2-Methylbutane, $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH{-}CH_2CH_3}$, has one tertiary hydrogen, at C-2.

The tertiary radical $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2\dot{C}{-}CH_2CH_3}$ is the most stable, so it forms almost exclusively and then takes up Br.

The major product is 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CBr{-}CH_2CH_3}$.

questions.text: The major product obtained in the photo catalysed bromination of 2-methylbutane is :
questions.solution:
Photochemical bromination is a free-radical substitution, and $\mathrm{Br^\bullet}$ is highly selective: it removes the H that gives the most stable radical.

2-Methylbutane, $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CHCH_2CH_3}$, has one tertiary H, on C-2.

Its removal gives the $3^\circ$ radical $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2\dot{C}CH_2CH_3}$, which then takes Br from $\mathrm{Br_2}$.

Relative reactivity of $3^\circ : 2^\circ : 1^\circ$ H towards $\mathrm{Br^\bullet}$ is about $1600 : 82 : 1$, so the tertiary bromide dominates.

So the major product is 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, $\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CBrCH_2CH_3}$.

questions.text: 5 L of an alkane requires 25 L of oxygen for its complete combustion. If all volumes are measured at constant temperature and pressure, the alkane is :
questions.solution:
We know, combustion of Hydrocarbon

C x H y + (x + $${y \over 4}$$)O 2  $$ \to $$  x CO 2 + $${y \over 2}$$ H₂O

So, to consume 1 mole of C x H y we need

(x + $${y \over 4}$$) mole of O 2 gas.

As both C x H y and O 2 are gas,

So avogadro's law is applicable on them.

At constant temperature and pressure according to avogadro's law, volume $$ \propto $$ mole

So, for 5L of C x H y the

volume of O 2 = 5(x + $${y \over 4}$$)

According to the question,

5(x + $${y \over 4}$$) = 25

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ (x + $${y \over 4}$$) = 5 . . . . . (1)

For Ethane (C₂H₆ ), x = 2 and y = 6

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ x + $${y \over 4}$$ = 2 + $${6 \over 4}$$ $$ \ne $$ 5

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ C₂H₆ can't be the required alkane.

For Propane (C₃H₈ ), x = 3. and y = 8

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ x + $${y \over 4}$$ = 3 + $${8 \over 4}$$ = 5

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ Propane (C₃H₈ ) is the right alkane.

Similarly for Butane (C₄H 10 ) and Isobutane (C₄H 10 ) you can check

x + $${y \over 4}$$ $$ \ne $$ 5.

questions.text: The addition of HI in the presence of peroxide catalyst does not follow anti-Markovnikov's rule because :

options.text: HI is a strong reducing agent.
H-I bond is too strong to be broken homolytically.
I atom combines with H atom to give back HI.
Iodine atom is not reactive enough to add across a double bond.

questions.solution:
The anti-Markovnikov (peroxide) addition needs the halogen radical to add to the alkene.

The H–I bond is weak, so iodine radicals form easily; bond strength is not the problem.

But the iodine atom is large and not reactive enough to attack the double bond; addition would be endothermic.

Iodine atoms instead combine to give $\mathrm{I_2}$, so the radical chain does not run and ionic Markovnikov addition occurs.

Answer: the iodine atom is not reactive enough to add across a double bond.

questions.text: In the presence of peroxide, HCl and HI do not give anti-Markownikoff's addition to alkenes because :

options.text: One of the steps is endothermic in HCl and HI
Both HCl and HI are strong acids
HCl is oxidizing and the HI is reducing
All the steps are exothermic in HCl and HI

questions.solution:
Peroxide (Kharasch) addition is a free-radical chain: $\mathrm{X^\bullet}$ adds to the alkene, then the carbon radical abstracts H from $\mathrm{HX}$.

For $\mathrm{HBr}$ both propagation steps are exothermic, so the chain continues.

For $\mathrm{HCl}$ the H–Cl bond ($431\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$) is too strong, so H-abstraction by the carbon radical is endothermic.

For $\mathrm{HI}$ the H–I bond is weak, but addition of $\mathrm{I^\bullet}$ to the C=C bond is endothermic, and the iodine atoms simply combine to $\mathrm{I_2}$.

So HCl and HI give no anti-Markovnikov addition because one of the chain steps is endothermic for them.

questions.text: The stereoisomers that are formed by electrophilic addition of bromine to trans-but-2-ene is/are :

Bromine adds to an alkene through a cyclic bromonium ion, which $\ce{Br-}$ opens from the opposite face, so the two Br atoms add anti.

Anti addition to trans-but-2-ene gives (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane, which has a plane of symmetry and is the meso compound.

Attack of $\ce{Br-}$ at either carbon of the bromonium ion, and bromonium formation on either face of the alkene, lead to this same meso compound; no enantiomers are formed. The products are therefore two identical meso forms.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: The hydrocarbon which can react with sodium in liquid ammonia is

options.text: CH 3 CH 2 CH 2 C≡CCH 2 CH 2 CH 3

questions.solution:
Sodium in liquid ammonia reduces an internal alkyne to the trans-alkene, and it converts a terminal alkyne, whose $\equiv$C–H hydrogen is acidic, into the sodium alkynide.

(
A) Oct-4-yne, $\ce{CH3CH2CH2C#CCH2CH2CH3}$, is reduced by sodium in liquid ammonia to trans-oct-4-ene, $\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH=CHCH2CH2CH3}$.

(
B) But-1-yne is a terminal alkyne; its acidic $\equiv$C–H reacts with sodium to form sodium but-1-ynide with evolution of hydrogen:

$$\ce{2CH3CH2C#CH + 2Na -> 2CH3CH2C#CNa + H2}$$

(
D) Hex-3-yne, $\ce{CH3CH2C#CCH2CH3}$, is reduced in the same way as oct-4-yne to trans-hex-3-ene, $\ce{CH3CH2CH=CHCH2CH3}$.

(
C) But-2-ene has neither an acidic hydrogen nor a C$\equiv$C bond, and its C=C bond is not reduced by sodium in liquid ammonia, so it does not react.

Hence, the correct options are (A), (
B) and (D).

Among CH $$ \equiv $$ CH and CH 2 = CH 2 , in CH $$ \equiv $$ CH compound H atom is attached with sp hybridised C atom and in CH 2 = CH 2 compound H atom is attached with sp 2 hybridised C atom.

As we know, electronegitivity of sp carbon is more compare to sp 2 carbon atom and that H is more acidic which is attached with more electronegative carbon atom. So CH $$ \equiv $$ CH is more acidic than CH 2 = CH 2 .

Among CH $$ \equiv $$ CH and CH 3 –C $$ \equiv $$ CH, in CH $$ \equiv $$ CH both the H atom is connected to sp carbon atom but in CH 3 –C $$ \equiv $$ CH, with one sp carbon atom H atom attached and with other sp carbon atom -CH 3 group attached which have +I effect and we know +I effect decreases acidic strength.

questions.text: Which of these will not react with acetylene ?
questions.solution: Acetylene reacts with the other three as :

questions.text: Acetylene does not react with :
questions.solution:
1. Acetylene reacts with sodium :

$$\mathrm{2CH} \equiv \mathrm{CH} + 2\mathrm{Na} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{CH} \equiv \mathrm{C}^{-}\mathrm{Na}^{+} + \mathrm{H}_2$$

Here, acetylene reacts with sodium to produce sodium acetylide and hydrogen gas.

2. Acetylene reacts with ammoniacal silver nitrate :

$$\mathrm{CH} \equiv \mathrm{CH} + 2\mathrm{AgNO}_3 \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ag}_2\mathrm{C}_2 + 2\mathrm{HNO}_3$$

In this reaction, acetylene reacts with ammoniacal silver nitrate to form a white precipitate of silver acetylide and nitric acid.

3. Acetylene reaction with hydrochloric acid in the presence of a $\mathrm{Hg}^{2+}$ catalyst (oxymercuration-demercuration) :

$$\mathrm{CH} \equiv \mathrm{CH} + \mathrm{Hg(OAc)_2} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{OH} + \mathrm{HgOAc}$$

$$\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{OH} + \mathrm{NaBH}_4 \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{H} + \mathrm{B(OH)_3} + \mathrm{NaOAc}$$

Acetylene does not readily react with $\mathrm{HCl}$. However, in the presence of a catalyst like $\mathrm{Hg}^{2+}$, a specific type of electrophilic addition known as oxymercuration can occur. The result is vinyl chloride. Note that $\mathrm{NaBH}_4$ is used to reduce the mercurinium ion intermediate and to replace the $\mathrm{Hg}$ group with a hydrogen atom.

4. Acetylene does not react with sodium hydroxide :

$$\mathrm{CH} \equiv \mathrm{CH} + \mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \text { no reaction }$$

According to the principles of the Hard and Soft Acids and Bases (HSAB) theory, soft acids prefer to bind with soft bases and hard acids prefer to bind with hard bases. In this case, $\mathrm{OH}^-$ is a hard base, while the $\mathrm{C}$ in acetylene is a soft acid, so they are not particularly reactive with each other.

5. Acetylene reacts with sodium amide :

$$\mathrm{CH} \equiv \mathrm{CH} + \mathrm{NaNH}_2 \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH} \equiv \mathrm{C}^{-}\mathrm{Na}^{+} + \mathrm{NH}_3$$

Here, sodium amide acts as a strong base and nucleophile, deprotonating the acetylene to form sodium acetylide and ammonia.

questions.text: The correct sequence of reagents used in the preparation of 4-bromo-2-nitroethyl benzene from benzene is :
questions.solution:
The target is ethylbenzene carrying $-\ce{NO2}$ ortho (C-2) and Br para (C-4) to the ethyl group.

The ethyl group is introduced as an acetyl group by Friedel–Crafts acylation ($\ce{CH3COCl/AlCl3}$) and then reduced to $-\ce{CH2CH3}$ by Clemmensen reduction ($\ce{Zn-Hg/HCl}$), which avoids the rearrangement and polysubstitution of direct alkylation.

Ethyl is ortho/para-directing, so bromination ($\ce{Br2/AlBr3}$) gives mainly 4-bromoethylbenzene.

On nitration ($\ce{HNO3/H2SO4}$), the activating ethyl group directs $-\ce{NO2}$ ortho to itself (C-2), giving 4-bromo-2-nitroethylbenzene:

In (
A) and (
C) the meta-directing acetyl group is still present during substitution and $\ce{Zn/HCl}$ also reduces $-\ce{NO2}$; in (
D) nitrobenzene does not undergo Friedel–Crafts acylation.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

Complete inversion requires a pure $S_N2$ path (backside attack); DMF, a polar aprotic solvent, favours $S_N2$ for an unhindered carbon.

$\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2Br}$ is a primary benzylic halide with an unhindered carbon, so it reacts entirely by $S_N2$ with inversion.

$\mathrm{C_6H_5CH(CH_3)Br}$ and $\mathrm{C_6H_5CH(C_6H_5)Br}$ are secondary benzylic halides that give stabilised carbocations, so partial $S_N1$ causes some racemisation.

$\mathrm{C_6H_5C(CH_3)(C_6H_5)Br}$ is tertiary and reacts by $S_N1$, giving racemisation.

So $\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2Br}$ undergoes complete inversion of configuration.

questions.solution:
Williamson synthesis is an $S_N2$ attack of an alkoxide ion on an alkyl halide.

With a tertiary halide the back-side attack is sterically blocked.

The alkoxide acts as a strong base instead, causing E2 elimination.

C oxidises to ethanoic acid, so C is ethanol: the other group is ethyl.

The alkoxide ion is a strong nucleophile; it attacks the carbon bearing the halogen and the halide ion leaves.

questions.text: The predominant intermolecular forces present in ethyl acetate, a liquid, are:

options.text: London dispersion, dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonding

questions.solution:
Ethyl acetate (CH 3 COOCH 2 CH 3 ) is an organic compound with a molecular structure that does not include any hydrogen atoms bonded directly to highly electronegative atoms like nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine. Because of this, it cannot form hydrogen bonds. However, ethyl acetate does possess a polar carbonyl group (C=O), which contributes to dipole-dipole interactions, and like all molecules, it can experience London dispersion forces. Therefore, the predominant intermolecular forces present in ethyl acetate are dipole-dipole interactions and London dispersion forces.

Hence, the correct option is :

Option D: London dispersion and dipole-dipole

questions.text: Among the following the order of reactivity towards nucleophilic addition is
questions.solution:
Reactivity towards nucleophilic addition depends on how electrophilic and how crowded the carbonyl carbon is.

Each $\mathrm{CH_3}$ group releases electrons ($+I$ effect and hyperconjugation) and lowers the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon.

Each $\mathrm{CH_3}$ group also hinders the approach of the nucleophile and crowds the tetrahedral product.

$\mathrm{HCHO}$ has no alkyl group, $\mathrm{CH_3CHO}$ has one and $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$ has two.

So the order is $\mathrm{HCHO \gt CH_3CHO \gt CH_3COCH_3}$.

questions.text: Which is the major product formed when acetone is heated with iodine and potassium hydroxide ?
questions.solution:
Acetone, $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}$, contains a $\mathrm{CH_3CO-}$ group, so it gives the iodoform reaction.

The $\mathrm{CH_3}$ group is tri-iodinated to $\mathrm{CI_3COCH_3}$, which is cleaved by $\mathrm{OH^-}$.

$\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3 + 3I_2 + 4KOH \rightarrow CHI_3 + CH_3COOK + 3KI + 3H_2O}$

So the major product is iodoform, $\mathrm{CHI_3}$ (yellow precipitate).

questions.text: Which one of the following reactions will not result in the formation of carbon $$-$$ carbon bond ?
questions.solution:
Reimer–Tiemann: phenol with $\mathrm{CHCl_3/NaOH}$ introduces a $\mathrm{-CHO}$ group on the ring, a new $\mathrm{C-C}$ bond.

Friedel–Crafts acylation: $\mathrm{ArH + RCOCl} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{AlCl_3}} \mathrm{ArCOR + HCl}$, a new $\mathrm{C-C}$ bond.

Wurtz: $\mathrm{2RX + 2Na \rightarrow R-R + 2NaX}$, a new $\mathrm{C-C}$ bond.

Cannizzaro: $\mathrm{2HCHO + NaOH \rightarrow HCOONa + CH_3OH}$; only a hydride ion is transferred, no $\mathrm{C-C}$ bond forms.

So the Cannizzaro reaction does not form a carbon–carbon bond.

questions.solution:
Reactivity towards nucleophilic addition increases with the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon and decreases with crowding around it.

Ketones carry two electron-releasing alkyl groups on the carbonyl carbon and are less reactive than aldehydes; butanone, with the larger ethyl group, is less reactive than propanone.

Increasing order: butanone < propanone < benzaldehyde < propanal.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
The number of stereoisomers formed in a reaction of $$(±)\mathrm{Ph}(\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}) \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{OH})(\mathrm{CN}) \mathrm{Ph}$$ with $$\mathrm{HCN}$$ is ___________.

[where $$\mathrm{Ph}$$ is $$-\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{5}$$]
questions.solution:
HCN adds across the C=O group of the cyanohydrin ketone, so the product is $\ce{Ph-C(OH)(CN)-C(OH)(CN)-Ph}$.

The product has two stereocentres, each carrying the same set of groups ($\ce{Ph}$, $\ce{OH}$, $\ce{CN}$ and the other half of the molecule), so the two halves of the molecule are identical.

A molecule with two identical stereocentres exists as one pair of enantiomers, (R,R) and (S,S), and one optically inactive meso form, (R,S), which has an internal plane of symmetry.

Number of stereoisomers $= 2 + 1 = 3$.

Hence, the answer is 3.

In the presence of a small amount of phosphorus, aliphatic carboxylic acids
react with chlorine or bromine to yield a compound in which $$\alpha $$ - hydrogen has been replaced by halogen. This reaction is known as :

Carboxylic acids having an $\alpha$-hydrogen react with $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ or $\mathrm{Br_2}$ in the presence of a small amount of red phosphorus.

$\mathrm{RCH_2COOH + X_2 \xrightarrow{P} RCH(X)COOH + HX}$, where $\mathrm{X = Cl}$ or $\mathrm{Br}$.

Phosphorus first forms the acyl halide, which enolises; the enol takes up the halogen at the $\alpha$-carbon.

This $\alpha$-halogenation of carboxylic acids is known as the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction.
