questions.text: If the $${2^{nd}},{5^{th}}\,and\,{9^{th}}$$ terms of a non-constant A.P. are in G.P., then the common ratio of this G.P. is :
questions.solution:
The terms of an Arithmetic Progression (A.P.) are given by $a$, $a + d$, $a + 2d$, ..., where $a$ is the first term and $d$ is the common difference.

Given that the 2nd, 5th and 9th terms of an A.P. are in Geometric Progression (G.P.), we can denote them as follows :

2nd term = $a + d$

5th term = $a + 4d$

9th term = $a + 8d$

For three numbers to be in G.P., the square of the middle term must be equal to the product of the other two terms. So,

$(a + 4d)^2 = (a + d)(a + 8d)$

Expanding and simplifying :

$a^2 + 8ad + 16d^2 = a^2 + 9ad + 8d^2$

$8ad + 16d^2 = a^2 + 9ad + 8d^2$

$8ad - 9ad = 8d^2 - 16d^2$

$-ad = -8d^2$

$a = 8d$

The common ratio of the G.P. is the ratio of the 5th term to the 2nd term, or $(a + 4d) / (a + d)$. Substituting $a = 8d$ gives :

$(8d + 4d) / (8d + d) = 12d / 9d = 4 / 3$

So, the common ratio of the G.P. is $4 / 3$. The answer is option D.

questions.solution:
For $375x^2 - 25x - 2 = 0$:

$$\alpha + \beta = \dfrac{25}{375} = \dfrac{1}{15}, \qquad \alpha\beta = -\dfrac{2}{375}$$

The roots are $\dfrac{25 \pm \sqrt{3625}}{750}$, approximately $0.114$ and $-0.047$, so $|\alpha| < 1$ and $|\beta| < 1$ and both geometric series converge:

$$\dfrac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha} + \dfrac{\beta}{1 - \beta} = \dfrac{(\alpha + \beta) - 2\alpha\beta}{1 - (\alpha + \beta) + \alpha\beta}$$

The numerator is $\dfrac{1}{15} + \dfrac{4}{375} = \dfrac{29}{375}$ and the denominator is $1 - \dfrac{25}{375} - \dfrac{2}{375} = \dfrac{348}{375}$.

$$\text{Sum} = \dfrac{29}{348} = \dfrac{1}{12}$$

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: Consider an arithmetic series and a geometric series having four initial terms from the set {11, 8, 21, 16, 26, 32, 4}. If the last terms of these series are the maximum possible four digit numbers, then the number of common terms in these two series is equal to ___________.
questions.solution:
The four terms in A.P. are $11, 16, 21, 26$ (common difference $5$) and the four terms in G.P. are $4, 8, 16, 32$ (common ratio $2$).

The A.P. terms are $11 + 5k$; the largest four-digit one is $11 + 5 \times 1997 = 9996$. So the A.P. is $11, 16, 21, \ldots, 9996$: every number from $11$ to $9996$ that leaves remainder $1$ on division by $5$.

The G.P. terms are $2^m$; the largest four-digit one is $2^{13} = 8192$. So the G.P. is $2^m$ for $m = 2, 3, \ldots, 13$.

The remainders of $2^m$ on division by $5$ repeat as $2, 4, 3, 1$ for $m = 1, 2, 3, 4$, so $2^m$ leaves remainder $1$ only when $m$ is a multiple of $4$.

For $2 \le m \le 13$ this gives $m = 4, 8, 12$, i.e. the common terms $16, 256, 4096$, all lying between $11$ and $9996$.

Hence, the answer is 3.

$$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,$$ $$ = n\left[ {148 - n + 1} \right]$$

$$ \Rightarrow n = 125,24$$

questions.text: A man saves ₹ 200 in each of the first three months of his service. In each of the subsequent months his saving increases by ₹ 40 more than the saving of immediately previous month. His total saving from the start of service will be ₹ 11040 after
questions.solution:
Let required number of months $$=n$$

$$\therefore$$ $$200 \times 3 + \left( {240 + 280 + 320 + ...} \right.$$

$$\left. {\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, + {{\left( {n - 3} \right)}^{th}}\,term} \right) = 11040$$

$$ \Rightarrow {{n - 3} \over 2}\left[ {2 \times 240 + \left( {n - 4} \right) \times 40} \right]$$

$$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = 11040 - 600$$

$$ \Rightarrow \left( {n - 3} \right)\left[ {240 + 20n - 80} \right] = 10440$$

$$ \Rightarrow \left( {n - 3} \right)\left( {20n + 160} \right) = 10440$$

$$ \Rightarrow \left( {n - 3} \right)\left( {n + 8} \right) = 522$$

$$ \Rightarrow {n^2} + 5n - 546 = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow \left( {n + 26} \right)\left( {n - 21} \right) = 0$$

$$\therefore$$ $$n = 21$$

questions.text: If the A.M. between $$p^{\text{th}}$$ and $$q^{\text{th}}$$ terms of an A.P. is equal to the A.M. between $$r^{\text{th}}$$ and $$s^{\text{th}}$$ terms of the same A.P., then $$p+q$$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Let the A.P. have first term $a$ and common difference $d$, so $T_k=a+(k-1)d$.

Given $\dfrac{T_p+T_q}{2}=\dfrac{T_r+T_s}{2}$.

So $2a+(p+q-2)d=2a+(r+s-2)d$.

For a non-constant A.P. ($d\neq 0$), $p+q-2=r+s-2$.

Hence $p+q=r+s$.

questions.text: If 100 times the 100th term of an AP with non zero common difference equals the 50 times its 50th term, then the 150th term of this AP is :
questions.solution:
Let the first term be $a$ and the common difference be $d \ne 0$.

Given $100(a+99d)=50(a+49d)$.

So $2a+198d=a+49d$, which gives $a+149d=0$.

But $T_{150}=a+149d$.

Hence the 150th term of the AP is $0$.

questions.text: If a 1 , a 2 , a 3 , ...... , a n , .... are in A.P, such that a 4 - a 7 + a 10 = m, then the sum of first 13 terms of this A.P. is :
Given sum of the first n terms of an A.P. is 2n + 3n 2 . Another A.P. is formed with the same first term and double of the common difference, the sum of n terms of the new A.P. is:
questions.solution:
$S_n = 2n + 3n^2$, so the first term is $a = S_1 = 5$.

$S_2 = 4 + 12 = 16$, so the second term is $16 - 5 = 11$ and the common difference is $d = 6$.

The new A.P. has first term $5$ and common difference $2d = 12$.

Its sum of $n$ terms is $\dfrac{n}{2}\left[2(5) + (n - 1)(12)\right] = \dfrac{n}{2}(12n - 2)$.

So the sum of $n$ terms of the new A.P. is $6n^2 - n$.

questions.text: The number of terms in an A.P. is even; the sum of the odd terms in it is 24 and that of the even terms is 30. If the last term exceeds the first term by 10$${1 \over 2}$$, then the number of terms in the A.P. is :
questions.solution:
Let a, d and 2n be the first term, common difference and total number of terms of an A.P. respectively i.e.

a + (a + d) + (a + 2d) + . . . .+ (a + (2n $$-$$ 1)d)

No. of even terms = n, No. of odd terms = n Sum of odd terms :

S 0 = $${n \over 2}\left[ {2a + \left( {n - 1} \right)\left( {2d} \right)} \right] = 24$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$  n [a + (n $$-$$ 1) d] = 24         . . . . .(1)

Sum of even terms :

S e = $${n \over 2}\left[ {2\left( {a + d} \right) + \left( {n - 1} \right)2d} \right] = 30$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$    n [a + d + (n $$-$$ 1) d] = 30       . . . . .(2)

Subtracting equation (1) from (2),

we get nd = 6    . . . . (3)

Also, given that last term exceeds the first term by $${{21} \over 2}$$

a + (2n $$-$$ 1) d = a + $${{21} \over 2}$$

2nd $$-$$ d = $${{21} \over 2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$   2 $$ \times $$ 6 $$-$$ $${{21} \over 2}$$ = d     ($$ \because $$   nd = 6)

d = $${3 \over 2}$$

Putting value of d in equation (3)

n = $${{6 \times 2} \over 3}$$ = 4

Total no. of terms = 2n = 2 $$ \times $$ 4 = 8

questions.text: Given an A.P. whose terms are all positive integers. The sum of the first nine terms is greater than 200 and less than 220. If the second term in it is 12, then its 4 th term is :
questions.solution:
Let a be the first term and d be the common difference of given A.P.

Second term, a + d = 12      . . . .(1)

Sum of first nine terms,

S 9 = $${9 \over 2}$$ (2a + 8d) = 9(a + 4d)

Given that S 9 is more than 200 and less than 220

$$ \Rightarrow $$   200 < S 9 < 220

$$ \Rightarrow $$ 200 < 9 (a + 4d) < 220

$$ \Rightarrow $$    200 < 9 (a + d + 3d) < 220

Putting value of (a + d) from equation (1)

200 < 9 (12 + 3d) < 220

$$ \Rightarrow $$   200 < 108 + 27d < 220

$$ \Rightarrow $$    200 $$-$$ 108 < 108 + 27d $$-$$ 108 < 220 $$-$$ 108

$$ \Rightarrow $$   92 < 27d < 112

Possible value of d is 4

27 $$ \times $$ 4 = 108

Thus, 92 < 108 < 112

Putting value of d in equation (1)

a + d = 12

a = 12 $$-$$ 4 = 8

4 th term = a + 3d = 8 + 3 $$ \times $$ 4 = 20

questions.text: Let the sum of the first three terms of an A.P. be 39 and the sum of its last four terms be 178. If the first term of this A.P. is 10, then the median of the A.P. is :
questions.solution:
Let the A.P. have first term $10$, common difference $d$, $n$ terms and last term $l$.

First three terms: $3\cdot10+3d=39\Rightarrow d=3$.

Last four terms: $l+(l-d)+(l-2d)+(l-3d)=4l-6d=178\Rightarrow 4l=196\Rightarrow l=49$.

$49=10+(n-1)\cdot3\Rightarrow n=14$, so the median is the mean of the 7th and 8th terms: $\dfrac{28+31}{2}=29.5$.

Check: for an A.P. the median is $\dfrac{10+49}{2}=29.5$. So the median is $29.5$.

$$ \because $$$$\,\,\,$$ $${1 \over {{x_1}}},{1 \over {{x_2}}},{1 \over {{x_3}}},.....,{1 \over {{x_n}}}$$ are in A.P.

x 1 = 4 and x 21 = 20

$$ \Rightarrow $$$$\,\,\,$$ d = $${1 \over {20}}$$ $$ \times $$ $$\left( {{1 \over {20}} - {1 \over 4}} \right)$$ $$ \Rightarrow $$ d = $$-$$ $${1 \over {100}}$$

Also x n > 50(given).

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ $${1 \over {{x_n}}} = {1 \over {{x_1}}} + \left[ {\left( {n - 1} \right) \times d} \right]$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$$$\,\,\,$$ x n = $${{{x_1}} \over {1 + \left( {n - 1} \right) \times d \times {x_1}}}$$

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ $${{{x_1}} \over {1 + \left( {n - 1} \right) \times d \times {x_1}}} > 50$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$$$\,\,\,$$ $${4 \over {1 + \left( {n - 1} \right) \times \left( { - {1 \over {100}}} \right) \times 4}} > 50$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$$$\,\,\,$$ 1 + (n $$-$$ 1) $$ \times $$ ($$-$$ $${1 \over {100}}$$) $$ \times $$ 4 < $${4 \over {50}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$$$\,\,\,$$ $$-$$ $${1 \over {100}}$$(n $$-$$ 1) < $$-$$ $${{23} \over {100}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$$$\,\,\,$$ n $$-$$ 1 > 23   $$ \Rightarrow $$  n > 24

Therefore$$\,\,\,$$ n = 25.

$$ \Rightarrow $$$$\,\,\,$$$$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{25} {{1 \over {{x_i}}}} $$ = $${{25} \over 2}\left[ {\left( {2 \times {1 \over 4}} \right) + \left( {25 - 1} \right) \times \left( { - {1 \over {100}}} \right)} \right]$$ = $${{13} \over 4}$$

questions.text: Different A.P.'s are constructed with the first term 100, the last term 199, and integral common differences. The sum of the common differences of all such A.P.'s having at least 3 terms and at most 33 terms is ___________.

Let $$a, b$$ be two non-zero real numbers. If $$p$$ and $$r$$ are the roots of the equation $$x^{2}-8 \mathrm{a} x+2 \mathrm{a}=0$$ and $$\mathrm{q}$$ and s are the roots of the equation $$x^{2}+12 \mathrm{~b} x+6 \mathrm{~b}=0$$, such that $$\frac{1}{\mathrm{p}}, \frac{1}{\mathrm{q}}, \frac{1}{\mathrm{r}}, \frac{1}{\mathrm{~s}}$$ are in A.P., then $$\mathrm{a}^{-1}-\mathrm{b}^{-1}$$ is equal to _____________.
questions.solution:
Replacing $x$ by $\dfrac{1}{x}$ in an equation replaces each root by its reciprocal. From $x^2-8ax+2a=0$ this gives $1-8ax+2ax^2=0$, i.e. $2ax^2-8ax+1=0$, whose roots are $\dfrac1p,\dfrac1r$. So $\dfrac1p+\dfrac1r=4$ and $\dfrac1p\cdot\dfrac1r=\dfrac{1}{2a}$.

In the same way, $x^2+12bx+6b=0$ gives $6bx^2+12bx+1=0$, whose roots are $\dfrac1q,\dfrac1s$. So $\dfrac1q+\dfrac1s=-2$ and $\dfrac1q\cdot\dfrac1s=\dfrac{1}{6b}$.

Take the A.P. $\dfrac1p,\dfrac1q,\dfrac1r,\dfrac1s$ as $\alpha-3\beta,\ \alpha-\beta,\ \alpha+\beta,\ \alpha+3\beta$. Then $2\alpha-2\beta=4$ and $2\alpha+2\beta=-2$, so $\alpha=\dfrac12$ and $\beta=-\dfrac32$.

So $\dfrac1p=5,\ \dfrac1q=2,\ \dfrac1r=-1,\ \dfrac1s=-4$.

Then $\dfrac{1}{2a}=5\times(-1)=-5 \Rightarrow \dfrac1a=-10$, and $\dfrac{1}{6b}=2\times(-4)=-8 \Rightarrow \dfrac1b=-48$.

$$a^{-1}-b^{-1}=-10+48=38$$

Hence, the answer is 38.

questions.text:
Let G be the geometric mean of two positive numbers a and b, and M be the arithmetic mean of $${1 \over a}$$ and $${1 \over b}$$.

If   $${1 \over M}$$ : G is 4 : 5, then a : b can be :
questions.solution:
G = $$\sqrt {ab} $$

M = $${{{1 \over a} + {1 \over b}} \over 2}$$

M = $${{a + b} \over {2ab}}$$

Given that $${1 \over M}:$$ G = 4 : 5

$${{2ab} \over {\left( {a + b} \right)\sqrt {ab} }} = {4 \over 5}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$   $${{a + b} \over {2\sqrt {ab} }} = {5 \over 4}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$    $${{a + b + 2\sqrt {ab} } \over {a + b - 2\sqrt {ab} }}$$ = $${{5 + 4} \over {5 - 4}}$$

{Using Componendo & Dividendo}

$$ \Rightarrow $$    $${{{{\left( {\sqrt a } \right)}^2} + {{\left( {\sqrt b } \right)}^2} + 2\sqrt {ab} } \over {{{\left( {\sqrt a } \right)}^2} + {{\left( {\sqrt b } \right)}^2} - 2\sqrt {ab} }} = {9 \over 1}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$    $${\left( {{{\sqrt b + \sqrt a } \over {\sqrt b - \sqrt a }}} \right)^2} = {9 \over 1} \Rightarrow {{\sqrt b + \sqrt a } \over {\sqrt b - \sqrt a }} = {3 \over 1}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {{\sqrt b + \sqrt a + \sqrt b - \sqrt a } \over {\sqrt b + \sqrt a - \sqrt b + \sqrt a }} = {{3 + 1} \over {3 - 1}}$$

{Using Componendo & Dividendo}

$$\sqrt {{b \over a}} = {4 \over 2} = 2$$

$${b \over a} = {4 \over 1}$$

$${a \over b} = {1 \over 4} \Rightarrow a:b = 1:4$$

questions.text: Let x, y, z be positive real numbers such that x + y + z = 12 and x 3 y 4 z 5 = (0.1) (600) 3 . Then x 3 + y 3 + z 3 is equal to :
questions.solution:
As we know

AM  $$ \ge $$  GM

$$ \Rightarrow $$   $${{3\left( {{x \over 3}} \right) + 4\left( {{y \over 4}} \right) + 5\left( {{z \over 5}} \right)} \over {12}}$$  $$ \ge $$  $${\left[ {{{\left( {{x \over 3}} \right)}^3}{{\left( {{y \over 4}} \right)}^4}{{\left( {{z \over 5}} \right)}^5}} \right]^{{1 \over {12}}}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$   1  $$ \ge $$  $${{{x^3}{y^4}{z^5}} \over {{3^3}{4^4}{5^5}}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$   x 3  y 4  z 5   $$ \le $$  3 3  . 4 4  . 5 5

$$ \Rightarrow $$   x 3 y 4 z 5   $$ \le $$  (0.1)(600) 3

but given that,

x 3 y 4 z 5 = (0.1) (600) 3

$$ \therefore $$   AM  $$=$$  GM

$$ \Rightarrow $$   All the number are equal.

$$ \therefore $$   $${x \over 3} = {y \over 4} = {z \over 5} = k$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$  x $$=$$ 3k, y = 4k, z = 5k

given that,

        x + y + z $$=$$ 12

$$ \Rightarrow $$   3k + 4k + 5k $$=$$ 12

$$ \Rightarrow $$   12k $$=$$ 12

$$ \Rightarrow $$   k = 1

$$ \therefore $$   x $$=$$   3,  y $$=$$ 4,   z $$=$$ 5

So, x 3 + y 3 + z 3

$$=$$ 3 3 + 4 3 + 5 3

$$=$$ 216

questions.text:
If sin 4 $$\alpha $$ + 4 cos 4 $$\beta $$ + 2 = 4$$\sqrt 2 $$ sin $$\alpha $$ cos $$\beta $$; $$\alpha $$, $$\beta $$ $$ \in $$ [0, $$\pi $$],

then cos($$\alpha $$ + $$\beta $$) $$-$$ cos($$\alpha $$ $$-$$ $$\beta $$) is equal to :
questions.solution:
For the non-negative numbers $\sin^4\alpha,\ 4\cos^4\beta,\ 1,\ 1$, A.M. $\ge$ G.M. gives

$$\sin^4\alpha+4\cos^4\beta+1+1\ge4\left(4\sin^4\alpha\cos^4\beta\right)^{1/4}=4\sqrt2\,\left|\sin\alpha\cos\beta\right|\ge4\sqrt2\sin\alpha\cos\beta.$$

The given equation says equality holds throughout, so the four numbers are equal, $\sin^4\alpha=4\cos^4\beta=1$, and $\sin\alpha\cos\beta\ge0$.

Since $\alpha\in[0,\pi]$, $\sin\alpha\ge0$, so $\sin\alpha=1$, i.e. $\alpha=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

$\cos^4\beta=\dfrac14 \Rightarrow \cos\beta=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, and $\sin\alpha\cos\beta\ge0$ gives $\cos\beta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, so $\beta=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $\sin\beta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$.

$$\cos(\alpha+\beta)-\cos(\alpha-\beta)=-2\sin\alpha\sin\beta=-2(1)\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)=-\sqrt2.$$

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: The coefficients of $${x^p}$$ and $${x^q}$$ in the expansion of $${\left( {1 + x} \right)^{p + q}}$$ are
questions.solution:

The general term = $${T_{r + 1}} = {}^{p + q}{C_r}.{\left( x \right)^r}$$

$$\therefore$$ $${x^p}$$ will be present in the term = $${}^{p + q}{C_p}.{\left( x \right)^p}$$

And $${x^q}$$ will be present in the term = $${}^{p + q}{C_q}.{\left( x \right)^q}$$

$$\therefore$$ coefficient of $${x^q}$$ = $${}^{p + q}{C_q}$$

We know $${}^n{C_r}$$ = $${}^n{C_{n - r}}$$

$$\therefore$$ $${}^{p + q}{C_q}$$ = $${}^{p + q}{C_{\left( {p + q} \right) - q}}$$ = $${}^{p + q}{C_p}$$

So coefficients of $${x^p}$$ and $${x^q}$$ are equal.

questions.text: The number of integral terms in the expansion of $${\left( {\sqrt 3 + \root 8 \of 5 } \right)^{256}}$$ is
questions.solution:
General term = $${}^{256}{C_r}.{\left( {\sqrt 3 } \right)^{256 - r}}.{\left( {\root 8 \of 5 } \right)^r}$$

= $${}^{256}{C_r}.{\left( 3 \right)^{{{256 - r} \over 2}}}.{\left( 5 \right)^{{r \over 8}}}$$

When $${{{256 - r} \over 2}}$$ is integer then $${\left( 3 \right)^{{{256 - r} \over 2}}}$$ is integer.

And when $${{r \over 8}}$$ is integer then $${\left( 5 \right)^{{r \over 8}}}$$ is integer.

Entire general term will be integer when $${{{256 - r} \over 2}}$$ and $${{r \over 8}}$$ both are integer.

$${{{256 - r} \over 2}}$$ is integer when r = 0, 2, 4, 6, ......, 256

$${{r \over 8}}$$ is integer when r = 0, 8, 16 ,......., 256

Now both $${{{256 - r} \over 2}}$$ and $${{r \over 8}}$$ will be integer when r = 0, 8, 16, ...., 256 (This is an AP)

$$\therefore$$ 256 = 0 + (n - 1)8 using formula of AP, t n = a + (n - 1)d

$$\therefore$$ n = $${{256} \over 8} + 1$$ = 32 + 1 = 33

questions.text: The coefficient of $${x^n}$$ in expansion of $$\left( {1 + x} \right){\left( {1 - x} \right)^n}$$ is
questions.solution:
Given $$\left( {1 + x} \right){\left( {1 - x} \right)^n}$$

= $${\left( {1 - x} \right)^n}$$ + $$x{\left( {1 - x} \right)^n}$$

General term of $${\left( {1 - x} \right)^n}$$ = $${}^n{C_r}.{\left( { - 1} \right)^r}.{x^r}$$

$$\therefore$$ Term containing $${x^n}$$ in $${\left( {1 - x} \right)^n}$$ = $${}^n{C_n}.{\left( { - 1} \right)^n}.{x^n}$$

So coefficient of $${x^n}$$ in $${\left( {1 - x} \right)^n}$$ = $${}^n{C_n}.{\left( { - 1} \right)^n}$$

General term of $$x{\left( {1 - x} \right)^n}$$ = $${}^n{C_r}.{\left( { - 1} \right)^r}.{x^{r + 1}}$$

$$\therefore$$ Term containing $${x^n}$$ in $$x{\left( {1 - x} \right)^n}$$ = $${}^n{C_{n - 1}}.{\left( { - 1} \right)^{n - 1}}.{x^n}$$

So coefficient of $${x^n}$$ in $$x{\left( {1 - x} \right)^n}$$ = $${}^n{C_{n - 1}}.{\left( { - 1} \right)^{n - 1}}$$

$$\therefore$$ coefficient of $${x^n}$$ in $${\left( {1 - x} \right)^n}$$ + $$x{\left( {1 - x} \right)^n}$$

= $${}^n{C_n}.{\left( { - 1} \right)^n}$$ + $${}^n{C_{n - 1}}.{\left( { - 1} \right)^{n - 1}}$$

= $${\left( { - 1} \right)^{n - 1}}\left[ {{}^n{C_{n - 1}} - {}^n{C_n}} \right]$$

= $${\left( { - 1} \right)^{n - 1}}\left[ {n - 1} \right]$$

= $${\left( { - 1} \right)^n}\left[ {1 - n} \right]$$

questions.text: If the coefficients of r th , (r+1) th , and (r + 2) th terms in the binomial expansion of $${{\rm{(1 + y )}}^m}$$ are in A.P., then m and r satisfy the equation
questions.solution:
Let r = 2

$$\therefore$$ 2nd, 3rd and 4th terms are in AP.

2nd term = T 2 = $${}^m{C_1}.y$$

Coefficient of T 2 = $${}^m{C_1}$$

3rd term = T 3 = $${}^m{C_2}.{y^2}$$

Coefficient of T 3 = $${}^m{C_2}$$

4th term = T 4 = $${}^m{C_3}.{y^3}$$

Coefficient of T 4 = $${}^m{C_3}$$

$$\therefore$$ 2.$${}^m{C_2}$$ = $${}^m{C_1}$$ + $${}^m{C_3}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$2.{{m\left( {m - 1} \right)} \over {1.2}}$$ = $${m \over 1}$$ + $${{m\left( {m - 1} \right)\left( {m - 2} \right)} \over {1.2.3}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ 6m 2 - 6m = 6m +m(m 2 - 3m + 2)

$$ \Rightarrow $$ 6m 2 - 6m = 6m + m 3 - 3m 2 + 2m

$$ \Rightarrow $$ 6m - 6 = 6 + m 2 - 3m + 2

$$ \Rightarrow $$ m 2 - 9m + 14 = 0

Now put r = 2 at each option and find answer.

In option C, $${m^2} - m(4r + 1) + 4\,{r^2} - 2 = 0$$ putting r = 2 we get

m 2 - 9m + 14 = 0. So Option C is correct.

questions.text: If the coefficient of $${x^7}$$ in $${\left[ {a{x^2} + \left( {{1 \over {bx}}} \right)} \right]^{11}}$$ equals the coefficient of $${x^{ - 7}}$$ in $${\left[ {ax - \left( {{1 \over {b{x^2}}}} \right)} \right]^{11}}$$, then $$a$$ and $$b$$ satisfy the relation
questions.solution:
General term of $${\left[ {a{x^2} + \left( {{1 \over {bx}}} \right)} \right]^{11}}$$ is T r+1 .

T r+1 = $${}^{11}{C_r}{\left( {a{x^2}} \right)^{11 - r}}{\left( {{1 \over {bx}}} \right)^r}$$

= $${}^{11}{C_r}{\left( a \right)^{11 - r}}{\left( b \right)^{ - r}}{\left( x \right)^{22 - 3r}}$$

For the coefficient of x 7 ,

$$ \Rightarrow $$ 22 - 3r = 7

$$ \Rightarrow $$ r = 5

So coefficient of x 7 = $${}^{11}{C_5}{\left( a \right)^6}{\left( b \right)^{ - 5}}$$ ......(1)

Now General term of $${\left[ {ax - \left( {{1 \over {b{x^2}}}} \right)} \right]^{11}}$$ is T r+1 .

T r+1 = $${}^{11}{C_r}{\left( {a{x}} \right)^{11 - r}}{\left( { - {1 \over {b{x^2}}}} \right)^r}$$

= $${}^{11}{C_r}{\left( a \right)^{11 - r}}{\left( { - 1} \right)^r}{\left( b \right)^{ - r}}{\left( x \right)^{11 - r}}{\left( x \right)^{ - 2r}}$$

For the coefficient of x -7 ,

11 - 3r = -7

$$ \Rightarrow $$ r = 6

$$\therefore$$ Coefficient of x -7 = $${}^{11}{C_6}{\left( a \right)^5}{\left( { - 1} \right)^6}{\left( b \right)^{ - 6}}$$

According to question,

Coefficient of x 7 = Coefficient of x -7

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $${}^{11}{C_5}{\left( a \right)^6}{\left( b \right)^{ - 5}}$$ = $${}^{11}{C_6}{\left( a \right)^5}{\left( { - 1} \right)^6}{\left( b \right)^{ - 6}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$ab = 1$$

questions.text: The number of terms in the expansion of $$\left(y^{1/5}+x^{1/10}\right)^{55}$$, in which powers of $$x$$ and $$y$$ are free from radical signs are
questions.solution:
General term: $T_{r+1}={}^{55}C_r\,y^{\frac{55-r}{5}}\,x^{\frac{r}{10}}$, $0\le r\le 55$.

The power of $x$ is an integer only when $r$ is a multiple of $10$.

For such $r$, $55-r$ is a multiple of $5$, so the power of $y$ is an integer too.

So $r=0,10,20,30,40,50$.

Hence there are $6$ such terms.

questions.text: The sum of the rational terms in the binomial expansion of $${\left( {{2^{{1 \over 2}}} + {3^{{1 \over 5}}}} \right)^{10}}$$ is
questions.solution:
The general term is $T_{r+1} = {}^{10}C_r\, 2^{\frac{10 - r}{2}}\, 3^{\frac{r}{5}}$, $0 \le r \le 10$.

It is rational only when $\dfrac{10 - r}{2}$ and $\dfrac{r}{5}$ are both integers, i.e. $r$ is even and a multiple of $5$: $r = 0$ or $r = 10$.

$r = 0$: $T_1 = 2^5 = 32$; $r = 10$: $T_{11} = 3^2 = 9$.

So the sum of the rational terms is $32 + 9 = 41$.

questions.text: If the 7th terms in the binomial expansion of $${\left( {{3 \over {\root 3 \of {84} }} + \sqrt 3 \ln x} \right)^9}$$, x > 0, is equal to 729, then x can be:
questions.solution:
$T_7 = {}^9C_6\left(\dfrac{3}{\sqrt[3]{84}}\right)^3\left(\sqrt{3}\ln x\right)^6$.

$= 84 \times \dfrac{27}{84} \times 27(\ln x)^6 = 729(\ln x)^6$.

Given $T_7 = 729$: $(\ln x)^6 = 1 \Rightarrow \ln x = \pm 1$.

So $x = e$ or $x = \dfrac{1}{e}$; hence $x$ can be $e$.

questions.text: The ratio of the coefficient of x 15 to the term independent of x in the expansion of $${\left( {{x^2} + {2 \over x}} \right)^{15}}$$ is
questions.solution:
$T_{r+1} = \binom{15}{r}(x^2)^{15 - r}\left(\dfrac{2}{x}\right)^r = \binom{15}{r}2^r x^{30 - 3r}$.

For $x^{15}$: $30 - 3r = 15 \Rightarrow r = 5$, so the coefficient is $\binom{15}{5}2^5$.

For the term independent of $x$: $30 - 3r = 0 \Rightarrow r = 10$, so the term is $\binom{15}{10}2^{10}$.

Since $\binom{15}{5} = \binom{15}{10}$, the ratio is $\dfrac{2^5}{2^{10}} = \dfrac{1}{32}$.

So the required ratio is $1 : 32$.

questions.text:
The term independent of $$x$$ in expansion of

$${\left( {{{x + 1} \over {{x^{2/3}} - {x^{1/3}} + 1}} - {{x - 1} \over {x - {x^{1/2}}}}} \right)^{10}}$$ is
questions.solution:
$${\left( {{{x + 1} \over {{x^{2/3}} - {x^{1/3}} + 1}} - {{x - 1} \over {x - {x^{1/2}}}}} \right)^{10}}$$

= $${\left( {{{\left( {{x^{1/3}} + 1} \right)\left( {{x^{2/3}} - {x^{1/3}} + 1} \right)} \over {{x^{2/3}} - {x^{1/3}} + 1}} - {{\left( {\sqrt x + 1} \right)\left( {\sqrt x - 1} \right)} \over {\sqrt x \left( {\sqrt x - 1} \right)}}} \right)^{10}}$$

= $${\left( {\left( {{x^{1/3}} + 1} \right) - {{\left( {\sqrt x + 1} \right)} \over {\sqrt x }}} \right)^{10}}$$

= $${\left( {\left( {{x^{1/3}} + 1} \right) - \left( {1 + {1 \over {\sqrt x }}} \right)} \right)^{10}}$$

= $${\left( {{x^{1/3}} - {1 \over {{x^{1/2}}}}} \right)^{10}}$$

[ Note:

For $${\left( {{x^\alpha } \pm {1 \over {{x^\beta }}}} \right)^n}$$ the $$\left( {r + 1} \right)$$ th term with power m of x is

$$r = {{n\alpha - m} \over {\alpha + \beta }}$$]

Here $$\alpha = {1 \over 3}$$, $$\beta = {1 \over 2}$$ and m = 0

then $$r = {{10 \times {1 \over 3} - 0} \over {{1 \over 3} + {1 \over 2}}}$$ = $${{10} \over 3} \times {6 \over 5}$$ = 4

questions.text: If  $${\left( {2 + {x \over 3}} \right)^{55}}$$ is expanded in the ascending powers of x and the coefficients of powers of x in two consecutive terms of the expansion are equal, then these terms are :
questions.solution:
$T_{r+1} = {}^{55}C_r\, 2^{55-r} \left(\dfrac{x}{3}\right)^r$, so the coefficient of $x^r$ is ${}^{55}C_r\, \dfrac{2^{55-r}}{3^r}$.

Equal coefficients in $T_{r+1}$ and $T_{r+2}$: ${}^{55}C_r\, \dfrac{2^{55-r}}{3^r} = {}^{55}C_{r+1}\, \dfrac{2^{54-r}}{3^{r+1}}$.

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{{}^{55}C_{r+1}}{{}^{55}C_r} = 6 \Rightarrow \dfrac{55 - r}{r + 1} = 6 \Rightarrow 7r = 49 \Rightarrow r = 7$.

So the terms are $T_8$ and $T_9$, i.e. the 8th and 9th terms.

questions.text: If 1 + x 4 + x 5 = $$\sum\limits_{i = 0}^5 {{a_i}} $$ (1 + x) i , for all x in R , then a 2 is :

The number of terms in the expansion of

(1 + x) 101 (1 + x 2 $$-$$ x) 100 in powers of x is :
questions.solution:
$(1+x)^{101}(1-x+x^2)^{100}=(1+x)\left[(1+x)(1-x+x^2)\right]^{100}=(1+x)(1+x^3)^{100}$.

$(1+x^3)^{100}$ has $101$ terms, with powers $x^0,x^3,x^6,\dots,x^{300}$.

Multiplying by $(1+x)$ gives powers $3r$ and $3r+1$ for $r=0,1,\dots,100$; these are all different, so no terms combine.

Number of terms $=2\times 101=202$.

questions.text:
The term independent of x in the binomial expansion of

(1 $$-$$ $${1 \over x}$$ + 3x 5 ) $${\left( {2{x^2} - {1 \over x}} \right)^8}$$
questions.solution:
In $\left(2x^2-\dfrac{1}{x}\right)^8$, $T_{r+1}={}^8C_r\,2^{8-r}(-1)^r x^{16-3r}$.

With $1$ we need $x^0$: $16-3r=0$ has no integer solution, so no contribution.

With $-\dfrac{1}{x}$ we need $x^1$, i.e. $r=5$: $-\left({}^8C_5\cdot 2^3\cdot(-1)^5\right)=448$.

With $3x^5$ we need $x^{-5}$, i.e. $r=7$: $3\left({}^8C_7\cdot 2\cdot(-1)^7\right)=-48$.

So the term independent of $x$ is $448-48=400$.

questions.text: If the coefficients of x −2 and x −4 in the expansion of $${\left( {{x^{{1 \over 3}}} + {1 \over {2{x^{{1 \over 3}}}}}} \right)^{18}},\left( {x > 0} \right),$$ are m and n respectively, then $${m \over n}$$ is equal to :

For coefficient of x $$-$$4 ,

questions.text: The smallest natural number n, such that the coefficient of x in the expansion of $${\left( {{x^2} + {1 \over {{x^3}}}} \right)^n}$$ is n C 23 , is :

(x > 0) is 20 × 8 7 , then a value of

If the fourth term in the binomial expansion of

$${\left( {\sqrt {{x^{\left( {{1 \over {1 + {{\log }_{10}}x}}} \right)}}} + {x^{{1 \over {12}}}}} \right)^6}$$ is equal to 200, and x > 1,
then the value of x is :
questions.solution:
Fourth term (T 4 )

= $${}^6{C_3}{\left( {\sqrt {{x^{\left( {{1 \over {1 + {{\log }_{10}}x}}} \right)}}} } \right)^3}{\left( {{x^{{1 \over {12}}}}} \right)^3}$$

= $$20{\left( {{x^{\left( {{1 \over {1 + {{\log }_{10}}x}}} \right)}}} \right)^{{3 \over 2}}}\left( {{x^{{1 \over 4}}}} \right)$$

= $$20 \times {x^{\left( {{1 \over {1 + {{\log }_{10}}x}}} \right){3 \over 2}}} \times {x^{{1 \over 4}}}$$

= $$20 \times {x^{\left( {{3 \over {2\left( {1 + {{\log }_{10}}x} \right)}} + {1 \over 4}} \right)}}$$

Given, T 4 = 200

$$ \therefore $$ $$20 \times {x^{\left( {{3 \over {2\left( {1 + {{\log }_{10}}x} \right)}} + {1 \over 4}} \right)}}$$ = 200

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $${x^{\left( {{3 \over {2\left( {1 + {{\log }_{10}}x} \right)}} + {1 \over 4}} \right)}}$$ = 10

Taking log 10 on both sides

$$\left( {{3 \over {2\left( {1 + {{\log }_{10}}x} \right)}} + {1 \over 4}} \right){\log _{10}}x$$ = 1

put log 10 x = t

$$\left( {{3 \over {2\left( {1 + t} \right)}} + {1 \over 4}} \right)t$$ = 1

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$\left( {{{\left( {1 + t} \right) + 6} \over {4\left( {1 + t} \right)}}} \right) \times t$$ = 1

$$ \Rightarrow $$ t 2 + 7t = 4 + 4t

$$ \Rightarrow $$ t 2 + 3t - 4 = 0

$$ \Rightarrow $$ (t + 4)(t - 1) = 0

$$ \Rightarrow $$ t = 1 or t = - 4

$$ \therefore $$ log 10 x = 1

$$ \Rightarrow $$ x = 10

or log 10 x = - 4

$$ \Rightarrow $$ x = 10 -4

But as x > 1 so x $$ \ne $$ 10 -4

$$ \therefore $$ x = 10

questions.text: A ratio of the 5th term from the beginning to the 5th term from the end in the binomial expansion of $${\left( {{2^{1/3}} + {1 \over {2{{\left( 3 \right)}^{1/3}}}}} \right)^{10}}$$ is :

The positive value of $$\lambda $$ for which the co-efficient of x 2
in the expression x 2 $${\left( {\sqrt x + {\lambda \over {{x^2}}}} \right)^{10}}$$ is 720, is -
questions.solution:
The general term in the expansion of the binomial expression $(a+b)^n$ is

$$
T_{r+1}={ }^n C_r a^{n-r} b^r
$$

Therefore, the general term in the expansion of the binomial expression

$x^2\left(\sqrt{x}+\frac{\lambda}{x^2}\right)^{10}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_{r+1} & =x^2\left({ }^{10} C_r(\sqrt{x})^{10-r}\left(\frac{\lambda}{x^2}\right)^r\right) \\\\
& ={ }^{10} C_r x^2 \cdot x^{\frac{10-r}{2}} \lambda^r x^{-2 r} \\\\
& ={ }^{10} C_r \lambda^r x^{2+\frac{10-r}{2}-2 r}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, for the coefficient of $x^2$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
2+\frac{10-r}{2}-2 r =2 \\\\
\Rightarrow \frac{10-r}{2}-2 r =0 \\\\
\Rightarrow 10-r =4 r \Rightarrow r=2
\end{aligned}
$$

So, the coefficient of $x^2$ is ${ }^{10} C_2 \lambda^2=720$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow & \frac{10 !}{2 ! 8 !} \lambda^2 =720 \\\\
\Rightarrow & \frac{10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 !}{2 \cdot 8 !} \lambda^2 =720 \\\\
\Rightarrow & 45 \lambda^2 =720 \\\\
\Rightarrow & \lambda^2 =16 \\\\
\Rightarrow & \lambda = \pm 4

$$

With $y=\sqrt{x^2-1}$, the odd powers of $y$ cancel in the sum:

$$(x+y)^6+(x-y)^6=2\left[x^6+{}^6C_2\,x^4y^2+{}^6C_4\,x^2y^4+y^6\right].$$

Putting $y^2=x^2-1$:

$$=2\left[x^6+15x^4(x^2-1)+15x^2(x^2-1)^2+(x^2-1)^3\right]$$

$$=2\left[x^6+(15x^6-15x^4)+(15x^6-30x^4+15x^2)+(x^6-3x^4+3x^2-1)\right]$$

$$=2\left[32x^6-48x^4+18x^2-1\right]=64x^6-96x^4+36x^2-2.$$

So $\alpha=-96$ and $\beta=36$, which give $\alpha+\beta=-60$ and $\alpha-\beta=-132$.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.solution:
The first term of the binomial is $3^{\log_3\sqrt{25^{x-1}+7}} = \sqrt{25^{x-1}+7}$ and the second is $3^{-\frac{1}{8}\log_3\left(5^{x-1}+1\right)} = \left(5^{x-1}+1\right)^{-1/8}$.

In increasing powers of the second term, $T_{r+1} = {}^{10}C_r\left(\sqrt{25^{x-1}+7}\right)^{10-r}\left(5^{x-1}+1\right)^{-r/8}$, so the ninth term ($r = 8$) is

$$T_9 = {}^{10}C_8\left(25^{x-1}+7\right)\left(5^{x-1}+1\right)^{-1} = 180$$

Since ${}^{10}C_8 = 45$, putting $t = 5^{x-1}$ (so $25^{x-1} = t^2$):

$$\dfrac{t^2+7}{t+1} = 4 \Rightarrow t^2 - 4t + 3 = 0 \Rightarrow t = 1 \text{ or } t = 3$$

$t = 1$ gives $5^{x-1} = 1$, i.e. $x = 1$; $t = 3$ gives $x = 1 + \log_5 3$, which is not among the options.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

Given Binomial Expansion

$$ = {\left( {{{\sqrt x } \over {{5^{{1 \over 4}}}}} + {{\sqrt 5 } \over {{x^{{1 \over 3}}}}}} \right)^{60}}$$

Also given that, l is coprime to 5 means l can't be multiple of 5. So we have to find all the factors of 5 in 60!, 24! and 36!

[Note : Formula for exponent or degree of prime number in n!.

Exponent of p in $$n! = \left\lfloor {{n \over p}} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor {{n \over {{p^2}}}} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor {{n \over {{p^3}}}} \right\rfloor + $$ ..... until 0 comes

here p is a prime number. ]

$$\therefore$$ Exponent of 5 in 60!

$$= \left\lfloor {{{60} \over 5}} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor {{{60} \over {{5^2}}}} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor {{{60} \over {{5^3}}}} \right\rfloor + $$ .....

$$ = 12 + 2 + 0 + $$ .....

$$ = \left\lfloor {{{24} \over 5}} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor {{{24} \over {{5^2}}}} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor {{{24} \over {{5^3}}}} \right\rfloor + $$ ......

$$ = 4 + 0 + 0$$ ......

$$ = 4$$

$$ = \left\lfloor {{{36} \over 5}} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor {{{36} \over {{5^2}}}} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor {{{36} \over {{5^3}}}} \right\rfloor + $$ .......

$$ = 7 + 1 + 0$$ ......

$$ = 8$$

$$\therefore$$ From equation (1), exponent of 5 overall

$${{{5^{14}}} \over {{5^4}\,.\,{5^8}}}\,.\,{5^3} = {5^k}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {5^5} = {5^k}$$

$$ \Rightarrow k = 5$$

questions.solution:
Using the binomial theorem,

$$ \left(1+\frac{1}{10000}\right)^{10000} =1+1+\sum\limits_{r=2}^{10000}\binom{10000}{r}\frac{1}{10000^r}. $$

All terms in the summation are positive, so the value is greater than $2$.

Also,

$$ \binom{10000}{r}\frac{1}{10000^r}<\frac{1}{r!}. $$

Hence,

$$ \left(1+\frac{1}{10000}\right)^{10000} <2+\frac1{2!}+\frac1{3!}+\cdots<3. $$

Thus,

$$ 2<\left(1+0.0001\right)^{10000}<3. $$

So the positive integer just greater than the given number is

$$ \boxed{3} $$

Hence, Option D is correct.

questions.text: The coefficient of x 1012 in the expansion of (1 + x n + x 253 ) 10 , (where n $$ \le $$ 22 is any positive integer), is :
questions.solution:
A general term is $\dfrac{10!}{p!\,q!\,s!}x^{nq+253s}$ with $p+q+s=10$.

We need $nq+253s=1012$; as $n\le 22$, $nq\le 22\times 10=220$.

$253s\le 1012\Rightarrow s\le 4$. For $s\le 3$, $nq\ge 1012-759=253\gt 220$, which is impossible.

So $s=4$, $nq=0$, i.e. $q=0,\ p=6$.

So the coefficient is $\dfrac{10!}{6!\,4!}={}^{10}C_4$.

questions.solution:
The general term of $\left(3x^3 - 2x^2 + \dfrac{5}{x^5}\right)^{10}$ is

$$\dfrac{10!}{n_1!\,n_2!\,n_3!}\,(3x^3)^{n_1}(-2x^2)^{n_2}\left(\dfrac{5}{x^5}\right)^{n_3}, \quad n_1 + n_2 + n_3 = 10$$

The power of $x$ is $3n_1 + 2n_2 - 5n_3$. For the constant term, $3n_1 + 2n_2 = 5n_3 = 5(10 - n_1 - n_2)$, i.e. $8n_1 + 7n_2 = 50$.

Checking $n_1 = 0, 1, \ldots, 6$, the only non-negative integer solution is $n_1 = 1$, $n_2 = 6$, which gives $n_3 = 3$.

$$\text{Constant term} = \dfrac{10!}{1!\,6!\,3!}\,(3)(-2)^6(5)^3 = 840 \times 3 \times 2^6 \times 5^3$$

Since $840 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7$, the constant term is $2^9 \times \left(3^2 \times 5^4 \times 7\right) = 2^9 \cdot l$, where $l = 3^2 \times 5^4 \times 7$ is odd.

So $k = 9$.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The number of $$3 \times 3$$ non-singular matrices, with four entries as $$1$$ and all other entries as $$0$$, is :

Let $$A=\left[\begin{array}{lll}
1 & a & a \\
0 & 1 & b \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{array}\right], a, b \in \mathbb{R}$$. If for some

$$n \in \mathbb{N}, A^{n}=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}
1 & 48 & 2160 \\
0 & 1 & 96 \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{array}\right]
$$ then $$n+a+b$$ is equal to ____________.
questions.solution:
Write $A = I + B$, where

$$B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & a & a \\ 0 & 0 & b \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix},\quad B^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & ab \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix},\quad B^3 = O$$

Since $I$ and $B$ commute, the binomial expansion of $(I + B)^n$ stops after the $B^2$ term:

$$A^n = I + nB + \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}B^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & na & na + \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}ab \\ 0 & 1 & nb \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$$

Comparing with the given matrix: $na = 48$, $nb = 96$ and $na + \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}ab = 2160$.

With $a = \dfrac{48}{n}$ and $b = \dfrac{96}{n}$, so that $ab = \dfrac{4608}{n^2}$, the last equation becomes

$$48 + \dfrac{2304(n-1)}{n} = 2160 \Rightarrow 2304(n-1) = 2112n \Rightarrow 192n = 2304 \Rightarrow n = 12$$

Then $a = \dfrac{48}{12} = 4$ and $b = \dfrac{96}{12} = 8$, so $n + a + b = 12 + 4 + 8 = 24$.

Hence, the answer is 24.

Check: the product of two lower triangular matrices is lower triangular with diagonal $1\cdot1=1$, which agrees.

questions.text:
Let $$A$$ and $$B$$ be real matrices of the form $$\begin{bmatrix}\alpha & 0\\ 0 & \beta\end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\begin{bmatrix}0 & \gamma\\ \delta & 0\end{bmatrix}$$, respectively.
Statement 1: $$AB-BA$$ is always an invertible matrix.
Statement 2: $$AB-BA$$ is never an identity matrix.

options.text: Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is false, Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true; Statement 2 is a correct explanation of Statement 1.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true; Statement 2 is not a correct explanation of Statement 1.

questions.solution:
$AB=\begin{bmatrix}0&\alpha\gamma\\ \beta\delta&0\end{bmatrix}$ and $BA=\begin{bmatrix}0&\beta\gamma\\ \alpha\delta&0\end{bmatrix}$.

So $AB-BA=\begin{bmatrix}0&\gamma(\alpha-\beta)\\ \delta(\beta-\alpha)&0\end{bmatrix}$ and $|AB-BA|=\gamma\delta(\alpha-\beta)^2$.

This is $0$ whenever $\alpha=\beta$ or $\gamma\delta=0$ (for example $A=I$ gives $AB-BA=O$), so $AB-BA$ is not always invertible: Statement 1 is false.

Both diagonal entries of $AB-BA$ are always $0$, so it can never equal $I$: Statement 2 is true.

So Statement 1 is false and Statement 2 is true.

questions.text:
If   B is a 3 $$ \times $$ 3 matrix such that   B 2 = 0,

then det. [(I + B) 50 $$-$$ 50B] is equal to :
questions.solution:
$I$ (the $3\times 3$ identity matrix) and $B$ commute, so by the binomial theorem $(I+B)^{50}=I+50B+\binom{50}{2}B^2+\dots$

Since $B^2=O$, every higher power of $B$ is also $O$, so $(I+B)^{50}=I+50B$.

Hence $(I+B)^{50}-50B=I$.

So $\det[(I+B)^{50}-50B]=\det I=1$.

By direct multiplication $A^2=-I$, so $A^3=-A$ and $A^4=I$.

$A^4-I=O$ and $A^2+I=O$: true.

$A^3-I=-A-I$ and $A(A-I)=A^2-A=-I-A$: true.

$A^3+I=I-A$ and $A(A^3-I)=A^4-A=I-A$: true.

$A^2+I=O$ but $A(A^2-I)=A(-2I)=-2A\ne O$: false.

So the statement that is not correct is $A^2+I=A(A^2-I)$.

The matrix $B=\begin{bmatrix}\alpha\\\beta\end{bmatrix}$ is a non-zero $2\times1$ column, so $AB$ is defined, and $AB=B$ gives $(A-I)B=O$.

If $A-I$ were invertible, $B=(A-I)^{-1}O=O$, which is not the case; so

$$\det(A-I)=\begin{vmatrix}a-1&b\\c&d-1\end{vmatrix}=(a-1)(d-1)-bc=0.$$

Expanding, $ad-bc-(a+d)+1=0$, so

$$ad-bc=(a+d)-1=2021-1=2020.$$

Hence, the answer is 2020.

questions.solution:
Since $A$ is symmetric, $A^TA=A^2=I$. Comparing entries,

$$a^2+b^2+c^2=1,\qquad ab+bc+ca=0.$$

Then $(a+b+c)^2=1+2(0)=1$, so $a+b+c=\pm1$, and

$$a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc=(a+b+c)(a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca)=\pm1.$$

With $a^3+b^3+c^3=2$, this gives $2-3abc=\pm1$, so $abc=\dfrac13$ or $abc=1$. Only $\dfrac13$ is among the options.

Note: strictly, the given data are inconsistent. $a^2+b^2+c^2=1$ forces $|a|,|b|,|c|\le1$, so $|a^3+b^3+c^3|\le|a|^3+|b|^3+|c|^3\le a^2+b^2+c^2=1$, and $a^3+b^3+c^3=2$ cannot hold for real $a,b,c$. The intended answer, which is also NTA's key, is the one the algebra above gives.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

Let A and B be 3 $$\times$$ 3 real matrices such that A is symmetric matrix and B is skew-symmetric matrix. Then the system of linear equations (A₂B₂ $$-$$ B₂A₂ ) X = O, where X is a 3 $$\times$$ 1 column matrix of unknown variables and O is a 3 $$\times$$ 1 null matrix, has :
questions.solution:
$A^T=A$ and $B^T=-B$, so $(A^2)^T=(A^T)^2=A^2$ and $(B^2)^T=(B^T)^2=(-B)^2=B^2$.

Let $P=A^2B^2-B^2A^2$. Then

$$P^T=(B^2)^T(A^2)^T-(A^2)^T(B^2)^T=B^2A^2-A^2B^2=-P,$$

so $P$ is a $3\times 3$ skew-symmetric matrix.

For a skew-symmetric matrix of odd order, $|P|=|P^T|=|-P|=(-1)^3|P|=-|P|$, so $|P|=0$.

$PX=O$ is a homogeneous system, so it always has the solution $X=O$; since $|P|=0$, it also has non-zero solutions, and hence infinitely many solutions.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: Let $$\mathrm{A}$$ and $$\mathrm{B}$$ be any two $$3 \times 3$$ symmetric and skew symmetric matrices respectively. Then which of the following is NOT true?
questions.solution:
Given $A^T = A$ and $B^T = -B$, so $(A^n)^T = A^n$ and $(B^n)^T = (-B)^n = (-1)^n B^n$.

(A): $(A^4 - B^4)^T = A^4 - B^4$, so $A^4 - B^4$ is symmetric (true).

(B): $(AB - BA)^T = B^T A^T - A^T B^T = -BA + AB = AB - BA$, so $AB - BA$ is symmetric (true).

(D): $(AB + BA)^T = B^T A^T + A^T B^T = -BA - AB = -(AB + BA)$, so $AB + BA$ is skew-symmetric (true).

(C): $(B^5 - A^5)^T = -B^5 - A^5$, while $-(B^5 - A^5) = -B^5 + A^5$. These are equal only when $A^5 = O$; for $A = I$ they differ, so $B^5 - A^5$ is not skew-symmetric in general (not true).

Hence, the correct option is (C).

If $$A^T$$ denotes the transpose of the matrix $$A=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&a\\0&b&c\\d&e&f\end{bmatrix}$$, where $$a,b,c,d,e$$ and $$f$$ are integers such that $$abd\neq 0$$, then the number of such matrices for which $$A^{-1}=A^T$$ is
questions.solution:
$A^{-1}=A^T$ means $AA^T=I$: the rows of $A$ are unit vectors, perpendicular to each other.

Row 1 $(0,0,a)$: $a^2=1$. Rows 1 and 2: $ac=0\Rightarrow c=0$, then $b^2+c^2=1\Rightarrow b^2=1$.

Rows 1 and 3: $af=0\Rightarrow f=0$; rows 2 and 3: $be+cf=be=0\Rightarrow e=0$.

Then $d^2+e^2+f^2=1\Rightarrow d^2=1$.

So $a,b,d\in\{1,-1\}$ and $c=e=f=0$, giving $2\times2\times2$ matrices.

So the number of such matrices is $2^3=8$.

Let $M=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\0&2&3\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}$ and $P=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&1\\1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix}$, so $AM=P$.

Then $A=PM^{-1}$, hence $A^{-1}=MP^{-1}$.

$P$ is a permutation matrix, so $P^{-1}=P^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&1\\1&0&0\end{bmatrix}$.

Multiplying, $MP^{T}$ has rows $(3,1,2)$, $(3,0,2)$, $(1,0,1)$; check: this matrix times $P$ gives back $M$.

So $A^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}3&1&2\\3&0&2\\1&0&1\end{bmatrix}$.

questions.text: The number of matrices $$A=\left(\begin{array}{ll}a & b \\ c & d\end{array}\right)$$, where $$a, b, c, d \in\{-1,0,1,2,3, \ldots \ldots, 10\}$$, such that $$A=A^{-1}$$, is ___________.
questions.solution:
$A = A^{-1}$ means $A^2 = I$:

$$A^2 = \begin{pmatrix} a^2 + bc & b(a + d) \\ c(a + d) & d^2 + bc \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$$

If $a + d \ne 0$, then $b = c = 0$ and $a^2 = d^2 = 1$ with $a = d$, giving $a = d = 1$ or $a = d = -1$: 2 matrices.

If $a + d = 0$, then $d = -a$ must also lie in $\{-1, 0, 1, \ldots, 10\}$, so $a \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$, and $a^2 + bc = 1$.

For $a = d = 0$: $bc = 1$, so $(b, c) = (1, 1)$ or $(-1, -1)$: 2 matrices.

For $(a, d) = (1, -1)$ or $(-1, 1)$: $bc = 0$, and with 12 values available for each entry the pairs with $b = 0$ or $c = 0$ number $12 + 12 - 1 = 23$, giving $2 \times 23 = 46$ matrices.

Total $= 2 + 2 + 46 = 50$.

Hence, the answer is 50.

questions.solution:
Let $A$ have rows $(a, b)$ and $(c, d)$. Then $A^2 = I$ gives $a^2 + bc = 1$, $d^2 + bc = 1$, $b(a + d) = 0$, $c(a + d) = 0$.

If $a + d \ne 0$, then $b = c = 0$, $a^2 = d^2 = 1$ and $a = d = \pm 1$, i.e. $A = \pm I$, which is excluded.

So $a + d = 0$, i.e. $\mathrm{Tr}(A) = 0$: Statement 1 is true.

With $d = -a$, $\det A = ad - bc = -(a^2 + bc) = -1$: Statement 2 is true.

Statement 1 follows from the off-diagonal entries of $A^2 = I$, not from $\det A = -1$.

So both statements are true, but Statement 2 is not a correct explanation of Statement 1.

questions.solution:
Expanding along the first row,

$$\begin{vmatrix} 0 & \cos x & -\sin x \\ \sin x & 0 & \cos x \\ \cos x & \sin x & 0 \end{vmatrix} = -\cos x\,(0 - \cos^2 x) - \sin x\,(\sin^2 x - 0) = \cos^3 x - \sin^3 x$$

$\cos^3 x - \sin^3 x = (\cos x - \sin x)(1 + \sin x \cos x)$ and $1 + \sin x \cos x = 1 + \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x > 0$, so the determinant vanishes only when $\tan x = 1$.

In $[0, 2\pi]$, $S = \left\{\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right\}$.

$$\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} + \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) = \dfrac{\sqrt{3} + 1}{1 - \sqrt{3}} = \dfrac{(\sqrt{3} + 1)^2}{1 - 3} = -2 - \sqrt{3}$$

Since $\tan$ has period $\pi$, $\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} + \dfrac{5\pi}{4}\right) = -2 - \sqrt{3}$ as well.

$$\sum\limits_{x \in S} \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} + x\right) = 2\left(-2 - \sqrt{3}\right) = -4 - 2\sqrt{3}$$

Hence, the correct option is (D).

Let p and p + 2 be prime numbers and let

$$
\Delta=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\mathrm{p} ! & (\mathrm{p}+1) ! & (\mathrm{p}+2) ! \\

(\mathrm{p}+2) ! & (\mathrm{p}+3) ! & (\mathrm{p}+4) !
\end{array}\right|
$$

Then the sum of the maximum values of $$\alpha$$ and $$\beta$$, such that $$\mathrm{p}^{\alpha}$$ and $$(\mathrm{p}+2)^{\beta}$$ divide $$\Delta$$, is __________.

questions.solution:
$A$ is $2\times 3$ and $B$ is $3\times 2$, so $AB$ is $2\times 2$:

$$AB = \begin{bmatrix} 2+2+4\alpha & \alpha-4-5\alpha \\ 2\alpha-2-4 & \alpha^2+4+5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4\alpha+4 & -4\alpha-4 \\ 2\alpha-6 & \alpha^2+9 \end{bmatrix}.$$

$$\det(AB) = (4\alpha+4)(\alpha^2+9) + (4\alpha+4)(2\alpha-6) = 4(\alpha+1)(\alpha^2+2\alpha+3).$$

$\det(AB) = 0$ gives $\alpha = -1$ or $\alpha^2+2\alpha+3 = 0$. The quadratic has discriminant $4-12 < 0$, so its two roots are non-real complex numbers (allowed, since $\alpha \in \mathbb{C}$) with sum $-2$.

Sum of all values of $\alpha$ $= -1 + (-2) = -3$, whose absolute value is $3$.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

Statement 2: A system of three homogeneous equations in three variables has a non trivial solution if the determinant of the coefficient matrix is zero.

options.text: Statement 1 is false, Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is a correct explanation for Statement 1.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is not a correct explanation for Statement 1.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is false.

questions.solution:
Statement 2 is the standard result: a homogeneous system has a nontrivial solution when the determinant of its coefficients is $0$. So Statement 2 is true.

For this system the condition is $\begin{vmatrix}1&k&3\\3&k&-2\\2&3&-4\end{vmatrix}=0$.

Expanding: $1(-4k+6)-k(-12+4)+3(9-2k)=-4k+6+8k+27-6k=33-2k$.

So $k=\dfrac{33}{2}$, not $\dfrac{31}{2}$.

Check: with $k=\dfrac{31}{2}$ the determinant is $33-31=2\neq 0$, so only the trivial solution exists; Statement 1 is false.

So Statement 1 is false and Statement 2 is true.

questions.text:
Consider the system of equations:

x + ay = 0, y + az = 0 and z + ax = 0. Then the set of all real values of 'a' for which the system has a unique solution is
questions.solution:
The system is homogeneous, so it has a unique (the trivial) solution exactly when the coefficient determinant $\Delta \ne 0$.

The rows of the coefficient matrix are $(1, a, 0)$, $(0, 1, a)$, $(a, 0, 1)$.

Expanding along the first row, $\Delta = 1(1 - 0) - a(0 - a^2) + 0 = 1 + a^3$.

$\Delta = 0 \Leftrightarrow a^3 = -1 \Leftrightarrow a = -1$ for real $a$.

So the required set is $\mathbb{R} - \{-1\}$.

Statement 1: The system of linear equations

x + (sin $$\alpha $$) y + (cos $$\alpha $$) z = 0

x - (sin $$\alpha $$) y - (cos $$\alpha $$) z = 0

has a non-trivial solution for only one value of $$\alpha $$ lying in the interval $$\left( {0,{\pi \over 2}} \right)$$

Statement 2: The equation in $$\alpha $$

$$\left| {\matrix{
{\cos \alpha } & {\sin \alpha } & {\cos \alpha } \cr
{\sin \alpha } & {\cos \alpha } & {\sin \alpha } \cr
{\cos \alpha } & { - \sin \alpha } & { - \cos \alpha } \cr

} } \right| = 0$$

has only one solution lying in the interval $$\left( {0,{\pi \over 2}} \right)$$

options.text: Statement 1 is true; Statement 2 is true; Statement 2 is not correct explanation for Statement 1
Statement 1 is true; Statement 2 is true; Statement 2 is correct explanation for Statement 1
Statement 1 is true; Statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; Statement 2 is true

questions.solution:
Statement 1: the homogeneous system has a non-trivial solution iff its coefficient determinant $\Delta_1 = 0$.

With $R_2 \to R_2 - R_1$, $R_3 \to R_3 - R_1$ and expanding along the first column, $\Delta_1 = -2\cos\alpha(\cos\alpha - \sin\alpha) + 2\sin\alpha(\sin\alpha - \cos\alpha) = -2\cos 2\alpha$.

In $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $\cos 2\alpha = 0$ only at $\alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so Statement 1 is true.

Statement 2: with $C_1 \to C_1 - C_3$ the first column becomes $(0, 0, 2\cos\alpha)$, so the determinant $= 2\cos\alpha(\sin^2\alpha - \cos^2\alpha) = -2\cos\alpha\cos 2\alpha$.

As $\cos\alpha \ne 0$ in $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, its only root there is $\alpha = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so Statement 2 is also true.

But this determinant is not the coefficient determinant of the system, so Statement 2 is not the reason Statement 1 holds.

So both statements are true, and Statement 2 is not a correct explanation of Statement 1.

If the system of linear equations:

x 1 + 2x 2 + 3x 3 = 6

x 1 + 3x 2 + 5x 3 = 9

2x 1 + 5x 2 + ax 3 = b

is consistent and has infinite number of solutions, then:

options.text: a = 8, b can be any real number
b = 15, a can be any real number

questions.solution:
Subtracting the first equation from the second: $x_2 + 2x_3 = 3$; adding them: $2x_1 + 5x_2 + 8x_3 = 15$.

Subtracting this from the third equation: $(a - 8)x_3 = b - 15$.

If $a \ne 8$, $x_3$ is fixed and the solution is unique; if $a = 8$ and $b \ne 15$, there is no solution.

Check: the determinant of coefficients is $3a - 25 - 2(a - 10) - 3 = a - 8$, which is $0$ only for $a = 8$.

So the system has infinitely many solutions exactly when $a = 8$ and $b = 15$.

For non-zero solution

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$\left| {\matrix{

$$ \therefore $$ $${1 \over a},{1 \over b},{1 \over c}$$ are in A.P.

x + (cos $$\gamma$$)y + (cos $$\beta$$)z = 0

(cos $$\gamma$$)x + y + (cos $$\alpha$$)z = 0

(cos $$\beta$$)x + (cos $$\alpha$$)y + z = 0

questions.solution:
Given $$\alpha$$ + $$\beta$$ + $$\gamma$$ = 2$$\pi$$

$$\Delta = \left| {\matrix{
1 & {\cos \gamma } & {\cos \beta } \cr
{\cos \gamma } & 1 & {\cos \alpha } \cr
{\cos \beta } & {\cos \alpha } & 1 \cr

} } \right|$$

$$ = 1 - {\cos ^2}\alpha - \cos \gamma (\cos \gamma - \cos \alpha \cos \beta ) + \cos \beta (\cos \alpha \cos \gamma - \cos \beta )$$

$$ = 1 - {\cos ^2}\alpha - {\cos ^2}\beta - {\cos ^2}\gamma + 2\cos \alpha \cos \beta \cos \gamma $$

$$ = {\sin ^2}\alpha - {\cos ^2}\beta - \cos \gamma (\cos \gamma - 2\cos \alpha \cos \beta )$$

$$ = - \cos (\alpha + \beta )\cos (\alpha - \beta ) - \cos \gamma (\cos (2\pi - (\alpha - \beta )) - 2\cos \alpha \cos \beta )$$

$$ = - \cos (2\pi - \gamma )\cos (\alpha - \beta ) - \cos \gamma (\cos (\alpha + \beta ) - 2\cos \alpha \cos \beta )$$

$$ = - \cos \gamma \cos (\alpha - \beta ) + \cos \gamma (\cos \alpha \cos \beta + \sin \alpha \sin \beta )$$

$$ = - \cos \gamma \cos (\alpha - \beta ) + \cos \gamma \cos (\alpha - \beta )$$

$$ = 0$$

So, the system of equation has infinitely many solutions.

questions.text:
Let [$$\lambda$$] be the greatest integer less than or equal to $$\lambda$$. The set of all values of $$\lambda$$ for which the system of linear equations
x + y + z = 4,
3x + 2y + 5z = 3,
9x + 4y + (28 + [$$\lambda$$])z = [$$\lambda$$] has a solution is :
questions.solution:
Let $k = [\lambda]$, an integer. The determinant of coefficients is

$$D = \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 5 \\ 9 & 4 & 28+k \end{vmatrix} = (36 + 2k) - (39 + 3k) + (12 - 18) = -(k + 9)$$

If $k \ne -9$, then $D \ne 0$ and the system has a unique solution.

If $k = -9$, the third equation is $9x + 4y + 19z = -9$. Writing $E_1: x + y + z = 4$ and $E_2: 3x + 2y + 5z = 3$, the combination $5E_2 - 6E_1$ gives $9x + 4y + 19z = 15 - 24 = -9$, which is exactly the third equation. The system then reduces to the two independent equations $E_1$ and $E_2$ and has infinitely many solutions.

So a solution exists for every integer value of $[\lambda]$, that is, for every real $\lambda$, and the required set is $\mathbb{R}$.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

$x-y-3z=2$

has infinitely many solutions, then the equation of the line passing through the points $(\lambda+2\mu,\ 2\lambda+\mu)$ and $(1,\ \lambda\mu)$ is
questions.solution:
For infinitely many solutions, $\Delta=\begin{vmatrix}\lambda&1&-1\\1&-1&-3\\-1&1&1\end{vmatrix}=2\lambda+2=0\Rightarrow\lambda=-1$.

With $\lambda=-1$: adding the first two equations gives $-4z=1$; adding the last two gives $-2z=2+\mu$.

Consistency: $z=-\dfrac{1}{4}\Rightarrow 2+\mu=\dfrac{1}{2}\Rightarrow\mu=-\dfrac{3}{2}$.

Points: $(\lambda+2\mu,\,2\lambda+\mu)=\left(-4,-\dfrac{7}{2}\right)$ and $(1,\lambda\mu)=\left(1,\dfrac{3}{2}\right)$; slope $=\dfrac{\frac{3}{2}+\frac{7}{2}}{1+4}=1$.

Line: $y-\dfrac{3}{2}=x-1\Rightarrow 2x-2y=-1$.

If $A$ were invertible, $B=A^{-1}(AB)=A^{-1}O=O$, contradicting $B\neq O$; so $|A|=0$. Similarly, if $B$ were invertible, $A=(AB)B^{-1}=O$; so $|B|=0$ and (
C) is false.

Since $AB=O$ and $B\neq O$, any non-zero column $X_0$ of $B$ satisfies $AX_0=O$, and so does every $kX_0$. The homogeneous system $AX=O$ therefore has infinitely many solutions: (
A) is false and (
B) is true.

For a $3\times3$ matrix, $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^{2}=0$, so $\operatorname{adj}A$ is not invertible and (
D) is false.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

The number of $$\theta \in(0,4 \pi)$$ for which the system of linear equations

&3(\cos 2 \theta) x+4 y+3 z=3 \\\\
&6 x+7 y+7 z=9
\end{aligned}

questions.solution:
Given,

$$3(\sin 3\theta )x - y + z = 2$$

$$3(\cos 2\theta )x + 4y + 3z = 3$$

$$6x + 7y + 7z = 9$$

For no solutions determinant of coefficient will be = 0

$$\therefore$$ $$D = \left| {\matrix{
{3\sin 3\theta } & { - 1} & 1 \cr
{3\cos 2\theta } & 4 & 3 \cr
6 & 7 & 7 \cr

} } \right| = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow 3\sin 3\theta (28 - 21) + 1(21\cos 2\theta - 18) + 1(21\cos 2\theta - 24) = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow 21\sin 3\theta + 42\cos 2\theta - 42 = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow \sin 3\theta + 2\cos 2\theta - 2 = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow 3\sin \theta - 4{\sin ^3}\theta + 2(1 - 2{\sin ^2}\theta ) - 2 = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow 3\sin \theta - 4{\sin ^3}\theta - 4{\sin ^2}\theta = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow 4{\sin ^3}\theta + 4{\sin ^2}\theta - 3\sin \theta = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow \sin \theta (4{\sin ^2}\theta + 4\sin \theta - 3) = 0$$

$$\therefore$$ $$\sin \theta = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow \theta = \pi ,2\pi ,3\pi $$ when $$\theta \in (0,4\pi )$$

or,

$$4{\sin ^2}\theta + 4\sin \theta - 3 = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow 4{\sin ^2}\theta + 6\sin \theta - 2\sin \theta - 3 = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow 2\sin \theta (2\sin \theta + 3) - 1(2\sin \theta + 3) = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow (2\sin \theta - 1)(2\sin \theta + 3) = 0$$

$$\therefore$$ $$\sin \theta = {1 \over 2}$$

or,

$$\sin \theta = - {3 \over 2}$$ [not possible as $$\sin \in [ - 1,1]$$]

$$\therefore$$ $$\sin \theta = {1 \over 2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \theta = {\pi \over 6},{{5\pi } \over 6},{{13\pi } \over 6},{{17\pi } \over 6}$$

$$\therefore$$ Possible values of $$\theta = \pi ,2\pi ,3\pi ,{\pi \over 6},{{5\pi } \over 6},{{13\pi } \over 6},{{17\pi } \over 6}$$

$$\therefore$$ Total 7 values of $$\theta$$ possible.

questions.text:
If the system of linear equations

2x + y $$-$$ z = 7

x $$-$$ 3y + 2z = 1

x + 4y + $$\delta$$z = k, where $$\delta$$, k $$\in$$ R has infinitely many solutions, then $$\delta$$ + k is equal to:
questions.solution:
$$2x + y - z = 7$$

$$x - 3y + 2z = 1$$

$$x + 4y + \delta z = k$$

$$\Delta = \left| {\matrix{
2 & 1 & { - 1} \cr
1 & { - 3} & 2 \cr
1 & 4 & \delta \cr

} } \right| = - 7\delta - 21 = 0$$

$$\delta = - 3$$

$${\Delta _1} = \left| {\matrix{
7 & 1 & { - 1} \cr
1 & { - 3} & 2 \cr
k & 4 & { - 3} \cr

} } \right|$$

$$ \Rightarrow 6 - k = 0 \Rightarrow k = 6$$

$$\delta + k = - 3 + 6 = 3$$

of | 9$$\alpha$$ + 3$$\beta$$ + 5$$\gamma$$ | is equal to ____________.
questions.solution:
If 2x $$-$$ 3y = $$\gamma$$ + 5 and $$\alpha$$x + 5y = $$\beta$$ + 1 have infinitely many solutions then

$${2 \over \alpha } = {{ - 3} \over 5} = {{\gamma + 5} \over {\beta + 1}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \alpha = - {{10} \over 3}$$ and $$3\beta + 5\gamma = - 28$$

So $$|9\alpha + 3\beta + 5\gamma | = | - 30 - 28| = 58$$

If the system of linear equations

$$2x + 3y - z = - 2$$

$$x + y + z = 4$$

$$x - y + |\lambda |z = 4\lambda - 4$$

where, $$\lambda$$ $$\in$$ R, has no solution, then
questions.solution:
$$\Delta = \left| {\matrix{
2 & 3 & { - 1} \cr
1 & 1 & 1 \cr
1 & { - 1} & {|\lambda |} \cr

} } \right| = 0 \Rightarrow |\lambda | = 7$$

But at $$\lambda = 7,\,{D_x} = {D_y} = {D_z} = 0$$

$${P_1}:2x + 3y - z = - 2$$

$${P_2}:x + y + z = 4$$

$${P_3}:x - y + |\lambda |z = 4\lambda - 4$$

So clearly $$5{P_2} - 2{P_1} = {P_3}$$, so at $$\lambda = 7$$, system of equation is having infinite solutions.

So $$\lambda = - 7$$ is correct answer.

Let the system of linear equations
$$x + 2y + z = 2$$,
$$\alpha x + 3y - z = \alpha $$,
$$ - \alpha x + y + 2z = - \alpha $$
be inconsistent. Then $$\alpha$$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
$$x + 2y + z = 2$$

$$\alpha x + 3y - z = \alpha $$

$$ - \alpha x + y + 2z = - \alpha $$

$$\Delta = \left| {\matrix{
1 & 2 & 1 \cr
\alpha & 3 & { - 1} \cr
{ - \alpha } & 1 & 2 \cr

} } \right| = 1(6 + 1) - 2(2\alpha - \alpha ) + 1(\alpha + 3\alpha )$$

$$ = 7 + 2\alpha $$

$$\Delta = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha = - {7 \over 2}$$

$${\Delta _1} = \left| {\matrix{
2 & 2 & 1 \cr
\alpha & 3 & { - 1} \cr
{ - \alpha } & 1 & 2 \cr

} } \right| = 14 + 2\alpha \ne 0$$ for $$\alpha = - {7 \over 2}$$

$$\therefore$$ For no solution $$\alpha = - {7 \over 2}$$

If the system of equations

$$\alpha$$x + y + z = 5, x + 2y + 3z = 4, x + 3y + 5z = $$\beta$$

has infinitely many solutions, then the ordered pair ($$\alpha$$, $$\beta$$) is equal to :
questions.solution:
Given system of equations

$$\alpha x + y + z = 5$$

$$x + 2y + 3z = 4$$, has infinite solution

$$x + 3y + 5z = \beta $$

$$\therefore$$ $$\Delta = \left| {\matrix{
\alpha & 1 & 1 \cr
1 & 2 & 3 \cr
1 & 3 & 5 \cr

} } \right| = 0 \Rightarrow \alpha (1) - 1(2) + 1(1) = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow \alpha = 1$$

and $${\Delta _1} = \left| {\matrix{
5 & 1 & 1 \cr
4 & 2 & 3 \cr
\beta & 3 & 5 \cr

} } \right| = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow 5(1) - 1(20 - 3\beta ) + 1(12 - 2\beta ) = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow \beta = 3$$

and $${\Delta _2} = \left| {\matrix{
1 & 5 & 1 \cr
1 & 4 & 3 \cr
1 & \beta & 5 \cr

} } \right| = 0 \Rightarrow (20 - 3\beta ) - 5(2) + 1(\beta - 4) = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow - 2\beta + 6 = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow \beta = 3$$

Similarly,

$$ \Rightarrow {\Delta _3} = \left| {\matrix{
1 & 1 & 5 \cr
1 & 2 & 4 \cr
1 & 3 & \beta \cr

} } \right| = 0 \Rightarrow \beta = 3$$

$$\therefore$$ ($$\alpha$$, $$\beta$$) = (1, 3)

The ordered pair (a, b), for which the system of linear equations

3x $$-$$ 2y + z = b

5x $$-$$ 8y + 9z = 3

2x + y + az = $$-$$1

has no solution, is :
questions.solution:
$$\left| {\matrix{
3 & { - 2} & 1 \cr
5 & { - 8} & 9 \cr
2 & 1 & a \cr

} } \right| = 0 \Rightarrow - 14a - 42 = 0 \Rightarrow a = - 3$$

Now 3 (equation (1)) $$-$$ (equation (2)) $$-$$ 2 (equation (3)) is

$$3(3x - 2y + z - b) - (5x - 8y + 9z - 3) - 2(2x + y + az + 1) = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow - 3b + 3 - 2 = 0 \Rightarrow b = {1 \over 3}$$

So for no solution $$a = - 3$$ and $$b \ne {1 \over 3}$$

questions.text:
Let the system of linear equations

x + y + $$\alpha$$z = 2

3x + y + z = 4

x + 2z = 1

have a unique solution (x$$^ * $$, y$$^ * $$, z$$^ * $$). If ($$\alpha$$, x$$^ * $$), (y$$^ * $$, $$\alpha$$) and (x$$^ * $$, $$-$$y$$^ * $$) are collinear points, then the sum of absolute values of all possible values of $$\alpha$$ is
questions.solution:
The coefficient determinant is

$$\Delta=\begin{vmatrix}1&1&\alpha\\3&1&1\\1&0&2\end{vmatrix}=1(2-0)-1(6-1)+\alpha(0-1)=-3-\alpha,$$

so a unique solution requires $\alpha\neq-3$.

Subtracting the first equation from the second gives $2x+(1-\alpha)z=2$, and the third gives $x=1-2z$. Then $2-4z+(1-\alpha)z=2$, i.e. $-(3+\alpha)z=0$, so $z^*=0$, $x^*=1$, and the second equation gives $y^*=4-3=1$.

The points $(\alpha,1)$, $(1,\alpha)$ and $(1,-1)$ are collinear, so

$$\begin{vmatrix}\alpha&1&1\\1&\alpha&1\\1&-1&1\end{vmatrix}=\alpha(\alpha+1)-1(1-1)+1(-1-\alpha)=\alpha^2-1=0.$$

Thus $\alpha=\pm1$, both different from $-3$, and the sum of the absolute values is $1+1=2$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

x + 3$$\alpha$$y + 5z = 4

is inconsistent, is
questions.solution:
$\Delta=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 1 & 1 \\ \alpha & 2 \alpha & 3 \\ 1 & 3 \alpha & 5\end{array}\right|$

$$
\begin{aligned}
&=1(10 \alpha-9 \alpha)-1(5 \alpha-3)+1\left(3 \alpha^{2}-2 \alpha\right) \\\\
&=\alpha-5 \alpha+3+3 \alpha^{2}-2 \alpha \\\\
&=3 \alpha^{2}-6 \alpha+3
\end{aligned}
$$

For inconsistency $\Delta=0$ i.e. $\alpha=1$

Now check for $\alpha=1$

$$
x+y+z=1\quad\quad...(i)
$$

$x+2 y+3 z=-1\quad\quad...(ii)$

$x+3 y+5 z=4\quad\quad...(iii)$

By (ii) $\times 2-$ (i) $\times 1$

$$
x+3 y+5 z=-3
$$

so equations are inconsistent for $\alpha=1$

questions.text:
Statement 1: If $$A$$ and $$B$$ be two sets having $$p$$ and $$q$$ elements respectively, where $$q\gt p$$. Then the total number of functions from set $$A$$ to set $$B$$ is $$q^{p}$$.
Statement 2: The total number of selections of $$p$$ different objects out of $$q$$ objects is $${}^{q}C_{p}$$.

options.text: Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is false.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true; Statement 2 is not a correct explanation of Statement 1.
Statement 1 is false, Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true; Statement 2 is a correct explanation of Statement 1.

questions.solution:
Statement 2 is the standard count of selections: $p$ different objects can be chosen out of $q$ in ${}^{q}C_{p}$ ways, so it is true.

To form a function from $A$ to $B$, each of the $p$ elements of $A$ selects its image from the $q$ elements of $B$.

By Statement 2 with one object selected, each element has ${}^{q}C_{1}=q$ choices, and the $p$ choices are independent.

So the number of functions is $q\times q\times\cdots\times q=q^{p}$, and Statement 1 is true.

Statement 1 is obtained by using the selection count of Statement 2 for each element, so both statements are true and Statement 2 is a correct explanation of Statement 1.

questions.text: 5 - digit numbers are to be formed using 2, 3, 5, 7, 9 without repeating the digits. If p be the number of such numbers that exceed 20000 and q be the number of those that lie between 30000 and 90000, then p : q is :
questions.solution:
The smallest number formed with the digits 2, 3, 5, 7, 9 is $23579 \gt 20000$, so all such numbers exceed 20000: $p = 5! = 120$.

A number between 30000 and 90000 must begin with 3, 5 or 7, and the other four digits can be arranged in $4!$ ways: $q = 3 \times 4! = 72$.

So $p : q = 120 : 72 = 5 : 3$.

The total number of 3-digit numbers, whose

Let xyz is 3 digits number.

and if 8-character long $$ = {10^8} - {5^8}$$

Number of password $$ = ({10^6} + {10^7} + {10^8}) - ({5^6} + {5^7} + {5^8})$$

$$ = {5^6}(64 + 640 + 6400 - 31)$$

$$ = 7073 \times {5^6}$$

$$\therefore$$ $$\alpha = 7073$$.

questions.text: The letters of the word 'MANKIND' are written in all possible orders and arranged in serial order as in an English dictionary. Then the serial number of the word 'MANKIND' is _____________.
questions.solution:
Step 1 :

Write all the alphabets in alphabetical order.

Step 2 :

Give a number to each alphabet starting from 0 in alphabetical order.

Step 3 :

In word "MANKIND" first alphabet is "M" which is present in the 4 th position in the Alphabet Box. And after "M", in the word "MANKIND" there are 6 alphabets "ANKIND" which can be arrange in $${{6!} \over {2!}}$$ ways. Here $$2!$$ present because two N presents.

So for alphabet "M" we write $$4.{{6!} \over {2!}}$$

Step 4 :

As in word "MANKIND" we calculated "M", so delete "M" from alphabet box and check remaining alphabets got right numbers or not in alphabet box.

As you can see after deleting "M", 4 th position in the alphabet box is missing so we create a new alphabet box.

Step 5 :

Now next alphabet after "M" in word "MANKIND" is "A" which is present in the 0 th position in the new alphabet box. And after "A" in the word "MANKIND" there are 5 alphabets "NKIND" which can be arrange in $${{5!} \over {2!}}$$ ways.

So, for alphabet "A" we write $$0.{{5!} \over {2!}}$$

Step 6 :

Now in word "MANKIND" we calculated "A", so delete "A" from previous new alphabet box and check remaining alphabets got right numbers or not in alphabet box.

As you can see after deleting "A", 0 th position in the alphabet box is missing, so we have to create a new alphabet box.

Step 7 :

Now next alphabet after "A" in word "MANKIND" is "N" which is present in the 3 rd and 4 th position in the alphabet box. We have to choose minimum position for "N" in the alphabet box. So, we choose 3 rd position "N". And after "N" in the word "MANKIND" there are 4 alphabets "KIND" which can be arrange $${{4!} \over {2!}}$$ ways. Here $$2!$$ used because of 2 N's (one "N" is that "N" which we are considering and other "N" which is present in the word "KIND")

So for alphabet "N" we write $$3\, \times \,{{4!} \over {2!}}$$

Step 8 :

Now in word "MANKIND" we calculated "N", so delete 3 rd "N" from alphabet box and check remaining alphabets got right number or not in alphabet box. As you can see after deleting 3 rd "N", 3 rd position is missing in the alphabet box so we have to create a new alphabet box.

Step 9 :

Now next alphabet after "N" in word "MANKIND" is "K" which is present at the 2 nd position in the new alphabet box. And after "K" in the word "MANKIND" there are 3 alphabets "IND" which we can arrange $$3!$$ ways.

So for alphabet "K" we write $$2\times3!$$

Step 10 :

Now, in word "MANKIND" we calculated "K", so delete "K" from alphabet box and check remaining alphabets got right number or not in alphabet box. As you can see after deleting "K", 2 nd position in the alphabet box is missing so we have to create a new alphabet box.

Step 11 :

Now next alphabet after "K" in word "MANKIND" is "I" which is present at 1 st position in the new alphabet box. And after "I" in the word "MANKIND" there are 2 alphabets "ND" which we can arrange in $$2!$$ ways.

So for alphabet "I" we write $$1\times2!$$

Step 12 :

Now in word "MANKIND" we calculated "I", so delete "I" from alphabet box and check remaining alphabets got right numbers or not in alphabet box. As you can see after deleting "I", 1 st position in the alphabet box is missing so we have to create a new alphabet box.

Step 13 :

Now next alphabet after "I" in word "MANKIND" is "N" which is present at 1 st position in the new alphabet box. And after "N" in the word "MANKIND" there is 1 alphabet "D" which we can arrange in $$1!$$ ways.

So for alphabet "N" we write $$1\times1!$$.

Step 14 :

Now in word "MANKIND" we calculated "N", so delete "N" from alphabet box and check remaining alphabets got right numbering or not in alphabet box. As you can see after deleting "N", remaining alphabet "D" got correct numbering so new alphabet box will be same.

Step 15 :

Now next alphabet after "N" in word "MANKIND" is "D" which is present at the 0 th position in the new alphabet box. And after "D" in the word "MANKIND" there is no alphabet so it is the last alphabet.

So for last alphabet we always write $$0!$$

$$\therefore$$ Position of the word "MANKIND" in the dictionary

$$ = 4\,.\,{{6!} \over {2!}} + 0\,.\,{{5!} \over {2!}} + 3\,.\,{{4!} \over {2!}} + 2\,.\,3!\, + 1\,.\,2!\, + \,1\,.\,1!\, + \,0!$$

$$ = 1440 + 0 + 36 + 12 + 2 + 1 + 1$$

$$ = 1492$$

questions.text: Numbers greater than 1000 but less than 4000 are formed using the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 (repetition allowed). Their number is :
questions.solution:
We need to find the total number of integers that are greater than $1000$ and less than $4000$, using the given digits $0, 1, 2, 3,$ and $4$. Notice that all such numbers will be $4$-digit numbers.

Let us imagine four vacant places representing the thousands, hundreds, tens, and units places of our $4$-digit number.

First, let us look at the thousands place. Since the number has to be greater than $1000$ and less than $4000$, the thousands place cannot be filled by $0$ (as that would make it a $3$-digit number) and it cannot be filled by $4$ (as the smallest number starting with $4$ is $4000$, and we need numbers strictly less than $4000$). So, the thousands place can only be filled using the digits $1, 2,$ or $3$. This gives us $3$ ways to fill the thousands place.

Since repetition of digits is allowed, we can use any of the five given digits ($0, 1, 2, 3, 4$) for the remaining places.

The hundreds place can be filled in $5$ ways.

The tens place can be filled in $5$ ways.

The units place can also be filled in $5$ ways.

By the fundamental principle of counting, the total number of $4$-digit numbers we can form this way is:

$$\text{Total numbers} = 3 \times 5 \times 5 \times 5 = 375$$

Now, we must be very careful about one small detail. The question asks for numbers greater than $1000$.

In our calculation of $375$ numbers, the smallest number formed is when we choose $1$ for the thousands place and $0$ for the hundreds, tens, and units places. This gives the number $1000$ itself. Since the number must be strictly greater than $1000$, we have to exclude the number $1000$ from our count.

So, we subtract $1$ from the total numbers we found:

$$\text{Required numbers} = 375 - 1 = 374$$

Hence, the correct option is Option C .

questions.text: How many different words can be formed by jumbling the letters in the word MISSISSIPPI in which no two S are adjacent?

Here, I = 4 times, S = 4 times, P = 2 times, M = 1 time

_M_I_I_I_I_P_P_

Those seven letters M, I, I, I, I, P, P can be arranged in $${{7!} \over {4!2!}}$$ ways

Those seven letters creates 8 gaps and we have to choose 4 gaps from those 8 gaps to put those four 'S' letters.

This can be done $${}^8{C_4}$$ ways.

After placing those four 'S' letters we can arrange them in $${{4!} \over {4!}}$$ ways.

Therefore, required number of words

$$ = {{7!} \over {4!2!}} \times {}^8{C_4} \times {{4!} \over {4!}}$$

$$ = {{7\,.\,6!} \over {4!2!}} \times {}^8{C_4}$$

questions.text:
The number of 6 digit numbers that can be formed using the digits 0, 1, 2, 5, 7 and 9 which are divisible by
11 and no digit is repeated is :
questions.solution:
All six digits 0, 1, 2, 5, 7, 9 are used once; write the number as $a_1a_2a_3a_4a_5a_6$. It is divisible by 11 when $(a_1 + a_3 + a_5) - (a_2 + a_4 + a_6)$ is a multiple of 11.

The two sums add up to $0 + 1 + 2 + 5 + 7 + 9 = 24$, so their difference is even and can only be $0$ or $\pm 22$. A difference of 22 needs a triple with sum 1, which is impossible (the smallest triple sum is $0 + 1 + 2 = 3$). So each triple has sum 12.

The triple containing 0 needs two digits adding to 12, which only 5 and 7 do. The only split is $\{0, 5, 7\}$ and $\{1, 2, 9\}$.

$\{1, 2, 9\}$ in the odd places and $\{0, 5, 7\}$ in the even places: $3! \times 3! = 36$ numbers.

$\{0, 5, 7\}$ in the odd places: $a_1 \neq 0$ gives 2 choices for $a_1$, then 2 ways for $a_3, a_5$, and $3!$ ways for the even places: $2 \times 2 \times 6 = 24$ numbers.

Total $= 36 + 24 = 60$.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

Total $= 216 + 72 + 18 + 4 = 310$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: All the arrangements, with or without meaning, of the word FARMER are written excluding any word that has two R appearing together. The arrangements are listed serially in the alphabetic order as in the English dictionary. Then the serial number of the word FARMER in this list is ___________.
questions.solution:
The letters of FARMER in alphabetical order are A, E, F, M, R, R, and a word is left out when its two R's are adjacent.

Words beginning with A: the letters E, F, M, R, R give $\dfrac{5!}{2!} = 60$ arrangements, of which $4! = 24$ have the two R's together (RR taken as one block). This leaves $60 - 24 = 36$.

Words beginning with E: in the same way, $36$.

Words beginning with FAE: M, R, R can follow as MRR, RMR or RRM; only RMR keeps the R's apart, so $1$ word (FAERMR).

Words beginning with FAM: E, R, R can follow as ERR, RER or RRE; only RER is allowed, so $1$ word (FAMRER).

Words beginning with FARE: M and R follow in $2! = 2$ ways (FAREMR, FARERM), neither with the R's together.

Words beginning with FARM: E, R follow as ER or RE, and the first of these is FARMER itself.

$$\text{Serial number} = 36 + 36 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 77$$

Hence, the answer is 77.

questions.solution:
A number is a multiple of 6 when it is even and its digit sum is a multiple of 3.

The six digits sum to $1 + 2 + 3 + 5 + 6 + 7 = 24$. A 5-digit number leaves out one digit $d$, and $24 - d$ is a multiple of 3 only for $d = 3$ or $d = 6$.

Leaving out 3, the digits are 1, 2, 5, 6, 7 (sum 21). The units digit is 2 or 6, and the other four digits fill the remaining places in $4! = 24$ ways, giving $2 \times 24 = 48$ numbers.

Leaving out 6, the digits are 1, 2, 3, 5, 7 (sum 18). The units digit must be 2, giving $4! = 24$ numbers.

$$\text{Total} = 48 + 24 = 72$$

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: The number of 7-digit numbers which are multiples of 11 and are formed using all the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7 and 9 is _____________.
questions.solution:
The digit sum is $1+2+3+4+5+7+9=31$. Let $S_1$ be the sum of the digits in the four odd places (1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th) and $S_2$ the sum in the three even places, so $S_1+S_2=31$.

The number is divisible by 11 exactly when $S_1-S_2=2S_1-31$ is a multiple of 11. Since $1+2+3+4\le S_1\le4+5+7+9$, i.e. $10\le S_1\le25$, this gives $S_1-S_2=\pm11$.

Case $S_1=21,\ S_2=10$: the three even-place digits are $\{1,2,7\}$, $\{1,4,5\}$ or $\{2,3,5\}$, leaving $\{3,4,5,9\}$, $\{2,3,7,9\}$ or $\{1,4,7,9\}$ for the odd places. Count $=3\times3!\times4!=432$.

Case $S_1=10,\ S_2=21$: the only three digits with sum 21 are $\{5,7,9\}$, leaving $\{1,2,3,4\}$ for the odd places. Count $=3!\times4!=144$.

Total $=432+144=576$.

Hence, the answer is 576.

$11$ lies in $[10,12]$ (not in the open interval $(11,13)$), so the number of men lies in $[10,12]$.

questions.text: A committee of 4 persons is to be formed from 2 ladies, 2 old men and 4 young men such that it includes at least 1 lady, at least 1 old man and at most 2 young men. Then the total number of ways in which this committee can be formed is
questions.solution:
Let the committee have $l$ ladies, $m$ old men and $y$ young men, with $l + m + y = 4$, $l, m \ge 1$ and $y \le 2$.

$(l, m, y) = (1, 1, 2)$: $\binom{2}{1}\binom{2}{1}\binom{4}{2} = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 6 = 24$.

$(l, m, y) = (2, 1, 1)$: $\binom{2}{2}\binom{2}{1}\binom{4}{1} = 8$.

$(l, m, y) = (1, 2, 1)$: $\binom{2}{1}\binom{2}{2}\binom{4}{1} = 8$.

$(l, m, y) = (2, 2, 0)$: $\binom{2}{2}\binom{2}{2} = 1$.

So the total number of ways is $24 + 8 + 8 + 1 = 41$.

questions.text: The total number of positive integral solutions (x, y, z) such that xyz = 24 is :
questions.solution:
$24 = 2^3 \times 3$, so each of $x, y, z$ is of the form $2^a\,3^b$, where the exponents of 2 add up to 3 and the exponents of 3 add up to 1.

The three factors 2 are shared among $x, y, z$ (each may receive 0, 1, 2 or 3 of them) in ${}^{3+3-1}C_{3-1} = {}^5C_2 = 10$ ways.

The single factor 3 goes to one of $x, y, z$ in 3 ways.

Number of ordered triples $= 10 \times 3 = 30$. These are the orderings of $\{1, 1, 24\}$ and $\{2, 2, 6\}$ (3 each) and of $\{1, 2, 12\}$, $\{1, 3, 8\}$, $\{1, 4, 6\}$, $\{2, 3, 4\}$ (6 each): $6 + 24 = 30$.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

Let group C have $r$ students, $r=1,2,3$; they are chosen in ${}^{10}C_{r}$ ways.

Each of the remaining $10-r$ students goes to A or B in $2^{10-r}$ ways; removing the 2 ways in which A or B is empty leaves $2^{10-r}-2$ ways.

$r=1$: ${}^{10}C_{1}\,(2^{9}-2)=10\times510=5100$

$r=2$: ${}^{10}C_{2}\,(2^{8}-2)=45\times254=11430$

$r=3$: ${}^{10}C_{3}\,(2^{7}-2)=120\times126=15120$

$$\text{Total}=5100+11430+15120=31650$$

Hence, the answer is 31650.

questions.text: The number of ways to distribute 30 identical candies among four children C 1 , C 2 , C 3 and C 4 so that C 2 receives at least 4 and at most 7 candies, C 3 receives at least 2 and at most 6 candies, is equal to :
questions.solution:
Let $C_2$ receive $c_2 \in \{4, 5, 6, 7\}$ candies and $C_3$ receive $c_3 \in \{2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$ candies.

The remaining $30 - c_2 - c_3$ candies go to $C_1$ and $C_4$ without restriction: $C_1$ can get $0, 1, \ldots, 30 - c_2 - c_3$, so there are $31 - c_2 - c_3$ ways.

Summing over the $4 \times 5 = 20$ pairs $(c_2, c_3)$, each $c_2$ occurs with 5 values of $c_3$ and each $c_3$ with 4 values of $c_2$:

$$\sum\limits_{c_2 = 4}^{7}\sum\limits_{c_3 = 2}^{6}(31 - c_2 - c_3) = 20 \times 31 - 5(4 + 5 + 6 + 7) - 4(2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6)$$

$$= 620 - 110 - 80 = 430$$

Hence, the correct option is (D).

$$\because$$ Sum of all entries of matrix A must be prime p such that 2 < p < 8 then sum of entries may be 3, 5 or 7.

(0, 0, 0, 5), (0, 0, 1, 4), (0, 0, 2, 3), (0, 1, 1, 3), (0, 1, 2, 2) and (1, 1, 1, 2).

$$\therefore$$ Total number of matrices = 4 + 12 + 12 + 12 + 12 + 4 = 56

If sum is 7 then possible entries are

(0, 0, 2, 5), (0, 0, 3, 4), (0, 1, 1, 5), (0, 3, 3, 1), (0, 2, 2, 3), (1, 1, 1, 4), (1, 2, 2, 2), (1, 1, 2, 3) and (0, 1, 2, 4).

Total number of matrices with sum 7 = 104

$$\therefore$$ Total number of required matrices

= 20 + 56 + 104

= 180

questions.text: An eight digit number divisible by 9 is to be formed using digits from 0 to 9 without repeating the digits. The number of ways in which this can be done is :
questions.solution:
The sum of all the digits $0,1,2,\dots,9$ is $45$, a multiple of $9$.

An eight digit number uses 8 distinct digits, so the two digits left out must have a sum divisible by $9$, i.e. a sum of $9$.

Possible pairs left out: $(0,9),(1,8),(2,7),(3,6),(4,5)$.

Leaving out $(0,9)$: the digits $1$ to $8$ give $8!=8\cdot7!$ numbers.

Each of the other 4 pairs leaves $0$ in the set, so $0$ cannot be first: $8!-7!=7\cdot7!$ numbers each, $28\cdot7!$ in all.

So the number of ways is $8\cdot7!+28\cdot7!=36\,(7!)$.

questions.text: Let A = {x 1 , x 2 , . . . ., x 7 } and B = {y 1 , y 2 , y 3 } be two sets containing seven and three distinct elements respectively. Then the total number of functions f : A $$ \to $$ B that are onto, if there exist exactly three elements x in A such that f(x) = y 2 , is equal to :

Choose the 3 elements of $A$ that map to $y_2$: this can be done in ${}^7C_3$ ways.

Each of the remaining 4 elements must map to $y_1$ or $y_3$, and both must be used for $f$ to be onto.

So the number of onto functions is $14\cdot {}^7C_3$.

questions.text: The number of ways in which an examiner can assign 30 marks to 8 questions, giving not less than 2 marks to any question, is:
questions.solution:
Let the marks be $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_8$ with each $x_i \ge 2$ and $x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_8 = 30$.

Put $x_i = y_i + 2$ with $y_i \ge 0$: then $y_1 + y_2 + \cdots + y_8 = 30 - 16 = 14$.

The number of non-negative integer solutions of 8 variables with sum 14 is ${}^{14 + 8 - 1}C_{8 - 1}$.

So the number of ways is ${}^{21}C_7$.

questions.text: The sum of the digits in the unit's place of all the 4-digit numbers formed by using the numbers 3, 4, 5 and 6, without repetition, is :

So each digit appears $6$ times in the unit's place (total $4!=24$ numbers).

Sum of unit's digits $=6(3+4+5+6)=6\times 18=108$.

questions.text: On the sides AB, BC, CA of a $$\triangle$$ ABC, 3, 4, 5 distinct points (excluding vertices A, B, C) are respectively chosen. The number of triangles that can be constructed using these chosen points as vertices are:

In all $3 + 4 + 5 = 12$ points are chosen; any $3$ of them form a triangle unless all three lie on the same side.

Total selections $= {}^{12}C_3 = 220$.

Collinear selections $= {}^{3}C_3 + {}^{4}C_3 + {}^{5}C_3 = 1 + 4 + 10 = 15$.

So the number of triangles $= 220 - 15 = 205$.

questions.text: If in a regular polygon the number of diagonals is 54, then the number of sides of this polygon is :

A polygon with $n$ sides has ${}^nC_2-n=\dfrac{n(n-3)}{2}$ diagonals.

$\dfrac{n(n-3)}{2}=54\Rightarrow n^2-3n-108=0$.

$(n-12)(n+9)=0\Rightarrow n=12$, since $n\gt 0$.

So the polygon has $12$ sides.

questions.text: Let P 1 , P 2 , ......, P 15 be 15 points on a circle. The number of distinct triangles formed by points P i , P j , P k such that i +j + k $$\ne$$ 15, is :
questions.solution:
The 15 points lie on a circle, so no three are collinear and the total number of triangles is ${}^{15}C_3 = 455$.

Triangles with $i + j + k = 15$ correspond to sets of distinct indices $i < j < k$ with sum 15:

With $i = 1$: $\{1, 2, 12\}, \{1, 3, 11\}, \{1, 4, 10\}, \{1, 5, 9\}, \{1, 6, 8\}$, that is 5 sets.

With $i = 2$: $\{2, 3, 10\}, \{2, 4, 9\}, \{2, 5, 8\}, \{2, 6, 7\}$, that is 4 sets.

With $i = 3$: $\{3, 4, 8\}, \{3, 5, 7\}$, that is 2 sets.

With $i = 4$: $\{4, 5, 6\}$, that is 1 set.

No set has $i \ge 5$, since then $i + j + k \ge 5 + 6 + 7 = 18$. So $5 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 12$ triangles have $i + j + k = 15$.

Required number $= 455 - 12 = 443$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).
