questions.text: The mean and standard deviation of 50 observations are 15 and 2 respectively. It was found that one incorrect observation was taken such that the sum of correct and incorrect observations is 70. If the correct mean is 16, then the correct variance is equal to :
questions.solution:
Given $$\overline x = 15,\,\sigma = 2 \Rightarrow {\sigma ^2} = 4$$

$$\therefore$$ $${x_2} + {x_2} + \,\,.....\,\, + \,\,{x_{50}} = 15 \times 50 = 750$$

$$4 = {{x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \,\,.....\,\, + \,\,x_{50}^2} \over {50}} - 225$$

$$\therefore$$ $$x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \,\,.....\,\, + \,\,x_{50}^2 = 50 \times 229$$

Let a be the correct observation and b is the incorrect observation

then $$a + b = 70$$

and $$16 = {{750 - b + a} \over {50}}$$

$$\therefore$$ $$a - b = 50 \Rightarrow a = 60,\,b = 10$$

$$\therefore$$ Correct variance $$ = {{50 \times 229 + {{60}^2} - {{10}^2}} \over {50}} - 256 = 43$$

questions.text: The mean of the numbers a, b, 8, 5, 10 is 6 and their variance is 6.8. If M is the mean deviation of the numbers about the mean, then 25 M is equal to :

$$\because$$ $$\overline x = 6 = {{a + b + 8 + 5 + 10} \over 5} \Rightarrow a + b = 7$$ ...... (i)

And $${\sigma ^2} = {{{a^2} + {b^2} + {8^2} + {5^2} + {{10}^2}} \over 5} - {6^2} = 6.8$$

$$ \Rightarrow {a^2} + {b^2} = 25$$ ..... (ii)

From (i) and (ii) (a, b) = (3, 4) or (4, 3)

Now mean deviation about mean

$$M = {1 \over 5}(3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 4) = {{12} \over 5}$$

$$ \Rightarrow 25M = 60$$

questions.text: The median of 100 observations grouped in classes of equal width is 25. If the median class interval is 20-30 and the number of observations less than 20 is 45, then the frequency of median class is
questions.solution:
Median $=l+\dfrac{\frac{N}{2}-C}{f}\times h$ with $l=20$, $h=10$, $N=100$, $C=45$.

$25=20+\dfrac{50-45}{f}\times10$.

$5=\dfrac{50}{f}\Rightarrow f=10$.

So the frequency of the median class is $10$.

questions.text:
The frequency distribution of daily working expenditure of families in a locality is as follows:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Expenditure (in Rs.) } (x) & \text{0-50} & \text{50-100} & \text{100-150} & \text{150-200} & \text{200-250} \\ \hline \text{No. of families } (f) & 24 & 33 & 37 & b & 25 \\ \hline\end{array}$$
If the mode of the distribution is Rs. 140, then the value of $$b$$ is
questions.solution:
The mode $140$ lies in the class $100\text{-}150$, so this is the modal class.

$\text{Mode}=l+\dfrac{f_1-f_0}{2f_1-f_0-f_2}\times h$ with $l=100$, $f_1=37$, $f_0=33$, $f_2=b$, $h=50$.

$140=100+\dfrac{4}{41-b}\times 50$, so $\dfrac{200}{41-b}=40$ and $41-b=5$.

Thus $b=36$; check: $36 \lt 37$, so $100\text{-}150$ is indeed the class of highest frequency.

So $b=36$.

questions.text: If the median and the range of four numbers {x, y, 2x + y, x - y}, where 0 < y < x < 2y, are 10 and 28 respectively, then the mean of the numbers is:
questions.solution:
Since $x \lt 2y$, $x - y \lt y$; so in increasing order the numbers are $x - y,\ y,\ x,\ 2x + y$.

Median $= \dfrac{y + x}{2} = 10 \Rightarrow x + y = 20$.

Range $= (2x + y) - (x - y) = x + 2y = 28$.

Solving, $y = 8$ and $x = 12$ (and $0 \lt 8 \lt 12 \lt 16$ holds).

The numbers are $4, 8, 12, 32$, so the mean $= \dfrac{56}{4} = 14$.

questions.text: The mean of a data set consisting of 20 observations is 40. If one observation 53 was wrongly recorded as 33, then the correct mean will be:
questions.solution:
Incorrect sum of the observations $= 20 \times 40 = 800$.

Correct sum $= 800 - 33 + 53 = 820$.

Correct mean $= \dfrac{820}{20} = 41$ (equivalently, the mean rises by $\dfrac{53 - 33}{20} = 1$).

So the correct mean is $41$.

questions.text: In a set of 2n distinct observations, each of the observation below the median of all the observations is increased by 5 and each of the remaining observations is decreased by 3. Then the mean of the new set of observations :

With $2n$ distinct observations, exactly $n$ lie below the median and the other $n$ lie above it.

Change in the total $=5n-3n=2n$.

Change in the mean $=\dfrac{2n}{2n}=1$.

So the mean increases by $1$.

questions.text: A factory is operating in two shifts, day and night, with 70 and 30 workers respectively. If per day mean wage of the day shift workers is ₹ 54 and per day mean wage of all the workers is ₹ 60, then per day mean wage of the night shift workers (in ₹) is :
questions.solution:
Total daily wage of all workers $=100\times60=6000$.

Day shift total $=70\times54=3780$, so night shift total $=6000-3780=2220$.

Mean wage of the night shift $=\dfrac{2220}{30}=74$; check: $\dfrac{70\cdot54+30\cdot74}{100}=60$.

So the per day mean wage of the night shift workers is ₹ 74.

questions.text:
The mean of the data set comprising of 16 observations is 16. If one of the observation valued 16 is deleted
and three new observations valued 3, 4 and 5 are added to the data, then the mean of the resultant data, is :
questions.solution:
Initially we have $$16$$ observations and among them one is $$16.$$

So, we have $$15$$ unknowns. Let those are $${a_1},a{}_2,{a_3}.....{a_{15}}$$

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ Mean of $$16$$ datal set

$$ = {{{a_1} + {a_2} + .....{a_{15}} + 16} \over {16}}$$

According to the question,

$${{{a_1} + {a_2} + .....{a_{15}} + 16} \over {16}} = 16$$

$$ \Rightarrow {a_1} + {a_2} + ...... + {a_{15}} = 256 - 16 = 240$$

Now we deleted $$16$$ and replaced by there new numbers $$3,4,$$ and $$5.$$

So, new mean

$$ = {{{a_1} + {a_2} + .......{a_{15}} + \left( {3 + 4 + 5} \right)} \over {18}}$$

$$ = {{240 + \left( {3 + 4 + 5} \right)} \over {18}}$$

$$ = {{240 + 12} \over {18}}$$

$$=14$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ A = 35

questions.text: If $$0 < x < \pi $$ and $$\cos x + \sin x = {1 \over 2},$$ then $$\tan x$$ is :
questions.solution:
$$\cos x + \sin x = {1 \over 2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {\left( {\cos x + {\mathop{\rm sinx}\nolimits} } \right)^2} = {1 \over 4}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {\cos ^2}x + {\sin ^2}x + 2\cos x\sin x = {1 \over 4}$$

$$\left[ \because {{{\cos }^2}x + {{\sin }^2}x = 1\, \,and \,\,2\cos x\sin x = \sin 2x} \right]$$

$$ \Rightarrow 1 + \sin 2x = {1 \over 4}$$

$${{2\tan x} \over {1 + {{\tan }^2}x}} = - {3 \over 4}$$

$$\therefore$$ $$\tan x = {{ - 8 \pm \sqrt {64 - 36} } \over 6}$$

$$ = {{ - 4 \pm \sqrt 7 } \over 3}$$

as $$\tan x < 0\,$$

If 2 cos $$\theta $$ + sin $$\theta $$ = 1 $$\left( {\theta \ne {\pi \over 2}} \right)$$

then 7 cos $$\theta $$ + 6 sin $$\theta $$ is equal to :

Let $t=\tan\dfrac{\theta}{2}$, so $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$ and $\sin\theta=\dfrac{2t}{1+t^2}$.

$2(1-t^2)+2t=1+t^2\Rightarrow 3t^2-2t-1=0\Rightarrow t=1$ or $t=-\dfrac{1}{3}$.

$t=1$ gives $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, which is excluded; so $t=-\dfrac{1}{3}$.

Then $\cos\theta=\dfrac{8/9}{10/9}=\dfrac{4}{5}$ and $\sin\theta=\dfrac{-2/3}{10/9}=-\dfrac{3}{5}$ (check: $\dfrac{8}{5}-\dfrac{3}{5}=1$).

$7\cos\theta+6\sin\theta=\dfrac{28}{5}-\dfrac{18}{5}=2$.

So $7\cos\theta+6\sin\theta$ is equal to $2$.

& \Rightarrow 9 \sin ^4 \alpha+4 \cos ^4 \alpha-12 \sin ^2 \alpha \cos ^2 \alpha=0 \\\\
& \Rightarrow \quad\left(3 \sin ^2 \alpha-2 \cos ^2 \alpha\right)^2=0 \\\\
& \Rightarrow \quad 3 \sin ^2 \alpha-2 \cos ^2 \alpha=0 \\\\
& \Rightarrow \quad 3 \sin ^2 \alpha=2 \cos ^2 \alpha \\\\
& \Rightarrow \quad \tan ^2 \alpha=2 / 3 \\\\
& \therefore \quad \cot ^2 \alpha=3 / 2 \\\\
& \text { Now, } 27 \sec ^6 \alpha+8 \operatorname{cosec}^6 \alpha=27\left(\sec ^2 \alpha\right)^3+8\left(\operatorname{cosec}^2 \alpha\right)^3 \\\\
& =27\left(1+\tan ^2 \alpha\right)^3+8\left(1+\cot ^2 \alpha\right)^3 \\\\
& =27\left(1+\frac{2}{3}\right)^3+8\left(1+\frac{3}{2}\right)^3=250
\end{aligned}
$$

questions.text: If for x $$\in$$ $$\left( {0,{\pi \over 2}} \right)$$, log 10 sinx + log 10 cosx = $$-$$1 and log 10 (sinx + cosx) = $${1 \over 2}$$(log 10 n $$-$$ 1), n > 0, then the value of n is equal to :

& \Rightarrow \log _{10}(\sin x+\cos x)^2=\log _{10}({n \over {10}}) \\\\

& \Rightarrow 1+2({1 \over {10}})={n \over {10}} \Rightarrow {12 \over {10}}={n \over {10}} \\\\
& \therefore n=12

$$

questions.text: $$\alpha = \sin 36^\circ $$ is a root of which of the following equation?
questions.solution:
Given that $\alpha = \sin 36^\circ$, we need to determine which equation it is a root of.

We start with the known relationship for $\cos 72^\circ$:

$ \cos 72^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{4} $

Using the double-angle formula for cosine:

$ \cos 72^\circ = 1 - 2 \sin^2 36^\circ $

Substitute $\alpha$ for $\sin 36^\circ$:

$ 1 - 2\alpha^2 = \frac{\sqrt{5}-1}{4} $

Multiply both sides by 4:

$ 4 - 8\alpha^2 = \sqrt{5} - 1 $

Add 1 to both sides:

$ 5 - 8\alpha^2 = \sqrt{5} $

Square both sides to eliminate the radical:

$ (5 - 8\alpha^2)^2 = 5 $

Expand the left side:

$ 25 + 64\alpha^4 - 80\alpha^2 = 5 $

Simplify by subtracting 5 from both sides:

$ 64\alpha^4 - 80\alpha^2 + 20 = 0 $

Divide the entire equation by 4:

$ 16\alpha^4 - 20\alpha^2 + 5 = 0 $

Thus, the equation $16\alpha^4 - 20\alpha^2 + 5 = 0$ is the one for which $\alpha = \sin 36^\circ$ is a root.

questions.text: The value of 2sin (12$$^\circ$$) $$-$$ sin (72$$^\circ$$) is :

Write $2\sin 12^\circ-\sin 72^\circ=\sin 12^\circ-\left(\sin 72^\circ-\sin 12^\circ\right)$ and use $\sin C-\sin D=2\cos\dfrac{C+D}{2}\sin\dfrac{C-D}{2}$:

$$\sin 72^\circ-\sin 12^\circ=2\cos 42^\circ\sin 30^\circ=\cos 42^\circ=\sin 48^\circ$$

So the value is

$$\sin 12^\circ-\sin 48^\circ=2\cos 30^\circ\sin\left(-18^\circ\right)=-2\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{5}-1}{4}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}\left(1-\sqrt{5}\right)}{4}$$

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: If $$\tan \left( {{\pi \over 9}} \right),x,\tan \left( {{{7\pi } \over {18}}} \right)$$ are in arithmetic progression and $$\tan \left( {{\pi \over 9}} \right),y,\tan \left( {{{5\pi } \over {18}}} \right)$$ are also in arithmetic progression, then $$|x - 2y|$$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
Since $\dfrac{\pi}{9}=20^\circ$, $\dfrac{7\pi}{18}=70^\circ$ and $\dfrac{5\pi}{18}=50^\circ$, the two arithmetic progressions give

$$2x=\tan 20^\circ+\tan 70^\circ,\qquad 2y=\tan 20^\circ+\tan 50^\circ$$

so

$$x-2y=\dfrac{\tan 70^\circ-\tan 20^\circ-2\tan 50^\circ}{2}$$

As $70^\circ=20^\circ+50^\circ$,

$$\tan 70^\circ=\dfrac{\tan 20^\circ+\tan 50^\circ}{1-\tan 20^\circ\tan 50^\circ}\Rightarrow \tan 70^\circ-\tan 70^\circ\tan 20^\circ\tan 50^\circ=\tan 20^\circ+\tan 50^\circ$$

Since $\tan 70^\circ=\cot 20^\circ$, $\tan 70^\circ\tan 20^\circ=1$, so $\tan 70^\circ-\tan 50^\circ=\tan 20^\circ+\tan 50^\circ$, that is, $\tan 70^\circ-\tan 20^\circ-2\tan 50^\circ=0$.

Therefore $x-2y=0$ and $|x-2y|=0$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: If 0 < x, y < $$\pi$$ and cosx + cosy $$-$$ cos(x + y) = $${3 \over 2}$$, then sinx + cosy is equal to :
questions.solution:
Let $u=\cos\dfrac{x+y}{2}$ and $v=\cos\dfrac{x-y}{2}$. Then $\cos x+\cos y=2uv$ and $\cos(x+y)=2u^2-1$, so the condition becomes

$$2uv-(2u^2-1)=\dfrac{3}{2}\Rightarrow 4u^2-4uv+1=0\Rightarrow (2u-v)^2+(1-v^2)=0$$

Both terms are non-negative since $v^2\le 1$, so $v^2=1$ and $2u=v$.

As $0<x,y<\pi$, $\left|\dfrac{x-y}{2}\right|<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $v>0$; hence $v=1$, which gives $x=y$, and then $u=\cos x=\dfrac{1}{2}$, so $x=y=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$.

Check: $\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}+\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{3}{2}$.

$$\sin x+\cos y=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{1+\sqrt{3}}{2}$$

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: Suppose $$\theta$$ and $$\phi\,(\neq 0)$$ are such that $$\sec(\theta+\phi)$$, $$\sec\theta$$ and $$\sec(\theta-\phi)$$ are in A.P. If $$\cos\theta=k\cos\left(\frac{\phi}{2}\right)$$ for some $$k$$, then $$k$$ is equal to
questions.solution:
A.P. condition: $\sec(\theta+\phi)+\sec(\theta-\phi)=2\sec\theta$.

Left side $=\dfrac{\cos(\theta-\phi)+\cos(\theta+\phi)}{\cos(\theta+\phi)\cos(\theta-\phi)}=\dfrac{2\cos\theta\cos\phi}{\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\phi}$.

So $\cos^2\theta\cos\phi=\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\phi$, i.e. $\cos^2\theta(1-\cos\phi)=(1-\cos\phi)(1+\cos\phi)$.

As $\phi\neq 0$, cancel $1-\cos\phi$: $\cos^2\theta=1+\cos\phi=2\cos^2\dfrac{\phi}{2}$.

Thus $\cos\theta=\pm\sqrt{2}\cos\dfrac{\phi}{2}$.

So $k=\pm\sqrt{2}$.

questions.text:
If    cos$$\alpha $$ + cos$$\beta $$ = $${3 \over 2}$$ and sin $$\alpha $$ + sin$$\beta $$ = $${1 \over 2}$$

and $$\theta $$ is the arithmetic mean of $$\alpha $$ and $$\beta $$,

then sin2$$\theta $$ + cos2$$\theta $$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
$\cos\alpha+\cos\beta=2\cos\dfrac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\cos\dfrac{\alpha-\beta}{2}=\dfrac{3}{2}$ and $\sin\alpha+\sin\beta=2\sin\dfrac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\cos\dfrac{\alpha-\beta}{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Dividing, $\tan\theta=\tan\dfrac{\alpha+\beta}{2}=\dfrac{1}{3}$.

$\sin 2\theta=\dfrac{2\tan\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta}=\dfrac{2/3}{10/9}=\dfrac{3}{5}$ and $\cos 2\theta=\dfrac{1-\tan^2\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta}=\dfrac{8/9}{10/9}=\dfrac{4}{5}$.

So $\sin 2\theta+\cos 2\theta=\dfrac{3}{5}+\dfrac{4}{5}=\dfrac{7}{5}$.

questions.text: $$2 \sin \left(\frac{\pi}{22}\right) \sin \left(\frac{3 \pi}{22}\right) \sin \left(\frac{5 \pi}{22}\right) \sin \left(\frac{7 \pi}{22}\right) \sin \left(\frac{9 \pi}{22}\right)$$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
Let $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{11}$, so $11\theta=\pi$. Using $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-t\right)=\cos t$:

$$\sin\dfrac{\pi}{22}=\cos 5\theta,\quad \sin\dfrac{3\pi}{22}=\cos 4\theta,\quad \sin\dfrac{5\pi}{22}=\cos 3\theta,\quad \sin\dfrac{7\pi}{22}=\cos 2\theta,\quad \sin\dfrac{9\pi}{22}=\cos\theta$$

So the expression is $P=2\cos\theta\cos 2\theta\cos 3\theta\cos 4\theta\cos 5\theta$.

Since $3\theta=\pi-8\theta$, $\cos 3\theta=-\cos 8\theta$; since $5\theta=\pi-6\theta$ and $16\theta=2\pi-6\theta$, $\cos 5\theta=-\cos 6\theta=-\cos 16\theta$. Hence $\cos 3\theta\cos 5\theta=\cos 8\theta\cos 16\theta$ and

$$P=2\cos\theta\cos 2\theta\cos 4\theta\cos 8\theta\cos 16\theta$$

Multiplying and dividing by $\sin\theta$ and applying $2\sin A\cos A=\sin 2A$ five times:

$$\cos\theta\cos 2\theta\cos 4\theta\cos 8\theta\cos 16\theta=\dfrac{\sin 32\theta}{2^5\sin\theta}$$

As $32\theta=2\pi+\dfrac{10\pi}{11}$, $\sin 32\theta=\sin\dfrac{10\pi}{11}=\sin\dfrac{\pi}{11}=\sin\theta$, so the product of cosines is $\dfrac{1}{32}$.

$$P=2\times\dfrac{1}{32}=\dfrac{1}{16}$$

Hence, the correct option is (B).

questions.text: $$16\sin (20^\circ )\sin (40^\circ )\sin (80^\circ )$$ is equal to :
If $${\sin ^2}(10^\circ )\sin (20^\circ )\sin (40^\circ )\sin (50^\circ )\sin (70^\circ ) = \alpha - {1 \over {16}}\sin (10^\circ )$$, then $$16 + {\alpha ^{ - 1}}$$ is equal to __________.
questions.solution:
Using $\sin\theta \sin(60^\circ - \theta)\sin(60^\circ + \theta) = \dfrac{1}{4}\sin 3\theta$ with $\theta = 10^\circ$:

$$\sin 10^\circ \sin 50^\circ \sin 70^\circ = \dfrac{1}{4}\sin 30^\circ = \dfrac{1}{8}$$

For the remaining factor, $2\sin 20^\circ \sin 40^\circ = \cos 20^\circ - \cos 60^\circ$, so

$$\sin 10^\circ \sin 20^\circ \sin 40^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 10^\circ \cos 20^\circ - \dfrac{1}{4}\sin 10^\circ$$

With $2\sin 10^\circ \cos 20^\circ = \sin 30^\circ - \sin 10^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2} - \sin 10^\circ$:

$$\sin 10^\circ \sin 20^\circ \sin 40^\circ = \dfrac{1}{4}\left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \sin 10^\circ\right) - \dfrac{1}{4}\sin 10^\circ = \dfrac{1}{8} - \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 10^\circ$$

Multiplying the two factors,

$$\sin^2 10^\circ \sin 20^\circ \sin 40^\circ \sin 50^\circ \sin 70^\circ = \dfrac{1}{8}\left(\dfrac{1}{8} - \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 10^\circ\right) = \dfrac{1}{64} - \dfrac{1}{16}\sin 10^\circ$$

Comparing with $\alpha - \dfrac{1}{16}\sin 10^\circ$ gives $\alpha = \dfrac{1}{64}$, so $16 + \alpha^{-1} = 16 + 64 = 80$.

Hence, the answer is 80.

questions.text: If $$\operatorname{cosec}\theta = {{p + q} \over {p - q}}$$ $$(p \ne q,\ p \ne 0)$$, then $$\left| {\cot \left( {{\pi \over 4} + {\theta \over 2}} \right)} \right|$$ is equal to :

questions.text:
If $$5\left( {{{\tan }^2}x - {{\cos }^2}x} \right) = 2\cos 2x + 9$$,

then the value of $$\cos 4x$$ is :
questions.solution:
Given that,

$$5\left( {{{\tan }^2}x - {{\cos }^2}x} \right) = 2\cos 2x + 9$$

$$ \Rightarrow 5\left( {{{{{\sin }^2}x} \over {{{\cos }^2}x}} - {{\cos }^2}x} \right) = 2\left( {2{{\cos }^2}x - 1} \right) + 9$$

Let $${\cos ^2}x = t,$$ then we have

$$5\left( {{{1 - t} \over t} - t} \right) = 2\left( {2t - 1} \right) + 9$$

$$ \Rightarrow 5\left( {{{1 - t - {t^2}} \over t}} \right) = 4t - 2 + 9$$

$$ \Rightarrow 5 - 5t - 5{t^2} = 4{t^2} + 7t$$

$$ \Rightarrow 9{t^2} + 12t - 5 = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow 9{t^2} + 15t - 3t - 5 = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow 3t\left( {3t + 5} \right) - 1\left( {3t + 5} \right) = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow \left( {3t + 5} \right)\left( {3t - 1} \right) = 0$$

$$\therefore$$ $$t = {1 \over 3}$$ and $$t = - {5 \over 3}$$

If $$t = - {5 \over 3}$$ then $${\cos ^2}x$$ is negative

So , $$t$$ can not be $$ - {5 \over 3}$$.

So, correct value of $$t = {1 \over 3}$$ then $$\cos {}^2x = t = {1 \over 3}$$

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ $$\cos 4x$$

$$ = 2{\cos ^2}2x - 1$$

$$ = 2{\left[ {2{{\cos }^2}x - 1} \right]^2} - 1$$

$$ = 2.{\left[ {2.{1 \over 3} - 1} \right]^2} - 1$$

$$ = 2.{\left( { - {1 \over 3}} \right)^2} - 1$$

$$ = {2 \over 9} - 1$$

$$ = - {7 \over 9}$$

questions.solution:
There are three cases possible for $$x \in [ - 1,1]$$

Case I : $$x \in \left[ { - 1, - \sqrt {{2 \over 3}} } \right)$$

$$ \therefore $$ $${\sin ^{ - 1}}(1) + {\cos ^{ - 1}}(0) = {x^2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {x^2} = {\pi \over 2} + {\pi \over 2} = \pi $$

$$ \Rightarrow x = \pm \sqrt \pi $$ $$ \to $$ (Reject)

Case II : $$x \in \left( { - \sqrt {{2 \over 3}} ,\sqrt {{2 \over 3}} } \right)$$

$$ \therefore $$ $${\sin ^{ - 1}}(0) + {\cos ^{ - 1}}( - 1) = {x^2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow 0 + \pi = {x^2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow x = \pm \sqrt \pi $$ $$ \to $$ (Reject)

Case III : $$x \in \left( {\sqrt {{2 \over 3}} ,1} \right)$$

$$ \therefore $$ $${\sin ^{ - 1}}(1) + {\cos ^{ - 1}}(0) = {x^2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {x^2} = \pi \Rightarrow x = \pm \sqrt \pi $$ (Reject)

questions.text: The domain of the function $$f(x)=\sin ^{-1}\left[2 x^{2}-3\right]+\log _{2}\left(\log _{\frac{1}{2}}\left(x^{2}-5 x+5\right)\right)$$, where [t] is the greatest integer function, is :
questions.solution:
For $\sin^{-1}[2x^2 - 3]$, the integer $[2x^2 - 3]$ must lie in $[-1, 1]$, i.e. be $-1$, $0$ or $1$. This holds exactly when $-1 \le 2x^2 - 3 < 2$, because $[t] \le 1$ for every $t < 2$:

$$2 \le 2x^2 < 5 \Rightarrow 1 \le x^2 < \dfrac{5}{2} \Rightarrow x \in \left(-\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{2}},\,-1\right] \cup \left[1,\,\sqrt{\dfrac{5}{2}}\right)$$

For $\log_2\left(\log_{1/2}(x^2 - 5x + 5)\right)$, the inner logarithm must be positive: $\log_{1/2}(x^2 - 5x + 5) > 0 \Rightarrow 0 < x^2 - 5x + 5 < 1$.

$x^2 - 5x + 5 > 0 \Rightarrow x < \dfrac{5 - \sqrt{5}}{2}$ or $x > \dfrac{5 + \sqrt{5}}{2}$.

$x^2 - 5x + 4 < 0 \Rightarrow (x - 1)(x - 4) < 0 \Rightarrow 1 < x < 4$.

Together: $x \in \left(1, \dfrac{5 - \sqrt{5}}{2}\right) \cup \left(\dfrac{5 + \sqrt{5}}{2}, 4\right)$, roughly $(1, 1.38) \cup (3.62, 4)$.

Intersecting with the first set, where $\sqrt{5/2} \approx 1.58$, leaves only $x \in \left(1, \dfrac{5 - \sqrt{5}}{2}\right)$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: The domain of the function $${\cos ^{ - 1}}\left( {{{2{{\sin }^{ - 1}}\left( {{1 \over {4{x^2} - 1}}} \right)} \over \pi }} \right)$$ is :

$$ \Rightarrow - {\pi \over 2} \le {\sin ^{ - 1}}\left( {{1 \over {4{x^2} - 1}}} \right) \le {\pi \over 2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow - 1 \le {1 \over {4{x^2} - 1}} \le 1$$

$$\therefore$$ $${1 \over {4{x^2} - 1}} + 1 \ge 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow {{1 + 4{x^2} - 1} \over {4{x^2} - 1}} \ge 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow {{4{x^2}} \over {4{x^2} - 1}} \ge 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $${{4{x^2}} \over {\left( {2x + 1} \right)\left( {2x - 1} \right)}} \ge 0$$ ...... (1)

$$\therefore$$ $$x \in \left( { - \infty , - {1 \over 2}} \right) \cup \{ 0\} \cup \left( {{1 \over 2},\infty } \right)$$ .....(2)

And $${1 \over {4{x^2} - 1}} - 1 \le 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow {{1 - 4{x^2} + 1} \over {4{x^2} - 1}} \le 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow {{2 - 4{x^2}} \over {4{x^2} - 1}} \le 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow {{2{x^2} - 1} \over {4{x^2} - 1}} \ge 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $${{\left( {\sqrt 2 x + 1} \right)\left( {\sqrt 2 x - 1} \right)} \over {\left( {2x + 1} \right)\left( {2x - 1} \right)}} \ge 0$$ ...... (3)

$$x \in \left( { - \infty , - {1 \over {\sqrt 2 }}} \right] \cup \left( { - {1 \over 2},{1 \over 2}} \right) \cup \left[ {{1 \over {\sqrt 2 }},\infty } \right)$$ .....(4)

From (2) and (4), we get

$$\therefore$$ $$x \in \left( { - \infty , - {1 \over {\sqrt 2 }}} \right] \cup \left[ {{1 \over {\sqrt 2 }},\infty } \right) \cup \{ 0\} $$

questions.text:
The domain of the function

$$f(x) = {{{{\cos }^{ - 1}}\left( {{{{x^2} - 5x + 6} \over {{x^2} - 9}}} \right)} \over {{{\log }_e}({x^2} - 3x + 2)}}$$ is :
questions.solution:
Since $x^2-5x+6=(x-2)(x-3)$ and $x^2-9=(x-3)(x+3)$, the argument of $\cos^{-1}$ is defined only for $x\neq\pm3$, where it equals $\dfrac{x-2}{x+3}$, and it must satisfy $-1\le\dfrac{x-2}{x+3}\le1$.

$\dfrac{x-2}{x+3}\le1\Leftrightarrow\dfrac{-5}{x+3}\le0\Leftrightarrow x>-3$.

$\dfrac{x-2}{x+3}\ge-1\Leftrightarrow\dfrac{2x+1}{x+3}\ge0\Leftrightarrow x<-3$ or $x\ge-\dfrac{1}{2}$.

So the numerator needs $x\in\left[-\dfrac{1}{2},\infty\right)-\{3\}$.

For the denominator, $x^2-3x+2=(x-1)(x-2)>0$ gives $x\in(-\infty,1)\cup(2,\infty)$, and $\log_e(x^2-3x+2)\neq0$ needs $x^2-3x+1\neq0$, that is $x\neq\dfrac{3\pm\sqrt5}{2}$.

Here $\dfrac{3-\sqrt5}{2}\approx0.38$ lies in $\left[-\dfrac{1}{2},1\right)$, while $\dfrac{3+\sqrt5}{2}\approx2.62$ and $3$ lie in $(2,\infty)$, so the domain is

$$\left[-\frac{1}{2},1\right)\cup(2,\infty)-\left\{3,\frac{3+\sqrt5}{2},\frac{3-\sqrt5}{2}\right\}.$$

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.text: Considering the principal values of the inverse trigonometric functions, the sum of all the solutions of the equation $$\cos ^{-1}(x)-2 \sin ^{-1}(x)=\cos ^{-1}(2 x)$$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
$${\cos ^{ - 1}}x - 2{\sin ^{ - 1}}x = {\cos ^{ - 1}}2x$$

For Domain : $$x \in \left[ {{{ - 1} \over 2},{1 \over 2}} \right]$$

$${\cos ^{ - 1}}x - 2\left( {{\pi \over 2} - {{\cos }^{ - 1}}x} \right) = {\cos ^{ - 1}}(2x)$$

$$ \Rightarrow {\cos ^{ - 1}}x + 2{\cos ^{ - 1}}x = \pi + {\cos ^{ - 1}}2x$$

$$ \Rightarrow \cos (3{\cos ^{ - 1}}x) = - \cos ({\cos ^{ - 1}}2x)$$

$$ \Rightarrow 4{x^3} = x$$

$$ \Rightarrow x = 0,\, \pm \,{1 \over 2}$$

questions.text: For $$k \in \mathbb{R}$$, let the solutions of the equation $$\cos \left(\sin ^{-1}\left(x \cot \left(\tan ^{-1}\left(\cos \left(\sin ^{-1} x\right)\right)\right)\right)\right)=k, 0<|x|<\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$$ be $$\alpha$$ and $$\beta$$, where the inverse trigonometric functions take only principal values. If the solutions of the equation $$x^{2}-b x-5=0$$ are $$\frac{1}{\alpha^{2}}+\frac{1}{\beta^{2}}$$ and $$\frac{\alpha}{\beta}$$, then $$\frac{b}{k^{2}}$$ is equal to ____________.
questions.solution:
For $0<|x|<\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$, $\cos(\sin^{-1}x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}>0$, and $\cot(\tan^{-1}u)=\dfrac{1}{u}$ for $u>0$, so

$$x\cot\left(\tan^{-1}\sqrt{1-x^2}\right)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}.$$

Since $x^2<\dfrac12$, $\left|\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\right|<1$, and $\cos(\sin^{-1}y)=\sqrt{1-y^2}$ gives

$$k=\sqrt{1-\frac{x^2}{1-x^2}}=\sqrt{\frac{1-2x^2}{1-x^2}}.$$

Squaring, $k^2(1-x^2)=1-2x^2\Rightarrow x^2=\dfrac{1-k^2}{2-k^2}$, so the two solutions are $\alpha=-\beta$ with $\alpha^2=\beta^2=\dfrac{1-k^2}{2-k^2}$.

Therefore $\dfrac{1}{\alpha^2}+\dfrac{1}{\beta^2}=\dfrac{2(2-k^2)}{1-k^2}$ and $\dfrac{\alpha}{\beta}=-1$.

These are the roots of $x^2-bx-5=0$, so their product is $-5$:

$$-\frac{2(2-k^2)}{1-k^2}=-5\Rightarrow 4-2k^2=5-5k^2\Rightarrow k^2=\frac13.$$

Then $\dfrac{1}{\alpha^2}+\dfrac{1}{\beta^2}=5$, and $b$ is the sum of the roots: $b=5+(-1)=4$.

$$\frac{b}{k^2}=\frac{4}{1/3}=12$$

Hence, the answer is 12.

questions.text: Let $$\alpha = \tan \left( {{{5\pi } \over {16}}\sin \left( {2{{\cos }^{ - 1}}\left( {{1 \over {\sqrt 5 }}} \right)} \right)} \right)$$ and $$\beta = \cos \left( {{{\sin }^{ - 1}}\left( {{4 \over 5}} \right) + {{\sec }^{ - 1}}\left( {{5 \over 3}} \right)} \right)$$ where the inverse trigonometric functions take principal values. Then, the equation whose roots are $$\alpha$$ and $$\beta$$ is :
questions.solution:
Given,

$$\alpha = \tan \left( {{{5\pi } \over {16}}\sin \left( {2{{\cos }^{ - 1}}\left( {{1 \over {\sqrt 5 }}} \right)} \right)} \right)$$

We know, $$2{\cos ^{ - 1}}x = {\cos ^{ - 1}}(2{x^2} - 1)$$

$$\therefore$$ $$2{\cos ^{ - 1}}\left( {{1 \over {\sqrt 5 }}} \right) = {\cos ^{ - 1}}\left( {2 \times {1 \over 5} - 1} \right) = {\cos ^{ - 1}}\left( { - {3 \over 5}} \right)$$

$$\therefore$$ $$\alpha = \tan \left( {{{5\pi } \over {16}}\sin \left( {{{\cos }^{ - 1}}\left( { - {3 \over 5}} \right)} \right.} \right)$$

$$ = \tan \left( {{{5\pi } \over {16}}\sin \left( {\pi - {{\cos }^{ - 1}}\left( { {3 \over 5}} \right)} \right.} \right)$$

$$ = \tan \left( {{{5\pi } \over {16}}\sin \left( {{{\cos }^{ - 1}}\left( {{3 \over 5}} \right)} \right.} \right)$$

$$ = \tan \left( {{{5\pi } \over {16}}\sin \left( {{{\sin }^{ - 1}}\left( {{4 \over 5}} \right)} \right.} \right)$$

$$ = \tan \left( {{{5\pi } \over {16}} \times {4 \over 5}} \right)$$

$$ = \tan \left( {{\pi \over 4}} \right)$$

$$ = 1$$

$$\therefore$$ $$\alpha = 1$$

Also given,

$$\beta = \cos \left( {{{\sin }^{ - 1}}\left( {{4 \over 5}} \right) + {{\sec }^{ - 1}}\left( {{5 \over 3}} \right)} \right)$$

$$ = \cos \left( {{{\cos }^{ - 1}}\left( {{3 \over 5}} \right) + {{\cos }^{ - 1}}\left( {{3 \over 5}} \right)} \right)$$

$$ = \cos \left( {2{{\cos }^{ - 1}}\left( {{3 \over 5}} \right)} \right)$$

$$ = \cos \left( {{{\cos }^{ - 1}}\left( {2\left. {{{\left( {{3 \over 5}} \right)}^2} - 1} \right)} \right.} \right)$$

$$ = \cos \left( {{{\cos }^{-1}}\left( {{{18} \over {25}} - 1} \right.} \right)$$

$$ = {{18} \over {25}} - 1$$

$$ = {{18 - 25} \over {25}}$$

$$ = - {7 \over {25}}$$

$$\therefore$$ $$\beta = - {7 \over {25}}$$

$$\therefore$$ The quadratic equation with roots $$\alpha$$ and $$\beta$$ is

$${x^2} - (\alpha + \beta )x + \alpha \beta = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow {x^2} - \left( {1 - {7 \over {25}}} \right)x + 1 \times \left( { - {7 \over {25}}} \right) = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow 25{x^2} - 18x - 7 = 0$$

questions.text: $${\cot ^{ - 1}}\left( {\sqrt {\cos \alpha } } \right) - {\tan ^{ - 1}}\left( {\sqrt {\cos \alpha } } \right) = x,$$ then sin x is equal to :
questions.solution:
Given that,

$${\cot ^{ - 1}}\left( {\sqrt {\cos \alpha} } \right) - {\tan ^{ - 1}}\left( \sqrt{\cos \alpha} \right) = x\,\,\,\,...\left( 1 \right)$$

We know,

$${\cot ^{ - 1}}x + {\tan ^{ - 1}}x = {\pi \over 2}$$

$$\therefore$$ $$\,\,\,$$ $${\cot ^{ - 1}}\left( {\sqrt {\cos \alpha} } \right) + {\tan ^{ - 1}}\left( {\sqrt {\cos \alpha} } \right) = {\pi \over 2}\,\,\,...\left( 2 \right)$$

Adding $$(1)$$ and $$(2),$$ we get,

$$2{\cot ^{ - 1}}\left( {\sqrt {\cos \alpha} } \right) = x + {\pi \over 2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,{\cot ^{ - 1}}\left( {\sqrt {\cos \alpha} } \right) = {x \over 2} + {\pi \over 4}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,\sqrt {\cos \alpha} = \cot \left( {{x \over 2} + {\pi \over 4}} \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,\sqrt {\cos \alpha} = {{\cot {x \over 2} - 1} \over {1 + \cot {x \over 2}}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,\sqrt {\cos \alpha} = {{\cos {x \over 2} - \sin {x \over 2}} \over {\cos {x \over 2} + \sin {x \over 2}}}$$

Squaring both sides we get,

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,\cos \alpha = {{1 - 2\sin {x \over 2}\cos {x \over 2}} \over {1 + 2\sin {x \over 2}\cos {x \over 2}}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,\cos \alpha = {{1 - \sin x} \over {1 + \sin x}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,{{1 - {{\tan }^2}{\alpha \over 2}} \over {1 + {{\tan }^2}{\alpha \over 2}}} = {{1 - \sin x} \over {1 + \sin x}}$$

Applying componendo and dividendo rule,

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,{{2\sin x} \over 2} = {{2{{\tan }^2}{\alpha \over 2}} \over 2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow \,\,\sin x = {\tan ^2}{\alpha \over 2}$$

Other Method :

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text { Since, } \cot ^{-1}(\sqrt{\cos \alpha})-\tan ^{-1}(\sqrt{\cos \alpha})=x \\\\
& \Rightarrow \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\cos \alpha}}\right)-\tan ^{-1}(\sqrt{\cos \alpha})=x \\\\
& \Rightarrow \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{\cos \alpha}}-\sqrt{\cos \alpha}}{1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{\cos \alpha}} \cdot \sqrt{\cos \alpha}}\right)=x \\\\
& \Rightarrow \frac{1-\cos \alpha}{2 \sqrt{\cos \alpha}}=\tan x \\\\
& \Rightarrow \cot x=\frac{2 \sqrt{\cos \alpha}}{1-\cos \alpha} \\\\
& \because \operatorname{cosec} x=\sqrt{1+\cot { }^2 x} \\\\
& \therefore \operatorname{cosec} x=\frac{1+\cos \alpha}{1-\cos \alpha} \\\\
& \Rightarrow \sin x=\frac{1-\cos \alpha}{1+\cos \alpha}=\tan ^2 \frac{\alpha}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

questions.text: If $${\cos ^{ - 1}}x - {\cos ^{ - 1}}{y \over 2} = \alpha ,$$ then $$4{x^2} - 4xy\cos \alpha + {y^2}$$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
As we know,

$${\cos ^{ - 1}}A - {\cos ^{ - 1}}B$$

$$ = {\cos ^{ - 1}}\left( {AB + \sqrt {1 - {A^2}} .\sqrt {1 - {B^2}} } \right)$$

Given, $${\cos ^{ - 1}}x - {\cos ^{ - 1}}{y \over 2} = \alpha $$

$$ \Rightarrow {\cos ^{ - 1}}\left( {x.{y \over 2} + \sqrt {1 - {x^2}} .\sqrt {1 - {{{y^2}} \over 4}} } \right) = \alpha $$

$$ \Rightarrow {{xy} \over 2} + \sqrt {1 - {x^2}} \sqrt {1 - {{y{}^2} \over 4}} = \cos \,\alpha $$

$$ \Rightarrow {\left( {\cos \alpha - {{xy} \over 2}} \right)^2} = \left( {1 - {x^2}} \right)\left( {1 - {{{y^2}} \over 4}} \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow {\cos ^2}\alpha + {{{x^2}{y^2}} \over 4} - 2.\cos \alpha .{{xy} \over 2}$$

$$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = 1 - {x^2} - {{{y^2}} \over 4} + {{{x^2}{y^2}} \over 4}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {x^2} + {{{y^2}} \over 4} - xy\,\cos \alpha = 1 - {\cos ^2}\alpha $$

$$ \Rightarrow {x^2} + {{{y^2}} \over 4} - xy\cos \alpha = {\sin ^2}\alpha $$

$$ \Rightarrow 4{x^2} + y{}^2 - 4xy\cos \alpha = 4{\sin ^2}\alpha $$

questions.text: Let x $$ \in $$ (0, 1). The set of all x such that sin -1 x > cos -1 x, is the interval:
questions.solution:
For $x \in (0, 1)$, $\cos^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \sin^{-1}x$.

So $\sin^{-1}x \gt \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \sin^{-1}x \Rightarrow \sin^{-1}x \gt \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Since $\sin^{-1}x$ is increasing, $x \gt \sin\dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$.

So the required interval is $\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, 1\right)$.

questions.text: If $$x, y, z$$ are in A.P. and $${\tan ^{ - 1}}x,{\tan ^{ - 1}}y$$ and $${\tan ^{ - 1}}z$$ are also in A.P., then :
questions.solution:
Given that, $$x,y,z\,\,$$ are in $$AP$$

So, $$\,\,\,$$ $$2y = x + z$$

Also given that,

$${\tan ^{ - 1}}x,{\tan ^{ - 1}}y\,\,$$ and $$\,\,\,{\tan ^{ - 1}}z\,\,$$ are in $$AP$$

So, $$2{\tan ^{ - 1}}y = {\tan ^{ - 1}}x + {\tan ^{ - 1}}z$$

$$ \Rightarrow {{2y} \over {1 - {y^2}}} = {{x + z} \over {1 - xz}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {{x + z} \over {1 - {y^2}}} = {{x + z} \over {1 - xz}}$$

[ as $$\,\,\,\,$$ $$2y = x + z$$]

$$ \Rightarrow 1 - {y^2} = 1 - xz$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $${y^2} = xz$$

As we get $${y^2} = xz,$$ so, $$x,y,z$$ are in $$GP.$$

questions.text:
Statement I : The equation (sin $$-$$1 x) 3 + (cos $$-$$1 x) 3 $$-$$ a$$\pi $$ 3 = 0 has a solution for all a $$ \ge $$ $${1 \over {32}}$$.

Statement II : For any x $$ \in $$ R ,

sin $$-$$1 x + cos $$-$$1 x = $${\pi \over 2}$$ and

$$0 \le {\left( {{{\sin }^{ - 1}}x - {\pi \over 4}} \right)^2} \le {{9{\pi ^2}} \over {16}}$$.

options.text: Both statements I and II are true.
Both statements I and II are false.
Statement I is true and statement II is false.
Statement I is false and statement II is true.

questions.solution:
Let $u = \sin^{-1}x \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$. Then $\cos^{-1}x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - u$, so the first part of Statement II is true.

Let $t = u - \dfrac{\pi}{4} \in \left[-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{4}\right]$; then $0 \le t^2 \le \dfrac{9\pi^2}{16}$, so the second part of Statement II is also true.

$(\sin^{-1}x)^3 + (\cos^{-1}x)^3 = \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} + t\right)^3 + \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4} - t\right)^3 = \dfrac{\pi^3}{32} + \dfrac{3\pi}{2}t^2$.

So this sum takes values only in $\left[\dfrac{\pi^3}{32}, \dfrac{7\pi^3}{8}\right]$, and the equation has a solution only for $\dfrac{1}{32} \le a \le \dfrac{7}{8}$.

For example, $a = 1$ gives no solution, so Statement I is false.

So Statement I is false and Statement II is true.

questions.text: If f(x) = 2tan $$-$$1 x + sin $$-$$1 $$\left( {{{2x} \over {1 + {x^2}}}} \right),$$ x > 1, then f (5) is equal to :
questions.solution:
Let $x=\tan\theta$; for $x\gt 1$, $\theta\in\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and $2\theta\in\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2},\pi\right)$.

$\sin^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}=\sin^{-1}(\sin2\theta)=\pi-2\theta$, since $\pi-2\theta\in\left(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$.

So $f(x)=2\theta+\pi-2\theta=\pi$ for every $x\gt 1$.

Check at $x=5$: $\sin(2\tan^{-1}5)=\dfrac{10}{26}=\dfrac{5}{13}$ with $2\tan^{-1}5\gt\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $2\tan^{-1}5=\pi-\sin^{-1}\dfrac{5}{13}$.

So $f(5)=\pi$.

Given $$a = {({\sin ^{ - 1}}x)^2} - {({\cos ^{ - 1}}x)^2}$$

questions.text: The value of $$\tan \left( {2{{\tan }^{ - 1}}\left( {{3 \over 5}} \right) + {{\sin }^{ - 1}}\left( {{5 \over {13}}} \right)} \right)$$ is equal to :

The sum of possible values of x for

tan $$-$$1 (x + 1) + cot $$-$$1 $$\left( {{1 \over {x - 1}}} \right)$$ = tan $$-$$1 $$\left( {{8 \over {31}}} \right)$$ is :
questions.solution:
The term $\cot^{-1}\dfrac{1}{x-1}$ needs $x\neq1$, and $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{8}{31}<\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

For $x>1$: $\cot^{-1}\dfrac{1}{x-1}=\tan^{-1}(x-1)>0$ and $\tan^{-1}(x+1)>\tan^{-1}2>\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so the left side exceeds the right side and there is no solution.

For $x<1$: $\dfrac{1}{x-1}<0$, so $\cot^{-1}\dfrac{1}{x-1}=\pi+\tan^{-1}(x-1)$ and the equation becomes

$$\tan^{-1}(x+1)+\tan^{-1}(x-1)=\tan^{-1}\frac{8}{31}-\pi.$$

The right side lies in $\left(-\pi,-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, which requires $x+1<0$, $x-1<0$ and $(x+1)(x-1)>1$, that is $x<-1$ and $x^2>2$.

Taking the tangent of both sides:

$$\frac{(x+1)+(x-1)}{1-(x^2-1)}=\frac{8}{31}\Rightarrow\frac{2x}{2-x^2}=\frac{8}{31}\Rightarrow 4x^2+31x-8=0\Rightarrow(x+8)(4x-1)=0.$$

Only $x=-8$ satisfies $x<-1$, $x^2>2$; indeed $\tan^{-1}(-7)+\tan^{-1}(-9)=-\pi+\tan^{-1}\dfrac{-16}{1-63}=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{8}{31}-\pi$.

At $x=\dfrac14$ the left side is $\tan^{-1}\dfrac54+\pi-\tan^{-1}\dfrac34>\pi$, so $x=\dfrac14$ is not a solution.

The sum of the possible values is $-8=-\dfrac{32}{4}$.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text:
Let $S=\left\{\theta\in[0, 2\pi]-\left\{\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{3\pi}{2}\right\}:\sin^{-1}(\sin\theta)+\cos^{-1}(\cos\theta)+\tan^{-1}(\tan\theta)=\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\right\}$.

Then $\dfrac{30}{\pi}\displaystyle\sum_{\theta\in S}\theta$ is equal to ________.
questions.solution:
$\theta\in\left[0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$: sum $=\theta+\theta+\theta=3\theta=\dfrac{4\pi}{5}\Rightarrow\theta=\dfrac{4\pi}{15}$ (valid).

$\theta\in\left(\tfrac{\pi}{2},\pi\right]$: sum $=(\pi-\theta)+\theta+(\theta-\pi)=\theta\Rightarrow\theta=\dfrac{4\pi}{5}$ (valid).

$\theta\in\left(\pi,\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\right)$: sum $=(\pi-\theta)+(2\pi-\theta)+(\theta-\pi)=2\pi-\theta\Rightarrow\theta=\dfrac{6\pi}{5}$ (valid).

$\theta\in\left(\tfrac{3\pi}{2},2\pi\right]$: sum $=(\theta-2\pi)+(2\pi-\theta)+(\theta-2\pi)=\theta-2\pi\le 0$: no solution.

$\dfrac{30}{\pi}\displaystyle\sum_{\theta\in S}\theta=\dfrac{30}{\pi}\cdot\dfrac{(4+12+18)\pi}{15}=68$.

questions.text: The sum of the absolute maximum and absolute minimum values of the function $$f(x)=\tan ^{-1}(\sin x-\cos x)$$ in the interval $$[0, \pi]$$ is :
questions.solution:
$g(x)=\sin x-\cos x=\sqrt2\sin\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$. For $x\in[0,\pi]$, $x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\in\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right]$, so $\sin\left(x-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\in\left[-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2},1\right]$ and $g(x)\in[-1,\sqrt2]$, with $-1$ at $x=0$ and $\sqrt2$ at $x=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.

Since $\tan^{-1}$ is increasing, $f_{\min}=\tan^{-1}(-1)=-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$ and $f_{\max}=\tan^{-1}\sqrt2$.

For $\theta=\tan^{-1}\sqrt2\in\left(0,\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+\tan^2\theta}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, so $\tan^{-1}\sqrt2=\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)$.

$$f_{\max}+f_{\min}=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\right)-\frac{\pi}{4}$$

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text: If $$0 < x < {1 \over {\sqrt 2 }}$$ and $${{{{\sin }^{ - 1}}x} \over \alpha } = {{{{\cos }^{ - 1}}x} \over \beta }$$, then the value of $$\sin \left( {{{2\pi \alpha } \over {\alpha + \beta }}} \right)$$ is :
questions.solution:
Let $${{{{\sin }^{ - 1}}x} \over \alpha } = {{{{\cos }^{ - 1}}x} \over \beta } = k \Rightarrow {\sin ^{ - 1}}x + {\cos ^{ - 1}}x = k(\alpha + \beta )$$

$$ \Rightarrow \alpha + \beta = {\pi \over {2k}}$$

Now, $${{2\pi \,\alpha } \over {\alpha + \beta }} = {{2\pi \,\alpha } \over {{\pi \over {2k}}}} = 4k\alpha = 4{\sin ^{ - 1}}x$$

Here $$\sin \left( {{{2\pi \,\alpha } \over {\alpha + \beta }}} \right) = \sin (4{\sin ^{ - 1}}x)$$

Let $${\sin ^{ - 1}}x = \theta $$

$$\because$$ $$x \in \left( {0,{1 \over {\sqrt 2 }}} \right) \Rightarrow \theta \in \left( {0,{\pi \over 4}} \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow x = \sin \theta $$

$$ \Rightarrow \cos \theta = \sqrt {1 - {x^2}} $$

$$ \Rightarrow \sin 2\theta = 2x\,.\,\sqrt {1 - {x^2}} $$

$$ \Rightarrow \cos 2\theta = \sqrt {1 - 4{x^2}(1 - {x^2})} = \sqrt {{{(2{x^2} - 1)}^2}} = 1 - 2{x^2}$$

$$\because$$ $$\left( {\cos 2\theta > 0\,\mathrm{as}\,2\theta \in \left( {0,{\pi \over 2}} \right)} \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow \sin 4\theta = 2\,.\,2x\sqrt {1 - {x^2}} (1 - 2{x^2})$$

$$ = 4x\sqrt {1 - {x^2}} (1 - 2{x^2})$$

questions.text: $$\tan \left(2 \tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{5}+\sec ^{-1} \frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}+2 \tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{8}\right)$$ is equal to :

Let $$x = \sin (2{\tan ^{ - 1}}\alpha )$$ and $$y = \sin \left( {{1 \over 2}{{\tan }^{ - 1}}{4 \over 3}} \right)$$. If $$S = \{ \alpha \in R:{y^2} = 1 - x\} $$, then $$\sum\limits_{\alpha \in S}^{} {16{\alpha ^3}} $$ is equal to _______________.
questions.solution:
$$\because$$ $$x = \sin \left( {2{{\tan }^{ - 1}}\alpha } \right) = {{2\alpha } \over {1 + {\alpha ^2}}}$$ ...... (i)

and $$y = \sin \left( {{1 \over 2}{{\tan }^{ - 1}}{4 \over 3}} \right) = \sin \left( {{{\sin }^{ - 1}}{1 \over {\sqrt 5 }}} \right) = {1 \over {\sqrt 5 }}$$

Now, $${y^2} = 1 - x$$

$${1 \over 5} = 1 - {{2\alpha } \over {1 + {\alpha ^2}}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow 1 + {\alpha ^2} = 5 + 5{\alpha ^2} - 10\alpha $$

$$ \Rightarrow 2{\alpha ^2} - 5\alpha + 2 = 0$$

$$\therefore$$ $$\alpha = 2,{1 \over 2}$$

$$\therefore$$ $$\sum\limits_{\alpha \in S} {16{\alpha ^3} = 16 \times {2^3} + 16 \times {1 \over {{2^3}}} = 130} $$

questions.text: Let m and M respectively be the minimum and the maximum values of $$f(x) = {\sin ^{ - 1}}2x + \sin 2x + {\cos ^{ - 1}}2x + \cos 2x,\,x \in \left[ {0,{\pi \over 8}} \right]$$. Then m + M is equal to :
questions.solution:
$$f(x) = {\sin ^{ - 1}}(2x) + \sin 2x + {\cos ^{ - 1}}(2x) + \cos 2x$$

$$ = {\sin ^{ - 1}}(2x) + {\cos ^{ - 1}}(2x) + \sin 2x + \cos 2x$$

$$ = {\pi \over 2} + \sqrt 2 \left( {{1 \over {\sqrt 2 }}\sin 2x + {1 \over {\sqrt 2 }}\cos 2x} \right)$$

$$ = {\pi \over 2} + \sqrt 2 \left( {\cos {\pi \over 4}\sin 2x + \sin {\pi \over 4}\cos 2x} \right)$$

$$ = {\pi \over 2} + \sqrt 2 \,.\,\sin \left( {2x + {\pi \over 4}} \right)$$

f(x) is maximum when $$\sin \left( {2x + {\pi \over 4}} \right)$$ is maximum means $$x = {\pi \over 8}$$ or $$\sin \left( {2 \times {\pi \over 8} + {\pi \over 4}} \right) = \sin {\pi \over 2} = 1$$

$$\therefore$$ $${\left[ {f(x)} \right]_{\max }} = {\pi \over 2} + \sqrt 2 \,.\,1 = {\pi \over 2} + \sqrt 2 = M$$

f(x) is minimum when $$\sin \left( {2x + {\pi \over 4}} \right)$$ is minimum means $$x = 0$$ or $$\sin \left( {2 \times 0 + {\pi \over 4}} \right) = {1 \over {\sqrt 2 }}$$

$$\therefore$$ $${\left[ {f(x)} \right]_{\min }} = {\pi \over 2} + \sqrt 2 \,.\,{1 \over {\sqrt 2 }} = {\pi \over 2} + 1 = m$$

$$\therefore$$ $$m + M = {\pi \over 2} + \sqrt 2 + {\pi \over 2} + 1 = \pi + \sqrt 2 + 1$$

Where $2 \alpha=\tan ^{-1} 2 \sqrt{2}$

questions.text: The value of $${\tan ^{ - 1}}\left( {{{\cos \left( {{{15\pi } \over 4}} \right) - 1} \over {\sin \left( {{\pi \over 4}} \right)}}} \right)$$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
$${\tan ^{ - 1}}\left( {{{\cos \left( {{{15\pi } \over 4}} \right) - 1} \over {\sin {\pi \over 4}}}} \right)$$

$$ = {\tan ^{ - 1}}\left( {{{{1 \over {\sqrt 2 }} - 1} \over {{1 \over {\sqrt 2 }}}}} \right)$$

$$ = {\tan ^{ - 1}}(1 - \sqrt 2 ) = - {\tan ^{ - 1}}(\sqrt 2 - 1)$$

$$ = - {\pi \over 8}$$

The star "*" in this context represents a binary operation, similar to addition (+), subtraction (-), multiplication (×), and division (÷). It is a custom operation defined by the problem statement, and the specific rules of the operation are provided in the problem.

In this case, the operation "*" is defined by the equation $x * y = x^2 + y^3$, which means if you have two numbers $x$ and $y$, then the result of applying the "*" operation to them is $x^2 + y^3$.

The problem also specifies an additional rule for this operation: $(x * 1) * 1 = x * (1 * 1)$, which needs to be taken into account when solving the problem. This is a type of "associativity" condition.
Given,

$$x\, * \,y = {x^2} + {y^3}$$

$$\therefore$$ $$x\, * \,1 = {x^2} + {1^3} = {x^2} + 1$$

Now, $$(x\, * \,1)\, * \,1 = ({x^2} + 1)\, * \,1$$

$$ \Rightarrow (x\, * \,1)\, * \,1 = {({x^2} + 1)^2} + {1^3}$$

$$ \Rightarrow (x\, * \,1)\, * \,1 = {x^4} + 1 + 2{x^2} + 1$$

Also, $$x\, * \,(1\, * \,1)$$

$$ = x\, * \,({1^2} + {1^3})$$

$$ = x\, * \,2$$

$$ = {x^2} + {2^3}$$

$$ = {x^2} + 8$$

Given that,

$$(x\, * \,1)\, * \,1 = x\, * \,(1\, * \,1)$$

$$\therefore$$ $${x^4} + 1 + 2{x^2} + 1 = {x^2} + 8$$

$$ \Rightarrow {x^4} + {x^2} - 6 = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow {x^4} + 3{x^2} - 2{x^2} - 6 = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow {x^2}({x^2} + 3) - 2({x^2} + 3) = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow ({x^2} + 3)({x^2} - 2) = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow {x^2} = 2,\, - 3$$

[$${x^2} = -3$$ not possible as square of anything should be always positive]

$$\therefore$$ $${x^2} = 2$$

$$\therefore$$ Now,

$$2{\sin ^{ - 1}}\left( {{{{x^4} + {x^2} - 2} \over {{x^4} + {x^2} + 2}}} \right)$$

$$ = 2{\sin ^{ - 1}}\left( {{{{2^2} + 2 - 2} \over {{2^2} + 2 + 2}}} \right)$$

$$ = 2{\sin ^{ - 1}}\left( {{4 \over 8}} \right)$$

$$ = 2{\sin ^{ - 1}}\left( {{1 \over 2}} \right)$$

$$ = 2 \times {\pi \over 6}$$

$$ = {\pi \over 3}$$

questions.text:
The set of all values of k for which

$${({\tan ^{ - 1}}x)^3} + {({\cot ^{ - 1}}x)^3} = k{\pi ^3},\,x \in R$$, is the interval :
questions.solution:
$${({\tan ^{ - 1}}x)^3} + {({\cot ^{ - 1}}x)^3} = k{\pi ^3}$$

Let $$f(t) = {t^3} + {\left( {{\pi \over 2} - t} \right)^3}$$

Where $$t = {\tan ^{ - 1}}x$$ ; $$t \in \left( { - {\pi \over 2},{\pi \over 2}} \right)$$

$$ = {t^3} + {\left( {{\pi \over 2}} \right)^3} - {{3{\pi ^2}t} \over 4} + {{3\pi } \over 2}{t^2} - {t^3}$$

$$f(t) = {{3\pi } \over 2}{t^2} - {{3{\pi ^2}} \over 4}\,.\,t + {{{\pi ^3}} \over 8}$$

This is a quadratic equation of t.

Here, coefficient of t 2 term is $${{3\pi } \over 2}$$ which is > 0.

$$\therefore$$ It is an upward parabola.

Now, $$f'(t) = 3\pi t - {{3{\pi ^2}} \over 4}$$

$$f''(t) = 3\pi > 0$$

$$\therefore$$ $$3\pi t - {{3{\pi ^2}} \over 4} = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow t = {\pi \over 4}$$ (minima)

$$\therefore$$ vertex of graph at $${\pi \over 4}$$

$$\therefore$$ Minimum value at $${\pi \over 4}$$ and maximum value at $$-$$$${\pi \over 2}$$.

$$\therefore$$ $$f\left( {{\pi \over 4}} \right) = {{{\pi ^3}} \over {64}} + {\left( {{\pi \over 2} - {\pi \over 4}} \right)^3} = {{{\pi ^3}} \over {32}}$$

$$f\left( { - {\pi \over 2}} \right) = - {{{\pi ^3}} \over 8} + {\pi ^3}$$

$$ = {{7{\pi ^3}} \over 8}$$

$$\therefore$$ $$k{\pi ^3} \in \left[ {{{{\pi ^3}} \over {32}},\,{{7{\pi ^3}} \over 8}} \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow k \in \left[ {{1 \over {32}},\,{7 \over 8}} \right)$$

questions.text: The number of solutions of the equation, sin -1 x = 2 tan -1 x (in principal values) is:
questions.solution:
The equation needs $-1 \le x \le 1$; for such $x$, $2\tan^{-1}x = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1 + x^2}\right)$.

So $\sin^{-1}x = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1 + x^2}\right) \Rightarrow x = \dfrac{2x}{1 + x^2}$.

$\Rightarrow x(1 + x^2) = 2x \Rightarrow x(x^2 - 1) = 0 \Rightarrow x = 0, 1, -1$.

Check: $\sin^{-1}(\pm 1) = \pm\dfrac{\pi}{2} = 2\tan^{-1}(\pm 1)$, and $x = 0$ gives $0 = 0$.

So the equation has $3$ solutions.

questions.text: The value of x for which $$\sin \left( {{{\cot }^{ - 1}}(1 + x)} \right) = \cos ({\tan ^{ - 1}}x)$$ is
questions.solution:
Let $\cot^{-1}(1 + x) = \alpha$, so $\cot\alpha = 1 + x$ and $\sin\alpha = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (1 + x)^2}}$ (positive, as $0 \lt \alpha \lt \pi$).

Let $\tan^{-1}x = \beta$, so $\cos\beta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 + x^2}}$ (positive, as $-\dfrac{\pi}{2} \lt \beta \lt \dfrac{\pi}{2}$).

Equating: $(1 + x)^2 = x^2 \Rightarrow 1 + 2x = 0 \Rightarrow x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Check: $\sin\left(\cot^{-1}\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \cos\left(\tan^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right) = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt 5}$.

So $x = -\dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.text: $$S = {\tan ^{ - 1}}\left( {{1 \over {{n^2} + n + 1}}} \right)$$ $$ + {\tan ^{ - 1}}\left( {{1 \over {{n^2} + 3n + 1}}} \right)$$ + .... $${\tan ^{ - 1}}\left( {{1 \over {1 + (n + 19)(n + 20)}}} \right)$$, then tan S is equal to:
questions.solution:
Since $n^2 + n + 1 = 1 + n(n + 1)$ and $n^2 + 3n + 1 = 1 + (n + 1)(n + 2)$, the $r$-th term is $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{1 + (n + r - 1)(n + r)}$, $r = 1, 2, \ldots, 20$.

$\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{1 + (n + r - 1)(n + r)} = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{(n + r) - (n + r - 1)}{1 + (n + r)(n + r - 1)} = \tan^{-1}(n + r) - \tan^{-1}(n + r - 1)$.

Adding, the intermediate terms cancel: $S = \tan^{-1}(n + 20) - \tan^{-1}n$.

$\tan S = \dfrac{(n + 20) - n}{1 + n(n + 20)}$.

So $\tan S = \dfrac{20}{n^2 + 20n + 1}$.

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: The perpendicular bisector of the line segment joining P(1, 4) and Q(k, 3) has y-intercept -4. Then a possible value of k is :
questions.solution:
Slope of $$PQ = {{3 - 4} \over {k - 1}} = {{ - 1} \over {k - 1}}$$

$$\therefore$$ Slope of perpendicular bisector of

$$PQ = \left( {k - 1} \right)$$

Also mid point of

$$PQ\left( {{{k + 1} \over 2},{7 \over 2}} \right).$$

Equation of perpendicular bisector is

$$y - {7 \over 2} = \left( {k - 1} \right)\left( {x - {{k + 1} \over 2}} \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow 2y - 7 = 2\left( {k - 1} \right)x - \left( {{k^2} - 1} \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow 2\left( {k - 1} \right)x - 2y + \left( {8 - {k^2}} \right) = 0$$

$$\therefore$$ $$y$$-intercept $$ = {{8 - {k^2}} \over 2} = - 4$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$8 - {k^2} = - 8$$ or $${k^2} = 16 \Rightarrow k = \pm 4$$

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: If the line $$2x + y = k$$ passes through the point which divides the line segment joining the points $$(1, 1)$$ and $$(2, 4)$$ in the ratio $$3 : 2$$, then $$k$$ equals :
questions.solution:
The point which divides the line segment joining the points (1, 1) and (2, 4) in the ratio 3 : 2 is

$$ = \left( {{{3 \times 2 + 2 \times 1} \over {3 + 2}},{{3 \times 4 + 2 \times 1} \over {3 + 2}}} \right)$$

$$ = \left( {{{6 + 2} \over 5},{{12 + 2} \over 5}} \right) = \left( {{8 \over 5},{{14} \over 5}} \right)$$

Since the line 2x + y = k passes through this point,

$$\therefore$$ $$2 \times {8 \over 5} + {{14} \over 5} = k$$ or $${{30} \over 5} = k$$ or, k = 6

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: Let $$PS$$ be the median of the triangle with vertices $$P(2, 2)$$, $$Q(6, -1)$$ and $$R(7, 3)$$. The equation of the line passing through $$(1, -1)$$ and parallel to PS is :
questions.solution:
Let $$P,Q,R,$$ be the vertices of $$\Delta PQR$$

Since $$PS$$ is the median, $$S$$ is mid-point of $$QR$$

So, $$S = \left( {{{7 + 6} \over 2},{{3 - 1} \over 2}} \right) = \left( {{{13} \over 2},1} \right)$$

Now, slope of $$PS$$ $$ = {{2 - 1} \over {2 - {{13} \over 2}}} = - {2 \over 9}$$

Since, required line is parallel to $$PS$$ therefore slope of required line $$=$$ slope of
$$PS$$

Now, equation of line passing through $$(1, -1)$$ and having slope $$ - {2 \over 9}$$ is

$$y - \left( { - 1} \right) = - {2 \over 9}\left( {x - 1} \right)$$

$$9y + 9 = - 2x + 2$$

$$ \Rightarrow 2x + 9y + 7 = 0$$

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: A straight line through origin O meets the lines 3y = 10 − 4x and 8x + 6y + 5 = 0 at points A and B respectively. Then O divides the segment AB in the ratio :
questions.solution:
The lines 4x + 3y $$-$$ 10 = 0 and

8x + 6y + 5 = 0 , are parallel as

    $${4 \over 8}$$  =  $${3 \over 6}$$

Now length of perpendicular from

(0, 0, 0) to 4x + 3y $$-$$ 10 = 0 is,

P 1   =   $$\left| {{{4\left( 0 \right) + 3\left( 0 \right) - 10} \over {\sqrt {{4^2} + {3^2}} }}} \right|$$  =  $${{10} \over 5}$$  =  2

Length of perpendicular from

0 (0, 0) to 8x + 6y + 5 = 0 is

P 2   =  $$\left| {{{8\left( 0 \right) + 6\left( 0 \right) + 5} \over {\sqrt {{6^2} + {8^2}} }}} \right|$$   =  $${5 \over {10}}$$   =  $${1 \over 2}$$

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ P 1 : P 2   =   2 : $${1 \over 2}$$   =   4 : 1

questions.text: A ray of light passing through the point P(2, 3) reflects on the x-axis at point A and the reflected ray passes through the point Q(5, 4). Let the co-ordinates of the foot of the perpendicular M from R on the bisector of the angle PAQ be ($$\alpha$$, $$\beta$$). Then, the value of 7$$\alpha$$ + 3$$\beta$$ is equal to ____________.
questions.solution:
$${4 \over {5 - \alpha }} = {3 \over {\alpha - 2}} \Rightarrow 4\alpha - 8 = 15 - 3\alpha $$

$$\alpha = {{23} \over 7}$$

$$A = \left( {{{23} \over 7},0} \right)\,Q = (5,4)$$

$$R = \left( {{{10 + {{23} \over 7}} \over 3},{8 \over 3}} \right)$$

$$ = \left( {{{31} \over 7},{8 \over 3}} \right)$$

Bisector of angle PAQ is $$X = {{23} \over 7}$$

$$ \Rightarrow M = \left( {{{23} \over 7},{8 \over 3}} \right)$$

So, $$7\alpha + 3\beta = 31$$

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: If two vertices of a triangle are $$(5, -1)$$ and $$(-2, 3)$$ and its orthocentre is at $$(0, 0)$$, then the third vertex is
questions.solution:
Let $A(5,-1)$, $B(-2,3)$, $H(0,0)$ and let the third vertex be $C(h,k)$.

$AH\perp BC$: $(5,-1)\cdot(h+2,k-3)=0\Rightarrow 5h-k+13=0$.

$BH\perp AC$: $(-2,3)\cdot(h-5,k+1)=0\Rightarrow -2h+3k+13=0$.

From the first, $k=5h+13$; substituting, $13h+52=0$, so $h=-4$, $k=-7$.

Check: $CH$ along $(4,7)$ and $AB$ along $(-7,4)$ have dot product $0$.

So the third vertex is $(-4,-7)$.

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: Let A(-3, 2) and B(-2, 1) be the vertices of a triangle ABC. If the centroid of this triangle lies on the line 3x + 4y + 2 = 0, then the vertex C lies on the line:

Let C = (x 1 , y 1 )

Centroid, E = $$\left( {{{{x_1} - 5} \over 3},{{{y_1} + 3} \over 3}} \right)$$

Since centroid lies on the line

3x + 4y + 2 = 0

$$ \therefore $$    $$3\left( {{{{x_1} - 5} \over 3}} \right)$$ + $$4\left( {{{{y_1} + 3} \over 3}} \right)$$ + 2 = 0

$$ \Rightarrow $$    3x 1 + 4y 1 + 3 = 0

Hence vertex (x 1 , y 1 ) lies on the line

3x + 4y + 3 = 0

questions.text: The circumcenter of a triangle lies at the origin and its centroid is the mid point of the line segment joining the points (a 2 + 1, a 2 + 1) and (2a, $$-$$ 2a), a $$ \ne $$ 0. Then for any a, the orthocenter of this triangle lies on the line :

Centroid (G) and orthocenter (H) of a triangle lie on the line joining the O and G.

questions.text: Let k be an integer such that the triangle with vertices (k, – 3k), (5, k) and (–k, 2) has area 28 sq. units. Then the orthocentre of this triangle is at the point :
questions.solution:
Given, vertices of triangle are (k, – 3k), (5, k) and (–k, 2).

$${1 \over 2}\left| {\matrix{
k & { - 3k} & 1 \cr
5 & k & 1 \cr
{ - k} & 2 & 1 \cr

} } \right| = \pm 28$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ k(k - 2) + 3k(5 + k) + 1(10 + k 2 ) = $$ \pm $$ 56

$$ \Rightarrow $$ 5k 2 + 13k + 10 = $$ \pm $$ 56

$$ \Rightarrow $$ 5k 2 + 13k - 66 = 0

$$ \Rightarrow $$ k = $${{ - 13 \pm \sqrt { - 1151} } \over {10}}$$

So no real solution exist.

or 5k 2 + 13k - 46 = 0

$$ \therefore $$ k = $${{ - 23} \over 5}$$ or k = 2

since k is an integer $$ \therefore $$ k = 2

Thus, the coordinate of vertices of triangle are

A(2, -6), B(5, 2) and C(-2, 2).

Now, equation of altitude from vertex A is

y - (-6) = $${{ - 1} \over {\left( {{{2 - 2} \over { - 2 - 5}}} \right)}}\left( {x - 2} \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ x = 2 .......(1)

Equation of altitude from vertex B is

y - 2 = $${{ - 1} \over {\left( {{{2 + 6} \over { - 2 - 2}}} \right)}}\left( {x - 5} \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ 2y - 4 = x - 5

$$ \Rightarrow $$ x - 2y = 1 .......(2)

Point H($$\alpha $$, $$\beta $$) lies on both (1) and (2),

$$ \therefore $$ $$\alpha $$ = 2 .........(3)

$$\alpha $$ - 2$$\beta $$ = 1 ......(4)

Solving (3) and (4), we get

$$\alpha $$ = 2 , $$\beta $$ = $${1 \over 2}$$

$$ \therefore $$ Orthocentre is $$\left( {2,{1 \over 2}} \right)$$.

questions.text: A point P moves on the line 2x – 3y + 4 = 0. If Q(1, 4) and R (3, – 2) are fixed points, then the locus of the centroid of $$\Delta $$PQR is a line :

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: Let the centroid of an equilateral triangle ABC be at the origin. Let one of the sides of the equilateral triangle be along the straight line x + y = 3. If R and r be the radius of circumcircle and incircle respectively of $$\Delta$$ABC, then (R + r) is equal to :

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: Let tan$$\alpha$$, tan$$\beta$$ and tan$$\gamma$$; $$\alpha$$, $$\beta$$, $$\gamma$$ $$\ne$$ $${{(2n - 1)\pi } \over 2}$$, n$$\in$$N be the slopes of three line segments OA, OB and OC, respectively, where O is origin. If circumcentre of $$\Delta$$ABC coincides with origin and its orthocentre lies on y-axis, then the value of $${\left( {{{\cos 3\alpha + \cos 3\beta + \cos 3\gamma } \over {\cos \alpha \cos \beta \cos \gamma }}} \right)^2}$$ is equal to ____________.
questions.solution:
Since orthocentre and circumcentre both lies on y-axis.

$$ \Rightarrow $$ Centroid also lies on y-axis.

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$\sum {\cos \alpha = 0} $$

cos$$\alpha$$ + cos$$\beta$$ + cos$$\gamma$$ = 0

$$ \Rightarrow $$ cos 3 $$\alpha$$ + cos 3 $$\beta$$ + cos 3 $$\gamma$$ = 3cos$$\alpha$$cos$$\beta$$cos$$\gamma$$

$$ \therefore $$ $${{\cos 3\alpha + \cos 3\beta + \cos 3\gamma } \over {\cos \alpha \cos \beta \cos \gamma }}$$

$$ = {{4({{\cos }^3}\alpha + {{\cos }^3}\beta + {{\cos }^3}\gamma ) - 3(\cos \alpha + \cos \beta + \cos \gamma )} \over {\cos \alpha \cos \beta \cos \gamma }} = 12$$

then, $${\left( {{{\cos 3\alpha + \cos 3\beta + \cos 3\gamma } \over {\cos \alpha \cos \beta \cos \gamma }}} \right)^2} = 144$$

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: In a triangle PQR, the co-ordinates of the points P and Q are ($$-$$2, 4) and (4, $$-$$2) respectively. If the equation of the perpendicular bisector of PR is 2x $$-$$ y + 2 = 0, then the centre of the circumcircle of the $$\Delta$$PQR is :

Solving with perpendicular bisector of PR,

2x $$-$$ y + 2 = 0

Circumcentre is ($$-$$2, $$-$$2)

$$

Circumradius $=\frac{10}{2}=5$

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: The equations of the sides $$\mathrm{AB}, \mathrm{BC}$$ and CA of a triangle ABC are $$2 x+y=0, x+\mathrm{p} y=39$$ and $$x-y=3$$ respectively and $$\mathrm{P}(2,3)$$ is its circumcentre. Then which of the following is NOT true?
questions.solution:
$A$ is the intersection of $2x + y = 0$ and $x - y = 3$: $A(1, -2)$.

The circumcentre $P(2, 3)$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of every side, so $B$ is the reflection of $A$ in the line through $P$ perpendicular to $AB$, and $C$ is the reflection of $A$ in the line through $P$ perpendicular to $AC$.

$AB$ has slope $-2$, so the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ is $y - 3 = \dfrac{1}{2}(x - 2)$, i.e. $x - 2y + 4 = 0$. Reflecting $A$:

$$\dfrac{x - 1}{1} = \dfrac{y + 2}{-2} = \dfrac{-2(1 + 4 + 4)}{5} = -\dfrac{18}{5} \Rightarrow B\left(-\dfrac{13}{5}, \dfrac{26}{5}\right)$$

$AC$ has slope 1, so the perpendicular bisector of $AC$ is $x + y = 5$. Reflecting $A$:

$$\dfrac{x - 1}{1} = \dfrac{y + 2}{1} = \dfrac{-2(1 - 2 - 5)}{2} = 6 \Rightarrow C(7, 4)$$

Slope of $BC = \dfrac{4 - 26/5}{7 + 13/5} = -\dfrac{1}{8}$, so $BC$ is $x + 8y = 39$ and $p = 8$. Also $AC^2 = 6^2 + 6^2 = 72$.

(
A) $9p = 72 = AC^2$: true. (
B) $AC^2 + p^2 = 72 + 64 = 136$: true.

$$\text{Area} = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|1\left(\dfrac{26}{5} - 4\right) - \dfrac{13}{5}(4 + 2) + 7\left(-2 - \dfrac{26}{5}\right)\right| = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|\dfrac{6 - 78 - 252}{5}\right| = \dfrac{162}{5} = 32.4$$

(
C) $32 < 32.4 < 36$: true. (
D) $34 < 32.4$ fails, so (
D) is not true.

Hence, the correct option is (D).

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: The equations of the sides $$\mathrm{AB}, \mathrm{BC}$$ and $$\mathrm{CA}$$ of a triangle $$\mathrm{ABC}$$ are $$2 x+y=0, x+\mathrm{p} y=15 \mathrm{a}$$ and $$x-y=3$$ respectively. If its orthocentre is $$(2, a),-\frac{1}{2}<\mathrm{a}<2$$, then $$\mathrm{p}$$ is equal to ______________.
questions.solution:
Vertex A is the intersection of $2x+y=0$ and $x-y=3$, so $A=(1,-2)$.

$AH \perp BC$: slope of $AH=\dfrac{a+2}{2-1}=a+2$ and slope of $BC=-\dfrac{1}{p}$, so $(a+2)\left(-\dfrac{1}{p}\right)=-1 \Rightarrow p=a+2$, i.e. $a=p-2$.

Vertex C: putting $x=y+3$ in $x+py=15a$ gives $y=\dfrac{15a-3}{p+1}=\dfrac{15p-33}{p+1}$ and $x=y+3=\dfrac{18p-30}{p+1}$.

$CH \perp AB$, and $AB$ has slope $-2$, so the slope of $CH$ is $\dfrac{1}{2}$:

$$\dfrac{\dfrac{15p-33}{p+1}-(p-2)}{\dfrac{18p-30}{p+1}-2}=\dfrac{15p-33-(p-2)(p+1)}{16p-32}=\dfrac{-p^2+16p-31}{16p-32}=\dfrac{1}{2}$$

$$-2p^2+32p-62=16p-32 \Rightarrow p^2-8p+15=0 \Rightarrow p=3 \text{ or } 5$$

$p=5$ gives $a=3$, outside $-\dfrac{1}{2}<a<2$; $p=3$ gives $a=1$, which is allowed.

Hence, the answer is 3.

questions.text: The distance of the origin from the centroid of the triangle whose two sides have the equations $$x - 2y + 1 = 0$$ and $$2x - y - 1 = 0$$ and whose orthocenter is $$\left( {{7 \over 3},{7 \over 3}} \right)$$ is :

Solving equation (1) and (4), we get

x = 2, y = 3.

$$\therefore$$ Point B = (2, 3)

Altitude from C to line AB is perpendicular to line AB.

$$\therefore$$ Equation of altitude CH is

x + 2y + $$\lambda$$ = 0 ...... (5)

It passes through point $$H\left( {{7 \over 3},{7 \over 3}} \right)$$ so it satisfy equation (5).

$$\Rightarrow$$ $$\lambda$$ = $$-$$7

$$\therefore$$ Altitude CH = x + 2y $$-$$ 7 = 0 ...... (6)

Solving equation (2) and (6), we get

x = 3, y = 2

$$\therefore$$ Point C = (3, 2)

Centroid G (x, y) of triangle A (1, 1), B (2, 3) and C (3, 2) is

Now, distance of point G (2, 2) from center O (0, 0) is

$$OG = \sqrt {{2^2} + {2^2}} = 2\sqrt 2 $$

questions.text: Let A be the set of all points ($$\alpha$$, $$\beta$$) such that the area of triangle formed by the points (5, 6), (3, 2) and ($$\alpha$$, $$\beta$$) is 12 square units. Then the least possible length of a line segment joining the origin to a point in A, is :
questions.solution:
For the triangle with vertices $(5,6)$, $(3,2)$ and $(\alpha,\beta)$:

$$\dfrac{1}{2}\left|\begin{vmatrix}5&6&1\\3&2&1\\\alpha&\beta&1\end{vmatrix}\right|=12$$

The determinant is $5(2-\beta)-6(3-\alpha)+(3\beta-2\alpha)=4\alpha-2\beta-8$, so $|4\alpha-2\beta-8|=24$.

Hence $2\alpha-\beta=16$ or $2\alpha-\beta=-8$: the set A is the union of the parallel lines $2x-y-16=0$ and $2x-y+8=0$.

The shortest segment from the origin to a point of A is the smaller of the perpendicular distances from the origin to these lines, $\dfrac{16}{\sqrt{5}}$ and $\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{5}}$, which is $\dfrac{8}{\sqrt{5}}$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

questions.text:
Let A($$-$$1, 1), B(3, 4) and C(2, 0) be given three points.
A line y = mx, m > 0, intersects lines AC and BC at point P and Q respectively. Let A 1 and A 2 be the areas of $$\Delta$$ABC and $$\Delta$$PQC respectively, such that A 1 = 3A 2 , then the value of m is equal to :
questions.solution:
Area of triangle ABC:

$$A_1 = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|(-1)(4-0) + 3(0-1) + 2(1-4)\right| = \dfrac{1}{2}\left|-4-3-6\right| = \dfrac{13}{2}$$

Line AC is $y = -\dfrac{1}{3}(x-2)$; with $y = mx$ it gives $P = \left(\dfrac{2}{3m+1}, \dfrac{2m}{3m+1}\right)$.

Line BC is $y = 4(x-2)$; with $y = mx$ it gives $Q = \left(\dfrac{8}{4-m}, \dfrac{8m}{4-m}\right)$.

Triangles PQC and ABC share the angle at C, with P on line CA and Q on line CB, so

$$\dfrac{A_2}{A_1} = \left|\dfrac{CP}{CA}\right| \cdot \left|\dfrac{CQ}{CB}\right|, \qquad \dfrac{CP}{CA} = \dfrac{2 - x_P}{2 - (-1)} = \dfrac{2m}{3m+1}, \qquad \dfrac{CQ}{CB} = \dfrac{x_Q - 2}{3 - 2} = \dfrac{2m}{4-m}$$

$A_1 = 3A_2$ gives

$$\dfrac{4m^2}{\left|(3m+1)(4-m)\right|} = \dfrac{1}{3} \Rightarrow 12m^2 = \left|-3m^2 + 11m + 4\right|$$

The sign $12m^2 = 3m^2 - 11m - 4$ gives $9m^2 + 11m + 4 = 0$, which has no real root (discriminant $121 - 144 < 0$). The other sign gives

$$15m^2 - 11m - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow (m-1)(15m+4) = 0 \Rightarrow m = 1 \text{ or } -\dfrac{4}{15}$$

Since $m > 0$, $m = 1$, with $P = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ and $Q = \left(\dfrac{8}{3}, \dfrac{8}{3}\right)$.

Hence, the correct option is (A).

questions.text: Let $$\alpha$$ 1 , $$\alpha$$ 2 ($$\alpha$$ 1 < $$\alpha$$ 2 ) be the values of $$\alpha$$ for the points ($$\alpha$$, $$-$$3), (2, 0) and (1, $$\alpha$$) to be collinear. Then the equation of the line, passing through ($$\alpha$$ 1 , $$\alpha$$ 2 ) and making an angle of $${\pi \over 3}$$ with the positive direction of the x-axis, is :
questions.solution:
Points A($$\alpha$$, $$-$$3), B(2, 0) and C(1, $$\alpha$$) are collinear.

$$\therefore$$ Slope of AB = Slope of BC

$$ \Rightarrow {{0 + 3} \over {2 - \alpha }} = {{\alpha - 0} \over {1 - 2}}$$

$$ \Rightarrow - 3 = \alpha (2 - \alpha )$$

$$ \Rightarrow - 3 = 2\alpha - {\alpha ^2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {\alpha ^2} - 2\alpha - 3 = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow {\alpha ^2} - 3\alpha + \alpha - 3 = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow \alpha (\alpha - 3) + 1(\alpha - 3) = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow (\alpha + 1)(\alpha - 3) = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow \alpha = - 1,\,3$$

Given, $${\alpha _1} < {\alpha _2}$$

$$\therefore$$ $${\alpha _1} = -1$$ and $${\alpha _2} = 3$$

$$\therefore$$ $$\left( {{\alpha _1},\,{\alpha _2}} \right) = ( - 1,\,3)$$

Now, equation of the line passing through ($$-$$1, 3) and making angle $${\pi \over 3}$$ with positive x-axis is

$$(y - {y_1}) = m(x - {x_1})$$

$$ \Rightarrow y - 3 = \left( {\tan {\pi \over 3}} \right)(x + 1)$$

$$ \Rightarrow y - 3 = \sqrt 3 (x + 1)$$

$$ \Rightarrow \sqrt 3 x - y + \sqrt 3 + 3 = 0$$

questions.text: Let the area of the triangle with vertices A(1, $$\alpha$$), B($$\alpha$$, 0) and C(0, $$\alpha$$) be 4 sq. units. If the points ($$\alpha$$, $$-$$$$\alpha$$), ($$-$$$$\alpha$$, $$\alpha$$) and ($$\alpha$$ 2 , $$\beta$$) are collinear, then $$\beta$$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
$$\because$$ A(1, $$\alpha$$), B($$\alpha$$, 0) and C(0, $$\alpha$$) are the vertices of $$\Delta$$ABC and area of $$\Delta$$ABC = 4

$$\therefore$$ $$\left| {{1 \over 2}\left| {\matrix{
1 & \alpha & 1 \cr
\alpha & 0 & 1 \cr
0 & \alpha & 1 \cr

} } \right|} \right| = 4$$

$$ \Rightarrow \left| {1(0 - \alpha ) - \alpha (\alpha ) + {\alpha ^2}} \right| = 8$$

$$ \Rightarrow \alpha = \, \pm \,8$$

Now, $$(\alpha ,\, - \alpha ),\,( - \alpha ,\alpha )$$ and $$({\alpha ^2},\beta )$$ are collinear

$$\therefore$$ $$\left| {\matrix{
8 & { - 8} & 1 \cr
{ - 8} & 8 & 1 \cr
{64} & \beta & 1 \cr

} } \right| = 0 = \left| {\matrix{
{ - 8} & 8 & 1 \cr
8 & { - 8} & 1 \cr
{64} & \beta & 1 \cr

} } \right|$$

$$ \Rightarrow 8(8 - \beta ) + 8( - 8 - 64) + 1( - 8\beta - 8 \times 64) = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow 8 - \beta - 72 - \beta - 64 = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow \beta = - 64$$

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: Let $$A\left( {{3 \over {\sqrt a }},\sqrt a } \right),\,a > 0$$, be a fixed point in the xy-plane. The image of A in y-axis be B and the image of B in x-axis be C. If $$D(3\cos \theta ,a\sin \theta )$$ is a point in the fourth quadrant such that the maximum area of $$\Delta$$ACD is 12 square units, then a is equal to ____________.
questions.solution:
$B=\left(-\dfrac{3}{\sqrt a},\sqrt a\right)$ and $C=\left(-\dfrac{3}{\sqrt a},-\sqrt a\right)$, so $C$ is the reflection of $A$ in the origin.

Area of $\triangle ACD$ is $\Delta=\dfrac12|M|$, where

$$M=\begin{vmatrix}\dfrac{3}{\sqrt a}&\sqrt a&1\\ -\dfrac{3}{\sqrt a}&-\sqrt a&1\\ 3\cos\theta&a\sin\theta&1\end{vmatrix}$$

Applying $R_1\to R_1+R_2$ makes the first row $(0,\ 0,\ 2)$, so

$$M=2\left[-\frac{3}{\sqrt a}\cdot a\sin\theta+\sqrt a\cdot 3\cos\theta\right]=6\sqrt a\,(\cos\theta-\sin\theta)$$

So $\Delta=3\sqrt a\,|\cos\theta-\sin\theta|$.

For $D$ in the fourth quadrant, $\theta\in\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right)$, and $\cos\theta-\sin\theta=\sqrt2\cos\left(\theta+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ has maximum $\sqrt2$, reached at $\theta=-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

$$\Delta_{\max}=3\sqrt{2a}=12 \Rightarrow 2a=16 \Rightarrow a=8$$

Hence, the answer is 8.

and slope of line joining $$(x,y)$$ and $$(xr, yr)$$

$$ = {{y\left( {r - 1} \right)} \over {x\left( {r - 1} \right)}} = {y \over x}$$

$$\therefore$$ $${m_1} = {m_2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ Points lie on the straight line.

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: A square of side a lies above the $$x$$-axis and has one vertex at the origin. The side passing through the origin makes an angle $$\alpha \left( {0 < \alpha < {\pi \over 4}} \right)$$ with the positive direction of x-axis. The equation of its diagonal not passing through the origin is :
questions.solution:
Co-ordinate of $$A = \left( {a\,\cos \,\alpha ,\,\,a\,\sin \,\alpha } \right)$$

Equation of $$OB,$$

$$y = \tan \left( {{\pi \over 4} + \alpha } \right)x$$

$$CA{ \bot ^r}$$ to $$OB$$

$$\therefore$$ slope of $$CA=-$$ $$\cot \left( {{\pi \over 4} + \alpha } \right)$$

Equation of $$CA$$

$$y - a\sin \alpha = - cot\left( {{\pi \over 4} + \alpha } \right)\left( {x - a\,\cos \,\alpha } \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow \left( {y - a\sin \alpha } \right)\left( {\tan \left( {{\pi \over 4} + \alpha } \right)} \right) = \left( {a\,\cos \,\alpha - x} \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow \left( {y - a\sin \alpha } \right)\left( {{{\tan {\pi \over 4} + \tan \alpha } \over {1 - \tan {\pi \over 4}\tan \alpha }}} \right)\left( {a\,\cos \,\alpha - x} \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow \left( {y - a\sin \alpha } \right)\left( {1 + \tan \alpha } \right) = \left( {a\cos \alpha - x} \right)\left( {1 - \tan \alpha } \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow \left( {y - a\sin \alpha } \right)\left( {\cos \alpha + \sin \alpha } \right) = \left( {a\cos \alpha - x} \right)\left( {\cos \alpha - \sin \alpha } \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow y\left( {\cos + \sin \alpha } \right) - a\sin \alpha \cos \alpha - a{\sin ^2}\alpha $$

$$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, = a{\cos ^2}\alpha - a\cos \alpha \sin \alpha - x\left( {\cos \alpha - \sin \alpha } \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow y\left( {\cos \alpha + sin\alpha } \right) + x\left( {\cos \alpha - \sin \alpha } \right) = a$$

$$y\left( {\sin \alpha + \cos \alpha } \right) + x\left( {\cos \alpha - \sin \alpha } \right) = a.$$

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: The equation of the straight line passing through the point $$(4, 3)$$ and making intercepts on the co-ordinate axes whose sum is $$-1$$ is :
questions.solution:
Let the required line be $${x \over a} + {y \over b} = 1.......\left( 1 \right)$$

then $$a+b=-1$$ $$\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,.........\left( 2 \right)$$

$$(1)$$ passes through $$(4,3), $$ $$ \Rightarrow {4 \over a} + {3 \over b} = 1$$

$$ \Rightarrow 4b + 3a = ab\,\,...............\left( 3 \right)$$

Eliminating $$b$$ from $$(2)$$ and $$(3),$$ we get

$${a^2} - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow a = \pm 2 \Rightarrow b = - 3$$, $$1$$

$$\therefore$$ Equation of straight lines are

$${x \over 2} + {y \over { - 3}} = 1$$

or $${x \over { - 2}} + {y \over 1} = 1$$

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: If non zero numbers $$a, b, c$$ are in $$H.P.,$$ then the straight line $${x \over a} + {y \over b} + {1 \over c} = 0$$ always passes through a fixed point. That point is :
questions.solution:
$$a,b,c$$ are in $$H.P. \Rightarrow {1 \over a}.{1 \over b},{1 \over c}$$ are in $$A.P.$$

$$ \Rightarrow {2 \over b} = {1 \over a} + {1 \over c}$$

$$ \Rightarrow {1 \over a} - {2 \over b} + {1 \over c} = 0$$

$$\therefore$$ $${x \over a} + {y \over a} + {1 \over c} = 0$$ passes through $$\left( {1, - 2} \right)$$

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: The line parallel to the $$x$$ - axis and passing through the intersection of the lines $$ax + 2by + 3b = 0$$ and $$bx - 2ay - 3a = 0,$$ where $$(a, b)$$ $$ \ne $$ $$(0, 0)$$ is :

options.text: below the $$x$$ - axis at a distance of $${3 \over 2}$$ from it
below the $$x$$ - axis at a distance of $${2 \over 3}$$ from it
above the $$x$$ - axis at a distance of $${3 \over 2}$$ from it
above the $$x$$ - axis at a distance of $${2 \over 3}$$ from it

questions.solution:
The line passing through the intersection of lines

$$ax + 2by = 3b = 0$$

and $$bx - 2ay - 3a = 0$$ is

$$ax + 2by + 3b + \lambda \left( {bx - 2ay - 3a} \right) = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow \left( {a + b\lambda } \right)x + \left( {2b - 2a\lambda } \right)y + 3b - 3\lambda a = 0$$

As this line is parallel to $$x$$-axis.

$$\therefore$$ $$a + b\lambda = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda = - a/b$$

$$ \Rightarrow ax + 2by + 3b - {a \over b}\left( {bx - 2ay - 3a} \right) = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow ax + 2by + 3b - ax + {{2{a^2}} \over b}y + {{3{a^2}} \over b} = 0$$

$$y\left( {2b + {{2{a^2}} \over b}} \right) + 3b + {{3{a^2}} \over b} = 0$$

$$y\left( {{{2{b^2} + 2{a^2}} \over b}} \right) = - \left( {{{3{b^2} + 3{a^2}} \over b}} \right)$$

$$y = {{ - 3\left( {{a^2} + {b^2}} \right)} \over {2\left( {{b^2} + {a^2}} \right)}} = {{ - 3} \over 2}$$

So it is $$3/2$$ units below $$x$$-axis.

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: The point of intersection of the lines $$\left(a^3+3\right)x+ay+a-3=0$$ and $$\left(a^5+2\right)x+(a+2)y+2a+3=0$$ ($$a$$ real) lies on the $$y$$-axis for
questions.solution:
On the $y$-axis $x=0$, so the point must satisfy $ay=3-a$ and $(a+2)y=-(2a+3)$.

For $a=0$ the first line is $3x-3=0$, i.e. $x=1\neq 0$; so $a\neq 0$ and $y=\dfrac{3-a}{a}$.

Then $(a+2)(3-a)=-a(2a+3)$, which simplifies to $a^2+4a+6=0$.

Its discriminant is $16-24=-8 \lt 0$, so no real $a$ works.

So the point lies on the $y$-axis for no value of $a$.

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: If the x-intercept of some line L is double as that of the line, 3x + 4y = 12 and the y-intercept of L is half as that of the same line, then the slope of L is:
questions.solution:
Given line 3x + 4y = 12 can be rewritten as

$${{3x} \over {12}} + {{4y} \over {12}}$$ = 1   $$ \Rightarrow $$  $${x \over 4} + {y \over 3}$$ = 1

$$ \Rightarrow $$   x-intercept = 4 and y-intercept = 3

Let the required line be

L : $${x \over a} + {y \over b} = 1$$ where

a = x-intercept and b = y-intercept

According to the question

a = 4 $$ \times $$ 2 = 8   and   b = 3/2

$$ \therefore $$    Required line is $${x \over 8} + {{2y} \over 3}$$ = 1

$$ \Rightarrow $$   3x + 16y = 24

$$ \Rightarrow $$   y = $${{ - 3} \over {16}}$$ x + $${{24} \over {16}}$$

Hence, required slope = $${{ - 3} \over {16}}$$.

questions.text: A light ray emerging from the point source placed at P(1, 3) is reflected at a point Q in the axis of x. If the reflected ray passes through the point R(6,7), then the abscissa of Q is:
questions.solution:
Let abscissa of Q = x

$$ \therefore $$   Q = (x, 0)

tan $$\theta $$ = $${{0 - 7} \over {x - 6}},$$ tan (180 o $$-$$ $$\theta $$) = $${{0 - 3} \over {x - 1}}$$

Now, tan (180 o $$-$$ $$\theta $$) = $$-$$ tan $$\theta $$

$$ \therefore $$    $${{ - 3} \over {x - 1}}$$ = $${7 \over {x - 6}}$$ $$ \Rightarrow $$ x = $${5 \over 2}$$

questions.solution:
Since the point of intersection lies on fourth quadrant and equidistant from the two axes,

i.e., let the point be (k, $$-$$k) and this point satisfies the two equations of the given lines.

$$\therefore$$ 4ak $$-$$ 2ak + c = 0 ......... (1)

and 5bk $$-$$ 2bk + d = 0 ..... (2)

From (1) we get, $$k = {{ - c} \over {2a}}$$

Putting the value of k in (2) we get,

$$5b\left( { - {c \over {2a}}} \right) - 2b\left( { - {c \over {2a}}} \right) + d = 0$$

or, $$ - {{5bc} \over {2a}} + {{2bc} \over {2a}} + d = 0$$ or, $$ - {{3bc} \over {2a}} + d = 0$$

or, $$ - 3bc + 2ad = 0$$ or, $$3bc - 2ad = 0$$

questions.text:
A square, of each side 2, lies above the x-axis and has one vertex at the origin. If
one of the sides passing through the origin makes an angle 30 o with the positive direction of the x-axis, then the sum of the x-coordinates of the vertices of the square is :
questions.solution:
Let, coordinate of point A = (x, y).

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ For point A,

$${x \over {\cos {{30}^ \circ }}}$$ = $${y \over {\sin {{30}^ \circ }}}$$ = 2

$$ \Rightarrow $$ x = $$\sqrt 3 $$

and y = 1

Similarly, For point B,

$${x \over {\cos {{75}^ \circ }}}$$ = $${y \over {\sin {{75}^ \circ }}}$$ = 2$$\sqrt 2 $$

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ x = $$\sqrt 3 - 1$$

y = $$\sqrt 3 + 1$$

For point C,

$${x \over {cos{{120}^ \circ }}}$$ = $${y \over {sin{{120}^ \circ }}}$$ = 2

$$ \Rightarrow $$$$\,\,\,$$ x = $$-$$1

y = $$\sqrt 3 $$

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ Sum of the x - coordinate of the vertices

= 0 + $$\sqrt 3 $$ + $$\sqrt 3 $$ $$-$$ 1 + ($$-$$ 1) = 2$$\sqrt 3 $$ $$-$$ 2

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text: The sides of a rhombus ABCD are parallel to the lines, x $$-$$ y + 2 = 0 and 7x $$-$$ y + 3 = 0. If the diagonals of the rhombus intersect at P(1, 2) and the vertex A (different from the origin) is on the y-axis, then the ordinate of A is :
questions.solution:
Let the coordinate A be (0, c)

Equations of the given lines are

x $$-$$ y + 2 = 0 and 7x $$-$$ y + 3 = 0

We know that the diagonals of the rhombus will be parallel to the angle bisectors of the two given lines; y = x + 2 and y = 7x + 3

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ equation of angle bisectors is given as :

$${{x - y + 2} \over {\sqrt 2 }} = \pm {{7x - y + 3} \over {5\sqrt 2 }}$$

5x $$-$$ 5y + 10 = $$ \pm $$ (7x $$-$$ y + 3)

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ Parallel equations of the diagonals are 2x + 4y $$-$$ 7 = 0

and 12x $$-$$ 6y + 13 = 0

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ slopes of diagonals are $${{ - 1} \over 2}$$ and 2.

Now, slope of the diagonal from A(0, c) and passing through P(1, 2) is (2 $$-$$ c)

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ 2 $$-$$ c = 2 $$ \Rightarrow $$ c = 0 (not possible)

$$ \therefore $$$$\,\,\,$$ 2 $$-$$ c = $${{ - 1} \over 2}$$ $$ \Rightarrow $$ c = $${5 \over 2}$$

$$\therefore\,\,\,$$ Ordinate of A is $${5 \over 2}$$.

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text:
A straight line L at a distance of 4 units from the origin makes positive intercepts on the coordinate axes and
the perpendicular from the origin to this line makes an angle of 60 o with the line x + y = 0. Then an equation
of the line L is :
questions.solution:
Since $L$ is at distance 4 from the origin and makes positive intercepts on both axes, its normal form is

$$x\cos\theta + y\sin\theta = 4, \qquad 0^\circ < \theta < 90^\circ$$

where $\theta$ is the inclination of the perpendicular from the origin to $L$.

The line $x + y = 0$ has inclination $135^\circ$. The perpendicular makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with it when the difference of inclinations is $60^\circ$ or $180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ$, so within $0^\circ < \theta < 90^\circ$:

$$\theta = 135^\circ - 60^\circ = 75^\circ \quad \text{or} \quad \theta = 135^\circ - 120^\circ = 15^\circ$$

Using $\cos 75^\circ = \sin 15^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3} - 1}{2\sqrt{2}}$ and $\sin 75^\circ = \cos 15^\circ = \dfrac{\sqrt{3} + 1}{2\sqrt{2}}$, $\theta = 75^\circ$ gives

$$(\sqrt{3} - 1)x + (\sqrt{3} + 1)y = 8\sqrt{2}$$

which is option (D), and $\theta = 15^\circ$ gives

$$(\sqrt{3} + 1)x + (\sqrt{3} - 1)y = 8\sqrt{2}$$

which is option (C). Both lines are at distance 4 from the origin, have positive intercepts and satisfy the angle condition.

Options (
A) and (
B) correspond to $\theta = 60^\circ$ and $\theta = 30^\circ$, whose perpendiculars make $75^\circ$ with $x + y = 0$.

Hence, the correct options are (
C) and (D).

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text:
Slope of a line passing through P(2, 3) and
intersecting the line, x + y = 7 at a distance of
4 units from P, is :
questions.solution:
We know parametric form of straight line is

$${{x - {x_1}} \over {\cos \theta }} = {{y - {y_1}} \over {\sin \theta }} = r$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $${{x - 2} \over {\cos \theta }} = {{y - 3} \over {\sin \theta }} = 4$$

$$ \therefore $$ x = 2 + 4cos$$\theta $$

y = 3 + 4sin$$\theta $$

$$ \therefore $$ Point A = (2 + 4cos$$\theta $$, 3 + 4sin$$\theta $$)

Point A lies on line x + y = 7,

$$ \therefore $$ (2 + 4cos$$\theta $$) + (3 + 4sin$$\theta $$) = 7

$$ \Rightarrow $$ sin$$\theta $$ + cos$$\theta $$ = $${1 \over 2}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $${\sin ^2}\theta + {\cos ^2}\theta $$ + 2sin$$\theta $$cos$$\theta $$ = $${1 \over 4}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ 1 + sin 2$$\theta $$ = $${1 \over 4}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ sin 2$$\theta $$ = $$ - {3 \over 4}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $${{2\tan \theta } \over {1 + {{\tan }^2}\theta }}$$ = $$ - {3 \over 4}$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ 3tan 2 $$\theta $$ + 8tan$$\theta $$ + 3 = 0

$$ \Rightarrow $$ tan$$\theta $$ = $${{ - 8 \pm 2\sqrt 7 } \over 6}$$

So slope = $${{ - 8 \pm 2\sqrt 7 } \over 6}$$

By checking each options,

Slope = $${{1 - \sqrt 7 } \over {1 + \sqrt 7 }}$$

As $${{1 - \sqrt 7 } \over {1 + \sqrt 7 }}$$ = $${{{{\left( {1 - \sqrt 7 } \right)}^2}} \over {1 - 7}}$$ = $${{8 - 2\sqrt 7 } \over { - 6}}$$ = $${{ - 8 + 2\sqrt 7 } \over 6}$$

questions.chapterName: Straight Lines and Pair of Straight Lines
questions.text:
The point P (a, b) undergoes the following three transformations successively :

(a) reflection about the line y = x.

(b) translation through 2 units along the positive direction of x-axis.

(c) rotation through angle $${\pi \over 4}$$ about the origin in the anti-clockwise direction.

If the co-ordinates of the final position of the point P are $$\left( { - {1 \over {\sqrt 2 }},{7 \over {\sqrt 2 }}} \right)$$, then the value of 2a + b is equal to :
questions.solution:
Image of A(a, b) along y = x is B(b, a). Translating it 2 units it becomes C(b + 2, a).

Now, applying rotation theorem

$$ - {1 \over {\sqrt 2 }} + {7 \over {\sqrt 2 }}i = \left( {(b + 2) + ai} \right)\left( {\cos {\pi \over 4} + i\sin {\pi \over 4}} \right)$$

$$ - {1 \over {\sqrt 2 }} + {7 \over {\sqrt 2 }}i = \left( {{{b + 2} \over {\sqrt 2 }} - {a \over {\sqrt 2 }}} \right) + i\left( {{{b + 2} \over {\sqrt 2 }} + {a \over {\sqrt 2 }}} \right)$$

$$\Rightarrow$$ b $$-$$ a + 2 = $$-$$1 ......(i)

and b + 2 + a = 7 ...... (ii)

$$\Rightarrow$$ a = 4; b = 1

$$\Rightarrow$$ 2a + b = 9

x $$ \ge $$ 0, y $$ \ge $$ 0

Feasible region is shown in the graph
